stories.title: Canadians gather for Remembrance Day ceremonies across the country
stories.summary: Canadians across the country are gathering today to reflect on the legacy of war and remember the men and women who served and died defending this country.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — Canadians across the country are gathering today to reflect on the legacy of war and remember the men and women who served and died defending this country.

Canadians will mark 25 years since the start of the Afghanistan war, a conflict in which 40,000 Canadian Armed Forces members served and 159 lost their lives.

The Afghanistan conflict, which lasted more than 12 years, was the longest in Canadian history and saw the largest deployment of Canadian troops since the Second World War.

Three Second World War veterans are expected to attend the ceremony in Ottawa and Prime Minister Mark Carney, Gov. Gen. Louise Arbour and other dignitaries will lay wreaths at the National War Memorial.

CF-18 fighter jets and a Black Hawk helicopter will perform flypasts over the national ceremony, while Griffon, Chinook and Cormorant helicopters and other Rcaf aircraft will conduct flyovers at local ceremonies across the country.

This year is also the 100th anniversary of the Royal Canadian Legion — founded in 1926 to create one main advocacy group for veterans’ benefits — and the 150th anniversary of the Royal Military College.

Some 300 cadets are expected to attend the parade to mark that anniversary, which is about 200 more cadets than usual.

This year’s ceremonies take place just weeks after a tragic fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright claimed the lives of four soldiers and injured dozens of others during a training exercise.

Three separate investigations, including one by military police, are looking into the accident at CFB Wainwright.

Sgt. Morgan Wong of Edmonton, Pte. Shaun Farrell of Prince Albert, Sask., Pte. Aidan Goulding of North Vancouver and Pte. Hayden Lykkemark of Langley, B.C., were killed at the Alberta training base last month.

They died when strong winds suddenly swept up a grass fire that was burning on the automatic grenade launcher range and carried it across the training area.

The last update from National Defence on Nov. 4 said of the 39 injured, 14 had been released from hospital while another 25 remained in hospital.

A separate ceremony is planned for today at CFB Wainwright. Federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre is set to attend, along with other dignitaries, military members and veterans.

This year’s Silver Cross Mother, Virginia Hicks, will lay a wreath at the cenotaph in Ottawa on behalf of all mothers who lost a child who served in the military.

Hicks lost her daughter during a training incident at CFB Petawawa in 2002. She was chosen by the Royal Canadian Legion months before the Wainwright accident took place.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 11, 2026.

stories.title: ‘Deeply disappointing’: Ross Atkins weighs in on Santander’s anti-Muslim posts
stories.summary: Speaking to reporters at the GM meetings, Atkins said "there really aren't words to express my level of disappointment."
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Posted November 11, 2026 5:25 am.

Toronto Blue Jays general manager Ross Atkins says it’s “concerning” and “deeply disappointing” that outfielder Anthony Santander posted anti-Muslim videos on his social media feed.

Speaking to reporters Tuesday at the Major League Baseball GM meetings, Atkins said “there really aren’t words to express my level of disappointment.”

“I’ve expressed that to him. I think anything [exacerbating] some level of hate, anti-Islamic, is just extremely concerning,” Atkins said.

“I also talked to Anthony about his lack of awareness, realizing that he has a very large microphone, what that meant,” Atkins added. “We’re working exceptionally hard internally to ensure, and we have been, that it’s a safe environment, that baseball is for everyone. It’s very important to us. It’s a part of our organizational values, and his behaviour did not align with that.”

Santander posted the videos in the aftermath of the U.S. midterm elections last Tuesday. He deleted them two days later but so far has not apologized or otherwise commented.

Santander, a 32-year-old from Venezuela, didn’t play at the big-league level last season due to injuries.

He signed a five-year, US$92.5-million deal with the Blue Jays in January 2025.

stories.title: A generation apart, these Palestinian Canadians found purpose through the military
stories.summary: Ten years after immigrating to Canada, Yousef Shaath gave up his job as an accountant to enlist in the army. He was 45 years old, going through basic training with recruits who had just entered adulthood.
stories.author: Judy Trinh
stories.content:
Ottawa – The most recent data from the Department of National Defence show that 28 per cent of new recruits are visible minorities.

Many of them joined the Canadian Armed Forces (CAF) because of a fierce sense of patriotism instilled in them by their immigrant parents.

That’s the case for Palestinian Canadians Yousef Shaath, 66, and George Al-Koura, 39. The veterans are a generation apart but both found a shared purpose through military service.

Ten years after immigrating to Canada, Shaath gave up his job as an accountant to enlist in the army.

He was 45 years old, going through basic training with recruits who had just entered adulthood.

Shaath said he was inspired by his cousin, Wafa Dabbagh, the first Muslim woman wearing a hijab in CAF . He was determined to “embed his footsteps” into Canada, energized by his fellow recruits who were more than half his age.

“I enjoyed every minute of it … if there’s a hurdle, you persist,” Shaath said in an interview with CTV News.

Over his 14-year career as a logistics officer, Shaath was deployed in Kuwait and Lebanon. He helped move weapons and equipment out of Afghanistan after Canada wound down its combat operation in Kandahar.

Shaath said his last deployment was the most meaningful to him. In 2015, he was sent to Lebanon to help the federal government conduct security checks on Syrian refugees.

Displaced by escalating violence in their homeland, Shaath’s parents fled from Palestine to Egypt in 1936. Shaath said his family history impressed upon him the importance of the work he was doing in helping Canada vet Syrian refugees for its sponsorship group.

“It was most rewarding … being helpful, to put up a hand to help others – that made me more loyal, more loving to the Canadian Forces.”

‘I’m Canadian first’

That shared sense of being uprooted – then falling in love with a new country – is a feeling that is also ingrained in Al-Koura.

In 2005, he joined the military just a few weeks before turning 18 years old. He sought adventure and to put into practice the lessons his parents taught him.

His parents, also Palestinian refugees, instilled in him the importance of protecting the freedom they found in the “cultural mosaic” of Canada.

stories.title: From Pearson to Prison: Toronto man faces 15 years in Albania after luggage tag switch
stories.summary: A young Toronto couple’s family vacation quickly turned into a nightmare in Albania. In part, because they followed travel advice from the Canadian government.
stories.author: Avery Haines, Jack Hauen
stories.content:
What happens when a simple trip turns into a nightmare? Part one of W5’s five-part investigation on CTVNews.CA follows travellers who say they went from passenger to prisoner, caught in a scheme that crossed borders and changed lives forever.

A young Toronto couple’s family vacation quickly turned into a nightmare in Albania. In part, because they followed travel advice from the Canadian government.

W5’s recent investigation into a bag-tag switching scheme involving innocent passengers and corrupt airport workers led the Canadian government to issue a warning that “criminal networks exploit luggage tags at the airport to move drugs.”

“Protect yourself from luggage swaps,” the Canadian government’s advice reads , “by taking clear photos or videos of your bags and their attached baggage tags … before they leave your possession.”

Kristian and Adriana Gjoni watched the W5 documentary and followed Ottawa’s travel advice and yet he still ended up in solitary confinement in Tirana, Albania.

Their ordeal began this summer, when the couple flew on one of Air Transat’s first direct flights from Toronto to Tirana, to share with family in Albania the news that they were pregnant with their first child.

Shortly after they touched down, an Albanian customs officer asked why one of their four bags was missing a tag.

“And I told him, I’m not an employee of Pearson or Air Transat,” Kristian said. “How would I know?”

The couple was detained for two and a half hours, until an officer led Kristian to the baggage carousel and ordered him to pick up a lone bag still circling the belt.

Kristian, a soft-spoken I.T. businessman who is originally from Albania, said that wasn’t his bag. But it didn’t matter.

An officer opened the lone bag, which was stuffed with 23.15 kilograms of cannabis.

Authorities whipped out their cameras.

“Think of the red carpet in Hollywood, where you have hundreds of people taking pictures all around and a single suitcase being opened,” he said.

Thankfully, Kristian thought, they were prepared with photos of their luggage.

It didn’t work. In fact, the Albanian police thought it was “extremely suspicious,” Kristian said.

“They asked me, ‘Why did you take pictures of your bags?’ And I told them, because it’s been all over the news and it’s a security risk right now in Canada,” he said.

Here’s how tag switching works: a corrupt worker smuggles a bag of drugs into an airport, takes the tag off an unsuspecting passenger’s luggage and attaches it to a suitcase full of drugs.

If the drug bag makes it through, a mule waiting at the destination picks it up. If not, the innocent passenger is left to explain themselves.

If you have any information regarding tag switching or corruption at Canadian airports, please reach out to avery.haines@bellmedia.CA and jack.hauen@bellmedia.CA .

A cell with no window

Despite Kristian’s protests, police whisked him to a nearby jail where he said he spent four days in solitary confinement. His new reality was an eight-by-nine-foot cell with no window and a fluorescent light that was never turned off.

It was a shocking change of scenery for the Toronto businessman, whose rap sheet, until that point, consisted of a few parking tickets. In a flash, he became an alleged international drug smuggler — ensnared in what Albanian police dubbed Operation Suitcases.

To stay sane in solitary, Kristian said he played chess with himself on a board he made with cigarette ash and paint rubbed off the walls.

Making matters worse, Adriana was taken to a local hospital with severe cramping. Doctors there performed an ultrasound, but not a blood test, and told police that she was not pregnant.

Albanian cops publicly allege couple lied about pregnancy

Kristian’s name was blasted out in the Albanian press, along with an allegation from police that they lied about the pregnancy.

Kristian “allegedly attempted to avoid inspection by claiming that his wife was pregnant,” reads one article. “Medical examinations later determined that the claim was false, authorities said.”

“So, the whole narrative was built before we even were questioned and was even released to the press,” he said. “News outlets, TV stations, social media, everywhere.”

Meanwhile, with Kristian still in jail, Adriana was released from emergency back into police custody.

“What got me through it was, ‘I’m going to get out. At least we’re still having our family. We’re going to have our baby,’” he said.

They discharged Adriana 12 hours later — but by that time, she was feeling unwell again and was rushed to another hospital.

A blood test there proved she was pregnant, but it was too late. Adriana had a miscarriage.

W5 has seen the hospital documents from Toronto and Albania that confirmed Adriana’s pregnancy and her miscarriage. Kristian believes the baggage ordeal caused it.

“We still haven’t moved past it,” he said. “I don’t think we’re ever going to fully move past it.”

Another Canadian passenger on the flight was also detained because her tag was on another suitcase with 23 kilograms of cannabis. She was released without charges.

All told, the cannabis was worth almost C$400,000, Albanian police said.

Fighting the charges using W5’s research

Eventually, Kristian was released from prison on bail after his lawyer presented evidence that includes dozens of links to W5’s reporting on bag-tag switching and corruption at Pearson Airport.

He is back in Toronto, but must regularly return to Tirana to sign in with police. Initially, authorities required a monthly check-in, but that has recently been relaxed to once every four months.

W5 went with Kristian last month for one of these trips. After a 12-hour journey, the check-in process took just minutes. An officer wrote his name down in a book and Kristian was free to leave.

Kristian has hired prominent Albanian anti-corruption lawyer Ndue Pjetra, who said his legal arguments will borrow heavily from W5’s reporting on bag-tag switching.

Pjetra has submitted information to the court about “serious concerns regarding security at Canadian airports.”

He’ll also have a helpful letter from the Mounties. The RCMP said it has verified that the couple only checked in the four bags they picked up, and agrees with Kristian’s version of events.

“The RCMP believes that you were the victim of a bag-tag switch incident where the baggage tag from your checked in suitcase was placed on to a suitcase which you did not check in,” an officer wrote in an email to Kristian in October.

Albania is a country known for its corruption, Kristian noted. “But I never thought that I’d have to travel back here because of corruption … within Canadian airports.”

Kristian’s trial is expected to begin in early 2027. He faces up to 15 years behind bars.

An Air Transat spokesperson said the airline takes allegations of interference with the baggage system “very seriously.”

“We recognize the distress this situation has caused Mr. Gjoni and his family,” Stéphanie Dussault said.

“Although airlines are responsible for transporting checked baggage,” the luggage system also includes “airport authorities, security partners and government agencies,” she noted.

Watch the one-hour special presentation of W5’s Avery Haines Investigates Sunday at 10 p.m. ET live on W5’s official YouTube channel and on CTV and Crave following the Grey Cup.

ByCalvi Leon Staff Reporter

Canadian ex-Olympian Ryan Wedding was charged a $100,000 monthly fee to join a secret network of Mexican cartel leaders, gain access to stolen police intelligence and receive alerts on impending arrests as authorities across North America closed in on his cocaine empire, U.S. authorities claim.

The explosive allegations are contained in an indictment unveiled Tuesday against Edgar Aarón Vazquez, an associate of the Sinaloa Cartel identified as the founder of the New Empire Cartel in Mexico City.

Known by the aliases “the General” and “Mini,” Vazquez was shot dead last Thursday in what Mexico’s top government security official called an exchange of gunfire with federal police. Secretariat of Security and Citizen Protection Omar García Harfuch said the officers were carrying out a warrant for Vazquez’s arrest on U.S. charges.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Angine de Poitrine debut third member in Toronto

Wedding is accused of running a drug ring that worked with Mexican cartels and ordered multiple murders around the globe — including the mistaken identity killings of an innocent Indian couple in Caledon, Ont., and the assassination of a U.S. federal witness who helped dismantle part of the network.

Once one of the FBI’s most-wanted fugitives and the subject of a $15-million reward, Wedding was arrested in Mexico in January.

Vazquez was sanctioned by the U.S. Treasury Department last year over his links to Wedding’s alleged cocaine empire. At the time, the department said Vazquez provided protection for the then-fugitive and used his police contacts to help locate murder targets for the drug ring.

Star Exclusive

Shortly before the murders of Jagtar Sidhu and Harbhajan Kaur Sidhu, a pair of Peel police officers knocked on their door looking for a man named

While the circumstances of the takedown remain unclear, the indictment against Vazquez offers the most detailed picture yet of both his role and how Wedding allegedly evaded capture under the protection of some of Mexico’s most notorious criminals.

According to the indictment, the New Empire Cartel is a violent organization that grew under the protection of “certain Mexican authorities.”

After his death, Mexican officials described Vazquez as the mastermind behind the high-profile murder of police commissioner Milton Morales Figueroa, head of the Mexico City police’s Tactical Strategy and Special Operations Unit.

Behind the scenes, the 42-year-old Vazquez allegedly maintained a network of corrupt public officials and private individuals who had access to sensitive information held by Mexican and international law enforcement agencies.

The indictment says he’d sell the information to organized crime leaders who paid subscription-like fees for his services.

According to the indictment, Vazquez charged Wedding a one-time initiation fee of $500,000 (US), followed by an average monthly fee of $100,000.

For that payment, Vazquez gave up details of ongoing enforcement operations, including arrests, outstanding warrants, active investigations and more, “oftentimes in exchange for an extortionate supplemental fee.”

The documents do not describe who else paid for Vazquez’s services, but refer to the group as a “collective of organized crime leaders.”

Live Updates

MONTREAL—The life of a “co-operating witness” is dangerous — especially if you’re double-crossing a drug cartel.

Prosecutors allege Wedding’s organization worked with Mexican drug cartels to move hundreds of kilos of cocaine from Colombia to Mexico at a time via boats and planes. From there, truckers would collect the drugs in stash houses in southern California and elsewhere along the U.S.-Canada border before moving the shipments northward into Canada.

That trucking network became the focus of a joint investigation by the FBI and RCMP that eventually took down Wedding’s alleged operation.

In Mexico, Vazquez was accused of providing Wedding’s group with “near-daily, rotating code words” for drug couriers to relay to Mexican law enforcement and military personnel at checkpoints, to secure their passage.

He also gave members of Wedding’s operation authentic law enforcement credentials — altered to bear their names and likenesses — to permit them to pass through Mexican security checkpoints, the indictment alleges.

Vazquez paid public officials to slow down criminal investigations and eliminate or manipulate evidence.

Also Tuesday, U.S. prosecutors unveiled a six-count federal indictment claiming that alleged Los Angeles gangster Roberto Gomez, 51, routinely obtained intelligence about law enforcement operations from Mexican and American authorities before relaying it to Wedding.

The indictment claims Gomez communicated with leaders of the Sinaloa Cartel and Cártel de Jalisco Nueva Generación (CJNG) and corrupt law enforcement officials to obtain information related to arrests, drug seizures, warrants and charges, then relayed those details to co-conspirators, including Wedding.

As of Tuesday, a spokesperson at the U.S. Attorney’s Office said Gomez was still at large.

The recent developments reveal an investigation that has expanded greatly in scope since Wedding’s arrest to include allegations of sweeping corruption inside Mexico.

Vazquez’s death came the same day that U.S. authorities announced the arrest of a Mexican judge for allegedly accepting a $2-million bribe to release Wedding’s Canadian right-hand man from Mexican custody.

After his arrest in January 2026, Wedding pleaded not guilty to 17 federal felony counts of murder, running a criminal enterprise, drug trafficking and other alleged crimes.

His lawyer, Anthony Colombo, told the Star in a brief statement on Tuesday that while the latest allegations are “not new,” his client’s plea of not guilty remains.

Calvi Leon is a Toronto-based general assignment reporter for the Star. Reach her via email: cleon@thestar.ca

stories.title: Canada’s legions have been struggling. So they made civilians an offer that was hard to refuse

ByFrancine Kopun Senior Writer

At the front of a plain square room, silent actors use hand motions to convey the routine, discipline and repetition of military service.

They mimic weapons drills and polishing boots, signal incoming helicopters and stand at attention before telling their stories.

The audience leans into the performance.

“I’m young. He’s younger,” says one actor, a retired medic. “I hold onto his wrist, not just to know when the end happens, but to offer some kind of touch until the end happens.”

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Angine de Poitrine debut third member in Toronto

The performance captures the crushing repetition of military life, punctuated by the horror of combat, the carnage of an improvised explosive device.

The show, at the Royal Canadian Legion Branch 344 on Lake Shore West on the Friday before Remembrance Day, is a production of the MiCiv Project, which brings military and civilian artists together, at a time when the civilian population of the Canadian Legion has surged.

One hundred years after it was incorporated in 1926, the Royal Canadian Legion — which advocates for the welfare of military members, veterans and their families, and operates legion halls across the country where they can gather— undertook a membership drive. The campaign has added 130,000 members in 2026 so far, bringing the total to 300,000. They did it with a simple offer: First year of membership is free; if you pay for a second year — about $55 online— you’re entered in a draw to win a Ford F150. Existing members are entered if they renew.

“It has just taken off like wildfire,” said Lynn McClellan, president of the Ontario Provincial Command of the Royal Canadian Legion, based in Elora. “I heard that a lot of these folks are within the ages of 40 to 60, which is really encouraging.”

Even with the offer, legion membership in Canada’s largest veterans organization is only half of what it was in 1982-84, when it totalled 600,000. Hundreds of branches have been closed over the decades, down to 1,350 across the country today.

“Without opening our doors to everybody, the branches would be closing far faster than they already are,” said Alan Roy, a veteran and president of the Royal Canadian Legion Branch 101, in Etobicoke.

With 1,040 members, 101 is the largest legion in Toronto and one of the few still operating seven days a week.

“We can’t seem to encourage the newer veterans, the newer soldiers, to come into the branch.”

Legions, for those who have never been in one, are generally free-standing buildings, with fairly utilitarian spaces, where members can drop by for a drink, or in some spots, play darts, pool, euchre, or dance to a live band on a Friday night.

They are humble. At 1395 Lake Shore Blvd., framed pictures of soldiers, Spitfires, Lancasters and destroyers deck the walls, highlighting the exploits, tragedy and heroism of local veterans.

At Royal Canadian Legion Branch 101 in Etobicoke, glass cases hold guns, gas masks, bayonets and artillery shells, as well as the cribbage boards that were a popular pastime in trenches and mess halls for soldiers and sailors in the First World War.

The displays aren’t meant to glorify war. The mementos are kept as a sacred tribute to the men who held them in their hands.

Many of the people connected to legions today have deep military roots.

Roy is a veteran whose grandfather fought in the first and second world wars. His father fought in the second, along with all his uncles. Roy wears a poppy, with a black string of mourning drawn through it in support of the four Canadian Armed Forces members killed on Oct. 17 in a fast-moving grass fire that overtook troops during a training exercise at CFB Wainwright.

The legion held a blood drive in support of the injured.

Live bands play here every Friday night. There are dart boards, pool tables, euchre tournaments, bus trips to the casino. They rent their hall to community groups to earn money to keep the lights on. Legions are not-for-profit.

On Friday night, a table of middle-aged women were whooping it up next to the band Redpath Traffic.

“If the band is good, we’re here,” said Debbie Fitzgerald. “If not, we go to bingo.”

At a table nearby were two new members, Kim and Jay Perry.

Jay says they joined due to the recent surge in patriotism in the country.

“We wanted to do something to support Canada.”

Legions support and advocate for veterans and work closely with their communities, sponsoring local sports teams and supporting local charities. They run the annual poppy campaign.

After being incorporated in 1926 to serve veterans of the First World War, the legion was expanded to include veterans of the Second World War, the Korean War, the RCMP and modern Canadian Armed Forces personnel.

In 1973 membership was opened to families— sons, daughters, spouses and parents of veterans. Today, anyone over 18 can join.

Laura Rutherford joined 16 years ago, though she has no familial connection the military.

“I sincerely value what our veterans have done and are continuing to do,” said Rutherford.

She had just moved to the city when she joined on a whim.

“I didn’t know a soul in Toronto. I came here for work. And this place has become my surrogate family.”

She made a circle of friends.

“This is such a huge part of my life and it has brought me more than I can ever express.”

Cassandra Anderton, president of the Royal Canadian Legion Branch 344, whose grandmother was president for more than 25 years, says membership offers an antidote to being online.

“Being able to sit and have conversations with people, especially in a world where we’re enveloped in our technology, this is where you make connections,” she said.

Younger veterans say they want a wider variety of programs— they want activities that get them outdoors, more activities that aren’t centred around a bar.

Pamela Sweeny, executive director of The Royal Canadian Legion Ontario Provincial Command, says the success of the membership drive has proven that the legion is still relevant. About 60 per cent of the new members are under 60. She said legion branches are being encouraged to offer new activities for new members— like video game nights and bands that younger members want to hear.

“You have to listen to fresh new ideas. Now that we have this wonderful opportunity, we’re focused on retaining those wonderful people that have joined.”

Francine Kopun is a Toronto Star journalist and senior writer, based in Toronto. Follow her on Twitter: @KopunF

stories.title: Wealth advisor sues Cibc for $18.7-million following his termination
stories.summary: Darren Luck has since landed at Wellington-Altus
stories.author: Michael McKiernan
stories.content:
Darren Luck, an advisor in Windsor, Ont., is suing Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce for $18.7-million following his messy exit from the firm at which he built his $350-million book of business.

In a statement of claim filed with the Ontario Superior Court of Justice, Mr. Luck alleges his suspension and ultimate termination for cause by CIBC earlier this year were part of a “calculated plan to subvert his book of business, ruin his reputation and throw his licence in limbo.”

Mr. Luck, a former senior wealth advisor with CIBC Wood Gundy, is seeking $7.1-million for fees and deferred stock payments he would have earned during a 36-month reasonable notice period, plus a further $10.6-million for the loss of value in his book of business and $1-million in bad faith and punitive damages related to the manner of his dismissal. He joined Wellington-Altus Private Wealth Inc. earlier this year.

According to Mr. Luck’s claim, CIBC had been looking for a way to force him out long before leaping on “innocuous conduct” involving the use of a personal e-mail address.

He also alleges CIBC interfered with the transfer of his Canadian Investment Regulatory Organization (CIRO) licence by including the “meritless” for-cause termination on its F1 form to the regulator, clearing the way for the bank to distribute Mr. Luck’s clients among competing advisors in the CIBC office where he worked.

By the time CIRO had unconditionally reinstated his licence, 16 weeks had passed and “the damage was done,” Mr. Luck’s claim reads.

In a statement sent to The Globe by e-mail, CIBC spokesperson Stephanie Marcus said the company was unable to comment as the matter was before the courts, but that “we will defend ourselves fully.”

In a statement of defence filed with the court, CIBC World Markets Inc. (CIBC WMI) characterizes Mr. Luck’s just-cause firing as the culmination of a six-year period of “repeated and escalating” misconduct, during which he was coached or disciplined for “three separate confidentiality breaches, repeated inappropriate political commentary through CIBC-affiliated accounts and unprofessional workplace communications.”

Leading up to Mr. Luck’s termination, the bank alleges he demonstrated a “blatant disregard” for CIBC policies and ultimately concluded he was “unmanageable.”

The firm also denies any interference with Mr. Luck’s licence, claiming it followed CIRO’s guidelines in its F1 submission regarding his departure.

In any case, the firm disputes Mr. Luck’s claim for damages related to his book of business, claiming his role as an investment advisor was to serve a group of the firm’s clients, for whom he “had no proprietary interest or goodwill.”

None of the allegations in either document have been proven in court.

Toronto employment lawyer Howard Levitt, who is acting for Mr. Luck, said the episode has left his client feeling “frustrated, enraged, outraged and disappointed.”

“He thinks the way he’s been treated is reprehensible,” Mr. Levitt says, adding that Mr. Luck joined Wellington-Altus without taking many of his former clients.

Even considering the cumulative disciplinary issues, the bank has fallen way short of establishing cause, according to Mr. Levitt.

“Is what he did so egregious as to suggest he’s ungovernable? It’s all pretty trivial stuff,” he says.

Since starting his career with Midland Walwyn Inc. in 1991, Mr. Luck has featured in prestigious industry rankings, including appearances on The Globe and Mail’s Canada’s Top Wealth Advisors: Best in Province ranking in 2022.

In his statement of claim, Mr. Luck attributes much of his success to the “Income Accelerator” investment strategy he adopted in the aftermath of the 2008 global financial crisis, which he communicated to clients in a personalized client statement he called “Wealth Tracks.”

Since 2009, Mr. Luck says his assets under management ballooned from $100-million to $350-million at the time of his firing. In 2025, Mr. Luck generated around $2.3-million in fee-based revenue from his 80-basis-point advisory fee, which was shared equally with the bank under a 50-50 fee-splitting agreement.

However, Mr. Luck’s claim says his strategy – which focused on keeping client fees low, only promoted higher-fee in-house products “very selectively” and outperformed CIBC’s average investment fund “dramatically” – did not go down well at the bank.

“[...] CIBC was not content as [it] wanted a greater share of those earnings. It had previously taken issue with Mr. Luck’s approach, which prioritized his clients rather than CIBC’s bottom line,” he alleges in the document. “Rather than appreciating Mr. Luck’s incredible performance as one of its best investment advisors, CIBC started treating him as a competitor.”

Mr. Luck’s claim alleges CIBC found its opportunity to act in January after his IT clerk sent some of his Wealth Tracks marketing material to Mr. Luck’s personal e-mail address. Mr. Luck’s claim says there was no confidential information in the e-mail, but after the e-mail was flagged, he was suspended on Jan. 24 pending an investigation.

In the following days, Mr. Luck alleges his team was dismantled, leaving nobody to serve his clients. Meanwhile, he alleges clients were told he was on administrative leave, “suggesting some serious ethical impropriety on Mr. Luck’s part, to motivate these clients to move to [different] CIBC advisors” before Mr. Luck’s termination on Feb. 2.

CIBC WMI denies Mr. Luck’s account. In its telling, the timeline for Mr. Luck’s termination started in 2020, when he first received coaching after sending confidential client information from his CIBC e-mail address to a personal e-mail address.

The bank says he received further coaching early during the COVID-19 pandemic after allowing clients to visit him in person at the office at a time when the bank had closed the Windsor branch to the public.

In the summer of 2024, Mr. Luck ran into trouble over an e-mail he forwarded from his CIBC e-mail address to a client and another employee containing disparaging comments about then-U.S. President Joe Biden and his family. Shortly after, CIBC WMI says a district manager instructed Mr. Luck to cease all political commentary and delete a comment on a LinkedIn post about the Liberal government’s commitment to welcome Gazan refugees to Canada, in which Mr. Luck wrote, “We cannot stand for this. Soon Trudeau will be gone living on one of Aga Khans islands and we will be stuck with an entire population of terrists [sic].”

According to the firm, Mr. Luck received his first formal written warning in early 2025 after it found he had continued to make comments and communications endorsing political views, in breach of its code of conduct and marketing guidelines.

A second formal warning followed in December, 2025, after the bank discovered Mr. Luck had tried to send a collection of e-mails from his CIBC work account to his personal e-mail account while preparing his response to a separate review of workplace harassment complaints by three fellow CIBC employees. Those complaints regarded Mr. Luck’s alleged yelling, intimidation and condescending remarks.

The statement of defence says the bank found the allegations in the underlying complaints did not amount to harassment. However, CIBC did conclude Mr. Luck’s manner of communication with colleagues was “inappropriate and did not meet the professional standards expected,” earning Mr. Luck his third formal warning just a week before his suspension.

That came, according to the statement of defence, after Mr. Luck’s IT clerk sent three PDFs, including a Wealth Tracks, to Mr. Luck’s personal e-mail address in January, 2026.

The firm claims Mr. Luck’s “Income Accelerator” strategy was actually a standard dividend reinvestment plan and had warned him that it was misleading to market the strategy as his own. One of the PDFs used the “Income Accelerator” marketing, while the others showed the performance of an anonymized investment portfolio.

Although the parties disagree on whether Mr. Luck had permission to use proxy study cases for comparing portfolio returns, CIBC alleges his “ongoing failure to acknowledge the seriousness of his actions” and repeated misconduct were cause for termination.

Toronto employment lawyer Howard Levitt, who is acting for Mr. Luck, said the episode has left his client feeling “frustrated, enraged, outraged and disappointed.”
“He thinks the way he’s been treated is reprehensible,” Mr. Levitt says, adding that Mr. Luck joined Wellington-Altus without taking many of his former clients.
Even considering the cumulative disciplinary issues, the bank has fallen way short of establishing cause, according to Mr. Levitt.
“Is what he did so egregious as to suggest he’s ungovernable? It’s all pretty trivial stuff,” he says.

Since starting his career with Midland Walwyn Inc. in 1991, Mr. Luck has featured in prestigious industry rankings, including appearances on The Globe and Mail’s Canada’s Top Wealth Advisors: Best in Province ranking in 2022.

In his statement of claim, Mr. Luck attributes much of his success to the “Income Accelerator” investment strategy he adopted in the aftermath of the 2008 global financial crisis, which he communicated to clients in a personalized client statement he called “Wealth Tracks.”

Since 2009, Mr. Luck says his assets under management ballooned from $100-million to $350-million at the time of his firing. In 2025, Mr. Luck generated around $2.3-million in fee-based revenue from his 80-basis-point advisory fee, which was shared equally with the bank under a 50-50 fee-splitting agreement.

However, Mr. Luck’s claim says his strategy – which focused on keeping client fees low, only promoted higher-fee in-house products “very selectively” and outperformed CIBC’s average investment fund “dramatically” – did not go down well at the bank.

“[...] CIBC was not content as [it] wanted a greater share of those earnings. It had previously taken issue with Mr. Luck’s approach, which prioritized his clients rather than CIBC’s bottom line,” he alleges in the document. “Rather than appreciating Mr. Luck’s incredible performance as one of its best investment advisors, CIBC started treating him as a competitor.”

Mr. Luck’s claim alleges CIBC found its opportunity to act in January after his IT clerk sent some of his Wealth Tracks marketing material to Mr. Luck’s personal e-mail address. Mr. Luck’s claim says there was no confidential information in the e-mail, but after the e-mail was flagged, he was suspended on Jan. 24 pending an investigation.

In the following days, Mr. Luck alleges his team was dismantled, leaving nobody to serve his clients. Meanwhile, he alleges clients were told he was on administrative leave, “suggesting some serious ethical impropriety on Mr. Luck’s part, to motivate these clients to move to [different] CIBC advisors” before Mr. Luck’s termination on Feb. 2.

CIBC WMI denies Mr. Luck’s account. In its telling, the timeline for Mr. Luck’s termination started in 2020, when he first received coaching after sending confidential client information from his CIBC e-mail address to a personal e-mail address.

The bank says he received further coaching early during the COVID-19 pandemic after allowing clients to visit him in person at the office at a time when the bank had closed the Windsor branch to the public.

In the summer of 2024, Mr. Luck ran into trouble over an e-mail he forwarded from his CIBC e-mail address to a client and another employee containing disparaging comments about then-U.S. President Joe Biden and his family. Shortly after, CIBC WMI says a district manager instructed Mr. Luck to cease all political commentary and delete a comment on a LinkedIn post about the Liberal government’s commitment to welcome Gazan refugees to Canada, in which Mr. Luck wrote, “We cannot stand for this. Soon Trudeau will be gone living on one of Aga Khans islands and we will be stuck with an entire population of terrists [sic].”

According to the firm, Mr. Luck received his first formal written warning in early 2025 after it found he had continued to make comments and communications endorsing political views, in breach of its code of conduct and marketing guidelines.

A second formal warning followed in December, 2025, after the bank discovered Mr. Luck had tried to send a collection of e-mails from his CIBC work account to his personal e-mail account while preparing his response to a separate review of workplace harassment complaints by three fellow CIBC employees. Those complaints regarded Mr. Luck’s alleged yelling, intimidation and condescending remarks.

The statement of defence says the bank found the allegations in the underlying complaints did not amount to harassment. However, CIBC did conclude Mr. Luck’s manner of communication with colleagues was “inappropriate and did not meet the professional standards expected,” earning Mr. Luck his third formal warning just a week before his suspension.
That came, according to the statement of defence, after Mr. Luck’s IT clerk sent three PDFs, including a Wealth Tracks, to Mr. Luck’s personal e-mail address in January, 2026.

The firm claims Mr. Luck’s “Income Accelerator” strategy was actually a standard dividend reinvestment plan and had warned him that it was misleading to market the strategy as his own. One of the PDFs used the “Income Accelerator” marketing, while the others showed the performance of an anonymized investment portfolio.

Although the parties disagree on whether Mr. Luck had permission to use proxy study cases for comparing portfolio returns, CIBC alleges his “ongoing failure to acknowledge the seriousness of his actions” and repeated misconduct were cause for termination.

stories.title: On the Move: Advisor team focused on longevity moves to Wellington-Altus
stories.summary: Neela White worked in long-term care before becoming an advisor
stories.author: Deanne Gage
stories.content:
On the Move is Globe Advisor’s roundup of notable hires and departures across Canada’s financial services industry.

Neela White works mainly with seniors, specializing in longevity issues and navigating Canada’s health care system. She sees this focus as essential to advisory practices for the future.

“It’s really being able to guide clients through the idea of what happens when a health care diagnosis [occurs],” the senior wealth advisor says.

She and business partner Derek Rennie moved their 150-client-household practice, Blue Wing Advisory Group in Toronto, to Wellington-Altus Private Wealth Inc. from Raymond James Ltd. earlier this month.

Ms. White has worked in the longevity space for years and says she wanted more marketing and technology support.

“As demand grows for advice that goes beyond traditional wealth management, particularly in my specialty areas, we’re excited to have the resources and support needed to deepen our expertise and deliver even greater value to clients and their families,” she says.

Longevity isn’t an area of focus for many advisors, says Ms. White, who was a primary caregiver and advocate to her own parents for a decade, and worked in long-term care doing activation and assessments.

Advisors tend to focus on areas in which they’re comfortable and can thrive, she says, and the topic of aging pushes some out of their comfort zone.

“Unless we have a really strong, open relationship with our client, these are difficult conversations to bring up because the conversations can be quite emotional,” she says. “How far should our conversations extend? That’s one of the areas our industry is exploring.”

Nevertheless, some uncomfortable conversations are getting easier. Ms. White says cancer used to be a taboo word, but as treatments have improved, the conversations have become normalized.

Today, she finds a dementia diagnosis the bigger taboo, with discussions about what’s needed and developing a plan with family members particularly challenging.

“The subject is not taboo for us,” she says. “Whatever the client diagnosis, it’s still our client and we’re there to protect them.”

On Nov. 3, Benjamin Felix was promoted to president of PWL Capital Inc. , at which he will retain his role as chief investment officer. Mr. Felix will work with chief executive officer Cameron Passmore on the company’s strategic growth and major client initiatives.

Robert Noel , Hudson Noel and Scott Buhler from Alderwood Wealth Partners in Warman, Sask., have joined Q Wealth Partners from CI Assante Wealth Management Ltd. In Winnipeg, Dave Holt and Aaron Migie moved to Q Wealth, establishing Aleris Private Wealth at which they’re managing partners. Mr. Holt was previously at Canaccord Genuity Wealth Management Canada and Mr. Migie hailed from CI Assante Wealth Management.

Terry Wright incorporated his firm, LT Wealth Management Partners Inc., becoming an independent portfolio manager registered with various provincial securities commissions. He was previously with Raymond James Ltd., which remains the custodian for his client accounts.

Recently switched firms? Got a big promotion? Left to start your own firm? Or retired to start that side hustle? Send the details to: dgage@globeandmail.com and put “On the Move” in the subject line. We look forward to hearing about your next chapter.

Nov. 11, 2026

JOH[](https://www.thestar.com/news/canada/british-columbia/rain-hammering-b-c-south-coast-may-taper-but-more-on-the-way-meteorologist/article_ed66d491-ee3f-5145-b45c-13df6aaa2c67.html)

By The Canadian Press

Environment Canada meteorologist Michael Gismondi says there will be a possible lull this morning before the rain is expected to re-intensify later.

It’s part of a series of atmospheric river systems that have been battering the coast this week, and Gismondi says the wet conditions are expected to persist into the weekend.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Angine de Poitrine debut third member in Toronto

Orange rainfall warnings that were raised by Environment Canada on Monday remain in place for Howe Sound and the Sea to Sky regions, with upwards of 160 millimetres of rain predicted, as well as western and inland Vancouver Island, where amounts could top 250 millimetres.

The weather office also warns residents of central B.C. that a “strong and slow-moving” system is bringing damaging winds, with gusts reaching around 100 kilometres an hour in some areas, before easing tonight.

It says utility outages are likely and driving may be difficult as there is risk of injury due to falling debris.

B.C.‘s Transportation Ministry is also urging drivers to monitor conditions and prepare for high winds, heavy rainfall and possible flooding in southern coastal regions for the rest of the week.

Flood watches continue to cover much of Vancouver Island and the South Coast.

On Tuesday, British Columbia’s River Forecast Centre issued high streamflow advisories for southern Vancouver Island and the Fraser Valley.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 11, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Carney takes off Wednesday for summits in Ireland, Philippines, Cambodia and China
stories.summary: Ottawa — Prime Minister Mark Carney takes off Wednesday for summits in Asia and Ireland where he'll look to advance trade and security ties.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By Dylan Robertson, The Canadian Press

Posted November 11, 2026 4:00 am.

Last Updated November 11, 2026 5:17 am.

OTTAWA — Prime Minister Mark Carney takes off Wednesday for summits in Asia and Ireland where he’ll look to advance trade and security ties.

His travels will take him to four countries and put him on the ground as high-stakes diplomacy takes place between the United States, China and Russia.

Vina Nadjibulla, co-founder of the Centre for Strategic Statecraft, said the trip is Canada’s chance to build on new agreements and partnerships it has signed with countries around the world.

“We’re now entering a much more consequential phase of actually implementing and delivering on all of these agreements, and sustaining the momentum,” she said.

“When Prime Minister Carney speaks about diversifying our relationships, it’s not just about Europe.”

The prime minister is set to depart for Dublin shortly after the Remembrance Day ceremony in Ottawa.

Carney will attend the European Political Community summit in Dublin, set for Nov. 12. For the second time, Canada will be the only non-European country represented at the table. Carney joined the group’s last meeting in Armenia in May.

The EPC summits have taken place roughly every six months since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

The informal meetings are aimed at discussing strategic co-operation in politics, security and infrastructure.

Carney and European Union leaders have floated Canada becoming an “associate member” of the EU since the last summit — a title they have yet to define.

The Philippines

After Dublin, Carney will cross both the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans to visit Manila, where the Philippines is hosting Canada as a guest at the Nov. 15–18 summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations.

ASEAN is a bloc of 11 countries that focuses on trade, regional peace and international norms. Canada is set to finalize negotiations on two trade deals while Carney is in Manila, one with the ASEAN bloc and another bilateral deal with the Philippines. He could even sign one of them while he’s there.

The prime minister has a meeting scheduled for Saturday with Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and will address ASEAN leaders on Sunday.

Queen’s University professor Stéphanie Martel, who studies Southeast Asia and the Asia-Pacific, said the visit will help shape the Indo-Pacific strategy the Trudeau government released four years ago. That strategy focused on making Ottawa a relevant partner in the region after years of sporadic engagement.

“It’s becoming kind of a cliché to refer to Canada as this fairweather friend,” she said.

Martel said Carney has focused on trade and maritime defence but less on local concerns about climate change resilience and gender-inclusive militaries.

“There’s a lot of action in terms of specific trade deals and specific sectors. But the overall engagement and the ability of Canada to be seen as this serious, comprehensive contributor to the region is still up for debate,” she said.

In the Philippines, Carney will be joined by Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu and Gender Minister Rechie Valdez, who is of Filipino origin.

Carney will then visit the Francophonie summit in Cambodia set for Nov. 14 to 16. He’s expected to meet with leaders from Africa and other continents while in the capital Phnom Penh.

Canada is hosting the next Francophonie summit in 2028 in the Ottawa area. Carney is expected to use the gathering to advance Canada’s strategic autonomy and protect the role of French in the growing digital economy.

Francophonie members will elect their next leader in Cambodia and Ottawa says it is staying neutral to avoid affecting the next summit.

On Sunday, the prime minister is set to address CEOs at the FrancoTech innovation event at the summit. On Monday, he is set to give plenary remarks.

Dominique Caouette, Indo-Pacific studies chair at the University of Montreal’s political science department, said the Francophonie summit is an opportunity for Canada and Quebec to advance economic interests.

“The Francophonie could also serve as a platform for Mr. Carney toward the middle powers. There are several that are part of the Francophonie. It’s another space where Canada could play an influential role,” Caouette said in a French-language interview.

The summit will feature both Carney and Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, who was elected on a sovereigntist mandate aimed at pushing back on Ottawa. Caouette said he doesn’t expect the two to clash.

“It’s not in the Canadian or Quebec tradition to air one’s dirty laundry in public,” he said.

Carney will be joined in Cambodia by Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand and her parliamentary secretary Mona Fortier. Before his arrival, Gov. Gen. Louise Arbour will lead Canada’s delegation at the summit.

Carney’s last stop will be China’s tech hub of Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation summit, set for Nov. 18 to 19. Leaders from across the Pacific Rim will gather in the city bordering Hong Kong to take stock of an increasingly disordered trading system.

Nadjibulla said the summit allows for bilateral and “minilateral” discussions that bring leaders together in small groups to advance common goals. She said the APEC meetings themselves have taken on less importance, thanks to the diverging interests of Russia, the U.S. and China.

U.S. President Donald Trump is set to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin at the summit.

The meeting has European leaders worried about a possible impact on Moscow’s war against Ukraine. Analysts are also watching for any updates on Trump’s war on Iran.

Carney’s visit will come just days after China extended a deal to provide market access to Canadian imports such as canola meal and lobster, in exchange for Canadian market access for Chinese steel and aluminum.

Xi and Carney are set to meet Tuesday and he will address business leaders the next day.

Nadjibulla said she’ll be watching for any economic announcements, such as a move to allow more Chinese vehicles into Canada or new Chinese investments in energy and technology.

“The warming, the recalibration of the relationship has been moving at a rapid pace,” Nadjibulla said, adding that any moves could affect trade talks with the U.S.

In China, Carney will be joined by his parliamentary secretary Kody Blois and Anand.

Carney is set to return to Ottawa on Nov. 19.

The federal Conservatives have criticized Carney’s overseas deals, arguing that the signed agreements have not yielded significant gains and are distracting the government’s attention from the affordability crisis.

The Liberals argue facetime between leaders is critical to diversifying trade and building more resilient supply chains and security partnerships.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 11, 2026.

— With files from Caroline Plante in Quebec City

Dylan Robertson, The Canadian Press

Carney and European Union leaders have floated Canada becoming an “associate member” of the EU since the last summit — a title they have yet to define.
The Philippines

After Dublin, Carney will cross both the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans to visit Manila, where the Philippines is hosting Canada as a guest at the Nov. 15–18 summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations.

ASEAN is a bloc of 11 countries that focuses on trade, regional peace and international norms. Canada is set to finalize negotiations on two trade deals while Carney is in Manila, one with the ASEAN bloc and another bilateral deal with the Philippines. He could even sign one of them while he’s there.
The prime minister has a meeting scheduled for Saturday with Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and will address ASEAN leaders on Sunday.

Queen’s University professor Stéphanie Martel, who studies Southeast Asia and the Asia-Pacific, said the visit will help shape the Indo-Pacific strategy the Trudeau government released four years ago. That strategy focused on making Ottawa a relevant partner in the region after years of sporadic engagement.
“It’s becoming kind of a cliché to refer to Canada as this fairweather friend,” she said.
Martel said Carney has focused on trade and maritime defence but less on local concerns about climate change resilience and gender-inclusive militaries.

“There’s a lot of action in terms of specific trade deals and specific sectors. But the overall engagement and the ability of Canada to be seen as this serious, comprehensive contributor to the region is still up for debate,” she said.
In the Philippines, Carney will be joined by Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu and Gender Minister Rechie Valdez, who is of Filipino origin.
Carney will then visit the Francophonie summit in Cambodia set for Nov. 14 to 16. He’s expected to meet with leaders from Africa and other continents while in the capital Phnom Penh.

Canada is hosting the next Francophonie summit in 2028 in the Ottawa area. Carney is expected to use the gathering to advance Canada’s strategic autonomy and protect the role of French in the growing digital economy.
Francophonie members will elect their next leader in Cambodia and Ottawa says it is staying neutral to avoid affecting the next summit.
On Sunday, the prime minister is set to address CEOs at the FrancoTech innovation event at the summit. On Monday, he is set to give plenary remarks.

Dominique Caouette, Indo-Pacific studies chair at the University of Montreal’s political science department, said the Francophonie summit is an opportunity for Canada and Quebec to advance economic interests.

“The Francophonie could also serve as a platform for Mr. Carney toward the middle powers. There are several that are part of the Francophonie. It’s another space where Canada could play an influential role,” Caouette said in a French-language interview.

The summit will feature both Carney and Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, who was elected on a sovereigntist mandate aimed at pushing back on Ottawa. Caouette said he doesn’t expect the two to clash.
“It’s not in the Canadian or Quebec tradition to air one’s dirty laundry in public,” he said.

Carney will be joined in Cambodia by Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand and her parliamentary secretary Mona Fortier. Before his arrival, Gov. Gen. Louise Arbour will lead Canada’s delegation at the summit.

Carney’s last stop will be China’s tech hub of Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation summit, set for Nov. 18 to 19. Leaders from across the Pacific Rim will gather in the city bordering Hong Kong to take stock of an increasingly disordered trading system.

Nadjibulla said the summit allows for bilateral and “minilateral” discussions that bring leaders together in small groups to advance common goals. She said the APEC meetings themselves have taken on less importance, thanks to the diverging interests of Russia, the U.S. and China.
U.S. President Donald Trump is set to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin at the summit.
The meeting has European leaders worried about a possible impact on Moscow’s war against Ukraine. Analysts are also watching for any updates on Trump’s war on Iran.

Carney’s visit will come just days after China extended a deal to provide market access to Canadian imports such as canola meal and lobster, in exchange for Canadian market access for Chinese steel and aluminum.
Xi and Carney are set to meet Tuesday and he will address business leaders the next day.
Nadjibulla said she’ll be watching for any economic announcements, such as a move to allow more Chinese vehicles into Canada or new Chinese investments in energy and technology.
“The warming, the recalibration of the relationship has been moving at a rapid pace,” Nadjibulla said, adding that any moves could affect trade talks with the U.S.
In China, Carney will be joined by his parliamentary secretary Kody Blois and Anand.
Carney is set to return to Ottawa on Nov. 19.

The federal Conservatives have criticized Carney’s overseas deals, arguing that the signed agreements have not yielded significant gains and are distracting the government’s attention from the affordability crisis.
The Liberals argue facetime between leaders is critical to diversifying trade and building more resilient supply chains and security partnerships.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 11, 2026.

stories.title: Budget 2026 shifts Liberal government’s language on home construction targets
stories.summary: Ottawa — The federal housing minister's office is reasserting Ottawa's goal of doubling the pace of home construction — even though references to the Liberals' hallmark affordability pledge were missing from Budget 2026.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By Craig Lord, The Canadian Press

Posted November 11, 2026 4:00 am.

Last Updated November 11, 2026 5:17 am.

Ottawa — The federal housing minister’s office is reasserting Ottawa’s goal of doubling the pace of home construction — even though references to the Liberals’ hallmark affordability pledge were missing from Budget 2026.

The budget, which was tabled last week, dropped any mention of that original target, which was introduced in the Liberals’ 2025 election platform and repeated numerous times in that year’s budget.

Instead, the 511-page document outlines a new plan to triple the pace of non-market housing construction to 24,000 starts per year over the next decade.

Non-market housing is usually more affordable and relies on government support to get built, but those homes account for only a small share of the overall number of units built in a year.

The Canadian Press asked Housing Minister Gregor Robertson’s office whether Ottawa is abandoning its goal of doubling the annual pace of overall home building.

After repeated requests, his office pointed to a six-month-old statement given to The Canadian Press in May confirming that the government was still “working toward doubling homebuilding over the next decade.”

At the time, The Canadian Press had asked Robertson’s office about Ottawa’s commitment to the target because April’s spring economic update also lacked references to the goal.

Parliamentary Budget Officer Annette Ryan pointed out then that while the government’s fiscal update included plenty of talk about affordability supports, “no specific targets or metrics for the pace of home building were provided.”

Housing affordability has been a hot-button issue since the COVID-19 pandemic, which saw rents and resale prices rapidly escalate — boxing out many young Canadians trying to become homeowners.

On Tuesday, Robertson’s office pointed to statistics showing national housing starts are up more than 20 per cent since the pre-pandemic period, rental construction is setting a record pace and rents have trended lower over the past few years.

“Since forming government, we launched an ambitious national plan to focus our efforts and spur co-ordinated action between governments, homebuilders, and communities. We moved quickly to increase housing supply and improve access to safe, warm, affordable homes,” his office said.

MP Scott Aitchison, the Conservative housing critic, accused the Liberals of quietly dropping the promise to double home building and replacing it with the smaller non-market target.

“Their announcements and promises have turned into another Liberal housing illusion. Tripling the speed of slow is still unbearably slow and will not restore affordability,” Aitchison said in a statement to The Canadian Press.

“Canadians need homes they can afford, not more failed Liberal targets and broken promises.”

In its fall housing supply report, the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corp. wrote that the country is entering a “new phase” where slowing population growth is leading to more balance in Canadian rental markets.

But the Crown corporation warned that the annual pace of housing starts is well short of levels needed to restore pre-pandemic affordability to the market in the next 10 years.

The Cmhc’s “business-as-usual” forecast sees Canada breaking ground on 231,000 homes per year, which it estimates would leave the market up to 238,000 homes short of affordable levels by 2036.

Affordability will remain out of reach if Canada fails to take advantage of this moment to rapidly build housing supply ahead of the next surge in demand, the Cmhc said.

Mike Moffatt, founding director of the Missing Middle Institute, said he always viewed the Liberals’ goal of doubling home building levels as a tough one to achieve. It would mean bringing the annual number of housing starts up to 500,000 in a given year, when Canada has so far topped out around 300,000.

Moffatt said the target May also be “excessive,” given that the government can effectively control the pace of population growth, which dictates how much supply is really needed to serve the Canadian market.

The headline number also doesn’t specify what kinds of homes Canada needs to build to actually meet Canadians’ needs, he added.

“I never loved the target. I felt it was probably too high and missed some important nuances,” Moffatt said.

The federal Liberals have instituted a number of policy changes aimed at stimulating home building since Prime Minister Mark Carney came to office in March 2025.

They include waiving the GST on many newly built homes, establishing new funds for local infrastructure and setting up Build Canada Homes, a new Crown corporation tasked with reversing years of lagging non-market home construction.

Budget 2026 proposed giving another $13 billion over 10 years to Build Canada Homes and pledged tens of billions of dollars over the coming decade to an effort to end homelessness across the country.

Andy Yan, director of the City Program at Simon Fraser University, also said he considered Ottawa’s original home building goal “more aspirational than realistic.”

“You can set a target, but do you have the capacity to meet those targets?” he said.

Yan said policies like the Housing Accelerator Fund and the Apartment Construction Loan Program have been “fairly successful” in getting more homes built, particularly on the rental side.

The Housing Accelerator Fund, which ties federal cash to pro-development policy changes, was one of Ottawa’s tools for addressing the fact that barriers to building often lie at the municipal level.

Many of the other levers for stimulating home building are also not directly in the federal government’s hands.

Building material costs have grown in response to U.S. tariffs, while a soft labour market is dampening buyer demand for new homes.

Interest rates — a critical factor for developers weighing the business case for a new build — are set independently by the Bank of Canada. The central bank delivered its first rate hike in more than three years last month and signalled more could be on the way.

Moffatt warned that many of the constraints holding back broader construction apply to social housing as well.

“There’s no non-market drywall, right? There’s no non-market lumber, there’s no non market electrician,” he said.

“A non-market social housing target is more in the government’s control, but it’s hardly a slam dunk.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 10, 2026.

Craig Lord, The Canadian Press

content_blocks.html: The budget, which was tabled last week, dropped any mention of that original target, which was introduced in the Liberals’ 2025 election platform and repeated numerous times in that year’s budget.

content_blocks.text: Instead, the 511-page document outlines a new plan to triple the pace of non-market housing construction to 24,000 starts per year over the next decade.
content_blocks.html: Instead, the 511-page document outlines a new plan to triple the pace of non-market housing construction to 24,000 starts per year over the next decade.

content_blocks.text: Non-market housing is usually more affordable and relies on government support to get built, but those homes account for only a small share of the overall number of units built in a year.

content_blocks.text: The Canadian Press asked Housing Minister Gregor Robertson’s office whether Ottawa is abandoning its goal of doubling the annual pace of overall home building.
content_blocks.html: The Canadian Press asked Housing Minister Gregor Robertson’s office whether Ottawa is abandoning its goal of doubling the annual pace of overall home building.

content_blocks.text: After repeated requests, his office pointed to a six-month-old statement given to The Canadian Press in May confirming that the government was still “working toward doubling homebuilding over the next decade.”
content_blocks.html: After repeated requests, his office pointed to a six-month-old statement given to The Canadian Press in May confirming that the government was still “working toward doubling homebuilding over the next decade.”

content_blocks.text: At the time, The Canadian Press had asked Robertson’s office about Ottawa’s commitment to the target because April’s spring economic update also lacked references to the goal.

content_blocks.text: Parliamentary Budget Officer Annette Ryan pointed out then that while the government’s fiscal update included plenty of talk about affordability supports, “no specific targets or metrics for the pace of home building were provided.”
content_blocks.html: Parliamentary Budget Officer Annette Ryan pointed out then that while the government’s fiscal update included plenty of talk about affordability supports, “no specific targets or metrics for the pace of home building were provided.”

content_blocks.text: Housing affordability has been a hot-button issue since the COVID-19 pandemic, which saw rents and resale prices rapidly escalate — boxing out many young Canadians trying to become homeowners.
content_blocks.html: Housing affordability has been a hot-button issue since the COVID-19 pandemic, which saw rents and resale prices rapidly escalate — boxing out many young Canadians trying to become homeowners.

content_blocks.text: On Tuesday, Robertson’s office pointed to statistics showing national housing starts are up more than 20 per cent since the pre-pandemic period, rental construction is setting a record pace and rents have trended lower over the past few years.
content_blocks.html: On Tuesday, Robertson’s office pointed to statistics showing national housing starts are up more than 20 per cent since the pre-pandemic period, rental construction is setting a record pace and rents have trended lower over the past few years.

content_blocks.text: “Since forming government, we launched an ambitious national plan to focus our efforts and spur co-ordinated action between governments, homebuilders, and communities. content_blocks.html: MP Scott Aitchison, the Conservative housing critic, accused the Liberals of quietly dropping the promise to double home building and replacing it with the smaller non-market target.

content_blocks.text: “Their announcements and promises have turned into another Liberal housing illusion. Tripling the speed of slow is still unbearably slow and will not restore affordability,” Aitchison said in a statement to The Canadian Press.
content_blocks.html: “Their announcements and promises have turned into another Liberal housing illusion. Tripling the speed of slow is still unbearably slow and will not restore affordability,” Aitchison said in a statement to The Canadian Press.

content_blocks.text: “Canadians need homes they can afford, not more failed Liberal targets and broken promises.”

content_blocks.text: But the Crown corporation warned that the annual pace of housing starts is well short of levels needed to restore pre-pandemic affordability to the market in the next 10 years.

content_blocks.text: The Cmhc’s “business-as-usual” forecast sees Canada breaking ground on 231,000 homes per year, which it estimates would leave the market up to 238,000 homes short of affordable levels by 2036.

content_blocks.text: Affordability will remain out of reach if Canada fails to take advantage of this moment to rapidly build housing supply ahead of the next surge in demand, the Cmhc said.

content_blocks.text: Mike Moffatt, founding director of the Missing Middle Institute, said he always viewed the Liberals’ goal of doubling home building levels as a tough one to achieve. It would mean bringing the annual number of housing starts up to 500,000 in a given year, when Canada has so far topped out around 300,000.

content_blocks.text: The federal Liberals have instituted a number of policy changes aimed at stimulating home building since Prime Minister Mark Carney came to office in March 2025.

By Bill Graveland The Canadian Press

Federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre is set to attend along with other dignitaries, military members and veterans.

On Oct. 17, a strong wind sent flames from a grass fire racing onto troops at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, southeast of Edmonton.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Angine de Poitrine debut third member in Toronto

Pte. Shaun Farrell, 23, of Prince Albert, Sask.; Pte. Aidan Goulding, 23, of North Vancouver; and Pte. Hayden Lykkemark, 19, of Langley, B.C.; and Sgt. Morgan Wong, 26, of Edmonton died in the blaze.

Thirty-nine others were injured, and many are still recovering in hospital.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has called it one of the worst tragedies for the Armed Forces on Canadian soil during peacetime. Three investigations are looking into what happened.

Wainwright Mayor Bruce Pugh said the town’s annual Remembrance Day service is expected to be the most solemn one in its recent history.

“It will be different this year just with the weight of what happened,” he said.

“I think it’s a reminder of that willingness and that sacrifice that never stops.”

Poilievre visited Wainwright shortly after the fire and met some of the injured soldiers. He said he heard astonishing stories of bravery.

“The courage of soldiers who literally ran into walls of fire to pull their brothers and sisters out of danger,” he said at the time.

“Soldiers who were burned head to toe in the hospital, some with their vision lost, actually joking around with the nurses to try and make the nurses feel more comfortable.”

Roughly 84 soldiers with the Charlie Company unit of the 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry were taking part in attack training, when the military says the fast-moving fire basically landed on top of them.

Roughly 300 members of the regiment are set to attend a Remembrance Day service in St. Albert, a bedroom community northwest of Edmonton.

The military says they are to march in a parade to the city’s cenotaph. There will also be a memorial Air Force flypast.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 11, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: From activist to academic, Bessie Borwein never stopped connecting people
stories.summary: Her family remembers her as a fierce, brilliant, loving woman who made lives better by her presence in them
stories.author: The Globe and Mail
stories.content:
Bessie Borwein: Matriarch. Scientist. Communicator. Connector. Born March 17, 1927, in Johannesburg, South Africa; died June 9, 2026, in London, Ont., of natural causes; aged 99.

Bessie Flax – not short for Elizabeth or Beatrice, just Bessie − grew up under the dual shadows of apartheid and the Holocaust, danced with Nelson Mandela in her student activist days, married at 19 and spent the next 75 years building a life defined by a relentless impulse to make the world a better place.

Bessie and David Borwein grew up together in the Johannesburg Jewish community. David was three years older and tutored her in math when she was an undergrad at University of Witwatersrand in Johannesburg. They married in 1946.

The couple left South Africa two years later to live in London where David pursued a DPhil in mathematics and Bessie started a PhD in botany. After the Nationalist Party came to power in 1948, David used to say that they could never go back as Bessie would have spent her life in jail – a statement he made with equal parts pride and genuine assessment of the risks.

David’s first teaching position was at the University of St. Andrews in Scotland. Bessie cried when she heard the news – she did not want to go somewhere so cold and dark and small. In the end, they loved it and spent 15 happy years there, welcoming three children, Jon, Peter and Sarah. Bessie and her family also became British citizens.

Ever adventurous, in the 1960s, the family of five immigrated to Canada – to London, Ont., a place they had never heard of – for a one-year sabbatical at Western University. They decided to make Canada their home and became Canadian citizens in 1982.

In London, Bessie began working as a lab technician and a professor at the university encouraged her to pursue graduate work. She completed her PhD in anatomy in 1973. Bessie studied the eyes of Anableps anableps , a quirky fish that swims at the water’s surface and thus sees two worlds at once. This was something that her daughter always found fitting.

Bessie was the answer to anyone who ever said it was too late to start. She had an extraordinary, illustrious career that didn’t start until she was nearly 50. She became an associate professor at Western University then associate dean of medical research. She served on the Research Ethics Review Board, founded a non-profit that educated the public on science, worked with the Alzheimer’s Society in Ontario, the Ontario Breast Screening Program, Madame Vanier Children’s Services and the Youth Science Foundation, among other gigs. She also won a list of awards and recognitions too long to recount here.

Bessie was a do-er. If there was a problem, she needed to help solve it. In 1968, when a neighbourhood child went missing, she spearheaded the Block Parent program, a network of safe homes each marked by a sign in the window. London was the first city in Canada to have it and it spread across the country.

She never stopped connecting people to each other – spotting the invisible thread between two people and pulling until they met. Bessie often sent packages of random newspaper clippings to her children, simply to say she was thinking of them. She signed every note “YDM” (for Your Devoted Mother). She also took in a cousin’s daughter and rewrote two futures in a single act of kindness – hers, and Sarah’s, as they became as close as sisters.

Bessie took infectious joy in her grandchildren and became a devoted and loving grandmother to all nine of them. Her home was a haven, full of warmth, heated political argument and David’s dry wit. He used to say their 75-year marriage worked because of the division of labour: He did the division, she did the labour.

She outlived her sons Jon and Peter, and David. Bessie carried those profound losses in her body and over the years, slipped away from the world. But the Bessie her family remembers was a fierce, brilliant, loving woman who made lives better by her presence in them.

Bessie was close to 100 before she died. Had she been a little more present, she might have held on for that telegram from the king.

Sarah Borwein is Bessie Borwein’s daughter.

To submit a Lives Lived: lives@globeandmail.com

Lives Lived celebrates the everyday, extraordinary, unheralded lives of Canadians who have recently passed. To learn how to share the story of a family member or friend, go to tgam.CA/livesguide .
