On Nov. 1, 2019, child welfare took custody of both boys. They were severely malnourished because of needless diet restrictions, stunted in height and using walkers, wheelchairs and leg braces at the time.

The brothers spent more than a month in hospital, where “it was ultimately determined by medical professionals that neither boy had the vast majority of health issues that C.D. alleged they had, and neither boy required any mobility aid or any incontinence product or any soothing aid or any medication that he had previously been prescribed,” Conlan wrote. None of the illnesses were verified, except for very mild cerebral palsy in one son.

Their medical histories showed a high suspicion for caregiver fabricated illness at the hands of their mother, according to a review of their medical records from birth until age 21 by a pediatrician at Toronto’s Hospital for Sick Children and the Scan (Suspected Child Abuse and Neglect) Program.

Reported symptoms in the children couldn’t be fully explained or verified by test results. One twin was prescribed at least seven different seizure medications based on C.D.’ s persistent reports that he was making abnormal movements, even though several CT scans and other tests were normal.

An investigation of the family home by child protection and police revealed an apartment set up for toddlers: stuffed animals on the bed, puzzles and toys for young children, low hanging hooks for back packs.
Their mother appeared to be in control “from the moment they woke up until they had ‘quiet time’ and went to bed,” a child psychologist wrote in a report requested by the Crown.

The boys had been homeschooled since after kindergarten, had no friends, rarely left the house and were bathed by their mother, even as teenagers. The family moved around; the boys were seen by different doctors in different cities. “The sheer volume of medical contacts in their medical histories was shocking,” psychologist Louise Sas wrote.
There were no play dates growing up and the twins wrongly believed they couldn’t manage without wheelchairs and walkers.

Some medical procedures carried out on the twins were intrusive, experts wrote. At one point, C.D. tried to convince surgeons to insert a feeding tube into one boy’s stomach, claiming he had severe reflux and a tendency to aspirate.
The brothers, who will turn 24 in December, continue to struggle and need community supports, Conlan wrote.
For years and years and years, this mother betrayed her position of trust and authority and, essentially, ruined the lives of her twin sons
In victim impact statements, the brothers said their mother convinced them that their wheelchairs, tests and medications were needed.
“One of the hardest things to understand is that we did not know what was happening was wrong because it was the Only life we knew,” one wrote.
“She was supposed to protect my brother and me, but instead she hurt us,” another said.
They were kept from their maternal grandmother. When people began to question things, their mother would move them to a new city.
The mother, now 45, is clearly “not a healthy person, whether physically or psychologically,” the judge said.

According to her medical records, she has a host of ailments, including gastrointestinal and bladder issues. She has a feeding tube, uses a motorized scooter, has multiple mental health conditions including borderline personality disorder and recently applied for Maid, for which her psychiatrist told court she would likely be deemed eligible.

She also has factitious disorder, in which a person intentionally feigns being sick to garner sympathy, care and support. “This is why the medical records in this case must, to a certain extent, be viewed cautiously,” the judge wrote.

Nonetheless, Conlan accepted that C.D. “is a very unhealthy person, mentally and physically,” that she has been the victim of past intimate partner violence and was left to raise her twins alone when the father effectively abandoned the family. She has abided by a “no-contact” order with her boys since they were taken into care.
However, the offences against her sons “were grave” and her moral blameworthiness high, Conlan wrote.
C.D. pleaded guilty, and Colan accepted that mental illness played a part in her crime.
She apologized in court to her sons, expressed regret for what she did and acknowledged harm done to the boys, the judge noted.

“I did find it interesting, however, that most of the lengthy statement that was read aloud by C.D. focused on her own physical and psychological problems and amounted, more than anything else, to a plea for mercy from the Court,” Conlan wrote.
In the end, he agreed with the Crown. “This is one of those cases that just demands a carceral sentence in a real jail.”
The defence had argued C.D. should serve her sentence under house arrest for the maximum length of a conditional sentence — two years less one day — to be followed by up to three years’ probation.

“The aggravating features of this case are extreme,” Conlan wrote. “For years and years and years, this mother betrayed her position of trust and authority and, essentially, ruined the lives of her twin sons by subjecting them to abuse in a myriad of ways.
“Denunciation and deterrence in this particular case simply demand a penitentiary sentence.”
Given her health issues, he tempered her sentence to 3.5 years for each of the two convictions, to be served concurrently — the lower end of the range the Crown was seeking.

Once widely known as Munchausen syndrome by proxy, fabricated illness in a child is rare. It’s often unrecognized and, even when spotted, often goes unreported, according to the authors of an influential paper on the condition.
“There is often a significant delay from months to years between when the child presents with initial symptoms to the time of diagnosis,” they wrote.

The reported incidence is up to two per 100,000 children younger than 16, researchers said. While mothers are the most common offenders, there have been cases where both parents have colluded to fabricate illness.
Some thrive on the attention of doctors; others insist their children can’t cope without their ongoing attention.
Fabricated illness can be difficult to detect. People can switch doctors, or report symptoms that seem bizarre, or symptoms that doctors don’t actually see when they examine the child.

Children can suffer serious harm, even death. It carries a six to nine per cent mortality rate. There have been reports of parents intentionally poisoning their kids with sedatives, opioids or other drugs.

stories.title: Emerge Canada, senior executives improperly borrowed millions from ETFs, securities watchdog rules
stories.summary: Most of the money has not been repaid and investors remain unsecured creditors
stories.author: Clare O’Hara
stories.content:
Ontario’s securities watchdog has ruled that Toronto-based fund manager Emerge Canada Inc. and two executives, including founder Lisa Langley, had breached their responsibilities to investors when they improperly borrowed almost $6-million of investor money to cover operating expenses.

On Tuesday, Ontario’s Capital Markets Tribunal – an independent division of the Ontario Securities Commission that handles adjudicative matters – found that Emerge Canada, Ms. Langley and chief financial officer Desmond Alvares violated a number of securities regulations, including failing to act in the best interest of the funds, borrowing investor money and insufficient record keeping.

However, the tribunal decision found that three members of Emerge’s independent review committee (IRC) – Marie Rounding, Monique Hutchins and Bruce Friesen – did not fail in their duties to oversee conflicts of interest, saying they were not informed about what was happening with the loans. All fund companies are required to have IRCs, which are responsible for reviewing a fund manager’s potential conflicts of interest on behalf of unitholders.

The OSC had accused Ms. Langley and Emerge of improperly borrowing millions from a group of exchange-traded funds named Emerge ARK, investments that were launched with U.S.-based ARK Investment Management LLC, which is run by prominent U.S. investor Cathie Wood.

Most of the money has not been repaid and investors remain unsecured creditors.

“We find that Langley was not familiar with the regulations and the compliance policies and procedures of her own firm,” the tribunal said in its findings.

“She had a complete misapprehension about what was a conflict, the nature of conflicts in fund management and the process for managing conflicts, including the purpose of an independent review committee.”

The tribunal said Ms. Langley failed to meet her obligations as an ultimate designated person and chief compliance officer. She also failed to identify the loan – known as a receivable – as a conflict and manage the conflict appropriately, and misunderstood the nature and permissibility of expenses charged to the funds, it added.

“The fact that she prioritized the launching of new funds using money borrowed from the funds and thereby significantly growing the receivable, after committing to paying down the receivable in the face of concerns expressed by Royal Bank of Canada and the Emerge Canada IRC, is a glaring example that she did not possess or exercise the level of competence, awareness, or diligence required of her roles,” it said.

The tribunal also rejected Mr. Alvares’s defence that he should not be held responsible because he took direction from Ms. Langley as her subordinate.

“It is not a defence that he deferred, or May have felt he had to defer, to Langley’s direction,” the tribunal said.

The tribunal added that Mr. Alvares’s explanation that he signed off on certain documents to authorize wire transfers out of the fund is a “clear example of Alvares permitting or acquiescing to the conduct that was occurring.”

Ms. Langley did not respond to a request for comment Tuesday, while Cheyenne Parsons, a lawyer at Crawley MacKewn Brush LLP and legal counsel for Mr. Alvares, declined to comment.

Adam Chisholm, a lawyer with McMillan LLP and legal counsel for the IRC members Ms. Hutchins and Ms. Rounding, said his clients are relieved at the outcome.

“These are accomplished, professional women whose reputations were squarely attacked by the publication of these proceedings, which we have always believed were misplaced,” he said in an e-mail.

It was the first time the OSC had launched an enforcement case against IRC members, and industry experts were closely monitoring the outcome for its impact on IRC members at other funds.

The OSC argued that Emerge had sent a referral of a conflict-of-interest matter to the IRC regarding the $6-million loan in 2021. However, the tribunal found that executives at Emerge did not flag any conflict issues to the IRC.

“This case should never have been brought,” said Rahul Shastri, a lawyer with Kagan Shastri DeMelo Winer Park LLP and legal counsel for Mr. Friesen. “The Commission publicly blamed the IRC for depriving investors of protection, but the Tribunal found there was never a referral and that the Irc’s duties were never engaged. Independent professionals who serve on IRCs deserve better from their regulator.”

Problems at Emerge first became known to investors on April 14, 2023, when the OSC imposed a temporary trading halt – known as a cease-trade order – on the company’s 11 exchange-traded funds.

The Globe initially reported that Emerge Canada, which managed about $118-million in assets, owed a total of $2.53-million to its six Emerge ARK funds.

A month later, the OSC suspended Emerge Canada’s operating licence. The regulator revealed that the amount owed at that time was $5.5-million.

The OSC said Emerge Canada began to transfer investor money from the investment funds’ bank accounts into its own bank accounts and those of its U.S. affiliate shortly after launching the ARK funds in 2019.

The transfers continued for four years until December 2022, when the company’s auditor, BDO Canada LLP, resigned. Over that time, the loans had grown to about $6-million, about 6.1 per cent of the funds’ total net asset value.

At the end of 2023, Emerge Canada was still unable to pay back the remaining loan balance and it shut down the ETFs on Dec. 29 of that year.

The OSC has not yet set a date for a penalty hearing for Emerge Canada, Ms. Langley or Mr. Alvares.

stories.title: Wartime mystery solved as divers find wreck of ship torpedoed by German U-boat
stories.summary: The steamboat was heading from Barbados to New Brunswick in December 1944 when it was torpedoed by a German U-boat. Its wreckage was found this year.
stories.author: Rebecca Lau, Heidi Petracek
stories.content:
For more than 80 years, the final resting place of S.S. Cornwallis and her crew was unknown.

The steamboat was heading from Barbados to New Brunswick in December 1944 when it was torpedoed by a German U-boat, which had just dropped off two Nazi spies in Maine.

Only five of the ship’s 48 crew members survived. They were among the more than 1,600 merchant mariners who were responsible for moving much-needed supplies, killed during the Second World War.

Now, an American team of volunteer divers has revealed its discovery — offering family members of the men some closure.

“It was almost as if our grandfather had spoken, ‘Hey, don’t forget about me,'” said Donald Stewart, the grandson of David. H. Stewart, who was lost with the steamship.

Robert Stewart was just 15 years old when he learned in a telegram that his father, David H. Stewart, was among the dead.

“Devastating, to say the least,” he said about the news.

“My mother had a tremendously good singing voice, but I don’t think I ever heard her sing that much after that.”

Nova Scotia native James Roy, 34, was also on board the ship.

“My dad used to speak of him a lot. My dad wasn’t very emotional about it, but he spoke of him. He’d say, ‘Oh, I wish you had met Jimmy, my brother,'” said his nephew, Glenn Roy.

Roy said his father never forgot his older brother. Over the years, Roy became interested in studying genealogy and learning about his family’s history.

Among his collection of treasured items is the telegram sent to his grandmother informing her James had died, as well as documentation of the pension she later received.

For more than eight decades, no one knew the exact location of Cornwallis’ watery grave until 2019, when a group of divers made it their mission to find the wreck in the Atlantic Ocean.

“The big thing is that someone has taken an interest in finding this location and putting a place on a map,” said Danny Allan, of the Nomad Exploration Team.

It wasn’t an easy task. The team spent years researching the ship and conducted a painstaking grid search over five days in the Gulf of Maine.

This past July, just when they were about to move to a new location, they spotted something on the sonar about 16 kilometres from a small island off the coast of Maine, submerged 122 metres below the surface.

“It was very evident from that you could see the superstructure of the wreck — the structure over where the engines were,” recalled Allan.

“And we were able to put divers on the numbers that we had found and we are able to verify with 100 per cent certainty that this was indeed the Cornwallis.”

He said identifying the ship meant checking blueprints from the original builders in British Columbia, and finding identifying characteristics.

“In a perfect world, you would find the ship’s bell that says, S.S. Cornwallis. In this case, I don’t think the bell is on the ship because it was torpedoed and the front end is broken off, so I’d be shocked if the bell was still there,” said Allan.

“This one is easy simply because it’s a 400-foot wreck with a 50-foot beam. There’s not many ships of that size.”

For the families of the crew members, that certainty helps bring a sense of closure.

“At least somebody was thinking about him,” said Roy about his uncle.

“He didn’t leave anything, you know what I mean. It was only this stuff that I have — a little bit of memories, a few pieces of paper. No family, no kids or anything. So I keep it going.”

stories.title: Lucan Poppy Project pays tribute to veterans
stories.summary: Visitors to cenotaphs in Lucan and Granton this Remembrance Day will have an opportunity to take in the community’s first Poppy Project.
stories.author: Bryan Bicknell
stories.content:
Visitors to cenotaphs in Lucan and Granton this Remembrance Day will have an opportunity to take in the community’s first Poppy Project.

“The Poppy Project is a community project where people crochet or knit poppies. And then the poppies get tied onto nets or fastened onto backings of some sort, and displayed on Remembrance Day,” explained Jane Corbett, treasurer for the Lucan Area Heritage Society, and one of a group of several local women involved in the Poppy Project.

It began as a way to say thanks to veterans, but quickly turned into a community-wide tribute. Gail Lewis, President of the Lucan Legion Branch 540 says the visual display is moving.

“And I didn’t know that they’d put them up yet, and I drove up, it’s just like ‘wow, it’s stunning,’ it’s visually stunning,” she exclaimed.

The project taps into a trend in communities across Canada. It began in the Lucan area late last year. Members of the Lucan Heritage Donnelly Museum came up with the idea to knit or crochet 1,111 poppies for display at the Lucan cenotaph.

“The 11th hour of the 11th day of the 11th month,” said Corbett.

Before they knew it, they had more than 3,000 poppies. A decision was made to bring 1,111 to the nearby Granton cenotaph, according to Museum president Margaret Paul.

“Well, I think they just wanted to recognize that our life is better now because of the veterans,” Paul said.

About 30 people formed the core group producing the hand-made poppies. But as many as 100 people from the area took part, sending in one or two poppies at a time as their way of saying thanks to veterans.

“To have so many people, organizations, individuals, volunteers come together from every different backround, every demographic to support this project- it’s just been incredible,” said Leigh Robinson, one of the volunteers and the branch supervisor at the Lucan Library.

Lucan-Biddulph Mayor Cathy Burghardt-Jesson says the project highlights the best in the community.

“Recognition, the celebration, the remembrance of our veterans doesn’t just happen on November 11th, it happens all year long. Because these poppies weren’t made just yesterday. It took time and effort for our volunteers to do that,” said Burghardt-Jesson.

Remembrance Day services in Lucan-Biddulph take place at the Granton cenotaph Wednesday at 9:30 a.m., and at the Lucan cenotaph beginning at 10:30 a.m.

stories.title: Carney awarded satirical ‘fossil of the day’ title by activists over absence at UN Climate Conference
stories.summary: The title, given to ‘absent leaders of wealthy countries,’ was also awarded to Germany, France, Japan and Denmark
stories.author: Catherine Morrison
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney and several other world leaders who failed to attend the UN Climate Conference in Turkey have been awarded the “fossil of the day” title.

Climate Action Network International, which has handed out the satirical award since 1999, says Tuesday’s edition went to the “absent leaders of wealthy countries,” including Canada, Germany, France, Japan and Denmark.

“Despite widespread public demands for stronger climate action, these countries’ empty chairs send a dismal signal about their commitment to international climate co-operation,” said a Climate Action Network International press release.

“They haven’t gone as far as the United States in abandoning the Paris Agreement altogether, but they appear to have decided that COP31 is no longer important enough to warrant their presence.”

The press release said the leaders’ summit is where heads of government set political direction, build alliances and “earn the trust that unlocks progress in the negotiations.”

“It is also where they can sit down with their peers from vulnerable countries and hear their priorities first-hand,” it said. “With multilateral co-operation under growing strain, that matters more than ever.”

Canada’s reputation as a global climate leader took a hit last year when it was awarded the “fossil of the day” award at the UN Climate Conference in Brazil.

At the time, Climate Action Network International said Canada was singled out for the first time in more than a decade for “flushing years of climate action down the drain.”

New Zealand received the award on Monday, as Climate Action Network International said its government has dismantled its climate commitments by gutting methane targets and changing the law to shield corporations from climate litigation.

Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin is attending the first week of the conference and some climate activists say Canada can expect some criticism there from other nations over its recent climate policy shifts.

Since taking office, Carney has rolled back or cancelled a number of climate policies enacted by former prime minister Justin Trudeau, including the consumer carbon tax, an electric vehicle sales mandate and an emissions cap on oil and gas production.

Canada’s environment commissioner issued a report last month which said the government abandoned work in 2024 on a 2021 pledge to ban exports of thermal coal, without any record of having a directive to do so.

Ottawa said that work is only “paused,” though the report also said Ottawa formalized the end of the work in August 2025 as part of budget cuts.

Carney was in Montreal Tuesday where he hosted a discussion with leaders in Canada’s cultural sector to highlight investments in the federal budget that support Canadian culture.

On Wednesday, he will participate in a national Remembrance Day ceremony in Ottawa before leaving on a 10-day overseas trip that does not include travel to COP in Turkey.

He will attend the European Political Community summit in Dublin, Ireland, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit in Manila, Philippines, the biennial Francophonie summit of French-speaking nations in Phnom Penh, Cambodia, and finally the Asia-Pacific Economic Coooperation summit in Shenzhen, China.

stories.title: Climate activists award Carney, other absent world leaders 'fossil of the day' title
stories.summary: Ottawa - Prime Minister Mark Carney and several other world leaders who failed to attend the UN Climate Conference in Turkey have been awarded the "fossil of the day" title.
stories.author: Catherine Morrison The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - Prime Minister Mark Carney and several other world leaders who failed to attend the UN Climate Conference in Turkey have been awarded the “fossil of the day” title.

Climate Action Network International, which has handed out the satirical award since 1999, says Tuesday’s edition went to the “absent leaders of wealthy countries,” including Canada, Germany, France, Japan and Denmark.

“Despite widespread public demands for stronger climate action, these countries’ empty chairs send a dismal signal about their commitment to international climate co-operation,” said a Climate Action Network International press release.

“They haven’t gone as far as the United States in abandoning the Paris Agreement altogether, but they appear to have decided that COP31 is no longer important enough to warrant their presence.”

The press release said the leaders’ summit is where heads of government set political direction, build alliances and “earn the trust that unlocks progress in the negotiations.”

“It is also where they can sit down with their peers from vulnerable countries and hear their priorities first-hand,” it said. “With multilateral co-operation under growing strain, that matters more than ever.”

Canada’s reputation as a global climate leader took a hit last year when it was awarded the “fossil of the day” award at the UN Climate Conference in Brazil.

At the time, Climate Action Network International said Canada was singled out for the first time in more than a decade for “flushing years of climate action down the drain.”

New Zealand received the award on Monday, as Climate Action Network International said its government has dismantled its climate commitments by gutting methane targets and changing the law to shield corporations from climate litigation.

Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin is attending the first week of the conference and some climate activists say Canada can expect some criticism there from other nations over its recent climate policy shifts.

Since taking office, Carney has rolled back or cancelled a number of climate policies enacted by former prime minister Justin Trudeau, including the consumer carbon tax, an electric vehicle sales mandate and an emissions cap on oil and gas production.

Canada’s environment commissioner issued a report last month which said the government abandoned work in 2024 on a 2021 pledge to ban exports of thermal coal, without any record of having a directive to do so.

Ottawa said that work is only “paused,” though the report also said Ottawa formalized the end of the work in August 2025 as part of budget cuts.

Carney was in Montreal Tuesday where he hosted a discussion with leaders in Canada’s cultural sector to highlight investments in the federal budget that support Canadian culture.

On Wednesday, he will participate in a national Remembrance Day ceremony in Ottawa before leaving on a 10-day overseas trip that does not include travel to COP in Turkey.

He will attend the European Political Community summit in Dublin, Ireland, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit in Manila, Philippines, the biennial Francophonie summit of French-speaking nations in Phnom Penh, Cambodia, and finally the Asia-Pacific Economic Coooperation summit in Shenzhen, China.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 10, 2026.

-With files from Nick Murray and Dylan Robertson

'Mr. Carney would prefer that we not put on our skates or even step onto the ice, because he wants the rink all to himself,' the Quebec premier said.

Prime Minister Mark Carney announces funding for the arts and culture community at Atelier Belleville in Montreal, ON Tuesday, November 10, 2026. (Allen McInnis / Montreal Gazette)

Catherine Lévesque

November 10, 2026 at 5:47 p.m.

Ottawa — Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon reached out directly to 59 newly elected or reelected U.S. governors and senators of states that have ties to his province, a move that seemed to irritate Prime Minister Mark Carney on Tuesday.

National Post obtained copies of two of these letters, first revealed by Le Journal de Québec, which essentially congratulate the officials for their midterm elections and invite them to collaborate with the government of Quebec to advance shared goals.

For instance, the letter sent by St-Pierre Plamondon to Abdul El-Sayed, senator-elect for the State of Michigan, mentions that Quebec and Michigan’s economies are well-integrated with trade reaching nearly U.S. $4.6 billion in 2025.

“As you begin your term, Quebec welcomes the opportunity to work with your team to advance our shared goals and to discuss new projects and initiatives that will benefit both our populations,” reads the missive, which was sent in English and French.

The letter concludes by referring the governors and senators to their closest Quebec government office representative — in Chicago, Boston or elsewhere.

This initial contact is intended to lay the ground for a “diplomatic offensive” south of the border, according to Le Journal de Québec. That will soon be followed by the unveiling of a “Team Quebec” led by chief negotiator Pascal Paradis.

Asked in Montreal whether these diplomatic efforts from Quebec could impact trade negotiations between Canada and the U.S., Carney responded in the affirmative.

“First, what’s clear is that the decision-makers of commercial agreements and initiatives for the next two, three years is the executive of the U.S. That’s clear,” he said during an unrelated press conference. “It’s not necessarily the legislators.”

“Second, in any negotiation, it is always a good idea to have a single negotiator. For this reason, such matters fall within the purview of the federal government,” he added.

St-Pierre Plamondon shot back, saying that the letters he sent to the U.S. officials was consistent with the actions of previous Quebec governments.

“Mr. Carney is not my boss, and he will not stop Quebec from doing what it has always done — maintaining an international presence that allows our interests to be represented,” he told reporters in Quebec City.

“In the coming months, expect to see Quebec taking its place on the world stage.”

St-Pierre Plamondon made these comments alongside Bloc Québécois Leader Yves-François Blanchet, with whom he was meeting in the provincial capital.

“Mr. Carney would prefer that we not put on our skates or even step onto the ice, because he wants the rink all to himself. Welcome to Quebec. We have always asserted our place,” St-Pierre Plamondon said.

It is on that frosty note that the Quebec premier is expected to meet Carney in the coming days, ON the margins of the Francophonie Summit in Cambodia.

Both men had tried to match their schedules to meet beforehand, with Carney offering to meet St-Pierre Plamondon in the Ottawa-Gatineau region or in the Montreal area but the Quebec premier insisted that Carney should be the one to visit him in Quebec City.

St-Pierre Plamondon still managed to find time to travel to Toronto to visit Ontario Premier Doug Ford on Friday and to attend a hockey game between the Toronto Maple Leafs and the Montreal Canadiens with his father and one of his sons over the weekend.

Carney, for his part, spent the day Tuesday in Montreal to announce $4 billion in investments in culture in the budget and to make brief campaign stops with each of his three candidates for the federal byelections taking place in Quebec next month.

Catherine Lévesque covers federal-Quebec relations for National Post. She joined the parliamentary bureau in Ottawa in 2022, after a decade spent in French media in Montreal, Quebec City and Ottawa.

stories.title: NDP Leader Marit Stiles engages London businesses on economy, social issues
stories.summary: met with London business leaders Tuesday for a closed-door roundtable discussion focused on economic challenges and pressing social issues facing the community.
stories.author: Gerry Dewan
stories.content:
met with London business leaders Tuesday for a closed-door roundtable discussion focused on economic challenges and pressing social issues facing the community.

Stiles emphasized the need for a coordinated government response to issues ranging from tariff pressures to the escalating housing and healthcare crises.

The meeting, held at the London Chamber of Commerce headquarters was part of Stiles’ ongoing tour across Ontario, with similar community meetings also occurring Tuesday in Sarnia .

Stiles reported that while she anticipated hearing concerns about tariff pressures impacting the local economy, these worries were indeed a significant part of the discussion.

“It’s really, really important that we have a coordinated response and we need the provincial government to step up,” Stiles stated, highlighting the necessity for provincial leadership.

Beyond economic pressures, the NDP leader noted that many concerns raised were universal across communities. “That street crisis that we see in every part of our communities; homelessness, addiction, mental health crisis. They’re really on the front line,” Stiles remarked.

She specifically pointed to the demand for more affordable housing, “missing middle” housing options, and improved healthcare services to address these widespread challenges.

stories.title: Canada’s veterinarian shortage just forced a beloved St. John’s area animal hospital to close after nearly 40 years
stories.summary: Mount Pearl, N.L.- One of Newfoundland and Labrador’s longest-running vet clinics is set to shut its doors this week.
stories.author: Garrett Barry
stories.content:
Mount Pearl, N.L.- One of Newfoundland and Labrador’s longest-running vet clinics is set to shut its doors this week.

Sunrise Animal Hospital, based in Mount Pearl, has told clients it will close on Nov. 13, due to a shortage of qualified veterinarians who could keep services running.

Corporate owner VetStrategy said in a statement that the closure was temporary and the organization was “focused on putting the right resources in place to support a return.”

There’s no timeline for when the clinic May reopen, and the owners will face a highly competitive labour market as they try to lure new vets to the clinic. The industry is facing a nationwide shortage of trained veterinarians, according to the Canadian Veterinary Medical Association (Cvma).

Relying on analysis from Ottawa’s Canadian Occupational Projection System, the Cvma says Canada has faced a shortage of veterinarians since 2021. Updated statistics from the Canadian Occupational Projection System suggest there is a strong risk the shortage will continue until 2035.

“There’s also been a change in how the workforce works,” said Maggie Brown-Bury, a Newfoundland-based veterinarian who is set to become the next president of the Cvma.

“You’re no longer just a general small-animal vet who does everything. You May become an ophthalmologist or a radiologist or a surgeon… so now we need more veterinarians to do what veterinary medicine can do, than we needed 20 years ago.”

Closure evokes ‘an emotional reaction’

Though there are other clinics in the St. John’s area with capacity to take on clients left behind by the Sunrise Animal Hospital’s closure, Brown-Burry says shuttering a long-standing institution is resonating with pet owners.

“I think it’s more of an emotional reaction to a long-standing institution closing its doors,” she said “There’s a lot of pet owners in the St. John’s, Mount Pearl area that have been going there for years. So it’s kind of the end of an era.”

Brown-Burry said more rural and remote areas are struggling even harder — like the Newfoundland town of Marystown, which lost its vet and clinic last fall.

The community’s town council has been working to find a replacement.

“It created a big void since then,” councillor Gary Myles said. “People, nowadays, they take care of their animals, their pets are family. Not like family, they’re family.”

The clinic’s closure means pet owners are forced to drive along a rural highway to the town of Clarenville, about two hours away, for routine or emergency care.

“With an emergency, you could be headed down the highway at 8 o’clock at night,” Myles said.

The obstacles facing foreign vets

While internationally trained veterinarians can help fill the shortage in Canada, long waitlists for licensing exams have seriously slowed the flow of foreign vets into the country.

In a submission to a House of Commons committee in December 2025, Gillian Muir, the Dean of the Western College of Veterinary Medicine at the University of Saskatchewan, wrote that the university is keeping a waitlist of between eight months to a year for international graduates wanting to write the test.

She recommended the federal government take steps to establish a specialized testing centre at the University of Saskatchewan that could triple the number of tests offered each year.

Brown-Burry says the Cvma is building resources to support new veterinary graduates inside of Canada with the business side of their future practice.

“Like how to communicate with people, how to deal with difficult conversations, how to deal with the conversations around money, because we don’t learn that in veterinary school — but if you go into clinical practice, that is going to be a conversation you end up having to have,” she said.

“There’s only so much we can do with bringing in new, we also have to look at retention.”

stories.title: Hundreds of students using Fanshawe’s renewed breakfast program
stories.summary: Fanshawe Student Union saw hundreds at their biweekly breakfast program. the FSU breakfast program was reintro...
stories.author: Samantha Luis
stories.content:
Fanshawe Student Union saw hundreds at their biweekly breakfast program. the FSU breakfast program was reintroduced at the start of the 2026 fall term. Students pay an ancillary fee and everything is divided into the services provided for students.

“Doing the breakfast program, before even setting up, students were already sitting and waiting for breakfast. It shows there is a real need for it,” said FSU President Shadé Dias. “It’s very important because there’s a lot of students on campus that don’t have a meal because they don’t have a job. Especially coming into winter, we find students that don’t have a lot of money as the start of term in September.”

She said roughly 750 breakfasts have been served since the program was reintroduced in September. Students from all demographics access the breakfast program, she said.

Students seemed to be enjoying the breakfast program Tuesday, walking away with apples and yogurts. They said they appreciated the convenient and free option, especially with costs of food being higher than normal.

“It’s important after a test,” said Alex Lam, who was among a group of students in the area. “We need nutrients to fuel our brains.”

Previously, the breakfast program ran once a month, but Dias increased the frequency to every other Tuesday to meet more demand.

Shadé Dias, FSU president (Credit: Torey Joseph Legarrie)

She said she would consider adding more days if needed. “If there is more demand, I’m sure the organization will look into possibly revamping the operations of it.”

“Having a breakfast program is just a great way of connecting with students and letting them know that we are here to support them in whatever way,” said Dias.

FSU does student satisfaction surveys to touch base with students and make sure needs are met, she said.

“One of the feedbacks from last year, was to improve our presence in different college areas. We’re moving it from Forwell hall, and we’re going to be in Innovation Village just to boost visibility and let students know that we’re here for them, listening to them, and supporting them as this is a major concern.”

Through Fanshawe, students can get discounts with their student ID at different grocery stores including; Food Basics, Metro, Real Canadian Superstore, and BulkBarn.

stories.title: N.S. group apologizes for inviting convicted killer to speak at panel
stories.summary: The Elizabeth Fry Society of Mainland Nova Scotia is now apologizing after an event included Marissa Shephard, who was convicted in the 2015 killing of a Moncton, N.B. teenager.
stories.author: Rebecca Lau, Reeti Rohilla
stories.content:
A Nova Scotia organization that supports women and girls who are involved with the justice system is facing backlash over who it invited to speak at a panel discussion on navigating the legal system.

The Elizabeth Fry Society of Mainland Nova Scotia is now apologizing after the event included Marissa Shephard , who was convicted in the 2015 killing of a Moncton, N.B. teenager.

The event at Dalhousie University last week was entitled “Navigating the Legal System & Community Supports After Violence, Victimization, and Loss” and was supported by a fund in partnership with the family of Logan Russell. On its website, the organization said Russell lost her life “in an act of horrifying violence perpetrated by her male partner.”

In a post on Facebook, Russell’s mother, Maureen MacTaggart, said she was “beyond disappointed and heartbroken that they would use Logan’s legacy in connection with someone like (Shephard).”

“We feel deceived by this decision and not being made aware of this ahead of time and given the choice to participate or not. Had we been made aware, it would have never been associated with Logan or our family,” she wrote.

Shephard received a 12-year sentence in 2021 after pleading guilty to manslaughter and arson in the death of 18-year-old Baylee Wylie.

Court documents say Wylie was tied to a chair, beaten, and stabbed about 200 times.

His body was found in Shephard’s burned-out Moncton townhouse in December 2015.

Shephard was one of three people sentenced in connection with Wylie’s killing. A 2024 Parole Board of Canada decision states Shephard wasn’t present for the fatal assault but helped start the fire.

The Parole Board required supervised housing on statutory release to manage Shephard’s risk to the community, citing poor institutional behaviour, including aggression, manipulation and intimidation in custody.

In its public statement, the Nova Scotia chapter of the Elizabeth Fry Society said it made a “serious mistake” in planning the event.

“We made a decision about panel participants without consulting Logan’s family, who had entrusted us with Logan’s memory,” the statement reads in part.

“An event meant to honour a loved one instead caused more pain, and re-opened grief for other families across the Maritimes who lost someone to violence,” the organization went on to say.

“Our work asks us to consider everyone who May be affected by violence, and above all, to do no further harm. With this event, our actions did not reflect that, and we have harmed those we support.”

The society declined Global News’ request for an interview, saying it is prioritizing staff safety because it has received threats of violence over the event.

In a message to Global News, Russell’s aunt, Darlene MacTaggart, said while she understands that the Elizabeth Fry Society’s focus is rehabilitation, having Shephard as a guest on the panel was a “poor decision.”

“It is our hope that going forward we can keep Logan and Baylee’s memories alive and continue to say their names. We will work hard to continue to support education on Intimate Partner Violence in Logan’s memory,” she wrote.

The family has also asked the society to stop using Logan’s name and image.

On its website, the organization said Russell lost her life “in an act of horrifying violence perpetrated by her male partner.”

content_blocks.text: In a post on Facebook, Russell’s mother, Maureen MacTaggart, said she was “beyond disappointed and heartbroken that they would use Logan’s legacy in connection with someone like (Shephard).”

“We feel deceived by this decision and not being made aware of this ahead of time and given the choice to participate or not. Had we been made aware, it would have never been associated with Logan or our family,” she wrote.
Pleaded guilty to manslaughter
Shephard received a 12-year sentence in 2021 after pleading guilty to manslaughter and arson in the death of 18-year-old Baylee Wylie.
content_blocks.html: Shephard received a 12-year sentence in 2021 after pleading guilty to manslaughter and arson in the death of 18-year-old Baylee Wylie.

content_blocks.text: Court documents say Wylie was tied to a chair, beaten, and stabbed about 200 times.
His body was found in Shephard’s burned-out Moncton townhouse in December 2015.
Shephard was one of three people sentenced in connection with Wylie’s killing. A 2024 Parole Board of Canada decision states Shephard wasn’t present for the fatal assault but helped start the fire.

The Parole Board required supervised housing on statutory release to manage Shephard’s risk to the community, citing poor institutional behaviour, including aggression, manipulation and intimidation in custody.
Society says it made a ‘serious mistake’
In its public statement, the Nova Scotia chapter of the Elizabeth Fry Society said it made a “serious mistake” in planning the event.
“We made a decision about panel participants without consulting Logan’s family, who had entrusted us with Logan’s memory,” the statement reads in part.
“An event meant to honour a loved one instead caused more pain, and re-opened grief for other families across the Maritimes who lost someone to violence,” the organization went on to say.
“Our work asks us to consider everyone who May be affected by violence, and above all, to do no further harm. With this event, our actions did not reflect that, and we have harmed those we support.”

content_blocks.text: The society declined Global News’ request for an interview, saying it is prioritizing staff safety because it has received threats of violence over the event.

In a message to Global News, Russell’s aunt, Darlene MacTaggart, said while she understands that the Elizabeth Fry Society’s focus is rehabilitation, having Shephard as a guest on the panel was a “poor decision.”

“It is our hope that going forward we can keep Logan and Baylee’s memories alive and continue to say their names. We will work hard to continue to support education on Intimate Partner Violence in Logan’s memory,” she wrote.
The family has also asked the society to stop using Logan’s name and image.

stories.title: As countries urge residents to prepare for emergencies, what should Canadians do?
stories.summary: Governments around the world are renewing calls for residents to prepare for at least 72 hours without essential services. A Canadian disaster recovery expert explains why the advice is not new, what risks households should consider and why Canadians should not panic.
stories.author: Archie Niari
stories.content:
As governments in several countries urge residents to prepare for emergencies by keeping at least three days’ worth of supplies at home, Canadian officials say the advice is nothing new, but experts warn households should take it seriously.

Recent preparedness campaigns in the United Kingdom , France and Japan have renewed attention on the importance of being self-sufficient during a crisis, including potential disruptions caused by extreme weather, cyberattacks and other emergencies.

🚨KIT D’urgence 72H: ÊTES-Vous PRÊTS? 🎒Préparez un sac contenant l’essentiel pour faire face à une situation d’urgence pendant 72 heures: - Eau potable et nourriture non périssable, - Lampe de poche et radio à piles, - Trousse de premiers secours et médicaments, - Vêtements… pic.twitter.com/feouRKffKX — Préfet de Normandie et de la Seine-Maritime (@Prefet76) October 27, 2026

Public Safety Canada continues to advise Canadians to be prepared to go at least 72 hours without essential services such as running water and electricity.

However, Suzanne Bernier, an instructor with the Disaster Recovery Institute of Canada, told CTV Your Morning on Nov. 4 that the message has been around for decades.

The 72-hour rule is nothing new

Bernier said the recommendation for households to be prepared to manage independently for three days is a longstanding guidance in Canada and elsewhere.

“That message ... that we’re hearing all over around the world, and in Canada, is nothing new. It’s the exact same messaging that we’d given out ... 30 years ago,” she said.

She added that emergency preparedness has traditionally included having an emergency kit ready to go in case residents are suddenly forced to evacuate.

Cyberattacks among growing concerns

While severe weather and natural disasters remain important considerations, Bernier said cybersecurity threats are increasingly part of the emergency preparedness conversation.

“We know that at any given time, at some point soon in the future, each and every one of us will have been impacted, either directly or indirectly, by one of those potential cybersecurity attacks,” she said.

Bernier added Canada is making progress in understanding the risks associated with cybersecurity, alongside other potential threats.

Canadians should not panic

Bernier said the renewed attention on emergency preparedness should not be a reason for people to become alarmed.

Instead, she said, it is an opportunity to revisit whether households are adequately prepared to manage if emergency services cannot reach them immediately.

“And another reason why this message is going out reminding people about having 72-hour kids prepared, is that we haven’t really moved the bar that much ahead over the past 30 years,” she said.

Her advice to Canadians hearing the renewed warnings is straightforward: “Not to be upset about it, or to be nervous about it, and just to remember, it’s something that we try to remind people regularly.”

stories.title: Charity that builds housing for homeless veterans struggles to find land for Toronto location
stories.summary: Veterans are more than four times as likely to experience homelessness than other Canadians, according to federal data
stories.author: Jameson Berkow
stories.content:
Hundreds of homeless veterans in Toronto will be spending Remembrance Day on the streets while a charity devoted to housing them struggles to find land.

Veterans’ House Canada opened its first location on the site of Ottawa’s former Canadian Forces Base Rockcliffe in 2021. Alan Mulawyshyn, the charity’s executive director and a former brigadier-general in the Canadian Armed Forces, said Toronto was the obvious place to go for a second location in 2022. It’s estimated there are approximately 500 homeless vets in the city, which also has the country’s largest unhoused population.

“We’ve talked to the city, talked to the province, talked to the feds, talked to private developers, talked to Legions, trying to figure out if we can just get that place to plant a flag. But nothing has come up. Nobody has come up with anything,” Mr. Mulawyshyn said in an interview.

“Everyone is supportive of the idea, they’ve been quite supportive, but at the end of the day we haven’t been able to get that land secured.”

While the Toronto plan has spent years in limbo, Veterans’ House has managed to secure land in Edmonton and build a $16-million location in the Alberta capital over a period of about 18 months. It opened its doors on Monday. The facility, essentially a copy of the Ottawa location, consists of 40 studio apartments with amenities that include a community garden, a dog park, a gym and a library.

Veterans’ House was incorporated in 2020 and is geared toward long-term solutions. It also offers residents addiction and mental health therapy, as well as on-site employment programs.

“We are negotiating with the City of Halifax for an acre of land in downtown Halifax right now, so Halifax May get ahead of Toronto as well,” Mr. Mulawyshyn said.

Toronto city councillor Josh Matlow is among those trying to help Veterans’ House find a home in Canada’s largest city. In late 2025, he advanced a motion that was unanimously approved by council, directing the deputy city manager to help identify a site for homeless veteran housing. It specifically requested direct consultation with Veterans’ House.

In an e-mailed response to a request for an update on the search process, Toronto housing secretariat executive director Doug Rollins said an “initial review” of potential properties has been completed and that “work on site selection is ongoing.”

Mr. Matlow said the inability to secure a Toronto Veterans’ House is not due to lack of effort.

“The challenge is very simple,” he said in an interview. “The city has just not been able to identify a site that will work that the city owns.”

“Right now, either city sites are in use for one reason or another. Or those that have been declared surplus over the past several years have been part of the city’s initiative to redevelop those sites for affordable housing, so there just aren’t a lot of city sites just kind of sitting around,” he said. “And there haven’t been many new ones declared surplus to open it up for a project like a Veterans’ House. That has been our biggest challenge.”

Privately owned sites are another option being considered, Mr. Matlow said. Despite the fact that the housing market downturn has left numerous private developments stalled or outright cancelled, he said the sheer cost of land in Toronto is adding to the difficulty.

“The property value in Toronto, compared to most other jurisdictions, is enormously high,” Mr. Matlow said. “To pull off a project of any magnitude costs just so much more than it would in other, say, mid-sized Canadian cities.”

Karen Chapple, director of the University of Toronto’s school of cities and a professor of geography and planning, said the market downturn will actually make it more difficult for a charity like Veterans’ House to find a private developer willing to part with a precious parcel of land.

“Developers tend to prefer to hold on to whatever they can get,” Prof. Chapple said in an interview. “In fact, developers, right now, while there is no work in actually building stuff, a lot of developers are working right now to acquire even more land because it is relatively cheap right now.”

“Developers, they will hold land for decades. They’ve already been holding land for decades,” she said.

Veterans’ House does not have decades to wait. Although veterans make up only about 1 per cent of the Canadian population, they represent approximately 4.4 per cent of the country’s homeless population, according to data the charity compiled from federal government sources. In simple terms, that means veterans are more than four times as likely to experience homelessness than other Canadians.

That equates to between 3,000 and 5,000 homeless veterans across Canada, Mr. Mulawyshyn said. It also takes years for Veterans’ House to raise enough money for construction, he said, which cannot begin in earnest until a site is found.

“Before you can really get a project going, apply for funding and have a fundraising campaign, you need a place to put the coming soon sign,” Mr. Mulawyshyn said.

Mr. Matlow said despite the apparent impasse, he remains committed to finding a Toronto Veterans’ House location.

“There are some really good people who work for the city who are actively working on this. It has been challenging, but we are not done. I’m still hopeful that by the next Remembrance Day, we can have something really exciting to announce.”

stories.title: Two weeks before opening, London’s Home for Homeless Veterans receives $1M pledge
stories.summary: In two weeks, London’s new Homes for Heroes Veterans Village will welcome its first residents to a new facility near Parkwood Hospital.
stories.author: Sean Irvine
stories.content:
In two weeks, London’s new Homes for Heroes Veterans Village will welcome its first residents to a new facility near Parkwood Hospital.

The village will offer support and care to 25 at-risk veterans and those transitioning from homelessness.

Pat O’Hagan, one of the village’s earliest backers, can’t believe the day he waited for is almost here.

“Recently I stood in the parking lot and cried my eyes out, I actually broke down.”

Built for $6 million, the village will require additional funds to operate support programs.

On Tuesday, just before Remembrance Day, the Wsib stepped up.

“I am pleased to announce the Wsib is investing $1 million in the Homes for Heroes Foundation to support the Veterans Village right here in London, Ontario,” said Jeff Lang, president and CEO.

Community support has gone a long way towards creating the village. A $4 million anonymous donation was made earlier this year.

But it’s the collective backing of Londoners that truly impresses Brad Field, the president and CEO of HFH.

“It is an investment that is a gamechanger,” he told those gathered at the village. “And it will help our men and women that have served this country move forward in their journey and reintegration towards civilian life.”

Training for onsite staff begins next week.

“It warms my heart, and it will warm my heart when the official ribbon cutting takes place. It will warm my heart when these homes are occupied by veterans that deserve the care that Canada and Homes for Heroes will deliver,” said HFH committee member and Retired Lieutenant General Peter Devilin.

The pledge to care brought O’Hagan to tears.

“It’s happening; it’s incredible, Sean; I can’t believe it!”

stories.title: Canadian businesses have ‘cushion’ to absorb costs, limit inflation: report
stories.summary: The report suggests many wholesale and retailers have created a "cushion" with profit margins allowing them to absorb more cost before passing it to consumers.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
Canadian businesses’ profits likely give them a “cushion” to absorb more inflation cost increases without passing those hikes onto consumers, a new Cibc report suggests.

The Cibc Capital Markets report notes the Bank of Canada recently reported inflation could stay above three per cent in 2027, leading companies to push costs onto consumers. But the report says doing that for a longer period of time could prove challenging.

“In the kind of economy we have now, which is soft, labour incomes not growing quickly, and profit margins pretty wide by historic standards, we’ll probably see more of those cost increases absorbed by businesses and less of an inflation threat for prices other than energy,” said Avery Shenfeld, one of the report’s co-authors and Cibc chief economist.

Canada’s inflation rate was last measured at 3.1 per cent in September.

The report says many wholesale and retail companies’ operating profit margins are higher than in the past.

Retail profit margins are above the average they were a decade ago, the report shows.

Wholesale trade price index is at about 7.3 per cent year over year and consumer goods entering from abroad sit at about 8.9 per cent.

Shenfeld told Global News that the state of the economy is different from three to five years ago, such as when Russia invaded Ukraine resulting in a big spike in oil and grain prices. But with a lower unemployment rate in 2022 at 5.5 per cent and wage increases, more customers were willing to pay those increased costs.

“There was a lot of spending power in the economy that had actually already escalated inflation,” he said. “If you go back to some prior episodes where the economy was softer and there were more unemployed people and wages were not growing in pace with prices, price increases didn’t stick as easily.”

The economy in 2011 was more similar to where Canada currently sits, the report says, citing supply disruptions from the Arab Spring. Unemployment at the time sat between seven and 7.6 per cent.

Unemployment was at about 6.7 per cent in October 2026.

Shenfeld said while businesses will often try to pass on cost increases to avoid changing their own margins, now isn’t the right time.

“I wouldn’t be surprsied to see some price increases coming, but whether they’re successful in retaining enough customers to sustain those prices, that’s really the question mark,” Shenfeld said. “Businesses will really have to see how consumers react and whether they have the buying power to pay more, not only for gasoline, but everything else they’re shopping for.”

Two weeks ago, the Bank of Canada hiked interest rates by 0.2 per cent to 2.5 per cent, the first change in a year and first increase in three years.

Governor Tiff Macklem cited the need to get inflation down and prevent higher energy prices, spurred by the Iran war and other geopolitical conflicts, from spreading to other goods and services.

He told MPs during a parliamentary committee meeting last week that businesses have “mostly absorbed” higher input costs so far, but past experience and Bank surveys suggest those costs will pass through to consumers next year.

That is possible, Shenfeld said, but it depends if inflation continues to rise. The report suggests a slacking labour market and moderate income growth will lead to inflation remaining weaker than the Bank of Canada expects.

“The Bank of Canada’s 3% core inflation forecast is driven off a very sizeable acceleration in core goods prices, one that would be more akin to what we would expect in a hotter economy than what we are facing right now,” the report says.

Should there be a resolution in the Middle East and oil prices continue to drop, inflation likely won’t take off to the level the Bank suggests. But Shenfeld cautions, if energy prices do rise, there will be more of an “inflation problem” and more rate hikes could occur.

stories.title: Carney to raise foreign interference concerns with Xi in meeting
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney and President Xi Jinping are expected to meet in person at the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China.
stories.author: Anja Karadeglija
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney said he will raise concerns about foreign interference in Canada when he meets next week with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Carney and Xi are expected to meet in person at the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China.

“The advantage of these meetings is you can raise issues directly and frankly,” Carney told a press conference in Montreal on Tuesday.

Carney said he would be raising the importance Canada attaches “to the non-interference in our affairs by China and other countries.”

The prime minister said he also will discuss with Xi the global security climate and the economic partnership between the two countries. He said that partnership “is something that is deepening but has clear guardrails in terms of the areas in which we’re involved.”

Carney last met with Xi in January. The two leaders also spoke at last year’s Apec summit — the first formal meeting between the leaders of Canada and China since 2017.

Carney has been rebuilding Canada’s relationship with China, including increasing trade between the two nations.

Carney said at the time he and Xi discussed foreign interference but Beijing didn’t understand how seriously Canadians take the issue.

In January 2025, a public inquiry identified China as the top perpetrator of foreign interference targeting Canadian democratic institutions, and concluded Beijing tried to meddle in some Canadian elections.

A recent report by the organization Safeguard Defenders said China has expanded illegal police stations it operates around the world, including in Canada. The Spain-based non-governmental organization said the stations are used by China to monitor the diaspora in a bid to control them.

Carney also told reporters in Montreal that his government has chosen a new ambassador to China and will announce the appointment soon. The post has been vacant since this spring.

“It’s a little longer than we would have liked. We wanted to get the right person and we have found that right person,” he told the press conference.

U.S. President Donald Trump will also be at the summit. Carney said he and Trump are expected to have a conversation at Apec or at the Asean summit in the Philippines, which takes place a few days earlier.

“I have an ability to engage with the president in multiple occasions and on a running basis, so yes, it’s good to sit down but it’s not absolutely necessary,” Carney said.

The Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit will take place in the Philippines from Nov. 16 to 18, and the Apec summit will bring leaders from across Asia, South America and the South Pacific together in Shenzhen, China from Nov. 18 to 19.

stories.title: This Remembrance Day, learn the history of Canada’s rarest military medals
stories.summary: The awards recognize important events in the country’s history and outstanding acts of bravery
stories.author: Sarah Wallace
stories.content:
The history of Canada’s military medals is as storied as the country itself. Thousands of medals have been awarded for both military members and civilians since the country’s inception, and continue to be handed out today.

“The orders, decorations and medals that are awarded to Canadian military personnel are just one of the ways in which we honour the service and sacrifice of those who protect our country both at home and abroad,” said Caitlin Pilkington, a collection specialist for medals, ceremonial and photos at the Canadian War Museum.

“They can recognize outstanding achievements, acts of bravery and courage or service in a particular conflict or operation, but they can also commemorate important events in Canadian history or acknowledge long service and devotion to duty.”

This Remembrance Day , we’re showcasing some of the rare medals service members and civilians can earn, and what they represent.

The Victoria Cross, or VC, is the highest military award in the Canadian honour system. It’s awarded to a service member who commits a daring act of bravery in the presence of the enemy, and is the rarest medal to be awarded.

The VC has two iterations: the British version, established in 1856 near the end of the Crimean War and eliminated in 1972, and the Canadian version, which was established in 1993.

The Canadian honour system was completely overhauled by the federal government in 1972 to make the military awards independent from the British, Ms. Pilkington said.

The thought process at the time was that awards that were being given to Canadians should be distinctly Canadian, she said.

Ms. Pilkington added that the nomination process for the VC takes 12 to 18 months.

Ninety-nine service members received the British VC for conflicts from the Crimean War through to the Second World War. The Canadian version has never been awarded.

In May, parliamentary secretary to the minister of national defence Sherry Romanado said that the federal government would establish a review board to re-evaluate cases of Afghanistan war veterans who May have met the VC award criteria. The announcement comes after years of pressure from veterans and members of parliament to review dozens of veterans’ cases.

The Cross of Valour, or CV, is the second-rarest military honour awarded. It’s also the highest civilian honour that can be bestowed.

The CV is awarded for a conspicuous act of bravery in circumstances of extreme peril, but off the battlefield.

“For some of the medals that are still awarded or that are currently awarded, there is a distinction made between actions that are done in the presence of the enemy and actions that are done away from the front lines,” Pilkington said.

It’s been awarded 21 times since the medal was established with the Canadian honour system overhaul in 1972.

The CV can be awarded to Canadian citizens and non-citizens, and anyone can be nominated on the Governor-General’s website . A nomination must occur within two years of the act of bravery, and is reviewed by the Canadian Decorations Advisory Committee.

The Meritorious Service Cross, or MSC, like the Cross of Valour, can be awarded to both military members and civilians. It is awarded for high standards of performance that considerably benefit the Canadian Forces.

“For a lot of these medals, the criteria is left quite broad, so that there’s opportunity for more people to be eligible for them,” Ms. Pilkington said.

The military version of the MSC was created in 1984, and the civilian version in 1991 . Astronaut Chris Hadfield became the first Canadian to hold both the civilian and military versions of the medal in 2013, for “his extraordinary achievements and the record number of experiments conducted” on the International Space Station.

The Sacrifice Medal, or SM, is one of the newest medals awarded to Canadian military members, and was established in 2008. It’s given to military members who suffered wounds or death in hostile actions starting on Oct. 7, 2001, after Canada entered Afghanistan.

The SM replaces the wound stripe, which would be worn on the uniform to signify that military member had been wounded in action, Ms. Pilkington said.

A SM can also be awarded to members of the forces who took their own lives from mental-health disorders caused from their service.

A 2017 Globe and Mail investigation found that more than 70 Canadian soldiers and veterans who served in the Afghanistan operation later took their own lives.

A General Campaign Star, or GCS, is a medal issued for service in a specific campaign, and was first established in 2004. It can be awarded to those on the front lines and in support roles in the presence of the enemy.

There are two types of GCS: Allied Forces and Expedition . Allied Forces is awarded to fighter pilots or crew members in “Operation Allied Force” – an aerial bombing campaign in Kosovo – in 1999, Ms. Pilkington said.

Missions can have multiple campaigns where a GCS can be awarded – the Second World War had nine different campaign stars based on where the solider was stationed, Ms. Pilkington said.

The Canadian Forces’ Decoration, or CD, is a service medal for the Canadian Forces . Members receive the medal after 12 years of service, and an added gold bar to the ribbon of the medal for every additional 10 years of qualifying service.

The CD was created by King George VI in the aftermath of the Second World War. The effigy of the monarch on the medal has changed three times with each ascension to the throne: King George VI, Queen Elizabeth II and now King Charles III.

'A kid beating up cadets that are trying to serve our country? It is the most disgusting thing you could ever do,' Ford said

Ontario’s Premier Doug Ford speaking at the Empire Club in Toronto. This week, he said the male youths who allegedly attacked air cadets selling poppies in Hamilton should get an "ass-whooping" from their parents. (Peter J Thompson/National Post)

November 10, 2026 at 4:05 p.m.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford says the vicious assault on a Hamilton air cadet commander last week was “absolutely disgusting.”

He says two male youths who allegedly blew an air horn in the faces of the cadets selling poppies, an incident that then led to the assault on Capt. Ken Kunkel, should be harshly disciplined.

He asked where their parents were and said they “should be ashamed that they’ve raised their kids to beat up cadets.”

Ford made the comments when asked about the incident at a press conference in Peterborough, Ont., reports Global News.

He added that the parents “should give your kids a little ass-whooping in the woodshed as far as I’m concerned,” according to Toronto Life magazine.

Kunkel was supporting two air cadets selling poppies in advance of Remembrance Day. After the suspects blew the air horn into the cadets’ ears, Kunkel followed the boys into a nearby restaurant to speak with them.

The 59-year-old Kunkel was then physically attacked by one of the boys, as well as an adult woman not related to the initial incident.

“She proceeded to assault the victim, causing him to fall to the ground. One of the male youths then struck the victim several times before leaving the restaurant,” said Hamilton Police in a statement.

The assault caused “life-altering injuries,” said police, and required emergency spinal surgery, National Post previously reported.

Kunkel is “strong willed and determined to walk,” Selina Peters, the organizer of a GoFundMe page for Kunkel and his family, told National Post last Friday.

As of Monday afternoon the page has received almost $283,000 in donations, surpassing its goal of $250,000.

Stewart Lewis is a writer and editor with National Post. A journalist and lawyer, he has worked in newspapers, radio and TV, and served a legal stint with Global Affairs Canada at the United Nations in New York City.

stories.title: Ottawa restores sanctions on Iran it lifted a decade ago
stories.summary: Canada will impose sanctions on 11 Iranian entities accused of contributing to Tehran’s pursuit of nuclear and ballistic missiles or of financing violence abroad.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — Canada will impose sanctions on 11 Iranian entities accused of contributing to Tehran’s pursuit of nuclear and ballistic missiles or of financing violence abroad.

The sanctions prohibit Canadians from engaging financially with the named Iranian organizations.

The organizations include banks, insurance providers and a tanker company.

The federal government cut ties with Iran in 2012 over its nuclear program, its human rights violations and its position on the Syrian civil war.

Canada closed its embassy in Iran, expelled Iranian diplomats and labelled the country a state sponsor of terrorism when it severed the relationship.

Ottawa relaxed economic sanctions on Iran in 2016 after reporting that Iran had showed progress on maintaining a peaceful nuclear program.

Iran is not allowed to develop or acquire nuclear weapons under the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons.

Global Affairs Canada says the announced sanctions align with G7 nations’ efforts to get Iran to co-operate with the International Atomic Energy Agency.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 10, 2026.

Alyssa Wheeler, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Bank of Canada staying cautious but considering more rate hikes: summary
stories.summary: The Bank of Canada’s governing council thinks it might need to raise interest rates further but it's proceeding carefully, according to a summary from its last meeting.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
The Bank of Canada ’s governing council thinks it might need to raise interest rates further but it’s proceeding carefully, according to a summary of deliberations of its recent decision to raise its key policy rate for the first time since 2023.

According to the report released Tuesday, the council acknowledged it faced considerable uncertainty and said it would take its monetary policy decisions one meeting at a time.

“Members underlined that their outlook was still subject to considerable uncertainty about the war in the Middle East, Canada‑U.S. trade relations, global financial conditions, the speed and extent of pass‑through and how businesses and households would react to these developments,” the summary said of the governing council.

“They agreed they would need to continue to take these sources of uncertainty into account when setting monetary policy.”

The Bank of Canada raised its policy interest rate by a quarter of a percentage point to 2.5 per cent last month to reduce the risk that stubbornly high oil prices become persistent inflation.

The central bank has said since the war in the Middle East began that it would “look through” the direct and immediate impact on inflation, but it would not let higher energy prices turn into broad-based and persistent inflation.

“With the war in its eighth month and no resolution on the horizon, members exchanged views on whether a higher policy interest rate was needed to mitigate the risk that higher energy costs would spread to other goods and services,” the summary of deliberations said.

The report said the council members agreed that monetary policy cannot lower global energy prices, but can prevent them from leading to generalized inflation.

The decision came as the Bank of Canada raised its outlook for the annual inflation rate to hit 3.5 per cent at the end of this year and remain above three per cent for much of 2027.

The summary of deliberations said higher costs largely haven’t been passed through to consumers so far, but the bank’s surveys suggest businesses expect to raise some prices over the next year.

The Bank of Canada’s next scheduled interest rate decision is set for Dec. 9.

stories.title: Ottawa to reimpose sanctions on Iran after lifting them a decade prior
stories.summary: Canada relaxed economic sanctions in 2016 after reporting that Tehran had showed progress on maintaining a peaceful nuclear program
stories.author: Alyssa Wheeler
stories.content:
Canada will impose sanctions on 11 Iranian entities accused of contributing to Tehran’s pursuit of nuclear and ballistic missiles or of financing violence abroad.

The sanctions prohibit Canadians from engaging financially with the named Iranian organizations.

The organizations include banks, insurance providers and a tanker company.

The federal government cut ties with Iran in 2012 over its nuclear program, its human rights violations and its position on the Syrian civil war.

Canada closed its embassy in Iran, expelled Iranian diplomats and labelled the country a state sponsor of terrorism when it severed the relationship.

Ottawa relaxed economic sanctions on Iran in 2016 after reporting that Iran had showed progress on maintaining a peaceful nuclear program.

Iran is not allowed to develop or acquire nuclear weapons under the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons.

Global Affairs Canada says the announced sanctions align with G7 nations’ efforts to get Iran to co-operate with the International Atomic Energy Agency.

stories.title: Ottawa releases list of companies lending staff to major projects office
stories.summary: The federal government has released a list of the private sector companies lending staff to the major projects office after initially refusing to do so.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — The federal government has released a list of the private sector companies lending staff to the major projects office after initially refusing to do so.

Conservative and Bloc Québécois MPs have for months pressed Ottawa to reveal the list, citing concerns about conflicts of interest.

A copy of the list obtained by The Canadian Press, first reported on by The Toronto Star, shows nine employees from the Bank of Montreal, two from RBC and one from Scotiabank.

The list also includes four staffers from the Government of Yukon and one each from the governments of British Columbia and the Northwest Territories.

Major projects office officials have insisted their employees are not in conflicts and that they’ve been cleared by human resources in the Privy Council Office.

Federal Energy Minister Tim Hodgson dismissed calls for the list last week and accused opposition MPs of peddling “conspiracy theories.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 10, 2026.

Nick Murray, The Canadian Press
