stories.title: Deadline to make a claim in a Cibc class action settlement is days away
stories.summary: Time is running out for those who qualify to submit a claim for compensation from an $11 million Cibc class-action settlement involving mutual fund commissions.
stories.author: Ariel Rabinovitch
stories.content:
Time is running out for those who qualify to submit a claim for compensation from an $11 million Cibc class-action settlement involving mutual fund commissions paid to discount brokers.

Eligible claims need to be submitted by Nov. 18, 2026 to qualify for compensation.

With about one week left to file a claim, here’s everything to know.

The lawsuit alleged Cibc and Renaissance mutual funds paid trailing commissions to discount brokers that were “excessive, inflated and/or unearned,” as these brokers generally do not provide personalized investment advice – the service those fees are typically intended to compensate.

Cibc and its affiliates denied wrongdoing, and a settlement agreement is not necessarily an admission otherwise. Usually, a settlement agreement happens when legal parties negotiate satisfactory terms that avoids the need to fight the lawsuit in court.

Examples of discount brokers, according to the settlement website, are BMO InvestorLine, Cibc Investor’s Edge, National Bank Direct Brokerage, RBC Direct Investing, Scotia iTRADE, TD Direct Investing, CI Direct Trading, Qtrade, Desjardins Online Brokerage, Hsbc InvestDirect, Laurentian Bank Discount Brokerage, Wealthsimple, Questrade, and Interactive Brokers. They May have had different names in the past.

Cibc and its asset management arm was allegedly using money from mutual fund assets to pay these trailing commissions to discount brokers.

This would be a normal practice provided the brokers were giving clients a service of personalized and sometimes ongoing investment advice and services, but the settlement documents say these brokers typically provide “order-execution only services.”

A similar class-action settlement involving trailing commissions involved TD last year.

Investors who qualify for a payout generally would have held, or are still holding eligible mutual funds outside of discount brokerage accounts, such as through bank branches or full-service advisors, starting up to or before Sept. 5, 2025.

Those who currently hold mutual funds through Cibc and current or former Renaissance fund holders will be compensated automatically without needing to file a claim and will see the funds deposited through their respective mutual funds or other related funds.

However, former Cibc mutual fund holders who no longer have those investment products with the firm have until Nov. 18, 2026 to file a claim for compensation. Those eligible claims will be paid by cheque or e-transfer where applicable.

Although the settlement about is $11 million, the amount that winds up being distributed among eligible claimants is determined after related legal fees, administrative expenses and other costs are deducted.

It also isn’t clear how much eligible claims could be worth because the number of potential claimants who qualify have not been disclosed.

However, the settlement’s plan of allocation document suggests each eligible claim could potentially be entitled to compensation of about $32.

“If the Net Former Holder Cibc Fund is sufficient to make payment of $32.00 to each eligible Claimant, the Administrator shall issue payment of $32.00 by e-transfer or cheque to each eligible Claimant,” the document says.

Eligible claims May wind up being less than $32 if there isn’t enough money to pay every claim.

“If the Net Former Cibc Holder Fund is insufficient to make payment of $32.00 to each eligible Claimant, the Administrator shall calculate each Former Cibc Holder’s payment by pro rating the Net Former Cibc Holder Fund between each eligible Claimant, and the Administrator shall send each Claimant an e-transfer or cheque of this pro rated amount.”

Those investors who think they May be entitled to compensation can file a claim online before the deadline.

stories.title: Fact File: Military chaplains can't lead prayers on Remembrance Day; no blanket ban
stories.summary: Recent social media posts claim Canadian Armed Forces chaplains have been banned from saying prayers on Remembrance Day, or that prayers and references to God are banned among members. A policy directive issued by the military in July does instruct military chaplains not to say prayers during official ceremonies or events, including Remembrance Day. Instead…
stories.author: Marissa Birnie The Canadian Press
stories.content: Recent social media posts claim Canadian Armed Forces chaplains have been banned from saying prayers on Remembrance Day, or that prayers and references to God are banned among members. A policy directive issued by the military in July does instruct military chaplains not to say prayers during official ceremonies or events, including Remembrance Day. Instead they are told to offer “spiritual reflections” that use neutral language and do not refer to God. Chaplains May still pray and refer to God at funerals or faith-specific events, and the directive does not limit members’ personal religious beliefs.

stories.title: Son of Holocaust survivors, who feels failed by Canadian leaders, says allyship between Jews and non-Jews is the way forward
stories.summary: 'Today, when my community needs the federal government to stand firmly beside us, I do not feel it has met the moment,' says Rick Ekstein
stories.author: Courtney Greenberg
stories.content:
A Canadian businessman and the son of Holocaust survivors, who is building bridges between the Jewish community and non-Jewish allies, says he feels failed by the federal government.

“My grandparents saw the warning signs in Europe in 1933. They saw what happens when hatred is allowed to grow, when institutions fail to act, and when ordinary people look away. They saw. Then they were murdered,” said Rick Ekstein, speaking to a crowd in Brussels last week at the European Coalition for Israel.

He was there to introduce and sign the Brussels Declaration, a pact between Jews and Christians, inspired by his family history.

In a similar move this week, Italian Canadians pledged their support to combat hate and antisemitism, with dozens of business owners and community leaders saying they would stand with their Jewish friends and neighbours.

Standing together against antisemitism and hate matters now more than ever. Italian Canadian business and community leaders have come together to launch Italians Stand Against Antisemitism and Hate, an initiative demonstrating solidarity with Canada's Jewish community. These… pic.twitter.com/pMBzz3gP2X — UJA Federation of Greater Toronto (@UJAFederation) November 10, 2026

Ekstein told National Post it was important for him to go to Europe for the pledge because that is where his mother’s story began.

Equally important, he said, is rooting out antisemitism in Canada — a country where his family was able to rebuild after the Second World War.

“Today, when my community needs the federal government to stand firmly beside us, I do not feel it has met the moment,” he said.

He added that he doesn’t believe Prime Minister Mark Carney “fully appreciates either the danger or the depth of fear within our community.”

In September, the federal government released a progress report for its National Commitments to Combat Antisemitism. Although it was welcomed by many in the community, Jewish Canadians “should not have to keep asking for protection or reassurance that we still belong here,” said Ekstein.

Only a week before the report was released, a gunman opened fire at a synagogue in Belleville, Ont. in a hate-motivated, targeted attack. stories.title: Toronto airport gold heist fugitive arrested in Mexico resort hotspot
stories.summary: Prasath Paramalingam disappeared in 2024 after he was released on bail
stories.author: Adrian Humphreys
stories.content:
A fugitive wanted for the Toronto airport gold heist has been arrested in Mexico after fleeing Canada when released on bail. He was hiding out in “one of the most privileged locations” of the resort hotspot of Cancun.

Prasath Paramalingam, 37, of Brampton, Ont., was first arrested in Canada in 2024, ON the first anniversary of the spectacular heist in which a shipping crate of gold bullion and foreign cash worth more than $22.5 million was stolen from Air Canada’s cargo warehouse — but he disappeared after his release on bail.

An arrest warrant was issued against him in Canada, but he was also wanted in the United States, where he was accused in a plot to smuggle handguns into Canada.

Mexican authorities said Paramalingam entered Mexico illegally by land, travelling from San Diego into Tijuana, before relocating to the popular resort city of Cancun, where he was arrested in early October by agents of the Quintana Roo State Prosecutor’s Office at the request of U.S. authorities.

He was arrested on Huayacán Avenue, one of Cancun’s fast-growing areas filled with modern and gated homes. A real estate company describes it as “one of the most privileged locations in town.” The circumstances of his arrest are not yet known.

He was held in immigration detention in Mexico until he was turned over to U.S. Marshals.

Authorities say the Canadian gold heist and the U.S. gun plot are connected, with three Canadian men accused of participating in both.

An indictment against Paramalingam in the U.S. for gun-running was filed on April 10, 2024, naming him and Durante King-Mclean, who is also accused of being the get-away driver who made off with the gold crate on April 17, 2023.

U.S. prosecutors claim King-Mclean conspired with Paramalingam and others starting around the date of the gold heist to smuggle handguns from the U.S across the border into Canada.

When Peel Regional Police announced arrests in the gold heist, Paramalingam was among those arrested in Canada. He was charged with accessory after the fact for allegedly helping to arrange an out-of-the-way farm where the gold crate was opened and divided up.

Canadian officials linked the two cases directly, alleging that proceeds from the heist were used to fund the gun-running venture, leading to an official calling it “reverse alchemy” for turning gold into guns.

Paramalingam was released on bail but failed to appear in court in Brampton as ordered on Aug. 19, 2024. He is now considered a fugitive in Canada.

Although wanted in both Canada and the United States, Paramalingam was sent by Mexico to the United States; accompanied by U.S. Marshals, he landed in Houston, Texas, where he was formally arrested on Oct. 5.

He appeared in court in Houston later that day.

His appearance was brief. He was quickly ordered detained and sent to Pennsylvania, where his charges in the gun plot were filed.

He was brought to court again in Harrisburg, Penn., where he pleaded not guilty to two firearm trafficking charges on Oct. 28.

Paramalingam asked for assistance from a public defender after declaring he did not have the money to pay for a lawyer.

Prosecutors said Paramalingam should remain in custody until his trial because his charges are considered a crime of violence because they involved guns, that he poses a serious risk of fleeing, and faces a lengthy prison sentenced if convicted.

Court heard that he had significant family and other ties outside of the United States and few such ties in the country. He also has no legal status in the U.S. and would be subject to deportation after serving any sentence, if found guilty. Paramalingam was born in India but immigrated to Canada, where he became a Canadian citizen.

Paramalingam did not oppose his continued detention, and it was ordered by the judge. His lawyer in the U.S. did not respond to a request for comment.

A tentative jury trial date was scheduled for January.

Documents in Canada and the United States outline several links between the gold and gun plots.

After the gold heist, one of the admitted masterminds behind it, Arsalan Chaudhary, said he arranged for an Airbnb in Florida for King-Mclean to hide out in because he was under police scrutiny for the gold theft. The booking for the Airbnb safehouse in Fort Lauderdale expired in late August 2023.

On Sept. 2, 2023, King-Mclean was heading back to Canada in a rented Nissan Sentra when he was pulled over on Interstate 81 by Pennsylvania state troopers. He fled the car on foot but was caught after a brief chase. When troopers opened the Nissan’s trunk, they found 65 illegal handguns, each stuffed in a sock.

The U.S. indictment alleges that Paramalingam discussed King-Mclean’s illegal entry into the U.S. just five days after the heist using an encrypted messaging app called Threema, where he used the name “Stunner.” By August there were coded communications about buying guns, the indictment alleges. The two men shared photos of guns and bundles of cash.

Authorities said that after King-Mclean left the Airbnb he drove to a U-Haul storage facility in Atlanta and collected a backpack. After the traffic stop, about half of the handguns police seized were inside the backpack. Two of the guns had been converted to fire fully automatically and were classed as machine guns by authorities.

The indictment also accuses another Canadian gold heist suspect of helping in the plot, also after the fact. Archit Grover, authorities allege, alerted others to King-Mclean’s arrest, removing evidence from the Airbnb, and arranging to pay $1,000 to the car rental agency.

Grover is scheduled for a trial in Brampton next year. His lawyer said he intends to plead not guilty.

King-Mclean pleaded guilty in U.S. federal court to firearms trafficking charges and is serving more than 13 years in prison.

Adrian Humphreys, a founding journalist at National Post in 1998, is a senior national reporter focusing on crime, policing and justice stories, and investigative journalism. He is the author of three non-fiction bestsellers about organized crime, and runs a popular YouTube channel about global gangsters.

stories.title: Legion branch founded by Japanese Canadian veterans is reinstated after 84 years
stories.summary: Victoria - A descendant of a decorated soldier who fought at Vimy Ridge says the revival of a British Columbia Legion branch founded by Japanese Canadian veterans like his grandfather helps correct an injustice.
stories.author: Wolfgang Depner The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Victoria - Masumi Mitsui was a decorated veteran of Vimy Ridge, but he never took part in a public Remembrance Day ceremony, his grandson David Mitsui said.

The British Columbia Legion Branch that fellow Japanese Canadian veterans founded in 1926 had been disbanded during the Second World War, Masumi Mitsui and other members by then regarded not as heroes but as “enemy aliens.”

They could not stand alongside fellow Legion members as representatives of Branch No. 9.

“But on Remembrance Day, when I was growing up and we would visit him, he had on his uniform, he had on his Legion beret, and he had shined up his First World War medals, and he honoured his fallen comrades … in the privacy of his own home,” said David Mitsui.

This year’s Remembrance Day will be different — Legion Branch No. 9 is being represented for the first time in at least 84 years, and almost exactly a century after it was founded.

Like his late grandfather, David Mitsui serves as president of the branch following its recent restoration, which will be marked by a public ceremony in February.

Mitsui said the restoration corrects an injustice and will allow descendants of Japanese Canadian veterans to fully honour the sacrifices of their ancestors, standing with members of other Legion branches.

“It gives us great pride to be able to represent Legion No. 9 and all of the veterans in an official capacity,” he said.

Mitsui’s grandfather was among about 200 soldiers of Japanese descent who fought for Canada during the First World War. Fifty-four did not return, while 92 were wounded.

When these sacrifices were not immediately recognized after the war, the surviving veterans organized themselves by forming Branch No. 9, which was officially chartered in December 1926, Mitsui said.

Masumi Mitsui was part of a delegation that successfully lobbied provincial legislators to grant Japanese Canadian war veterans the right to vote in 1931.

But just over a decade later, Branch No. 9 surrendered its charter under duress after Japan’s attack on Pearl Harbor, while the Canadian government declared Japanese Canadians “enemy aliens” and placed them in internment camps.

David Mitsui said his grandfather did not resist the surrender of the charter because he did not want to embarrass the Legion.

When Manami Mitsui was taken to Vancouver’s Hastings Park as part of his family’s internment as Japanese Canadians, “he slammed his First World War medals on the table,” David Mitsui said.

“They flew off (the table) onto the floor, and he said ‘What good are these?’”

Mitsui said the Legion had promised to restore the charter after the end of the Second World War, but historian Debbie Jiang found newspaper clippings last year showing the promised reinstatement was denied in 1948.

Jiang said this was because the federal government had not yet lifted mobility restrictions on Japanese Canadians.

“The measures taken against these Canadian heroes of Vimy Ridge were undemocratic to say the least, treating them like criminals, taking away not only their life’s work, but their dignity and demeaning the service they gave to a country that did not even allow full citizenship rights,” she said.

Jiang got in touch with Legion leadership after making her discovery about the fate of Branch No. 9 last year. Mitsui said she championed the revival of the branch by researching its history, then getting descendants of the founders to submit an application for a charter.

Jiang says the restoration of the branch’s charter in July showed that it was never too late to right a wrong.

The branch has about 60 members, most of them descendants of veterans, and while it lacks physical premises due to a lack of funds, the first official meeting is scheduled for Dec. 2.

It will take place over Zoom, because members are spread across Canada, Jiang said.

While the branch is still sorting out its future, one of its goals is education, she said.

“Legion No. 9 exists now not only to tell history, but to motivate Canadians to learn its own untaught history by living it in the present, by joining as a member, and being part of the projects we have in plan,” she said.

David Mitsui will take part in Remembrance Day ceremonies on Wednesday with his daughter.

His grandfather May never have done so, but there was a moment of recognition for his service on Aug. 2, 1985.

Masumi Mitsui was invited to re-light the lantern on top of the cenotaph when the Japanese Canadian War Memorial in Vancouver was rededicated. It had been extinguished in 1942.

“He was in a wheelchair, but he stood proudly below the cenotaph,” David Mitsui recalled.

“He saluted and he said, ‘I have done my last duty for my comrades. They are gone, but not forgotten.’”

stories.title: No more amendments expected for police search powers bill, minister says, despite calls from watchdogs
stories.summary: 'The privacy of Canadians is a central concern,' said Intelligence Commissioner Simon Noel
stories.author: Christopher Nardi
stories.content:
Ottawa — Days after two government watchdogs recommended changes to the Liberals’ lawful access bill in the Senate, Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree said he did not anticipate any further amendments to the controversial legislation.

“I don’t, at this point, anticipate amendments to be coming through the Senate” on lawful access reform Bill C-22, Anandasangaree told National Post last week.

The minister said that he’d “look” at any amendments that May come out of the Senate’s review of C-22. But he asserted that amendments by MPs in the late spring meant the bill strikes the right balance between privacy rights and helping police and intelligence agencies do their work.

Days earlier, the federal privacy and intelligence commissioners argued the opposite, telling Senators that additional changes were necessary to better protect Canadians’ privacy rights while providing security and intelligence authorities with the necessary tools.

“The privacy of Canadians is a central concern,” said Intelligence Commissioner Simon Noel.

Lawful access is one of the most intrusive powers afforded to police and intelligence agencies. Creating such a regime for the digital age in Canada has been the subject of fierce debate for decades.

Bill C-22 proposes a new lawful access regime which would make it easier for police and intelligence agencies to intercept private communications or personal data as part of their investigations.

It has been applauded by police forces as a long-overdue fix to growing obstacles to investigations, but panned by civil liberties advocates as an attack on privacy and encryption.

The legislation proposes that police and the Canadian Security Intelligence Service (Csis) be able to approach telecommunications companies and ask them if, yes or no, an individual is a client before having to get a warrant for more information.

The bill then sets out a new path for authorities to obtain subscriber information from the companies such as a client’s name, address and the types of services provided with the appropriate warrant.

While he was encouraged by changes to the bill made by MPs in June, Privacy Commissioner Philippe Dufresne told the Senate committee that the new path for authorities to obtain subscriber information remains too broad.

One of his five recommendations was that the government limit the power to only target telecommunications providers or carve out medical and privileged information. Furthermore, authorities should only be allowed to obtain a “finite list of discrete identifiers”.

“Depending on the nature of the service providers in question, which include health-care providers, lawyers, financial institutions and dating apps, such information could reasonably attract a heightened expectation of privacy due to its sensitivity,” Dufresne said.

Bill C-22 also proposes new obligations to electronic service providers to organize and retain various types of client data for up to one year in a way that makes it obtainable by law enforcement or Csis with a warrant.

That means that if passed, the bill would compel electronic service providers to store and make information like device locations or cameras available to police or Csis with the requisite warrant. That could be used to track a person’s live location in case they pose a threat to national security or are considered to be in danger, the government has said.

It also allows the minister to issue a secret order compelling any electronic service provider to create such a capacity and retain users’ metadata for up to six months.

Critics, including tech companies such as Apple, Meta and Signal, have argued that the bill would compel them to create a new “backdoor” into their systems and undermine encryption. The minister has rejected those concerns and clarified in the bill that the government cannot mandate a solution that would lessen or crack encryption.

At the Senate, Dufresne and Noel recommended the government be forced to consider necessity and proportionality when making new lawful access regulations or orders under C-22.

Such a change would require the minister to justify his decision to issue a secret order and consider if it strikes the right balance between privacy rights and public safety needs.

“This requires that, whenever an order is issued or a regulation is adopted, an assessment must be carried out: is it absolutely essential or necessary?” Dufresne said.

Intelligence Commissioner Simon Noel seconded many of Dufresne’s suggestions. He also argued that there should be a higher bar for the public safety minister to make a secret order to a company required to set up intercept capacities for authorities.

“In principle, a decision-maker such as a minister must act publicly. Only in exceptional cases May they act confidentially,” said Noel.

Christopher Nardi is a senior parliamentary reporter with National Post in Ottawa. He has worked in both French and English media, speaks Italian and writes about politics, national security, justice and how things work (or don't) in government.

stories.title: Canada joins AI safety declaration but without ‘teeth,’ what can it do?
stories.summary: 'Go talk to the families in Tumbler Ridge' if you want to know how effective the AI industry’s voluntary standards are.
stories.author: Alex Boutilier
stories.content:
Canada has signed on to an international AI safety declaration committing companies and nations to greater information sharing and “early warning systems” to flag “serious cyber and AI control incidents.”

The France-led initiative drew initial endorsements from national governments — including Japan, Norway, the Netherlands and Bahrain — as well as major U.S.-based AI companies like Anthropic, OpenAI, Microsoft and Canada’s Cohere.

However, experts are skeptical that its voluntary nature and say without teeth, such agreements will not work.

Florian Martin-Bariteau, the director of the University of Ottawa’s Centre for Law, Technology and Society, said in an interview that while non-binding statements do send a signal about the Carney government’s approach to AI, they do not replace the need for serious regulation for the industry.

Martin-Bariteau said you can “go talk to the families in Tumbler Ridge” if you want to know how effective the AI industry’s voluntary standards are.

“It doesn’t work. The prime minister doesn’t seem to like actual regulators,” Martin-Bariteau said.

“I have nothing against anything in the statement, this is what we need … but if there is no teeth, if there are no people to do the follow-ups, the regulators, it will never work. Because it hasn’t worked before.”

The non-binding communiqué suggests agreement between governments and frontier AI companies in three general areas: a common risk management framework for the technology’s development, the principles of “responsibility and accountability” for all actors in the “AI ecosystem,” and increased information sharing to flag major threats.

On risk management, signatories said the would work to develop a public repository of non-sensitive information about AI risk assessments, with a standardized format to compare different models — something that would cut through the cryptic warnings AI companies often issue about the danger posed by their own models.

“Frontier models transcend national borders in their development, deployment and impact, and their opportunities and risks are therefore inherently global,” the statement, released by the Prime Minister’s Office on Monday, read.

“We all have a role in protecting our societies while enabling research, innovation and the wider use of AI.”

The declaration also stresses the need for governments to develop legal frameworks that give AI companies “certainty” about their development — as well as protect citizens “in case of large-scale damages.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney and his government have repeatedly touted the potential for AI to drive economic growth and innovation, launching the national “AI for All” strategy in June.

After well-publicized opposition to the construction of AI data centres in Canada and the United States, AI Minister Evan Solomon announced an agreement — again, a completely voluntary one — with leading AI companies to limit the environmental and noise pollution from new data centres, and to work with communities over concerns about the facilities’ water and electricity needs.

Ahead of last week’s federal budget, Carney announced that the federal government would make a $1.6 billion investment in Canadian AI company Cohere.

“We are not waiting for the future of AI to be decided somewhere else by those we don’t know or by whom we don’t trust. We’re building it right here in the right way,” Carney told reporters last month.

The France-led initiative drew initial endorsements from national governments — including Japan, Norway, the Netherlands and Bahrain — as well as major U.S.-based AI companies like Anthropic, OpenAI, Microsoft and Canada’s Cohere.

stories.title: Why winning all three federal byelections in Quebec could be an ‘uphill battle’ for the Liberals
stories.summary: Liberals have high hopes for these three byelections, judging by their prior electoral successes in Terrebonne and Chicoutimi—Le Fjord earlier this year.
stories.author: Catherine Lévesque
stories.content:
Welcome to our new, improved site!

Read a note from our editor-in-chief

Liberals have high hopes for these three byelections, judging by their prior electoral successes in Terrebonne and Chicoutimi—Le Fjord earlier this year.

Prime Minister Mark Carney and Guy Cormier, the Liberal candidate in Laurier-Sainte-Marie, prepare to pull a short espresso as they visit Cafe Club in Montreal, ON Tuesday, November 10, 2026. (Allen McInnis / Montreal Gazette)

November 10, 2026 at 2:46 p.m.

Ottawa — Prime Minister Mark Carney was in campaign mode in Quebec on Tuesday before he jets off for a whirlwind trip to Europe and Asia in the coming days.

After making an announcement on culture in Montreal, he put his Liberal leader cap on to make three pit stops in Laurier—Ste-Marie, Rosemont—La Petite-Patrie and Saint-Hyacinthe—Bagot—Acton ahead of the federal byelections that will be held on Dec. 7.

“We really hope to go three-for-three in Quebec,” one Liberal organizer confided.

Bloc Québécois Leader Yves-François Blanchet has said his party is competitive in all three ridings, while the NDP is prepared to put up a fight in Montreal especially.

Jonathan Kalles, a former Quebec adviser to prime minister Justin Trudeau, said while it is possible for the Liberals to sweep the board in Quebec, he thinks it will be an “uphill battle” to win in Rosemont—La Petite-Patrie and Saint-Hyacinthe—Bagot—Acton.

Liberals are fairly confident they will be able to hold on to the downtown Montreal riding of Laurier—Ste-Marie thanks to Guy Cormier, the former president and CEO of Desjardins. He answered Carney’s call after closing the door on running for provincial politics.

The riding was previously held by former environment minister Steven Guilbeault, who stepped down earlier this year because of disagreements on Carney’s climate policies.

Kalles said while Cormier is a “star candidate,” he doesn’t think it’ll be an “easy” ride.

Laurier—Ste-Marie is a very progressive riding that elected former Bloc Québécois leader Gilles Duceppe for years before he was defeated by the New Democrats in 2011. Provincially, it is home to left-wing and sovereigntist party Québec Solidaire, he said.

“I think Guy Cormier is a great candidate, but it’s going to be harder for somebody who’s not from the far-left,” Kalles said. “I’m not trying to lower expectations. I just think that, ultimately, the core demographics of (the riding) still remain a challenge.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney meets with Rosemont-La Petite Patrie riding candidate Jean-Sébastien Vallée at Milano in Little Italy in Montreal on Nov. 10, 2026. Tim Snow / Montreal Gazette

But Philippe J. Fournier, editor-in-chief of 338Canada, notes that Laurier—Ste-Marie has had new electoral boundaries since last year which include part of the Old Montreal neighbourhood and therefore makes it more fertile ground for the Liberals.

“It’s a different riding than when Mr. Guilbeault first ran,” he said. “It’s richer. It is gentrified. It’s still very much francophone, but it’s more diverse.”

Cormier will be facing Bloc Québécois candidate Zumretay Arkin, who is the former vice president of the World Uyghur Congress, as well as Nimâ Machouf, an epidemiologist who is once again running for the NDP in the riding.

Liberals are also eyeing Rosemont—La Petite-Patrie which has been vacant since former NDP MP Alexandre Boulerice made the switch to provincial politics.

Fournier thinks there is a “really good chance of a pickup” for the Liberals in the riding. The party is counting on Jean-Sébastien Vallée, a human rights advocate and community organizer who also ran for the Liberals in 2025, to try to make that happen.

“The ‘Boulerice effect’ is real, and so if you take that away in Rosemont, it’s almost impossible to see the NDP holding that,” Fournier said.

But the New Democrats are determined to hold on to their turf.

“We were so ready for the election call to come,” said NDP Leader Avi Lewis last week. “I think some of the crews in Montreal might have been up in the middle of the night getting signs up for dawn to break in Rosemont—La Petite Patrie.”

Their candidate is Pierre Céré, a longtime advocate for the rights of the unemployed.

Lewis spent three weeks in Montreal over the summer to campaign with Machouf and Céré, and he said he “can’t wait to get back to Montreal” to do just that.

“People in those neighbourhoods in Montreal did not vote for a new pipeline, did not vote for an all-in on AI strategy, did not vote for dismantling our entire climate policy in Canada. And that’s why Steven Guilbeault resigned in the first place,” he said.

“So, I think this a chance for the people of those two Montreal ridings to send a message to Ottawa,” he added.

The Bloc might also prove to be stiff competition to both the Liberals and the NDP in Rosemont—La Petite-Patrie with their candidate Alexandre Curzi, ON leave as director-general of l’Union des artistes and the son of actor Pierre Curzi.

Then, there is Saint-Hyacinthe—Bagot—Acton, a rural riding east of Montreal.

Former Bloc MP Simon-Pierre Savard-Tremblay resigned to run for the Parti Québécois and is now Quebec’s minister responsible for relations with First Nations and Inuit.

The Bloc has recruited Caroline Emond, former Delegate General of Quebec in Brussels and former Director General of the International Dairy Federation. She will be running against Chantal Soucy, a former CAQ MNA who joined the federal Liberals.

Fournier said that in normal times, the Liberals would not win this Bloc stronghold.

But he said the results of the August byelection in Chicoutimi—Le Fjord — where the Liberals handily won with more than 50 per cent of the vote — has given him “pause.”

“Could the Liberals pull off another ‘Chicoutimi’ and really surprise us? It’s possible, but I would say that the Liberals have not won there since 1980,” he said.

“It’s extra gravy if they win it.”

Catherine Lévesque covers federal-Quebec relations for National Post. She joined the parliamentary bureau in Ottawa in 2022, after a decade spent in French media in Montreal, Quebec City and Ottawa.

The RCMP interviewed Alex O’Driscoll about a Facebook comment in which he allegedly said he'd 'shoot Trump on sight' if the U.S. invaded Canada

Alex O'Driscoll, 56, is no fan of U.S. President Donald Trump, but definitely not a threat to him. (Alex O'Driscoll)

November 10, 2026 at 2:45 p.m.

Alex O’Driscoll hasn’t set foot in the U.S. since 2005 and the man from St. John’s, N.L., had no intention of returning.

“I have no interest in ever going back there,” he told National Post Tuesday.

Now, even should he have a change of heart and decide to visit family there, he likely won’t be allowed entry because of a social media comment he made about U.S. President Donald Trump roughly 18 months ago.

Last month, the 56-year-old dog groomer returned home to find an RCMP business card tacked to his door.

“I’m like, ‘What do they want me for? I haven’t done anything that I’m aware of,’” he said.

Upon contacting the officer, O’Driscoll was told the U.S. Secret Service had contacted the RCMP about a Facebook comment he’d allegedly made in response to a hypothetical question: “What would you do if Trump showed up and took over Canada?”

The Secret Service alleged that O’Driscoll replied, “I would shoot him on sight.”

O’Driscoll laughed at first, thinking it was surely a joke, but the officer told him he was serious.

He said that while he dislikes Trump “immensely,” he has no desire to shoot him. He doesn’t even own a gun.

“I’m not a threat to Trump,” he said.

As for the comment, O’Driscoll said it’s possible he made it, though having abandoned Facebook and all social media some time ago, he can’t remember it nor find any record.

Even the RCMP officer, he said, didn’t have a physical printout of the alleged comment, just a letter from the Secret Service that he wasn’t permitted to see.

After a 10-minute chat, the officer determined O’Driscoll wasn’t a threat and said he would send a recording of the conversation to the Secret Service as evidence.

They also told him that he “May possibly be banned from ever entering the U.S. again.”

“Which I’ll take as a bad badge of honour at this point,” O’Driscoll.

The RCMP was not able to comment on O’Driscoll’s situation, but said it “takes all threats against public officials seriously.”

Under the RCMP Federal Policing mandate, we have the responsibility to investigate criminal code matters involving foreign public officials, when they are visiting Canada and therefore designated an internationally protected person,” they wrote.

The RCMP could not say how many times such investigations have been carried out regarding the U.S. President.

A spokesperson for the Secret Service told National Post in an email that it does not discuss matters of protective intelligence out of concern for operational security.

A few days after the incident, O’Driscoll decided to commemorate his 15 minutes of notoriety by ordering a bright orange hoodie emblazoned with the words: “Trump is marked safe from Alex.”

stories.title: Canadian Army slashing reserves as it builds up regular forces
stories.summary: 'The reality is they have no plan whatsoever to increase the size of the reserves,' says Bryan Brulotte, a retired infantry captain
stories.author: Chris Lambie
stories.content:
The Canadian Army is cancelling training and cutting reserve jobs on the eve of Remembrance Day and at a time of unprecedented military spending.

In an effort to grow the regular army, the military is targeting the reserves “because it’s easier to cut,” said Bryan Brulotte, a retired infantry captain who spent a combined 30 years in the regular force and army reserves.

“The regular army’s budget for personnel is very difficult to manipulate and to cut,” said Brulotte.

The cuts are “not in line, at all,” with promises to grow the reserves, said Brulotte, who, in his civilian life, founded MaxSys, a national staffing and human resources company that grew to $100 million in annual revenue.

“They’re very clever at using smoke and mirrors to discuss it or present it differently,” he said.

The reserve cuts come as the “Canadian Armed Forces writ large have sent out a note for 10 per cent cuts on expenditures between now and the end of the fiscal year,” Brulotte said.

“The purpose of that is they want to redirect money towards what they believe are higher priorities — and that would be money for operations and maintenance or to capital budgets.”

The army’s 2nd Canadian Division, which includes all the regular and reserve units within Quebec, “is the one that’s going to get hit the most,” Brulotte said. “It’s roughly 141 reserve units that are going to get cut. They’re going to cut on their Class B, which is full-time reservists. And they’re going to get cut on Class-A, which is the part-time reservists that parade one day a week, one weekend a month and two weeks in the summer.”

But the cuts are looming for reserve units “all over the country,” he said.

Laura McIntyre-Grills, who speaks for National Defence, confirmed in an email that the army is reviewing its funding allocations “to prioritize readiness” within its available resources.

“Ultimately, the overall available Reserve pay allocation within the Army is being directed toward the highest readiness priorities,” she said. “In effect, the Army is reducing activities that have been deemed to be lower priority, including some locally authorized temporary Class B employment positions, and some individual training days or short-duration training exercises.”

National Defence has yet to provide a number on how many reserve jobs will be cut.

Exercises between two and nine days long “May be reduced in scope or cancelled,” McIntyre-Grills said.

“As well some existing Class B contracts will end as scheduled without renewal. These decisions are being made as part of a broader effort to responsibly align available resources with the Army’s highest readiness and modernization priorities. This does not affect all Class B employment, and the Army continues to employ Reservists in a range of part-time and full-time roles.”

The army “recognizes that predictability is critical for both the part-time and full-time members of the Army Reserve, and that this can have a financial impact on reservists and their families,” McIntyre-Grills said.

“The Army will be updating its planning guidance for temporary full-time employment for reserve members, with the intent to reduce expenditures for locally generated short-term contracts up to 364 days and instead use those funds to support the highest priorities of the Canadian Army with more structured and consistent employment opportunities, while also funding the traditional part-time reserve program,” she said.

“This May include existing 3-year term employment positions being eliminated at the end of their terms, so that reserve military pay funding can be reinvested in higher priority reserve employment opportunities. The Army has also directed that the number of Regular Force members posted to Army Reserve units to provide daily support be increased during the 2027 military posting season.”

The reserves “are the easier target to strip because its more flexible spending, more discretionary spending,” said Brulotte, who concluded his military service by spending a decade as Honorary Colonel of the Governor General’s Foot Guards.

“Under that kind of bureaucratese, they’re saying, ‘No, we’re not cutting; what we’re doing is simply redirecting to higher priority areas 10 per cent of budgets. What that really means is that they’re cutting in certain areas and reallocating it to other areas. And where they’re cutting is the reserves.”

The military has roughly 25,000 reservists, but they’re authorized to grow that to 30,000, Brulotte said.

“With these cuts what they’re really doing is there’s less time for training, less time for recruiting, less time for maintenance, less time for everything. So, it downgrades the reserves and brings them to a lower level of operational efficiency.”

The military doesn’t appear to be closing reserve units, he said.

“What I have seen is they’re closing down programs and they’re amalgamating units under something called tactical groupings.”

Senior leadership in the reserves will likely be targeted, Brulotte said.

“If you no longer have senior leadership in an armoury, then it’s really tough to put together a training team and administer and grow the unit,” he said.

By consolidating “what they’re really doing is getting rid of the infrastructure to increase the size of the reserves, which goes against what the Chief of the Defence Staff Jennie Carignan said 18 months ago when she talked about a primary reserve of 100,000,” Brulotte said.

“You can’t grow the reserves by shrinking it.”

He doubts the reserve numbers will hit Carignan’s lofty target and suspects the money will go towards standing up the 1st Canadian Division, which was announced in September as the army’s primary deployable division.

“The reality is they have no plan whatsoever to increase the size of the reserves and the growth of the 1st Canadian Manoeuvre Division, which is the big sizzle, is going to be done on the back of 2nd Division – 2nd Division’s going to suffer,” Brulotte said.

The recent federal budget lays out a plan to push defence spending above 4.1 per cent of GDP by 2030-31, including $99.2 billion in core defence spending and another $58.3 billion in defence-related and security funding.

Chris Lambie is Atlantic bureau chief for National Post. He has worked for news organizations from Newfoundland to the Northwest Territories and is a three-time National Newspaper Award nominee, with a win for local reporting.

stories.title: Federal report offers 'first step' toward health strategy for men and boys: advocate
stories.summary: Ottawa - The federal government has released a report outlining challenges related to boys' and men's health as it works toward a national strategy to be release next year.
stories.author: Catherine Morrison The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - The federal government has released a report outlining challenges related to boys’ and men’s health as it works toward a national strategy to be released next year.

The report, published last week, raises concerns about stereotypes about masculinity and highlights the need for increased access to support and community spaces.

The report took into account the experiences of nearly 6,000 people and organizations who took part in roundtables, filled out an online questionnaire and shared written submissions.

The group Movember is working with Ottawa on the strategy as an independent convening partner. Its director of policy and advocacy, Catherine Corriveau, called the report a good “first step.”

“I think this is the first step of a very long staircase to understanding the scope of men and boys’ health in Canada,” she said.

Corriveau said the government needs to consider the different experiences of men and boys across Canada, since the report could not share all perspectives gathered through feedback from 6,000 individuals and organizations.

“I really don’t think there’s many barriers to this strategy,” she said. “There’s definitely clear buckets that have been identified for funding as well and very feasible policy changes and pathways that have been laid out for government to take.”

Corriveau noted that health didn’t seem to be a critical issue in the federal government’s budget released last week.

“My hope is that they want to make that when this strategy comes out, it has serious funding tied to it so we’re not just putting a piece of paper on a shelf and calling it a day,” she said.

Health Canada says the country’s first federal health strategy for men and boys will be released in early 2027. Health Minister Marjorie Michel previously said it would be released later this year.

Bijan Rafii, executive director of the Canadian Centre for Men and Families, York Region, said the initiative is “very long overdue.”

He said that while the report was “comprehensive,” there were some issues that were not mentioned that he hopes will be addressed in the strategy. They include intimate partner violence and the impact of divorce on men and boys.

Conservative MP Jamil Jivani has called for a national health strategy for men and boys. He hosted town halls with other members of Parliament to encourage participation in the government’s consultation process for the strategy.

In June, he sent a letter to Michel outlining the issues he said had come up over and over in the consultations and adding he hoped they would be addressed in the strategy. They included recognizing and respecting “traditional masculinity,” defunding safe supply and safe injection sites, and ending diversity, equity and inclusion in the workforce.

Speaking to The Canadian Press, Jivani said that while there are good things in the report, those issues were not covered.

“That’s my primary source of frustration and then you combine that with the fact that they delayed the announcement of the strategy to 2027,” he said. “It’s not building a lot of confidence that they’re taking this thing as seriously as I wish they were.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 10, 2026.

stories.title: Dresden keeps up landfill battle as project seeks Ontario approvals
stories.summary: A southwestern Ontario town is pushing back on the latest step to advance a controversial landfill and transfer station project, as Premier Doug Ford's government ramps up a search for garbage space.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A southwestern Ontario town is pushing back on the latest step to advance a controversial landfill and waste transfer station project, as Premier Doug Ford’s government ramps up a search for garbage space.

Waste company York1 wants to revive and expand a dormant landfill less than a kilometre from Dresden and pack it over the next decade with enough waste to fill Toronto’s Rogers Centre, despite local opposition.

“It’s a beautiful town, fantastic community, and this is just a few hundred metres north of town,” said Dave Taylor, deputy chief administrative officer for Chatham-Kent, the municipality encompassing Dresden.

“Our council has been unanimously opposed to the project since York1 proposed it.”

The landfill would be mostly soils, such as excavated earth from worksites along with other construction waste, according to the company’s site plans. The proposed transfer station would also sort and clean up construction debris, scrap wood, blue box material and dirt, before sending it to recyclers or landfillers.

Municipal officials have argued the company relied on outdated permits, granted decades ago, to bypass a full environmental assessment. The Ford government, which backtracked last year on a promise to complete that assessment, is now seeking public comment on whether to amend the permits.

“The York1 project is an expansion of an existing facility and can mobilize quickly to expand Ontario’s waste management capacity, as active landfill waste permissions are already in place, and it would not require a new environmental assessment that would take nearly a decade to complete,” Juliana Wilson, spokesperson for Environment Minister Todd McCarthy, said in a statement.

A spokesperson for York1 said “nothing is more important than safety” and encouraged people to take part in the public review.

“Ontario is running short of landfill space, and keeping recyclable materials out of landfill is part of the answer. We think this site can do that safely, and the provincial review is where that gets tested,” their statement read.

The proposal comes as the province prepares to overhaul landfill approvals, and as the minister warns Ontario could hit its capacity in the next 10 years, or sooner if the United States keeps up tariffs on Canadian garbage. Ontario shipped about a quarter of its landfill waste to the United States in 2024, an industry report said.

New omnibus legislation would repeal a municipal veto over new dumps, initially granted by the Ford government in 2020. Under recent regulatory changes, landfills looking to expand their service area or increase how much waste they take no longer need to undergo an environmental assessment, and would instead only be subject to amendments to narrower environmental compliance approvals.

Environmental assessments decide if a landfill project should happen at all, weighing environmental, social and economic impacts together and exploring alternatives. A compliance approval governs how it operates, by setting limits on garbage intake, air pollution or stormwater runoff.

While the Dresden site’s existing approvals are still in place, the municipality says the small landfill has been dormant so long it should be treated as a new project.

Under the proposal, the small landfill dating back to the 1960s, which holds an estimated 40,000 cubic metres of waste, would expand to a maximum capacity of 1.6 million cubic metres, the volume of the Rogers Centre. Up to 3,000 tonnes of waste per day would be accepted and then sorted at the site’s proposed waste transfer station. About 20 two-way truck trips would pass through the site each hour during peak times, a traffic report commissioned by the company suggests.

Locals have balked at the site’s proximity to homes and schools and raised a number of concerns, including about traffic and water impacts. A tributary to the Sydenham River runs along the site.

“We still hold out hope that by us raising those issues that we know are there, that will still factor into the provincial decision as to whether or not to ultimately grant the environmental compliance approvals,” Taylor, the municipality’s deputy chief administrative officer, said in an interview this week.

The public comment period on the amended permits is open until Dec. 21. If greenlit, the municipality says the landfill will still be subject to local zoning requirements, after York1 recently dropped a lawsuit where it argued those local approvals should not apply.

The province initially announced in March 2024 it would pursue an environmental assessment for the project, citing community concerns. Shortly after that, the premier called a byelection in the local riding of Lambton-Kent-Middlesex, where the successful Progressive Conservative candidate Steve Pinsonneault campaigned against the expansion.

Then, in a surprise after the election last year, the government cancelled that assessment as part of an omnibus bill. Pinsonneault spoke out against the decision but was absent from the legislature when it was voted on.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 10, 2026.

Note to readers:This is a corrected story. A previous version said Dave Taylor is the chief administrative officer for Chatham-Kent. In fact, he’s the deputy chief administrative officer.

stories.title: Warm, sunny weather to continue before cooler temperatures arrive later this week
stories.summary: Another mild day is expected across southern Ontario Tuesday, with temperatures reaching 14 C in London before cooler air moves in later this week, according to CTV News meteorologist Julie Atchison.
stories.author: Koylan Azofeifa Rueda
stories.content:
Southern Ontario is enjoying temperatures well above seasonal norms this week, with sunshine and mild conditions expected to continue through Remembrance Day, according to CTV News London meteorologist Julie Atchison.

“It’s nice and mild out there in London,” Atchison said, noting temperatures had reached 14 C in London by Tuesday afternoon, while Sarnia and Windsor were already reporting 17 C.

The sunny weather is expected to continue through Tuesday before skies become partly cloudy overnight. Residents can expect a mix of sun and cloud Wednesday morning, with increasing cloud cover developing through the afternoon.

Atchison said moisture moving out of the American Midwest will bring mainly cloudy skies for Remembrance Day ceremonies on Wednesday, but conditions should remain pleasant.

“There is a slight chance for some showers towards Grey and Bruce County,” she said. “However, I am expecting the majority of the rainfall to hold off until later in the day.”

Steadier rain is expected to develop north of London, including parts of Huron and Perth counties, by late afternoon, with Grey and Bruce counties also expected to see rainfall. London faces only a 40 per cent chance of showers, Atchison said.

Temperatures are expected to reach about 9 C by late Wednesday morning, with light and variable winds, generally from the south.

A significant cool-down is forecast to arrive later in the week. Thursday’s high is expected to reach just 7 C, followed by 4 C on Friday under a mix of sun and cloud.

Overnight temperatures are forecast to fall between -2 C and 1 C, creating the potential for lake-effect precipitation, particularly in areas north of London.

“Any time you get that cold flow coming off Lake Huron, we could get into some mixing,” Atchison said.

While a slight chance of lake-effect rain or snow will remain in the forecast through the weekend, Atchison said residents planning outdoor activities should still be able to enjoy some sunshine.

Overnight temperatures are forecast to fall between -2 C and 1 C, creating the potential for lake-effect precipitation, particularly in areas north of London.
“Any time you get that cold flow coming off Lake Huron, we could get into some mixing,” Atchison said.
While a slight chance of lake-effect rain or snow will remain in the forecast through the weekend, Atchison said residents planning outdoor activities should still be able to enjoy some sunshine.

stories.title: Fatal B.C. attack involved 4 bears displaying ‘predatory behaviour,’ officials say
stories.summary: A GoFundMe page identified the victims as Jenny Balcarras and her daughter, Selah Reed. One person’s remains were found in the Snooka West Trail area last Monday.
stories.author: Amy Judd
stories.content:
The B.C. Conservation Officer Service says four bears were involved in the deadly attack in Bella Coola last week in which a mother and her daughter were killed .

The service said the bears have been “dispatched.”

“Evidence from the investigation, as well as animal DNA, was analyzed and conclusively linked to a sow and its three offspring,” Insp. Jeff Tyre with the BC Conservation Officer Service said at an update on Tuesday.

“After considering all the evidence and in accordance with provincial human wildlife conflict response guidelines, these bears have been dispatched to protect the public.”

Tyre also said this attack “likely involved predatory behaviour,” which is very rare.

“That is to say, we don’t know how it started, but we know how ended,” he said.

One person’s remains were found in the Snooka West Trail area last Monday.

The second person’s remains were found on Tuesday afternoon during search efforts by conservation officers and the RCMP.

A GoFundMe page identified the victims as Jenny Balcarras and her daughter, Selah Reed.

A family member started the fundraiser and said Balcarras recently moved to Bella Coola to start a new career and begin a new chapter in her life.

“Selah was just 20 years old, with her whole life ahead of her. She was only beginning her journey into adulthood, making this loss even more heartbreaking,” the crowdfunding campaign reads.

“Jenny leaves behind three young adult children — a son and two daughters — as well as a grandchild. They are now faced with the devastating loss of their mother and sister while also having to navigate the unexpected financial burden of arranging funeral services and covering the associated expenses for both Jenny and Selah.”

Tyre said the four bears were not involved in the 2025 attack in the same area, whith involved school children .

More to come.

stories.title: Four bears involved in fatal B.C. attack that left mother and daughter dead
stories.summary: DNA tests link female grizzly and three yearling cubs to deadly attack, with all four killed to protect public, authorities say
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The B.C. Conservation Officer Service says four grizzly bears that it captured in Bella Coola in recent days were all involved in a deadly attack that claimed the lives of a mother and daughter in the community this month.

Insp. Jeff Tyre with the service said DNA tests had conclusively linked the female grizzly and her three yearling cubs to the attack and all had been killed to protect the public.

“Our investigation also found that this attack likely involved predatory behaviour, which I can tell you is very rare,” Tyre told an online briefing.

“That is to say, we don’t know how it started, but we know how it ended.”

The bodies of art therapist Jenny Balcarras and her adult daughter, Selah Reed, were found last week about 150 metres apart after they were reported missing on Nov. 1.

Their remains were found in an area of trails outside the northern B.C. community, where local authorities imposed a voluntary curfew and police had been escorting children to school last week in the wake of the attack.

Tyre said the DNA tests showed the bears were not involved in a 2025 attack on a group of schoolchildren in the same area of Bella Coola, which is about 1,000 kilometres north of Vancouver.

Tlhmtimut Samuel Schooner, elected Chief Councillor of the Nuxalk Nation, said the investigation into the recent attack “was carried out with the utmost care and respect.”

“This attack has been deeply re-triggering for our community members as we continue to recover from last year’s attack,” he told the briefing.

“Our thoughts remain with the victims’ family. We still have community supports in place, and they will remain there until we feel the time is right to remove them. Our community is rightly still deeply affected and will be for generations.”

Tyre said bears involved in fatal attacks on people “cannot be rehabilitated or relocated.”

“This type of behaviour represents an extreme risk to the public, and such bears are dispatched to protect the public and prevent similar attacks in the future.”

The B.C. Conservation Officer Service says a rare predatory attack by a grizzly sow and her three yearling cubs was behind the deaths of Jenny Balcarra and her adult daughter, Selah …

The 2025 attack by a grizzly on a group of about 20 elementary school students and teachers last November left an adult and three children badly injured.

Nicholas Scapillati, executive director of the B.C.-based Grizzly Bear Foundation, said in an interview on Tuesday that the tragedy in Bella Coola was an “extremely challenging” situation.

He commended the Conservation Officer Service for their investigation, and “helping these rural communities where they clearly need our help in co-existing with the bears.”

“Rural communities co-existing or working to co-exist with grizzly bears in Western North America have great challenges and they need our help,” Scapillati said. Education was necessary, he said, “but we also need community programs that further co-existence and safety.”

Scapillati said B.C.’s Bear Smart program, which helps educate communities about staying safe and co-existing with bears, is effective.

But “this past year, the B.C. government stopped putting energy into that program and actually paused it,” he said.

He said the timing of the attack was significant.

“Bears are heading toward hibernation. Their behaviour is significantly different at this time of year and communities need to be safe and that’s a critical message for everyone in Western Canada, in Western North America right now that lives close to a grizzly bear,” he said.

“In the fall, it’s a more challenging time to co-exist with them.”

He said the incoming B.C. Conservative provincial government could have a “great opportunity” to do more to help rural communities avoid similar tragedies.

Schoone said in a statement on Tuesday that the First Nation was thankful to the conservation officer service for finding the bears and bringing some resolution to the community.

The statement said community members should “take all necessary precautions outdoors, stay close to young children, and ensure our spaces are free of any attractants.”

stories.title: How a small poppy project bloomed into a community event and nearly 11,000 handmade flowers
stories.summary: An initiative kick-started by three friends for Remembrance Day sparks fellowship in the Ontario town of Bobcaygeon
stories.author: Mira Miller, Photography by Justine Rines
stories.content:
When Maggie Burns suggested to friends at her local curling club that their town of Bobcaygeon, Ont., should knit and crochet poppies for Remembrance Day , she never imagined how it would take off.

Last January, 74-year-old Burns, and her friends Alison Williams and Andrea DeFalco, 61 and 71, kick-started the initiative, making a Facebook group to spread word of the project and share the patterns. The group has since grown to 449 members and helped to organize poppy-making events and local business participation.

Now, after almost a year of hard work, the town of just 3,576 people has made nearly 11,000 poppies. At the beginning of November, volunteers set up thousands of poppies on display at seven different locations throughout Bobcaygeon, where they’ll remain for all to admire until Nov. 15.

“The way everybody jumped on board, I was shocked, really,” Burns said. “The participation was just unbelievable.”

Burns took part in a similar poppy project a few years ago, when she briefly lived in St. Marys, Ont. She had also heard of similar installations in other Ontario cities, including Stratford and Niagara Falls . When she returned to Bobcaygeon in September 2025, she was inspired to bring the project home with her.

Burns first requested and received the necessary approvals from the Royal Canadian Legion, the City of Kawartha Lakes and Parks Canada. She needed permission to use the red poppy, as it is a registered trademark owned by the Legion, and because the poppies would be displayed on public property. She got the go-ahead without issue and began recruiting her friends, involving others soon after.

The historic stone archway entrance to the Boyd Heritage Museum and the swing bridge crossing the Trent-Severn Waterway are decorated with poppies.

“It just snowballed and the poppies started pouring in,” said Burns, a retired software-test manager who picked up crochet again during the pandemic, after first learning it in the seventies. The poppies are about four inches across and each take roughly 30 minutes to make, depending on whether they’re crocheted or knitted and the crafter’s skill level.

Throughout the winter, the trio held monthly social events at local businesses where people could gather to knit and crochet together. Several of those businesses also operated as drop-off locations, so residents could leave their poppies to be collected when they were done.

Williams, Burns and DeFalco have been putting their time and talents into creating the poppies as a tribute to those who served and sacrificed.

“It became very social,” Williams said. “People loved it because it was just a tiny thing they could do to be part of a great big community event.”

The initial goal was 5,000 poppies, a target the volunteers reached by July, so they set a new objective of 10,000. They hit that by the end of September.

The final official count at the end of October came in at 10,899, though Williams said they’ve received even more since then.

In September, Burns, Williams, DeFalco and other volunteers started meeting up twice a week to sew the poppies onto pieces of mesh for display.

“We’d just sit and chat and stitch and a lot of the ladies became friends,” Burns said. “They were exchanging numbers at the end.”

Burns said the town is proud to pay their respects to veterans in this way and pass down important history to younger generations.

“It’s just a really good feeling,” she said. “My father was in the services and it’s an honour to do this on behalf of the Legion and the veterans who sacrificed so much for us.”

Volunteers also made poppy garlands and 100 poppy sticks that have been placed behind the town’s cenotaph, where the Remembrance Day ceremony is held, to honour the 100th anniversary of the Legion.

The project was met with enthusiasm from community members of all kinds, from residents at the local retirement home to children as young as eight years old. Many also got involved by donating yarn from Granny Bird’s Wool Shoppe in town.

Janet Wilson, 69, hadn’t crocheted in more than 40 years when she heard of the initiative at the curling club – so she decided to relearn. “I made around 180 poppies and really enjoyed the participation of our town in this unique project,” she said.

stories.title: CP NewsAlert: Four bears involved in deadly attack in Bella Coola, B.C.
stories.summary: Bella Coola - The B.C. Conservation Officer Service says four grizzly bears that it captured in Bella Coola in recent days were all involved in a deadly attack that claimed the lives of a mother and daughter in the community this month.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The B.C. Conservation Officer Service says four grizzly bears that it captured in Bella Coola in recent days were all involved in a deadly attack that claimed the lives of a mother and daughter in the community this month.

Insp. Jeff Tyre with the service said DNA tests had conclusively linked the female grizzly and her three yearling cubs to the attack and all had been killed to protect the public.

“Our investigation also found that this attack likely involved predatory behaviour, which I can tell you is very rare,” Tyre told an online briefing.

“That is to say, we don’t know how it started, but we know how it ended.”

The bodies of art therapist Jenny Balcarras and her adult daughter, Selah Reed, were found last week about 150 metres apart after they were reported missing on Nov. 1.

Their remains were found in an area of trails outside the northern B.C. community, where local authorities imposed a voluntary curfew and police had been escorting children to school last week in the wake of the attack.

Tyre said the DNA tests showed the bears were not involved in a 2025 attack on a group of schoolchildren in the same area of Bella Coola, which is about 1,000 kilometres north of Vancouver.

Tlhmtimut Samuel Schooner, elected Chief Councillor of the Nuxalk Nation, said the investigation into the recent attack “was carried out with the utmost care and respect.”

“This attack has been deeply re-triggering for our community members as we continue to recover from last year’s attack,” he told the briefing.

“Our thoughts remain with the victims’ family. We still have community supports in place, and they will remain there until we feel the time is right to remove them. Our community is rightly still deeply affected and will be for generations.”

Tyre said bears involved in fatal attacks on people “cannot be rehabilitated or relocated.”

“This type of behaviour represents an extreme risk to the public, and such bears are dispatched to protect the public and prevent similar attacks in the future.”

The 2025 attack by a grizzly on a group of about 20 elementary school students and teachers last November left an adult and three children badly injured.

Nicholas Scapillati, executive director of the B.C.-based Grizzly Bear Foundation, said in an interview on Tuesday that the tragedy in Bella Coola was an “extremely challenging” situation.

He commended the Conservation Officer Service for their investigation, and “helping these rural communities where they clearly need our help in co-existing with the bears.”

“Rural communities co-existing or working to co-exist with grizzly bears in Western North America have great challenges and they need our help,” Scapillati said. Education was necessary, he said, “but we also need community programs that further co-existence and safety.”

Scapillati said B.C.‘s Bear Smart program, which helps educate communities about staying safe and co-existing with bears, is effective.

But “this past year, the B.C. government stopped putting energy into that program and actually paused it,” he said.

He said the timing of the attack was significant.

“Bears are heading toward hibernation. Their behaviour is significantly different at this time of year and communities need to be safe and that’s a critical message for everyone in Western Canada, in Western North America right now that lives close to a grizzly bear,” he said.

“In the fall, it’s a more challenging time to co-exist with them.”

He said the incoming B.C. Conservative provincial government could have a “great opportunity” to do more to help rural communities avoid similar tragedies.

Schoone said in a statement on Tuesday that the First Nation was thankful to the conservation officer service for finding the bears and bringing some resolution to the community.

The statement said community members should “take all necessary precautions outdoors, stay close to young children, and ensure our spaces are free of any attractants.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 10, 2026.

stories.title: 15-year-old faces impaired driving charges after fatal crash
stories.summary: Oneida Police Service and Middlesex County OPP say officers responded to a crash on Oneida Road at about 6:40 a.m. on Nov. 7.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
A 17-year-old from London has been identified as the person killed in a single-vehicle crash on Oneida Nation of the Thames First Nation.

Oneida Police Service and Middlesex County OPP say officers responded to a crash on Oneida Road at about 6:40 a.m. on Nov. 7.

Police said one passenger was pronounced dead at the scene. The victim has been identified as a 17-year-old from London.

Three other occupants of the vehicle were taken to hospital.

Investigators allege the driver, a 15-year-old from Oneida Nation of the Thames First Nation, was impaired at the time of the crash.

The youth has been charged with operation while impaired with a blood-alcohol concentration exceeding the legal limit, operation while impaired causing death, dangerous operation causing death, driving without a licence, driving with a blood-alcohol concentration above zero as a novice driver, using a licence plate not authorized for the vehicle, and driving a motor vehicle with liquor readily available.

The accused was held for a bail hearing.

The identity of the accused is protected under the Youth Criminal Justice Act.

Police are asking anyone with information or dashcam footage of the vehicle involved before the collision to contact the Oneida Police Service or OPP.

Tyre said bears involved in fatal attacks on people “cannot be rehabilitated or relocated.”

“This type of behaviour represents an extreme risk to the public, and such bears are dispatched to protect the public and prevent similar attacks in the future.”

The 2025 attack by a grizzly on a group of about 20 elementary school students and teachers last November left an adult and three children badly injured.

Nicholas Scapillati, executive director of the B.C.-based Grizzly Bear Foundation, said in an interview on Tuesday that the tragedy in Bella Coola was an “extremely challenging” situation.

He commended the Conservation Officer Service for their investigation, and “helping these rural communities where they clearly need our help in co-existing with the bears.”

“Rural communities co-existing or working to co-exist with grizzly bears in Western North America have great challenges and they need our help,” Scapillati said. Education was necessary, he said, “but we also need community programs that further co-existence and safety.”

Scapillati said B.C.’s Bear Smart program, which helps educate communities about staying safe and co-existing with bears, is effective.

But “this past year, the B.C. government stopped putting energy into that program and actually paused it,” he said.

He said the timing of the attack was significant.

“Bears are heading toward hibernation. Their behaviour is significantly different at this time of year and communities need to be safe and that’s a critical message for everyone in Western Canada, in Western North America right now that lives close to a grizzly bear,” he said.

“In the fall, it’s a more challenging time to co-exist with them.”

He said the incoming B.C. Conservative provincial government could have a “great opportunity” to do more to help rural communities avoid similar tragedies.

Schoone said in a statement on Tuesday that the First Nation was thankful to the conservation officer service for finding the bears and bringing some resolution to the community.

The statement said community members should “take all necessary precautions outdoors, stay close to young children, and ensure our spaces are free of any attractants.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 10, 2026.
