stories.title: Carney to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping next week
stories.summary: Ottawa — Prime Minister Mark Carney says he will raise concerns about foreign interference in Canada when he meets next week with Chinese President Xi Jinping.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — Prime Minister Mark Carney said Tuesday he will raise concerns about foreign interference in Canada when he meets next week with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Carney and Xi are expected to meet in person at the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China.

“The advantage of these meetings is you can raise issues directly and frankly,” Carney told a press conference in Montreal.

Carney said he would bring up with Xi the importance Canada attaches “to the non-interference in our affairs by China and other countries.”

The prime minister said he also will discuss with Xi the global security climate and the economic partnership between the two countries. He said that partnership “is something that is deepening but has clear guardrails in terms of the areas in which we’re involved.”

Carney last met with Xi in January. The two leaders also spoke at last year’s Apec summit — the first formal meeting between the leaders of Canada and China since 2017.

Carney said at the time he and Xi discussed foreign interference but Beijing didn’t understand how seriously Canadians take the issue.

Carney’s government has been rebuilding Canada’s relationship with China and is pursuing increased trade between the two nations.

In January 2025, a public inquiry identified China as the top perpetrator of foreign interference targeting Canadian democratic institutions, and concluded Beijing tried to meddle in some Canadian elections.

A recent report by the organization Safeguard Defenders said China has expanded the network of illegal police stations it operates around the world, including in Canada. The Spain-based non-governmental organization said the stations are used by China to monitor the diaspora in a bid to control them.

Carney also told reporters in Montreal that his government has chosen a new ambassador to China and will announce the appointment soon. The post has been vacant since the spring.

“It’s a little longer than we would have liked. We wanted to get the right person and we have found that right person,” he said.

U.S. President Donald Trump will also be at the summit. Carney said he and Trump are expected to have a conversation at Apec or at the Asean summit in the Philippines, which takes place a few days earlier.

“I have an ability to engage with the president in multiple occasions and on a running basis, so yes, it’s good to sit down but it’s not absolutely necessary,” Carney said.

Carney said he spoke briefly with Trump over the weekend.

That conversation came a few days after the U.S. midterm elections where Trump’s Republicans lost badly in a vote widely believed to be a referendum on many of his policies, including the tariffs on Canada.

Trade talks between Canada and the U.S. collapsed in August. In the days since the U.S. midterm elections gave the Democrats firm control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate, several party officials have indicated repealing Trump’s tariffs on Canadian products is a priority.

Carney told reporters last week that “more intense” trade negotiations with the United States have restarted.

The Association of Southeast Asian Nations, or Asean, summit will take place in the Philippines from Nov. 16 to 18. The Apec summit will bring leaders from across Asia, South America and the South Pacific together in Shenzhen, China from Nov. 18 to 19.

China has confirmed that it is discussing a possible meeting between Xi, Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin, which would take place at the Apec summit.

Carney was in Montreal Tuesday to tout the $4 billion in funding for culture and recreation outlined in last week’s federal budget. It includes new tax credits, and $600 million in annual funding for Canadian content.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 10, 2026.

— With files from The Associated Press and Catherine Morrison

Anja Karadeglija, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Ontario appoints eight regional chairs, including outgoing Conservative MP Scott Aitchison
stories.summary: Ford’s government recently gave itself powers to appoint regional chairs in Durham, Halton, Muskoka and Waterloo
stories.author: Allison Jones
stories.content:
Ontario Premier Doug Ford’s government has appointed eight regional heads of council, including Conservative MP Scott Aitchison.

Aitchison had announced he would resign his Parry Sound-Muskoka seat at the end of the fall sitting of Parliament, and the Ontario government says he will be sworn in as Muskoka District chair on Dec. 1.

Ford’s government recently gave itself powers to appoint regional chairs in Durham, Halton, Muskoka and Waterloo, also extending an existing power to appoint the chairs in Niagara, Peel and York regions.

The regional chairs will also get so-called strong chair powers, including to appoint or fire the chief administrative officer and division heads, direct staff, veto certain bylaws and propose the municipal budget.

Appointed chairs who are serving as mayors in their communities will hold both roles, including Pickering Mayor Kevin Ashe as Durham regional chair and Vaughan Mayor Steven Del Duca as York regional chair.

Former Oakville mayor Ann Mulvale will become Halton regional chair, outgoing Orillia Mayor Don McIsaac will serve as Simcoe County chair, outgoing Welland Mayor Frank Campion will serve as Niagara regional chair, Kitchener city Coun. Scott Davey will serve as Waterloo regional chair, and current Peel regional chair Nando Iannicca will stay in the role.

stories.title: Two charged after $70,000 worth of construction equipment stolen in Strathroy-Caradoc
stories.summary: The Strathroy-Caradoc Police Service says the investigation began on Sept. 28 after officers received a report that construction equipment and materials had been stolen several days earlier.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
Two people are facing charges after an investigation into the theft of approximately $70,000 worth of construction equipment and materials in Strathroy-Caradoc.

The Strathroy-Caradoc Police Service says the investigation began on Sept. 28 after officers received a report that construction equipment and materials had been stolen several days earlier.

The case was later assigned to the force’s criminal investigation division.

As a result of the investigation, police arrested a 48-year-old Thedford resident and a 28-year-old Lambton Shores resident.

Both men have been charged with possession of property obtained by crime and trafficking in property obtained by crime.

Police say several stolen items were recovered during the investigation, including a significant amount of copper wire.

The accused are scheduled to appear in a London court in late December.

stories.title: Global conflict pushes countries to focus on domestic energy security, report finds
stories.summary: Shift to nuclear and other renewable sources stands to reduce carbon emissions, according to Wood Mackenzie analysis
stories.author: Joy SpearChief-Morris
stories.content:
Global conflicts and supply-chain pressures are pushing some countries to shift away from a dependency on fossil fuels and helping to reduce their carbon emissions more than with climate-specific policies alone, a new report finds.

Research group Wood Mackenzie’s annual Energy Transition Outlook found trade conflict and the U.S.-Iran war have led some major economies to become less reliant on global energy markets, focusing more on domestically produced energy, including nuclear and other low-carbon sources.

“The world now confronts an energy landscape of unprecedented complexity, where emissions trajectories continue deteriorating, climate targets drift further from reach, and market volatility has reached extraordinary levels,” said Prakash Sharma, Wood Mackenzie vice-president and head of scenarios and technologies and one of the report’s lead authors.

“We believe the government thinking has moved in parallel with these market pressures.”

Mr. Sharma said climate policy and net-zero objectives require stronger policy supports and incentives, and “the current global order, we believe, is not designed to support that alternative.”

Canada is one of almost 200 countries that have committed to net zero carbon emissions by 2050 as signatories to the 2015 Paris Agreement, which seeks to limit a global average temperature rise to between 1.5 and 2 degrees above preindustrial levels.

Wood Mackenzie’s independent assessment, which outlines five distinct energy transition scenarios across 105 energy markets to 2060, found the energy security scenario – one which focuses on domestic renewable sources – would result in a projected warming of 2.5 degrees by 2100, lower than their base-case scenario of 2.6 degrees.

The security scenario accounts for a boost in investment in nuclear and geothermal energy sources over technologies such as hydrogen and carbon capture, which it said rely on stronger climate policies and incentives.

The scenario that accounts for countries choosing to focus on economic expansion, such as major investments in data centres for artificial intelligence and robotics, is projected to lead to warming of 3 degrees since fossil fuel usage continues longer, delaying investment in renewable sources.

The report states electricity demand is expected to grow by 15 per cent between now and 2030, with data centres accounting for about one-third of that increase.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has been shifting Canada’s policies away from a climate-focused approach to one prioritizing investment in major projects, including fossil fuels, with new oil and natural gas pipelines to the West Coast announced recently.

However, the 2026 federal budget tabled Nov. 5 outlined billions in new money for Canada’s electricity system, including $40-billion over 10 years starting in 2027-28 for infrastructure expansion.

It also extended tax credits for clean electricity investment through 2040, with an expected cost of $2.4-billion from 2027-28 to 2030-31 and $36.1-billion from 2031-32 to 2041-42.

Lindsey Entwistle, Wood Mackenzie’s principal analyst of scenarios and technologies and another of the report’s lead authors, said electrification is “clearly the solution to many of the challenges of energy security, decarbonization, and economic growth.”

The Canadian Climate Institute’s annual early emissions report found the country was well short of its carbon-emissions-reduction goals for 2030, and also turned to clean electrification as a solution.

Sachi Gibson, mitigation research director at the environmental think tank, said technology such as electric vehicles and heat pumps has driven power demand in Canada, although the transition has not been as rapid as in other countries.

“Folks are electrifying for many reasons, not just climate concerns,” Ms. Gibson said.

“There’s multiple drivers at play. It can be climate policy, it can be energy security concerns, it could also be affordability.”

Wood Mackenzie said data centres and AI are expected to double global power demand by 2060, with the U.S., China and India accounting for more than half of that growth.

“There’s an immediate scramble for electricity supply and real fears around high energy prices,” Ms. Entwistle said.

The federal budget also included a commitment to support data centre developers to build 500 megawatts of processing power for Canadian AI companies, though it did not put a dollar figure behind the program.

November 10, 2026 at 12:53 p.m.

Ottawa — Since the spring, two separate groups have asked Parliament to reconsider how we honour our veterans. The first wants Canada to finally award the Victoria Cross, our highest military decoration for valour. The second campaign wants the government to reclassify past conflicts as wars, elevating veterans of those fights as war veterans.

In this video, we explain why this is happening now and what it will mean for veterans.

Let’s start with the Victoria Cross. The original medal was struck by Queen Victoria in 1856 to award valour in the Crimean War. Echoing present conflicts, that was a war where the allies tried to evict Russian occupiers out of the Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea.

These medals are highly prized and worth about a half million dollars on the open market though they rarely go up for sale. Lord Michael Ashcroft has 245 of them that he collected to preserve the legacy that they honour.

The Canadian War Museum purchased Robert Shankland’s VC when it came up for auction in 2009. Shankland is part of a trio of Victoria Cross winners, coincidentally all born in the 700 block of Winnipeg’s Pine Street. The museum was also able to acquire the medals of Leo Clarke and Frederick William Hall to celebrate the heroism of the men who May never have physically met, but all performed the greatest acts of bravery. In 1925, Winnipeg renamed Pine Street Valour Road in their honour.

The VC was Britain’s highest honour, and as a former colony, it was also Canada’s. Our winners had to visit Buckingham Palace to receive their award. Ninety-nine Canadians would be awarded this ultimate honour, the last one in the dying days of World War II.

Then, in 1993, Canada created its own version, the Canadian Victoria Cross. But not a single one was ever awarded.

Aghan vet Bruce Moncur made it his personal mission to change this, and he enlisted his former boss Chief Of Defence Staff Rick Hillier to help.

Moncur’s team strategized that the best way to win this battle was to pick a single hero to champion for a VC, and they chose North Bay Ontario’s Jess Larochelle.

North Bay MP Pauline Rochefort entered the fray after an earlier bill by former Conservative leader Erin O’Toole failed to convince the Trudeau government to act. This time the request was for a review of past honours, not just VCs.

Her bill was referred to committee where it would receive unanimous consent.

Upon returning to the House, it passed, also with unanimous consent. On Nov. 2, Defence Minister David McGuinty announced that in the coming months, the government will begin developing a process to consult with veterans, serving members, stakeholders and historians to examine potential criteria for the review and classification of past conflicts and military operations.

Canada has not officially designated any military operation as “wartime service” since the Korean War, which ended in 1953. Everything after that, including the Gulf War and the war in Afghanistan, have been classified as “special duty service.” While changing the designation won’t affect benefits or pensions, for those affected, this is a badge of honour of great importance to them.

Mick Gzowski is a video reporter for the National Post's parliamentary bureau in Ottawa.

Everything after that, including the Gulf War and the war in Afghanistan, have been classified as “special duty service.” While changing the designation won’t affect benefits or pensions, for those affected, this is a badge of honour of great importance to them.
Mick Gzowski is a video reporter for the National Post's parliamentary bureau in Ottawa.

stories.title: Stegh president and CEO announces retirement
stories.summary: In a statement, Karen Davies informed the hospital’s board of directors of her decision to step down from the role.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
The president and chief executive officer of St. Thomas Elgin General Hospital has announced plans to retire.

In a statement, Karen Davies informed the hospital’s board of directors of her decision to step down from the role. Davies said she will remain in the position during the transition period and continue supporting the hospital’s strategic priorities while assisting with the onboarding of new leadership.

Board chair Amy Dale praised Davies’ leadership and contributions to the hospital.

“Karen has provided transformational leadership at Stegh, and her vision, steadfastness, calm nature and commitment to putting people first have created a very strong hospital and bright future for care in our community,” Dale said in a statement.

Davies joined the hospital in 2012 as chief nursing executive and vice-president. She served in that position for nine years before becoming president and CEO in 2021.

According to the hospital, Davies helped strengthen its focus on quality of care, emergency department performance, patient experience, staff experience and operational excellence during her tenure.

“Serving this hospital and community has been one of the greatest privileges of my life,” Davies said in a statement.

“I have been fortunate to work alongside exceptional staff, physicians, volunteers, leaders, board members and community partners who share an unwavering commitment to providing exemplary care.”

The hospital’s board of directors said it will begin a search for a new president and CEO in the coming weeks.

stories.title: Morgan proposes dividing London’s deputy mayor role, nominates new budget chair, in council re-organization
stories.summary: Morgan is nominating two councillors to become his deputy mayors, Coun. Shawn Lewis and Coun. Corrine Rahman, and Coun. Steve Lehman to be his new Budget Chair.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
Mayor Josh Morgan will ask the newly elected city council to endorse his re-organization of senior council positions at the start of the new term.

Morgan is nominating two councillors to become his deputy mayors, Coun. Shawn Lewis and Coun. Corrine Rahman, and Coun. Steve Lehman to be his new Budget Chair.

Lewis served as the city’s sole deputy mayor throughout the four-year term.

“Having a second deputy mayor position is going to allow us to spread the work across multiple individuals,” Morgan explained. “At a very high level, one of the deputy mayors would be helping with a lot of advocacy and organization of external groups.”

Morgan said the second deputy mayor position will have a greater focus on council decision-making, “Making sure our meetings are efficient, that we’re getting the things done that people want us to work on. This is an opportunity for leadership in a way to help reinforce that, and to be very streamlined and focused on those things.”

The mayor’s decision to add a second deputy mayor position, and his nominations for the three roles, will all require endorsement from city council.

Lewis says he’s honoured to be nominated for a second consecutive four-year term.

However, his role would evolve, “I’ll be doing a little bit more outside the walls of City Hall. That will include some engagement with AMO (Association of Municipalities of Ontario) and provincial leadership. It will also include some advocacy and some work with leadership within our community.”

Some of his previous role, including chairing the Strategic Priorities and Policy Committee (Sppc) would become the responsibility of the other deputy mayor he added, “One of the things I’ve talked to the mayor about already is setting up a process improvement table with the construction trades and our (city) staff to start to sort out these traffic issues so that we can move London around better.”

She emphasized that improving the efficiency of committee meetings will be high on her priority list.

Asked about being London’s first female deputy mayor in about a decade she replies, “I’m a visible minority woman. So, that’s not something that we have experienced in the city in a deputy mayor role. So, it will be different from that perspective, but we bring our identities to the table with us and that’s something that I bring.”

Lehman says he’s excited about being nominated to be budget chair, but recognizes there are expectations from the public to achieve the mayor’s tax pledge that would keep increases in the three per cent range.

“It’s going to be a challenge. There’s no question,” Lehman acknowledged. “We’re going to get out of the gate right now with the final year of our four year budget, and then we get into the really heavy lifting for crafting the next four year budget.”

He added, “I think affordability was top of priority list, not just for the mayor, but for myself. I think people that have been elected. But also I looked at the campaign platforms of those running across the city, and it was there as well.

Coun. Elizabeth Peloza was the previous budget chair from 2020 until 2026.

Regarding his decision to change his budget chair Morgan said, “I think [councillor] Peloza served the city very well in the budget chair position. She’s got a constituency that’s got a lot of work to do. She’s got BRT [bus rapid transit] coming to fruition, she’s got a lot of development in her ward. She’s a great leader on council and I think she’ll continue to lead in many different ways.”

In a statement to CTV News, Peloza expressed gratitude for serving in the role, and that it has been a privilege to play a part in upholding London’s AAA credit rating that keeps borrowing costs low.

Peloza offered Lehman her congratulations and best wishes.

She added, “My commitment to London and its residents remains unwavering. Public service has never been about a title or a position, it is about the responsibility we have to our community and the difference we can make.”

Each of the three roles would pay $101,759 per year, an eight per cent top-up above the new $94,222 base pay of a city councillor.

Since the elimination of London’s Board of Control, mayors have structured senior council leadership positions differently each term.

From 2010 to 2014, the city had no deputy mayor and instead used a rotating acting mayor system. From 2014 to 2018, there were two deputy mayors. Between 2018 and 2022, council had one deputy mayor and one budget chair serving two-year terms, while the 2022-26 term featured one deputy mayor and one budget chair serving four-year terms.

stories.title: 'Unimaginable savagery': Man gets life sentence for murdering pregnant wife in 2024
stories.summary: Montreal - A man who admitted to stabbing his pregnant wife nearly 50 times in Montreal in 2024 has been sentenced to life in prison with no chance of parole for at least 22 years.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - Narjes Ben Yedder was supporting her mother through a cancer fight and was about to become a mother herself when her husband stabbed her to death in an act of “unimaginable savagery,” a Montreal court heard Tuesday at a sentencing hearing.

Ben Yedder’s friends and family, some of whom travelled from Tunisia to attend, were present in court as Mustapha Khalil Mechken was sentenced to life in prison with no chance of parole for at least 22 years.

Khalil Mechken pleaded guilty earlier this month to second-degree murder after stabbing Ben Yedder nearly 50 times as she slept in their home while she was about 10 weeks pregnant. He admitted in a statement of facts that he didn’t want to become a father.

Ben Yedder’s family and friends delivered emotional victim impact statements, describing the 32-year-old as a ray of light and a pillar of support for her friends and family.

Ben Yedder’s mother told the court in a letter that her daughter had been her source of strength during her recent cancer battle.

“You gave me moral support when I lost hope. You found the words to comfort me when fear was taking over,” Neila Ladhari’s letter read.

“You were much more than my daughter. You were my support, my confidante, my strength in the days that I didn’t think I had any.”

Ladhari said she still felt “total incomprehension” at the savagery of her daughter’s murder at the hands of her husband.

“You lost your life from the violent actions of the one who was supposed to love you, to respect you, to protect you,” she said in the letter, which was read for her by a family member as she sat in the viewing area.

Khalil Mechken sat in the prisoner’s box with his head in his hands throughout the testimony, sometimes appearing to cover his ears. Later, through his lawyer, he asked the family for forgiveness.

“I hope God forgives me too. I still love you. Lately, my mental health hasn’t been the best,” he told the family in a statement. His lawyer noted that he had no criminal record and had pleaded guilty, eliminating the need for a trial.

Superior Court Justice Marc-André Blanchard delivered the sentence, which was a joint recommendation from the Crown and the defence.

“Femicide, and that’s what we’re dealing with here, is a broad, vile, and odious crime,” he said, adding that the 22-year parole ineligibility is on the higher end for a second-degree murder conviction.

When he pleaded guilty, Khalil Mechken acknowledged in a statement of facts that he didn’t feel ready to have a child and was worried that a maternity leave would hurt the couple’s finances.

He stabbed Ben Yedder 49 times with two kitchen knives on Jan. 26, 2024, and then called 911 and told the operator he’d killed his wife.

The statement of facts says Khalil Mechken had made a number of internet searches in the days leading up to the crime, including on whether a spouse inherits a deceased’s partner’s bank account.

He also looked up sleep troubles, intrusive thoughts, signs of burnout and depression.

One of his Google searches, five days before he killed her, read “I don’t want to take care of my little one.”

Ben Yedder’s family and friends on Tuesday expressed deep grief at not only losing her, but also her future child.

”(This child) should have heard her heart, known her arms, grown up with love,” her cousin Olfa Ben Yedder said. “He should have known my children and grown up with them, shared childhood memories, like you and I,” she said, describing the victim as like a sister to her.

A friend, Khaoula Lamairi, described Ben Yedder as someone who loved surprising her friends, organizing gatherings, and making people smile.

“For almost three years, we’ve been waiting for answers, waiting for justice to be done,” she said. “And today, even if the truth is recognized, I realize it changes nothing about her absence. Narjes won’t come back.”

Speaking outside the courtroom, members of Ben Yedder’s family who had travelled from Tunisia said they were satisfied with the sentence and relieved that the court proceedings were over.

One of her cousins also expressed skepticism at the killer’s apology, and said mental health concerns don’t explain the “savagery” of his action.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 10, 2026.

stories.title: Western Fair Association honoured with provincial agriculture award
stories.summary: Presented by the Ontario Ministry of Agriculture, Food and Agribusiness, the awards recognize efforts that advance Ontario’s agriculture and food sector while raising awareness of its contribution to the provincial economy.
stories.author: CTVNewsLondon.ca Staff
stories.content:
The Western Fair Association has received a 2026 Excellence in Agriculture Award from the Ontario government in the Agribusiness Excellence category.

Presented by the Ontario Ministry of Agriculture, Food and Agribusiness, the awards recognize efforts that advance Ontario’s agriculture and food sector while raising awareness of its contribution to the provincial economy.

“This recognition is a reflection of what can happen when we bring people, ideas and resources together around a shared purpose,” said Western Fair Association CEO Reg Ash in a statement.

“Agriculture has always been part of who we are, but our role continues to evolve. We’re proud to help entrepreneurs turn great ideas into growing businesses, connect farmers with new technologies, and build partnerships that strengthen Ontario’s food economy.”

The association’s agricultural initiatives are also expanding. In May, the Government of Canada announced an additional $8-million investment in Grove 2.0, a project that will increase production capacity and add cold-storage facilities aimed at helping more Ontario food and beverage businesses grow and access new markets.

Beyond The Grove, the Western Fair Association said it supports agricultural innovation through Innovation Farms Ontario and the AgRobotics Working Group, bringing together farmers, researchers and technology companies to develop and test new solutions.

The organization also hosts industry and community events, including the London Farm Show, the National Poultry Show, The Market and the annual Western Fair.

stories.title: Ottawa puts sharper focus on permanent residency for privately sponsored refugees
stories.summary: Ottawa — The federal government is increasing the number of privately sponsored refugees eligible for permanent residency in the coming years as it reduces the number of eligible government-sponsored refugees.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — The federal government is increasing the number of privately sponsored refugees eligible for permanent residency in the coming years as it reduces the number of eligible government-sponsored refugees.

The 2027 immigration levels plan, released last week, says about 29,000 refugees and another 20,000 protected persons and family members will be granted permanent residency status annually through 2029.

Overall, the number is similar to last year but within that number, the government is making adjustments to who is eligible for permanent residency.

The number of privately sponsored refugees eligible will increase to 17,500 from 16,000 last year, while the number of eligible government-sponsored refugees will fall to just under 12,000 from more than 13,000 in 2025.

Groups, such as religious societies and community organizations, that privately sponsor refugees help them find housing and provide them with food, rent, clothing and other essentials during their first year in Canada.

Renze Nauta, a program director for the non-partisan think tank Cardus, said increasing the number of privately sponsored refugees is a good idea because they tend to be more successful at integration than those who are aided by the government.

Nauta said Cardus wrote Immigration Minister Lena Diab in September asking that the percentage of privately sponsored refugees be increased after it was reduced last year.

“I think this is an example of where governments do leverage civil society and Canadians who support them, and I think we should do more of that,” he said.

But Lauren Lallemand, co-executive director of the Canadian Council for Refugees, said the shift to privately sponsored refugees suggests the government is off-loading its responsibility onto civil society groups.

“The government has a moral and international law obligation to resettle refugees,” Lallemand said.

“We’re disappointed to see what we interpret as a further kind of reduction in the state’s ownership of their responsibility in making sure that people receive protection in Canada and basically just transferring it on to communities and members of civil society.”

Nauta said there is evidence privately sponsored refugees do better at settling in because they receive more direct, personalized support.

“That will allow for a growth in immigration if that’s what the government calls for later on,” he said. “But it does start with that integration. That’s hard to do but Canadians have shown for the last several decades that they’re willing to do it, they have the heart to do, it and they have the means.”

Citing declining rates of newcomers — including refugees — since 2024, both Prime Minister Mark Carney and Immigration Minister Lena Diab have argued the immigration system is back under control.

Lallemand said it’s disconcerting to hear the government point to declining numbers of refugees as part of its immigration narrative.

“There are several global crises happening now that mean that there are far more displaced people than there were even 10 years ago, for example, or 15 years ago,” she said.

“The acceptance rate for refugees who apply through asylum is quite high. It’s above 70 per cent. And so kind of implying that you are getting immigration under control by further blocking people from accessing safety is very troubling.”

The government passed a law last year that says conventional asylum claims must be filed within a year of the claimant’s first arrival in Canada. Those applying after that time can still obtain protection through a pre-removal risk assessment — the appeal mechanism for a rejected asylum claim.

The government has justified the new power by pointing to a major spike in asylum claims after the COVID-19 pandemic — a spike that included people using the system to extend their time in Canada when their visas were set to expire.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 10, 2026.

David Baxter, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Calgary budget proposes 15% property tax increase in 2027
stories.summary: If approved as proposed, Calgary's budget could result in a 37 per cent increase to city property taxes over the next four years.
stories.author: Adam MacVicar
stories.content:
Calgarians could be facing a double-digit property tax increase next year as the four-year budget is presented to city council with spending focused on infrastructure and public safety.

The budget proposal, the first year of a four-year spending plan, includes nearly $600 million in new spending in 2027 as well as a total $4.4 billion in capital funding for city infrastructure like water, roads and recreation facilities.

It proposes a 15 per cent property tax increase in the first year, a 10 per cent increase in 2028, a 7.7 per cent hike in 2029 and a 6 per cent increase in the budget’s final year in 2030.

Those figures are subject to change during budget deliberations later this month.

As proposed, the budget would result in an extra $53 cost per month for the typical residential property assessed at the median of $688,000 in 2027, which includes an additional $16 per month due to a proposed increase in waste and recycling fees as well as water bills.

Calgary Transit fares are also set to increase by 3.8 per cent, and adult leisure centre admission is expected to cost Calgarians an extra 3.1 per cent in 2027.

The proposed property tax increase is set to pay for a portion of the slew of investments included in next year’s budget including $188 million in new funding for the Calgary Police Service and Calgary Fire Department, a $134 million boost for Calgary Transit, as well as $256.3 million in ongoing operating and one-time funding for infrastructure.

The four-year budget also proposes $21 billion in recommended capital spending over four years, including $13 billion in new capital infrastructure.

The four-year capital budget includes $1.7 billion for the Pine Creek and Fish Creek wastewater treatment plant, $420 million for roadway improvements, $102 million for new fire and emergency response stations and $300 million to purchase new transit buses.

The Calgary Police Service is also projected to receive its entire $192 million requested increase to its capital budget, a jump of 73 per cent over four years, as well as its full operating budget request.

According to the budget proposal, city debt is expected to rise from $4.2 billion in 2027 to $10 billion in 2030 to help pay for long-term infrastructure, including major water utility projects and the Green Line.

The budget document warns that although debt remains within council-approved limits, more debt will increase the amount required for debt payments and “reduce the funding flexibility available for future priorities.” Property values in Calgary are expected to decline slightly in 2027, with preliminary figures showing the assessed value of a single residential property is expected to drop 2.5 per cent from $706,000 in 2026 to $688,000. The typical condo assessment is also projected to drop 5.6 per cent in 2027 to $327,500.

The lower assessments are expected to result in a reduced education property tax payment for Calgarians after the provincial government announced a standardized rate that is frozen for the next three years.

According to city officials, the provincial property tax is expected to drop 6.4 per cent due to the change in assessments and projected to result in $125 in savings for the typical homeowner in 2027.

More to come…

stories.title: Ontario student accused of working for Chinese official pleads not guilty in U.S.
stories.summary: An Ontario student accused of working for someone he believed to be a Chinese government official has pleaded not guilty in the United States to making false statements.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
An Ontario student accused of working for someone he believed to be a Chinese government official has pleaded not guilty in the United States to making false statements.

Documents from a Michigan court show Weiheng Zeng entered his plea at his arraignment on Monday.

Zeng, a Chinese citizen who was studying at the University of Waterloo , was arrested after allegedly taking photos of Toronto’s Pearson airport and Chicago’s O’Hare airport at the request of a mysterious Chinese contact he’d met on an online forum.

In an affidavit filed earlier this year, an FBI agent said Zeng was first flagged by authorities in connection with an incident at O’Hare in April, when a man was seen taking photos, climbing a forklift and trying to open locked trailers at a FedEx facility.

The affidavit said Zeng, who had driven into the United States about 10 days before the incident, was later linked to a minivan seen at the site.

It said that when Zeng tried to drive into the country with the same vehicle in August, he was pulled aside for several interviews, during which he allegedly gave conflicting statements. The allegations have not yet been tested in court.

stories.title: Volunteer cleaners of Canada’s war graves keep the names of the fallen fresh
stories.summary: A new program enlists Canadians to tend the headstones of those who died in two world wars
stories.author: Marcus Gee, Photography by Fred Lum
stories.content:
In a corner of Toronto’s Prospect Cemetery, a collection of granite headstones stand in a broad lawn shaded by tall, old trees. Most bear the Maple Leaf logo that identifies them as fallen warriors of the First World War.

On a gentle fall afternoon last week, Helen Williams walked among them, stopping to scrape lichen from the stone. The Commonwealth War Graves Commission is responsible for caring for 15,000 such graves at nearly 3,000 Canadian sites. Until recently, tending them meant dispatching staff all over the country, including 10 provinces and the Yukon, a strain on both the commission’s budget and the country’s environment.

So the commission put out a call for volunteer grave tenders, spreading the word through social media and chapters of the Royal Canadian Legion. Spokeswoman Katrielle Ethier says the program has been a “resounding success.”

Since it started last year, more than 600 people have stepped up. Like sons and daughters caring for the resting place of a beloved parent, they look after the graves of long-dead warriors, scrubbing their headstones and trimming the weeds around their plots.

Ms. Williams, 59, joined the program last year, just after her husband retired from the army . Richard Williams, a signals officer, served for 36 years, doing stints in Haiti, Afghanistan and Norway, as well as numerous Canadian posts, eventually rising to the rank of lieutenant colonel.

The couple, married now for close to 40 years, visited war graves around Canada and the world as Mr. Williams hopped from place to place. They were moved by the painstaking care that went into memorials such as those near Juno Beach in Normandy, where Canadian forces came ashore on D-Day, and at Beaumont-Hamel, where soldiers of the Newfoundland Regiment were mowed down in the Battle of the Somme.

The couple wanted to help make sure that fallen soldiers buried at home in Canada got the same measure of respect. Ms. Williams was assigned 20 graves in Prospect Cemetery, which spreads north of Toronto’s St. Clair Avenue West. Mr. Williams got the same number in Mount Pleasant Cemetery, the lovely oasis in North Toronto where people come to walk and bicycle.

He says the work gives them the chance to honour those who gave their lives and to “make sure they’re remembered in some way, shape or form.” These Canadians made the “ultimate sacrifice,” he says, and we need to “reflect on that every time we get a chance . ”

His wife adds that, because Canada never suffered foreign occupation during the world wars, it is sometimes hard to remember why deaths like these matter. Visiting the graves in Prospect and other places like it reminds us.

“When we learn from history,” she says, “sometimes we can avoid making the same mistakes.”

Ms. Williams brings a knife to cut away the turf that encroaches on the headstones and a dishwashing brush and plastic scraper to remove the moss, lichen and dirt that accumulates on the grey granite. She uses a special app on her phone to document and report any bigger issues. If the inscription on a headstone is becoming too worn to be legible or a marker is listing and threatening to fall over, the commission will send professionals to make things right.

Tending the graves of her 20 warriors, she often wonders who they were, what they did and who they left behind. She also thinks of the times her husband went out the door to do his job and how she and her children worried whether he would be coming back.

What was originally called the Imperial War Graves Commission was founded in 1917. Throughout most of history, the bodies of those who were killed in battle lay where they had fallen, unmarked and unremembered except by those who loved them.

After the mass slaughter of the First World War, the war’s victors decided that that must change. Prodded by a visionary Englishman, Fabian Ware, who had served in a wartime ambulance unit, they set up the commission with the goal of honouring all of those who died, regardless of their rank. It combed the battlefields for bodies and reburied those that could be recovered, memorializing them in the lush cemeteries with rows of neat tombstones that have come to symbolize the scale of the loss.

Today, the commission oversees 23,000 cemeteries and memorials around the world, paying tribute to 1.7 million casualties of both the First and Second World Wars. To keep those graves in good condition, it relies on an army of inspectors, masons and gardeners.

Most of the more than 60,000 Canadians killed in the first war lie in Europe. By agreement, the bodies of those who died overseas were not repatriated to their home countries. But thousands lie in Canada, too. Some sustained wounds or contracted illnesses during the war and died after coming home. Others died while training in Canada. Still others perished at sea. Six out of 10 commission sites consist of just a single grave, like that of Lieutenant Roy Leslie Rogers, who died in 1919 and is buried in a small cemetery in Oxbow, Sask. Other sites have hundreds.

Prospect Cemetery contains the dead of both world wars. Many of the men buried there are from Earlscourt, a local community with many working-class immigrants from Britain. They went off to the First World War in droves.

In the park where Ms. Williams works, one headstone marks the resting place of Private Frederick Armes, 45, who died of pneumonia while serving at a Toronto training camp, according to the Veteran Affairs website. His son William, fighting in Europe, died a month later.

Another commemorates George Veals, who left his job at a tram service, the Toronto Street Railway Company, to join the navy. He was in Halifax completing his training as a wireless telegraph operator when two ships, one of them carrying munitions, collided in the harbour, setting off an explosion that killed close to 2,000 people, including Mr. Veals, on Dec. 6, 1917.

Yet another bears the name of trapper and guide Bertie Nakogee of the Northern Ontario’s Taykwa Tagamou First Nation. He enlisted in Moose Factory, Ont., and died, also of pneumonia, in the hospital at his Toronto base the day after Christmas 1916. Though he was buried with military honours, he did not get a proper headstone until 2012, after an amateur historian uncovered his story and told the commission. The day Ms. Williams visited, a small Canadian flag fluttered beside the marker.

Visiting such graves, she always takes care to say the name on the headstones out loud, something she did when she visited overseas war cemeteries on her travels. When asked why, her eyes grow misty. Finally, she answers: “No one is ever really gone as long as somebody says their name.”

stories.title: Ontario appoints regional council chairs, including outgoing Conservative MP
stories.summary: Ontario Premier Doug Ford's government has appointed eight regional heads of council, including outgoing Conservative MP Scott Aitchison.
stories.author: Allison Jones
stories.content:
Ontario Premier Doug Ford’s government has appointed eight regional heads of council, including Conservative MP Scott Aitchison.

Aitchison had announced he would resign his Parry Sound-Muskoka seat at the end of the fall sitting of Parliament, and the Ontario government says he will be sworn in as Muskoka District chair on Dec. 1.

Ford’s government recently gave itself powers to appoint regional chairs in Durham, Halton, Muskoka and Waterloo, also extending an existing power to appoint the chairs in Niagara, Peel and York regions.

The regional chairs will also get so-called strong chair powers, including to appoint or fire the chief administrative officer and division heads, direct staff, veto certain bylaws and propose the municipal budget.

Appointed chairs who are serving as mayors in their communities will hold both roles, including Pickering Mayor Kevin Ashe as Durham regional chair and Vaughan Mayor Steven Del Duca as York regional chair.

Former Oakville mayor Ann Mulvale will become Halton regional chair, outgoing Orillia Mayor Don McIsaac will serve as Simcoe County chair, outgoing Welland Mayor Frank Campion will serve as Niagara regional chair, Kitchener city Coun. Scott Davey will serve as Waterloo regional chair, and current Peel regional chair Nando Iannicca will stay in the role.

stories.title: ‘We just want to play,’ Ovechkin says on Russian participation at Iihf events
stories.summary: Ottawa — Washington Capitals star forward Alexander Ovechkin said Russian athletes just want to represent their country, but he didn't weigh in on the decision to allow his countrymen back into Iihf tournaments.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — Washington Capitals star forward Alex Ovechkin said Tuesday that Russian athletes just want to represent their country, but declined to weigh in when asked about the decision to allow Russia back into international hockey tournaments.

Ovechkin took questions from reporters in Ottawa ahead of Washington’s game against the Senators.

Last month, the Court of Arbitration for Sport overturned the International Ice Hockey Federation’s ban on Russia competing in its events.

Russia has been excluded from international hockey tournaments since it invaded Ukraine in 2022. Belarus has also been banned from competing, but the CAS ruling only addressed the Russian ban.

Asked about the Canadian government’s decision not to allow Russian players to compete at the upcoming world junior hockey championship in Alberta next month, Ovechkin said fans want to see the world’s best athletes compete.

“I don’t know how it’s going to work out, but I’m pretty sure if you ask the fans, the fans want to see the best players out there,” Ovechkin told reporters.

“The fans want to see young generation players who are going to be future stars, future NHLers. But you know it’s not up to us.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney was unequivocal earlier this month in saying Russian players would not be at the world juniors in Edmonton.

The decision to ban them drew support from the NHL’s all-time points leader.

“I understand the stance the prime minister is taking, and good for him. He’s made that stance, and he’s made it clear,” Wayne Gretzky said at an event in Toronto.

“I think a lot of the players and the people of Canada feel the same way.”

Gretzky and Ovechkin have a unique relationship. Gretzky publicly supported Ovechkin as he chased down the NHL’s all-time goal-scoring record last year, personally encouraging him along the way.

Asked about Carney’s decision, Ovechkin declined to take a position.

“It’s his thoughts, his decisions,” Ovechkin said.

Other countries have also opposed Russia’s return to international competition. On Sunday, the Swedish Ice Hockey Association said it would refuse to play Russia if the teams meet at the world juniors. Finland and Czechia have also threatened boycotts.

Canada’s secretary of state for sport, Adam van Koeverden, said last week the decision to ban Russia stems from accusations the Kremlin has used sporting success for “propaganda” purposes to garner domestic support for the war in Ukraine — a charge Ovechkin denied when asked Tuesday.

“As an athlete, you want to represent your country,” Ovechkin said.

“It doesn’t matter which — world championship, Olympic Games, European championship. You just want to go out there and play and represent your country.”

Tuesday night’s game against the Senators marks the start of the Canadian leg of Ovechkin’s farewell tour, with the NHL’s all-time leading goal scorer saying this will be his final season.

The CAS decision to reinstate Russia has prompted some hockey pundits to wonder whether the move could open the door for the NHL to include Russia in the 2028 World Cup of Hockey, which is not an Iihf event.

Asked whether he would represent Russia one final time if it competes, Ovechkin ruled it out.

“No. One hundred per cent, no,” he said, smiling.

Tuesday night’s game in Ottawa also drew attention off the ice.

The Ukrainian Canadian Congress organized a demonstration outside the Canadian Tire Centre called “No War Crimes in Hockey” to protest Ovechkin’s support for Russian President Vladimir Putin.

The organization has held demonstrations around Ottawa, usually to protest Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. A rally in February marking the fourth anniversary of the invasion drew 300 people to Parliament Hill.

Tuesday’s protest drew fewer than two dozen people on a rainy, windy evening in the Ottawa suburb of Kanata.

“People should be making choices and understand whether to support stuff like that for pleasure, for destruction, of ruining of childhood, and causing devastation,” said Mike Ryndzak, one of the demonstrators.

“Winter is coming. People have nothing. No food, no electricity, no heat, no water … and it’s absolutely not acceptable. It’s obvious that it has to stop at some point.”

Ryndzak acknowledged the low turnout at the protest, but said the Ukrainian Canadian Congress was also holding a fundraising event Tuesday which most members opted to attend.

Ovechkin publicly backed Putin in 2017 when he launched a social movement called “Putin Team.” At the time, he told reporters from The Associated Press and The Washington Post, “I just support my country.”

When Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, Ovechkin said, “Please, no more war,” when asked about the invasion. Asked about his relationship with Putin, Ovechkin said: “He’s my president, but I’m not in politics. I’m an athlete.”

Ovechkin also appeared in an ad earlier this year for a political party aligned with Putin. He told reporters in September that he was asked to participate and agreed to do so.

— With files from Abdulhamid Ibrahim and Josh Clipperton in Toronto, and The Associated Press.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 10, 2026.

Nick Murray, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Real estate association forecasts B.C. home sales to slide 4.5 per cent this year
stories.summary: Vancouver - The B.C. Real Estate Association expects home sales in the province to continue to slide this year, warning of "mounting headwinds" for the market, while hoping for a pick-up in both prices and sales in 2027.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Vancouver - The B.C. Real Estate Association expects home sales in the province to continue to slide this year, warning of “mounting headwinds” for the market, while hoping for a pick-up in both prices and sales in 2027.

The association says in its fourth-quarter forecast that sales are expected to fall 4.5 per cent this year from 2025 levels, to just over 67,000 units sold.

stories.title: Stellantis to repay Ottawa after sale of auto plant to defence contractor
stories.summary: The government contributed money to retool automaker’s Brampton, Ont., facility, but work was halted after U.S. introduced auto tariffs
stories.author: Eric Atkins
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney called Stellantis NV’s Stla-N sale of its car plant in Brampton, Ont., to defence contractor Roshel Inc. “completely outrageous,” vowing to protect workers and ensure subsidies to the automaker are returned.

“Stellantis is failing to respect their commitment to the workers of this plant and also to the Canadian government and Canadians,” Mr. Carney told reporters in Montreal.

Stellantis said on Monday that Roshel has bought the idled plant near Toronto for an undisclosed amount. There had been rumours for months about a sale of the factory, which closed for retooling in 2023. That work was paused in 2025, after U.S. President Donald Trump placed 25-per-cent tariffs on Canadian-made cars. Stellantis, based in the Netherlands and Michigan, then moved planned production of the Jeep Compass to Illinois.

The automaker said on Tuesday it has offered to repay money the federal government gave it to retool the plant, but did not say how much, citing confidentiality provisions.

“We recognize that Canadians expect accountability for public funding and that is why Stellantis has offered to voluntarily return the government support received for Brampton Assembly’s original retooling plan,” Stellantis said in a statement.

Mr. Carney said Stellantis’s abandonment of the plant violates “several” agreements Stellantis has made, including the funding arrangement. The Unifor union, which represents the plant’s workers, accuses Stellantis of violating its collective agreement.

“It’s a betrayal of the workers as it is a betrayal of the obligations to Canada and by extension to all Canadians,” Mr. Carney said. “We will fully enforce our rights in protection of those workers and protection of Canadian funds.”

The plant employed more than 3,000 people when it closed in 2023, and about 2,200 remain on layoff.

Ottawa contributed as much as $529-million to Stellantis for work on plants in Brampton and Windsor, Ont., according to the 2022 agreement obtained by The Globe and Mail under the Access to Information and Privacy law. The heavily redacted document says Stellantis must operate the Brampton plant until 2035, unless levies, adverse market conditions or other factors have a “material impact” on the plant.

It is not clear exactly how much money went to the Brampton plant, or if the government provided other subsidies.

Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said at the press conference in Montreal that she will convene a meeting in Toronto on Thursday with officials from Unifor, Stellantis and the Ontario government.

“Patience has its limits,” Ms. Joly said. “We’ve been working for more than a year now with Stellantis, with Unifor, to try and come to a solution. But Stellantis has decided to move forward and to once again violate their contract, the contract they signed with us.”

Ms. Joly said last year Stellantis’s move to shift production and leave the plant idle was a violation of the funding agreement. At the time, she threatened to take the carmaker to court.

“We’ll use all the means we have available to us to protect jobs but also to get justice for workers who for far too long now have been asking Stellantis to honour their commitments to them,” she said.

Unifor national president Lana Payne has repeatedly called on the federal government to save the plant, and called its sale a failure of the government strategy to protect jobs in the face of the U.S. trade war.

“Selling an auto assembly plant and losing vehicle production capacity is devastating for the Canadian industry, for our country, but mostly for the workers who have given so much to this company,” Ms. Payne said on Monday.

Roshel is a Brampton-based maker of armoured vehicles with factories in several countries. Company owner Roman Shimonov told The Globe and Mail he is seeking contracts for the plant, including a bid for the federal government’s light utility vehicle program, valued at about $5-billion.

“I have a lot of plans and they’re very solid,” he said by phone on Monday, “and they’re based on specific activities that are within defence and automotive.”

Unifor walked away from collective bargaining with Stellantis in September when the company confirmed it had a preliminary agreement to sell the plant. Workers then voted for a strike mandate, if needed.

Stellantis also operates a casting plant in Toronto and a minivan plant in Windsor. That factory’s assembly line is shut down this week – the sixth week since mid-September – owing to tariffs and sales.

stories.title: Ontario securities watchdog flags need to prepare for quantum computing threats
stories.summary: OSC report highlights need to defend against the harvesting of encrypted data that could one day be unlocked by new technologies
stories.author: Alexandra Posadzki, Sean Silcoff
stories.content:
Ontario’s securities watchdog is warning firms to be on the lookout for cybercriminals stealing encrypted data that they anticipate quantum computers will one day be capable of decrypting.

The emerging threat, which is referred to in the cybersecurity industry as “harvest now, decrypt later,” is highlighted in a report published Tuesday by the Ontario Securities Commission, or OSC.

In its first report about the technology, the regulator is urging firms in the capital markets sector to assess both the risks and opportunities associated with rapidly advancing quantum computing, and to prepare by taking steps such as creating inventories of their cryptographic assets.

The warning adds to mounting concerns about the cybersecurity threats posed by artificial intelligence, which could amplify the risks associated with quantum computing, the report notes.

“Quantum computing has the potential to drive significant innovation across the economy, including financial services,” Grant Vingoe, the Osc’s chief executive, said in a statement.

“At the same time, firms need to be thinking today about how future advances could affect cybersecurity, data protection and operational resilience,” he added.

Industry proponents have long promised that quantum computers, which derive their power by tapping into the peculiar properties of matter and light at microscopic scales, will some day solve tasks that remain out of reach of existing computers, opening up new applications in financial forecasting, drug and material discovery, and machine learning.

Quantum technology also has applications in sensing, communications and cybersecurity. Yet, advances the technology could bring are twinned with dread. That’s because quantum computers, once they reach commercial scale, could enable bad actors to pick the locks on cryptographic algorithms that secure the world’s digital economy.

Canada’s intelligence and defence agencies have recognized the threat for years, and governments and financial-sector players have been put on notice to quantum-proof their critical infrastructure.

There is no consensus as to when quantum computers will become powerful enough to break today’s widely used public-key cryptography.

Although that milestone, which is known as Q-Day, could be years or even decades away, some data that is encrypted today could remain valuable for a long time, according to the report. In the capital markets, such data could include trade secrets, client data, proprietary trading strategies, correspondence with regulators or communication relating to mergers and acquisitions.

The OSC is the latest in an expanding list of global financial and government players weighing in on the potential risks of quantum computing.

In June, the G7 Central Bank Quantum Technologies Working Group, which included the Bank of Canada, published a report titled Preparing for Quantum Technologies: Key Considerations for Financial Sector Participants.

The working group report aimed to establish a shared analytical framework to understand the potential implications of quantum technologies for central banking activities and for the overall financial ecosystem.

“In particular, the risk of ‘harvest now, decrypt later,’ whereby encrypted data collected today could be decrypted in the future, highlights the need to consider long-term data confidentiality,” the group said in a release at the time.

Royal Bank of Canada, meanwhile, announced in September that it had hired its first director of quantum strategy, Dr. Elizabeth Iwasawa.

Canada was an early leader in the development of quantum computers, and the Carney government has stressed that supporting its homegrown industry is of national importance.

Three domestic companies – Xanadu Quantum Technologies Ltd., Nord Quantique and Photonic Inc. – have advanced to the second stage of a U.S. Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, or Darpa, competition challenging developers to show they can build a commercial-grade quantum computer by 2033.

Last December, Ottawa committed up to $23-million apiece to those three companies (plus a fourth company that isn’t in the competition) to match what Darpa has offered those that complete the first two stages, as part of its Canadian Quantum Champions Program.

Companies that make it through a third and final leg of the Darpa process could qualify for another US$300-million each in U.S. government funding. The Canadian government announced in the budget last week the second stage of its champions program, which it said “will help ensure that Canada retains its quantum firms.”

Several U.S. states, including Illinois, Colorado and Maryland, have been aggressively courting quantum companies from Canada and elsewhere with incentives to locate in their jurisdictions.

The Canadian government has also provided additional funding to domestic quantum companies, including a repayable $195-million commitment announced in August to help Xanadu build a 158,000-square-foot advanced research development and manufacturing facility in Toronto.

stories.title: Carney must ‘fire’ industry minister, Poilievre says over Stellantis sale
stories.summary: Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said Tuesday that Prime Minister Mark Carney should 'fire' Mélanie Joly after Stellantis agreed to sell its Brampton plant to Roshel.
stories.author: Ariel Rabinovitch
stories.content:
Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said Tuesday that Prime Minister Mark Carney should “fire” his industry minister, Mélanie Joly, after a Stellantis agreement to sell its Brampton plant threatened thousands of job losses.

Stellantis , the parent company of Jeep and other automotive brands, announced on Monday a deal to sell its Brampton vehicle assembly plant to Canadian defence and armoured vehicle manufacturer Roshel.

The financial terms of that agreement have not been made public, and although there have been questions about whether some Stellantis workers May be grandfathered into Roshel’s operations, no specifics have been provided.

That deal came as contract talks between Stellantis and the union representing more than 9,000 of its workers in Canada remain at an impasse.

“This Liberal industry minister, just like Champagne before her and the entire Liberal government, is costing Canadians money and jobs and driving our economy into the ditch,” said Poilievre Tuesday in Brampton.

“She’s been threatening lawsuits for years. She’s done nothing. That is why today the official opposition is calling for the Liberal prime minister to fire his failed, costly job-killing Liberal industry minister.”

In 2023, Stellantis received a $15 billion joint commitment between the federal and Ontario provincial government over 10 years as a performance incentive to revive an electric vehicle battery facility in Windsor and prevent it from being moved to the U.S. That agreement also required Stellantis to maintain its footprint in the province through 2035, which includes the Brampton plant.

Unifor has previously written to Joly urging the government to block the potential sale and clarify whether Stellantis’ intentions to offload the plant breached its commitments to Ottawa.

The Brampton facility had been slated to be retooled for Jeep production, a process that began early in 2024, before the company paused the plan in early 2025. It later announced it was moving production of the Jeep Compass to Illinois, leaving the plant idled indefinitely.

In October 2025, Joly launched a dispute process and claimed Stellantis breached the terms of its agreement by moving the plant’s production out of the province and to the U.S.

– with files from Global’s Alessia Simona Maratta & Karen Bartko

stories.title: Cat dies after fire breaks out in basement of Calgary home
stories.summary: The Calgary Fire Department said its crews were called to the 100 block of Doverthorn Close SE around 4 a.m. Tuesday for reports of a fire.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
A cat is dead after a fire broke out in the basement of a Calgary home early Tuesday morning.

The Calgary Fire Department said its crews were called to the 100 block of Doverthorn Close SE around 4 a.m. for reports of a fire.

Firefighters noticed smoke showing from a single-family bungalow when they arrived on scene.

One resident from the home self-evacuated and was assessed by paramedics, the fire department said. Crews rescued two residents from the basement apartment who were transferred to paramedics for care. One cat was found dead.

Crews remained on scene Tuesday to ensure the fire stayed extinguished.

Department spokesperson Alex Kwan told reporters crews didn’t hear smoke alarms going off when they arrived on scene.

“Typically, a smoke alarm that’s working would be active in that type of fire,” he said.

“If you have two different suites or different families living in different areas of the home, having smoke alarms that are interconnected is critical in that if there is a fire in one area that everyone in the same building is going to be alerted to that.”

An investigation into the cause is underway.

stories.title: Pwhl expansion clubs Hamilton, Detroit, Vegas and San Jose unveil team nicknames
stories.summary: The four markets (Hamilton, San Jose, Vegas and Detroit) were selected this spring in expanding the Pwhl from eight to 12 teams.
stories.author: Lucas Casaletto
stories.content:
By The Associated Press

Posted November 10, 2026 9:23 am.

The Professional Women’s Hockey League’s (Pwhl) four new expansion teams finally have nicknames and logos to accompany them in preparing to make their on-ice debuts next month.

It’s game on for the Detroit Clutch, San Jose Sea Lions, Vegas Vanguards and Hamilton Havoc.

The four markets were selected this spring in expanding the Pwhl from eight to 12 teams, and doubling the league’s size since launching on Jan. 1, 2024. Season 4 begins with an opening weekend set for Dec. 5-6. The unveiling of the logos and nicknames on Tuesday comes a month after the Pwhl revealed the teams’ colour schemes.

Though merchandise featuring the logos and nicknames is now available for sale, they will not be incorporated on the expansion teams’ jerseys until next season due to the branding not being available when Pwhl jerseys were placed for order. The four teams will instead have their city names printed across the front.

“Each team’s unique identity was built with the spirit and legacy of the community a the center,” the Pwhl said in a news release. “Women-led Pwhl design teams were at the helm of the process to develop each city’s brand identity.”

The league said the Vegas and San Jose logo designs included collaboration from the creative agency of Doubleday and Cartwright.

— The Clutch offers a double meaning in being both a nod to Detroit’s automotive industry and the ability to deliver under pressure. The circular black and white logo features an automotive wheel outlined in red with the word “Clutch” written across in art deco-inspired typography.

Fine-tuned details. Swipe to see all the elements of our new logo! pic.twitter.com/bTEw9XLwT9 — Pwhl Detroit (@pwhl__detroit) November 10, 2026

— The Sea Lions tie in the mammals populating the Bay Area waters with a circular logo featuring a sea lion’s head and torso emerging from the waves with a color scheme of blue and sunset orange. The name also pays homage to the West Coast Negro Baseball Association’s San Francisco Sea Lions, who played in 1946 and featured Toni Stone, the first woman to play regularly in a major men’s professional league, the league said.

Swipe to see all the details of the Sea Lion logo ➡️ pic.twitter.com/bPg32VMfDe — Pwhl San Jose (@PWHL_SanJose) November 10, 2026

— Vanguards was inspired by the pioneering spirit that helped shape the West and features the primary colors of cactus green, desert gold and navy. The logo features a kit fox native to the Mojave Desert and known to thrive in difficult conditions. The fox’s ears are shaped in a ‘V’ to represent Vegas.

No details missed. Nothing left unexplored. pic.twitter.com/TuiygKKnA8 — Pwhl Las Vegas (@pwhl_lasvegas) November 10, 2026

— The league said the Havoc’s name was inspired by the “balance between the forces of industry and nature in Hamilton, as steel mills rise alongside the natural beauty of the Niagara Escarpment” in Ontario. The logo features Hamilton’s official bird, the peregrine falcon, perched atop steel-forged lettering spelling out Havoc, with a color scheme of rusted steel, tempered gold and orange.

The Havoc’s nickname was exclusively unveiled on Breakfast Television on Tuesday morning.

A logo formed for the city, rooted in nature and refined by industry. pic.twitter.com/GqRmJx1ei8 — Hamilton Havoc (@PWHL_Hamilton) November 10, 2026

stories.title: Can my company charge a fee if someone doesn’t show up for their shift?
stories.summary: Rules vary between jurisdictions and provinces but in Ontario the Employment Standards Act strictly limits deductions from pay, experts say
stories.author: Andrea Yu
stories.content:
Interested in more careers-related content? Check out our new weekly Work Life newsletter . Sent every Monday afternoon.

I work at a large restaurant and bar that has been having issues with people calling in sick last-minute. They just introduced a new policy that if you don’t give 24 hours’ notice that you can’t come in for your shift, they’ll deduct $50 from your next paycheque. They said that if you find someone else to cover your shift, then you won’t have to pay the fee. I know they’re just trying to deter people from calling in sick so often but this seems unfair and possibly illegal. Is a company allowed to charge a fee when someone doesn’t show up for their scheduled shift?

Thuraya S. A. Lutfi , Lawyer, Lutfi Law , Mississauga

Rules vary between jurisdictions and provinces but in Ontario the Employment Standards Act (ESA) strictly limits deductions from pay. It prevents an employer from deducting, withholding or causing an employee to return wages unless the deduction is required by law, authorized by a court order or covered by a valid written authorization.

The written authorization must state that a deduction can be made and must refer to a specific amount or a formula for calculating it; oral agreements and blanket authorizations in an employment agreement are not enforceable. A policy announcement alone is unlikely to meet these requirements, and refusing to sign an authorization allowing a deduction from your wages is protected activity under Ontario’s ESA.

A signed authorization May still be vulnerable. In the context of a resignation notice, the Ministry’s guidance states that a written authorization would be invalid if the amount to be deducted constituted a penalty rather than a genuine attempt to pre-estimate damages. Whether that reasoning extends to missed shifts has not been confirmed here.

Statutory sick leave adds further protection. Once an employee has completed two consecutive weeks with the employer, they are entitled to three unpaid sick days per calendar year and an employer can’t fire, discipline or penalize an employee because they properly exercised their ESA sick-leave rights. An employee must generally tell the employer before starting the leave, or as soon as possible afterward if that isn’t feasible, and will not lose the right to the leave by failing to do so. Absences beyond those three days are not protected by this provision. However, disability-related absences May engage the Human Rights Code.

Daniel Wong , partner and chair, employment law group, WeirFoulds LLP , Toronto

Employers have a legitimate interest in ensuring that scheduled shifts are covered. Last-minute absences can create operational challenges, increase labour costs and negatively affect customer service, particularly in industries such as hospitality where staffing levels can directly impact the business. It is understandable why an employer would want to minimize the impact to its business by employees who fail to report for their scheduled shifts with little to no notice.

That said, employers generally cannot impose financial penalties on employees simply because they miss a shift. In many Canadian jurisdictions, including Ontario, deductions from wages are heavily regulated. While employers May be permitted to make deductions that are required by law or authorized in certain circumstances, a policy that effectively imposes a $50 fine for a missed shift May be vulnerable to challenge. Calling the deduction a “fee” rather than a “penalty” does not necessarily change its legal character.

The analysis can become more complicated depending on the reason the employee is unable to report for their scheduled shift, such as an illness or a family emergency. Human rights and employment standards legislation each provide various protections for employees who are unable to work because of illness or reasons that constitute a protected ground. A policy that discourages employees from reporting legitimate absences could expose an employer to additional legal risk.

As with many workplace issues, practical considerations are important. Employers May be better served by addressing attendance issues through scheduling practices, attendance management programs and progressive discipline where appropriate, rather than attempting to recover money directly from employee wages. A policy that is intended to solve one workplace problem can sometimes create a different one altogether.

stories.title: Man arrested after $1K stolen from poppy box: Brandon police
stories.summary: A man was arrested Saturday morning for allegedly stealing roughly $1,000 in cash from a poppy donation box, police in Brandon., Man., say.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
A man was arrested Saturday for allegedly stealing roughly $1,000 in cash from a poppy donation box.

Brandon police said in a news release Nov. 7 that police were called at 10:52 a.m. that day regarding a theft complaint.

Police allege a man stole the cash from the box, which was in a business in the 1700 block of Highland Avenue.

A 46-year-old man was located nearby shortly afterwards and was arrested.

Police said the suspect was intoxicated at the time. He was placed in custody until he was sober.

He was later released on an undertaking.

stories.title: Hydro One’s third-quarter profit falls amid rising costs
stories.summary: Higher revenue partly offsets drop to 68 cents per diluted share from 70 cents a year earlier
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Hydro One Ltd. H-T reported its third-quarter profit fell compared with a year ago as it faced higher costs, offset in part by higher revenue.

The power utility says its net income attributable to common shareholders totalled $413-million or 68 cents per diluted share for the quarter ended Sept. 30.

The result compared with a profit of $421-million or 70 cents per diluted share in the third quarter of 2025.

Revenue for the quarter totalled $2.49-billion, up from $2.3-billion in the same quarter last year.

Revenue, net of purchased power, amounted to $1.29-billion, up from $1.22-billion a year earlier.

Hydro One is Ontario’s largest electricity transmission and distribution provider with 1.5 million customers.

stories.title: B.C. deluge could bring 250 mm of rain as forecasters predict flooding, landslides
stories.summary: A deluge hitting Vancouver Island and other parts of southwest B.C. could bring more than 250 millimetres of rain in some places, as forecasters warn of floods and landslides.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
A deluge hitting Vancouver Island and other parts of southwest British Columbia could bring more than 250 millimetres of rain in some places, as forecasters warn of floods and landslides.

Environment Canada has raised orange rainfall warnings in west and central Vancouver Island, Howe Sound and the Sea-to-Sky regions, meaning the “severe” storms are likely to cause significant damage and disruption.

The agency says parts of Vancouver Island could see more than 250 millimetres of rain, while Howe Sound and the Sea-to-Sky regions could see upwards of 160 millimetres.

Parts of Metro Vancouver could receive 120 millimetres, while Haida Gwaii and north Vancouver Island could get wind gusts of up to 110 kilometres an hour.

British Columbia’s River Forecast Centre has issued flood watches for much of Vancouver Island and the South Coast, with the worst weather expected to last into Wednesday before tapering off Thursday.

It’s part of a stretch of wild weather that turned deadly over the weekend after the driver of a car was killed Saturday by a falling tree in Surrey, and after the death of a pedestrian who was hit by a car Friday during a heavy downpour in Vancouver.

A canoeist remains missing in stormy waters off northern Vancouver Island after their disappearance was reported Friday.
