stories.title: ‘Things will never be the same’: Wainwright prepares for Remembrance Day after fire
stories.summary: The Alberta town of Wainwright is gearing up for what could be the most solemn Remembrance Day in its recent history, says Mayor Bruce Pugh.
stories.author: Fakiha Baig
stories.content:
The Alberta town of Wainwright is gearing up for what could be the most solemn Remembrance Day in its recent history, says Mayor Bruce Pugh.

A fire on Oct. 17 at the nearby Canadian Forces Base Wainwright killed four soldiers and injured 39. Officials said last week that 25 were still in various hospitals.

“It will be different this year just with the weight of what happened,” said Pugh.

“Wainwright is a military community and it’s a big family.

“I get a sense that things will never be the same.”

Hundreds of military personnel, residents and dignitaries are set to fill the local ice rink on Wednesday for the town’s annual Remembrance Day ceremony.

Flowers and wreaths are also to be placed at the town’s clock tower, said Pugh. The fieldstone tower, which commemorates Canadians who died in the First and Second World Wars, has been standing in the middle of a downtown roundabout for about a century.

Remembrance Day has been significant in Wainwright for many years.

The town of about 7,000 people, located 210 kilometres southeast of Edmonton, is home to one of the busiest Canadian Forces bases in the country, and its members are deeply intertwined in local life.

The children of Armed Forces members go to school and play hockey in town. And residents are accustomed to hearing artillery blasts and feeling their windows shake during training exercises.

“We’re worried about our CAF friends,” Pugh said.

“I know they have tremendous support and strength, but how can you go through an event like that and not have a scar?”

Roughly 84 soldiers with the Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry were taking part in a field exercise at the base, when strong and sudden winds whipped a grass fire into their path.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has called it one of the worst tragedies for the Armed Forces on Canadian soil during peacetime. Three investigations are looking into what happened.

The four killed were: Sgt. Morgan Wong, 26, of Edmonton; Pte. Shaun Farrell, 23, of Prince Albert, Sask.; Pte. Aidan Goulding, 23, of North Vancouver, B.C.; and Pte. Hayden Lykkemark, 19, of Langley, B.C.

Among the injured is Sean Hiatt, a 24-year-old corporal with the Loyal Edmonton Regiment, who also worked as a railway track maintenance supervisor with CN Rail.

The railway said it plans to station locomotives outside the Wainwright arena on Wednesday.

“We recognize that this year’s Remembrance Day comes at a particularly difficult time following the recent tragedy at CFB Wainwright,” the railway said in a statement.

Jennifer Ford, an archivist with the Wainwright and District Museum and Visitor Information Center, said the mood in Wainwright has been serious since the fire.

“I went to school with people whose families served in the military and they were just involved in community,” she said.

“It’s a very close-knit community.”

Before CFB Wainwright was a military base, she said, it was Buffalo National Park. The Department of National Defence took over the area around 1939.

Near the end of the Second World War, the base temporarily transformed into a camp for prisoners of war. Britain asked Canada to host roughly 1,100 German officers at the site.

Ford said a guard recalled a very Canadian moment while describing life at the camp.

“On his first day (on the job), he noticed there was a hockey game taking place and it was between the guards and the prisoners,” Ford said. “He was kind of in shock.”

Some of the prisoners loved Canadians so much, they later decided to stay in the country, she said.

The site eventually grew into the base it is today.

Last week, the federal budget promised $25 million over two years to support those affected by the fire. Ottawa said it has a responsibility to support members of the military and the families who stand with them.

Pugh said he anticipates there will be a lot of attention on the town and the military this Remembrance Day.

“I recognize that this idea of freedom is not free,” the mayor said.

“There’s a cost that is paid, sadly, and those people are willing to do it. So they deserve our utmost respect.”

stories.title: Protests planned as Ovechkin makes first visit to Canada of final NHL season
stories.summary: Tuesday's game in Ottawa marks the 41-year-old Ovechkin's first visit to Canada since announcing his retirement. Washington plays in Ottawa once more this season, ON April 8.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Alexander Ovechkin’s first visit to Canada in his final NHL season comes amid plenty of controversy.

The Washington Capitals’ captain and the NHL’s all-time leading goal-scorer is retiring after this season, his 22nd in the league. But when the Capitals face the Senators in Ottawa tonight, the Russian star could face some hostility.

The Ukrainian Canadian Congress is organizing a demonstration outside the Canadian Tire Centre, called “No War Crimes in Hockey,” to protest Ovechkin’s support for Russian President Vladimir Putin.

A separate controversy is brewing around Russia’s reinstatement into international hockey by the Court of Arbitration for Sport. Russia has been banned from playing since its invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has said Russian players won’t be allowed to represent their country at next month’s world junior hockey championship in Alberta.

Tuesday’s game in Ottawa marks the 41-year-old Ovechkin’s first visit to Canada since announcing his retirement. Washington plays in Ottawa once more this season, ON April 8.

Connor Hellebuyck to address reporters before Devils play Jets Tuesday

Teams arrive in Calgary ahead of Grey Cup final

stories.title: Renovated Bloor West home on a ravine lands three bids on offer date
stories.summary: High park-swansea
stories.author: Sydnia Yu
stories.content:
109 Kennedy Ave., Toronto

Asking price: $1,998,000 (September 2026)

Selling price: $2,115,000 (September 2026)

Previous selling prices: $1,825,000 (November 2017); $1,201,000 (November 2015); $530,000 (May 2004); $194,000 (September 1987)

Taxes: $11,241 (2025)

Days on the market: 11

Listing agent: Andrew Ipekian, Keller Williams Referred Urban Realty

The sellers of this four-bedroom house on a 31- by 141-foot lot threw their doors open to potential buyers in September, setting a date within 10 days when they would consider any offers. About 60 guests came through and three made offers. The sellers took an offer that was $117,000 over their asking price.

“Sometimes offer dates fall flat, and sometimes they’re a big hit,” said agent Andrew Ipekian. “It really depends on the property and, more importantly, what’s competing around it.”

In this case, the home is one of few in the area to be right on a ravine, yet still within a few hundred metres of Runnymede subway station, restaurants and other amenities on Bloor Street West.

“The big selling feature of this property was it backed onto a ravine, and it happened to be walking distance to the subway and Bloor Street,” Mr. Ipekian said.

“Normally, you get one or the other, but to have these two [assets], it’s like having a unicorn.”

This two-storey house has an open-concept dining area and two entertaining spaces, including one with a fireplace.

The eat-in kitchen has an island, stainless-steel appliances and sliding doors to a deck.

There are four bathrooms, including one in the two-bedroom suite in the basement.

The property has access to a mutual driveway, but no private parking.

stories.title: Annex condo resale tops 2022 purchase price despite market conditions
stories.summary: ANNEX
stories.author: Sydnia Yu
stories.content:
77 McMurrich St. No. 313, Toronto

Asking price: $769,000 (September 2026)

Selling price: $749,000 (October 2026)

Previous selling prices: $720,000 (August 2022); $212,056 (January 2004)

Taxes: $3,936 (2026)

Days on the market: 30

Listing agent: Scott Hanton, Hanton Real Estate Inc.

Given the subdued condo market in Toronto this fall, agent Scott Hanton knew this one-bedroom-plus-den unit might be difficult to sell. But he felt that, with luck, there would be a buyer for one of these smaller models in a boutique building near Yonge Street. Listed for $769,000, it got off to a good start with guests checking out the interior every day.

“The last one-plus-one [condo] that was available [in the building] was a unit I sold about a year ago,” said Mr. Hanton.

“We had at least a showing a day, which doesn’t sound like a lot, but is actually a lot for this market.”

Some time after Thanksgiving Day, the 23-year-old unit received a conditional offer, at $20,000 below the asking price. Still, the $749,000 selling price handed the seller $29,000 more than they paid for the unit in 2022.

“There was a concern about how strong the current market was, and maybe they’d have to take a loss here,” Mr. Hanton said.

“This one bucked the trend and actually sold for $29,000 more than the seller bought it for in 2022. Some high-end renovations and staging made a huge difference.”

In 2023, this 740-square-foot unit was refinished with a new bathroom, laundry machines and hardwood flooring in the den, bedroom and living room.

The principal room also has sliding doors to a south-facing balcony.

The kitchen has granite flooring and countertops.

A storage locker and one parking spot comes with the unit. Monthly fees of $956 pay for water and heating, concierge and use of recreational amenities.

“The building is very safe, quiet and secure, and has a great reputation,” Mr. Hanton said.

“They are about to update the common areas. The budget for that has already been taken care of, so the new owners aren’t on the hook for anything.”

stories.title: Hydro One reports third-quarter profit down from year ago, revenue up
stories.summary: Toronto — Hydro One Ltd. reported its third-quarter profit fell compared with a year ago as it faced higher costs, offset in part by higher revenue.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Toronto — Hydro One Ltd. reported its third-quarter profit fell compared with a year ago as it faced higher costs, offset in part by higher revenue.

The power utility says its net income attributable to common shareholders totalled $413 million or 68 cents per diluted share for the quarter ended Sept. 30.

The result compared with a profit of $421 million or 70 cents per diluted share in the third quarter of 2025.

Revenue for the quarter totalled $2.49 billion, up from $2.30 billion in the same quarter last year.

Revenue, net of purchased power, amounted to $1.29 billion, up from $1.22 billion a year earlier.

Hydro One is Ontario’s largest electricity transmission and distribution provider with 1.5 million customers.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 10, 2026.

stories.title: Are Stelco jobs a bargaining chip?
stories.summary: The livelihoods of some 500 Stelco workers are the crux of a recent showdown between Industry Minister Melanie Joly and the CEO of Ohio-based steel producer Cleveland-Cliffs. Joly wants the company to reverse its layoff of Canadian workers, claiming it goes against the original agreement the company signed when they acquired Stelco back in 2024. […]
stories.author: Patricia D'Cunha
stories.content:
The livelihoods of some 500 Stelco workers are the crux of a recent showdown between Industry Minister Melanie Joly and the CEO of Ohio-based steel producer Cleveland-Cliffs.

Joly wants the company to reverse its layoff of Canadian workers, claiming it goes against the original agreement the company signed when they acquired Stelco back in 2024. Cleveland-Cliffs, however, says they haven’t broken any terms.

Host Caryn Ceolin speaks to Toronto Sta r business reporter Josh Rubin to breakdown the timeline of the Stelco drama, what legal action Ottawa could actually take against the steel giant, and whether or not the jobs lost are a chip within a complicated trade relationship.

stories.title: Dennis Crevits ready to tackle major projects in upcoming term as Central Elgin Mayor
stories.summary: A week before being sworn in as mayor of the Municipality of Central Elgin, Dennis Crevits is already becoming acquainted with municipal staff and preparing for the next four years.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
A week before being sworn in as mayor of the Municipality of Central Elgin, Dennis Crevits is already becoming acquainted with municipal staff and preparing for the next four years.

“A month ago, I didn’t have all these little red dots in my calendar, but now probably 75 per cent of the days are filled with meetings already and with what’s happening in the next four years,” said Crevits.

Crevits is familiar with the Elgin County administration building, having served as Central Elgin’s deputy mayor two decades ago and as a two-term ward councillor.

Across the street from his future office, the former St. Thomas Psychiatric Hospital lands are undergoing redevelopment.

With a request for proposals now before developers, Crevits said he hopes servicing will be in place on the property within two years.

“Something we’d like to see is the starting of the first phase where the main building is. We’d like to see a community, a village, a grocery store, commercial and then affordable housing, some seniors housing, perhaps a long-term-care home. We want a village, not just another subdivision, and that’s the important thing.”

Ontario Housing Minister Rob Flack, who knows Crevits and former Elgin County warden Tom Marks, said he is looking forward to working with the new council on the transformation of the hospital lands and expects to have an announcement in the coming weeks.

“This has been a labour of love, so to speak,” said Flack. “At the end of the day, I think we’re there, and it’s going to mean a great opportunity for people to buy affordable homes in the years ahead.”

Crevits said he has been hearing from residents about the issues they want addressed by the new council. Among the most common concerns are municipal water rates, an issue that has persisted through previous administrations led by Sally Martyn and Andrew Sloan.

“The water rates within the municipality, people still see them as extremely high,” said Crevits.

“It’s something that we have to focus on and we need to keep those in check. Something that I’d like to do is maybe work with the province and have a joint water board, but there’s different avenues that we will look into.”

With major industrial development expected in the region during his four-year term, Crevits said he is also monitoring progress on the Highway 3 bypass and is considering discussions with the City of St. Thomas regarding a potential business park at the St. Thomas Municipal Airport.

Central Elgin covers a large geographic area, and communities including Belmont, Lynhurst, Port Stanley and Sparta each face unique challenges.

“I’ve been contacting all the elected officials and the ones that have been acclaimed as well, and I’m starting to see some of the other issues that I wasn’t aware of,” said Crevits.

“There are some bridges that need replacing or repairing within the municipality. Another big thing is the disaster mitigation fund in Port Stanley with the flooding. That’s an ongoing process. We have one project going on down there on Bessie Street, but there’s other streets that are coming within the next couple of years.”

The new council is scheduled to be sworn in Nov. 18.

The new council is scheduled to be sworn in Nov. 18.

“A month ago, I didn’t have all these little red dots in my calendar, but now probably 75 per cent of the days are filled with meetings already and with what’s happening in the next four years,” said Crevits.
Crevits is familiar with the Elgin County administration building, having served as Central Elgin’s deputy mayor two decades ago and as a two-term ward councillor.

“Something we’d like to see is the starting of the first phase where the main building is. stories.title: Connor Hellebuyck to address reporters before Devils play Jets Tuesday
stories.summary: Connor Hellebuyck is expected to speak with the media after being traded to the New Jersey Devils and benched for their upcoming game against his former team, the Winnipeg Jets.
stories.author: Tavi Dhillon
stories.content:
Less than a month after being dealt to the New Jersey Devils, goaltender Connor Hellebuyck is returning to Winnipeg as his new team faces his former team.

The matchup, which has been circled on the calendars of Winnipeg Jets fans since the former league MVP was traded to the Devils late last month , will not feature number 37. The Devils announced Hellebuyck’s benching on social media Sunday with Sunny Mehta, general manager for New Jersey, citing a potential “reduction in our expected win probability.”

The U.S. gold medallist is expected to address the media in Winnipeg after practice on Tuesday morning.

Speaking with reporters in Toronto Sunday night, after the Devils shut out the Leafs 4-0, the three-time Vezina trophy winner said he must obey the instructions coming from management, despite his desire to play.

“At the end of the day, I have to listen to them, and I can only push so hard,” Hellebuyck said, adding that he will hold on to his “cherished” memories in the city.

“I’ve spent the majority of my career there and a lot of my accomplishments are from there. So, there is a lot to miss. But that being said, I am excited about the new chapter I’m in.”

Global News spoke with fans in Winnipeg ahead of Tuesday evening’s game.

Resident Mike Richardson said he doesn’t expect Hellebuyck’s absence to change fan reactions at Canada Life Centre.

“Everybody wanted that, just to ‘boo.’ However you feel about it, that’s the rivalry of hockey,” Richardson said. “I don’t doubt things may rain down on the ice, especially if he was there.”

“You’re going to hear a lot of chants about, well, I probably can’t say it on TV. But it’ll be a good game, but not the game everybody wanted.”

Blake Dowel is originally from the U.S., he said he is also looking forward to seeing the reactions Tuesday night.

“We’ve got to see some jerseys on ice, you know? Let’s do it. And I’m not even a natural Winnipeg Jets fan. I’m from the States. I just love hockey,” Dowel said.

Tuesday is the only time the Devils and Jets will face off in Winnipeg this season. They meet again in New Jersey on Nov. 28.

More to come.

stories.title: Landmark self-storage deal signals market strength
stories.summary: Canadian self-storage sees a boost amid high cap rates
stories.author: Zakiya Kassam
stories.content:
A landmark $1.67-billion deal is drawing attention to Canada’s self-storage market, signalling its strength at a time when other real estate asset classes are faltering.

In September, Texas-based real estate investment trust Public Storage – the world’s largest owner and operator of self-storage facilities – announced the acquisition of Public Storage Canada , adding 68 facilities across Toronto, Vancouver, Montreal, Calgary and Ottawa, and 5.3 million square feet of rentable space, to its portfolio.

The deal reflects a broader trend in the sector: Institutional investors and established real estate players are angling to expand within the Canadian self-storage market, where income upside is propped up by low supply and stable demand. Whether moving, downsizing, navigating major life changes or running out of room at home, people always need self-storage.

“In self-storage, you’re not constrained by long-term leases; you’re not constrained by any sort of legislation around rental rate increases,” says Oliver Tighe, national lead of self-storage advisory services at Colliers Canada . “I think investors are very interested in acquiring assets where they do have control over the income.”

That flexibility is increasingly attractive, Mr. Tighe says, as self-storage has become a more compelling investment compared to traditional asset classes such as office, retail, industrial and multifamily over the past five years.

The Public Storage Canada deal represents the third-major institutional self-storage portfolio sale in Canada over the past two years, says Mr. Tighe, pointing to real estate firm QuadReal ’s purchase of the 15-property Maple Leaf Self Storage last year and alternative investment manager Brookfield ’s more-recent acquisition of a stake in Montreal Mini-Storage.

Still, a recent Colliers report pegs the Public Storage Canada deal to be “one of the most significant self-storage deals in Canadian history.” It says the acquisition supports the depth of demand for large-scale self-storage investments in Canada and underscores institutional investors’ favour of the sector.

Across major Canadian cities, the appetite for self-storage real estate is supported by the industry posting higher cap rates – greater income-upside relative to purchase price – than traditional real estate asset classes. In Toronto, for example, Colliers reports self-storage cap rates sitting at 4.5 to 5.25 per cent, compared with 4 to 4.75 per cent for the multi-family segment. In Vancouver, the self-storage cap rates range from 4.5 to 5.25 per cent compared to 3.75 to 5 per cent for multi-family properties.

For investors, the appeal of acquiring self-storage extends beyond the properties themselves. Larger self-storage portfolios allow operators to spread marketing costs across multiple facilities, share management resources and direct customers to other locations when one site is full, says Mr. Tighe.

Meanwhile, developing a new facility can take as long as seven years to reach stabilized occupancy, making acquisitions a faster route to growth.

“There are benefits to having scale, and I think that’s what’s driving a lot of demand for these portfolios,” Mr. Tighe says.

As the Canadian self-storage market maintains momentum, Mr. Tighe expects the sector to see similar acquisitions to the Public Storage Canada deal.

“Over the last five years, the biggest trend has been consolidation – big owners of self-storage getting bigger,” he says. “Every time a portfolio comes up, it’ll trade from a regional owner, who might have three or four facilities, to a bigger owner who might have 20, 30 or even 100 facilities.”

Experts expect this trend to accelerate since many self-storage operators are either aging out of or leaving the business.

Over the next three to five years, this could result in “the largest transfer of self-storage assets from one owner to another in the history of the sector,” according to Colliers.

Nation-wide operators already own more than half of the self-storage facilities in the Greater Toronto Area, Mr. Tighe estimates, saying that share could climb to 70 to 75 per cent within the next five years.

Additionally, the growing presence of American companies, such as Public Storage, in Canada is another nod to the market’s changing ownership landscape.

California-based SmartStop Self Storage recently invested $74-million in a 14-property self-storage portfolio – a move that expands the company’s presence in Vancouver, Calgary and the Greater Toronto Area, and extends it into Halifax and Quebec City.

However, Simon Berman, chief executive and co-founder of Montreal Mini-Storage , says operators based in the United States May be underestimating the differences between the two markets.

“American investors recognize that Canada has considerably less self-storage space per capita than the United States – that’s an attractive starting point, but it can also be dangerously simplistic,” says Mr. Berman.

As of September, data provider StorTrack reported Canadian self-storage inventory sitting at 3.2 square-feet-per-capita, while U.S. inventory sits at an average of 7.8 square-feet-per-capita.

“A gap in supply isn’t automatically a gap in demand,” Mr. Berman adds. “The opportunity is real, but the assumption that Canadians will eventually consume storage exactly like our U.S. neighbours is a questionable investment thesis.”

Mr. Berman believes the Canadian self-storage sector has an enduring advantage: Demand is driven by life events, rather than the state of the economy.

“Self-storage is a surprisingly human business,” he says. “We often refer to the six Ds: death, divorce, displacement, disaster, disease and density.” Whether people are downsizing, moving, navigating transition or dealing with loss, the need for storage doesn’t disappear.

Still, operators are facing competition as new facilities enter the market.

Mr. Tighe says demand is highly localized, with some areas seeing an influx in new facilities as others remain underserved. New operators often offer steep introductory discounts to attract tenants, which puts pressure on established facilities to compete.

In Montreal, the competition is pronounced: 68 per cent of advertised storage units carried a promotion in September, according to Mr. Berman. He expects the arrival of more U.S. operators to add to that pressure.

Montreal Mini-Storage plans to respond by investing in technology, redeveloping underused properties and acquiring new ones. Mr. Berman says it is set to announce additional locations before the end of the year.

As U.S. operators gain a foothold in Canada, Mr. Berman believes Canadian stakeholders will have to lean on their local knowledge and relationships to differentiate themselves.

“They know the game, but we know the players,” he says.

stories.title: Jail ‘unreasonably harsh’ for Alberta man whose girlfriend, child died in botched at home abortion
stories.summary: The 27-year-old man pleaded guilty to disposing of the child’s body with intent to conceal
stories.author: Chris Lambie
stories.content:
A Lethbridge, Alta., man whose baby and girlfriend both died after she took an abortion medication sourced overseas has received a suspended sentence and 15 months’ probation after pleading guilty to disposing of the child’s body with intent to conceal.

The 27-year-old, whose identity is protected by a publication ban, argued in the Alberta Court of Justice for a conditional discharge followed by three years of probation. The Crown proposed three months of house arrest and 24 months of probation.

“If I were to impose only a conditional discharge, as defence has asked, I fear that public confidence in the administration of justice would be irreparably undermined. A discharge fails to reflect the seriousness of the offence and the social values engaged by it,” Justice Kristin Rae Ailsby wrote in an Oct. 29 decision.

“But the same is true of jail — which is the Crown’s position. If I were to impose a custodial sentence — no matter where it was served — that result would also undermine the administration of justice. Custody would be an unreasonably harsh result, and it would communicate that this court fails to understand the very real complex emotions, like fear and shame that women and their partners experience with and from unexpected pregnancies.”

The court heard the man and woman, who was 31 when she died, were in a romantic relationship.

“They met through family, dated for several months and, by all accounts, they enjoyed a loving relationship,” said the decision.

In January 2024, she learned she was pregnant with his child.

“Motivated by concerns related to costs, lack of medical coverage, family expectations, and community optics,” she decided to pursue an abortion.

He provided her with $500 to help pay for it. She used the money to purchase an “unknown medication from the Philippines,” said the decision.

She took it on June 10, 2024.

That evening she began to experience abdominal pain, which he “assumed was an expected response to the medication, even though he wasn’t aware of its risks or side effects.”

Over the next several days, her health worsened and the couple “continued to hide her pregnancy and abortion plans,” said the decision.

Her family members knew she wasn’t well, but the couple convinced them she “was simply experiencing stomach aches, diarrhea, and vertigo.”

Four days after taking the medication, she messaged her partner telling him she couldn’t get up.

He found her sitting on the bathroom floor and helped her into the bedroom, in the process, learning that she “had already discharged the fetus she was carrying,” said the decision.

“At no point” did she “ever disclose to her boyfriend where she had placed the child’s body.”

Indeed, according to an agreed statement of facts, she would not tell him what happened to the child’s remains.

Her health continued to worsen and by 7:30 p.m., the woman was “in an unresponsive state.”

A neighbour who was a nurse called 911. She went into cardiac arrest, and paramedics performed CPR before transporting her to the hospital.

Three weeks after taking the medication, the woman died at a long-term care facility.

It’s important to note her partner wasn’t charged with any offence related to her death, Ailsby said.

“He is accused of failing to report the discharged body of a child to police, making him a party to an offence of concealing the body of a child.”

His lawyer argued that he was in a “distressed state of mind at the time.”

He “loved his girlfriend, respected her agency and need for privacy, and was holding onto a shared secret about her condition and her health after forming a shared plan with her.”

The only aggravating factor the Crown pointed out was that he “failed to be honest or transparent, regarding his girlfriend’s pregnancy and abortion – exactly when (her) very life was at stake.”

His pre-sentence report describes him “as a good-natured, hard-working man who is deeply remorseful for his actions and mindful of the seriousness of his offence,” said the decision.

He was hospitalized the month after she died “due to suicidal ideations,” said the decision, which notes “he was diagnosed with depression directly relating” to his partner’s death.

He described hating “himself for his actions, does not believe is he worthy of forgiveness, and wants to make amends,” said the decision, which notes he “feels a profound loss from the death, the complexities of their child’s arrival into the world, and the loss of trust from his community and his family following this offence.”

According to the judge, “the sentencing goals of denunciation and deterrence are very much at play” in this case.

“This offence, which is very serious, engages several core community values,” Ailsby said. “The importance of healthy romantic relationships, the sanctity of children, the fragility of babies, and the competence of health care professionals to diagnose and care for hurt mothers and their babies, no matter the cause of that hurt.”

Because of those principles, which the judge dubbed “core Canadian values,” his sentence “must meaningfully communicate denunciation and deterrence.”

In this case, a suspended sentence “does just that,” Ailsby said.

“It is a conviction — and as such carries both the practical and symbolic effects of state sanction. Moreover, it’s a significant punishment that affirms Canadian values and state priorities.”

His motivation in committing this offence stemmed from his desire to respect his partner’s medical and bodily autonomy and the dignity she believed she’d achieve through privacy

Justice Kristin Rae Ailsby

A suspended sentence makes him “accountable to the state for concealing his child’s body, which thwarted the state from knowing the child’s cause of death — something which a peaceful state informed by charter values and engaged in public health wants and needs to know,” said the judge.

The man’s lawyer argued “very effectively, that his client’s criminality is an omission, not commission — that (he) failed to do something good, more than did something bad,” Ailsby said.

Throughout the afternoon after his partner took the medication, he didn’t inform anyone that she was “pregnant or had discharged the fetus, and allowed them to think that she was suffering from vertigo.”

Despite knowing the fetus had been discharged, he failed to report it to police or emergency medical services, said the judge.

“He is not the principal offender,” Ailsby said. “His personal degree of responsibility is uniquely attenuated by the fact that the abortion and the plan to conceal the child’s body appeared to be (his romantic partner’s) primary choices.”

He didn’t even know where she placed the child’s body, said the judge.

“But no matter what motivation inspired his decisions, the reality is that (he) engaged in criminality worthy of state condemnation.”

The judge lauded the victim’s mother for sharing insights about her daughter’s pregnancy and death.

“She has renewed my own hopes for justice and its relationship to women’s health,” Ailsby said.

“That is, I hope all pregnant women in Canada, and especially those confronted with the reality they are pregnant when they didn’t expect or want (it) to happen, not only feel lovingly supported in their communities, but also feel confident placing their trust in competent medical professionals who respect their autonomy, dignity, and wellness. This case has highlighted how very vigilant we, as a community, must remain in this hope.”

Chris Lambie is Atlantic bureau chief for National Post. He has worked for news organizations from Newfoundland to the Northwest Territories and is a three-time National Newspaper Award nominee, with a win for local reporting.

stories.title: ‘There’s zero’ for homeless veterans in Canada
stories.summary: Analysis: Veterans Affairs does nothing to help find housing for veterans, says a retired brigadier general in charge of a non-profit that is trying to fill the gap
stories.author: Donna Kennedy-Glans
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney spoke of compassion after the CFB Wainwright fire. “We stand in solidarity and compassion” with the wounded, he said, and in the House of Commons he pointed to the “acts of compassion that testify to the acts of service, selflessness and patriotism that our Armed Forces perform every day.”

“There can be a disconnect between compassion and bureaucracy when they bump into each other,” cautions retired Brig.-Gen. Alan Mulawyshyn. After 40 years in the Canadian Armed Forces — serving along the Iraq/Kuwait border, in Kosovo, and in Kandahar — he now heads Veterans’ House Canada, the non-profit that houses and supports homeless veterans.

“The day-to-day job is obviously housing homeless veterans, taking care of them, providing them supports,” he says, “but I think my second role is advocacy and awareness.” He has testified before the Senate subcommittee on veterans affairs and will talk to anyone who will listen to puncture the assumption that “there can’t be homeless veterans because of course why wouldn’t Veterans Affairs take care of them? We have a whole department. How can this be?”

Veterans Affairs Canada does some things well and some things poorly, he reports. Most veterans have case managers and can apply for disability and pain-and-suffering benefits; all good. The problem, he says, is that Veterans Affairs does nothing on the housing front: “There’s zero, there’s not a dollar in their budget for housing.”

Veterans’ House Canada, launched in 2020 as a project of Ottawa’s Multifaith Housing Initiative, was built to fill that gap. From the Ottawa site of its first 40-studio building, the Andy Carswell Building, Mulawyshyn sketches the coast-to-coast ambition: a second home in Edmonton opened Nov. 9; he’s in active discussions in Victoria, Halifax and Toronto; he wants a presence in Quebec.

There’s a veterans homelessness program, announced several budgets ago, he explains, that tops up some of the rents for the veterans the non-profit houses. “It took them a year and a half to actually implement it,” Mulawyshyn laments, “so a five-year program became a three-and-a-half-year program… the front date moved, but the end date didn’t.” Veterans Affairs wasn’t set up to run it, so the file went to Infrastructure Canada. The non-profit received some funding, but it is “a bit of a round peg in a square hole thing.” The program sunsets in 2028; “I really hope it gets extended,” he adds, “because it is valuable.” (Budget 2026 did renew the federal program for another decade.)

It’s about getting things done, solutions. You can sit and bitch about stuff, but I think solutions are what we want to see

Brig.-Gen. Alan Mulawyshyn

The non-profit fundraises for capital and operations. “We apply for grants, get donations from mom-and-pop businesses, collect donations from $5 to purposefully targeting defence corporations.” Lockheed Martin Canada and Boeing Canada contribute. One very generous supporter, John Carswell and Canso Investment Counsel, put up millions. Carswell is a veteran himself. “Mental health is a common theme,” he adds, “all of our programming, everything we do, has a mental health lens.” Just being part of a community, getting people out of their rooms, that is critical. “And it’s that double-edged sword, right, because you have a mental health issue and then you start self-medicating. Drugs and alcohol, which makes it worse, and then that gets rid of all your money, so you have to put affordability on top of that, and you have this vicious, vicious circle.”

Veterans’ House is a harm-reduction organization. “You do not have to be dry, you don’t have to be sober, to come to us.” If the rule were otherwise, he adds, “we might have an empty building.”

Military life is clear-cut. Wake up sick and the system books the appointment and lines you up for the flu shot. “It’s just a machine, right?” Leave the military, he continues, and “you get 90 days of your prescriptions, and if you can’t find a family doctor, if you don’t know how to navigate the system, there’s no one there for you, and that’s where this vicious cycle starts.

“Veterans Affairs Canada can help to make sure that continuity of care happens, but it doesn’t always happen,” he adds, “and part of it’s on the military member to accept help as well.” Veterans can be stubborn: “stoic self-reliance” is part of military culture.

The non-profit works with homeless shelters and the Royal Canadian Legion. “Veterans Affairs Canada case managers call us up and say we’ve got a client who’s homeless. We’ve had self-referrals…parents call us up for their kids.

“We basically do first come, first served. Otherwise you are playing God. ‘Who’s more needy? You served longer than she did.’ You just can’t do that.” It is permanent housing; residents can stay as long as they want, “but it’s not a jail sentence, they can leave whenever they want.” They have housed 87 homeless veterans in Ottawa since 2021; there is turnover. The average age is about 60 — he jokes that the average tenant is almost him, “a 60-year-old white male; that was the military 20 and 30 years ago.” The vast majority are junior non-commissioned officers, and about three-quarters are army.

In the United States the military pays a generous housing allowance. “Basically, if you live in a married quarter or a single quarter on the base, it’s free.” In Canada there have been no equivalent rent supplements or housing allowances, even while serving. “I moved14 times with my family in my career,” Mulawyshyn says. “We had to move from Petawawa to live in Toronto, and then back to Petawawa afterwards. It was really a slingshot thing,” and members “just have to suck it up.”

There is talk of ramping up investment in Canada’s military as part of the Nato commitment. Will that change the landscape? “I hope it’s sustainable,” he replies, “because I graduated RMC in 1987 and the ’87 white paper had just come out. Perrin Beatty (then defence minister) came and talked to us and we were young. We were getting nuclear submarines! I mean, this was an exciting time to be a newly commissioned officer, right? And two weeks later, that was all dead.”

Today the messages remain mixed. “The military is growing and growing but we just cut your budget by 10 per cent,” is what he hears. His entire military career was spent cutting and scrimping — unscrewing every second light bulb to save money.

“You can buy all the submarines and F-35s you want,” he concludes, but it is always about people. “It’s about getting things done, solutions. You can sit and bitch about stuff, but I think solutions are what we want to see.”

I don’t hear anger in his voice. I don’t even hear frustration. What I hear is determination to find a clearer path for soldiers and veterans. What I hear is compassion.

stories.title: A small Quebec town is grappling with fear after multiple restaurants were targeted by suspicious fires
stories.summary: Police will step up patrols in Ormstown after a string of suspected arsons shook the small community about 70 kilometres southwest of Montreal.
stories.author: Genevieve Beauchemin
stories.content:
Ormstown, QUE. - Police will step up patrols in Ormstown after a string of suspected arsons shook the small community about 70 kilometres southwest of Montreal.

The increased presence is a bid to support residents after Sara Pizzeria was reduced to rubble on Sunday morning. It is the latest alleged attack on restaurants located within metres of each other on a small street called rue Lambton.

Summer Eastwood, a lifelong Ormstown resident and owner of the nearby Taverne de la Ferme, a few blocks from the scene of the fires, said the situation is frightening.

“It’s scary,” Eastwood said. “I think both as a citizen and as a business owner, this is not the kind of environment we want to be living in. It’s very disconcerting not to know who is behind these attacks in our otherwise very peaceful and supportive community.”

A trend of suspicious attacks

Police said this is the second suspicious fire at Sara Pizzeria this month. Last week, a 27-year-old man was arrested moments after the first incident. He was suspected of throwing a Molotov cocktail at the restaurant. He remains in custody.

The recent fires follow one in September at an Italian restaurant doors away on rue Lambton and a July fire at another pizzeria across the street. No one has been injured in any of the suspected arsons.

“This is the first time since I have been in the department that we’ve had a serious problem like this,” said Ormstown Fire Chief Michael Greig, who has been a firefighter in town for 17 years.

Ormstown Mayor Philippe Besombes called on the provincial government to help his town.

“It’s very difficult because we are a little community,” Besombes said. “People don’t understand what happened.”

Quebec’s Minister of Domestic Security Guy Jr. Lapointe, a former police officer, travelled to Ormstown on Monday to meet with the mayor and to reassure the population.

“We are seeing more and more violent situations in regions, whether it is fires, or arsons,” Lapointe said after the meeting. “We are here for support, to have citizens feel safer. I think it is very important. We said we would have more police officers. We will do that. We are working on that presently.”

Arsons targeting restaurants in Montreal and other major cities are frequently linked to extortion attempts and organized crime. However, the Surete du Quebec, which is investigating the Ormstown fires, has not confirmed any links to criminal organizations or evidence of extortion.

Eastwood, a 20-year veteran of the restaurant industry, said her specialty is welcoming guests, offering diners top-tier service, and that she is not a security expert.

“I really hope our government is going to step up and look out for us,” she said. “I don’t think it is the job of restaurant owners to protect their businesses.”

She added that Ormstown remains one of the most beautiful places in Quebec, filled with warm and welcoming people, and she hopes people know that the arsons do not reflect the spirit of her town.

stories.title: Ford government’s Bill 140 gutting Ontario’s environmental rights, experts warn
stories.summary: The sweeping new bill is drawing sharp warnings from environmental advocates who say it will reverse decades of progress on environmental issues.
stories.author: Olivia Bowden, Colin D'Mello
stories.content:
A chorus of environmental advocates, legal experts and political parties are sounding the alarm over the Ford government’s latest red tape reduction laws, claiming the proposed bill would gut residents’ ability to challenge provincial decisions that affect the environment.

The Ford government tabled the Building Ontario Faster Act, ON Oct. 27, in an effort to fast-track infrastructure projects and cut down regulatory requirements.

The sweeping new bill, however, is drawing sharp warnings from environmental advocates who say it will reverse decades of progress on environmental issues and that could leave Ontarians more vulnerable to serious environmental harms.

“Eliminating the environmental rights of 16 million Canadians will destabilize the environment and the economy it’s built on,” said Joseph Castrilli, a lawyer at the Canadian Environmental Law Association.

If the legislation passes, “it’s pretty clear that decision-making will be more secretive and less beneficial to members of the public,” said Castrilli.

A key element of the legislation looks to overhaul the Environmental Bill of Rights, meant to give residents a firm legal voice in any environmental decision-making and the ability to hold Ontario accountable for protecting the environment.

Currently, the province has to comply with the bill of rights and the Auditor General monitors the Ford government’s compliance.

The Ford government, advocates say, is now looking to repeal much of the Environmental Bill of Rights, including the ability for the public to request environmental investigations, policy reviews, or to appeal any government permits.

stories.title: Some common forensics techniques aren't as reliable as courts presume: professor
stories.summary: A police dog sniffs out narcotics concealed in the depths of a nondescript car. An officer links a bullet found at a crime scene to a specific gun — and a specific suspect. An expert details the sequence of an attack based on the pattern of bloodstains in the area.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A police dog sniffs out narcotics concealed in the depths of a nondescript car. An officer links a bullet found at a crime scene to a specific gun — and a specific suspect. An expert details the sequence of an attack based on the pattern of bloodstains in the area.

Such scenarios have been mainstays in crime shows and court cases for years, but new research suggests these forensic and investigative techniques are far less reliable than many presume.

Sara Gordon, an associate professor of law at the University of British Columbia, examined how Canadian courts deal with evidence related to sniffer dogs, ballistics analysis and blood spatter patterns in a series of papers, one recently issued and two slated for publication.

“With all three of them I saw this sort of tendency of courts and attorneys generally to just sort of assume that all of these different techniques are reliable,” Gordon said in a recent interview.

“We’ve all seen ‘CSI.’ People just sort of automatically believe that if a police officer is testifying that a bullet was fired from a particular gun, they must be correct. And that’s just not the case with all of these different techniques.”

While they have the “veneer of science,” the vast majority of forensic techniques weren’t developed in a lab or university but in police departments, Gordon said.

It’s only in the last 10 to 20 years or so that their validity has been put to the test empirically, and “for many of them, the evidence isn’t supportive of the types of conclusions examiners tend to reach,” she said.

For one thing, each of these techniques is vulnerable to some form of bias, she noted.

“If the police officer is pretty sure that a person has narcotics, they might unintentionally signal that to the dog. They can do that, just something as simple as kind of slowing down when they walk past the person and that can, unconsciously on the human’s part ... cue the dog to alert maybe even if there’s not drugs present,” Gordon said.

In ballistics and bloodstain pattern analyses, there’s a risk of contextual bias, since the majority of examiners are police officers, she said.

“By virtue of their position, they have access to information about the crime scene that can be biasing,” she said.

“For instance, if a bloodstain examiner has information about the crime scene, you know, maybe who was involved, the relationship between the victim and the accused ... they might go into that crime scene with a preconceived expectation about what they might find, and that can bias their interpretation of what they see there at the crime scene.”

A couple of major reports in the United States flagged the lack of scientific support for several forensics techniques used throughout North America about a decade ago, setting off a flurry of research, Gordon said.

Courts, however, have largely not caught up to the science, said Gordon, adding she aims to provide that information with her papers so that judges and attorneys can make informed decisions about the admissibility of evidence.

The Supreme Court of Canada last looked at the constitutionality of sniffer dog searches in 2013, finding that police could conduct such searches with less cause than for others because they are minimally intrusive and accurate.

Since then, a number of studies across jurisdictions have shown sniffer dogs to be far less reliable than believed, Gordon said.

Successful dog alerts, meaning those that lead to the discovery of illicit drugs, “are often no better than chance,” according to her paper in the Alberta Law Review. An ombudsman’s review out of New South Wales in Australia examined more than 10,000 alerts by 17 drug detection dogs and found that dogs falsely alerted to the presence of narcotics 74 per cent of the time, the paper said.

“There are no national standards for the training, testing, and deployment of police sniffer dogs in Canada, nor any meaningful transparency about how these functions are carried out by the dozens of canine units around the country,” Gordon wrote in the paper.

Dog searches are also far from minimally intrusive, she said.

“It can be embarrassing, it can be humiliating, and it can really scary for people. And that’s especially the case for racialized people or people who are sort of often subject to enhanced police scrutiny,” she said in the interview.

As such, the same standard of reasonable and probable grounds should be applied to sniffer dog searches to make sure they comply with the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, she wrote in the paper.

Canadian courts have admitted ballistics evidence for nearly a century based primarily on examiners’ testimony that it’s reliable, “without subjecting those claims to meaningful scrutiny or limiting examiner conclusions to those that are empirically supported,” according to Gordon’s upcoming paper in the Dalhousie Law Journal.

While courts in the United States have started to push back, Gordon said she could only find one case in Canada where a judge refused to admit forensic firearms testimony due to concerns over the scientific validity of the technique.

The case, heard in Ontario five years ago, included testimony from a firearms examiner with the province’s Centre of Forensic Sciences, who said shell casings found at the scene were fired from a handgun found at the home of one of the accused, she wrote in the forthcoming paper.

Under cross-examination, the examiner said there was no specific number of “agreements,” or tiny corresponding markings on the two cartridge cases, required to conclude there was a match, the paper said.

That was one of the concerns raised by the judge in rejecting her testimony, the paper said. The judge also noted the examiner had not undergone proficiency testing, and that she had acknowledged the absence of a discipline-wide error rate for ballistics examiners, it said. He pointed to a landmark 2016 report in the United States that found no scientific support for the validity or reliability of firearms analysis.

Gordon’s paper said the validation studies ballistics examiners typically invoke to back up their expertise “suffer from significant methodological flaws,” including unrepresentative samples, testing conditions that don’t align with actual working conditions and the categorization of inconclusive results as correct. Meanwhile, examiners routinely present their conclusions in “highly certain terms” without disclosing the limitations of the technique, it said.

Ballistics examiners “will regularly testify in court that the error rate for that forensic technique is one per cent, one-and-a-half per cent,” the researcher said in the interview.

“It is absolutely not true that the error rates are that low. And forensic examiners just shouldn’t be permitted to testify to that.”

Recent studies on bloodstain pattern analysis have also shown very high levels of error, up to 32 per cent, Gordon wrote in another upcoming paper, this one for the Canadian Bar Review.

The technique does not appear to have received the scrutiny courts are required to apply to novel or contested scientific evidence, the paper said. Rather, courts have focused on the training and experience of the examiners in deciding whether to admit the evidence, “taking it for granted that the field is sufficiently reliable,” the paper said.

The principle underlying blood spatter analysis is said to be fluid dynamics, an “incredibly complicated” physics principle, Gordon said in the interview. While police officers receive training, some courses are as short as a weekend, and the vast majority of officers just don’t have the scientific training to apply those physics principles, she said.

“It’s a scientific language that dresses up this forensic technique, which is largely just the examiner ... looking at a particular pattern and saying, oh, that matches up with this other pattern that I’ve read about or that I studied,” she said.

“The problem is that they often try to go far beyond that and recreate crime scenes in really extreme detail,” she said. The science doesn’t support those kinds of conclusions, which are also particularly vulnerable to contextual bias, she said.

As a result, crime scene reconstruction based on bloodstain pattern analysis should generally be inadmissible, she wrote in the paper.

“A forensic technique with error rates exceeding 30 per cent should not be relied upon to establish guilt beyond a reasonable doubt,” the paper said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 10, 2026.

Paola Loriggio, The Canadian Press

He pointed to a landmark 2016 report in the United States that found no scientific support for the validity or reliability of firearms analysis.

Gordon’s paper said the validation studies ballistics examiners typically invoke to back up their expertise “suffer from significant methodological flaws,” including unrepresentative samples, testing conditions that don’t align with actual working conditions and the categorization of inconclusive results as correct. Meanwhile, examiners routinely present their conclusions in “highly certain terms” without disclosing the limitations of the technique, it said.
Ballistics examiners “will regularly testify in court that the error rate for that forensic technique is one per cent, one-and-a-half per cent,” the researcher said in the interview.
“It is absolutely not true that the error rates are that low. And forensic examiners just shouldn’t be permitted to testify to that.”
Recent studies on bloodstain pattern analysis have also shown very high levels of error, up to 32 per cent, Gordon wrote in another upcoming paper, this one for the Canadian Bar Review.

The technique does not appear to have received the scrutiny courts are required to apply to novel or contested scientific evidence, the paper said. Rather, courts have focused on the training and experience of the examiners in deciding whether to admit the evidence, “taking it for granted that the field is sufficiently reliable,” the paper said.

The principle underlying blood spatter analysis is said to be fluid dynamics, an “incredibly complicated” physics principle, Gordon said in the interview. While police officers receive training, some courses are as short as a weekend, and the vast majority of officers just don’t have the scientific training to apply those physics principles, she said.

“It’s a scientific language that dresses up this forensic technique, which is largely just the examiner ... looking at a particular pattern and saying, oh, that matches up with this other pattern that I’ve read about or that I studied,” she said.

“The problem is that they often try to go far beyond that and recreate crime scenes in really extreme detail,” she said. The science doesn’t support those kinds of conclusions, which are also particularly vulnerable to contextual bias, she said.
As a result, crime scene reconstruction based on bloodstain pattern analysis should generally be inadmissible, she wrote in the paper.
“A forensic technique with error rates exceeding 30 per cent should not be relied upon to establish guilt beyond a reasonable doubt,” the paper said.

stories.title: Milder temperatures before cooler weather returns
stories.summary: Another mild day is expected across southern Ontario Tuesday, with temperatures reaching 14 C in London before cooler air moves in later this week, according to CTV News meteorologist Julie Atchison.
stories.author: Koylan Azofeifa Rueda
stories.content:
Another mild day is expected across southern Ontario Tuesday, with temperatures reaching 14 C in London before cooler air moves in later this week, according to CTV News meteorologist Julie Atchison.

The day will start with some cloud cover before breaking into a mix of sun and cloud. Temperatures could reach 16 C in Sarnia, while Huron-Perth and Grey-Bruce counties are expected to see highs between 11 C and 12 C.

The chance of showers increases Wednesday, with a 40 per cent chance.

Temperatures will cool to 7 C Thursday, with showers possible, followed by a mix of sun and cloud Friday.

Atchison says overnight lows approaching the freezing mark could also bring a chance of snow mixing with rain.

“If we get into some action at night, we will likely see some flakes mixing in early next week,” she said.

A mix of sun and cloud is expected early next week, with a high of 9 C.

stories.title: Toronto’s Blue J Legal raises $176-million to expand AI offerings to tax professionals
stories.summary: Fast-growing company has expanded to 6,500 client firms, from 1,000 two years ago
stories.author: Sean Silcoff
stories.content:
Rapidly growing Toronto AI software company Blue J Legal Inc. has secured a nine-figure financing for the second straight year as it prepares to offer agentic products to its clientele of tax specialists.

The University of Toronto spinout led by tax law professor Benjamin Alarie has raised a US$176-million financing led by Baltimore-based JMI Equity. U.S. financiers Oak HC/FT and Sapphire Ventures, which co-led a US$122-million investment into Blue J last year, are participating, as well as past backer Intrepid Growth Partners, a Canadian AI-focused investor. The deal, set to be announced Tuesday, values Blue J at US$700-million.

Nearly US$100-million will go to buy shares from employees and early investors. Blue J plans to use its $80-million in proceeds to commercialize its nascent agent product and expand in the U.K. – its third market after the U.S. and Canada – and globally.

Blue J’s main clients are tax accountants, though it also sells to tax lawyers, making it one of several companies bringing AI-driven products to law firms to hasten the automation of often tedious, time-consuming work .

Mr. Alarie, a past associate dean of U of T’s faculty of law, founded Blue J in 2015 with fellow professors Albert Yoon and Anthony Niblett. They worked to develop AI software that would help lawyers and accountants speed up the process of researching complex taxation matters, powered by predictive analytics software. Blue J raised venture capital and generated modest sales.

Then in late 2022 OpenAI launched ChatGPT, the AI chatbot that answered text questions in seconds. Mr. Alarie realized Blue J could fold generative AI capabilities into its product to answer far more tax-research questions. “The technology wasn’t really there to allow us to create a system that could answer any arbitrary tax research question – until we saw the promise of LLMs,” he said.

Blue J rebuilt its product incorporating OpenAI’s large language models, relaunching it in mid-2023. The updated version produced answers in about 90 seconds, but they were wrong about half of the time, a by-product of the quirky tendency of LLMs to generate incorrect information.

The Toronto company set about refining its product, in part by licensing data from Tax Notes, a leading publisher of tax views and commentary, and benefiting from improvements to successive releases of LLMs. Many of its answers come from content licensed by several tax data and information providers, some in exclusive deals.

By the end of 2024, Blue J could produce answers within 10 seconds that were 95-per-cent-plus accurate and its users could have technical back-and-forth conversations about complex tax matters with the program. Some companies found users could save two hours a week each using Blue J, whose individual plans start at US$1,498 a year.

Mr. Alarie said error rates have come down by about 80 per cent this year as measured by “down votes” from users in response to its generated answers, which now occur 0.05 per cent of the time. “We can now confidently deliver an answer to just about any tax research question,” Mr. Alarie said.

Blue J’s increasing speed and accuracy spurred interest, and the number of client firms mushroomed from less than 100 three years ago to more than 1,000 at the end of 2024 and 4,000 a year later. It now serves more than 6,500 firms. Blue J’s annual recurring revenue has expanded by 165 per cent since its last financing in August 2025 and is now in the mid-eight-figure range.

JMI principal Jack Duane said his firm tracked Blue J for years, and received “resounding positive sentiment” when it spoke to its customers, “not just around Blue J’s technology and research platform but also around the company and team. What came through clearly is they are a trusted AI vendor in a space where trust is of the utmost performance.”

Asked of the competitive risk, including the threat that the LLM giants themselves will move into the space, Mr. Duane responded that Blue J’s offering is “extremely hard to replicate” due to its access to proprietary data “and most importantly, their unique domain expertise.”

JMI is one of the most successful foreign investors in the Canadian tech sector. Its portfolio here includes stakes in Clio, Pointclickcare, Jane, Safe Software and Benevity.

Blue J is close to launching its agentic offerings, which will expand its utility beyond simply generating tax answers to clients. Its new workflow product will also enable them to automatically draft other work using its answers, including memos and notices of assessment. “Blue J will be increasingly capable of assisting with just about any of those advisory workflows for which research is an essential input,” Mr. Alarie said.

With reports from Joe Castaldo

stories.title: Is your doctor working too much? Ontario seems to think so
stories.summary: We need to know if physicians’ billings are fair and justified, but should do so without persecuting hard-working doctors providing access to care in a crumbling system
stories.author: André Picard
stories.content:
Last week, the Ontario Ministry of Health sent “educational” letters to hundreds of physicians, flagging their “abnormal” billing practices.

The letters suggested they May be seeing too many patients, or working too many days.

Dr. Rebecca Hicks, president of the Ontario Medical Association, took to Instagram to vent her anger, telling patients that the “Ontario government is trying to limit the care you get.”

“The hours that we’re working to see patients, the extra hours we’re working on evenings and weekends, that’s not fraud. That’s patient care. That’s our job,” she told the CBC.

There is no doubt the letters are a bit ham-fisted. Singling out your hardest workers for criticism is a Management 101 failure.

But in 2025, Ontario paid out $19.5-billion to doctors. Their average gross payment was $469,000. Surely, when you’re spending eye-popping amounts of money like this, oversight and auditing is in order.

Physician billing can’t just be an open spigot, with no checks and balances. In fact, last year, provincial Auditor-General Shelley Spence harshly criticized the Ministry of Health for not auditing doctors whose billings raised obvious red flags.

She cited some shocking examples: Eighty-two doctors who claimed to have worked 24 hours or more in a single day; a diagnostic radiologist who billed for an average of 461 patients daily; and an ophthalmologist who billed $6.7-million in one year.

The Auditor-General criticized the Ministry for not conducting any random audits of physician billing. The process was complaints-driven until this year, when some doctors were flagged based on crude metrics, and sent the rage-provoking letters.

This is not exactly a witch hunt. From 2022 to 2025, the Ministry recouped only $8.1-million in overbilling, which is a pittance on total billings approaching $60-billion.

In other words, the chances of being investigated and fined for dubious practices are slim to nil. It’s doubtful there will even be follow-up on the letters sent last week.

There are even fewer cases that are referred to the provincial regulator or the courts. A Whitby, Ont., physician who routinely billed more than 24 hours a day was fined $6,000, voluntarily repaid $65,000 on top of an order to refund Ohip $6,000, and her license was suspended for 12 months .

In another highly publicized case, the Ministry went after Dr. Elaine Ma for billing $600,962 to operate 48 COVID-19 vaccination clinics during the pandemic. The courts threw out the case , saying the billing was justified in extenuating circumstances.

The large majority of Ontario’s 35,000 physicians are honest and hard-working . According to the Canadian Institute for Health Information, family doctors work an average 50.1 hours weekly, while specialists do 52.3 hours, and surgeons 64.2 hours. They are remunerated well for doing so.

But, like in every profession, there are some bad apples that make everyone look bad.

The challenge is: How do you weed them out?

In the wake of the Auditor-General’s criticism, the Ministry’s Payment Accountability and Fraud Control Unit adopted some metrics to help them flag over-billers.

These included billing for more than 15 hours of services in a day; seeing more than 100 unique patients in a day; and working a high volume of total days in a year. The doctors who surpassed these random metrics were flagged and sent a letter.

Most of the doctors singled out probably have perfectly reasonable explanations.

Dr. Adam Stewart, who has a bustling practice in Madoc, Ont., took to Instagram to say receiving a warning letter was “disheartening and demoralizing.”

What irked many doctors was the letters’ vague suggestion of wrongdoing, without any specific numbers, thresholds or comparative data.

There are no specific billing caps in Ontario because practices vary widely.

Dr. Stewart said he works almost every day of the year to ensure he is available to patients, and, “if anything, we should be getting letters of thank you.”

Like seemingly everything in health care, there is some history here. Until the early 2000s, the Ministry pursued doctors aggressively and unfairly, to the point where at least two died by suicide after being ordered to repay large amounts of money, even if their only failure was less-than-stellar recordkeeping.

A 2005 report prepared by former Supreme Court judge Peter Cory led to a revamping of the auditing system . But over time, it has become almost non-existent.

There needs to be a juste milieu , where taxpayers know physicians’ billings are fair and justified, and doctors are not persecuted for working long and hard – often too long and hard – to shore up a crumbling system.

stories.title: Claire Cruickshank and Betty McTaggart: In their 90s and still BFFs
stories.summary: Around the world, experts have declared loneliness a global epidemic – especially among older adults – but these ladies have no problem with it
stories.author: Ann Hui
stories.content:
Each month, generations reporter Ann Hui takes readers along to hang out with fascinating Canadians – regular people and celebrities, teens to seniors – joining them in their favourite pastime for up-close and candid conversations.

There are a lot of things that Claire Cruickshank, 94, has trouble remembering these days. It takes her a while to recall important dates and other details – what year she did what and when.

But there’s one thing she has no trouble remembering at all. As soon as she hears the first few notes of the song, she can sing every word by heart.

“Oh, we ain’t got a barrel of money. Maybe we’re ragged and funny.” She was singing on a recent weekday afternoon. “We’ll travel along, singin’ a song. Side by side.”

The song was Side By Side , sung by Kay Starr, and seated next to her on the couch, singing and bobbing along, was Betty McTaggart, her best friend of more than 75 years.

The two women first met as 19-year-olds, living across the hall from one another as nursing students in B.C. They’ve managed to remain, for more than seven decades since, the best of friends. And now they’re back living across the hall from one another – only now, rather than a student residence, they’re in an Uxbridge, Ont., retirement residence.

Around the world, experts have declared loneliness a global epidemic – linked with an increased risk of dementia, mood disorders, diabetes and cardiovascular disease – and, according to one well-known study, the health-risk equivalent of smoking 15 cigarettes each day.

Here in Canada, the problem is especially acute among two groups: Young people (between the ages of 15-24) and older adults. Older adults just like Betty and Claire. It’s a problem – loneliness – that medical experts and policy makers alike have struggled to understand.

But these ladies have had no problem with it. These days, the two women are together just about every single day. It takes less than 20 steps to walk between their apartments. They’re surrounded by other friends they’ve made at the retirement centre, too, who eat their meals together and take chair-yoga classes together. They play euchre together twice a week, and then bridge another night of the week.

So what’s the secret to their friendship?

Claire, who’s always been the quieter, shyer one – Thelma to Betty’s Louise – spoke first.

“We just liked each other,” she said. “It’s simple as that.”

Betty chimed in. “There were times, I’m sure, where we disagreed. But we got over it.”

She turned and faced her friend.

“You paid the rent on time, so you were okay.”

Still, they understand – especially from watching the younger people in their lives struggle – that friendship doesn’t always come so easily to everyone.

“I think the generations are so different,” Betty said. “When we were forming friendships, we didn’t have the same distractions.”

The two were on the couch in the billiards room at Aspira Douglas Crossing, the retirement centre where they live. They were killing time before a chair exercise class, huddled over old photos and reminiscing about the mischief they’d gotten into over the years.

There’s been a formula to their friendship, it seems. Part of it was good luck. But there were other important elements, too.

“I think you look for somebody that you can trust,” Betty said. “And a sense of humour. A sense of adventure.”

This latter point has been, in many ways, the secret ingredient. Over the years, one of them would have an idea. For an adventure, or a bit of fun. And the other would say yes. This dynamic was set early on in their friendship, after meeting as students in New Westminster, B.C. “It was clear,” Betty said – describing Claire – “that she was going to be a lot of fun.”

On one evening, that included explosions. Betty’s uncle, who lived in California, decided it would be a good idea to send some firecrackers to her student residence. And one of them – either Betty or Claire, depending who you ask – decided it would be a good idea to set them off inside.

“They went bang, bang, bang, bang, bang, bang, bang, bang, ” Betty said. “And everyone came running.”

“We got hell for that,” Claire said.

After graduation, after they began living together as roommates, there were other high jinks, too. “Foolish things,” Claire said.

They hitchhiked together. Drove off across the country together, twice. Moved back and forth from Vancouver to Toronto, twice. Worked as nurses together. Worked as flight attendants together. And then this is where the luck part comes in: In Toronto, the two women started dating – and eventually marrying – another set of best friends. Betty dated Bruce. And Claire began dating Bruce’s best friend since Grade 11, Don.

Even after both women started families of their own, they kept finding reasons to spend time together. They’d play golf together. Bridge together. Get together for dinner and a movie. They kept saying yes to each other.

Three years ago, after Betty’s husband Bruce passed, she decided to move into the Uxbridge retirement residence. A year and a half after that, Claire’s husband, Don, passed, too. So she decided to move into the same residence. Across the hall from one another again after all these years.

“Claire’s been such an integral part of my life. I kind of feel like we need each other,” Betty said. “Nothing ever fills in the loss of your husband. But it’s so nice to have her, to have someone I trust,” she said. “We can say anything to each other.”

Sometimes they can be found chatting in the billiards room. Other times they sit outside and enjoy the sun in silence. Other times still, they’re singing together, just like they did all those years ago – the Kay Starr song they’d play on road trips, or hum in the hallways at work. It’s become their theme song – a song they can sing together, even as other memories begin to fade.

At the end of the song, Betty said she hoped that stories like theirs might somehow be helpful to younger generations.

“I can see that young people today do need some help in making friendships.”

But it really doesn’t have to be difficult, Claire added. “Friendships become friendships because you like somebody, and you want to see them again,” she said.

“And we’ve just seen each other again, and again, and again.”

November 10, 2026 at 6:00 a.m.

Ottawa — Canadians support the construction of new pipelines to expand energy exports by a ratio of more than eight to one, a new poll has found.

The Ipsos poll to be released Tuesday found that 81 per cent of respondents said they “strongly” (45 per cent) or “somewhat” support (36 per cent) new pipelines and export terminals as a way to reduce Canada’s reliance on American customers. Only 10 per cent said they either strongly (3 per cent) or somewhat oppose (7 per cent) such projects.

The online poll, conducted Oct. 16 to 19 on behalf of the Montreal Economic Institute think tank, also found that the widespread support for new pipeline infrastructure extended across demographic groups and throughout the country.

Respondents from Ontario (84 per cent) were slightly more supportive of energy infrastructure than even those from energy-rich Western Canada (83 per cent). Residents of Quebec showed the least support (74 per cent) of the four regions, but they still showed an overwhelming majority in favour and included only 4 per cent of respondents who strongly oppose the idea.

Renaud Brossard, the Montreal institute’s vice-president of communications, said the poll suggests that many of Canada’s politicians lag behind the public on this issue and that opponents of energy infrastructure have not convinced the average person.

“There’s a need for the Canadian political discourse to catch up to where Canadians actually are.”

Brossard said support for energy and export infrastructure has been on the rise in recent years, spurred in part by the threats and tariffs from U.S. President Donald Trump. Wars in Ukraine and Iran have also raised concerns about energy reliance and supplies, he added.

Janetta McKenzie, director of oil and gas at the Pembina Institute, a Canadian think tank that specializes in environmental policy, said it’s no great surprise that Canadians are concerned about over-reliance on the U.S., but that support for pipeline infrastructure is more complicated than that. New pipelines and terminals take longer and May not be as cost-effective, she said, as investing in drag-reducing agents, pumping systems and other technologies that make existing pipelines more efficient.

“There are a whole bunch of options,” said McKenzie.

Since taking over from former prime minister Justin Trudeau less than two years ago, Mark Carney has tried to speed up the processes for building energy and other natural resource projects. The government has taken steps to shorten approval timelines, show a clearer path for completing such projects deemed to be nationally important and to eliminate the duplication between federal and provincial assessments. Ottawa has also made moves to make major investments in Canada more attractive, including the new productivity mega-deduction on investments that was formalized in last week’s budget.

The Ipsos poll also found strong support for speeding up the assessment process for major projects, with 71 per cent of respondents in favour and 12 per cent against.

Similarly strong support (78 per cent versus 11 per cent against) was found for increasing energy exports to countries such as Poland, South Korea, Japan, Germany and Ukraine.

The poll was based on a sample of 1,167 Canadian residents at least 18 years old between. The company says the poll’s results are accurate within 3.5 percentage points, 19 times out of 20.
