stories.title: Ottawa says 4,306 Canadian veterans of Second World War, Korea still alive today
stories.summary: The number of living Canadian veterans of the Second World War and the Korean War has fallen sharply since Remembrance Day last year.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — The number of living Canadian veterans of the Second World War and the Korean War has fallen sharply since Remembrance Day last year.

Veterans Affairs Canada says the estimated population of living Canadian veterans from those two wars has dropped to approximately 4,306.

Last year, the federal government department estimated that figure at 5,649.

Veterans Affairs said it did not have a specific breakdown this year for the separate conflicts, or of the numbers of men and women who served.

In 2025, the department said it believed there were 3,691 surviving Second World War veterans and another 1,909 from the Korean War.

Most veterans from the Second World War are at least in their late 90s now, while those who served in the Korean War are in their early to mid-90s.

The 2021 Census made a rare count of Canadians who served in the military and reported 461,240 Canadian Armed Forces vets living in Canada with an average age of 61.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 10, 2026.

stories.title: Collaboration helps cybercrime fighters 'paint full picture,' event participants say
stories.summary: A large video screen displays a running tally of statistics as dozens of people hunch over laptops, a freshly formed hivemind in the fight against cybercrime.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — A large video screen displays a running tally of statistics as dozens of people hunch over laptops, a freshly formed hivemind in the fight against cybercrime.

Operation Maple Disruption 2.0 is underway.

The event, which ran Nov. 2 to 6 in Ottawa, brought together partners working for more than 50 organizations — from banks and police forces to a large social media firm and securities commissions. It built on the first such event that took place last year.

It was organized by the RCMP’s National Cybercrime Co-ordination Centre and the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre to pinpoint and disable tools used to commit cybercrime and fraud such as investment scams and identity theft.

Organizers say over the course of the week, partners co-ordinated thousands of disruptive actions against a host of fraud enablers.

The measures included disabling email accounts associated with fraudulent activity, blocking phone numbers used to facilitate fraud, removing or blocking fraudulent websites, flagging, blocking, or cancelling suspicious transactions, and blocklisting cryptocurrency addresses connected to illicit activity.

In all, action was taken on 4,264 reports of fraudulent activity, with a total of $1.06 million recovered, the RCMP says.

Beyond these tallies, the organizers hope the connections forged during the week-long operation will carry over into future efforts to tackle online fraud — a battle that benefits from the combined expertise of specialists who might not otherwise cross paths.

Participant Octavia Howell, chief information security officer at credit data company Equifax Canada, said no one industry can fight online fraud alone, so bringing people together under one roof helps analysts draw better conclusions.

“The worst thing we would want to do is make an assumption that someone’s a fraudster, and they’re not,” she said. “So we’re able to paint a full picture because of the collaboration that’s in the room.”

Maple Disruption was designed with the idea of participants being equal partners, said Chris Lynam, director general of the National Cybercrime Co-ordination Centre and the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre.

Information of interest might be sent to all the banks taking part, prompting their representatives to compare notes and have a conversation, he said.

“They see that maybe the money was transferred from their bank to the next, and they go off into another room here and start figuring out, OK, like what can we do further as a sector?”

The RCMP’s Daniel Foy, officer in charge of the anti-fraud centre, said the collaborative nature of the event helps speed up investigations.

“When you consider the fact that we have to pick up the phone, send out emails, wait for days to get responses, now we can get answers right away sometimes or within minutes. So this is the value of what we’re doing here, and the partnerships that are created amongst the financial institutions, and seeing competitors work together for a common cause, that’s very important,” Foy said.

“The sidebar discussions that we see this week are, to me, great value because people are exchanging their best practices. They’re making links on the fly.”

Individual players concerned about cybercrime each have small pieces of the puzzle, said Graeme Bunton, executive Director of the NetBeacon Institute, an initiative dedicated to reducing online harms.

“Maple Disruption enabled us to get a bunch of those puzzle pieces together, so we can have a bigger view of the cybercrime that’s happening, and then take a good shot at trying to make that stop.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 10, 2026.

Jim Bronskill, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Muslim group calls Blue Jays’ Santander posts disconcerting, says there’s an opportunity at hand
stories.summary: Santander posted the videos in the aftermath of the U.S. midterm elections last Tuesday and deleted them two days later.
stories.author: Lucas Casaletto
stories.content:
By Gregory Strong and Sadeen Mohsen, The Canadian Press

Posted November 10, 2026 5:30 am.

A spokesperson for the National Council of Canadian Muslims said there is “a real opportunity here” in the wake of a series of anti-Muslim videos posted by Blue Jays outfielder Anthony Santander via social media.

Santander posted the videos in the aftermath of the U.S. midterm elections last Tuesday and deleted them two days later.

Steven Zhou, the Nccm’s media and communications lead, said while it was disappointing and “very disconcerting” to learn of the posts, the council was hopeful the situation could be turned into a positive.

“Generally I think the majority of our community wants to see a strengthened relationship basically — and education,” Zhou said Monday. “And above all, I think everybody wants to see an apology from him.”

A message left with Santander’s agent/sports management company wasn’t immediately returned. The Blue Jays issued a statement last Friday.

“Baseball is for everyone, and the Blue Jays have created an inclusive experience where all fans feel welcome at our ballpark,” the team said. “Individual comments do not represent our organization’s values and beliefs.”

The videos included a Christian preacher saying, “There is no such thing as kind Muslims,” with another suggesting Sharia law would be imposed on the U.S. after Abdul El-Sayed was elected to the Senate in Michigan.

El-Sayed, the son of Egyptian immigrants, will become the first Muslim American U.S. senator. He was the target of Islamophobic rhetoric on the campaign trail.

Santander, 32, who’s from Venezuela, didn’t play at the big-league level last season due to injuries. He signed a five-year, US$92.5-million deal with the Blue Jays in January 2025.

“Athletes and sports teams are supposed to be a symbol of unity — in a place like Toronto especially — where people of all different backgrounds come together to see ball games,” Zhou said.

“To see that juxtaposed and contrasted with this kind of thing, a narrative that Muslims identify with danger, with exclusion, and just that he May feel that way is just really unfortunate.”

Santander hit 44 homers for the Baltimore Orioles in 2024 but was limited to just 54 games with Toronto in 2025. He’s expected to be an everyday player again in 2027.

Emad Ahmed, a 26-year-old influencer from Oakville, said he was “appalled” when he saw the posts on Instagram.

“It just doesn’t rub you in the right way, especially being so emotionally invested as a Jay fan and as a Muslim,” he said. “Players that exhibit that kind of behaviour don’t make the sport as welcoming to join.”

Abdul Murad, the commissioner for a Toronto-area Muslim league called One Ummah Softball, said he was caught off guard to find Santander’s post circulating in the slew of online Islamophobic content after the elections.

“I didn’t expect to see a professional athlete, especially for one of the teams that I love so much, share that same sentiment,” he said.

Murad said many Muslim fans were upset with the team’s statement and lack of an announced reprimand.

Morgan McLellan, a managing partner at Sovereign, a strategic, financial and crisis communications advisory firm, felt the Blue Jays’ reaction to the Santander situation was “the bare minimum.”

“If the Blue Jays don’t tackle this with the seriousness that it deserves, I think you’re going to leave a lot of fans feeling disenfranchised and feeling left out,” he said. “And I think the Muslim community deserves a fulsome response and a clear action plan from the organization.”

It’s not the first time the Blue Jays have faced controversy over a player’s social media activity.

In May 2023, Blue Jays reliever Anthony Bass faced criticism after sharing a video supporting boycotts of companies that backed the Lgbtq+ community. Bass apologized and met with Pride Toronto representatives, but later said he stood by his personal beliefs.

Bass was designated for assignment before the start of the team’s Pride weekend and was later released. Atkins cited performance as the main reason for the move, but acknowledged the controversy was a factor.

It remained unclear if there might be any consequences for Santander.

“Realistically it’s a fine, a short suspension, or sensitivity training,” sports lawyer Emir Crowne said via email. “Anything heavier, he’ll grieve, and an arbitrator will ask whether the punishment fits.

“A genuine apology helps him there — and everywhere else.”

Zhou, meanwhile, remained hopeful that the National Council of Canadian Muslims would hear from the club.

“Our doors are absolutely open,” Zhou said. “We want to meet the player. We want to meet the ownership. We want to develop something going forward.”

stories.title: Ontario man locked up alone for more than 20 years 'not highly likely' to improve: independent psychiatrist
stories.summary: Camelott Hamblett, who has been locked in isolation at Waypoint for two decades, watched Monday’s hearing for eight hours without issue.
stories.author: Jacques Gallant
stories.content:
This story is part of 20 Years in Isolation , the Star’s ongoing investigation into the use of psychiatric seclusion at Waypoint Centre for Mental Health Care. The Star’s reporting has been met with calls for an independent review of Ontario’s mental health system .

There’s likely no end in sight for a man who has spent more than 20 years locked in isolation in his room at Ontario’s only maximum-security psychiatric hospital.

That was the stark conclusion revealed Monday by a forensic psychiatrist who conducted an independent assessment of Camelott Hamblett, a Toronto man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia who has been detained at Waypoint Centre for Mental Health Care in Penetanguishene since 2005.

Despite high doses of nearly every antipsychotic medication, Hamblett’s symptoms leading to his aggression have not lessened significantly, said Dr. Philip Klassen, who suggested modifications could be made to make his life as comfortable as possible with the hope that a new treatment will be created one day to finally improve his condition.

“I’m not saying there’s no chance” of Hamblett ever being released from seclusion, Klassen testified before the Ontario Review Board (ORB) .

“I’m saying, unfortunately, for us to have a good feeling about that question awaits a novel therapeutic approach to his mental illness.”

Camelott Hamblett

Hamblett was found not criminally responsible two decades ago for assault and sexual assault. He may well be the person who has spent the longest amount of time in isolation in any Ontario hospital. His story was the impetus for the Star’s ongoing investigation, 20 Years in Isolation , looking into the use of long-term seclusion at Waypoint.

Seclusion is meant to be the option of last resort to deal with a patient who poses an imminent risk of bodily harm to themselves or others, and to be used for as brief a time as possible. The Star’s investigation revealed that Waypoint has been keeping multiple patients with serious mental illness in seclusion for years. Leading experts have described the hospital’s practice as abusive, akin to torture, and unlike anything seen in other North American hospitals .

On Monday, the 44-year-old Hamblett patiently watched the virtual ORB hearing sitting at a table at Waypoint in a black T-shirt and wrist restraints; a wall behind him was covered with bumblebee stickers and the words “Bee-long.” His family, including his parents, aunt and sisters, also Zoomed in.

He listened as his treating psychiatrist, Dr. Stephanie Bouskill, acknowledged that his level of agitation has dropped in severity and that transitioning him out of seclusion remains the goal. He’s also been spending more time out of his room on seclusion relief; he especially likes going to the canteen and watching YouTube videos.

Hamblett may be the person who has spent the most time in psychiatric seclusion in any Ontario hospital. In a four-part series, the Star

Asked by Hamblett’s lawyer, Anita Szigeti, if the media attention and public scrutiny had caused Waypoint to focus more attention on Hamblett, Bouskill replied: “I don’t think I’m in a position to speak to causation or about media scrutiny.”

Hamblett nodded and smiled as his sister and substitute decision-maker, Cheyenne Phillip, addressed the hearing, saying she believes the coverage has played a key role in Hamblett’s improvement, and that the family continues to hope Hamblett will be well enough one day that he can be transferred to a facility closer to home.

“I feel now that the attention is being brought on the overuse of seclusion on him specifically in Waypoint, I feel like now there is more of a need to fix it,” Phillip said.

“Things are slowly on the upswing for him.”

Klassen, vice-president of medical affairs at Ontario Shores Centre for Mental Health Sciences in Whitby, described Hamblett’s psychiatric condition as “very unique.” His assessment described him as akin to a palliative care patient — a term Klassen retracted during his testimony, saying he didn’t want people to lose hope.

“We need to look for small gains,” he testified. “When you’ve had somebody who’s been in seclusion for so long, what can we do to make their life just a little bit more enjoyable?”

Camelott Hamblett, right, with his brother-in-law, Ebenezer Yamoah.

While Klassen’s report was focused on Hamblett, the Star has reported on other Waypoint patients who have spent over five years, and in at least one case over 10 years, in seclusion .

The ORB, made up of retired judges, doctors, lawyers, and laypersons, is responsible for the oversight of people found not criminally responsible or unfit to stand trial. All parties agreed Monday the board should order that Hamblett remain detained at Waypoint, but Szigeti asked that the board also order Waypoint to provide more detailed information about Hamblett’s time in seclusion.

The board had initially declined to order an independent assessment of Hamblett’s case, but was overturned in January by the Court of Appeal after the judges expressed shock at Hamblett’s living conditions, leading to the appointment of Klassen as the assessor.

Jake Gordon has been transferred closer to family just weeks after the Star published footage of

Szigeti told the five-member panel of the board she was surprised and somewhat alarmed by Klassen’s testimony — “We’re left with the evidence that Mr. Hamblett can be expected to die in seclusion because there’s nothing that can be done for him unless and until a new medication comes up.”

Klassen’s 12-page independent assessment report — which largely summarized Hamblett’s case history — recommended putting a TV behind Plexiglas in Hamblett’s room that could also facilitate video calls with his family. He also recommended an increase in the delivery of takeout food — something Hamblett enjoys.

“Mr. Hamblett has now been at Waypoint Centre for more than 20 years. There is no clear end in sight to his residency there,” says the assessment. “Highly unique circumstances invite unique responses.”

He also recommended better measurements of Hamblett’s aggressive episodes, and trying yet another drug, cariprazine; the hospital has said it intends to try it, but Klassen himself acknowledged that a positive response by Hamblett “is not highly likely.”

The doctor also said he believes the hospital could be letting Hamblett out of his room for greater periods of seclusion relief.

His assessment stands in contrast to the one completed by criminologist Andrea Monteiro in the case of patient Andrew Azevedo, who spent five years in seclusion at Waypoint . Monteiro’s 109-page report took a broad look at Waypoint’s seclusion policies. She concluded that Waypoint was using seclusion to pre-emptively manage patients who might become violent later — a practice now banned in many prisons — and that the hospital was detaining patients in conditions the United Nations has “deemed to constitute torture” in similar settings.

Camelott Hamblett being visited at Waypoint in 2024 by his sister, Cheyenne Phillip, left, nieces and nephew, and mother Audrey Watson-Pinnock.

A panel of the ORB relied heavily on Monteiro’s report in September in officially recognizing that seclusion is harmful , and ordering Waypoint to follow its own policies in Azevedo’s case . That same panel heard Hamblett’s case on Monday, but for one person — the chair of the panel this time was Michael Dambrot, the retired Superior Court judge who leads the ORB.

Hamblett spent well over six hours watching Monday’s Zoom hearing without issue, prompting Szigeti to ask Bouskill, his psychiatrist: Why would an order have been made Monday to keep Hamblett in seclusion?

She replied that the order would have been made by a different psychiatrist during “seclusion rounds,” when the cases of secluded patients are reviewed with staff to determine if seclusion orders should be renewed. The patients are not assessed during those rounds.

Bouskill ultimately found herself agreeing with Szigeti that Hamblett wasn’t displaying behaviour on camera that would pose an immediate risk of safety.

The ORB panel will deliver its decision at a later date.

The doctor also said he believes the hospital could be letting Hamblett out of his room for greater periods of seclusion relief.

His assessment stands in contrast to the one completed by criminologist Andrea Monteiro in the case of patient Andrew Azevedo, who spent five years in seclusion at Waypoint . Monteiro’s 109-page report took a broad look at Waypoint’s seclusion policies. She concluded that Waypoint was using seclusion to pre-emptively manage patients who might become violent later — a practice now banned in many prisons — and that the hospital was detaining patients in conditions the United Nations has “deemed to constitute torture” in similar settings.
Camelott Hamblett being visited at Waypoint in 2024 by his sister, Cheyenne Phillip, left, nieces and nephew, and mother Audrey Watson-Pinnock.

A panel of the ORB relied heavily on Monteiro’s report in September in officially recognizing that seclusion is harmful , and ordering Waypoint to follow its own policies in Azevedo’s case . That same panel heard Hamblett’s case on Monday, but for one person — the chair of the panel this time was Michael Dambrot, the retired Superior Court judge who leads the ORB.

Hamblett spent well over six hours watching Monday’s Zoom hearing without issue, prompting Szigeti to ask Bouskill, his psychiatrist: Why would an order have been made Monday to keep Hamblett in seclusion?

She replied that the order would have been made by a different psychiatrist during “seclusion rounds,” when the cases of secluded patients are reviewed with staff to determine if seclusion orders should be renewed. The patients are not assessed during those rounds.
Bouskill ultimately found herself agreeing with Szigeti that Hamblett wasn’t displaying behaviour on camera that would pose an immediate risk of safety.
The ORB panel will deliver its decision at a later date.

stories.title: Why the early flu season in Ontario has doctors confused
stories.summary: The season has officially started, weeks earlier than in recent years, with kids showing the highest positivity rates.
stories.author: Kerry Gillespie
stories.content:
But flu activity is still considered low, which May surprise families already coping with a house full of sickness thanks to the much higher rates among children.

Influenza positivity — the proportion of lab tests that come back positive — reached 7.1 per cent for the week ending Oct. 31, surpassing the five per cent threshold that officially marks the start of flu season. In the last three years, that threshold hasn’t been crossed before mid-November.

Positivity is higher among children: 22.9 per cent for five- to 11-year-olds and 15.7 per cent for one- to four-year-olds, according to Ontario’s respiratory virus tracker. (Positivity captures only people who get tested, and flu isn’t the only virus going around.)

By comparison, positivity hit 36 per cent during peak flu activity last year and for children it was 60 to 75 per cent, said Dr. Richard Mather, a public health physician with Public Health Ontario.

That suggests much more flu is coming. Experts are somewhat surprised that the flu’s early start has been followed by a slower-than-usual rise, especially given seasonal influenza started circulating before most people were eligible for a flu shot .

Once Ontario crosses the five per cent threshold, peak flu is typically about five weeks away.

“We think it will start increasing more rapidly at this point, but it has been a bit unusual what has happened so far with that slow increase so we can’t say for sure,” Mather said.

In the Southern Hemisphere, flu season was later than usual. Ontario’s early flu activity May reflect late-summer travellers returning with the virus, and the homegrown season hasn’t really taken off yet, Mather said.

“That’s one theory, but I don’t think we really know,” he said.

Whatever the reason, it’s encouraging news, he said, “because it gives more time for more people to get vaccinated.”

And early evidence continues to indicate this year’s flu shot is a good match for the most commonly circulating strains. Right now, that’s influenza A (H1N1).

It takes about two weeks from receiving the vaccine to benefiting from its full protection. So experts say now is a good time to get a free flu shot , the best protection against severe illness for individuals and for those around them.

“The important thing is that even though influenza activity is highest in kids, it’s older adults that see the most severe complications,” Mather said. Adults over 75 account for the most hospital admissions, followed by those ages 65 to 74.

With so much uncertainty about the season’s path, experts say getting vaccinated now is the safest bet.

As Dr. Isaac Bogoch, an infectious diseases specialist at Toronto General Hospital and the University of Toronto, puts it: flu “started a bit early, maybe it’ll peak early, maybe it’ll end early.”

But, he added, “if people want certainty, predicting respiratory viruses is not the place to be.”

Two other components of the respiratory virus season, COVID-19 (at 3.6 per cent positivity) and RSV (at 0.4 per cent), are considered low and projected to remain stable through Nov. 14.

stories.title: This retired advisor became an Honorary Colonel after being rescued from a helicopter crash
stories.summary: Diane McCurdy wrote a bestseller whose title was based on clients’ biggest question about retirement: How Much is Enough?
stories.author: Deanne Gage
stories.content:
In this ongoing series, Onward, advisors discuss their succession plans and transitions to retirement.

Diane McCurdy started her practice in 1976 when she was just 20 years old. She took on any client with a pulse, as the industry saying goes.

“That’s not what you do now. Today, you target more,” she says.

Her company, McCurdy Financial Planning Inc. in Vancouver, started with a focus on life insurance – specifically, ensuring businesses and families had solid risk management strategies. But she soon introduced financial planning. In 2000, she published a bestselling book whose title was based on several clients’ biggest question about retirement savings: How Much is Enough ?

In 2005, one of Ms. McCurdy’s longtime friends volunteered on Vancouver’s Board of Trade with Brandon Epp, who was looking to get into wealth management. The friend referred Mr. Epp to a hesitant Ms. McCurdy. Previous hires hadn’t matched her work ethic and client-first philosophy, which she brought to her 600 client households.

But after meeting Mr. Epp, she was impressed with his can-do approach and hired him.

“I couldn’t have asked for a better partner,” she says.

In 2021, Mr. Epp became the company’s president.

When Ms. McCurdy made a decision to sell in 2024, Mr. Epp chose not to pursue the purchase of the entire company. He valued the collaborative environment and the opportunity to work as part of a team rather than take on sole ownership, she explains.

So, Ms. McCurdy hired a brokerage firm to help with the sale. She eventually chose Vela Wealth Management Inc., an independent Vancouver firm that she says focuses on wealth accumulation, preservation and legacy for a high-end clientele.

“You’re trying to align everything and find the right buyers, who are aligned in thinking, philosophy and how they treat clients, staff and the team,” she says.

Negotiations took about a year.

Vela kept the name and branding for McCurdy Financial Planning. Mr. Epp continues to serve as company president. He also became an owner of Vela, continuing in his entrepreneurial journey in a partnership environment, Ms. McCurdy says.

Ms. McCurdy hasn’t visited since the transition took place in October, 2025.

“It’s for them to manage the way they see fit,” she says. “I know they’ll do it well.”

Still, Vela kept her on a 90-day contract as part of the deal, in case they needed to consult her. They never did.

“It just shows that the company was well set up and I was not required,” she says.

Ms. McCurdy’s priorities when leaving her business were to walk out the door but know that her clients and staff were well served. She says some retiring advisors struggle with letting go.

Advisors planning to sell should examine their practices objectively by asking whether they would buy back their own business, she says. If the answer is no, assess why.

She says advisors May first need to invest some time in hiring the right people, fixing systems and understanding newer technology, for example.

“It’s easy to get complacent because everything is working well, but in reality, you need to be changing constantly,” Ms. McCurdy says.

About 15 years ago, Ms. McCurdy’s husband chartered a helicopter to take them for a picnic at the top of a mountain as a surprise birthday gift. He was a geologist and had previously hiked to the spot; he wanted to share it with Ms. McCurdy. But the helicopter crashed in the B.C. interior.

The search and rescue effort introduced Ms. McCurdy to the Royal Canadian Air Force (Rcaf) and she became more involved with the military in the years that followed. After her recovery from the crash, she was invited to tour various bases and now serves as an Honorary Colonel in the Rcaf.

In this volunteer role, she acts as a liaison between the military and the broader community. Ms. McCurdy says she helps build awareness and appreciation of the military and its people, while supporting 442 Search and Rescue Squadron and 19 Wing Comox through a variety of initiatives.

Ms. McCurdy also serves on the board of the National Art Centre.

Retirees need to be careful to not overfill their schedules so they have time for friends and family, Ms. McCurdy says.

“As you get older, more things come your way,” she says. “You’re on committees, boards, your life gets more full. You only have 24 hours in a day and you have to [prioritize] what you are going to do.”

Candour, especially around the finances, is appreciated, and your name and photo will be used for the column. Please e-mail dgage@globeandmail.com and include a brief synopsis of your situation.

stories.title: Dabrusin defends Canada's climate record in advance of UN climate conference
stories.summary: Ottawa - Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin pointed to Canada's work on methane emissions and electrification Monday in defence of her government's climate policy before this week's annual United Nations climate conference.
stories.author: Nick Murray The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin pointed to Canada’s work on methane emissions and electrification Monday in defence of her government’s climate policy before this week’s annual United Nations climate conference.

Dabrusin will attend the first week of COP31 in Turkey this week. Some climate activists say Canada can expect some criticism there from other nations over its recent climate policy shifts.

Dabrusin disagreed with critics who say Canada has rolled back its climate commitments and argued that Canada is a leader on climate policy.

“When it comes to international climate finance, we’re one of only two countries that’s recommitted our international climate finance,” she told The Canadian Press.

“When it comes to methane, we’re co-conveners of the global methane pledge.”

Bangladesh, Kenya, Nigeria and Vanuatu joined Australia have backed a plan to double the number of homes with rooftop solar panels worldwide by 2030.

International climate finance refers to funding from wealthier countries, who are more responsible for greenhouse gas emissions to date, to help fight climate change in smaller, less developed nations which are often affected more by the effects of a warming planet.

Dabrusin will convene a ministerial meeting with the European Union of the Global Methane Pledge, a group of 159 countries committed to collectively reducing global methane emissions by 30 per cent below 2020 levels by 2030.

In June, UN Secretary-General António Guterres launched a global call to action on methane during an address at the London Climate Action Week.

Dabrusin also said Canada has been asked to lead consultations with Palau on oceans at COP31. Canada will host the 12th “Our Ocean” conference in May.

Canada and the United Kingdom are co-leaders of the Powering Past Coal Alliance, which seeks to accelerate the global transition away from coal power.

Canada’s environment commissioner issued a report last month which said the government abandoned work in 2024 on a 2021 pledge to ban exports of thermal coal, without any record of having a directive to do so.

Ottawa said that work is only “paused,” though the report also said Ottawa formalized the end of the work in August 2025 as part of budget cuts.

Ottawa - Prime Minister Mark Carney and several other world leaders who failed to attend the UN Climate Conference in Turkey have been awarded…

Canada has mostly phased out the burning of thermal coal to power its grid, one of the most polluting forms of electricity generation. Canada also has been accused of hypocrisy for exporting thermal coal to other parts of the world while taking a stance against it domestically.

When asked whether Canada told any of its international partners that the government had stopped work on banning exports of thermal coal, Dabrusin said only that the choice was made “by the previous” environment minister Steven Guilbeault — for whom Dabrusin worked parliamentary secretary.

Although Dabrusin was minister when Canada formally ended the work in August of 2025, she disagreed with the suggestion that she bore responsibility.

“I think that the choice was made to not pursue it under the previous government. And so making HR decisions around that — like, that was already work that wasn’t going ahead,” Dabrusin said.

“But what I will say is, we’re open to next steps. This is a new government, new minister, and we’re open to next steps on what we do.”

Antalya, Turkey (AP) — Climate activist Greta Thunberg arrived at U.N. climate talks on Tuesday, condemning the annual proceedings as hypocrit…

Some critics aren’t convinced.

“The hypocrisy in saying it’s too dirty for us, but we’re happy to make millions from it, and we’re happy to allow — because most of that thermal coal is U.S. thermal coal that they can’t ship out of their own ports. So talk about the opposite of the ‘elbows up,’” said Julia Levin, associate director of national climate at Environmental Defence.

She told The Canadian Press while Canada’s leadership on coal has helped other countries transition away from it, Ottawa’s reputation is vulnerable.

“Ideally, Canada should reaffirm the commitment to banning the export of thermal coal,” Levin said.

“If they refuse to do that, then they have no business chairing the (Powering Past Coal) Alliance.”

MP Patrick Bonin, the Bloc Québécois climate critic, also told The Canadian Press Canada should step away from the alliance.

“Very clearly Canada should step down. And short of that, we hope that the other member states that continue their commitments show Canada the door,” Bonin said in French.

“It’s as if there was a delinquent at the head of this initiative. It doesn’t make sense. For the good of this initiative, Canada should step aside.”

Bonin is also attending COP as part of the Canadian delegation. He acknowledged Canada has done work on reducing methane emissions — though he noted Ottawa has delayed the implementation of its methane regulations.

Dabrusin said other countries are still keen to work with Canada and many have turned to it as a reliable energy partner.

Asked how Canada reconciles responding to those calls with maintaining its climate goals, Dabrusin cited Canada’s electrification plans — to which Ottawa committed $50 billion in its latest budget, mostly through tax credits.

“We’re working on building our electricity grid. That actually allows for the switching to electrification, which needs to be done to reduce our emissions,” she said.

“We’re focused on … increasing energy efficiency. And then the innovation, which we do have a lot of the great strong clean tech companies to be able to do what we need to do to get to net zero. And we’re absolutely committed to our Paris commitments.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 10, 2026.

stories.title: ‘I can feel their heart’: Silver Cross mother offers condolences over Wainwright
stories.summary: Ottawa — Virginia Hicks did not know when the Royal Canadian Legion chose her as Canada's Silver Cross mother in June that a deadly training accident would soon cast a shadow over this year's Remembrance Day ceremonies.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — Virginia Hicks did not know when the Royal Canadian Legion chose her as Canada’s Silver Cross mother in June that a deadly training accident would soon cast a shadow over this year’s Remembrance Day ceremonies.

Hicks lost one of her own daughters, Mariebeth Short, in a military training accident 24 years ago.

Hicks said she was shocked to learn of the fire that broke out during a training exercise at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, Alta., last month, claiming four lives and injuring dozens more.

“When we were watching the news, my husband and I, we heard about the accident in Wainwright and it was like someone had poured cold water over you. It was like, oh my God, not again — and with such numbers.” Hicks told The Canadian Press in an interview.

“You think, those parents, I can feel their heart. I know what they’re going through.”

Hicks said many Canadians do not understand that “the grief is the same” when tragedy strikes during peacetime.

“When someone dies in theatre, everybody is very sad. Oh my God, he was in Kandahar, he was in Kabul, he was in Bosnia, he was in Latvia. That is tragic because they’ve died away from their loved ones. They’ve died in a different country,” she said.

“But when someone is in Canada and is training and they die in training, that’s just as important because they are training to go over to these places where the government has put our name on the line saying we can go.”

Hicks, who lives in Frankford, Ont., will lay a wreath at the National War Memorial during the Remembrance Day ceremonies in the capital on Wednesday on behalf of Canadian mothers whose children died in military service.

Her daughter Mariebeth Short, a sapper in a combat engineer regiment, died in 2002 when the light armoured vehicle she was travelling in rolled over in Petawawa, Ont.

Sapper Short was 4 foot 11 and about 95 pounds. Hicks described her daughter as smart, funny and extremely confident — a spirited personality who relished any opportunity to surprise those who underestimated her.

“You could never give her a task that she would not complete, regardless of how long it took her,” Hicks said. “Anybody that worked with her gave her 100 per cent credit because they at first assumed that she couldn’t do the hard jobs.

“She was just as big as the six-foot fellows in her unit and anybody else that wanted to contest her, she showed them they were wrong.”

Short was 22 when she died. She would have turned 46 in January.

Short joined the forces in 2000. She wanted to see the world and find a career she could be proud of, Hicks said.

Short came from four generations of military — both her parents served. Hicks had served for more than ten years when her daughter died,

On Sept. 23, 2002, Short called her mother at work and said she was really excited because she was first on the list to drive the LAV during training.

Just before the accident, Short had switched positions with another combat engineer so she could stand outside the gunner’s hatch to watch what was going on.

As the vehicle came down the hill, its tires caught in an old trench. The front left wheel assembly snapped off, causing the vehicle to roll over twice.

Hicks and her husband Brian had just moved into a new home in Halifax. Brian was finishing up some odd jobs outside the house at around 7 p.m. when a vehicle with military plates pulled into the driveway. He quickly recognized the padre from his collar badges.

Within 24 hours, a grieving Hicks and her husband were on a plane to Ottawa and headed to CFB Petawawa.

It still took just over a year after the accident for Short’s family to learn what the official investigation concluded. That news came on Nov. 11, 2003, a day before Hicks was deployed to Kabul, Afghanistan. It would take many more months for her to obtain the accident reports.

They concluded the vehicle’s front wheel assembly had a substandard weld.

The information changed Hicks’ view of the accident — it was not the fault of anyone involved in the training, she said, but was caused by someone on the factory floor.

The family tried to sue the manufacturer but the company went on to declare bankruptcy. She never got closure.

Every year, Hicks visits the site where the accident happened.

“They’ve allowed us go back into the regimental buildings and to the monument that they have created for their fallen members,” Hicks said of the Canadian Armed Forces. “For me, the military was more supportive than the manufacturer. There was never any, ‘I’m sorry.'”

The military has been accused of being too slow to release details about the incident in Wainwright, which is now subject to three separate investigations.

Sgt. Morgan Wong of Edmonton, Pte. Shaun Farrell of Prince Albert, Sask., Pte. Aidan Goulding of North Vancouver and Pte. Hayden Lykkemark of Langley, B.C., were killed in Wainwright last month when strong winds suddenly swept up a grass fire and carried it across the training range.

As of Nov. 4, 14 of the personnel who suffered burn injuries had been released from hospital while 25 remain hospitalized, according to the Department of National Defence.

Hicks said her message to those affected by the Wainwright tragedy is to hold tight and be patient, as difficult as that can be after a catastrophe.

“I know it’s a hard thing to say, but the military will find out what happened, why it happened,” Hicks said.

“Allow them the time to do the investigation so there’s no rumours or innuendoes or whatever is in your mind. Let them do their job. They’re good at their job.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 10, 2026.

Kyle Duggan, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Writers' Trust of Canada set to hand out eight book awards, more than $400K in cash
stories.summary: Toronto - The Writers' Trust of Canada is set to hand out eight literary awards and more than $400,000 in prize money at its annual awards ceremony tonight.
stories.author: Kaitlyn McGrath The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - Moments after Canadian-American author Zak Jones accepted the top fiction prize at this year’s Writers’ Trust Awards for his debut novel “Fancy Gap,” he quipped that many of his friends have told him “the acknowledgments are the best part of the book.”

“So many people keep telling me that,” he said as he accepted the $70,000 Atwood Gibson Writers’ Trust Fiction Prize. “So please pick it up at the library and read the acknowledgments.”

Of course, the Writers’ Trust jurors clearly thought the rest of the book was pretty good, too.

“Fancy Gap” tells the story of three estranged family members in Appalachia struggling with loss and poverty.

The jurors praised Jones, who grew up in rural North Carolina and now lives in Toronto, for bringing the setting alive through sight, sound, taste and smell in a slow burn that “leaves readers feeling as if they, too, are in detox from a world they’ve only ever heard whispered about.”

In his speech, Jones thanked readers who picked up his book.

“It’s very easy as Canadians to dismiss stories about the United States as frivolous and unnecessary,” he said.

In an interview after the awards, Jones said while the novel is set in the United States, it touches on universal themes.

“Canadian readers are some of the best readers in the world at finding universal messages, morals, feelings, stories in any given text,” said Jones, who won a Writers’ Trust award for emerging writers in 2023. “We owe a lot of that to the kind of diverse nature of our readership writ large.

“We have a culture here of allowing ourselves to explore other universes. And I would say that that extends to ‘Fancy Gap,’ just like any other book.”

Other finalists for the Atwood Gibson prize included “My Person” by Téa Mutonji; “Riverword” by Lisa Robertson; “Treat Them As Buffalo” by Blair Palmer Yoxall; and “Seven Heavens Away” by Ashraf Zaghal.

Jones was among the eight winners at the ceremony, hosted by artist and poet Moez Surani, that saw the Writers’ Trust of Canada hand out more than $400,000 in cash prizes at the CBC’s Glenn Gould Studio.

British Columbia-based author Robert Moor took home the $75,000 Hilary Weston Writers’ Trust Prize for Nonfiction for “In Trees: An Exploration,” a book he spent nine years writing that examines what trees can teach us about life.

After Moor took the stage, he told the audience he was so sure he wouldn’t win that he didn’t print his speech.

“Oh, this is a nightmare,” he said, stalling as he frantically scrolled his phone.

Once he found his prepared remarks, Moor acknowledged the strange climate writers are living in right now during the rise of “artificial so-called intelligence.”

“I know it sounds self-congratulatory and absurd when people all over the world are dying from wars and climate chaos, when children are drowning right now in Gaza, but I truly believe that reading and writing is an act of resistance,” Moor said.

The jurors in their citation praised his “exquisite and deeply erudite meditation on trees, but more importantly on humanity’s relationship with the natural world.”

In an interview after the ceremony, Moor called the recognition “life-changing.”

“It gives you that energy you need to keep going,” Moor said.

Misha Solomon won the $12,000 Dayne Ogilvie Prize for LGBTQ2S+ Emerging Writers for his collection of narrative poems in “My Great-Grandfather Danced Ballet,” which weaves a fictionalized portrait of Solomon’s great-grandfather with his own life in Montreal.

Meanwhile, writer, poet and editor Rachel Rose received the inaugural $25,000 Nancy Flight Writers’ Trust Prize for Nonfiction Editing for her work on Kirsten Johnson’s memoir “Humanitarienne: A Doctor’s Stories from the Conflict Zone,” about the physician’s work in war-torn and disaster-affected regions.

The award was introduced this year to recognize a group generally out of the spotlight.

Rose joked it was “the most Canadian of awards.”

“To recognize editors, those invisible people who work behind the scenes to make good books even better, who usually expect and get no recognition whatsoever,” Rose said. “All I can say is, go Canada.”

Several authors also won awards for career achievements.

Margaret Christakos received the $60,000 Latner Griffin Writers’ Trust Poetry Prize, while Maria Campbell took home the $40,000 Matt Cohen Award: In Celebration of a Writing Life.

Cherie Dimaline, author of “The Marrow Thieves,” snatched up the $40,000 Vicky Metcalf Award for Literature for Young People, and Shaena Lambert won the $25,000 Writers’ Trust Engel Findley Award.

The prize is given to an outstanding writer of fiction in their mid-career.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 10, 2026.

stories.title: New biopic shows Stallone's 'Rocky' rise was the real underdog story
stories.summary: Toronto - Five decades after it was released, “Rocky,” the film about a small-time boxer who takes on a world heavyweight champion, remains a tale cherished by underdogs everywhere.
stories.author: Kaitlyn McGrath The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - Five decades after it was released, “Rocky,” the film about a small-time boxer who takes on a world heavyweight champion, remains a tale cherished by underdogs everywhere.

Yet the true story of how Sylvester Stallone, then a struggling actor, wrote the screenplay and fought to star in the Academy Award-winning film, might be the more compelling against-the-odds narrative.

At least that’s the belief of Peter Farrelly, the director behind the crowd-pleasing biopic “I Play Rocky,” which hits Canadian theatres Friday.

‘Rocky’ is a classic film beloved by many. ‘I Play Rocky’ director Peter Farrelly discusses why he “wasn’t that afraid” to take on making a movie about the behind-the-scenes story of how Sylvester Stallone fought to star in the film after writing the screenplay. (Nov. 10, 2026)

“The reason I wanted to do it is because I felt this actually had a bigger arc. Rocky had a job in the beginning. He was a bone breaker, but he had a job. And, at the end, he doesn’t win, he survives. Stallone was homeless. He’s doing soft core porn. He is selling his dog. And he wins the Oscar,” Farrelly said.

“When I read this thing, I was like, this is better than ‘Rocky’ and gives you the same feeling,” the award-winning director said.

Up-and-comer Anthony Ippolito stars as Stallone and the 27-year-old actor has earned critical praise for his portrayal, particularly for capturing Stallone’s specific voice and mannerisms.

The movie follows a young Stallone trying to land acting parts when he’s encouraged by then-girlfriend, Sasha, played by AnnaSophia Robb, to write a part for himself. When his “Rocky” script impresses a pair of Hollywood producers, Stallone doesn’t back down until the studio lets the then-unknown actor play the titular role of Rocky Balboa.

Ippolito, who earned the part after sending a self-taped audition to the filmmakers, said playing the action star involved doing homework and undergoing a physical transformation to bulk up. But to embody Stallone, rather than merely impersonate him, Ippolito said he focused on connecting to the material.

“It’s just a great story and so just kind of deciding that you’re going to take a more organic approach to this and enter it from a more vulnerable place as opposed to from an external sort of portrayal,” he said.

Farrelly called Ippolito “a superstar”

“When he’s in a scene, he is in a scene,” the director said. “He’s not faking it, he’s there, and you feel his performance.”

Meanwhile, Toronto-born Stephan James stars in the film as athlete-turned-actor Carl Weathers, who played Apollo Creed, the heavyweight champion who challenges Balboa.

Crowd-pleasing biopic ‘I Play Rocky’ tells the real-life against-the-odds story of how Sylvester Stallone fought to star in ‘Rocky’ after penning its screenplay. Anthony Ippolito and Stephan James, who star in the new film, discuss why they believe people like to root for the underdog. (Nov. 10, 2026)

James watched footage of Weathers, who died in 2024, and said he tried to “offer up something different than what people are used to seeing from Carl.”

“Trying to balance what we know as Carl and then giving him a layer of humanity, frustration, insecurity, vulnerability, whatever that is to make him more relatable to people,” James said.

“I Play Rocky” premiered at the Toronto International Film Festival and finished first runner-up for the People’s Choice Award.

In 1976, “Rocky” launched Stallone to stardom and was the highest-grossing film of the year. It earned 10 Oscar nominations the following year, and won three, including best picture. The film spawned a franchise with sequels and spinoffs and is widely regarded as one of the all-time greatest movies.

Given its legacy, depicting the film’s making — under the watchful eye of diehard fans — could be a “slippery slope,” Farrelly said. But the veteran director said he wasn’t afraid to take on the challenge.

”’‘Rocky’s’ better, knowing what he went through. And that’s why I felt like (this film) wasn’t exploiting ‘Rocky,’ it was actually enhancing ‘Rocky,’” Farrelly said.

As for Stallone’s reaction, Farrelly said the 80-year-old actor has seen it and “he loved it.”

The film spawned a franchise with sequels and spinoffs and is widely regarded as one of the all-time greatest movies.

Given its legacy, depicting the film’s making — under the watchful eye of diehard fans — could be a “slippery slope,” Farrelly said. But the veteran director said he wasn’t afraid to take on the challenge.
”’‘Rocky’s’ better, knowing what he went through. And that’s why I felt like (this film) wasn’t exploiting ‘Rocky,’ it was actually enhancing ‘Rocky,’” Farrelly said.
As for Stallone’s reaction, Farrelly said the 80-year-old actor has seen it and “he loved it.”

stories.title: Ontario school’s idea for plantable Remembrance Day poppies is catching on
stories.summary: The project provides classrooms with kits to create wearable poppies from seed paper that can be planted in spring.
stories.author: Kristin Rushowy
stories.content:
It began as a sustainability project at Fanshawe College five years ago that has since blossomed into a Remembrance Day activity for kids in schools across the country.

The idea behind The Poppy Project is to provide classrooms with kits to create wearable poppies from seed paper that can later be planted as “seeds of hope” in their gardens in the spring. It has the approval of the Royal Canadian Legion and has raised about $8,000 to date.

Education Minister Paul Calandra told the Star he’d like to get the project into as many Ontario schools as possible for next Remembrance Day, given a new curriculum that in part encourages students to wear, and make, poppies.

He learned about it two weeks ago when Fanshawe representatives were at Queen’s Park, and said “I can see a time when maybe every kid is getting this — it’s such a cool project and I’d like to see if there’s a way I can get this into every single school, and every kid have an opportunity to do this.”

A number of MPPs and cabinet ministers, including Calandra, were seen wearing the sustainable poppies on their lapels last week at Queen’s Park.

Darlene O’Neill leads the Poppy Project at Fanshawe College in London, Ont., ON Nov. 5.

The project began in 2021 to mark the 100th anniversary of the poppy. Design instructor Wendy Sperry came up with the idea, and with the help of students, fine-tuned and marketed it. At that time, they sold for $10 a kit, with $2 donated to the legion, and they’re now priced at $12 a kit.

Some 225,000 poppies have now been made by thousands of children across Canada, and Fanshawe expects to bring in another $2,000-$3,000 this season.

Sperry, who has since retired, “tested and tested and figured out a way to make what she called a replantable poppy, so that after Remembrance Day, the whole philosophy is to plant seeds of hope,” said Darlene O’Neill of Fanshawe’s Military Connected Campus.

Students at Central Toronto Academy created ceramic poppies as part of a project that’s a local fundraiser for the legion.

The project now has Fanshawe students who are dedicated to marketing and promoting it across the country to schools, hospitals, corporate events and seniors homes, she said, adding the kits are now available in both official languages .

“It’s great to see children making their own poppies and learning about the history of the poppy” including the famous poem written by Ontarian Lt.-Col. John McCrae, “In Flanders Fields.”

“It’s empowering. It’s heartwarming to see the interest that the nation has in our veterans and in those who continue to serve,” added O’Neill. “To me, as a daughter of a veteran, I’m so proud to be related with this project and Fanshawe’s work on the Poppy Project, and I think it’s just continuing to bloom.”

stories.title: The ‘lost Canadians’ of the world wars: Inside the fight to claim citizenship for those ‘willing to die for Canada’
stories.summary: Inside the fight to claim citizenship for those ‘willing to die for Canada’
stories.author: Jason Miller
stories.content:
Douglas Jung was one of the many Chinese Canadians who enlisted to fight in the Second World War with the hope of being rewarded for their service with Canadian citizenship.

Even after volunteering to serve Canada, the Vancouver-born Jung, along with many others of Chinese descent, faced an uphill battle to gain legal status after returning from overseas.

While he survived, many soldiers died fighting for this country without status or as British subjects.

“They felt that if they showed that they were willing to die for Canada then a grateful nation would grant them full citizenship,” said his son, Arthur Calderwood.

These soldiers are known as the “lost Canadians,” said Don Chapman, an author who has launched a petition ahead of Remembrance Day, lobbying the federal government to recognize those who died fighting for Canada in the First and Second World War as citizens.

Douglas Jung is pictured in his uniform after returning to British Columbia from his deployment in Australia during the Second World War. His son said the photo was captured sometime in 1945.

He said Canadian citizenship rules at the time were particularly disenfranchising to some groups, such as Chinese veterans whose registration certificates indicated that they had no legal status in Canada.

“They were considered to be nothing more than stateless registered aliens,” Chapman said. “There are so many veterans that fought for Canada and died disenfranchised.”

Chapman said the petition, which had been signed by more than 475 people as of Monday, is calling on the Canadian government to change its interpretation of the law, which holds that citizenship didn’t officially exist until Jan. 1, 1947. Before 1947, when the first Canadian Citizenship Act officially came into effect, all individuals born or naturalized in Canada were considered British subjects; others, like those of Chinese descent, had no legal status due to discriminatory and racist legislation such as the Chinese Exclusion Act.

Chapman, who has dedicated more than two decades to fighting for reforms to Canadian citizenship regulations , said he’s gearing up to take the federal government to court over his bid for a resolution formally declaring that those killed in the service of Canada during two world wars were in fact citizens.

Chapman pointed out that while Canada commemorates the sacrifice made by these military members each Remembrance Day — some of their graves are even marked by maple leaves — they are still not officially considered citizens because of what he considers to be archaic rules.

Don Chapman (left) shares a moment with retired Canadian Lt.-Gen Roméo Dallaire.

He wants the approximately 110,000 who died for Canada in both world wars to be recognized, regardless of their status before 1947.

“We celebrate people as Canadian who the state says were not,” said Chapman, 72, a former airline pilot who authored “The Lost Canadians: A Struggle for Citizenship Rights” and founded the Lost Canadians movement . “This is a historic wrong. These are people who have fallen through the cracks.”

While earlier legislation, including the Canadian Nationals Act of 1921 and the Immigration Act of 1910, used the term “Canadian national” and, for immigration purposes, “Canadian citizen,” this did not establish Canadian citizenship, said Anahita Beladi, a spokesperson for Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada.

Beladi said while the Federal Court of Appeal and the Supreme Court of Canada have confirmed that Canadian citizenship did not exist as a legal status with general application before Jan. 1, 1947, “this in no way diminishes the profound sacrifices made by those who served.”

“Under the current Citizenship Act, there is no authority to grant or confer Canadian citizenship on deceased individuals,” Beladi said.

Calderwood, who took his mother’s maiden name, said his father’s registration certificate from 1924 stipulates that he did not have legal status in Canada at birth.

Jung joined the army as an 18-year-old and was deployed to Australia as part of Operation Oblivion but didn’t face active combat, Calderwood said.

Calderwood, who supports Chapman’s movement, said his father was among the fortunate soldiers of Chinese descent who made it home and lived to earn citizenship after 1947. Calderwood’s two uncles also served.

Douglas Jung is pictured in his registration certificate issued in June 1924.

“The entire Chinese-Canadian community were hoodwinked into believing that they were not Canadian citizens and that they were not worthy,” Calderwood said. “We should clarify and correct these discrepancies.”

Jung would go on to become Canada’s first Chinese member of Parliament in 1957. He died in 2002.

Chapman said his own experience with what he argues was Canada’s flawed citizenship regulations served as a catalyst for him to fight for the citizenship of all the people he saw as “lost Canadians.”

Born to Canadian parents in Vancouver, Chapman said he lost his citizenship in 1961 at six years old, when an obscure section of the Citizenship Act stripped him of his status after his parents relocated to the U.S. and his father took on American citizenship.

That law stated that any child whose father took out citizenship in another country would automatically lose his or her status as a Canadian, even if that child’s mother remained in Canada.

“It took me 47 years to get my citizenship back. These laws made no sense,” he said.

And then, along the way, “I discovered all these other categories of lost Canadians.”

Jung joined the army as an 18-year-old and was deployed to Australia as part of Operation Oblivion but didn’t face active combat, Calderwood said.

Calderwood, who supports Chapman’s movement, said his father was among the fortunate soldiers of Chinese descent who made it home and lived to earn citizenship after 1947. Calderwood’s two uncles also served.
Douglas Jung is pictured in his registration certificate issued in June 1924.

“The entire Chinese-Canadian community were hoodwinked into believing that they were not Canadian citizens and that they were not worthy,” Calderwood said. “We should clarify and correct these discrepancies.”
Jung would go on to become Canada’s first Chinese member of Parliament in 1957. He died in 2002.
Chapman said his own experience with what he argues was Canada’s flawed citizenship regulations served as a catalyst for him to fight for the citizenship of all the people he saw as “lost Canadians.”

Born to Canadian parents in Vancouver, Chapman said he lost his citizenship in 1961 at six years old, when an obscure section of the Citizenship Act stripped him of his status after his parents relocated to the U.S. and his father took on American citizenship.
That law stated that any child whose father took out citizenship in another country would automatically lose his or her status as a Canadian, even if that child’s mother remained in Canada.
“It took me 47 years to get my citizenship back. These laws made no sense,” he said.
And then, along the way, “I discovered all these other categories of lost Canadians.”

stories.title: Working at LHSC: From critical care nurse to Emergency Department Nurse Practitioner
stories.summary: November 10, 2026By Kendrah Krouskos
stories.content:
Kendrah Krouskos, Nurse Practitioner, in the Emergency Department.

November 10, 2026

By Kendrah Krouskos

As patient volumes and the complexity of care continue to grow, Nurse Practitioners (NP) are helping expand access to timely, high-quality care at LHSC. NPs are registered nurses with advanced education and clinical training who can assess patients, diagnose conditions, order and interpret tests, prescribe medications, and develop treatment plans. In LHSC's Emergency Department, NPs play an important role in improving access to care while helping patients navigate some of their most vulnerable moments.

I graduated from Western University's Bachelor of Science in Nursing program in 2004 and began my career at LHSC on the General Surgery unit at University Hospital. A few years later, I ventured into travel nursing in the United States, working in California, Colorado, North Carolina and South Carolina. The experience broadened my clinical perspective and even led me to meet my husband.

After returning to London in 2009, I joined the Critical Care Trauma Centre (CCTC), where I became involved in Critical Care Outreach, Critical Response Teams and CCRAID (Critical Care Response Against Infectious Disease), including infectious disease preparedness efforts during Canada's first suspected Ebola case.

I later spent five years as a Clinical Educator before moving into Nursing Professional Practice, focusing on policy development, standards of practice, nurse coaching and practice investigations. During the pandemic, I returned to critical care to support education initiatives related to PPE, vaccination clinics and nurse upskilling.

Each role gave me new opportunities to learn, support colleagues and contribute to patient care in different ways.

Although I enjoyed education and professional practice, I wasn't ready to step away from direct patient care. I loved teaching and mentoring others, but I also valued connecting with patients and helping them navigate difficult moments in their lives.

My experience in critical care had given me a strong foundation in autonomous practice and clinical decision-making, and becoming a Nurse Practitioner felt like a natural next step to build on those skills and take on greater clinical responsibility. Soon after, I enrolled in the Master of Nursing and Nurse Practitioner program at the University of Windsor while continuing to work full time, graduating in 2025 and completing my NP examinations shortly afterward.

LHSC's support made a tremendous difference throughout the process. My leaders provided flexibility, educational leave and encouragement, while the Learn and Stay Grant helped offset some of the costs of returning to school.

As a Nurse Practitioner in the Emergency Department, I independently assess, diagnose and treat patients with a range of concerns, from abdominal and chest pain to respiratory illnesses, headaches and women's health concerns. The role was introduced to expand access to care in a busy emergency setting while supporting patient flow and timely treatment.

Every day is different, which is one of the things I love most about my role. I enjoy learning, developing new skills and challenging myself clinically, whether expanding my knowledge of point-of-care ultrasound or building procedural skills like suturing. Most importantly, I value the connections I make with patients.

People often arrive in the Emergency Department during vulnerable and stressful moments. I want them to feel heard, respected and supported throughout their visit. I often tell patients, "This is a safe, judgment-free environment. I'll listen, I'll ask questions and I want you to be honest with me because that's the best way I can help." Sometimes that means providing treatment; other times, it's answering questions, connecting patients with community supports or ensuring they leave with a clear follow-up plan.

Collaboration is also essential to the role. I work alongside nurses, physicians, physiotherapists, occupational therapists, social workers and community partners to ensure patients receive the right care and support at the right time.

One of the things I hope people better understand about Nurse Practitioners is the unique role we play within the healthcare team. We bring an advanced clinical skill set while keeping nursing's patient-centred approach at the heart of everything we do. We can assess, diagnose, order tests, prescribe medications and develop treatment plans, while also focusing on education, communication, and helping patients navigate their healthcare journey.

Most importantly, I hope patients leave feeling listened to.

Emergency Departments are incredibly busy environments, and many patients are experiencing uncertainty, fear or frustration when they arrive. My goal is for everyone I care for to leave feeling listened to, supported and informed, even when we can't solve every problem in a single visit.

Looking back on my career, I'm grateful for every opportunity that helped shape the clinician I am today. From bedside nursing and education to professional practice and now emergency care, each experience has reinforced my passion for learning and for helping people when they need it most.

Stories November 10, 2026

Biobanks play a critical role in advancing health research by providing researchers with access to high-quality biological samples and detailed clinical data from consenting participants. These resources help researchers better understand disease, identify new approaches to diagnosis and treatment, and ultimately improve patient outcomes. At London Health Sciences Centre Research Institute (Lhscri), a growing network of biobanks supports research across a wide range of health conditions, including the London Urology BioSolutions Repository (Lubsr), a comprehensive urology biobank dedicated to advancing the understanding of genitourinary diseases. Supported by the Urology Clinical Research Unit team, Lubsr is building a robust collection of biospecimens and research data from both patients with urological conditions and healthy individuals. By collecting and preserving tissue, blood, urine, and associated health information, the repository is creating a valuable resource for researchers in London and across Canada working to better understand a wide range of urological conditions and support future discoveries in urological research.

Research Coordinator and Lubsr Program Coordinator, Kes Sebborn, gives us a behind the scenes look at the work happening in the urology biobank.

The Urology Clinical Research Unit team is part of a vibrant community through their work in both the Victoria Hospital Urology Department and the Cancer Research Laboratory Program at Lhscri’s Victoria Research Laboratories. Surrounded by scientists, clinicians, nurses, administrative professionals, research staff, and other colleagues working across a range of specialties, the team contributes to a shared culture of innovation, collaboration, and collective commitment to advancing the understanding of disease. These connections across both the clinical and research environments play an essential role in the success of the research program, helping researchers and clinicians work together to build a brighter future for patients with urological diseases.

Every study and sample collection at the urology biobank begins with a participant’s decision to contribute to research. Participants are at the heart of the work happening in the biobank, and those contributions drive progress in the prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of urological cancers. Research begins with a conversation. Before proceeding with sample collection, the team reviews the Letter of Information and Consent for the urology biobank and other research study materials with participants, giving them the opportunity to ask questions and make informed decisions about taking part in research. These conversations often lead to lasting connections, making participation engagement a rewarding part of the team’s work.

Once a patient has provided their consent, the team collects tissue samples, including blood samples, that are used for study-specific protocols and contributions to the urology biobank. Providing a comfortable and welcoming environment to patients who agree to participate in research is an important part of the process. The team works to ensure participants feel supported and at ease during sample collections, helping make participation a meaningful experience for those who choose to contribute to research.

Each sample donated to the biobank is handled with great care. Stored in a -80°C freezer, samples are placed in cryovials, organized in secure storage systems, and preserved for future research. The freezer can accommodate more than 80,000 samples and currently houses over 3,000. As the biobank continues to grow, each new sample helps expand the opportunities for future discoveries in urological research.

After being placed in the freezer, samples are carefully recorded in the team’s digital tracking system, ensuring it can be retrieved efficiently for future research. Using detailed search and filtering tools, the team can identify samples based on disease type, collection date, sample type, and other important characteristics. This allows researchers to access the right samples to answer specific research questions. A colour-coded system helps distinguish between the different types of samples being stored and managed. Each colour is assigned to a specific sample type, such as blood, tissue, or urine, providing an easy visual reference and helping keep the sample types clearly organized

Not all cancers are the same, and neither are the people affected by them. In one current prostate cancer clinical trial, the team is working on analyzing tissue samples to better understand the genetic features of each participant’s cancer. The results help clinicians select the most appropriate treatment from six possible options, moving away from a one-size-fits-all approach. This is an example of how science is helping LHSC’s clinical team deliver the right treatment to the right patient at the right time.

Although small, the Urology Clinical Research Unit team brings dedication and collaboration to its work, whether supporting patients, working alongside colleagues or contributing to research. That shared commitment is central to how the team operates, with members supporting one another and working toward a common goal of creating meaningful opportunities for research and improving the experience and outcomes of patients.

The team is also proud to support London Health Sciences Foundation (Lhsf) events that help fund and celebrate research contributions. From Dash 4 Dad to the Lexus of London Golf Classic Gala, events of this nature bring together patients, families, health-care professionals, and researchers with the shared goal of improving outcomes for future generations.

stories.title: This Honda once again tops Canada’s list of most stolen vehicles. Is yours on it?
stories.summary: The Honda CR-V SUV is a popular target for thieves because it's “globally serviceable,” Équité Association’s annual report found.
stories.author: Peter Edwards
stories.content:
The most stolen vehicle in Canada is once again the Honda CR-V, according to Équité Association, an insurance crime-and-fraud prevention group.

That’s one of the findings in a newly-released list of the top 10 most stolen vehicles in Canada in 2025 .

The Honda CR-V was also the most stolen vehicle in Canada in 2021 and 2022.

Leading the most-stolen list for 2025 were Honda CR-Vs at 2,137 thefts, followed by 1,813 stolen Honda Civics and 1,147 stolen Toyota Rav 4s, which was the country’s most stolen vehicle in 2024.

Organized crime groups target specific vehicles to maximize their profits through domestic and international resale, Équité Association said.

Gas-powered vehicles remain the most popular targets, pointing to a lack of charging stations for electric cars in resale markets overseas.

The Honda CR-V is also considered “globally serviceable,” Équité Association noted, explaining why it’s a popular target for thieves.

Rounding out the top 10 list of most stolen vehicles in Canada are: Ram 1500 Series trucks at 1,072; Ford F150 Series trucks at 1,057; Lexus RX Series autos at 964; Chevrolet/ GMC Silverado/ Sierra 1500 Series trucks at 927; Toyota Tundra trucks at 787; Jeep Wranglers at 603 and Hyundai Elantras at 484.

“We must make vehicles harder to steal,” said Heather Masterson, president and CEO of Équité Association, in a prepared statement.

“With auto theft remaining a low-risk high reward crime, organized networks continue to exploit vulnerabilities, leaving tens of thousands of Canadians victimized, and communities emotionally and financially affected,” Masterson said.

“Despite considerable collective efforts to combat auto theft, criminals continue to profit from the $900 million annually in stolen vehicles,” Masterson said.

Équité Association’s 2025 Auto Theft Trend Report revealed that national and industry initiatives resulted in an 18 per cent Canada-wide, year-over-year drop in auto theft when compared to 2024.

However, 72 per cent of Canadians polled feel that mandatory anti-theft technology should be built into their vehicles, not sold as an aftermarket add-on, Équité Association officials argued.

“We cannot let our guard down,” Bryan Gast, national VP of intelligence and investigations and Équité Association, said in a prepared statement.

“Canada is a source nation for stolen vehicles, which is why Équité, in collaboration with government partners, law enforcement and key stakeholders, is working hand-in-hand to disrupt these increasingly aggressive criminal networks,” Gast said.

stories.title: Man ‘squatting’ in fire-damaged building for months recounts second serious blaze this year
stories.summary: A former tenant says he wasn’t the only person living inside the boarded-up apartment building at 745 Dundas St. after it was damaged by a deadly fire this summer, and where another significant blaze broke out early Sunday morning.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
A former tenant says he wasn’t the only person living inside the boarded-up apartment building at 745 Dundas St. after it was damaged by a deadly fire this summer, and where another significant blaze broke out early Sunday morning.

His story suggests growing desperation among homeless Londoners to get indoors, and the need for more shelters that allow pets.

David, a 47-year-old Londoner, tells CTV News he rented an apartment on the main floor of the 13-unit building until the deadly fire that killed a local woman on July 17.

After the fire, he was unwilling to give up his three cats when offered space in a homeless shelter, so he resorted to using a poorly secured side window to return to his apartment.

“I’ve had to squat here with my cats,” David explained a day after the second fire in four months. “Yesterday, at around 6:30 in the morning, there was an explosion. (It) was just below my apartment.”

He believes someone was using a torch and propane tank to illegally cut copper pipes from the basement.

Two of his cats died in the fire, the third is temporarily staying with a friend.

David says he will not be returning inside the building because of the overwhelming odour.

Devastated, he struggled to hold back tears while describing his situation, “I can’t go anywhere. I’m just on the streets now. I have nowhere to go. No family left. And now my cats are gone. That’s all I had.”

Remarkably, David says he wasn’t alone living in the fire-damaged building that had a construction fend surrounding it and plywood covering the doors and windows.

According to him, there were three other people staying inside virtually every night.

Neighbour Nicholas Jeffery believes city hall should have done more to prevent people, including David, from being able to regain access to the building.

“They break-in these windows,” Jeffrey said. “It’s dangerous. (The building) could collapse.”

In response to the most recent fire, the City of London has issued an Order against the owner of the building, Radium-1 Development Ltd. of Scarborough, demanding a decision in 14 days to either demolish or repair the building.

Specifically it requires:

Immediately prohibit all access to the interior of the building and install a construction fence around the entire perimeter

Immediately obtain the services of a Professional Engineer to assess the structural condition of the building

Based on the engineer’s findings, obtain either a demolition permit or apply for a building permit to conduct repairs by November 23, 2026

In October, CTV News obtained fire inspection documents that identified 13 Ontario Fire Code violations at 745 Dundas St. since the beginning of 2025.

At the time, Yaso Somalingam, CEO of Radium-1 Development Ltd. said all of the deficiencies had been resolved prior to the July 17 fire that killed a 29-year-old woman and critically injured two other people.

“I did everything!” Somalingam said in October. “I did work with the city. I work with the fire department.”

So far, the London Fire Department has not determined the cause of the fire on Sunday morning.

The Order issued by city hall described extensive interior and structural damage.
