Gray cried as she testified Monday, saying it had been “so hard to watch” A.B.‘s mental health deteriorate in the lead-up to the trial underway in Vancouver.
A.B. had attempted suicide in February and she was hospitalized after another attempt in June, Gray told the court.
“Every day this year, pretty much, I’ve woken wondering … when it’s going to happen. Not if, but when,” Gray said.
Gray testified last week that she regretted some of her online posts about Galloway.

Her lawyer, Vanshika Dhawan, told the court last Thursday her client was no longer defending some of her online statements as responsible communications or arguing they were made honestly under “qualified privilege.”
But she said Gray was still defending certain statements as fair comment.
Gray concluded her testimony on Monday, and the trial will continue Tuesday.

stories.title: What luxury home sales tell us about Canada’s K-shaped real estate economy
stories.summary: Luxury home sales are on the rise in seven out of 13 of Canada’s largest real estate market, a new report from Remax Canada shows.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
It is no secret that Canada’s housing market has been dealing with headwinds, including the economic uncertainty caused by U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war against Canada. But one segment of the real estate sector seems to be bouncing back faster.

Luxury home sales are on the rise in seven out of 13 of Canada’s largest real estate market, a new report from Remax Canada shows.

The growth in the luxury real estate market is fastest outside of the two biggest markets, Toronto and Vancouver.

In five of these markets, the luxury real estate sector saw double digit growth rates in the first nine months of 2026.

Burlington, Ont., (26.3 per cent), St. John’s (21 per cent), Calgary (20.6 per cent), Edmonton (15.9 per cent) and Saskatoon (15.3 per cent) saw the largest increase in luxury home sales.

However, a closer look at the numbers shows that even in Canada’s biggest cities, luxury real estate is booming. The slowdown in the Toronto luxury market is concentrated in homes between $3 million and $7.5 million.

The Greater Toronto Area saw a 17.6 per cent increase in luxury sales of homes priced at $7.5 million or more. In the GTA, 18 homes sold for more than $10 million, with 15 of them within the city – the highest single year count for Toronto in a decade.

Get expert insights, Q&A on markets, housing, inflation, and personal finance information delivered to you every Saturday.

A single home in Toronto’s upscale Forest Hill neighbourhood sold for $23 million.

This data comes as the Canadian Real Estate Association reported a 2.3 per cent monthly decline in overall home sales in the country in September.

Rising fixed mortgage rates and economic uncertainty have “stretched” housing affordability in Canada, Crea said.

“The big question going forward is how much farther will the Bank have to go to keep a lid on inflation next year? Until that becomes clearer, this fresh round of uncertainty will likely send some buyers back to the sidelines,” said Shaun Cathcart, Crea’s senior economist.

While Trump’s trade war has continued to be “dark cloud” over many prospective buyers, those at the very top have more financial muscle they are able to flex, said Adil Ninani, realtor with Royal LePage West, based in British Columbia.

“Buyers of the $10 million price bracket have also done very well in the equity markets. They’re not all real estate concentrated. They’ve had other successes or wins in other asset classes that is allowing them to step into this price category,” he said.

2:07 Touring the $1.3M Bonus Prize luxury condo in midtown Toronto

Canada’s unemployment rate ticked up to 6.7 per cent last month.

In 2025, U.S. stocks appreciated 17 per cent, following a 23 per cent gain in 2024 and 24 per cent gain in 2026.

“Wealth enables a home purchase. Confidence and the right opportunity motivate it,” said Michael Altneu, vice president of luxury at Remax.

Buyers at the top also have “the stamina to work through a long, extended negotiation,” Dinani said.

With only a handful of buyers in the luxury market, buyers have the upper hand and can afford to drag out a negotiation and wear down the seller.

“We’ve had negotiations on high-end properties (in and around Vancouver) last multiple months,” he said,

The trend in the luxury home market can be seen as a “course correction” that could trickle down to other segments, he added.

“We are seeing assets worth $10 million plus throughout Metro Vancouver sell. But these were originally listed at $16 to $18 million them. We’ve seen a course correction on pricing expectation,” he said.

However, the thing that will ultimately move the needle on new buyers jumping into the market is a resolution of Trump’s trade war, Dinani said.

“The big thing we’re watching from a macro level is some sort of resolution with the United States. That, in itself, would lead to more folks coming back into the market,” he said.

stories.title: Montreal kosher pizza place vandalized in latest spate of attacks on Jewish businesses
stories.summary: Shattered window happened on the anniversary of Kristallnacht, the 1938 Nazi German attack on Jewish homes and businesses
stories.author: Chris Knight
stories.content:
Welcome to our new, improved site!

Read a note from our editor-in-chief

Shattered window happened on the anniversary of Kristallnacht, the 1938 Nazi German attack on Jewish homes and businesses

Shattered glass covers a table at Pizza Pita restaurant in Montreal (Handout/Uri Peretz)

November 9, 2026 at 2:42 p.m.

A kosher restaurant in Montreal’s Cote-des-Neiges neighbourhood has been vandalized, with a heavy rock thrown through the window early Monday morning.

Uri Peretz, who has owned the Pizza Pita Prime in Decarie Square since 2024, spoke to National Post Monday afternoon.

Peretz called it “quite peculiar that it happened on the anniversary of Kristallnacht, the Night of Broken Glass.”

On the night of Nov. 9, 1938, Nazi German leaders unleashed a nationwide reign of anti-Jewish state-sponsored vandalism, arson and terror.

The group Stand With Us Canada, which combats misinformation and antisemitism, also noted the connection in a post on social media, adding: “The circumstances surrounding last night’s incident remain unclear. We will continue to follow this developing story.”

Peretz said he was woken by a phone call at 3 a.m. on to let him know the restaurant’s alarm had been activated.

“I dispatched police right away,” he said. “By the time I arrived, we saw that one of our windows has been smashed with a big rock. And it doesn’t seem like it was a break-in. It was definitely vandalism.”

“I definitely condemn the vandalism,” Peretz said, adding: “We see that there’s been now a chain of incidents happening on Jewish institutions” in Montreal.

They include Mimimelon, a kosher bakery in Montreal’s Saint-Laurent neighbourhood, that was targeted in back-to-back suspected arson attacks on Nov. 3 and 4. And in August, the kosher Nöam Restaurant was also destroyed in an apparent arson attack.

A rock used to break a window sits on the floor of Pizza Pita restaurant in Montreal. handout / Uri Peretz

“One time is a coincidence,” Peretz said. “The second time, it’s not a coincidence anymore. And then the third time, and there will be a fourth time, I’m sure. But we have to stay resilient … we see what happens when we don’t.”

stories.title: Cool and cloudy start to the week in London weather
stories.summary: Get ready for a shift in weather in London, Ont., as the current conditions move from cool, grey skies to a much brighter and warmer Tuesday.
stories.author: Melanie Kentner, Julie Atchison
stories.content:
Get ready for a shift in weather in London, Ont., as the current conditions move from cool, grey skies to a much brighter and warmer Tuesday.

Monday features cool temperatures under generally grey skies and low cloud cover. While some areas like Windsor, Chatham, and Sarnia might see brief sunshine, cloudiness is expected over London.

Spotty light rain is possible in southern Huron County and parts of Middlesex.

Conditions will improve overnight as high pressure builds from the south, leading to breaking cloud cover and a shift in winds from northwest to southwest.

Expect a pleasant start to Tuesday with a nice mix of sun and cloud.

Conditions are forecast to be dry throughout the day. Temperatures will climb back above normal, reaching approximately 13-14 Celsius due to a southerly flow.

stories.title: A forgotten WWI fighter pilot, a 17-year mission and a new monument to honour Canada’s fallen soldiers
stories.summary: Lt.-Col. William Barker, Canada's most decorated war hero, shot down 50 enemy aircraft during the Great War
stories.author: Kenn Oliver
stories.content:
When the sun sets over Mount Pleasant Cemetery in Toronto on Tuesday, the eve of Remembrance Day, more than 400 solar-powered lights will twinkle to life near the grave markers of the Canadian veterans interred there.

The Royal Canadian Air Force Foundation (Rcaff), the guiding force behind the Light of Remembrance initiative, a first of its kind for Canada, said in a press release that “behind every light is a life of service — and a story worth remembering.”

One story coming into focus ahead of Nov. 11 is that of Lt.-Col. William Barker, a highly decorated, yet seldom-heralded WWI fighter pilot who was honoured with his own bronze public statue in Toronto’s Rosedale neighbourhood last week.

“Monuments can be put up on military bases that nobody sees, but you want to make sure that the public has a chance to own them like this,” said John Wright.

John Wright, left, and Rcaf Foundation CEO Jeremy Diamond in Scrivener Square with the newly unveiled statue of Lt.-Col. William Barker. John Wright

Wright, a long-time civilian advocate for the military and veterans, has been a driving force behind bringing Barker’s memory to the fore and turning it into something bigger for veterans and all Canadians since coming across the soldier’s final resting place in a mausoleum bearing his in-laws’ surname in 2009.

It’s why he likens the 17-year journey to see Barker properly honoured to Field of Dreams, the 1989 film starring Kevin Costner.

“This really is not just a field of dreams; it’s really a land of hope, and I think that’s really what all of this is supposed to mean,” said Wright, co-founder of Friends of William Barker, which has since evolved into the Rcaff, a not-for-profit which has provided Canadian students with a million dollars in scholarships for post-secondary studies in Stem, aviation and aeronautics.

Originally a farm boy from Dauphin, Man., with a penchant for horses and firearms, Barker was a 20-year-old Canadian Expeditionary Force soldier for the British Army in Belgium when he volunteered for the Royal Flying Corps in 1916. He became a gunner first, taking part in the assault on Beaumont-Hamel, and then completed flying school in the first four weeks of 1917.

Known for his aggressive style and tactical instinct, Barker quickly compiled a string of victories on the Western Front and in Italy, reaching 46 by August — all in a single aircraft, a Sopwith Camel.

His specific plane “has been declared by British aviation historians to be the most successful fighting aircraft in the RAF history,” according to biographer Wayne Ralph, and his Canadian piloting counterpart, Lt.-Col. Billy Bishop, once called him “the deadliest air fighter that ever lived.”

As a wing commander, he is credited with never losing a plane in his squadron.

Lt.-Col. Billy Bishop once called his fighter pilot counterpart Lt.-Col. William Barker “the deadliest air fighter that ever lived.”

But Barker was also something of a rebel.

On Christmas Day in 1917, he and another pilot conducted a “successful but unauthorized” patrol and attack on a German aerodrome in northern Italy. He was reprimanded, according to the Dictionary of Canadian Biography, but the bold action later earned him a Distinguished Service Order and a second bar on his Military Cross.

Wright said the audacity to attack the enemy as they were “all inside having schnapps” is part of what makes Barker “quintessentially Canadian.”

“Some people would see that as immodesty and recklessness, but what you have in Barker is somebody who … demonstrates a tenacity that I would say is typically Canadian,” he told National Post.

Barker’s days of tormenting the enemy ended not long after, however.

Back on the Western Front on Oct. 27, 1918, just two weeks before the Armistice was signed, Barker, who had a “roving commission to operate at will from any squadron,” took the skies over France on a solo flight in a different aircraft, according to Canada’s Aviation Hall of Fame.

After encountering and shooting down one enemy aircraft, he was attacked by a German fighter plane, suffering a wound to his right thigh.

Barker shot it down, only to find himself surrounded by roughly 15 more fighters, suffering three more bullet wounds in the ensuing dogfight. He took down another three enemies, but his wounds led him to fall unconscious and briefly lose control of his plane.

Lt.-Col. William Barker. Toronto Sun/QMI Agency

“On recovery he found himself being attacked again by a large formation, and, singling out one machine, he deliberately charged and drove it down in flames,” the official War Office citation reads, per the Hall of Fame.

“During this flight his left elbow was shattered and again he fainted, and on regaining consciousness he found himself still being attacked; but, notwithstanding that he was now severely wounded in both legs and his left arm rendered useless, he dived on the nearest machine and shot it down in flames.”

After another hard fight against the relentless Germans, Barker broke their formation and reached Allied territory where he crashed on landing.

He was awarded the Victoria Cross for his bravery and was promoted to Lt.-Col. but spent months recovering from his injuries, writing to a fellow squadron pilot from his hospital bed that the Germans “damn nearly” killed him, Ralph recounted.

“It May be nice to have the VC. But believe me I would sweep them all in the fire to stand once more fit. The agony I have gone through has been damnable,” wrote Barker, who returned to Canada in 1919 as its most decorated war hero, an honour he holds to this day.

His post-war life was marked by ups and downs, though he kept flying despite being essentially one-armed.

He entered commercial aviation with Bishop, who had visited him during his convalescence in England, but the airline, like many such ventures at the time, didn’t last long.

Billy Bishop, left, and William Barker. Archival photo

In 1922, he was appointed the Canadian Air Force’s acting director and helped found the Royal Canadian Air Force. After he resigned from military life in 1926, Conn Smythe, general manager of the Toronto Maple Leafs, who learned to fly from Barker during the war, appointed him the first president of the newly renamed hockey club in 1927, but that didn’t last long either.

In 1930, he returned to aviation with Montreal’s Fairchild Aircraft Limited of Canada, serving as its vice president and general manager. While demonstrating one of its new aircraft that March, Barker lost control and was instantly killed when the plane crashed into an ice-covered Ottawa River. More than 54,000 people reportedly attended his funeral, along with an honour guard of 2,000 service members, including six other VC recipients.

Barker’s statue in Scrivener Square is only steps away from the Summerhill Lcbo, in what was once the North Toronto railway station building, a place that happened to be connected to his story, Wright explained.

It was where he arrived in Toronto upon returning from the war, and the station he departed from on his way to Ottawa and the accident that killed him in 1930. His body also came through there when he returned to Toronto.

“It’s almost as if the statue itself wouldn’t go anywhere else until it fit there,” said Wright.

Barker’s nearly forgotten contributions have been recognized before now. After Wright and Vicky Ollers co-founded the Friends of William Barker, a 2011 memorial incorporating a Sopwith propeller was unveiled outside the mausoleum, with a plaque identifying Barker on the crypt door. A Remembrance Day ceremony has happened there every year since.

In April 2018, the Canadian Forces School of Aerospace Studies was renamed the Rcaf Wing Commander William G. Barker VC Aerospace College. He’s also recognized in a Billy Bishop Toronto City Airport exhibition and a bronze companion statue depicting Barker in his Expeditionary Force uniform was unveiled in Rockcliffe, near Ottawa, in October 2024.

But the Toronto statue, which depicts him in the “rare Canadian Air Force uniform he wore at Camp Borden and as acting director,” has always been the end goal, said Wright, who recognized several individuals and organizations for their part, including Barker’s grandsons, Alec, David and Ian Mackenzie, and great-grandson Henry.

Ian Mackenzie, grandson, left, and Henry Mackenzie, great grandson, right, beside the newly unveiled bronze statue of Lt.-Col. William Barker, a Canadian First World War flying ace, at Scrivener Square in Toronto. Jack Boland / Toronto Sun/Postmedia

With this passion project resolved, his next is the Lights for Remembrance, which he said is inspired by candlelight ceremonies in the Netherlands that began in 1995 to commemorate the country’s liberation by Canadian forces during Wwii.

“I think, given what (CFB) Wainwright brings to the table, we want to roll it out across the country and ask others to do likewise,” Wright said, referring to the tragedy that killed four soldiers and injured scores more at the Alberta base last month.

This year’s lights at Mount Pleasant Cemetery will go on at 4:30 p.m. Tuesday. Starting next year, the annual event will begin on Nov. 8, Indigenous Veterans Day, and continue throughout the month.

Kenn Oliver is a web editor and writer for National Post. He is a career journalist of more than 20 years, the bulk of which was spent as a sports writer, business reporter and web editor for the Telegram in St. John's, N.L.

“During this flight his left elbow was shattered and again he fainted, and on regaining consciousness he found himself still being attacked; but, notwithstanding that he was now severely wounded in both legs and his left arm rendered useless, he dived on the nearest machine and shot it down in flames.”
After another hard fight against the relentless Germans, Barker broke their formation and reached Allied territory where he crashed on landing.

He was awarded the Victoria Cross for his bravery and was promoted to Lt.-Col. but spent months recovering from his injuries, writing to a fellow squadron pilot from his hospital bed that the Germans “damn nearly” killed him, Ralph recounted.

“It May be nice to have the VC. But believe me I would sweep them all in the fire to stand once more fit. The agony I have gone through has been damnable,” wrote Barker, who returned to Canada in 1919 as its most decorated war hero, an honour he holds to this day.
His post-war life was marked by ups and downs, though he kept flying despite being essentially one-armed.
He entered commercial aviation with Bishop, who had visited him during his convalescence in England, but the airline, like many such ventures at the time, didn’t last long.
Billy Bishop, left, and William Barker. Archival photo

In 1922, he was appointed the Canadian Air Force’s acting director and helped found the Royal Canadian Air Force. After he resigned from military life in 1926, Conn Smythe, general manager of the Toronto Maple Leafs, who learned to fly from Barker during the war, appointed him the first president of the newly renamed hockey club in 1927, but that didn’t last long either.

In 1930, he returned to aviation with Montreal’s Fairchild Aircraft Limited of Canada, serving as its vice president and general manager. While demonstrating one of its new aircraft that March, Barker lost control and was instantly killed when the plane crashed into an ice-covered Ottawa River. More than 54,000 people reportedly attended his funeral, along with an honour guard of 2,000 service members, including six other VC recipients.

Barker’s statue in Scrivener Square is only steps away from the Summerhill Lcbo, in what was once the North Toronto railway station building, a place that happened to be connected to his story, Wright explained.
Editor’s Picks

It was where he arrived in Toronto upon returning from the war, and the station he departed from on his way to Ottawa and the accident that killed him in 1930. His body also came through there when he returned to Toronto.
“It’s almost as if the statue itself wouldn’t go anywhere else until it fit there,” said Wright.

Barker’s nearly forgotten contributions have been recognized before now. After Wright and Vicky Ollers co-founded the Friends of William Barker, a 2011 memorial incorporating a Sopwith propeller was unveiled outside the mausoleum, with a plaque identifying Barker on the crypt door. A Remembrance Day ceremony has happened there every year since.

In April 2018, the Canadian Forces School of Aerospace Studies was renamed the Rcaf Wing Commander William G. Barker VC Aerospace College. He’s also recognized in a Billy Bishop Toronto City Airport exhibition and a bronze companion statue depicting Barker in his Expeditionary Force uniform was unveiled in Rockcliffe, near Ottawa, in October 2024.

But the Toronto statue, which depicts him in the “rare Canadian Air Force uniform he wore at Camp Borden and as acting director,” has always been the end goal, said Wright, who recognized several individuals and organizations for their part, including Barker’s grandsons, Alec, David and Ian Mackenzie, and great-grandson Henry.

Ian Mackenzie, grandson, left, and Henry Mackenzie, great grandson, right, beside the newly unveiled bronze statue of Lt.-Col. William Barker, a Canadian First World War flying ace, at Scrivener Square in Toronto. Jack Boland / Toronto Sun/Postmedia

With this passion project resolved, his next is the Lights for Remembrance, which he said is inspired by candlelight ceremonies in the Netherlands that began in 1995 to commemorate the country’s liberation by Canadian forces during Wwii.

“I think, given what (CFB) Wainwright brings to the table, we want to roll it out across the country and ask others to do likewise,” Wright said, referring to the tragedy that killed four soldiers and injured scores more at the Alberta base last month.
This year’s lights at Mount Pleasant Cemetery will go on at 4:30 p.m. Tuesday. Starting next year, the annual event will begin on Nov. 8, Indigenous Veterans Day, and continue throughout the month.

Kenn Oliver is a web editor and writer for National Post. He is a career journalist of more than 20 years, the bulk of which was spent as a sports writer, business reporter and web editor for the Telegram in St. John's, N.L.

stories.title: Waterous Energy Fund consolidates heavy-oil holdings with Strathcona-Greenfire merger
stories.summary: A controlling shareholder in both oil sands companies, the fund is backing Strathcona’s purchase of Greenfire for about $2.4-billion
stories.author: Jeffrey Jones
stories.content:
Strathcona Resources Ltd. SCR-T is buying fellow heavy-oil producer Greenfire Resources Ltd. GFR-T for about $2.4-billion in cash and stock in a deal aimed at consolidating holdings controlled by Calgary-based Waterous Energy Fund.

The friendly transaction, the latest in a recent gusher of oil-patch takeover activity, will meld two oil companies with similar strategies, and the increased size is expected to improve access to capital, Strathcona said on Sunday. Waterous Energy Fund (WEF) owns 57 per cent of Strathcona and 72 per cent of Greenfire.

Part of the rationale is tied to Strathcona’s proposal for an oil-by-rail system to Prince Rupert from Alberta, said Adam Waterous, the company’s executive chairman and founder of WEF. Under that plan, known as Northern Express, 250,000 barrels of oil a day would be shipped on Canadian National Railway Co.’s tracks to the northwestern B.C. port.

The merger offers Strathcona the scale necessary for the company to pursue that project, which is still in its early stages, Mr. Waterous said in an interview.

The proposal calls for $2.5-billion to $3.5-billion in spending on rail, terminal and other infrastructure, and would require exemptions to a federal ban in that region on tanker loadings.

Mr. Waterous said he expects the combined Strathcona and Greenfire to have investment-grade credit ratings, a rarity in the Canadian oil and gas industry. That would lower borrowing costs for this project and other investments.

“Becoming investment-grade is a real marker for scale,” said the financier and former investment banker.

Strathcona is offering either 0.25 of one of its shares or $11 in cash for each Greenfire share. The first option yields a premium of 15 per cent over Greenfire’s Friday closing price on the Toronto Stock Exchange. The latter affords a lift of 39 per cent.

The Waterous fund is backing the deal and has elected to take Strathcona stock for its Greenfire holdings.

Strathcona will assume $550-million in Greenfire debt, increasing the value of the deal to as much as $2.9-billion.

Greenfire shares surged 38 per cent to a 52-week high of $10.94 on the TSX on Monday. Strathcona slipped about 1 per cent to $36.

By combining the two companies, Strathcona said it expects annual cost savings of $75-million a year and tax savings of as much as $400-million over four years.

The combined entity will have more than three billion barrels of proved-plus-probable reserves, representing a reserve life index of more than 54 years, Strathcona said. It expects production will increase from 153,000 barrels a day to 260,000 in five years.

“Overall, the transaction makes strategic sense and supports our view that this wave of consolidation will continue, driven by scarcity,” Travis Wood, analyst at National Bank Financial, said in a note to clients.

Takeover action has heated up with oil prices, which surged more than 40 per cent after the United States and Israel launched their attacks on Iran in late February. Iran retaliated by taking control of the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world’s main energy shipping corridors, and bringing tanker traffic to a virtual halt.

That has put Canada’s significant oil and gas resources in the global spotlight, and Prime Minister Mark Carney has prioritized bolstering exports. Mr. Waterous said that push bodes well for the oil-by-rail proposal.

Access to global markets for oil and natural gas is increasing with the expansion of the Trans Mountain pipeline to the West Coast and construction of new liquefied natural gas plants. Another million barrels a day of new oil export capacity could be built in the coming years if the Pacific Link pipeline is constructed, and the Shell PLC-led LNG Canada project has announced it is doubling its production capacity.

Among other recent energy deals: Shell acquired ARC Resources for US$16.4-billion, Cenovus Energy Inc. bought Athabasca Oil Corp. for $5.7-billion and, in late October, Ovintiv Inc. said it would acquire Logan Energy Corp. for US$890-million including assumed debt.

stories.title: Environmental economist tells trial Canada has limited power to alter climate change
stories.summary: Vancouver - An environmental economist testifying at Canada's first youth-led climate trial says the country has a limited ability to affect the climate inside its borders as it is largely determined by the choices of other countries.
stories.author: Brieanna Charlebois The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Vancouver - An environmental economist testifying at Canada’s first youth-led climate trial says the country has a limited ability to affect the climate inside its borders as it is largely determined by the choices of other countries.

David Anthoff, who studies climate change and environmental policy and is a professor at the University of California, Berkeley, is the first witness called by the federal government in the Federal Court trial in Vancouver.

The case was brought by 15 youth, who are arguing that federal legislation violates their constitutional rights by continuing the trajectory of greenhouse gas emissions.

Anthoff said Monday that Canada contributes about 1.4 per cent of global emissions.

“So Canada can have an impact on the global climate and an impact on Canada’s climate by changing its own emissions, but it’s relatively small compared to the overall size of the problem,” he said.

“Most of the climate change that Canada will experience, whether that is large or not, will be determined by the choices of other countries outside of Canada.”

Anthoff said it is not his view that “what Canada does doesn’t matter,” that it is futile or that there are no consequences to its emissions, but Canada would fare better if it managed a foreign policy initiative between several countries that agreed to a co-ordinated effort.

“Then something like that might be a much bigger lever than just the domestic greenhouse gases within Canada just because the vast majority of this problem is caused by emissions outside of Canada’s border,” he told the court.

Anthoff testified that mitigation policies require international co-ordination, while adaptation policies do not.

He said mitigation policies that reduce greenhouse gas emissions “are meant to slow down climate change or solve the root problem.”

“Mitigation outcomes are by definition a function of the choices of every country, and so effective mitigation policies will require some level of co-ordination or joint action to happen,” he said.

Meanwhile, Anthoff said adaptation policies are actions or reactions people or states have to climate change, and can be done without co-ordination, within one jurisdiction.

“It could be a province that solves some of these problems by itself,” he said.

On cross-examination, Anthoff agreed that delaying mitigation would “lead to more climate change and that will lead to a more harmful impacts from climate change.”

He noted the ability to adapt might reduce the level of mitigation needed as well as damage from climate change. But, he later said, “you will not find any study that would suggest we can adapt our way out of this problem.”

Asked if he agreed that reducing climate change would benefit younger generations who would be alive in the second half of the century when climate impacts are projected to worsen, he said that was likely true for most.

“Different population groups are impacted in different ways by climate change, but overall, if we add all of these effects together, it will be harmful,” Anthoff said.

Plaintiff lawyer Catherine Boies Parker told the court in her opening statement the case was not about the existence of climate change.

Rather, it hinges on whether the government is “constitutionally required to stop making it worse,” she said.

The plaintiff’s case was heard first and included testimony from youth from seven provinces and two territories on how they have suffered “specific harms connected directly to the government’s conduct.”

BJ Wray, counsel for Canada’s Department of Justice, told the court in opening arguments that the Charter was “never intended to solve existential crises,” and that providing the plaintiffs with a safe climate system” is not something the country can do on its own.

The trial comes about seven years after the case was first filed in 2019. It is expected to continue into late November, with closing arguments scheduled for February.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 9, 2026.

stories.title: Art Gallery of Ontario to open 5-floor expansion in September 2027
stories.summary: The Toronto museum says the Dani Reiss Modern and Contemporary Gallery will display nearly 400 artworks by Indigenous, Canadian and international artists.
stories.author: Alex Nino Gheciu
stories.content:
By Alex Nino Gheciu The Canadian Press

Posted November 9, 2026 1:27 pm

The Art Gallery of Ontario says its new five-floor expansion will open to the public next fall.

The 40,000 square feet of additional space is set to open on Sept. 25, 2027, showcasing the gallery’s growing collection of art.

The Toronto museum says the Dani Reiss Modern and Contemporary Gallery will display nearly 400 artworks by Indigenous, Canadian and international artists.

The project was launched in 2022 with a $35-million donation from Canada Goose chairman and CEO Dani Reiss.

The AGO says the expansion is now fully funded to cover ongoing operating costs, thanks to support from the federal and provincial governments and private donors.

The expansion, led by Diamond Schmitt, Selldorf Architects and Two Row Architect, will overlook Toronto’s Grange Park and connect to the museum’s existing Frank Gehry-designed building.

The AGO says the addition was designed to operate without burning fossil fuels and has received Zero Carbon Building Design certification, making it the first Canadian cultural institution of its size to earn the designation.

This is the seventh expansion the museum has undertaken since being founded in 1900.

stories.title: Honda Canada to retool Alliston, Ont. plant for expanded hybrid production
stories.summary: Honda Canada says it will retool its manufacturing facilities in Alliston, Ont., to expand production of hybrid-electric and gasoline-powered vehicles.
stories.author: Sammy Hudes
stories.content:
Honda Canada says it will retool its manufacturing facilities in Alliston, Ont., to expand production of hybrid-electric and gasoline-powered vehicles.

The Japanese automaker announced Monday it is partnering with the federal and provincial governments to fund plant upgrades, including the reintroduction of engine manufacturing, with an initial $166 million investment.

It said that funding is part of a broader $867-million commitment that will enhance quality, efficiency and manufacturing flexibility. Of that total, the federal government said it will provide $313 million, while the Ontario government is kicking in $156 million.

“This renewed investment reinforces Canada’s critical role in Honda’s North American growth and hybrid-electric vehicle strategy and helps position our operations for long-term competitiveness and future opportunities,” said Honda Canada president and CEO Dave Jamieson in a news release.

The funding will ensure Honda can maintain its workforce of 4,000 Canadian employees across two facilities at the Alliston plant, while supporting its Canadian auto production volumes.

The company said it will also strengthen the Alliston plant’s operations to help meet growing customer demand for hybrid-electric vehicles in North America.

“This investment will strengthen our automotive supply chains, support thousands of well-paying jobs in Ontario and across the country, and help build a strong Canadian auto sector where workers build the cars of the future,” said Industry Minister Mélanie Joly in a statement.

In May, Honda announced plans to introduce 15 new Honda and Acura hybrid models globally by 2030, with North America expected to be the primary market for many of those vehicles.

The automaker said it is investing across its manufacturing network in Canada, Ohio, Alabama and Georgia to support that strategy.

That same month, the company indefinitely suspended its plans for a $15-billion Canadian electric vehicle complex in response to dwindling demand.

Announced in 2024, Honda’s EV project would have included a vehicle assembly plant as well as battery production facilities. It had said that new EV plant could create 1,000 incremental manufacturing jobs in Alliston.

It was set to receive upwards of $5 billion in federal and Ontario funding, however no money had yet been transferred.

The decision to pause those plans did not affect current employment or production levels at the Alliston plant.

More than 400,000 vehicles were produced at the site last year. Honda is Canada’s second largest auto manufacturer by volume.

stories.title: All The Cows Are Dead is a melt-in-your-mouth new musical about meat
stories.summary: Mike Nadajewski and Taylor Garwood star in Ben Page’s exceptional musical about the circle of life – and the sanctity of beef
stories.author: Aisling Murphy
stories.content:
Title: All The Cows Are Dead

Book, music and lyrics by: Ben Page

Directed by: William Dao

Actors: Mike Nadajewski and Taylor Garwood

Company: Talk Is Free Theatre

Venue: Soul Provisions (68 Tycos Dr.)

City: Toronto

Year: Runs until Nov. 18

Critic’s Pick

Deep in the shank of Toronto’s northwest corner sits Soul Provisions, a one-stop shop for luxury popsicles and soups. The space is decidedly not a theatre – located at the back of a nondescript industrial complex just south of Yorkdale Shopping Centre, it’s about as far a cry from a Mirvish auditorium as you could possibly imagine.

But as a venue for All The Cows Are Dead , Ben Page’s melt-in-your-mouth new musical about a butcher and his quixotic nephew, the tiny space couldn’t be more suitable. The concrete floors and walls echo as if already familiar with the sounds of cleavers and grinders; the fluorescent overhead lights beat down incessantly, much more appropriate than traditional theatrical spotlights for slicing make-believe rib-eyes.

None of that is especially new territory for Talk Is Free Theatre. Based in Barrie, Ont., the company specializes in scrappy, site-specific work – in recent years, its Toronto productions have brought audiences to private living rooms, church basements and obscure warehouses for its shows, each seemingly more out-there than the last. ( Company , one of Talk Is Free’s few musicals to be staged in a traditional theatre space, was notably among its least successful .)

All The Cows Are Dead , which premiered in Barrie earlier this year, marks an all-time acme for Talk Is Free, which I suspect may need to start scouting a larger (if undoubtedly just as weird) venue for the work’s inevitable remount. A two-hander starring Mike Nadajewski and Taylor Garwood, the musical owes plenty to Stephen Sondheim’s Sweeney Todd : Eagle-eared audiences will notice more than a few passing references to that show’s meaty score before the end of Cows’ first song.

But Page, the 27-year-old child of Barenaked Ladies co-founder Steven Page, doesn’t let clever references overpower the story at hand – or their own extraordinary score. The work is mature beyond its years, and just as rich as the prime cuts of Broadway history that inspired it. Though Talk Is Free brings Page’s writing to life at an exceptional level, especially through Nadajewski’s and Garwood’s sensitively layered performances, the writing itself is undeniable: Page ought to be on the radar of every producer of musical theatre in this country.

We meet baby-faced Louis (Garwood) at the start of his apprenticeship with Anton (Nadajewski), whose affection for the dead cows in his care seems to contradict his vocation of choice. There’s little irony in Anton’s demeanour as he explains to his nephew the things that make cows happy – grass, milk, sunshine – while carving their carcasses into chuck roasts and tenderloins.

Nadajewski, a fixture of the Stratford and Shaw Festivals, places his trademark impish wit on full display as he works through Anton’s erratic moods. There’s not a moment in the show that’s not elevated by the actor’s giddy sense of humour or robust baritone voice – in the best, most satisfying ways, it’s often tricky to tell where Nadajewski stops and Anton begins.

Louis, meanwhile, has little desire to be a butcher, his aspirations set squarely on becoming a poet, or at the very least, handsome. But neither are likely to happen for him – he’s mostly accepted that, a fact Garwood makes achingly clear as he sings through Page’s intricate, melancholy score.

Maybe, just maybe, inspiration will strike. Maybe Louis will be able to show his uncle that his poetic longings aren’t mere fancy – that he’s destined for more than emptying scrap buckets full of muck. But for now, he’s stuck working in Anton’s shop, learning under duress what makes cows – and his uncle – tick.

So goes All The Cows Are Dead , whose individual vignettes coalesce into a gorgeous mosaic of what it means to live and die in harmony with the natural world. Anton is volatile, occasionally cruel, but unwaveringly determined to make a meatman of his bumbling heir. For a while, it’s unclear if the butcher could be capable of real, bleeding love.

But then he speaks of the cows – the young calves slaughtered solely for human consumption, the beasts murdered in the name of pleasure. His reverence for veal isn’t a love Louis can easily understand or even entirely recognize, but it’s love all the same, contradictory yet powerful in its depth.

Director William Dao steers the proceedings with little interest in naturalism or gore, instead choosing to represent meat through red and pink balloons. Some are succulent and supple, stuffed such that they approximate real steaks; others are brownish and floppy, destined to become balloon sausages seasoned with thyme. (Alessia Urbani is the set, costume and props designer.)

It’s a bold aesthetic risk that pays off in spades. While there’s always the fear that a latex roast or mince might pop, that tension only adds to the ever-changing relationship between Louis and Anton, their easy camaraderie forever on the edge of charring into bitterness.

There’s a moment when things click for Louis – when, just for a second, his higher purpose threatens to become clear. He’s concocted a special seasoning blend that his customers adore; he’s found a rhythm to butchery that nearly agrees with his idealistic virtues. “I’ve discovered something superb,” he sings happily as he inflates his creations.

In the aftermath of Page’s glorious chamber fantasia of meat, I’m inclined to say the same to just about anyone who will listen. All The Cows Are Dead is a vital meditation on the circle of life, and a poignant observation of how generations relate to each other – or don’t. Even staged inside a strangely remote urban retail store, it’s among the strongest, most tender new Canadian musicals of the decade.

Indeed, to echo Louis: It’s something superb.

Though Talk Is Free brings Page’s writing to life at an exceptional level, especially through Nadajewski’s and Garwood’s sensitively layered performances, the writing itself is undeniable: Page ought to be on the radar of every producer of musical theatre in this country.

We meet baby-faced Louis (Garwood) at the start of his apprenticeship with Anton (Nadajewski), whose affection for the dead cows in his care seems to contradict his vocation of choice. There’s little irony in Anton’s demeanour as he explains to his nephew the things that make cows happy – grass, milk, sunshine – while carving their carcasses into chuck roasts and tenderloins.

Nadajewski, a fixture of the Stratford and Shaw Festivals, places his trademark impish wit on full display as he works through Anton’s erratic moods. There’s not a moment in the show that’s not elevated by the actor’s giddy sense of humour or robust baritone voice – in the best, most satisfying ways, it’s often tricky to tell where Nadajewski stops and Anton begins.

Louis, meanwhile, has little desire to be a butcher, his aspirations set squarely on becoming a poet, or at the very least, handsome. But neither are likely to happen for him – he’s mostly accepted that, a fact Garwood makes achingly clear as he sings through Page’s intricate, melancholy score.

Maybe, just maybe, inspiration will strike. Maybe Louis will be able to show his uncle that his poetic longings aren’t mere fancy – that he’s destined for more than emptying scrap buckets full of muck. But for now, he’s stuck working in Anton’s shop, learning under duress what makes cows – and his uncle – tick.

So goes All The Cows Are Dead , whose individual vignettes coalesce into a gorgeous mosaic of what it means to live and die in harmony with the natural world. Anton is volatile, occasionally cruel, but unwaveringly determined to make a meatman of his bumbling heir. For a while, it’s unclear if the butcher could be capable of real, bleeding love.

But then he speaks of the cows – the young calves slaughtered solely for human consumption, the beasts murdered in the name of pleasure. His reverence for veal isn’t a love Louis can easily understand or even entirely recognize, but it’s love all the same, contradictory yet powerful in its depth.

Director William Dao steers the proceedings with little interest in naturalism or gore, instead choosing to represent meat through red and pink balloons. Some are succulent and supple, stuffed such that they approximate real steaks; others are brownish and floppy, destined to become balloon sausages seasoned with thyme. (Alessia Urbani is the set, costume and props designer.)

It’s a bold aesthetic risk that pays off in spades. While there’s always the fear that a latex roast or mince might pop, that tension only adds to the ever-changing relationship between Louis and Anton, their easy camaraderie forever on the edge of charring into bitterness.

There’s a moment when things click for Louis – when, just for a second, his higher purpose threatens to become clear. He’s concocted a special seasoning blend that his customers adore; he’s found a rhythm to butchery that nearly agrees with his idealistic virtues. “I’ve discovered something superb,” he sings happily as he inflates his creations.

In the aftermath of Page’s glorious chamber fantasia of meat, I’m inclined to say the same to just about anyone who will listen. All The Cows Are Dead is a vital meditation on the circle of life, and a poignant observation of how generations relate to each other – or don’t. Even staged inside a strangely remote urban retail store, it’s among the strongest, most tender new Canadian musicals of the decade.
Indeed, to echo Louis: It’s something superb.

content_blocks.text: Deep in the shank of Toronto’s northwest corner sits Soul Provisions, a one-stop shop for luxury popsicles and soups. The space is decidedly not a theatre – located at the back of a nondescript industrial complex just south of Yorkdale Shopping Centre, it’s about as far a cry from a Mirvish auditorium as you could possibly imagine.

The space is decidedly not a theatre – located at the back of a nondescript industrial complex just south of Yorkdale Shopping Centre, it’s about as far a cry from a Mirvish auditorium as you could possibly imagine.

content_blocks.text: But as a venue for All The Cows Are Dead , Ben Page’s melt-in-your-mouth new musical about a butcher and his quixotic nephew, the tiny space couldn’t be more suitable. The concrete floors and walls echo as if already familiar with the sounds of cleavers and grinders; the fluorescent overhead lights beat down incessantly, much more appropriate than traditional theatrical spotlights for slicing make-believe rib-eyes.

Based in Barrie, Ont., the company specializes in scrappy, site-specific work – in recent years, its Toronto productions have brought audiences to private living rooms, church basements and obscure warehouses for its shows, each seemingly more out-there than the last. ( Company , one of Talk Is Free’s few musicals to be staged in a traditional theatre space, was notably among its least successful .)

stories.title: ‘Absolutely disgusting’: Ford addresses Hamilton poppy drive assault
stories.summary: An assault that left an air cadet captain with life-altering injuries last week was “absolutely disgusting,” Premier Doug Ford says.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
An assault that left an air cadet captain with life-altering injuries last week was “absolutely disgusting,” Ontario Premier Doug Ford says.

Ford said Monday that the two youths who allegedly triggered the incident should be physically disciplined.

“It’s absolutely disgusting by a bunch of older kids. Where are the parents? The parents should be ashamed that they’ve raised their kids to beat up cadets. You’ve got to be kidding,” Ford told reporters at an unrelated news conference in Peterborough, Ont.

“I hope the parents are listening. You know, you should give your kids a little ass whooping in the woodshed as far as I’m concerned. A 14-year-old kid beating up cadets that are trying to serve our country? The most disgusting thing you could ever do.”

The alleged assault, which occurred on Nov. 1 in Hamilton, Ont., resulted in charges against a 12-year-old boy and a 48-year-old woman. Police did not announce charges against the second youth, whose age was not released. The ages of the cadets wasn’t released either.

Capt. Kenneth Kunkel was supervising the cadets outside a restaurant when two youths allegedly approached and blew an air horn directly into their ears. The 59-year-old followed the youths into the restaurant and confronted them.

During the ensuing struggle, an adult woman intervened and allegedly assaulted Kunkel, causing him to fall, before one youth allegedly struck him several times.

Kunkel’s son, Christopher, previously told Global News his father’s legs buckled and he lost movement during the confrontation after the woman allegedly became involved.

He said in a statement that his father told bystanders that he needed help and could not move his legs.

Kunkel underwent same-day spinal surgery and is now in rehabilitation, Christopher said.

“After an unforgettable Halloween evening where Captain Kenneth Kunkel walked his four grandchildren around the neighbourhood to visit friends and neighbours, we are decimated by the senseless attack that May have forever robbed four kids of their grandfather’s playful, loving tendencies,” he said.

His father has been helping cadets for almost 20 years, he said, adding Kenneth was instrumental in his own journey through the cadet program and into service with the Canadian Armed Forces.

Christopher said his father’s work also influenced former cadets who later joined municipal police services, the RCMP and the military, or became more involved in their communities.

“Even as he got older, Captain Kenneth Kunkel would physically prepare for weeks in advance so he could train with cadets and be a role model as they underwent fitness evaluations as part of the cadet program,” he said.

1:50 Cadet captain unable to walk after attack during Hamilton poppy drive

A crowdfunding campaign has been established to help financially support Kunkel’s recovery.

The 12-year-old boy was charged with assault level one as well as aggravated assault, while the woman was charged with aggravated assault.

The investigation is ongoing.

Anyone with information is asked to contact police.

stories.title: London resident charged after international child exploitation investigation
stories.summary: A 47-year-old London man is facing 11 charges following an investigation by the London Police Service Internet Child Exploitation Unit.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
A 47-year-old London man is facing 11 charges following an investigation by the London Police Service Internet Child Exploitation Unit.

According to police, the investigation began after Homeland Security Investigations conducted a probe between January and October 2025 into international child sex trafficking organizations that facilitate livestream child sexual abuse.

In October 2025, the Philippine National Bureau of Investigation’s Human Trafficking Division conducted an operation that resulted in the rescue of five children. Information related to alleged criminal offences was later provided to the RCMP National Child Exploitation Crime Centre’s Transnational Child Sex Offender Unit with assistance from the Child Rescue Coalition, Homeland Security Investigations and the Financial Transactions and Reports Analysis Centre of Canada.

During an RCMP-led investigation in Ottawa conducted in partnership with Homeland Security Investigations, investigators identified a London man who was allegedly sending money to a facilitator in the Philippines.

On June 9, 2026, the RCMP’s National Child Exploitation Crime Centre notified London police that the investigation involved a London resident.

Members of the London Police Service Internet Child Exploitation Unit executed a search warrant at a residence in the area of Grosvenor and Gammage streets on Nov. 5. A suspect was arrested and electronic devices were seized.

Police said investigators located evidence of child sexual abuse and exploitation material.

As a result of the investigation, Timothy Ryan Shirk, 47, of London, is charged with:

Three counts of agreement by telecommunication to commit specific criminal offences with another person under or believed to be under 16;

Publishing, printing or possessing for publication child sexual abuse material;

Possession of child sexual abuse and exploitation material;

Sexual assault as a party to an offence;

Sexual interference with a person under 16; and

Obtaining sexual services for consideration from a person under 18.

Police said the accused appeared in court on Nov. 5 and was later released on conditions, including that he not be within 20 metres of a public park, public swimming area, daycare centre, school grounds, playground or community centre. He is also prohibited from being alone with anyone under the age of 18 and from possessing weapons.

A photograph of the accused has been released by police because of the nature of the charges and the court-imposed conditions.

Shirk is scheduled to reappear in a London court on Jan. 28, 2027.

According to police, the investigation began after Homeland Security Investigations conducted a probe between January and October 2025 into international child sex trafficking organizations that facilitate livestream child sexual abuse.

In October 2025, the Philippine National Bureau of Investigation’s Human Trafficking Division conducted an operation that resulted in the rescue of five children. Information related to alleged criminal offences was later provided to the RCMP National Child Exploitation Crime Centre’s Transnational Child Sex Offender Unit with assistance from the Child Rescue Coalition, Homeland Security Investigations and the Financial Transactions and Reports Analysis Centre of Canada.

During an RCMP-led investigation in Ottawa conducted in partnership with Homeland Security Investigations, investigators identified a London man who was allegedly sending money to a facilitator in the Philippines.
On June 9, 2026, the RCMP’s National Child Exploitation Crime Centre notified London police that the investigation involved a London resident.

Members of the London Police Service Internet Child Exploitation Unit executed a search warrant at a residence in the area of Grosvenor and Gammage streets on Nov. 5. A suspect was arrested and electronic devices were seized.
Police said investigators located evidence of child sexual abuse and exploitation material.
As a result of the investigation, Timothy Ryan Shirk, 47, of London, is charged with:
Three counts of agreement by telecommunication to commit specific criminal offences with another person under or believed to be under 16;
Publishing, printing or possessing for publication child sexual abuse material;
Possession of child sexual abuse and exploitation material;
Sexual assault as a party to an offence;
Sexual interference with a person under 16; and
Obtaining sexual services for consideration from a person under 18.

Police said the accused appeared in court on Nov. 5 and was later released on conditions, including that he not be within 20 metres of a public park, public swimming area, daycare centre, school grounds, playground or community centre. He is also prohibited from being alone with anyone under the age of 18 and from possessing weapons.
A photograph of the accused has been released by police because of the nature of the charges and the court-imposed conditions.
Shirk is scheduled to reappear in a London court on Jan. 28, 2027.

stories.title: Honda to retool Ontario plant for production of new hybrid and gas-powered models
stories.summary: Carmaker will invest $166-million to restart the Alliston plant’s engine shop, keeping 4,000 jobs
stories.author: Eric Atkins
stories.content:
U.S. President Donald Trump has repeatedly said the United States doesn’t need Canadian automobiles . A new investment by Honda Motor Co. HMC-N in Alliston, Ont., and the reopening of Ford Motor Co.’s F-N assembly plant in Oakville tell a different story.

Ford’s factory west of Toronto, which closed for retooling in 2024, has reopened to make pickup trucks, most of which are destined for U.S. buyers. Even before the plant’s official launch later in November, the F-Series Super Duty trucks are already being shipped to dealers in Canada and the United States, bolstering production at plants in Kentucky and Ohio, which are running at full capacity. About 2,000 people are back on the job at the plant.

“This is a good news story,” said Fraser Johnson, a business professor at Western University.

The Oakville plant turned out 3,488 trucks in October, as Ford is set to make more than one million F-Series trucks in 2026, said Michael Ward, an analyst at Citi Research.

“They have ramped up nicely,” said Sam Fiorani, an analyst at Pennsylvania-based consultancy AutoForecast Solutions.

Honda, meanwhile, said it is spending $166-million at its Ontario auto plant to restart its engine shop and retool for updated models of hybrid-electric and gas-powered cars, part of an $867-million investment announced on Monday.

The investment will help the automaker meet demand while maintaining 4,000 jobs at the plant northwest of Toronto, Honda said Monday.

Honda is enjoying strong demand for the plant’s cars, the CRV and Civic, and ships much of its 400,000-plus production to the United States. The engine factory, which closed in 2024, will supply power motors to about one-quarter of the factory’s total for the Canadian market.

The federal and Ontario governments are contributing $313-million and $156-million, respectively, to the total.

The Ford plant, with annual capacity of 100,000 units, makes large versions of Ford’s best-selling pickups, including the F-250 and F-350, powered by diesel or gasoline engines. Ford’s Essex engine plant in Windsor, Ont., makes some of the trucks’ 7.3-litre V-8 gas engines, and has increased production to feed the Oakville factory after a US$500-million investment by the automaker. The diesel engines are made in Mexico, highlighting the integration of the North American auto industry.

Ford’s F-Series trucks are the best-selling vehicles in the U.S. and Canada. Canadians bought more than 138,000 of the trucks in 2025, beating the Toyota RAV4 SUV, and outselling the nearest truck competitors combined, the GMC Sierra and Chevrolet Silverado, according to DesRosiers Automotive Consultants Inc. “The F-Series is a tremendous product, with amazing customer loyalty and the ability to shrug off many of its would-be competitors,” said Andrew King, managing partner of DesRosiers.

Shahin Alizadeh, owner of dealership Downtown Ford Toronto, said sales of F-Series trucks have grown to comprise 25 to 30 per cent of his sales. “Loyalty is a big factor with Ford buyers,” he said.

Ford says it has invested $5-billion at the plant, in addition to a $464-million grant from the federal government . The plant made the Ford Edge until it closed in mid-2024 to be retooled to make electric vehicles and battery packs. That plan was delayed and then cancelled altogether amid slowing demand in the U.S. for EVs. Instead, Ford began remaking the assembly line to produce the large trucks, which will include those powered by hybrid and extended-range electric powertrains.

“We’re excited about the local production,” Mr. Alizadeh said. “I don’t know if Ford is, if the tariffs keep going.”

Mr. Trump said his tariffs of 25 per cent on cars made in Canada and elsewhere are intended to foster manufacturing in the U.S. The tariffs are opposed by the North American auto industry – including Detroit-based companies – as an unneeded expense that undermines decades of supply chain integration.

In Canada, General Motors GM-N and Stellantis NV Stla-N responded to the tariffs by reducing production and laying off workers. GM idled its electric van plant in Ingersoll, Ont., laying off more than 1,000 people. The Globe and Mail reported on Friday that Stellantis is expected this week to say it has sold its Brampton, Ont., plant, which has been idle since 2023, to defence contractor Roshel Inc.

Ford and the Unifor union, which represents more than 5,150 Canadian workers, agreed in recent collective bargaining talks to bring back all laid-off Oakville workers by next July. (The plant employed 3,200 Unifor members when it closed in 2024.) Full-rate production workers will make $50.20 an hour by the end of the three-year deal, while skilled trades employees will be paid $62.71.

The agreement also includes a renewed “no closure” clause for all Ford facilities, and a commitment to start a third shift at the Windsor engine plant, likely by 2029.

Industry observers say Ford made the investment in Oakville with the belief that tariffs aren’t forever, and because the F-Series is in high demand. The trucks, whose base models range in price from $62,000 to $128,400, are very profitable. This makes it easier for Ford to absorb part of the cost of the tariffs, although some is expected to be passed on to buyers.

“Given the margins on the product, Ford is able to some extent withstand the tariff costs, at least in the short term until there’s some resolution of the trade dispute with the U.S.,” Prof. Johnson said. “And they need the capacity to be able to protect the market share and sell their vehicles.”

Details of the U.S. content of the trucks were not available, but the industry says the average for cars made in Canada is about 50 per cent. This makes for an effective tariff rate of about 12.5 per cent.

Alicia Boler Davis, president of Ford Pro, the company’s work-truck division, said on a recent conference call with analysts the Oakville plant will help the automaker catch up to demand from large commercial buyers and rental companies. The Oakville trucks will also make up for lost production at U.S. plants slated to pause for upgrades.

“We’re excited about Oakville and that capacity because that’s going to allow us to really grow,” she said.

Honda, which recently marked its 40th year of making cars in Canada, is the country’s second-largest producer by volume.

Brendan Sweeney, who represents Honda and Toyota as head of the Pacific Manufacturing Association of Canada, said strong consumer demand for Hondas ensures the plants keep producing despite the tariffs.

“They’re not in a position to stop production,” he said. The Japanese corporate belief in looking long-term, to a time when the tariffs might be gone, is also a big factor, Mr. Sweeney said.

It’s an event where community members partner with the same athletes for whom they are fundraising.

“Motionball is a charity that supports Special Olympics Canada, and it’s our flagship event,” said Justin Mulligan, the London event organizer at Oakridge Secondary School.

“I like to describe it as recess-style games. It’s very inclusive, and people from all walks of life can play the games we offer. It’s all about the athletes, interacting with them and providing a safe environment for them.”

Over the past 25 years, the movement has raised close to $23 million for Special Olympics.

Motionball operates in 20 cities and on 30 university campuses, hosting more than 50 events each year.

Those recess-style games include bench ball, basketball, giant pong, ultimate frisbee, soccer and bean bag toss.

“Motionball was kind of exciting because the people were very, very happy to join us together,” said Surrey Barnham, a London Special Olympics athlete.

“Special Olympics is very fun. I would say it was pretty good because what people love about Special Olympics is they can do anything and be proud of themselves.”

Special Olympics athlete Riley Been was excited to participate for the first time.

“I’ve been playing basketball and bench ball and ping pong,” said Been. “I like Special Olympics because I can be with my friends.”

You would be hard-pressed to find a more enthusiastic athlete than Valentina Mejia.

Mulligan said reading about or seeing the event does not fully capture its spirit.

“You have to participate to understand the magnitude,” he said.

“They’re just so happy when they show up and they’re ready to go. They love life. They’re always smiling. We had somebody who came directly from the hospital today because he couldn’t miss this event. He had to get out of there and come here, and it just shows their spirit. They just want to have fun and participate.”

stories.title: Ford’s reopened Oakville truck plant gears up to supply U.S. market
stories.summary: About 2,000 workers are back on the job and vehicles are already being shipped south of border
stories.author: Eric Atkins
stories.content:
U.S. President Donald Trump has repeatedly said the United States doesn’t need Canadian automobiles . A new investment by Honda Motor Co. HMC-N in Alliston, Ont., and the reopening of Ford Motor Co.’s F-N assembly plant in Oakville tell a different story.

Ford’s factory west of Toronto, which closed for retooling in 2024, has reopened to make pickup trucks, most of which are destined for U.S. buyers. Even before the plant’s official launch later in November, the F-Series Super Duty trucks are already being shipped to dealers in Canada and the United States, bolstering production at plants in Kentucky and Ohio, which are running at full capacity. About 2,000 people are back on the job at the plant.

“This is a good news story,” said Fraser Johnson, a business professor at Western University.

The Oakville plant turned out 3,488 trucks in October, as Ford is set to make more than one million F-Series trucks in 2026, said Michael Ward, an analyst at Citi Research.

“They have ramped up nicely,” said Sam Fiorani, an analyst at Pennsylvania-based consultancy AutoForecast Solutions.

Honda, meanwhile, said it is spending $166-million at its Ontario auto plant to restart its engine shop and retool for updated models of hybrid-electric and gas-powered cars, part of an $867-million investment announced on Monday.

The investment will help the automaker meet demand while maintaining 4,000 jobs at the plant northwest of Toronto, Honda said Monday.

Honda is enjoying strong demand for the plant’s cars, the CRV and Civic, and ships much of its 400,000-plus production to the United States. The engine factory, which closed in 2024, will supply power motors to about one-quarter of the factory’s total for the Canadian market.

The federal and Ontario governments are contributing $313-million and $156-million, respectively, to the total.

The Ford plant, with annual capacity of 100,000 units, makes large versions of Ford’s best-selling pickups, including the F-250 and F-350, powered by diesel or gasoline engines. Ford’s Essex engine plant in Windsor, Ont., makes some of the trucks’ 7.3-litre V-8 gas engines, and has increased production to feed the Oakville factory after a US$500-million investment by the automaker. The diesel engines are made in Mexico, highlighting the integration of the North American auto industry.

Ford’s F-Series trucks are the best-selling vehicles in the U.S. and Canada. Canadians bought more than 138,000 of the trucks in 2025, beating the Toyota RAV4 SUV, and outselling the nearest truck competitors combined, the GMC Sierra and Chevrolet Silverado, according to DesRosiers Automotive Consultants Inc. “The F-Series is a tremendous product, with amazing customer loyalty and the ability to shrug off many of its would-be competitors,” said Andrew King, managing partner of DesRosiers.

Shahin Alizadeh, owner of dealership Downtown Ford Toronto, said sales of F-Series trucks have grown to comprise 25 to 30 per cent of his sales. “Loyalty is a big factor with Ford buyers,” he said.

Ford says it has invested $5-billion at the plant, in addition to a $464-million grant from the federal government . The plant made the Ford Edge until it closed in mid-2024 to be retooled to make electric vehicles and battery packs. That plan was delayed and then cancelled altogether amid slowing demand in the U.S. for EVs. Instead, Ford began remaking the assembly line to produce the large trucks, which will include those powered by hybrid and extended-range electric powertrains.

“We’re excited about the local production,” Mr. Alizadeh said. “I don’t know if Ford is, if the tariffs keep going.”

Mr. Trump said his tariffs of 25 per cent on cars made in Canada and elsewhere are intended to foster manufacturing in the U.S. The tariffs are opposed by the North American auto industry – including Detroit-based companies – as an unneeded expense that undermines decades of supply chain integration.

In Canada, General Motors GM-N and Stellantis NV Stla-N responded to the tariffs by reducing production and laying off workers. GM idled its electric van plant in Ingersoll, Ont., laying off more than 1,000 people. The Globe and Mail reported on Friday that Stellantis is expected this week to say it has sold its Brampton, Ont., plant, which has been idle since 2023, to defence contractor Roshel Inc.

Ford and the Unifor union, which represents more than 5,150 Canadian workers, agreed in recent collective bargaining talks to bring back all laid-off Oakville workers by next July. (The plant employed 3,200 Unifor members when it closed in 2024.) Full-rate production workers will make $50.20 an hour by the end of the three-year deal, while skilled trades employees will be paid $62.71.

The agreement also includes a renewed “no closure” clause for all Ford facilities, and a commitment to start a third shift at the Windsor engine plant, likely by 2029.

Industry observers say Ford made the investment in Oakville with the belief that tariffs aren’t forever, and because the F-Series is in high demand. The trucks, whose base models range in price from $62,000 to $128,400, are very profitable. This makes it easier for Ford to absorb part of the cost of the tariffs, although some is expected to be passed on to buyers.

“Given the margins on the product, Ford is able to some extent withstand the tariff costs, at least in the short term until there’s some resolution of the trade dispute with the U.S.,” Prof. Johnson said. “And they need the capacity to be able to protect the market share and sell their vehicles.”

Details of the U.S. content of the trucks were not available, but the industry says the average for cars made in Canada is about 50 per cent. This makes for an effective tariff rate of about 12.5 per cent.

Alicia Boler Davis, president of Ford Pro, the company’s work-truck division, said on a recent conference call with analysts the Oakville plant will help the automaker catch up to demand from large commercial buyers and rental companies. The Oakville trucks will also make up for lost production at U.S. plants slated to pause for upgrades.

“We’re excited about Oakville and that capacity because that’s going to allow us to really grow,” she said.

Honda, which recently marked its 40th year of making cars in Canada, is the country’s second-largest producer by volume.

Brendan Sweeney, who represents Honda and Toyota as head of the Pacific Manufacturing Association of Canada, said strong consumer demand for Hondas ensures the plants keep producing despite the tariffs.

“They’re not in a position to stop production,” he said. The Japanese corporate belief in looking long-term, to a time when the tariffs might be gone, is also a big factor, Mr. Sweeney said.

stories.title: Honda Canada to retool Alliston, Ont., plant to expand hybrid production
stories.summary: Markham — Honda Canada says it will retool its manufacturing facility in Alliston, Ont., to expand production of hybrid-electric and gasoline-powered vehicles.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Honda Canada says it will retool its manufacturing facilities in Alliston, Ont., to expand production of hybrid-electric and gasoline-powered vehicles.

The Japanese automaker announced Monday it is partnering with the federal and provincial governments to fund plant upgrades, including the reintroduction of engine manufacturing, with an initial $166 million investment.

It said that funding is part of a broader $867-million commitment that will enhance quality, efficiency and manufacturing flexibility. Of that total, the federal government said it will provide $313 million, while the Ontario government is kicking in $156 million.

“This renewed investment reinforces Canada’s critical role in Honda’s North American growth and hybrid-electric vehicle strategy and helps position our operations for long-term competitiveness and future opportunities,” said Honda Canada president and CEO Dave Jamieson in a news release.

The funding will ensure Honda can maintain its workforce of 4,000 Canadian employees across two facilities at the Alliston plant, while supporting its Canadian auto production volumes.

The company said it will also strengthen the Alliston plant’s operations to help meet growing customer demand for hybrid-electric vehicles in North America.

“This investment will strengthen our automotive supply chains, support thousands of well-paying jobs in Ontario and across the country, and help build a strong Canadian auto sector where workers build the cars of the future,” said Industry Minister Mélanie Joly in a statement.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford called the investment “a clear vote of confidence in the 4,000 world-class Ontario auto workers employed at the plant.”

“In the face of tariffs and economic uncertainty, we’re delivering on our plan to make Ontario more competitive so we can protect workers and attract job-creating investments like this one from around the globe,” he said in a statement on social media.

In May, Honda announced plans to introduce 15 new Honda and Acura hybrid models globally by 2030, with North America expected to be the primary market for many of those vehicles.

The automaker said it is investing across its manufacturing network in Canada, Ohio, Alabama and Georgia to support that strategy.

That same month, the company indefinitely suspended its plans for a $15-billion Canadian electric vehicle complex in response to dwindling demand.

Announced in 2024, Honda’s EV project would have included a vehicle assembly plant as well as battery production facilities. It had said that new EV plant could create 1,000 incremental manufacturing jobs in Alliston.

It was set to receive upwards of $5 billion in federal and Ontario funding, however no money had yet been transferred.

The decision to pause those plans did not affect current employment or production levels at the Alliston plant.

More than 400,000 vehicles were produced at the site last year. Honda is Canada’s second largest auto manufacturer by volume.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 9, 2026.

Sammy Hudes, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Carney reveals first CEO of Canada Strong Fund for sovereign wealth
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney has recruited another global investment executive to his government, this time to helm Canada's first sovereign wealth fund.
stories.author: Craig Lord
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney has recruited another global investment executive to his government, this time to helm Canada’s first sovereign wealth fund.

The Prime Minister’s Office announced today that Karen Karniol-Tambour will be the inaugural chief executive of the Canada Strong Fund.

Karniol-Tambour is the co-chief investment officer at U.S.-based Bridgewater Associates, one of the world’s largest asset managers.

A biography provided by Carney’s office says Karniol-Tambour is a Canadian citizen who has been named one of the 100 most influential women in U.S. finance for seven years running by the financial magazine Barron’s.

The Prime Minister’s Office says the Canada Strong Fund will be run at arm’s-length from government with its own independent board of directors.

Carney unveiled plans for the sovereign wealth fund last spring with an announcement of an initial capital commitment of $25 billion and a retail component that lets individual Canadians invest and potentially share in the fund’s returns.

stories.title: Neffy nasal spray for severe allergies now available without prescription
stories.summary: The National Association of Pharmacy Regulatory Authorities (Napra) classified Neffy as a Schedule II product across Canada, which means it can now be sold over the counter.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
Neffy , the epinephrine nasal spray for severe allergies , is now available without a prescription at pharmacies in Canada—but not for everyone.

The National Association of Pharmacy Regulatory Authorities (Napra) classified Neffy’s two milligram dose as a Schedule II product across Canada.

This means that the drug is now available without a prescription in provinces and territories where a prescription was previously required, ALK-Abelló Pharmaceuticals Inc. Canada said.

In April, Health Canada approved epinephrine nasal spray for use in adults and children with a body weight of 30 kilograms or 66 pounds for emergency treatment of severe allergic reactions, but it still needed classification from Napra.

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved the drug in the U.S. in 2024.

Allowing it to be sold behind the counter will give caregivers another way to carry and use epinephrine for first-line emergency treatment for severe allergic reactions, ALK Canada said.

Consumers will need to speak directly with the pharmacist who will conduct proper counselling before dispensing Neffy to patients without a prescription, the company added.

In 2024, results of four studies in 175 healthy adults, without anaphylaxis, showed Neffy worked about as well as injected epinephrine to boost heart rate and blood pressure, which counter severe reactions.

The two milligram dose of the Neffy nasal spray is equivalent to a 0.3 milligram dose in an epinephrine auto-injector, according to Food Allergy Canada.

The Neffy one milligram dose, which is not yet approved for use in Canada, can be used on patients weighing 15-30 kilograms. For now, the EpiPen Jr. with its 0.15 milligram dose, remains the only option for younger patients.

According to the FDA, some of the most common side effects of Neffy include throat irritation, tingling nose, headache, nasal discomfort, fatigue, runny nose, sneezing, abdominal pain, gum pain, numbness in the mouth, nasal congestion, dizziness, nausea and vomiting.
