stories.title: Gun users battle Ottawa’s firearms ban at Supreme Court
stories.summary: Challengers against 2020 regulations banning assault-style weapons have lost twice in the lower courts
stories.author: David Ebner
stories.content:
The federal government will defend its 2020 ban on assault-style firearms at the Supreme Court of Canada on Monday, taking on an array of challengers that argue Ottawa exceeded its legal authority.

The case, to be heard Monday and Tuesday, is the biggest hearing at the top court this fall. It centres around legal questions about the reasonable extent of Ottawa’s power to ban weapons such the AR-15, Beretta Cx4 Storm and other firearms to protect public safety despite the use of the guns in some cases for sport shooting or hunting.

The federal Liberals enacted the ban under former prime minister Justin Trudeau. “Assault-style firearms designed for military use have no place in Canada,” he said at the time. Ottawa invoked its regulatory powers, rather than legislation, to ban more than 1,500 types of firearms in 2020, and increased the list of banned guns to more than 2,500 in late 2024 and early 2025.

The lower courts have twice ruled in Ottawa’s favour. The Supreme Court in March agreed to hear the appeals.

A continuing amnesty period for the possession of the prohibited weapons is in effect until 90 days after a judgment from the Supreme Court. Businesses and individuals can dispose of their guns or permanently deactivate them, and Ottawa is also buying them back. As of mid-2026, the federal government had paid businesses $96-million for about 74,000 guns – an average of $1,300 per weapon.

The firearms case involves four different challengers and, unusually, includes several self-represented litigants who will argue in front of the nine judges of the Supreme Court without a lawyer. Five other gun groups as well as the provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Ontario also oppose the ban.

The appellant Christine Generoux, from Ottawa and in her late 30s, has been dubbed “an unlikely heroine of Canadian gun culture” by a sport shooting group. She is set to argue her case herself on Monday morning, and in her legal filing said there was no justification to deem the guns unreasonable for use in recreational purposes. She also spoke of what she called the sentimental, life-sustaining and cultural nature of guns.

“Sport shooting is destroyed and hunting disrupted,” Ms. Generoux stated. She further argued the issue goes deeper than reasonableness – a key legal question of whether Ottawa stayed within the limits of its powers. “It strikes at the heart of Parliamentary democracy and Canadian identity.”

The Canadian Coalition for Firearms Rights, an appellant that does have legal counsel, argued the heart of the firearms case goes beyond the individual rights of gun owners. The group said Ottawa’s regulations were too vague to be within its powers and described this as legality succumbing to “ambiguous administrative will, leaving people to navigate a standardless whim.”

The group stated that mass shootings are rare in Canada, “claims of firearm use in homicides are exaggerated” and most high-profile shootings involve illegal guns.

The ban “concerns the profound disruption of the lives of ordinary, law-abiding Canadians,” it argued in its appeal. “They are not extremists; they are farmers, veterans, competitive athletes, Indigenous harvesters, and neighbours in communities across Canada.”

The federal government’s response began by listing a series of deadly mass shootings in Canada and around the world where the killers wielded assault-style firms, starting with Portapique, N.S., in 2020, Montreal’s L’École Polytechnique in 1989 and the Islamic Culture Centre in Quebec City in 2017.

Ottawa’s response then addressed the core of the legal case: whether the federal cabinet was allowed to use regulations based on a section in the Criminal Code to achieve its public-safety policy objectives rather than through the legislative powers of Parliament. The minority Liberal government tried and failed to codify the banned assault-style firearms in law in 2023.

The federal government is arguing that Parliament has long empowered cabinet with broad discretionary authority to prohibit firearms in the interest of public safety, and that the exercise of that political power “was reasonable and justified by the serious public safety concerns these firearms pose.”

Ottawa has few allies at the top court. The Canadian Coalition for Gun Control, an intervener in the case, provides the only explicit backing, echoing the federal government’s position that the Criminal Code allows for the authority to pass regulations to ban the firearms. The group cited the overriding purpose of public safety and argued that the broad nature of the ban adheres with the rule of law.

The three provincial governments that intervened in the case are all conservative-led and are once more opposing the federal Liberals at the Supreme Court, as they had earlier this year in the landmark case on Quebec secularism and the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

Alberta and Saskatchewan said Ottawa overstepped its powers in the firearms ban, while Ontario more plainly stated: “The regulations are unconstitutional.”

Alberta hired veteran lawyer Guy Pratte at Borden Ladner Gervais in Ottawa to helm its arguments. His father, Yves, was a Supreme Court judge in the late 1970s, and earlier this year Mr. Pratte argued on behalf of the federal government in the Quebec secularism case.

Alberta’s legal filing said Ottawa “at the stroke of a pen” criminalized firearms ownership for more than 100,000 Canadians licensed to own such guns for hunting and sport shooting “without any evidence that these firearms users pose a threat to public safety.”

The province also said hunting and participation in shooting sports are “matters of exclusive provincial jurisdiction” and that the Criminal Code only allows cabinet to ban guns by regulation if they are not reasonable to use for those purposes, rather than in pursuit of a policy of public safety.

stories.title: Métis veteran reflects on Canada’s treatment of Indigenous veterans
stories.summary: For the Canadian Armed Forces veteran and Royal Canadian Legion Branch 101 president, remembering that service is also an opportunity to honour his Métis heritage.
stories.author: Kamil Karamali
stories.content:
Toronto – Looking through photographs of his father and grandfather, Alan Roy traces a family history of military service through faded images and medals that predate his own time in uniform.

His father served in the Second World War. His grandfather, Roy says, served in both world wars.

“Third generation in the military,” Roy, 64, said, describing his own place in that family tradition.

For the Canadian Armed Forces veteran and Royal Canadian Legion Branch 101 president, remembering that service is also an opportunity to honour his Métis heritage.

“My pride in being Canadian is only increased by the fact that we can say we have Métis heritage,” Roy said, who describes his own military experience as one of belonging. “I never felt that I was being ostracized because of whatever my background was at that time.”

But he also acknowledges a broader history of discrimination against Indigenous veterans — one that recognition today cannot erase.

“It’ll never go away. It’s part of our history now,” he said. “Many of them have suffered for their heritage. I know from personal experience, many of these people are upset over the way things happened. There are a lot of horror stories out there.”

Service abroad, barriers at home

Veterans Affairs Canada acknowledges that many Indigenous veterans did not receive equal treatment when they returned from military service.

First Nations veterans faced unequal access to land and benefits. After the First World War, reserve land was transferred to non-Indigenous veterans, while most First Nations veterans applying for equivalent land grants received permission to use land already belonging to their communities rather than ownership.

Métis veterans faced different barriers. In a 2019 apology, Ottawa acknowledged that postwar benefits were poorly designed to meet their needs. Many lacked the prerequisites to access education and training programs, against a backdrop of prejudice, poverty and limited educational opportunities.

Veterans Affairs estimates that more than 12,000 First Nations, Métis and Inuit people served in the major conflicts of the 20th century. At least 500 lost their lives.

Rob Baskey, a senator with the Métis Nation of Ontario Veterans’ Council and an Eagle Staff carrier, says ensuring veterans receive the benefits they deserve is part of reconciliation.

“I think we can always be better,” he said. “If Indigenous Veterans are finally receiving those benefits that they should have been receiving... I think that’s a positive step forward towards reconciliation. But we can always do better.”

Making remembrance more visible

Dozens of people gathered Sunday at the Spirit Garden outside Toronto City Hall to mark Indigenous Veterans Day.

For Baskey, the public ceremony is one part of a year-round responsibility to remember those who served – saying that Indigenous Veterans Day needs to attract greater awareness and attendance.

“There’s a crowd here but it’s not on the scale that it should be. If people knew about this ceremony, it’s going to happen today... it would be more people,” he said.

In a joint statement Sunday, federal ministers said: “The Government of Canada remains committed to ensuring that all Indigenous Veterans receive the recognition and support they deserve.”

Roy sees progress in the recognition of Indigenous service and identity within the military, pointing to visible expressions of that heritage on uniforms.

“Every step is a good one,” he said.

As he looks through his family’s photographs, that history remains close at hand: three generations of service, preserved for another generation to remember.

stories.title: Fanshawe welcomes prospective students
stories.summary: Prospective students and many family members filled the halls of Fanshawe College on Nov. 7 for the school's f...
stories.author: Samantha Luis
stories.content:
Prospective students and many family members filled the halls of Fanshawe College on Nov. 7 for the school’s fall open house. As visitors toured classrooms and met with faculty and student ambassadors, some already decided on specific programs while others still hadn’t made up their minds.

“I’m planning on being a future student at Fanshawe. I just wanted to take a look around. I have things in mind, but I haven’t decided. I thought of becoming

Hasan Alaliwat, prospective student (Credit: Samantha Luis/ XFM News) a social worker, but when I went around I saw lots of interesting things, so it will make it more difficult for me to decide. But anyway I do have to decide to start my plan,” said Hasan Alaliwat, a who is new to London and Canada.

For other prospective students, the open house provided the opportunity to discover programs, while also addressing the concerns about continuing education.

Sofia Sandoval, prospective student (Credit: Samantha Luis/ XFM News)

“I’m here to find a program that I like. I’m into arts and all that stuff. It’s a great open house; it changed my perspective on everything. I’m from Colombia and studied there. my biggest concern is having my diploma translate, but they helped me a lot here,” said Sofia Sandoval, a prospective student originally from Colombia.

Noela Mugisha, prospective student (Credit: Samantha Luis/ XFM News)

Those that did know their post-secondary future came with questions and concerns for what this new chapter May bring.

“I just applied for the MRI rad tech program, so I’m really excited. The only kind of concern I have is commuting or doing residency because I do live an hour and a half away,” said Noela Mugisha, a prospective student.

Staff and volunteers helped make open house easier for prospective students by giving directions and guided tours around the school.

“I’m helping people get from place to place. It’s important for our prospective students to be able to navigate the College and be able to get the information that they want,” said Karen Bieger, Csrsis at Fanshawe.

Karen Bieger, Csrsis at Fanshawe College (Credit: Samantha Luis/ XFM News)

Open houses are made to showcase the building and programs, while also building connections and relationships.

“It’s very important for us to do open houses because it allows us to show prospective students everything that we have on campus and everything that we have to offer.

Kate Traill, general arts and science program coordinator (Credit: Samantha Luis/ XFM News)

The halls were filled with hands full of Fanshawe merchandise and program information sheets.

“Roughly, I would say down this hallway is pretty quiet but I have probably seen a good 300-400 students,” said Bieger.

“Probably around 100 or 200 people, there’s been a line-up at the table almost all day.” said Traill, when asked how many people she’s spoken to at her booth.

Booths were lined up for each program with teachers and current students to answer any questions prospects May have.

Hallway during open house (Credit: Samantha Luis/ XFM News)

“I’ve been here all day answering questions about the general arts and science program, and just trying to promote our program as a flexible way for students to try and meet different learning goals,” said Traill.

“I had a lot of questions today about prerequisite courses. A lot of questions about pathways and what courses they can take in our program and how they would transfer to university,” said Traill, when asked what her most asked questions were.

Fanshawe’s next open house will take place on Apr. 3, 2027 to align with the seasonal recruitment cycle, and give prospective students a spring look at the campus ahead of application deadlines.

stories.title: Ottawa reveals details on long-promised $600-million for screen and music sectors
stories.summary: The funding was first announced in June after Ottawa ordered the Crtc to review a policy that would have raised streamers’ spending obligations in Canada
stories.author: Josh O’Kane
stories.content:
Ottawa announced details Sunday on how it would divvy up a long-promised $600-million funding package to help Canada’s film, television and music sectors produce original content and navigate the streaming era.

The Canada Media Fund, which assists the making of Canadian and Indigenous on-screen content, will be the biggest recipient, and is set to receive $213.4-million. The Department of Canadian Heritage said in its announcement that this would help the fund enhance existing programs and introduce new initiatives as it tries to mitigate declining contributions from private-sector cable and satellite companies.

Telefilm Canada is set to receive $68.5-million to put toward the growth, competitiveness and reach of Canadian and Indigenous productions. The Canada History Fund was allocated up to $5-million.

Independent production funds such as the Black Screen Office, Canadian Independent Screen Fund and Broadcasting Accessibility Fund, as well as several funds related to local news, will receive a cumulative $185.1-million.

The Indigenous Screen Office is set to get $51-million, while Heritage said that it would provide $10-million to the Northern Aboriginal Broadcasting program for Indigenous radio and television content.

The music industry, meanwhile, was promised $67-million through the Canada Music Fund to be distributed by its usual recipients, the Foundation Assisting Canadian Talent on Recordings (Factor) and Fondation Musicaction, as well as the Canadian Starmaker Fund, Fonds RadioStar and the Indigenous Music Office.

Opinion: The Crtc is right to make streaming giants pay more. What comes next, though?

The $600-million was first promised in June, after a whiplash two-week period in which the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission implemented a new framework for foreign streamers to contribute 15 per cent of their revenue earned in Canada to domestic content via the Online Streaming Act – only for the federal government to insist the regulator hold off and review the policy after criticism that it might become a trade irritant with the U.S.

At the time, Heritage said the money would provide stability for the sector until the federal government set new policy. By August, dozens of Canadian film and television organizations were on edge , issuing an open letter pressing for clear regulations to force streamers to pay for Canadian programming – and warning that the promised $600-million was not a sufficient replacement for legally enforceable obligations on streamers.

Heritage said in a statement Sunday that it planned to provide this kind of funding boost to the screen and music sectors annually until the government had finished developing its new streaming-funding policy.

Cultural industries had hoped for clarity on the matter in Thursday’s federal budget, but the destination of the $600-million was not among the fiscal document’s announcements . Those included a new tax credit for Canadian creative workers, $783.1-million for national museums and related institutions over five years, $60-million for the National Gallery of Canada, $20-million for the Canada Council for the Arts over three years, as well as $20-million over four years, plus $5-million ongoing, for the Canada Book Fund.

A file photo of a Toronto police cruiser. (Chris Doucette / Postmedia Network)

Courtney Greenberg

November 8, 2026 at 5:35 p.m.

A woman has been arrested at an anti-Israel protest in a predominantly Jewish neighbourhood in Toronto on Sunday.

Toronto police told National Post the arrest, for failure to comply at a demonstration, occurred just after 12 p.m. in the Bathurst St. and Sheppard Ave area.

While police did not identify the woman, videos circulating online showed the incident with officers on scene, leading a person with hands behind their back, into a Toronto Police Service vehicle.

There have been anti-Israel protests held in the Bathurst and Sheppard area since October 7. In March, police said that demonstrators would not be able to enter residential parts of the neighbourhood due to safety risks.

Courtney Greenberg is a Toronto-based journalist covering breaking news, with a focus on antisemitism in Canada. In 2026, she was a Postmedia Fellow with the Investigative Journalism Bureau, where she worked on in-depth investigations into women’s health and the justice system.

stories.title: Budget 2026: Ottawa plows money into power grids, but connecting them remains unclear
stories.summary: Intertie projects often spark debates about which province would reap most of the benefits, and how costs should therefore be divided
stories.author: Matthew McClearn
stories.content:
It was right there on the cover: The latest federal budget , released last week, featured red-and-white transmission towers and power lines running across a mountainous landscape near the Churchill Falls and Gull Island power project in Labrador.

The budget represents Ottawa’s latest efforts to promote expansion of the nation’s power grid, which it regards as too fragmented. The priciest measures include tweaking investment tax credits in ways that could benefit major transmission projects. The budget also set aside tens of millions of dollars for studies intended to help various levels of government to plan interprovincial links, also known as interties.

The federal government has promoted interties for nearly a decade now, but early signature projects flopped. The Atlantic Loop, introduced around 2020, contemplated 1,000 kilometres of two-way transmission lines connecting the Atlantic provinces to Quebec, but the price tag kept rising and crucial partners backed away a few years later.

But that did not cool Ottawa’s ardour: Several transmission-related proposals have been referred to the Major Projects Office for consideration as projects of national importance. In addition to individual projects, the new agency promotes the Transmission InterConnect Investment Strategy, which promises to “identify high priority transmission projects, as well as possible financial solutions to help them move forward.”

Tim Weis, senior director of the Pembina Institute’s industrial decarbonization group, said intertie projects are complicated to execute because they’re costly and require co-operation between two or more provinces with different regulatory systems governing their electricity markets. Intertie projects often become mired in debates about which province would reap most of the benefits, and how costs should therefore be apportioned.

Madeleine McPherson, an associate professor at the University of Victoria’s civil engineering department, has spent the last decade creating large models of power systems, mapping generators, transmission lines, power demand and a host of other factors. Those models reveal that interties make power more affordable, she said.

A more interconnected grid also allows better access to the lowest-cost resources, including wind power in the Prairies and Atlantic provinces, by pairing them with hydroelectricity that can compensate for their constantly changing output, according to Dr. McPherson. Power grids also become more reliable when neighbours can help one another during extreme weather events.

What’s missing, she said, is a consistent approach for weighing costs and benefits of proposed interties to determine which ones are truly worth pursuing, and who should pay for them. Such frameworks have been used by jurisdictions such as Australia that enjoyed greater success at improving grid integration over the last decade.

Opinion: It’s hard to be ‘masters of our destiny’ when our destiny is shaped in the U.S.

The budget included two items aimed at addressing such issues. It allocated $26.4-million over 10 years to the federal natural resources department to support data and modelling capacity to improve planning of electrical systems. And it earmarked $37-million during the next fiscal year “to support robust cost-benefit analysis of proposed interties and inform cross-border cost-allocation discussions.”

Absent from the budget were obvious new sources of federal capital to pay for intertie projects. But it did expand eligibility of investment tax credits for what it describes as “clean” energy, so that high-voltage intraprovincial transmission projects will qualify. (What qualifies as high-voltage varies drastically by province, reflecting the fact that grids use different technologies and serve vastly different users.) Eligible property would include cables, towers and transformers.

The government forecast that the cost of the tax credit changes will be substantial and grow significantly over time: a total of $2.4-billion from 2027 to 2031, and $36.1-billion over the following decade.

The tax credit changes were well-received by several energy think tanks. The Canadian Renewable Energy Association said they were “smart” and “practical” and would lower the cost of high-voltage transmission projects.

“Transmission connects the lowest-cost new power to the people and businesses who need it,” Vittoria Bellissimo, the organization’s president and chief executive officer, wrote in a statement.

François Bouffard, an associate professor in McGill University’s electrical and computer engineering department, said the tax credits will help developers, who face rising capital costs for intertie projects.

Dr. Bouffard said north-south transfers in electricity have long dominated the energy trade agenda across Canada, including in his home province of Quebec. But attitudes shifted significantly after Donald Trump’s return to the White House in 2025; energy sovereignty has gained importance. He observed a similar shift in neighbouring Ontario, where the provincial government had previously been averse to importing large amounts of electricity from Quebec.

“So perhaps there’s an alignment of planets that’s putting a lot more value in terms of our keeping our own electricity for ourselves.”

Keith Brooks, programs director at Environmental Defence, also welcomed the extension of the tax credits but said the government’s investments in electricity infrastructure were overshadowed by much larger funding toward oil and gas projects.

“Budget 2026 appears to be an attempt to paper over this government’s pro-fossil fuel agenda by dangling investments in clean electricity,” he wrote.

Dr. Weis at the Pembina Institute said the government’s sustained focus on interties is helpful to those projects, which can lose momentum if not continually pushed forward.

But he added: “There’s still a lot of work ahead to make these projects a reality.”

stories.title: ‘We’re ready to partner’: London wants piece of $17.8 billion offered by Ottawa for homelessness crisis
stories.summary: London Mayor Josh Morgan is ‘ready to partner’ to solve the city’s housing and homelessness crisis.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
London Mayor Josh Morgan is ‘ready to partner’ to solve the city’s housing and homelessness crisis.

“We know we can solve the country’s most complex problems when we work together,” said Morgan.

In the 2026 federal budget released Thursday, Prime Minister Mark Carney is offering $11.2 billion to tackle homelessness over four years, starting next year, and $17.8 billion over 10 years.

“We know what the challenges are on our streets, I can see it out front door in my office every single day,” said Morgan.

“People who walk the downtown, people who are suffering on our streets, so, we need to help them.”

With a lofty goal of ending homelessness within a decade, Ottawa will invest in mental health and addiction resources, supportive and affordable housing, as well as rent supports and continued support for the Veterans Homelessness Program.

“Everyone deserves to be in a home,” said Arielle Kayabaga, deputy house leader of the government and London West MP.

“Some people May say, you know, why are we spending all this money? We would be wrong not to do that.”

London was the first city in Canada to receive money from the Housing Accelerator Fund (HAF).

They hope they can be first to receive these funds. They could use it to partner with developers to create more affordable and supportive housing communities.”

“ Village Soho is a great model and a great example of what Londoners can do and an example of what we can achieve across the country through partnership,” said Peter Fragiskatos, London Centre MP.

“You have hundreds of units of housing here that are market based and non-market based and we’ve seen the cost of rent increase. Because of the budget, we’re going to see units for non-market housing go from 8,000 a year to 24,000 a year.”

That is great news for charitable developers like Homes Unlimited.

“We’re creators, not curators,” said Jim Foote, vice president of Homes Unlimited.

“We don’t sit around and watch things get dusty on a shelf. We like to build. We can use it [potential funding] on reimagining some of our existing [properties] and we would look to news sites. There’s potentially surplus municipal lands, federal lands that could be right here in the city that are underutilized, that we could look at development as well.”

To make this work the province will have to get on board with wraparound services and municipalities will have to find locations and execute the builds quickly.

“Our competitive advantage is we know how to partner,” said Morgan.

“We already know how to do it and we have been doing it. We were just waiting for the big the big announcement and now it’s here.”

stories.title: New exemption allows foreign buyers to purchase new homes but will it help affordability?: experts
stories.summary: When Lucy Hua started her career in real estate a decade ago, most of her clients were foreign buyers. That market dried up after Canada enacted a ban on foreign purchases of residential property in 2023.
stories.author: Michael Serapio
stories.content:
When Lucy Hua started her career in real estate a decade ago, most of her clients were foreign buyers. That market dried up after Canada enacted a ban on foreign purchases of residential property in 2023.

And Hua is skeptical those buyers will return, even with a new exemption announced by Ottawa this week.

“I wouldn’t say whether it’s going to work out or not,” said Hua, “Only time will tell.”

On Thursday, the federal government announced that it will allow foreign buyers to purchase residential homes for the first time in years. However, those purchases are limited to new homes.

The strategy comes from Australia and is widely referred to by policymakers as the “Australian model.”

By limiting foreign capital to brand new builds, advocates of the strategy say it keeps foreign wealth away from housing stock on the resale market, which protects Canadian buyers from foreign competition.

At the same time, by limiting foreign money to newly built homes, developers can meet the threshold for financing through pre-sales or sell out projects that are already built. Either way, foreign money allows developers to move on to new projects and increase the housing supply available to Canadian buyers.

“When those condos, those projects, are not selling, those developers cannot move forward with their future projects,” said Hua. “Without those new homes built in our marketplace, we’re not helping with affordability. We’re not helping with accessibility to our local market, to our local residents.”

Yinnon Geva, an assistant professor at the University of Toronto’s Institute for Management and Innovation, questions whether the exemption is really aimed at making housing more affordable for Canadians.

“The federal government is trying to keep the development industry afloat or at least keeping the business going. And the question is, how does this help affordability at the end of the day?,” he said. “We can’t be serious about bringing down prices if we keep propping up demand.”

If foreign buyers take advantage of this exemption, real estate developers could benefit.

Currently, there are thousands of unsold new condos in Toronto and Vancouver. According to RBC, unlike detached homes which finds themselves in a balanced market, the oversupply in condominiums has driven prices down significantly.

But whether foreign buyers will buy these unsold units, or presale units in a new development, is a big unknown.

Despite the exemption, Ottawa is maintaining its ban on foreign purchases of existing residential properties. The ban, which was set to expire in the new year, has also been extended and will now remain in place until 2029.

And Ottawa’s exemption does nothing to address provincial measures that have been enacted to dissuade foreign buyers.

“Across Ontario, we’re looking at 25 per cent foreign buyer taxes,” said Hua. “And in BC, in some specific regions, we’re looking at 20 per cent. So those have not been lifted or exempted.”

And Hua is skeptical those buyers will return, even with a new exemption announced by Ottawa this week.
“I wouldn’t say whether it’s going to work out or not,” said Hua, “Only time will tell.”
On Thursday, the federal government announced that it will allow foreign buyers to purchase residential homes for the first time in years. However, those purchases are limited to new homes.
The strategy comes from Australia and is widely referred to by policymakers as the “Australian model.”

By limiting foreign capital to brand new builds, advocates of the strategy say it keeps foreign wealth away from housing stock on the resale market, which protects Canadian buyers from foreign competition.

At the same time, by limiting foreign money to newly built homes, developers can meet the threshold for financing through pre-sales or sell out projects that are already built. Either way, foreign money allows developers to move on to new projects and increase the housing supply available to Canadian buyers.

stories.title: In B.C., shoebox units aren’t driving the unsold condos problem
stories.summary: Family-sized units outweigh ‘shoebox condos’ in B.C.’s standing inventory
stories.author: Howard Chai
stories.content:
The first step to solving a problem is admitting that it exists. The second step is understanding it and there has been some misunderstanding around the completed unsold condos problem in British Columbia.

Many – pundits, politicians, and others – have echoed the story that developers catered to investors by building studio and one-bedroom units, resulting in the current glut of unsold condos.

Data shared with The Globe and Mail from Real Property Data seems to disprove that narrative, however, at least in British Columbia.

As of the end of the third quarter of 2026, the Lower Mainland had 5,770 completed but unsold condos either in high-rise concrete buildings or low-rise wood-frame buildings. That total consists of 177 studio units, 88 junior one-bedroom units, 1,859 one-bedroom units, 2,865 two-bedroom units, 598 three-bedroom units, and 32 four-bedroom units. (The remaining 151 units could not be classified.)

Condos with one bedroom or less are the ones typically associated with investors, who buy them to rent out or flip, while most governments typically define “family-sized units” as those with two or more bedrooms.

Thus, 2,124 of the 5,770 completed unsold condos – 36.8 per cent – are investor-size units and 3,495 of the 5,770 completed unsold units – 60.6 per cent – are family-sized units.

The region is also home to 1,253 completed unsold townhouses, the vast majority of which have two or more bedrooms. Including townhouses, the split between investor-size and family-size units becomes 30.8 per cent and 66.3 per cent – an even starker contrast that suggests the true problem lies with the larger units.

The criticism of these investor-size condos as “shoebox” or “dog crate” condos is not just about the number of bedrooms, it is also about size and livability.

However, of the 5,770 completed unsold condos, 311 are below 500 sq. ft, 1,588 are between 500 and 700 sq. ft, 1,844 are between 700 and 900 sq. ft, and 1,854 are above 900 sq. ft. This means that 1,899 of the 5,770 units – 32.9 per cent – are investor-size units while 3,698 of the 5,770 units – 64.1 per cent – are family-size units, again indicating that there are twice as many family-size units as investor-size units.

The numbers do not include completed unsold townhouses, which again skew larger and would further increase the difference.

Asked whether there was any truth to developers overbuilding investor-size condos, Craig Anderson, VP of sales for Magnum Projects, which has been working with developers and lenders on moving standing inventory, called it “a misleading narrative.”

Indeed, new buildings generally have fewer family-size units and more investor-size units, but most of the latter have been pre-sold, and they are not the kind of units that are piling up now.

The family-sized units have been a bigger problem because many families do not want to live in a condo and instead prefer a home with a yard , Mr. Anderson points out. Housing prices have also come down across the board, in some cases substantially, and the price gap between a two-bedroom condo and a townhouse is not as large as it once was. Given the two options, most would likely opt for the townhouse.

People are generally aware that developers have to pre-sell a certain number of units in order to secure construction financing. That number is usually around 60 or 70 per cent, and that segment tends to include more studio and one-bedroom units.

The remaining 40 or 30 per cent, however, usually includes the larger units, and they are often held back to be sold after construction completes, when they are – in theory – more valuable.

“Three or four years ago, when the buildings were launched, studios and one-bedrooms were taken up because, of course, people thought they could flip them sooner,” said Mr. Anderson. “They’ve closed on those or walked away from them , but let’s say a majority have closed on them. Typically, what we’ve always been stuck with is the two-bedrooms or larger.”

“The fact that over 60 per cent of today’s standing inventory is made up of family-sized units is a clear rebuttal that condos don’t sell for the sole reason that they are ‘shoeboxes’ or ‘dog crates,’” said Joanne Shao, VP of development for Century Group, a Metro Vancouver developer with projects of all sizes.

Ms. Shao recognizes that family-sized units don’t necessarily have the same appeal as a townhouse, but said that B.C. has a limited amount of undeveloped land, so developers can’t just build townhouses and need to build density around mass transit.

If it were up to developers, they May not have built as many family-size units as they have, as costs increase with unit size and the returns on those costs decrease .

Ms. Shao says the problem is it’s not completely up to the developers, as many local governments have policies requiring a certain amount of family-size units.

“A problem we have right now is that policies are so restrictive that projects are pretty much designed by the city for us,” said Ms. Shao. “It’s not only the case that they have restrictions around the unit mix, but also whether or not bedrooms have windows, the minimum size of bedrooms, and the floor plate size. So when they ask for a minimum of 40 per cent family-size units, it’s not like we can just extend the floor plate in order to achieve the efficiency that we need to get the project to pencil and be financeable. ”

Echoing comments that have been made by many numerous other developers, Ms. Shao said all of the policies – whether it be regarding accessibility, energy or design – are reasonable on their own and well-meaning, but the policies compound and each adds to the cost of building, which then gets passed on to buyers.

Ms. Shao called the number of unsold units a “glaring red flag,” but said that attributing that to developers building too many “shoebox” or “dog crate” condos is an oversimplification of the problem and also the wrong take-away.

“The conclusion that there are 7,000 unsold units on the market because they must be undesirable is a conclusion that is not serving as well, because this is a symptom that’s trying to tell us so much more about how we deliver housing.”

stories.title: Mom says B.C. soldier who died at CFB Wainwright was her ‘bright light’
stories.summary: Goulding had been participating in live-fire exercises at CFB Wainwright last month as part of training for potential deployment overseas.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
Remembering her “bright light,” Pte. Aidan Goulding’s mother called her son fearless and someone who loved life.

Family, friends and members of the Canadian Armed Forces gathered in Vancouver Sunday for the funeral of one of the four men killed at CFB Wainwright during a deadly fire.

The 23-year-old’s mother started her eulogy by thanking those who had reached out in the past few weeks and for the “outpouring” of support.

“Aidan was never still,” said Sonia Monk. “He loved life and wanted to experience all of it. He was fearless, sometimes more fearless than I would have preferred.

“If there was a safe, sensible way to do something, Aidan usually found a more exhilarating way.”

Goulding had been participating in live-fire exercises at CFB Wainwright last month as part of training for potential deployment overseas.

A grassfire overtook soldiers during the exercise, killing Goulding as well as Sgt. Morgan Wong, Pte. Shaun Farrell and Pte. Hayden Lykkemark. Another 39 soldiers were taken to hospital at the time.

The funerals of Wong and Farrell have been held in recent weeks.

Monk told those gathered at Seaforth Armoury that Goulding’s best friend was his brother Wylder, who also spoke at the funeral.

Wylder recalled how the siblings would get to “all kinds of mischief” together when they were younger, from bike riding and tree climbing to skateboarding, often ending up hurting themselves in the process.

“He was my best friend, my worst enemy, my harshest critic and my fiercest competitor,” Wylder said.

“Aidan really did live his life to the fullest. He went places, met people, had adventures, and got himself into situations that most people probably couldn’t even imagine.”

Goulding served with the 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry (3PPCLI), which was part of the training that took place in Alberta that fateful day.

stories.title: Hundreds gather to remember B.C. soldier killed in Wainwright fire
stories.summary: Aidan Goulding was one of four soldiers killed after grass fire overtook troops during training exercise
stories.author: Nono Shen
stories.content:
A 23-year-old Canadian soldier was remembered Sunday as a globe-trotting, sporty and car-loving man with an infectious sense of humour and a fearless love for life.

Hundreds of military personnel, family and friends gathered at an armoury on a stormy day in Vancouver to remember Pte. Aidan Goulding, one of four soldiers killed last month after a grass fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta overtook troops during a training exercise.

His mother, Sonia Monk, described her son as someone with a great sense of humour, always open to a good laugh.

“Whenever I was disciplining him, he would start to laugh or he would try to say something. I could never properly discipline him,” she said.

“That’s something that our family is going to miss. Nothing is going replace that.”

The funeral for 23-year old Pte. Aidan Goulding took place at the Seaforth Armoury in Vancouver on Sunday. The Canadian Press

Monk said she was proud of her patriotic son who joined the army from a high-paying job.

“When he finally told me, he said, ‘I have one life to live, I want to do something important, and so I’m joining the army.’ I think that’s so unselfish of him,” she said.

After he joined the Canadian Armed Forces, Goulding felt like he found a place where he belonged, Monk said.

“It gave him a sense of purpose, a family and a place he truly felt at home.”

Goulding’s funeral started with soldiers carrying his flag-draped casket into the armoury, with the sounds of a bagpipe cascading, and some words from a rabbi.

Monk described his upbringing in North Vancouver with his brother, Wylder, who was also his best friend.

“They had each other’s backs,” she said. “Their relationship touched my heart deeply, and I was content in knowing that they would always be close.”

Growing up, he showed his competitive and curious side.

His family said in a statement he played many sports, including soccer and rugby, and developed a love for cars at a young age.

He spent many hours buying used cars, fixing them late into the night under the glow of a lamp on his family’s driveway and then reselling them.

The first car he fine-tuned was a used Chrysler 300C.

The modification: make it louder.

“He loved understanding how things worked and took great pride in making them his own,” his family said.

He was also stylish.

Monk said her son asked to wear a white suit on his first day of Grade 4. When he turned 21, he asked for a gold suit.

“He was unapologetically himself, and I admired that,” she said,

The family has also described Goulding as a globe-trotter.

In his short life, he explored many parts of the world, including Mexico, Germany, Austria, Italy, Croatia, Malta, the Netherlands, England and Spain.

Reagan Goulding, his aunt, said during the funeral that he often made those around him laugh.

She said it’s been hard knowing that he died at a young age.

“This is perhaps one of the hardest parts of losing someone so young,” she said. “It’s not just the memories we have lost, but the opportunity to make a relationship we still had time to build.”

Reagan Goulding said she could see her nephew, who she described as being “smart, ambitious, determined, and resourceful,” perhaps becoming a police officer or joining Csis.

“I truly believe great things were in his future. We wanted him to know that we all saw this in him, that we believed in him and became a proud follower of him,” she said.

She said her last message to Goulding was sent on the day of the tragedy, a text message that said, “Aidan, you better be OK.”

She never received a reply.

Reagan Goulding said if she knew this was her last message she would have said more, including telling him one more time how proud she was.

She also remembered the other soldiers killed in the fire.

They were: Pte. Hayden Lykkemark, 19, of Langley, B.C.; Sgt. Morgan Wong, 26, of Edmonton; and Pte. Shaun Farrell, 23, of Prince Albert, Sask.

“They were young men who matched their calling, who stood beside one another, and who were parts of the family themselves. Their loss is felt by their families, their friends, soldiers, and everyone who has been touched by this tragedy,” she said.

“Aidan and his fellow soldiers will not be forgotten,” she added.

Thirty-nine others were injured in the fire, and many remain in hospitals in Edmonton and Calgary.

As the soldiers carried the casket out of the armoury and reloaded it into a hearse to head to the cemetery, the sun broke through the clouds, casting its light over rainy Vancouver.

Monk, who spoke to media after the funeral, said she felt it was a sign from Goulding, encouraging her to move forward with life.

“Because I think through tragedy or hardship, he would always say things like that, ‘We’ll move forward.’ So, I think that’s what he was sort of saying to me today, actually, with the sun shining bright in my eyes.”

Monk said she felt “supported and lifted” after hearing stories from Goulding’s “brothers and sisters” in the army.

“I’m quite tired, I haven’t eaten a lot, I haven’t slept a lot. But all the support and seeing everybody here today, it’s remarkable. I can’t find a word other than remarkable,” said Monk, adding that “There’s lots of love in Canada.”

stories.title: Officer hurt in dangerous driving crash
stories.summary: An officer has sustained minor injuries in a dangerous driving crash in Hanover.
stories.author: Kate Otterbein
stories.content:
An officer has sustained minor injuries in a dangerous driving crash in Hanover.

On Sunday just before 2 a.m., Hanover Police tried to stop a vehicle on 4th Avenue, near 9th Street. An officer approached the vehicle, and the driver allegedly drove away at a high rate of speed.

An officer deployed a spike belt, the vehicle didn’t stop for a stop sign and hit a second responding police cruiser head-on in the 100 block of 10th Street, police said.

The vehicle then continued eastbound down 10th for several blocks before the suspects got out of the car and reportedly ran.

A short foot chase led to the arrest of a 28-year-old Haldimand County man, and a 23-year-old Cambridge woman shortly after.

The police officer involved in the crash was treated at hospital and later released. The suspects weren’t hurt and both vehicles sustained significant front-end damage.

stories.title: Local farm businesses recipients in Excellence in Agriculture awards
stories.summary: Local businesses have been given honours, part of the 2026 Excellence in Agriculture Awards from Ontario.
stories.author: Kate Otterbein
stories.content:
Local businesses have been given honours, part of the 2026 Excellence in Agriculture Awards from Ontario.

Local winners and honourable mentions are:

Drone Spray Canada, Blenheim – Minister’s Award

Western Fair Association (The Grove), Middlesex County – Agribusiness Excellence

Elite Agri Solutions Inc., Middlesex County – Agribusiness Excellence honourable mention

Wowbutter Foods, Perth County – Agribusiness Excellence honourable mention

Drone Spray Canada, Blenheim – Research and Innovation Excellence

Sandi Brock, Perth County – Education of Excellence honourable mention

Drone Spray Canada in Blenheim has been named the recipient of the Minister’s Award and the award for Research and Innovation Excellence.

“Drone Spray Canada is incredibly honoured to receive this award for our involvement in bringing a new and innovative technology to agriculture,” said Drone Spray Canada.

“It has been many years working with countless stakeholders to ensure we can integrate drones into our agricultural practices. This allows growers to increase efficacy, decrease costs and ultimately generate better products. We are excited to continue to see this industry take-off.”

The awards are given to businesses, farmers, and organizations that help protect and strengthen Ontario’s agri-food sector. They honour seven winners and six honourable mentions.

“The workers and innovators in Ontario’s agri-food sector are second to none, using world-class expertise and experience to bring fresh, nutritious and delicious food to tables across the province,” said Sam Oosterhoff, Minister of Agriculture, Food, and Agribusiness.

“These awards are a celebration of Ontario’s rich, multigenerational agricultural heritage being carried forward by the leaders of today, with a commitment to building a more secure and self-reliant agri-food sector for generations to come.”

In addition to the award announcements, Ontario also said it will be investing $2.3 million over the next three years in 4-H Ontario. 4-H offers youth engagement programs, preparing them to become agricultural leaders. This investment will help strengthen the skilled workforce and ensure long-term growth, competitiveness, and resilience in the agri-food sector, the province said.

“4-H Ontario is very appreciative of the continued support received from the Ontario Ministry of Agriculture, Food and Agribusiness,” said Evelyn Chambers, Acting Executive Director, 4-H Ontario.

“This funding will allow 4-H to continue to deliver opportunities for Ontario youth and develop the next workforce generation.”

stories.title: N.S. protests call for moratorium on data centre proposals in province
stories.summary: Protesters gathered in front of the provincial legislature at noon Saturday, taking up an entire block of Hollis Street before marching through the city’s downtown core.
stories.author: Tori Fitzpatrick
stories.content:
The chants of nearly 1,000 Nova Scotians drowned out the rain in downtown Halifax Saturday as residents took to the streets to protest a proposed artificial intelligence data centre in southern Cape Breton.

Protesters gathered in front of the provincial legislature at noon, taking up an entire block of Hollis Street before marching through the city’s downtown core.

They called for a moratorium on all large-scale AI data centre proposals in the province after proponent Everwind Fuels announced last month it plans to lease a data centre in Pont Tupper, N.S., to U.S. AI company Anthropic.

Ned Zimmerman, a tech worker from Dartmouth, N.S., and one of the organizers of the rally, said large-scale AI data centres are socially destructive and environmentally irresponsible.

“We feel that the push to integrate AI into everything raises a lot of concerns for society, and this is not the kind of thing that we want to see being imposed on our communities, ON our landscapes, our ecosystems, and our populations,” Zimmerman said.

Organizers of the rally said it was one of seven happening across the province on Saturday.

Everwind has described the $10-billion project as the largest private investment in provincial history. Anthropic has signed a 20-year lease for the 18,600-square-metre facility, which it will use to power its AI assistant Claude.

It is expected to come online in 2027 and draw 95 megawatts of electricity in its first phase. A 325-megawatt expansion is scheduled for mid-2028, bringing the total energy demand to 420 megawatts.

But it has faced backlash from Nova Scotians who are concerned about its potential impact on the environment and on power rates.

A petition to stop the development of AI data centres in Nova Scotia on Change.org garnered nearly 28,000 signatures.

Everwind says it will cover the cost of all electricity infrastructure, and the project will not increase power rates for customers.

A statement from Premier Tim Houston’s office said the data centre will only proceed if it meets provincial and federal guidelines, which it noted includes protecting the water, the environment, power rates and capacity.

Zimmerman said those guidelines are not enough for a project of this scale, adding that communication from the provincial government has been sparse. He also said Everwind has not done enough to consult with communities about the data centre, demonstrating a lack of transparency and accountability.

“It was kept closely under wraps. And broader community consent, community consultation was not engaged until the project was announced,” he said.

Everwind did not respond to request for comment about the protest.

Earlier this week, the company held two lengthy information sessions in Cape Breton. Some attendees said they were left with outstanding questions. Everwind’s engagement director said at a session Wednesday night that more consultations would be arranged.

Rebecca Lawrence from Dartmouth was among the protesters Saturday in Halifax. She said the provincial government is rushing the data centre project without acknowledging the potential harm it could cause.

She said she’s worried about potential noise pollution, as well as the centre’s impact on the local water supply.

Water from nearby Landrie Lake, which is also used to supply water to the town of Port Hawkesbury, will be used to cool the Point Tupper data centre’s servers. The system will use an average of 100,000 litres of water per day in the first phase, expanding to an average draw of 500,000 litres per day in its next phase.

“I think that one drop of drinking water wasted on generative AI is too much,” Lawrence said.

EverWind said the cooling system will be closed-loop, similar to a car’s radiator, with cooling fluid recycled or disposed of off-site, not in local waterways.

Ashley Drodge, another organizer of Saturday’s protest in Halifax, said said she’s concerned about the lack of binding regulations for AI data centre development and the absence of an environmental impact assessment for the project.

“This is short-sighted, money in your pocket development,” she said.

Earlier this month, Nova Scotia’s Minister of Environment, Timothy Halman, said that instead of an environmental impact assessment, the project requires industrial approval, a tool he described as the most appropriate for this type of project.

“What is being utilized here is a very robust regulatory tool to ensure safe construction and operation of a proposed facility,” he told reporters.

Houston has previously said he doesn’t know whether any new legislation is needed to regulate the data centre.

However, the statement from his office about the protest said the province would be open to legislative changes “should we find ourselves in a situation where we require them.”

Lawrence said Saturday her message to the premier is to listen to Nova Scotians.

“Nova Scotian’s are pretty vocal on the fact that we don’t want this,” she said. “On every side there’s people from all across the spectrum who are saying no to these data centres.”

stories.title: Toronto woman bought a $1.25-million duplex with her now ex-partner. Now they’re stuck with it
stories.summary: A breakup and falling home values have complicated plans to sell the Etobicoke property
stories.author: Zahra Khozema
stories.content:
In August 2023, at the age of 27, Mona and her then-partner purchased a three-bedroom, two-bathroom duplex in Toronto’s west end for $1.25-million.

They’d been together five years and envisioned eventually turning the property into their family home. But plans changed when they broke up a year later.

Today, Mona works in commercial real estate and earns around $135,000 a year. She lives in one of the duplex’s units alone, managing its expenses, renovations and upstairs tenants, while still sharing ownership with her ex.

She describes it as “the hardest thing I’ve ever gone through in my life.”

From when she arrived in Canada, Mona longed for a stable home, so she worked multiple jobs while studying and after graduation, sometimes six days a week. By 21, she had saved close to $14,000.

In 2021, Mona and her then-partner moved into a North York condo owned by his mother, where they paid $1,600 a month in rent between them. This helped them build a down payment.

When they began house hunting, they initially considered condos, but Mona, who has a real estate licence, was concerned about maintenance fees. She wanted a freehold property that could eventually become their family home. And after viewing more than 50 places, they found a house in Etobicoke where both units in the duplex were tenanted.

The two rentals were a big reason that made the purchase possible. At the time, Mona was making $60,000 annually while her then-partner earned close to $80,000. Because lenders consider rental income when assessing mortgage applications, the couple qualified to borrow more than they otherwise could.

Mona also acted as the purchasing agent, forgoing her commission and effectively reducing the $1.29-million selling price by $40,000 to $1.25-million.

They made a 20-per-cent down payment, splitting it down the middle. Mona withdrew her years of savings and investment, including $10,000 from her Rrsp. With closing costs, the two spent almost $300,000.

The couple secured a three-year fixed-rate mortgage at 4.89 per cent, amortized over 30 years. Their monthly payments were $5,260, and although the rent didn’t cover everything, it made things more manageable. Despite making additional payments, they’ve paid down just $65,500 in principal over three years. Refinancing in June lowered their monthly payments to $4,800.

The purchase wiped out their savings. Mona said they couldn’t afford to move in, so they stayed in the condo while tenants occupied both units of the duplex. They hoped to save enough to renovate the property – but their relationship ended before those plans materialized.

Following the breakup, Mona went back to stay with her parents, but she didn’t want to sell the Toronto house since its value had dropped to less than $1.1-million. She estimates that after selling costs, she and her ex would each walk away with just $61,000.

When one of the tenants moved out in October 2025, Mona and her ex started renovations on the vacant unit, replacing flooring, removing walls and upgrading appliances. Mona finally moved in this January while some work continued.

The remaining rental unit brings in $2,300 monthly, while her ex contributes $400 monthly. Mona says he told her he cannot afford to pay more at this time.

While they still co-own the property, Mona has taken on most responsibilities. The pressure of home ownership has been overwhelming, she said, leaving little time for herself or her personal life.

“I felt like I was really living in limbo for the past two years. I was walking around with a cloud on top of me,” she said.

Despite it all, she’s proud of what she accomplished as a young woman and immigrant. Mona hopes to rent out her unit by the end of the year, before her work relocation to the U.S. She would prefer if the house sold but continues to worry about financial loss.

“It’s a very expensive learning lesson.”

Purchase price: $1,250,000

Down payment: $250,000 (20 per cent) split equally

Legal fees: Approximately $5,000

Moving costs: Approximately $600

Land transfer tax: $21,475 ($17,475 after first-time home buyer rebate)

Repairs: Approximately $100,000

Furniture: Approximately $10,000

Home inspection: $550

Monthly ongoing costs

Mortgage: $4,800 after refinancing; previously $5,260

Home insurance: $110

Property taxes: $6,000 annually ($500 monthly)

Utilities: $150-$250 for hydro, $120-$150 for gas, $150 for waste, and $120 for WiFi

Advice: Mona cautions buyers to account for how rental income could affect their taxes and to keep their mortgage separate from their everyday banking.

If you fit the profile, we could contact you for a profile and yes, you can remain anonymous.

In 2021, Mona and her then-partner moved into a North York condo owned by his mother, where they paid $1,600 a month in rent between them. This helped them build a down payment.

When they began house hunting, they initially considered condos, but Mona, who has a real estate licence, was concerned about maintenance fees. She wanted a freehold property that could eventually become their family home. And after viewing more than 50 places, they found a house in Etobicoke where both units in the duplex were tenanted.

The two rentals were a big reason that made the purchase possible. At the time, Mona was making $60,000 annually while her then-partner earned close to $80,000. Because lenders consider rental income when assessing mortgage applications, the couple qualified to borrow more than they otherwise could.
Mona also acted as the purchasing agent, forgoing her commission and effectively reducing the $1.29-million selling price by $40,000 to $1.25-million.

They made a 20-per-cent down payment, splitting it down the middle. Mona withdrew her years of savings and investment, including $10,000 from her Rrsp. With closing costs, the two spent almost $300,000.

The couple secured a three-year fixed-rate mortgage at 4.89 per cent, amortized over 30 years. Their monthly payments were $5,260, and although the rent didn’t cover everything, it made things more manageable. Despite making additional payments, they’ve paid down just $65,500 in principal over three years. Refinancing in June lowered their monthly payments to $4,800.

The purchase wiped out their savings. Mona said they couldn’t afford to move in, so they stayed in the condo while tenants occupied both units of the duplex. They hoped to save enough to renovate the property – but their relationship ended before those plans materialized.

Following the breakup, Mona went back to stay with her parents, but she didn’t want to sell the Toronto house since its value had dropped to less than $1.1-million. She estimates that after selling costs, she and her ex would each walk away with just $61,000.

When one of the tenants moved out in October 2025, Mona and her ex started renovations on the vacant unit, replacing flooring, removing walls and upgrading appliances. Mona finally moved in this January while some work continued.
The remaining rental unit brings in $2,300 monthly, while her ex contributes $400 monthly. Mona says he told her he cannot afford to pay more at this time.
While they still co-own the property, Mona has taken on most responsibilities. The pressure of home ownership has been overwhelming, she said, leaving little time for herself or her personal life.
“I felt like I was really living in limbo for the past two years. I was walking around with a cloud on top of me,” she said.

Despite it all, she’s proud of what she accomplished as a young woman and immigrant. Mona hopes to rent out her unit by the end of the year, before her work relocation to the U.S. She would prefer if the house sold but continues to worry about financial loss.
“It’s a very expensive learning lesson.”

Furniture: Approximately $10,000

stories.title: Quebec minister ‘deeply shocked’ by more than 100 alleged fraud cases
stories.summary: Ex-Immigration Ministry bureaucrat Marilena Ida has been charged with breach of trust and document forgery after an investigation.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Quebec Immigration Minister Catherine Gentilcore says she is “deeply shocked” by alleged fraud incidents uncovered by the province’s anti-corruption agency.

In a news release this weekend, Gentilcore said the “necessary measures have been put in place” to ensure that about 100 cases of alleged immigration fraud linked to a former government employee remain an isolated incident.

Ex-Immigration Ministry bureaucrat Marilena Ida has been charged with breach of trust and document forgery after an investigation by Quebec’s anti-corruption commissioner.

The agency alleged last week that as an interim co-ordinator, Ida issued more than 100 false Quebec selection certificates to candidates who did not meet the requirements.

A certificate must be obtained from the province before applying to Ottawa for permanent residence in Quebec, with criteria including French proficiency, education and work history.

The agency alleges the incidents took place between August 2016 and February 2019. Ida is scheduled to appear in a Montreal courthouse on Dec. 10.

stories.title: Second in series of storms brings wind, rain and power outages to parts of B.C.
stories.summary: Zeballos - The second in a series of storms in British Columbia brought howling winds and torrential rainfall to parts of the province Sunday morning, while knocking out power for thousands of customers.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Zeballos - The wind that blew outside Gerry Sullivan’s bedroom in the Village of Zeballos on northwest Vancouver Island was enough to wake him up early Sunday morning.

“It was just howling, and we had thunder, we had lightning,” he said.

Sullivan and his wife Vicki said early Sunday that they hadn’t had power since Saturday afternoon as the second major storm to wallop parts of British Columbia over the last several days left thousands without electricity and one person dead when vehicles became trapped under a fallen tree.

The couple said they had two generators to keep the lights on and a wood stove for backup heat.

“I’m 72-years old and I’ve never ever experienced a wind like that,” Vicki Sullivan said, adding that she could hear trees falling outside their home Saturday.

On Sunday the Village of Zeballos amended an evacuation order issued on Friday due to the risk of landslides, lifting the order on some of the initial 22 properties but adding others.

As of Sunday afternoon, an evacuation order was in place for 30 properties including both homes and vacant or unaddressed lots. An evacuation alert covered 19 properties.

The Strathcona Regional District said in a statement that a geotechnical assessment of the affected area had been received and recommendations are being implemented.

“Emergency officials continue to monitor conditions closely, particularly with additional storm systems and heavy rainfall forecast throughout the week. Conditions will be reassessed as weather systems move through the area,” the statement said.

Gerry Sullivan said the village of about 120 residents is located about 42 kilometres away from the main highway along a forest service road. He said he wasn’t sure whether the road was passable after the most recent storm.

At about 8 a.m. Sunday, he said the wind had died down but it was still raining in Zeballos.

Environment Canada issued a rainfall warning Sunday morning for the Fraser Canyon between Boston Bar and Lytton, with rainfall amounts of up to 50 millimetres expected.

A wind warning for north central B.C. cautioned gusts reaching up to 90km/h until early Sunday evening. Additional warnings covered parts of the Lower Mainland, the Sunshine Coast and Vancouver Island.

The weather agency said more bad weather is on the way.

A special weather statement for the north, central and south coasts and Vancouver Island, said a “strong and potent series of storms” will move through the region from Tuesday through Thursday.

It said “significant rainfall accumulations” are expected, with upslope terrain and higher elevations expected to bit hit the hardest.

Police in Surrey, B.C., said one person died after two vehicles became trapped under a fallen tree during the storm on Saturday evening.

Officers were called to a report of downed wires and a fallen tree across a highway and found the vehicles trapped under the tree, a statement said.

One of the drivers was pronounced dead at the scene and the other was treated for minor injuries.

BC Hydro said approximately 30,000 customers remained were without power Sunday afternoon after the windstorms caused nearly 415,000 to lose power since Friday.

The provincial Crown utility said parts of Central Interior, particularly east and north of Prince George are facing “the most significant challenge” with crews dealing with extensive damage across a large area, including downed wire, numerous broken poles and other damaged electrical equipment.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 8, 2026.

stories.title: Unexploded shell recovered by military along St. Lawrence River
stories.summary: The town says the shell had been submerged under a rising tide in the Port Saint-François area across the St. Lawrence River from Trois-Rivières.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Quebec police say the military has recovered an unexploded shell along the banks of the St. Lawrence River near Trois-Rivières, Que.

Police, who were called to the town of Nicolet on Friday to form a security perimeter, have confirmed that soldiers recovered the object, which was deemed harmless.

The municipality says in a social media post that the Canadian Armed Forces would transport the shell to another location and destroy it.

The town says the shell had been submerged under a rising tide in the Port Saint-François area across the St. Lawrence River from Trois-Rivières.

Two shells were found within two days in the same area last July.

Between 1952 and 2000, the Defence Department conducted tests at a munitions test centre in Nicolet by firing into Lac Saint Pierre, through which the river flows.

The federal government says firing now takes place inside a sand-filled containment berm, where the munitions are then recovered.

stories.title: Ontario officials warn of possible measles exposure at Pearson airport
stories.summary: Local unimmunized child recently tested positive for virus after international trip, Durham Region Health Department says
stories.author: Sadeen Mohsen
stories.content:
Health officials in Ontario are warning the public, including people who passed through Pearson International Airport last week, about a possible exposure connected to a confirmed measles case.

The Durham Region Health Department says a local unimmunized child recently returned from an international trip and tested positive for the virus.

Officials say anyone who was on Ethiopian Airlines flight ET552 travelling to Toronto last Monday, or who was in Pearson International Airport on Tuesday between 7:30 a.m. and 11 a.m., must watch for symptoms until Nov. 24.

Also, anyone who was in the Lakeridge Health Ajax-Pickering emergency room on Tuesday between 10:40 a.m. and 5 p.m. must watch for symptoms.

Tale of two outbreaks: Canada stamps out measles while cases grow in the U.S.

Health officials say measles symptoms can start seven to 21 days after exposure and can include a high fever, cough and a runny nose.

They say they are investigating the exposure and have followed up with those who have been in contact with the child.

stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
QUÉBEC - Quebec Immigration Minister Catherine Gentilcore says she is “deeply shocked” by alleged fraud incidents uncovered by the province’s anti-corruption agency.

In a news release this weekend, Gentilcore said the “necessary measures have been put in place” to ensure that about 100 cases of alleged immigration fraud linked to a former government employee remain an isolated incident.

stories.title: Toronto Pearson, Durham region ER among possible measles exposure sites
stories.summary: Known contacts in the Durham Region have been contacted by the department, but officials are issuing the warning after determining there May have been further exposures.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
Health officials in the Greater Toronto Area are warning recent travellers of a potential measles exposure at Pearson International Airport last weekend.

The Durham Region Health Department said Saturday it had identified added exposure locations related to a confirmed measles case in a local unimmunized child who had travelled internationally.

One of the three exposure locations was traced to Ethiopian Airlines Flight ET552 from Addis Ababa to Toronto. The flight left Addis Ababa Nov. 2 at 11:32 p.m. East Africa time and landed in Toronto Nov. 3 at 7:30 a.m. EST.

Other exposure locations include terminal 1 of Toronto Pearson International Airport between 7:30 a.m. and 11 a.m., and the Lakeridge Health Ajax-Pickering emergency department waiting room from 10:40 a.m. to 5 p.m., both on Nov. 3.

People who were in these locations during these times are asked to watch for symptoms until Nov. 24.

Measles symptoms May include a high fever more than 38.3 C, a cough, runny nose, red rash lasting four to seven days and red, watery eyes and sensitivity to light. Symptoms typically begin seven to 21 days after infection.

They should also confirm they and their family members have received two doses of the MMR vaccine.

If symptoms develop, people are asked not to attend work or school and to call ahead before visiting a health clinic or their primary care provider.

People with questions about exposure at the airport should contact their local public health unit or Health 811.

Known contacts in the Durham Region have been contacted by the department, but officials are issuing the warning after determining there May have been further exposures.

stories.title: Thousands of B.C. residents without power as 2nd storm moves through
stories.summary: A number of storms have hit British Columbia this weekend leaving thousands without power after trees were downed by strong winds, with more wind gusts expected.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
Thousands of British Columbians remain without power after the second in a series of storms pelted the Lower Mainland and Vancouver Island.

Approximately 135,000 residents had no power at the height of the storm about 1 a.m. local time Sunday. That number had dropped to about 63,000 as of 7 a.m.

Surrey, Duncan, Port Hardy and Prince George were among the hardest hit, according to BC Hydro. Those areas saw strong winds bring down branches and trees that damaged power lines, poles and other electrical equipment.

Sunday’s power outages add to the more than 380,000 outages seen since Friday when the first of the storms started to hit the province. Approximately 317,000 customers have had their power restored so far, but winds are not expected to subside until later in the day, causing additional concern in some areas.

“We prepared for this storm and had crews and resources ready to respond immediately,” said Whitney Deane, spokesperson for BC Hydro. “Our crews are making good progress, but with strong winds continuing this morning, we expect to see additional damage and outages before conditions improve.”

The utility says it will provide updated restoration estimates as crews reach outage locations, but reminds people to stay at least 10 metres away from downed, damaged or low-hanging power lines and call 911 to report them.

This weekend’s storms have been the result of successive atmospheric rivers making their way across B.C. Coastal communities have been warned of rising water levels, while the mainland is facing damaging winds.

Environment Canada has issued a slew of wind and rainfall warnings for the island and Lower Mainland, with winds expected to gust up to 90 km/h. Rainfall amounts of up to 50 mm could be seen in some areas including parts of Metro Vancouver along the North Shore.

Special weather statements have also been forecast for the B.C. Interior including the Cariboo, Fraser Canyon, 100 Mile House, South Thompson, the Coquihalla Highway and the Okanagan Connector. The statement says wind gusts ranging from 60 to 80 km/h will blow through, but cautions winds will ease slightly before an incoming cold front brings a strong push of up to 90 km/h gusts late this morning for Western regions. The winds will ease by this evening.

After cautioning of potential cancellations Saturday, most BC Ferries services are operating Sunday. Those between Metro Vancouver and Nanaimo are proceeding, while the departures from Swartz Bay and Tsawwassen are also operating.

A third storm expected to hit Monday May bring a more prolonged period of rainfall across B.C.’s coast through next week, Environment Canada said.

— with files from Global News’ Rachel Morgan and Amy Judd

stories.title: Five things to watch for in the Canadian business world in the coming week
stories.summary: Canada
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
TORONTO - Five things to watch for in the Canadian business world in the coming week:

The parade of quarterly results from companies continues this week with Barrick Mining Corp. on Monday followed by Finning International Inc. and Hydro One Ltd. on Tuesday. CGI Inc., Cargojet Inc., CAE Inc. and Power Corp. of Canada will report its results on Wednesday. Brookfield Corp. and Canadian Tire Corp. Ltd. are scheduled for Thursday and Onex Corp. is set for Friday.

Bank of Canada

The Bank of Canada will release Tuesday its summary of deliberations for its interest rate decision last month. The central bank decided to increase its key interest rate by a quarter of a percentage point to 2.5 per cent as it worried elevated energy prices could spill over and become generalized inflation.

Defence economy

The Economic Club of Canada will hold a discussion Tuesday on how to turn defence spending into lasting economic value. The talk is expected to include MDA Space CEO Mike Greenley, Saab Canada president Cara Salci, executive director of Downsview Aerospace Innovation & Research Phil Arthurs and IMT Group chief financial officer Patricia Widmeyer.

Champagne speech

Federal cabinet ministers are fanning out across the country to pitch the Liberal’s budget to Canadians this week. Federal Finance Minister François‑Philippe Champagne will give a speech at the Empire Club of Canada in Toronto on Friday.

Economic data

Statistics Canada will release a pair of closely watched economic reports for September on Friday. The agency is set to publish its monthly survey of manufacturing and its report on wholesale trade for the month. The reports come as the economy faces headwinds from a fresh round of tariffs by U.S. President Donald Trump.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 8, 2026.
