stories.title: Canada’s war monuments highlighted in Nova Scotia photographer’s new book
stories.summary: Len Wagg’s ‘At Home and Beyond: Honouring Canada’s War Dead,’ tells stories of people who care for war monuments
stories.author: Devin Stevens
stories.content:
Nova Scotia author and photographer Len Wagg was on his day off 30 years ago when he discovered how powerful and poignant a war cemetery could be.

Wagg was on assignment for the Halifax Chronicle Herald in Italy when he accepted an invitation to visit the small Sicilian town of Agira.

A few hours later, he was walking through the Agira Canadian War Cemetery, an oasis of immaculately manicured lawns and pine trees, looking at row after row of headstones inscribed with the names of Canadians who served during the Second World War.

He wrote a story for the paper, and said the response to it stayed with him for years.

“I got calls from Nova Scotia and from the United States,” Wagg said in a recent interview at the Last Steps memorial in Halifax, where more than 350,000 First World War service members boarded ships to Europe, many never to return.

“People had said they knew their father had died overseas but they didn’t know where it was. And this picture of the headstone was the first time that they had seen where it was.”

Opinion: We should make Ottawa’s Peace Tower a true tribute to peace

For the past five years, Wagg has travelled across Canada and Europe photographing war graves, monuments and other sites for his new book, At Home and Beyond: Honouring Canada’s War Dead .

The book captures images of well-known sites such as Vimy Ridge, Juno Beach and the grave of poet John McCrae, who wrote In Flanders Fields . But it also tells the stories of the people who care for those monuments or make other contributions to honour Canada’s war dead.

More than 110,000 Canadians are buried overseas at more than 5,800 sites. Another 27,000 have no known graves, having gone into battle and disappeared.

Wagg said he’s not a historian, and didn’t want the book to focus only on war monuments. Instead, he focused on the people.

The book includes chapters dedicated to Canadian war nurses, the organizers behind relatively new memorials like the Last Steps, and the stories of individual soldiers like Pte. George Lawrence Price of Port Williams, N.S., the last Commonwealth soldier to die in the First World War. He was killed by a German sniper at 10:58 a.m. on Nov. 11, 1918 – two minutes before the armistice went into effect.

By coincidence, Price’s grave in Belgium is metres away from that of Pte. John Parr, a 17-year-old British soldier who became the first Commonwealth serviceman killed during the First World War, which had been declared less than a month earlier.

Wagg profiles Sarah Lockyer and her team at the Department of National Defence’s casualty identification unit in Ottawa. The group of historians and anthropologists use various tools, including DNA analysis, to identify Canadians whose unmarked graves are still being found in Europe. Once identified, those service members are given full military funerals in France.

“One of the quotes from (Lockyer) was, ‘They gave their lives for the country. It’s the least we can do to give them back their names.’ And that was something I found very powerful,” said Wagg.

The book’s foreword is written by Warren (Whitey) Bernard, the 91-year-old Tofino, B.C., resident who was the subject of a famous photo known as Wait for Me Daddy , taken in 1940.

The image, which has inspired a bronze statue, souvenir coins and a stamp, appeared on the front page of the Vancouver Province. It features a young Bernard breaking away from his mother to reach for his father’s hand as he marches off to war in New Westminster, B.C. Wagg said the photo once hung in every school in British Columbia.

Wagg said he wondered what happened to the little boy in the photo and set out to find him, calling his meeting with Bernard one of the high points of his career.

Bernard said he’s been interviewed many times over the years but was impressed by Wagg’s passion for the project.

“I appreciated the way he was taking this on,” Bernard said in an interview. “When guys like Len come along, they’re not trying to get the story for a five-minute or a two-minute shot.… They’re interested in the story. I was really impressed.”

Wagg said the way many people see Canada as a country today is a ripple of what the country did in the First and Second World Wars, especially in Europe, where graveyards are actively maintained and host various ceremonies every year.

Wagg said that from the beaches of Normandy to the buglers playing the Last Post every night at the Menin Gate memorial in Ypres, Belgium, he’s heard the same message from the young people involved in caring for war monuments.

“It’s a generational gratitude,” he said. “The reason why young people in their 30s and 40s are doing this is because of the stories they heard around the kitchen table from their parents and grandparents. It’s important for us to understand (that) part of who we are as Canadians comes from the ripples of their sacrifice.”

stories.title: London police looking to identify sexual assault, break-and-enter suspect
stories.summary: The London police is looking for help identifying a suspect wanted in connection with a sexual assault and break-and-enter.
stories.author: Kate Otterbein
stories.content:
The London police is looking for help identifying a suspect wanted in connection with a sexual assault and break-and-enter.

On Thursday around 3 p.m., police responded to a home in the 900-block of Blythwood Road after a break-and-enter report.

Police said the suspect went into a home and allegedly sexually assaulted a woman. Another resident heard the woman and went to the main floor, when the suspect ran.

The suspect was last seen heading westbound on Blythwood Road on a black push scooter. Multiple officers and the K9 unit searched the area but didn’t find the suspect.

The victim didn’t sustain any physical injuries.

Officers describe the suspect as a man with brown skin, around 25 years old, five-feet-eight-inches tall, with short black hair and dark eyes. He was clean shaven at the time of the incident and was wearing a white t-shirt and black pants. Police said he was also described as speaking English with an accent.

Anyone who was in the area or has dashcam or surveillance video that could help the investigation is asked to contact police at 519-661-5670.

stories.title: Western Mustangs advance to 118th Yates Cup with win over Windsor Lancers
stories.summary: The Western Mustangs are headed to the Yates Cup game for the 10th time in the last 11 years after a 43-33 win over Windsor at Alumni Field in London, Ont. Saturday.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
The Western Mustangs are headed to the Yates Cup game for the 10th time in the last 11 years after a 43-33 win over Windsor at Alumni Field in London, Ont. Saturday.

The Mustangs will travel to Kingston to face the Queen’s Gaels for the OUA title after grinding out a victory on their home field.

Running back Ethan Dolby rushed for three touchdowns including two in the final quarter which put Western ahead for good.

The Lancers had him bottled up with a strong defensive front, but he stayed patient and finally broke through the holes created by the offensive line.

“Those red zone carries you know you just got to find the crease,” said Dolby, who had 54 yards on 15 carries.

Western head coach Michael Faulds knew they had to be patient with the run game because they didn’t want to rely solely on the passing of quarterback Ben Casselman.Casselman threw for 345 yards and mixed in some key runs totalling 104 yards.

“Especially in the fourth quarter they had the wind,” said Faulds.

“Every single play in that fourth quarter, we snapped it inside of three seconds on the play clock. Ben did a good job managing that and our run game didn’t explode today. We had a couple young offensive linemen in there but proud that you know on that last drive that we scored the touchdown we were able to run the football.”

This game featured some crazy offensive plays including an 86-yard pass to Emmett Charles for a Western touchdown and a 108-yard score by Dasani McIntosh when it looked like the Mustangs May have to take a safety from their own two-yard line.

“I would love for it to be like an elaborate play where I did like something super high tech, but I just had a flat route in the flats and Ben led me up field,” said McIntosh.

“I saw a couple of defenders, Emmett Charles made a huge block, and I just flipped them and just wanted to get to the end zone.”

That play happened with Western up 22-19 and a safety would have meant a one-point game and Western kicking back to Windsor.

“We kind of felt we’re going to give up two points being on our one-yard line if we don’t get it,” recalled Faulds.

“So, I told [Offensive Coordinator Gaetan] Richard like let’s still throw the football. Let’s be aggressive. We put three receivers in the boundary, and they brought the Will [Linebacker], so as soon as they brought the Will I knew they were shorthanded. He broke two tackles and he’s one of the fastest guys in USports and the rest is history on that play.”

The game was filled with penalties, and Windsor took some key unsportsmanlike and unnecessary roughness penalties at crucial times to take them out of scoring range.

The Mustangs will now have to play the OUA final on the road after losing head-to-head against the Gaels 41-30 back on Oct. 3.

“They’re coached by [Londoner] Steve Snyder and have a great staff. They’ve got a fifth-year quarterback in Alex Vreeken, so we’re going to spend a lot of time this week obviously looking at the film. We had a close game with them, and Ben Casselman continues to grow as our quarterback. So that’s one of the big differences compared to the previous meeting.”

Faulds knows exactly what the Yates Cup means. He was a two-time game MVP as a player for Western and won two more Ontario titles as the head coach of Wilfrid Laurier.

“It’s super special because as most people know, it isn’t the Super Bowl that is the oldest football trophy and it isn’t the Grey Cup that is the oldest football trophy,” said Faulds.

stories.title: North Vancouver woman rescued after being swept creek during B.C. storm
stories.summary: Stormy conditions hit the province over the weekend, with more rain expected in some areas on Sunday
stories.author: Nono Shen
stories.content:
A North Vancouver woman is praising the quick actions of local firefighters for saving her life after she was swept down a fast-moving creek in the stormy weather that descended over parts of the province.

Brittany Craig was attempting to fix the line that brings water from a nearby creek into her home in the Woodlands community north of Deep Cove on Friday when she lifted a rock and the sudden release of water pushed her into the fast-moving creek.

“It was like out of a movie, when you see people go in a creek or river, and they go under, and then their head comes up for a second,” Craig said in an interview Saturday.

Craig said she was able to grab onto a log in the middle of the creek and managed to call 9-1-1 on her cellphone that was nearly out of battery.

She said she was eventually stranded on the log, pushed against a sheer bank with nowhere else to go.

She began waving her red hooded sweatshirt in the air and screaming for help when firefighters arrived, throwing her a life-jacket and supplies to keep her warm.

Dennis Cappellini, assistant fire chief for District of North Vancouver Fire and Rescue Services, said they got a call around 12:47 p.m. about a water rescue for a woman in the creek.

Cappellini said crews arrived to find the creek had already turned into a fast-moving river due to heavy rainfall.

They lowered a rescuer down on the rope, attached Craig, and hauled her out of the creek onto a trail.

Cappellini said a tree fell next to crew members as they performed the rescue.

“It was a pretty treacherous rescue, but all in all, it went very well,” he said.

Craig said she is overwhelmed with gratitude for the rescuing efforts.

“If they didn’t come here, I don’t think I would have been alive,” she said.

Strong winds and heavy storms across B.C. left tens of thousands of people without power Saturday.

BC Hydro said about 80,000 customers were without electricity at the peak of Friday’s storm, when high winds knocked down trees and branches, leading to widespread power outages across the province.

It said more than 190,000 customers have lost power since the storm began, and, as of Sunday morning, about 87,000 remain without power after another round of rough weather rolled through overnight.

The provincial Crown corporation said Prince George in northern B.C., as well as Port Hardy, Courtenay and Qualicum on Vancouver Island, are among the hardest-hit areas.

“Due to the extent of the damage and access challenges in some areas, some customers are expected to remain without power overnight,” said BC Hydro in a statement.

Parts of Vancouver Island have seen up to 210 millimetres of rain since Thursday in the first major weather system of British Columbia’s storm season, which could combine with high tides to soak some low-lying coastal areas.

B.C.’s River Forecast Centre said the rainfall is part of a series of atmospheric river systems expected to drench coastal areas in the coming days.

It said waterways are rising rapidly, with flows in parts of northern and Western Vancouver Island reaching two- to five-year return levels on Friday.

High streamflow advisories cover most of the island as well as the south and central coasts, including the Sea to Sky region and the lower Fraser River basin.

A wind warning for parts of Metro Vancouver said strong winds gusting up to 90 kilometres an hour would last until Sunday.

Environment Canada, meanwhile, issued a coastal flooding statement for much of Vancouver Island’s west coast, saying elevated ocean levels combined with strong winds and waves could push waters above the highest astronomical tides.

The river forecast centre said a second bout of rain would arrive later Saturday, stretching into Sunday, with the heaviest downpours expected on Vancouver Island and in the Sea to Sky and Howe Sound areas, along with the North Shore mountains.

A third storm that’s expected to hit Monday May bring a more prolonged period of rainfall across B.C.’s coast through next week, the forecaster said.

Whitney Deane, a spokeswoman with BC Hydro, said Friday’s storm caused significant damage, and customers are encouraged to be prepared.

“Additional weather systems are expected through mid-week, and some of the winds could be more impactful than what we’ve seen so far,” said Deane.

In the Village of Zeballos on northwest Vancouver Island, 22 properties remained under evacuation order after heavy rain and flooding on Friday raised landslide risk.

The Strathcona Regional District said in a statement on Saturday that a geotechnical engineer had completed their initial assessment and the district was awaiting the formal report.

One of the main roads in the area, Maquinna Avenue, was re-opened to essential travel, but the statement said stopping was strictly prohibited, “as there continues to be a risk to public safety.”

An earlier statement from the district said officials were also monitoring the forecasted heavy rainfall expected to begin later on Saturday.

BC Ferries cancelled multiple trips scheduled for Saturday night due to high winds and wave height in the Strait of Georgia, which lies between Vancouver Island and the southwestern mainland.

It warned that more cancellations were possible on Sunday.

Craig said she spent Friday night shaken up after what she experienced, but she took to social media to express her gratitude for the firefighters.

“I owe my life to the crew at District of North Vancouver Fire and Rescue. The power of these creeks right now is no joke; what looks manageable on the surface will take your feet right out from under you,” said Craig in a post on Facebook.

Cappellini said unexpected things can happen in water, especially after a heavy rain or when a high streamflow advisory is in place.

“The currents are strong; even if you have a dog that’s a really good swimmer, be careful with your pets as you would be with yourself, your children, and other loved ones,” he said.

stories.title: She argued masculinity is not a problem. Controversy ensued
stories.summary: Analysis: 'Men experience the world differently,' says writer Helen Andrews. 'We don’t need to understand it. We don’t need to like it. We just need to make space for it'
stories.author: Donna Kennedy-Glans
stories.content:
One year ago, American writer Helen Andrews published “The Great Feminization” in Compact magazine. Her claim was blunt: cancel culture is what women do when they reach critical mass in an institution. Wokeness is less an ideology than a byproduct of demographic change once universities, law schools, newsrooms and similar bodies tip majority-female.

The essay went viral in America and drew fire. When we spoke recently, Andrews said she had hoped the worst of the recent cycle was over. “I almost feel like it’s all ramping up again,” she says. “I have this horrible, portentous feeling that the Cornell episode is a sign it’s all going to come roaring back.”

The Cornell episode is straightforward. In 2024, a woman alleged gang rape at a fraternity house on the Cornell campus. The Tompkins County district attorney reviewed the file and concluded the evidence would not support charges. Two years later, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul revived the case and appointed Attorney General Letitia James as special prosecutor. Hochul, the first woman in the office, remarked that the image of two women examining the case gave people comfort: “Two women perhaps are looking at this differently than men would.”

Andrews does not claim a crime occurred; the original prosecutor already said it did not. What interests her is the decision to reopen a closed file with an explicit appeal to gender. “The Democratic Party gins up these hysterias in order to activate female voters in a closely contested midterm,” she says. “They know what they’re doing. Once the election is in the rearview mirror and it has served its purpose, they might be quite content to let it drop — especially since the facts in this case are so unfavourable.”

A few days after the midterms, James stepped back from the criminal investigation and appointed Jacqueline Kelly, a former federal prosecutor, to lead it.

Andrews sees the pattern elsewhere. Male institutions — fraternities, the military, certain sports — become targets when an opening appears. “Anytime there’s a chance to take them down a peg or seize more feminine control of them, people will jump at that chance.”

One line from her original essay drew particular heat. It is now legal, she wrote, for women to sue if their workplace feels like a fraternity house. It is not legal for men to sue if their workplace feels like a Montessori kindergarten. Many women who responded treated this as obvious: fraternity houses are bad; Montessori classrooms are good. Andrews’ reply was direct: “You think that because you are a woman and you are at home in that kind of soft, nurturing environment. Get it through your head that men experience the world differently.”

She does not treat the gender difference as a moral failing. “Women are more attuned to consensus, and female groups are much more willing to police consensus,” she asserts. “Men are stronger, so they don’t have to care if the people around them are mad at them. If you’re a weaker woman, you really do.” The Cornell fraternity members, she notes, did not break the law; they made people angry. In a feminized setting, that can be enough.

College administrators, now majority female in many places, have a further incentive. Women are, ON average, more risk-averse. Banning fraternity events reduces the chance of lawsuits. Andrews is not sentimental about the parties: “I am not a frat-party kind of gal,” she says. “But I’m enough of an adult to step back and say fraternities do good things for men. They teach leadership and brotherhood in an all-male atmosphere that does things for guys that I don’t fully understand, because I have two X chromosomes. We don’t need to understand it. We don’t need to like it. We just need to make space for it.”

That is the practical claim; she’s not arguing for male monopoly. She is arguing that once an institution tips, the habits that once made it function — open conflict, willingness to offend, tolerance for rough edges — tend to be redefined as problems.

Canada has not had the same debate over her thesis. Andrews has lived in Australia (her husband is Australian) and finds the Anglosphere countries recognizably similar yet not identical. Australians are blunter; Canadians are more polite. “It’s contrary to the Canadian spirit to stand up and say that the rules on sexual-assault complaints have swung too far and are now stacked against men in a way that is deeply unfair,” she says. “That’s a hard thing to talk about, and in some ways it’s un-Canadian because it’s mean. It involves being mean to some complainant.”

But, she observes, “It’s the price of civility. The feminists have been so aggressive in pushing the pendulum that they have made some kind of response necessary. They overreached. There’s no option but to push back, even if it involves being a little mean or impolite.”

She is aware of the Hockey Canada case. Five members of the 2018 World Junior team were charged after an encounter at a gala in London, Ont. Police initially closed the file, but in the midst of parliamentary hearings, a funding freeze, board resignations and sponsor withdrawals, charges were laid. In July 2025, Justice Maria Carroccia acquitted all five. She found the complainant neither credible nor reliable and concluded there was actual consent not impaired by fear. Hockey Canada’s separate code-of-conduct process nonetheless kept four of the players out of its programs for years. The organization also appointed its first female president and CEO, Katherine Henderson, and moved toward greater gender balance on the board.

Andrews does not treat that criminal law outcome as proof of her thesis, but she does call the judge “the hero of that case” for applying the law when public pressure ran the other way. She also observes a familiar institutional pattern: “People May be opportunistically using this case as proof that misogyny is rife in the hockey world and we need to make lots of changes to the entire institution,” she suggests. “Those kinds of changes are often implemented in the heat of a controversy and then you can’t undo them even after the heat has died down. That is how leftists burrow into institutions and take them over.”

She is not opposed, in principle, to leagues imposing standards beyond the criminal law. “I’m OK with league punishments even for players who are not found criminally liable,” she said. “A league can say, ‘You didn’t break the law, but you violated the moral standards we stand for.’ I think that is probably unfair in this particular case, and worse than these boys deserve, but in principle I don’t think it’s a wrong thing to do.”

Bringing a lighter tone to a serious topic, Andrews points out how Chrystia Freeland “made headlines in your country and even in my country … with her new book saying that crying was routine in Justin Trudeau’s cabinet … how embarrassing for Canada.”

“Is that a reflection of the Great Feminization?” she asks. Trudeau had made a point of assembling a gender-balanced cabinet, the first in Canadian history to reach rough parity. “Some people would say no, because that happened under a male prime minister,” she says. “But I look at that and think the gender dynamics had something to do with the fact people felt like crying in that room was appropriate.” The irony, she notes, is that Freeland — the woman — was the one recording the embarrassment.

Andrews has three sons. She says there are days she asks herself why she keeps writing about this. “It would make my life a lot easier to just give it up.” She has not; she believes she owes them a world that has not treated ordinary male traits as a problem to be managed. I, too, have three sons who are now young men. That is one reason I called her.

stories.title: Funeral Sunday for B.C. soldier killed in CFB Wainwright fire
stories.summary: The funeral for one of the four Canadian soldiers killed in a fire at a military base in Alberta is today in Vancouver.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Vancouver — The funeral for one of the four Canadian soldiers killed in a fire at a military base in Alberta is today in Vancouver.

The ceremony honouring 23-year-old Pte. Aidan Goulding will take place at the Seaforth Armoury where family, friends and members of the armed forces are expected to pay their respects.

Goulding was part of the 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry when he died after a grass fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright overtook a live-fire training exercise on a nearby grenade range.

Goulding is being remembered by his friends and family as an excellent athlete with a contagious laugh who was looking forward to peacekeeping in Latvia.

The other soldiers killed in the Oct. 17 fire were: Pte. Shaun Farrell, 23, of Prince Albert, Sask. Pte. Hayden Lykkemark, 19, of Langley, B.C.; and Sgt. Morgan Wong, 26, of Edmonton.

The fire left 39 others wounded, many with serious burns.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 8, 2026

stories.title: The sad story of Canada’s last captive whales
stories.summary: The tragedy of this country’s cetaceans, shipped abroad, shows how much humanity’s morality has evolved – and how far it has go
stories.author: The Editorial Board
stories.content:
There are moments in history that are simultaneously major progress and a reminder of how far humanity still has to go. A Canadian example of this happened in the summer, as an aquarium in Ontario shipped the last remaining captive whales out of the country.

Under a 2019 law , it is illegal for Canadian aquariums to own whales. Keeping such creatures in captivity is now – and hopefully forever – forbidden in Canada. Ideally, there will be no more.

That’s the good news. The tragic twist is that at least five of these whales have died since moving to their new homes, including one last month . And the underlying moral falling is that it took Canadians decades to realize that it is simply wrong to hold highly intelligent and social creatures, huge creatures, in small pens for our entertainment.

This is a reminder that morality evolves over time. What people find acceptable now May well be grounds for scathing criticism from their grandchildren or great-grandchildren. That is not a reason to excuse the actions of previous generations – because even in the heyday of historic evils, there were people who spoke out against a prevailing wisdom they realized was wrong – but to remember that in our own ways we May prove as flawed as them.

While none of us is perfectible, we are improvable. The lesson of these whales is that we have to examine our own blind spots and recognize our own failings.

In the 18th century, English philosopher Jeremy Bentham had already landed on a key theory that undercut millennia of justification for rendering irrelevant the concept of animal rights.

From biblical times – when the Old Testament God gave humans “dominion” over the animal kingdom – to human laws treating animals as nothing more than property, the assumption was that people could do with creatures what they wanted. It might be economically foolish to beat a draft animal to death, but nothing otherwise prevented such behaviour.

However, Bentham argued that the power of humans needed a leash. In his book An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation , he laid out the case that animals should not be treated as a class worse than humans for a simple reason : “The question is not, Can they reason? nor, Can they talk? but, Can they suffer? Why should the law refuse its protection to any sensitive being?”

This was a powerful call for a philosophical and legal realignment, one that is continuing to gather momentum more than two centuries later. In some cases, the impetus to change has been staring us in the face. The Dutch term for pacing nervously is ijsberen , which literally means “to polar bear.” Because what does this creature do in the zoo? It walks up and down its enclosure, up and down, up and down.

Not only did Bentham place human blindness about the well-being of animals on the moral spectrum with changing views about race, he explicitly called for people to live up to a better standard: “The time will come when humanity will extend its mantle over everything which breathes.”

That time is not yet here, but it is coming closer.

Animal welfare is now firmly established in law. In most countries, animals, while still legally property, are protected against willful harm. In Canada, the legislation against keeping whales in captivity was followed by a Senate bill prohibiting the same for elephants and great apes, while grandfathering animals currently in that situation. The bill made it to third reading in the upper house before the 2025 election and should be revived.

Court cases have been brought – so far, unsuccessfully – seeking to extend some of the rights of humans to other primates. Although they have failed, attitudes have changed enough that many historical norms around animal treatment seem barbaric.

Vivisection, the cutting apart of living animals, is rightly now seen as torture. Setting animals on each other to fight to the death still happens, but behind closed doors, because it is now illegal in most countries. Circuses, which once flexed the old dominion muscle by making animals perform undignified stunts to entertain the crowds, are being supplanted by ones that focus on human ability.

This is not to say that progress is complete.

The raising of animals for food will likely be viewed differently one day than it is now. Animal products are shunned already by vegans, a small but growing constituency, and meat is avoided by the larger group of vegetarians. Expectations around more humane treatment of farmed animals have become mainstream. Lab-grown meat May one day become indistinguishable from the traditional variety, however, for now, rearing animals in order to eat them remains firmly entrenched in culinary culture and the global economy.

Zoos, meanwhile, occupy an increasingly problematic space. Where once they were seen so benignly that a favourite of children’s literature – Curious George – realized after being captured in the wild and having an adventure in the big city that he would be happier in a zoo, they now prompt uncomfortable questions. In response, many present themselves as centres of research and conservation. Often, though, this strains credulity. Andrew Westoll, who has researched such claims, argues that most of these facilities fail as educational destinations and also at the preservation and propagation of endangered species.

Bentham’s point is also crucial because it points to the evolution of morality. That can be an awkward thought. Implicit here is the notion that what is seen as good today May not always be seen that way. That behaviour we consider good May be viewed differently in the future. But what is considered acceptable does change. It always has.

Consider the case of a U.S. congressman named Daniel Sickles who, in 1859, shot and killed the man he believed to be his wife’s lover. He pleaded temporary insanity and was acquitted. But what really scandalized the public was that he then reconciled with his wife.

In some early societies, a retaliatory killing was not seen as murder but as justice. As social groupings became bigger, though, and blood feuds could go on indefinitely, at great cost in lives and social disruption, the idea that such crimes should be punished by society and not the individual took hold.

Law and morality have tended to move in lockstep, with the legal codes evolving to reflect changing social views. And the history of the law shows that, rather than things being simply right or wrong, these judgments were often based on circumstance.

Did the biblical Ten Commandments forbid killing another person or forbid murder? Analyses vary, but the distinction illustrates that the same act can be two different things.

However, the law is an imperfect mirror of morality.

The term “outlaw” was originally applied to a person outside the protection of the law. They had no legal redress if wronged and, if they were slain, their killers could face no legal punishment. The law did not recognize their existence.

At various times in history, the best legal minds of their era deliberated and agreed that it was acceptable to enslave another person, that women should be denied the vote. In relatively recent living memory, the idea that a man could rape his wife was not recognized in Canadian law.

All of these things are, to our eye, abhorrent. Rightly so. What was once normal became morally unacceptable. Such changes are good; they bring society closer to its better angels.

But morality remains complicated. Many situations have competing priorities: allegiance to duty, to virtue, to loved ones, to the greater good. The last is particularly thorny, because an enduring effect of clan-based societies is division between us and them.

The famous trolley problem – a thought exercise that questions who is to be sacrificed in order to save others – assumes that most people don’t view all lives as equally important. Critics of “speciesism” argue that attributing fewer rights to animals than humans is a form of this.

A comforting way to think about morality is that it exists in an abstract perfection, that it is an ideal we must simply live up to. In that scenario, the people who fought unjust laws in previous centuries were seized with some morality greater than the law, greater than what they were taught by society. Something within them.

If that is the case, people alive today should not assume that we have risen perfectly to join them in achieving an innate moral virtue. More likely, we still have a long way to go. The sad and yet hopeful story of the whales shows us that.

stories.title: Funeral today for B.C. soldier killed in CFB Wainwright fire
stories.summary: Vancouver - The funeral for one of the four Canadian soldiers killed in a fire at a military base in Alberta is today in Vancouver.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Vancouver - A 23-year-old Canadian soldier was remembered Sunday as a globe-trotting, sporty and car-loving man with an infectious sense of humour and a fearless love for life.

Hundreds of military personnel, family and friends gathered at an armoury on a stormy day in Vancouver to remember Pte. Aidan Goulding, one of four soldiers killed last month after a grass fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta overtook troops during a training exercise.

His mother, Sonia Monk, described her son as someone with a great sense of humour, always open to a good laugh.

The funeral for 23-year old Pte. Aidan Goulding took place at the Seaforth Armoury in Vancouver. Goulding was one of four soldiers killed last month after a grass fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta overtook troops during a training exercise. (Nov. 8, 2026)

“Whenever I was disciplining him, he would start to laugh or he would try to say something. I could never properly discipline him,” she said.

“That’s something that our family is going to miss. Nothing is going replace that.”

Monk said she was proud of her patriotic son who joined the army from a high-paying job.

“When he finally told me, he said, ‘I have one life to live, I want to do something important, and so I’m joining the army.’ I think that’s so unselfish of him,” she said.

After he joined the Canadian Armed Forces, Goulding felt like he found a place where he belonged, Monk said.

“It gave him a sense of purpose, a family and a place he truly felt at home.”

Goulding’s funeral started with soldiers carrying his flag-draped casket into the armoury, with the sounds of a bagpipe cascading, and some words from a rabbi.

Monk described his upbringing in North Vancouver with his brother, Wylder, who was also his best friend.

“They had each other’s backs,” she said. “Their relationship touched my heart deeply, and I was content in knowing that they would always be close.”

Growing up, he showed his competitive and curious side.

His family said in a statement he played many sports, including soccer and rugby, and developed a love for cars at a young age.

He spent many hours buying used cars, fixing them late into the night under the glow of a lamp on his family’s driveway and then reselling them.

The first car he fine-tuned was a used Chrysler 300C.

The modification: make it louder.

“He loved understanding how things worked and took great pride in making them his own,” his family said.

He was also stylish.

Monk said her son asked to wear a white suit on his first day of Grade 4. When he turned 21, he asked for a gold suit.

“He was unapologetically himself, and I admired that,” she said,

The family has also described Goulding as a globe-trotter.

In his short life, he explored many parts of the world, including Mexico, Germany, Austria, Italy, Croatia, Malta, the Netherlands, England and Spain.

Reagan Goulding, his aunt, said during the funeral that he often made those around him laugh.

She said it’s been hard knowing that he died at a young age.

“This is perhaps one of the hardest parts of losing someone so young,” she said. “It’s not just the memories we have lost, but the opportunity to make a relationship we still had time to build.”

Reagan Goulding said she could see her nephew, who she described as being “smart, ambitious, determined, and resourceful,” perhaps becoming a police officer or joining Csis.

“I truly believe great things were in his future. We wanted him to know that we all saw this in him, that we believed in him and became a proud follower of him,” she said.

She said her last message to Goulding was sent on the day of the tragedy, a text message that said, “Aidan, you better be OK.”

She never received a reply.

Reagan Goulding said if she knew this was her last message she would have said more, including telling him one more time how proud she was.

She also remembered the other soldiers killed in the fire.

They were: Pte. Hayden Lykkemark, 19, of Langley, B.C.; Sgt. Morgan Wong, 26, of Edmonton; and Pte. Shaun Farrell, 23, of Prince Albert, Sask.

“They were young men who matched their calling, who stood beside one another, and who were parts of the family themselves. Their loss is felt by their families, their friends, soldiers, and everyone who has been touched by this tragedy,” she said.

“Aidan and his fellow soldiers will not be forgotten,” she added.

Thirty-nine others were injured in the fire, and many remain in hospitals in Edmonton and Calgary.

As the soldiers carried the casket out of the armoury and reloaded it into a hearse to head to the cemetery, the sun broke through the clouds, casting its light over rainy Vancouver.

Monk, who spoke to media after the funeral, said she felt it was a sign from Goulding, encouraging her to move forward with life.

“Because I think through tragedy or hardship, he would always say things like that, ‘We’ll move forward.’ So, I think that’s what he was sort of saying to me today, actually, with the sun shining bright in my eyes.”

Monk said she felt “supported and lifted” after hearing stories from Goulding’s “brothers and sisters” in the army.

“I’m quite tired, I haven’t eaten a lot, I haven’t slept a lot. But all the support and seeing everybody here today, it’s remarkable. I can’t find a word other than remarkable,” said Monk, adding that “There’s lots of love in Canada.”

— With files from Fakiha Baig in Edmonton

“I truly believe great things were in his future. We wanted him to know that we all saw this in him, that we believed in him and became a proud follower of him,” she said.

She said her last message to Goulding was sent on the day of the tragedy, a text message that said, “Aidan, you better be OK.”

She never received a reply.

Reagan Goulding said if she knew this was her last message she would have said more, including telling him one more time how proud she was.

She also remembered the other soldiers killed in the fire.

They were: Pte. Hayden Lykkemark, 19, of Langley, B.C.; Sgt. Morgan Wong, 26, of Edmonton; and Pte. Shaun Farrell, 23, of Prince Albert, Sask.

“They were young men who matched their calling, who stood beside one another, and who were parts of the family themselves. Their loss is felt by their families, their friends, soldiers, and everyone who has been touched by this tragedy,” she said.

“Aidan and his fellow soldiers will not be forgotten,” she added.

Thirty-nine others were injured in the fire, and many remain in hospitals in Edmonton and Calgary.

As the soldiers carried the casket out of the armoury and reloaded it into a hearse to head to the cemetery, the sun broke through the clouds, casting its light over rainy Vancouver.

Monk, who spoke to media after the funeral, said she felt it was a sign from Goulding, encouraging her to move forward with life.

“Because I think through tragedy or hardship, he would always say things like that, ‘We’ll move forward.’ So, I think that’s what he was sort of saying to me today, actually, with the sun shining bright in my eyes.”

Monk said she felt “supported and lifted” after hearing stories from Goulding’s “brothers and sisters” in the army.

“I’m quite tired, I haven’t eaten a lot, I haven’t slept a lot. But all the support and seeing everybody here today, it’s remarkable. I can’t find a word other than remarkable,” said Monk, adding that “There’s lots of love in Canada.”

Hundreds of military personnel, family and friends gathered at an armoury on a stormy day in Vancouver to remember Pte. Aidan Goulding, one of four soldiers killed last month after a grass fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta overtook troops during a training exercise.
His mother, Sonia Monk, described her son as someone with a great sense of humour, always open to a good laugh.
“Whenever I was disciplining him, he would start to laugh or he would try to say something. I could never properly discipline him,” she said.
“That’s something that our family is going to miss. Nothing is going replace that.”
Monk said she was proud of her patriotic son who joined the army from a high-paying job.
“When he finally told me, he said, ‘I have one life to live, I want to do something important, and so I’m joining the army.’ I think that’s so unselfish of him,” she said.
After he joined the Canadian Armed Forces, Goulding felt like he found a place where he belonged, Monk said.
“It gave him a sense of purpose, a family and a place he truly felt at home.”
Goulding’s funeral started with soldiers carrying his flag-draped casket into the armoury, with the sounds of a bagpipe cascading, and some words from a rabbi.
Monk described his upbringing in North Vancouver with his brother, Wylder, who was also his best friend.
“They had each other’s backs,” she said. “Their relationship touched my heart deeply, and I was content in knowing that they would always be close.”
Growing up, he showed his competitive and curious side.

stories.title: Americans in Canada hope for closer ties between two countries after midterms
stories.summary: When Lucia Lloyd immigrated to Canada in 2019, she thought she had moved far away enough from President Donald Trump’s America.
stories.author: Sharif Hassan The Canadian Press
stories.content:
When Lucia Lloyd immigrated to Canada in 2019, she thought she had moved far away enough from President Donald Trump’s America.

She said she was already upset when Trump first took office in 2017, but the president’s controversial nomination of Brett Kavanaugh to the U.S. Supreme Court and the judge’s subsequent confirmation amid sexual misconduct allegations was the last straw for her.

“So, that was the day that I started researching whether I could move to Canada, and it turned out to be the end,” said Lloyd, a Virginia native who is now a priest at an Anglican Church in Bowmanville, Ont., east of Toronto.

Ever since Trump launched the trade war with Canada in his second term and mused about annexing the country, Lloyd said she has been “horrified” by the way the president has treated her adopted home and Canadians.

“There is nothing that Canada has done to deserve this, there is no advantage to doing this,” she said in an interview. “It’s just Trump’s own personal meanness to go around insulting allies and trading partners and friends on this side of Lake Ontario.”

That’s why Lloyd said she was thrilled to see the Democrats’ sweeping victory in Tuesday’s midterm elections, which she hopes will put a check on Trump’s powers.

“I do feel a huge sense of relief,” she said, adding that the results also give her hope that the relationship between Canada and the United States might gradually improve after nearly two years of heightened tensions.

Lloyd said she is currently in Canada on a work permit while her permanent residency application is being processed, and she feels lucky that, unlike many immigrants in the United States, she doesn’t have to worry about being picked up by “masked federal agents” on the street and put into a detention centre.

While Canadians welcomed the blue wave in U.S. Congress, many expressed doubts that it would restore their trust in their neighbour any time soon.

Lloyd said she “absolutely” understands the sentiment given the extent of damage caused by the current U.S. administration.

“There’s a lot of work still to be done. I think it’s going to take a long time,” she said, adding that as long as Trump is in the White House, the path toward normalizing those ties won’t be easy.

Lloyd’s views were echoed by Kate Kitchen, an Ohio-born dual citizen who lives in Peterborough, Ont. She also thinks Canadians’ distrust of the U.S. is likely to stick around in the near future.

The shifting political landscape in the United States, however, makes her optimistic about mending the close economic and cultural relationship between two nations in the long run.

“I’m thinking these are trustworthy, intelligent, compassionate people who have taken over these jobs … let’s wait and see but I think people are hopeful,” she said.

Kitchen said she stayed awake past midnight Tuesday to watch the midterm results, particularly those in Ohio where she’d mailed her ballot and followed up to make sure it was received and counted.

She said she was “shocked in a good way” to see the Democrats win the House and the Senate with a majority that makes it hard for “the president to be able to mess” with.

“We hadn’t wanted to get our hopes up, but oh my gosh,” she said.

Matthew Lebo, a political scientist at Western University in London, Ont., whose research focuses on U.S. politics, said he was “more optimistic today than a week ago,” following the midterm results, but it is too soon to celebrate the future of the U.S.-Canada relationship.

“Two years ago they voted (Trump) in, Tuesday they voted out a bunch of Republicans and I don’t know what they’re going to do in two years,” he said.

It will take a few more elections to find out if American voters will roundly reject overt racism, threats to immigrants and cruelty in politics, Lebo said.

He said the ongoing tariff war is something that Canadians are mostly worried about.

“But the most important issue is whether or not we are living next to a full democracy,” he said, adding that the United States has been sliding toward an authoritarian system, and “that’s accelerated under Donald Trump.”

On trade talks, Lebo said while historically some Democrats have been more protectionist, it is possible that they will push back against Trump’s tariffs on Canadian goods and be successful.

“I think they should be helpful. They will try,” he said of the newly elected Democrats in Congress who have spoken out against the tariffs in recent days.

“But it’s still going to be Trump and the same people who will be negotiating with Canada,” he said. “It’s going to be a very confrontational two years … within the American government and maybe still between Canada and the U.S.”

stories.title: Turning back vulnerable refugees under a Canada-U.S. border pact is discriminatory, Supreme Court will hear this week
stories.summary: Safe Third Country Agreement has a discriminatory impact on some groups, opponents argue.
stories.author: Nicholas Keung
stories.content:
Women fleeing gender-based persecution are being denied asylum. Children seeking protection are held behind bars, sometimes separated from parents. Lgbtq refugees are outed by jail staff and sexually assaulted by other detainees.

These are the risks faced by particularly vulnerable asylum-seeking migrants when Canada sends them back to the U.S. at the land border, according to claims alleged in a lawsuit challenging the constitutionality of the Canada-U.S. Safe Third Country Agreement.

The bilateral pact, effective since 2004, requires refugee claimants to seek protection in the first country they arrive in — either Canada or the United States. Those who cross into the other country are turned back unless they meet one of a few narrow exemptions, such as having an immediate family member there or being an unaccompanied minor.

While the rules are meant to apply to everyone equally, the lawsuit claims that some groups face discriminatory impacts based on their gender, age and sexual orientation, hence the agreement violates section 15 of the Canadian Charter of Rights, which guarantees equality rights.

Family sent back to Honduras accuses Ottawa of violating rights by handing them to U.S. — despite what they claim is Trump administration's abuses.

“The agreement is not discriminatory on its face in the sense that it says, ‘Don’t let women in or Lgbtq people or whatever,’ but the way it works is that you have a law that disproportionately impacts particular groups,” said Asma Faizi, president of the Canadian Council for Refugees, in an interview. The council is one of three public interest groups leading the litigation.

“If a law is discriminating against these particular groups, then that entire law should be held to be unconstitutional.”

On Monday, the Federal Court will start a four-day hearing into their claims.

The bilateral agreement was the subject of two failed attempts to strike it down in court, in 2007 and 2020, but advocates say this case is particularly important now given the political landscape in the U.S.

Julia Sande, a lawyer with Amnesty International Canada, said the designation of the U.S. as a safe country has always been problematic because the U.S. asylum law is considered deficient and out of step with Canadian and international law.

But since President Donald Trump returned to the White House in January 2025, she said the conditions and treatment of refugees in the U.S. have further deteriorated, as documented in a recent report by her colleagues in the U.S.

“Everyone is aware of what’s going on in the U.S. as far as a really mass detention and deportation effort, a dismantling of the asylum system as a whole, and deportations to third countries where people have no connections to,” said Sande. Amnesty is also part of the lawsuit with the Canadian Council of Churches and two families from El Salvador and Syria.

“While we’ve had concerns the agreement has been unconstitutional throughout its lifetime, it’s so much worse now.”

The lawsuit follows a Supreme Court of Canada ruling in 2023. The court upheld the pact, saying it did not violate the Charter’s section 7 guarantees of liberty and security of the person , but sent the issue of whether it violated equality rights back to the Federal Court, noting the “profound seriousness of the matter.”

Prasanna Balasundaram, director of Downtown Legal Services.

The lawsuit focuses on the three most vulnerable subgroups — women, children and Lgbtq individuals — who are disproportionately disadvantaged by the system, the lawsuit argues.

Canada returned 4,323 claimants to the U.S. between Jan. 1, 2025, and March 30, 2026, according to court submissions. Of the total, 2,078 were recorded as female and 860 were children under 17; the majority were racial minorities.

The lawsuit said female refugee claimants fleeing gender-based persecution face additional hurdles to seek asylum protection under U.S. law, which treats their claims as “private matters outside the scope of protection.”

Refugee claimant children who are detained upon return face conditions such as lack of access to clean water, adequate food and hygiene supplies, which harm them disproportionately, causing long-term trauma, the lawsuit alleges.

In contrast, Canada was among the first countries to recognize gender-based persecution as a ground for refugee protection, and the detention of children is only a measure of last resort here, the lawsuit says.

The lawsuit also claimed detained Lgbtq migrants are 97 times more likely to be sexually assaulted than other detainees, and suffer abuse by jail staff who regularly put them in danger by outing them. In addition, it said trans people are being issued identity documents in the wrong gender, which put them at risk for mistreatment or discrimination.

“Imagine your kid is being fed food with worms, cloudy water,” Sande said in an interview. “And then it’s like, ‘Well, if you want to sign your rights away, that’s the best way to get your kid out of detention.’ And so we see that, and kids are separated from their parents.”

The litigants ask the Federal Court to declare that the designation of the U.S. as a safe third country is “invalid and of no force or effect” under Canadian immigration law if it rules the agreement breaches the equality rights under the Charter.

“These claimants face a disproportionate risk of abuse in American immigration detention, as well as barriers to obtaining refugee protection,” said Prasanna Balasundaram, director of Downtown Legal Services in Toronto. The legal clinic represents the Salvadoran family named only as “ABC, DE and FG” in the lawsuit.

“The courts have to examine how the laws operate in practice rather than assuming that a rule that applies equally to everyone produces equal consequences.”

In its submissions to court, the federal government said the guarantee of equality rights in Canada does not apply to foreign law or the actions of foreign governments.

It argued that both the Salvadoran and Syrian families who initiated the lawsuit did make it to Canada in the end and acquired permanent residence, so the court decision won’t affect them. In addition, there are mechanisms at a Canadian border officer’s discretion to avoid returning a claimant to the U.S. if there’s concern for the person’s wellbeing.

“The U.S.A. has enacted a comprehensive scheme to assess asylum claims complete with procedural safeguards for administering these provisions,” government lawyers said in court submissions.

“It is a democratic country with a system of checks and balances among its three branches of government, including an independent judiciary and constitutional guarantees of due process and equal protection under the law.”

The Immigration Department said the agreement keeps Canada’s border management orderly and avoids sudden spikes in asylum claims that could overwhelm border crossings, housing, and processing systems. It said it continues to monitor U.S. policy changes and their impacts on the refugee system, but declined to comment on the lawsuit.

stories.title: CTV News wins 42 Rtdna Canada awards, including wins for CTVNews.CA and W5
stories.summary: CTV News won eight National Awards of Excellence and six Best Canadian Local News awards from Rtdna Canada, the organization announced Saturday night at a gala event in Toronto.
stories.author: CTVNews.ca Staff
stories.content:
CTV News won eight National Awards of Excellence and six Best Canadian Local News awards from Rtdna Canada, the organization announced Saturday night at a gala event in Toronto.

CTV W5 won the Enterprise Journalism award in the Multiplatform category for “Avery Haines Investigates: Cartel Canada,” an investigation into how Canada became the largest exporter of meth to New Zealand in the world.

CTV W5 also won the Investigative Excellence award for “Avery Haines Investigates: Sleeping With The Enemy,” following an online network of men who are secretly drugging and videotaping their crimes.

Taking home the best ‘TV Newscast’ award was CTV National News with Omar Sachedina.

CTV News won the Breaking News award for coverage of Trudeau’s resignation, and the Excellence in Sports Reporting award for reporting on Pwhl player Abby “Hustles” Hustler.

Best Canadian Local News awards

CTV News Toronto won the Multiplatform award for Continuing Coverage (Large Market) for its coverage of the Toronto Blue Jays playoffs.

CTV News Saskatoon won the same award for Small/Medium Market for coverage of Saskatchewan wildfires.

In the Video category, CTV News Atlantic won the Feature News (Small/Medium Market) award for a feature on a sculpture-building mechanic.

CP24.com won a Live Special Events (Regional) Digital award for its coverage of Ontario’s provincial election.

Lifetime Achievement, Distinguished Service, Emerging Journalist awards

This year’s Lifetime Achievement Award was presented to CTV W5’s Avery Haines. The Award is presented to individuals who have “distinguished themselves through outstanding service and continued excellence during the course of their career,” Rtdna Canada says.

CTV News Vice-President Richard Gray was also honoured with the Distinguished Service Award, which Rtdna Canada says is given “in recognition and appreciation of outstanding contribution and exemplary distinguished service rendered for the benefit and advancement of electronic journalism and Rtdna.”

CTV News Social Content Coordinator Sydney Wray was presented with the Emerging Journalist Award, given in recognition of “the achievements and excellent work of Canadian journalists who are at the beginning stages of their career,” according to the organization.

Rtdna Canada, or the Radio Television Digital News Association of Canada, is the leading voice of journalists in Canada, fostering the best in Radio, Television and Digital News. The members of Rtdna Canada recognize the responsibility of journalists to promote and to protect the freedom to report independently about matters of public interest and to present a wide range of expressions, opinions and ideas.

stories.title: Festival of Lights, Festival of Growth: A look at Diwali’s business impact in Canada
stories.summary: As the Indian diaspora expands globally, this festive economic surge is no longer confined to the subcontinent - it is rapidly becoming a borderless retail and cultural phenomenon.
stories.author: John Marchesan
stories.content:
By Rashmeen Rupal, Omni News

Posted November 7, 2026 8:48 pm.

Sunday marks Diwali, or the Festival of Lights, for millions of people around the world. Often referred to as the ‘Festival of Growth’ in India, it is the time of peak festival shopping when big brands launch their most ambitious products and advertising agencies release the most creative storytelling with high end festive emotions.

The season is the centre of Indian commerce, where cultural celebrations create a boost for the economy.

As the Indian diaspora expands globally, this festive economic surge is no longer confined to the subcontinent — it is rapidly becoming a borderless retail and cultural phenomenon.

The car-buying trend during Diwali in India has crossed borders to Canada. A number of GTA car dealerships are leaning towards the festive buying trends with purchase offers and other incentives, like what Performance Auto Group in Ontario is doing, offering participating customers a one-ounce silver coin with the purchase or lease of a vehicle.

Indo-Canadian cultural commentator Darshan Maharaja points to the clothes, gifts and sweets people buy, along with promotions from major retailers, as signs of how visible Diwali has become in Canada’s shopping calendar.

“In a way, one can say that the Christmas spending season starts one month early because of Diwali,” he tells Omni News in an email.

A month of different festivities lead up to the auspicious day, and one such day is Dhanteras – which roughly translates to the Day of Wealth. On this day Indian families buy gold or silver, while another holiday tradition comes in the form of a box of Mithai, or South Asian sweets, to share with friends and family.

Though the affordability crisis has placed a tight squeeze on Canadian household budgets, families will not cancel Diwali; instead, they alter how they spend.

“People used to buy bigger products, now they are buying smaller things, but they are buying more of them,” said Vikram Rana, owner of Rana Jewelers in Brampton.

At the same time, some businesses are seeing the real impacts of global uncertainty.

“We used to get quite a lot of orders during the festive season, but now the orders have almost gone down 50 per cent,” said Soumya, who runs a small South Asian restaurant in downtown Toronto. She tells Omni News that rising costs and changes to immigration, including fewer international students, has affected their business.

In Canada, about 828,000 people reported Hinduism as their religion in the 2021 census. About 772,000 reported Sikhism and 8,300 reported Jainism. Diwali is a major Hindu festival, but at the same time, Sikhs mark Bandi Chhor Divas and Jains observe Mahavir Diwas, distinct religious occasions that also have traditions involving light.

Ontario’s Ministry of Tourism, gaming and culture told Omni News that the province’s diversity attracts visitors who stay in local accommodations, dine at restaurants, shop at local businesses and support main street economies.

“Since 2018, approximately $520,000 in funding support has been provided through Experience Ontario to Diwali-related festivals and events. Festivals and events supported through Experience Ontario help communities attract visitors who stay in local accommodations, dine at restaurants, shop at local businesses and support main street economies,” they said in a statement.

In Toronto, the celebrations began weeks before the main holiday. At Nathan Phillips Square, the Diwali Festival of Lights brought music, dance and vendors selling food and clothing to the city’s downtown before closing with fireworks on October 25. Another celebration at Mel Lastman Square featured 50 vendors and more than 150 performers. And Brampton, the Canadian city with the largest South Asian population, is hosting a Diwali Mela on November 8 .

stories.title: Province-wide protests call for moratorium on AI data centre proposals in N.S.
stories.summary: Halifax - The chants of nearly 1,000 Nova Scotians drowned out the rain in downtown Halifax Saturday as residents took to the streets to protest a proposed artificial intelligence data centre in southern Cape Breton.
stories.author: Tori Fitzpatrick The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Halifax - The chants of nearly 1,000 Nova Scotians drowned out the rain in downtown Halifax Saturday as residents took to the streets to protest a proposed artificial intelligence data centre in southern Cape Breton.

Protesters gathered in front of the provincial legislature at noon, taking up an entire block of Hollis Street before marching through the city’s downtown core.

They called for a moratorium on all large-scale AI data centre proposals in the province after proponent Everwind Fuels announced last month it plans to lease a data centre in Pont Tupper, N.S., to U.S. AI company Anthropic.

Hundreds of protesters in Halifax marched against a proposed AI data centre in southern Cape Breton. Organizers say it was one of at least seven protests planned across the province on Saturday calling for a moratorium on large-scale AI data centres. (Nov. 8, 2026)

Ned Zimmerman, a tech worker from Dartmouth, N.S., and one of the organizers of the rally, said large-scale AI data centres are socially destructive and environmentally irresponsible.

“We feel that the push to integrate AI into everything raises a lot of concerns for society, and this is not the kind of thing that we want to see being imposed on our communities, ON our landscapes, our ecosystems, and our populations,” Zimmerman said.

Organizers of the rally said it was one of seven happening across the province on Saturday.

Everwind has described the $10-billion project as the largest private investment in provincial history. Anthropic has signed a 20-year lease for the 18,600-square-metre facility, which it will use to power its AI assistant Claude.

It is expected to come online in 2027 and draw 95 megawatts of electricity in its first phase. A 325-megawatt expansion is scheduled for mid-2028, bringing the total energy demand to 420 megawatts.

But it has faced backlash from Nova Scotians who are concerned about its potential impact on the environment and on power rates.

A petition to stop the development of AI data centres in Nova Scotia on Change.org garnered nearly 28,000 signatures.

Everwind says it will cover the cost of all electricity infrastructure, and the project will not increase power rates for customers.

A statement from Premier Tim Houston’s office said the data centre will only proceed if it meets provincial and federal guidelines, which it noted includes protecting the water, the environment, power rates and capacity.

Zimmerman said those guidelines are not enough for a project of this scale, adding that communication from the provincial government has been sparse. He also said Everwind has not done enough to consult with communities about the data centre, demonstrating a lack of transparency and accountability.

“It was kept closely under wraps. And broader community consent, community consultation was not engaged until the project was announced,” he said.

Everwind did not respond to request for comment about the protest.

Earlier this week, the company held two lengthy information sessions in Cape Breton. Some attendees said they were left with outstanding questions. Everwind’s engagement director said at a session Wednesday night that more consultations would be arranged.

Rebecca Lawrence from Dartmouth was among the protesters Saturday in Halifax. She said the provincial government is rushing the data centre project without acknowledging the potential harm it could cause.

She said she’s worried about potential noise pollution, as well as the centre’s impact on the local water supply.

Water from nearby Landrie Lake, which is also used to supply water to the town of Port Hawkesbury, will be used to cool the Point Tupper data centre’s servers. The system will use an average of 100,000 litres of water per day in the first phase, expanding to an average draw of 500,000 litres per day in its next phase.

“I think that one drop of drinking water wasted on generative AI is too much,” Lawrence said.

EverWind said the cooling system will be closed-loop, similar to a car’s radiator, with cooling fluid recycled or disposed of off-site, not in local waterways.

Ashley Drodge, another organizer of Saturday’s protest in Halifax, said said she’s concerned about the lack of binding regulations for AI data centre development and the absence of an environmental impact assessment for the project.

“This is short-sighted, money in your pocket development,” she said.

Earlier this month, Nova Scotia’s Minister of Environment, Timothy Halman, said that instead of an environmental impact assessment, the project requires industrial approval, a tool he described as the most appropriate for this type of project.

“What is being utilized here is a very robust regulatory tool to ensure safe construction and operation of a proposed facility,” he told reporters.

Houston has previously said he doesn’t know whether any new legislation is needed to regulate the data centre.

However, the statement from his office about the protest said the province would be open to legislative changes “should we find ourselves in a situation where we require them.”

Lawrence said Saturday her message to the premier is to listen to Nova Scotians.

“Nova Scotian’s are pretty vocal on the fact that we don’t want this,” she said. “On every side there’s people from all across the spectrum who are saying no to these data centres.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 7, 202 6.

“It was kept closely under wraps. And broader community consent, community consultation was not engaged until the project was announced,” he said.
Everwind did not respond to request for comment about the protest.

Earlier this week, the company held two lengthy information sessions in Cape Breton. Some attendees said they were left with outstanding questions. Everwind’s engagement director said at a session Wednesday night that more consultations would be arranged.

Rebecca Lawrence from Dartmouth was among the protesters Saturday in Halifax. She said the provincial government is rushing the data centre project without acknowledging the potential harm it could cause.
She said she’s worried about potential noise pollution, as well as the centre’s impact on the local water supply.

Water from nearby Landrie Lake, which is also used to supply water to the town of Port Hawkesbury, will be used to cool the Point Tupper data centre’s servers. The system will use an average of 100,000 litres of water per day in the first phase, expanding to an average draw of 500,000 litres per day in its next phase.
“I think that one drop of drinking water wasted on generative AI is too much,” Lawrence said.
EverWind said the cooling system will be closed-loop, similar to a car’s radiator, with cooling fluid recycled or disposed of off-site, not in local waterways.

Ashley Drodge, another organizer of Saturday’s protest in Halifax, said said she’s concerned about the lack of binding regulations for AI data centre development and the absence of an environmental impact assessment for the project.
“This is short-sighted, money in your pocket development,” she said.

Earlier this month, Nova Scotia’s Minister of Environment, Timothy Halman, said that instead of an environmental impact assessment, the project requires industrial approval, a tool he described as the most appropriate for this type of project.
“What is being utilized here is a very robust regulatory tool to ensure safe construction and operation of a proposed facility,” he told reporters.
Houston has previously said he doesn’t know whether any new legislation is needed to regulate the data centre.
However, the statement from his office about the protest said the province would be open to legislative changes “should we find ourselves in a situation where we require them.”
Lawrence said Saturday her message to the premier is to listen to Nova Scotians.
“Nova Scotian’s are pretty vocal on the fact that we don’t want this,” she said. “On every side there’s people from all across the spectrum who are saying no to these data centres.”

stories.title: Daughter of Wwii veteran selling ‘door poppies’ to support local Legion
stories.summary: Margot Rockett’s father served in the Air Force in the Second World War. In the last few years of his life, Rockett said he lived at the Sunnybrook Veterans Centre.
stories.author: Rachel Morgan
stories.content:
As Remembrance Day approaches, Margot Rockett is working hard to keep up with the demand after her craftsmanship went viral on TikTok.

Rockett makes what she calls “door poppies”, large wreath-like poppies that can be hung on doors, walls and windows.

“It’s a bigger, bolder way to say I remember,” she told Global News.

Rockett’s father served in the Air Force in the Second World War. In the last few years of his life, Rockett said he lived at the Sunnybrook Veterans Centre.

“They took such good care of him and I really wanted to give back to the Poppy Fund and to the Legion,” she said.

During the pandemic, the “door poppy” was born.

“I just sort of tweaked a flower I made before and I made the door poppy,” Rockett said.

The $10 “door poppy” is officially licensed by the Legion.

“It’s a very rigid, strict policy because it is a trademarked image, and I respect that because they have to protect the poppy,” Rockett said.

All of the proceeds from the poppies go to Rockett’s Legion branch at Coxwell and Gerrard. She said all of the money stays in the community to support local veterans and their families.

That support is appreciated by those at the Legion.

“When Margot approached us a couple years ago, I thought it was pretty amazing and that all her proceeds were going to come to this branch specifically for our poppy campaign, it’s a huge income for us,” Shelley Lyons, vice-president at the Coxwell and Gerrard Legion, told Global News.

She said it’s been “disheartening” to see fewer people wearing poppies around Remembrance Day and hopes that Rockett’s initiative will encourage people to pay their respects.

She said as the First and Second World Wars fade further into history, a “lack of education and just memory knowledge” could be driving factors.

“It always makes me smile when I see someone wearing it,” she added.

For now, Rockett is working all hours to keep up with the demand, but she said she wouldn’t have it any other way.

“I think if my dad were here, he’d be really proud,” she said.

– With files from Global News’ Sean O’Shea

stories.title: ‘Extremely grateful’: Price, Bergeron headline 2026 Hockey Hall of Fame class
stories.summary: Carey Price spent a lot of his youth on the road and in the air. Growing up in a remote part of British Columbia, that’s what chasing his hockey dream required. When the phone rang in June to announce he would be joining the game’s greats, Price was fittingly in a familiar situation — driving. […]
stories.author: John Marchesan
stories.content:
By Joshua Clipperton, The Canadian Press

Posted November 7, 2026 5:34 pm.

Carey Price spent a lot of his youth on the road and in the air.

Growing up in a remote part of British Columbia, that’s what chasing his hockey dream required.

When the phone rang in June to announce he would be joining the game’s greats, Price was fittingly in a familiar situation — driving.

“I was on my way to go visit my grandmother at the hospital,” recalled the former Montreal Canadiens goaltender. “Hockey Hall of Fame came up with my caller ID in my truck, so pretty excited about that. Got to spend the rest of the day with my grandmother, who made a recovery.

“It was a blessed day.”

Price had plenty of those in the NHL and with Canada on the international stage. Now he will share another one Monday with the rest of the hall’s 2026 class.

The netminder headlines this year’s inductees alongside Patrice Bergeron, Pekka Rinne, Keith Tkachuk and Cindy Curley in the player category set to be enshrined Monday. Brian Burke will go in as a builder.

“A long road to get to this point,” Price, who starred in Montreal for all 15 of his NHL seasons and will enter the hall in his second year of eligibility, said Saturday. “I’m just extremely thankful for that journey and everything that I learned along the way — not only in hockey but in life.”

The No. 5 pick at the 2005 draft, Price won the Hart Trophy as league MVP and the Vezina Trophy as its top goaltender in 2015.

The 39-year-old from Anahim Lake, B.C., finished with a 361-261-79 record, .917 save percentage, 2.51 goals-against average and 49 shutouts across 712 regular-season games in a career that was, at times, hampered by injury.

Price had even better big-moment numbers before a knee issue forced him to stop playing beyond the 2021-22 campaign.

He owned a .919 save percentage, 2.39 GAA and eight shutouts in 92 playoff contests, with his final post-season act perhaps the most impressive — willing the underdog Canadiens on an improbable push to the 2021 Stanley Cup final.

Those gaudy numbers and achievements are a long way from the lonely roads and empty skies of his hockey-playing youth.

“A very large part of my childhood, spending time in planes and trucks and cars with my dad,” Price said. “He’d tell you that he wouldn’t have it any other way. But I’m grateful to him and the rest of my family for their support in getting here.”

A six-time Selke Trophy winner as the NHL’s top defensive forward after being selected 45th overall in 2003, Bergeron hoisted hockey’s holy grail with the Boston Bruins in 2011.

The 41-year-old former centre from L’Ancienne-Lorette, Que., registered 427 goals and 613 assists for 1,040 points in 1,294 regular-season games. He added 128 points (50 goals, 78 assists) in 170 playoff contests, including Boston’s run to the 2019 final, before retiring in 2023.

“A huge honour,” said Bergeron, who spent all 19 of his NHL campaigns with the Bruins and was in his first year of eligibility. “You look back at all the memories and the people that have helped you along the way.”

Price, who added the Ted Lindsay Award as the league’s most outstanding player voted on by the Nhlpa membership to his trophy case in 2015, and Bergeron also enjoyed success side-by-side sporting the red Maple Leaf.

The duo was on Canada’s juggernaut 2014 Olympic team that topped the field before capturing the World Cup of Hockey two years later.

“It was a lot more fun to be on his side with Team Canada,” Bergeron, who also claimed gold at the 2010 Games to go along with victories at the 2005 world junior hockey championship and the 2004 men’s worlds, said of Price. “A legendary career.”

Rinne, 43, owned a 369-213-75 record playing parts of 15 NHL seasons with the Nashville Predators. The 2018 Vezina-winning goaltender had a .917 save percentage and a 2.43 GAA in 683 regular-season games. He added a 45-44 playoff mark with a .914 save percentage, 2.49 GAA and five shutouts.

Tkachuk, whose NHL-playing sons Matthew and Brady will be in attendance Monday, registered 1,065 points (538 goals, 527 assists) in 1,201 contests in 18 NHL campaigns.

“They’ll probably be critiquing me when I’m up there speaking and making faces,” the 52-year-old Tkachuk joked of his sons before turning serious: “They’re great kids, they’re supportive, and I’m just glad they have the opportunity, with the schedule, to be here.”

A trailblazer in women’s hockey, Curley captained the U.S. to three silvers at the worlds in the 1990s.

“There’s just so many people that wouldn’t give up,” the 62-year-old said of her sport. “I just benefitted from their hard work. I’m truly grateful.”

Burke, 71, had a long career in NHL management that included stops with the Hartford Whalers, Vancouver Canucks, Anaheim Mighty Ducks, Toronto Maple Leafs, Calgary Flames and Pittsburgh Penguins following a stint at the league office.

“Still pinching myself,” said the Cup-winning GM with Anaheim in 2007. “Like a dream come true.”
