St-Pierre Plamondon was travelling to Toronto for personal and family reasons and took the opportunity to reach out to Ford for a meeting.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford speaks at the Grand Cru Culinary Wine Festival at Toronto's Enercare Centre on Oct. 29, 2026.

Catherine Lévesque

November 6, 2026 at 4:29 p.m.

Ottawa — While Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon would not travel to Ottawa or Montreal to hold a first in-person meeting with Prime Minister Mark Carney, he has agreed to meet with Ontario Premier Doug Ford in Toronto.

St-Pierre Plamondon and Ford were expected to meet at a luxurious Toronto hotel on Friday at 5 p.m. for a private meeting. There was initially speculation from Quebec officials about the premiers meeting at Queen’s Park, but that changed hours prior.

The Quebec premier’s spokesman, Alex Boissonneault, told Montreal radio station 98,5 FM that St-Pierre Plamondon was already travelling to Toronto for personal and family reasons this weekend and he took the opportunity to reach out to Ford for a meeting.

Both men had spoken on the phone after St-Pierre Plamondon’s victory last month.

Boissonneault said it was always the intention for both premiers to rapidly convene a meeting, since Quebec and Ontario have close economic ties. He also said it is fortunate that this encounter is happening the day after the federal budget.

The Quebec government has been grumbling about the lack of increase in federal health transfers and Ottawa’s unilateral decision to create a “productivity mega deduction” that would deprive Quebec of $1 billion per year.

St-Pierre Plamondon will probably hope to find an ally in Ford to push Ottawa for more funds, but Ford has generally been in agreement with many of Carney’s decisions.

There is no expectation of a photo opportunity or media availability after the meeting.

Ford had developed a close relationship with former Quebec premier François Legault during his tenure. They were photographed sipping beers — Ford’s was a non-alcoholic one — on the margins of an economic recovery summit in Toronto in 2020.

The photo had sparked controversy because Legault and Ford, even though they were outside, were not respecting the social distancing rules during the pandemic.

“Our mouths remained more than two meters apart,” justified Legault at the time.

Even though St-Pierre Plamondon and Ford will probably remain cordial in public, it remains unlikely that they will become as good friends since both are on opposite sides about whether Canada should remain a united country or Quebec should separate from it.

Back in January, Ford said “it would be a disaster for our countryif the separatists got elected,” referring to St-Pierre Plamondon’s Parti Québécois leading in the polls.

The PQ leader shot back, saying Ford was putting on a “bad show” and that it was “a bit of a caricature” for the premier of Ontario to suddenly tell Quebecers how to vote.

Ford changed his tune after St-Pierre Plamondon formed government in October.

Speaking to reporters after a meeting with Carney in Ottawa, Ford said he was looking forward to paying St-Pierre Plamondon a visit to discuss how Quebec and Ontario could grow their economies together.

“I love Quebecers,” he said. “There’s some connection there. I have come to the conclusion they’re passionate. They’re fighters. I’m passionate. I’m a fighter, and I just connect with them. So, we look forward to working with the premier.”

“What’s more important than anything to Quebecers and Ontarians is certainty and stability and jobs. And that’s what we’re going to work together on,” he added.

Things have not gone as smoothly with Carney, who will be meeting with St-Pierre Plamondon during the Francophonie Summit in Cambodia later in November.

Carney had offered for them to meet in the Ottawa-Gatineau area or in Montreal, but St-Pierre Plamondon insisted Carney travel to the capital of his province because of a provincial law that claims important meetings should take place in Quebec City.

Carney might pay a visit to the premier in Quebec City later this year.

Catherine Lévesque covers federal-Quebec relations for National Post. She joined the parliamentary bureau in Ottawa in 2022, after a decade spent in French media in Montreal, Quebec City and Ottawa.

St-Pierre Plamondon will probably hope to find an ally in Ford to push Ottawa for more funds, but Ford has generally been in agreement with many of Carney’s decisions.
There is no expectation of a photo opportunity or media availability after the meeting.

Ford had developed a close relationship with former Quebec premier François Legault during his tenure. They were photographed sipping beers — Ford’s was a non-alcoholic one — on the margins of an economic recovery summit in Toronto in 2020.
The photo had sparked controversy because Legault and Ford, even though they were outside, were not respecting the social distancing rules during the pandemic.
“Our mouths remained more than two meters apart,” justified Legault at the time.

Even though St-Pierre Plamondon and Ford will probably remain cordial in public, it remains unlikely that they will become as good friends since both are on opposite sides about whether Canada should remain a united country or Quebec should separate from it.
Back in January, Ford said “it would be a disaster for our countryif the separatists got elected,” referring to St-Pierre Plamondon’s Parti Québécois leading in the polls.
The PQ leader shot back, saying Ford was putting on a “bad show” and that it was “a bit of a caricature” for the premier of Ontario to suddenly tell Quebecers how to vote.
Ford changed his tune after St-Pierre Plamondon formed government in October.

Speaking to reporters after a meeting with Carney in Ottawa, Ford said he was looking forward to paying St-Pierre Plamondon a visit to discuss how Quebec and Ontario could grow their economies together.

“I love Quebecers,” he said. “There’s some connection there. I have come to the conclusion they’re passionate. They’re fighters. I’m passionate. I’m a fighter, and I just connect with them. So, we look forward to working with the premier.”
“What’s more important than anything to Quebecers and Ontarians is certainty and stability and jobs. And that’s what we’re going to work together on,” he added.
Things have not gone as smoothly with Carney, who will be meeting with St-Pierre Plamondon during the Francophonie Summit in Cambodia later in November.

Carney had offered for them to meet in the Ottawa-Gatineau area or in Montreal, but St-Pierre Plamondon insisted Carney travel to the capital of his province because of a provincial law that claims important meetings should take place in Quebec City.
Carney might pay a visit to the premier in Quebec City later this year.
Catherine Lévesque covers federal-Quebec relations for National Post. She joined the parliamentary bureau in Ottawa in 2022, after a decade spent in French media in Montreal, Quebec City and Ottawa.

stories.title: Carney says Canada welcomes ‘any moves’ to restore free trade after U.S. midterms
stories.summary: Ottawa — Prime Minister Mark Carney says his government welcomes "any moves" to restore free trade between Canada and the United States as officials south of the border push to end the trade war.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — Prime Minister Mark Carney says his government welcomes “any moves” to restore free trade between Canada and the United States as officials south of the border push to end the trade war.

In the days since the U.S. midterm elections gave the Democrats firm control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate, several party officials have indicated repealing President Donald Trump’s tariffs on Canadian products is a priority.

They include Sen. Ron Wyden, a Democrat from Oregon who is expected to chair the Senate finance committee when the new Congress is seated in January. The Wall Street Journal reported Thursday that Wyden was already talking to colleagues about legislation to combat Trump’s tariffs, including those on Canada.

Even if a bill is introduced, Trump retains the power to block it by issuing a veto. The president’s veto can only be overridden by a two-thirds vote in both chambers of Congress.

The Democrats likely will need more than 20 Republicans in the House, and 10 to 12 Republicans in the Senate, to vote with them to override a Trump veto. Some Republicans have said they know the tariffs are among the reasons their party lost.

“Tariffs have made everything too expensive,” longtime Texas Republican Sen. Ted Cruz said in his post-midterms statement.

Ahead of the elections, some Republican candidates also broke with Trump over his trade war with Canada, including failed Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers. Rogers loudly backed the tariffs in the summer but changed his tune in October.

Abdul El-Sayed, who defeated Rogers, has said ending what he called the “stupid tariffs on Canada” is among his priorities.

Speaking to reporters Friday, Carney said he hasn’t spoken with Democrats about plans to introduce legislation to end the tariffs.

He said a free-trade agreement is in the interests of both Canadians and Americans and his government will continue to work with Washington to get a deal that serves Canada.

“We welcome any moves to restore a free trading arrangement between Canada and the United States, which is in the interests of American families struggling with affordability. It’s in the interest of American workers looking for good, high-paying jobs and it’s fundamentally in the interest of Canadians,” said Carney.

Before the midterm results were known on Tuesday, Carney said more formal talks with the U.S. were restarting following a call with Trump. The prime minister indicated the Trump administration had softened its position and said the Americans were “asking less” and “offering more.”

Conservative MP Jamil Jivani, who has visited Washington in an attempt to move forward Canada-U.S. trade negotiations, said Ottawa still needs to find ways to work with Trump.

“I would love nothing more than for us to be able to get this done and move on because we got a lot of problems in our own country we need to solve,” said Jivani. “This whole U.S. thing has become a massive distraction from a lot of our own domestic issues.”

After trade talks between Canada and the U.S. collapsed in August, Trump slapped an array of Canadian goods with 50 per cent tariffs, banned imports of other Canadian products and signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America.

Ottawa responded with retaliatory tariffs on specific American imports.

Trump again escalated trade tensions the following month by banning imports of certain Canadian goods, including motorcycles and some liquor and whey products.

Last month, Trump lifted some tariffs on Canadian exports while adding tariffs to dozens of new products, including Canadian garbage and sewage.

A U.S. food importer also filed a legal challenge of Trump’s use of a Depression-era trade statute — Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 — to hit Canada with the heavy duties and trade embargoes.

Politicians on both sides of the border are looking at the midterm elections results as an opportunity to rebuild the Canada-U.S. relationship.

Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc said Wednesday the Liberal government’s push to diversify trade won’t change direction in the midterms’ wake. He also said recent talks with Trump’s administration have been productive and he looks forward to speaking more with his American counterparts in the coming days.

Trump said Friday that Stephen Miller would become White House chief of staff. Miller currently serves as White House deputy chief of staff for policy and oversees a broad portfolio, though he is best known for his role in Trump’s immigration policy.

After Carney met with Trump in Washington in May 2025, Miller told Fox News that it was like “watching a grandmaster in chess perform.”

“President Trump has opened up a completely new relationship with Canada because of his strength and because of his diplomacy,” he said.

Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand said Friday there is a need to address the sectoral tariffs that have been hitting Canadians “extremely hard,” including those on steel and aluminum.

Anand added that Canada has to “keep going with asserting Canadian interests.”

“We are standing for Canadian sovereignty, Canadian domestic economic resilience and our strategic autonomy,” she said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 6, 2026.

— With files from Kyle Duggan, Kelly Geraldine Malone and The Associated Press

Catherine Morrison, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Man convicted of murder in Toronto van attack drops appeal
stories.summary: Alek Minassian had filed notice of appeal in 2022 after he was sentenced to life in prison with no chance of parole for 25 years
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The man who carried out a deadly van attack in Toronto eight years ago is no longer challenging his more than two dozen convictions.

Ontario’s top court says Alek Minassian has abandoned the appeal of his convictions on 10 counts of first-degree murder and 16 of attempted murder.

Minassian had filed a notice of appeal in July 2022, about a month after he was sentenced to life in prison with no chance of parole for 25 years.

He was also sentenced to 20 years for 15 counts of attempted murder, to be served concurrently.

Eight women and two men died on April 23, 2018, when Minassian – enraged that women wouldn’t sleep with him and radicalized online – deliberately drove a rented van down a crowded sidewalk in his quest for infamy.

He admitted at trial that he planned and executed the attack, but argued that he should be found not criminally responsible due to his autism spectrum disorder.

Prosecutors, meanwhile, argued Minassian is a mass killer who knew right from wrong and happens to also have autism.

The presiding judge, Superior Court Justice Anne Molloy, rejected the defence’s argument that Minassian never developed empathy as a result of his autism and was unable to make rational decisions.

The 10 people killed in the rampage were Ji Hun Kim, 22; So He Chung, 22; Anne Marie D’Amico, 30; Andrea Bradden, 33; Chul Min “Eddie” Kang, 45; Renuka Amarasingha, 45; Dorothy Sewell, 80; Geraldine Brady, 83; Munir Najjar, 85; and Mary Elizabeth “Betty” Forsyth, 94.

Another victim, Amaresh Tesfamariam, died in 2021 from injuries sustained in the attack.

stories.title: Baby Brezza bottle sterilizer is being recalled in Canada and the U.S.
stories.summary: The Health Canada recall was issued alongside the company, Baby Brezza Enterprises LLC, and the United States Consumer Product Safety Commission.
stories.author: Rachel Morgan
stories.content:
Health Canada has issued a recall for a Baby Brezza bottle dryer and sterilizer due to a fire and burn hazard.

The recall was issued alongside the company, Baby Brezza Enterprises LLC, and the United States Consumer Product Safety Commission.

The Baby Brezza SuperFast Sterilizer Dryer dries and sterilizes baby bottles and their parts and accessories.

Health Canada said model number BRZ0083 is impacted by the recall.

“The product can overheat when plugged in and in use, posing fire and burn hazards,” Health Canada said in an alert on its website.

The company reported that 6,001 units of the affected products were sold in Canada and 29,000 were sold in the U.S. between September 2023 and November 2026.

As of Oct. 29, the company has received 20 reports of the product overheating and melting in Canada and 32 reports of incidents in the U.S. No injuries have been reported.

Health Canada said consumers should stop using the recalled product immediately and can contact EI Brand Management Inc. for instructions on how to receive a free replacement.

stories.title: Fanshawe students, staff wear poppies to honour veterans
stories.summary: The week before Rembrance Day, Fanshawe College staff and students were alrady donning poppies to show respect...
stories.author: Ben McFadden
stories.content:
The week before Rembrance Day, Fanshawe College staff and students were alrady donning poppies to show respect for those who “fought for the luxuries we have today.”

The Royal Canadian Legion’s annual poppy campaign started Oct. 24, and appeared to be in full swing on campus Friday. XFM News asked wearers what it meant to them.

Daniel Thuss, second year journalism student. (Benjamin McFadden/XFM News)

As cadet corps and volunteers spanned out across the city, numerous shops on campus had donation boxes as part of this year’s campaign. In addition, the Legion, which is celebrating its 100th-anniversary, created an interactive history page on its website.

“I think wearing a poppy represents a part of our nation’s history… it’s important to recognize those who fought for the luxuries we have today,” said student Callum Contursi.

The London-area has a rich military history. Many residents are veterans or family members of veterans.

“My great-grandparents met during World War II. If it was not for them, I wouldn’t be here right now, said student Daniel Thuss.

Poppy donations go toward services and supports for Canadian vets.

The Legion encourages those who are wearing poppies, to show respect by placing the pins over their hearts. The organization asks that people disposed of damaged poppies in a respectful way.

London Remembrance Day ceremonies will take place at the Cenotaph in Victoria Park on November 11, from 10:30 to 11:30, following a parade that will begin in front of the London Delta Armouries at 10 a.m., and end at the Cenotraph. The parade route is as follows:

10 a.m.- Assembly at London Delta Armouries.

10:30 a.m. – Parade marches east on Dundas St., up Waterloo and back down Dufferin towards the Cenoptah.

The new funding for Csis represents a whopping 60 per cent boost on average of the agency's annual spend.

Canadian Security Intelligence Service director Daniel Rogers (left) and Minister of Public Safety Gary Anandasangaree chat before the committee meeting on Foreign Election Interference at the West Block on Parliament Hill in Ottawa. (Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia)

November 6, 2026 at 3:56 p.m.

Ottawa — The federal government wants to grant Csis broader powers to collect more intelligence abroad and is open to eventually creating a Canadian human foreign intelligence agency, according to a senior intelligence official.

On Friday, top Privy Council office intelligence official Dominic Rochon provided more detail about the government’s plan to beef up the Canadian Security Intelligence Service (Csis) the day after it announced a $6 billion investment in the agency.

Speaking at the annual Canadian Association for Security and Intelligence Studies symposium, Rochon said Canada needs to better protect its economic security against foreign threats and shocks.

That will require a broadening of the spy agency’s powers in Canada and abroad, he said.

“From an economic security perspective, there is going to need to be some support from intelligence agencies such as Csis,” Rochon told attendees. He noted that the agency is currently “constrained” in what it can collect legally under the Csis Act.

“There will be legislative change that is going to be needed in order to be able to provide (Csis) with an extra five, 10 per cent of what their collection can be,” he added.

Though Csis already has some foreign operations, many of its powers in the Csis Act are limited to intelligence collection and addressing threats “within Canada.”

His comments come on the heels of an unexpected government commitment in Thursday’s federal budget of a massive, $6-billion influx of cash for Csis over the next 10 years.

Csis’s budget this fiscal year is roughly $1 billion, meaning the new funding represents a whopping 60 per cent boost on average of the agency’s annual spend.

With the budget investment, Prime Minister Mark Carney delivered a clear message to Canada’s spy agency: be prepared to grow and do a lot more, fast.

The major investment has intensified speculation about the government’s desire to boost Canada’s spy network abroad amid growing fears of the U.S. becoming an unreliable intelligence partner.

The foreign human intelligence mandate could be given to Csis (whose current powers are largely focused on domestic national security) or developed into a standalone agency akin to the US’s CIA or the UK’s MI6.

During his panel discussion on Friday, Rochon left the door open to the creation of a Canadian foreign human intelligence agency, noting that all options “are on the table” for Carney.

But, he argued, it would be “imprudent” to suddenly try to create a foreign human intelligence agency from scratch. Rather, Thursday’s funding boost for Csis is a signal of the government’s intention to build up that capacity gradually.

“I think what makes more sense is to give Csis incremental authorities and start developing that because it requires specific training,” he said.

“Instead of starting from zero, I think you evolve… you adjust legislation in a certain way, you can plan for potentially making those types of machinery changes somewhere down the road.”

But much of the money promised to Csis over the next decade will go to fix longstanding staffing, infrastructure and technological deficits.

Csis is expected to use the funds to build new regional offices across Canada, staff up faster and invest significantly in its classified IT systems. The agency could also open up more foreign offices, longtime national security researcher Wesley Wark speculated Thursday.

In a recent interview with National Post, Csis Director Dan Rogers said the spy agency is “strained”.

“We have an organization that is extremely overtaxed in an extraordinarily complex environment, and people do hard work in stressful environments every day,” he said.

He explained that the agency was still dealing with the repercussions of years of under-resourcing that hampered its ability to hire staff and maintain its IT and physical infrastructure.

“So this year we have (hiring) targets. Next year, we have more ambitious targets because we know that this year we’re going to take a bit of time to build the capacity because we hadn’t been doing it for a while. I expect that that trajectory gets better,” Rogers explained.

In recent months, various members of Carney’s government have expressed an interest in allowing Csis to do more intelligence collection abroad.

In a series of interviews with National Post in the spring, Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree said he supports the creation of a Canadian foreign spy capacity to lessen the country’s dependence on the U.S. for its intelligence.

“We are at a point where… our trusted friends are not the same level of trust and collaboration, or threats of non collaboration, that we need to be mindful of,” he told National Post in May.

Christopher Nardi is a senior parliamentary reporter with National Post in Ottawa. He has worked in both French and English media, speaks Italian and writes about politics, national security, justice and how things work (or don't) in government.

stories.title: Hamilton cadet leader injured in vicious attack ‘determined to walk’ after emergency spinal surgery
stories.summary: Capt. Ken Kunkel's daughter wrote on Facebook earlier this week: 'My dad is such a trooper'
stories.author: Stewart Lewis
stories.content:
Welcome to our new, improved site!

Read a note from our editor-in-chief

Ken Kunkel (centre), commanding officer of the 826 Griffin Squadron Royal Canadian Air Cadets, was badly injured in an assault in Hamilton on Nov. 1. Kunkel with his family, from left to right Son Christopher, wife Shelly, Ken, daughter Kimberly, son in law Tylor. (Source: GoFundMe)

November 6, 2026 at 3:56 p.m.

A Canadian Armed Forces member gravely assaulted during a poppy selling campaign is “determined to walk” after injuries from the attack has left him immobile for the unforeseeable future.

Capt. Ken Kunkel, an air cadet commander in Hamilton, Ont., was supporting two air cadets selling poppies on Sunday in advance of Remembrance Day, when according to Hamilton Police, the 59-year-old was attacked by a 12-year-old male youth and a 48-year-old female, who were arrested later that day.

The resulting “life-altering injuries” cited by police, required immediate spinal surgery.

“Ken is strong-willed, and he’s determined to walk. If community support was enough he’d be flying at the point!” Selina Peters, a friend of the family who set up a GoFundMe page, told National Post on Friday.

The public outrage over the vicious attack has resulted in more than $206,000 in donations and counting as of Friday afternoon.

Peters told National Post that “the family has been absolutely overwhelmed and incredibly humbled by the generosity and support shown by the community. They never imagined the fundraiser would reach this level, and they are deeply grateful to everyone who has donated, shared the campaign or reached out with words of encouragement.”

Ken Kunkel, commanding officer of the 826 Griffin Squadron Royal Canadian Air Cadets, was badly injured in an assault in Hamilton on Nov. 1. (Photo credit: GoFundMe) eyJpdiI6IktwQXNoK2k0WWhQVVV6d08x

Kunkel, a Commanding Officer of 826 Griffin Squadron Royal Canadian Air Cadets, is a husband, father of two, grandfather and a dedicated community volunteer.

Kunkel’s daughter, Kimberly Deitrich, wrote on her Facebook page earlier this week that the family’s lives “have been turned upside down” and as they “navigate through this difficult and uncertain time, we continue to wait and take his recovery each a day at a time … My dad is such a trooper, and we are so proud of his strength through all of this. We love you so much, Dad.”

Peters said the fundraising goal has been increased to $250,000, with the idea of anticipating the family’s needs and helping to “provide some financial security as the family navigates the months and potentially years ahead.

“As they begin to navigate the road ahead, it’s becoming clear that there will be significant accessibility and recovery-related expenses,” said Peters. “This May include an accessible vehicle, which can cost upwards of $150,000, along with wheelchair equipment, potential home modifications and other unforeseen expenses.”

Kimberly Deitrich, is Ken Kunkel’s daughter, has posted photos of Hamilton General Hospital and spinal unit where Kunkel is being treated. (Photo credit: Kimberly Deitrich/Facebook)

“The family wants everyone to know how deeply grateful they are. They never expected this level of generosity, and the kindness shown by this community has meant more than words can express,” Peters said.

In another post on her Facebook page, Dietrich thanked Hamilton East-Stoney Creek MP, Nate Kurac, for speaking about the attack in the House of Commons, adding that honouring veterans is important.

“Having my dad’s situation brought to the attention of the House of Commons is truly meaningful, and we cannot express how much we appreciate the recognition and the words that were shared,” Deitrich wrote. “What makes this situation particularly heartbreaking is that these young cadets were simply volunteering their time to support the Poppy Campaign, giving back to their community and helping honour those who served and sacrificed for our country. The importance of respecting the poppy and recognizing what it represents is a message that deserves to be heard.”

According to police, the attack on Kunkel began midday Sunday when two youths approached the young Air Cadets in front of a restaurant and blew an air horn into their ears.

Kunkel followed the youth suspects into the restaurant to speak to them about what they did, say police. But a struggle followed, with the adult female, who was not initially involved in the altercation. She assaulted Kunkel, causing him to fall to the ground. Then one of the male youths struck him several times before leaving the restaurant.

Police later arrested the youth and adult female suspects, charging them with causing Kunkel’s injuries.

The Youth Criminal Justice Act ensures that the identity of the youth cannot be published. National Post has reached out to the police service to confirm the identify of the woman.

Canadians 'disgusted' over vicious attack on Armed Forces member selling poppies with cadets

Donations continue for Wainwright victims as some recovering soldiers moved closer to home

Stewart Lewis is a writer and editor with National Post. A journalist and lawyer, he has worked in newspapers, radio and TV, and served a legal stint with Global Affairs Canada at the United Nations in New York City.

stories.title: Driver who helped B.C. bus crash victims credits firefighter training
stories.summary: Mackenzie - A Mackenzie, B.C., resident who was the first to respond to a crash that injured 20 people after a shuttle bus ran off the highway says he is grateful he was in the wrong place at the right time.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A man from Mackenzie, B.C., who was the first to respond to a crash that injured 20 people when a shuttle bus careened off the highway said he is grateful he was in the wrong place at the right time.

Rich Rogers was driving along Highway 39 with his wife and 11-year-old son on Wednesday, when they saw the bus flip on its side and veer off the route about four kilometres south of Mackenzie.

The bus struck a tree and fell into a ditch as Rogers and his family looked on.

Rich Rogers helped 20 injured passengers after he witnessed a shuttle bus crash on Highway 39 near Mackenzie, B.C., ON Nov. 4, 2026. (Nov. 6, 2026)

“My boy just started screaming ‘no, no, no’ over and over,” Rogers said in an interview on Friday.

The former firefighter, who works as a driver transporting mine workers, said his emergency training kicked in as he rushed to assess and triage the injured, while his wife called emergency services.

Rogers said he found one person who had been ejected from the bus and did not appear to be breathing, while three others were unconscious aboard the vehicle.

The bus was chartered by a contractor for a data centre company.

After turning off the still-running vehicle and identifying four passengers who needed critical care, Rogers said he encountered the driver, who was pacing back and forth and seemed to be in shock.

Police and emergency health services arrived and Rogers helped a paramedic treat the ejected passenger. He then stayed to help clean up debris from the road, later catching a ride back into town with the local fire department.

Rogers said he’d left his job as a firefighter in Prince George due to mental stress and moved to Mackenzie in September.

He said the crash had brought up tough emotions from his earlier work, but he was thankful for the training he’d received, because it allowed him to help give the injured patients a chance at recovery.

“I went through a lot of emotional stress that I feel that I didn’t get the support or help that I deserved,” he said of his previous job.

“I’m very thankful that my wife recognized it in me before I did that I was struggling, and we’re definitely going to have to watch for those types of emotions and feelings creeping in again.”

Returning to his job as a driver after the crash, Rogers said he reminded his passengers about the importance of seatbelts and asked that they wear them in his vehicle, which is very similar to the one involved in Wednesday’s crash.

Rogers said he does not think of himself as a hero and instead praised the efforts of first responders who helped control the chaos at the scene.

“I just think of myself as wrong place, right time, right skills,” he said.

“If it was me or my family in that position I hope somebody else that had skills would do anything they could to help us, which is basically all I could do,” he said.

Northern Health issued an update on Thursday saying 15 of the 20 people assessed and treated in its facilities after the crash had been discharged.

The crash, which happened in a remote part of northern B.C. about 1,000 kilometres north of Vancouver, had triggered Code Orange mass-casualty declarations at two hospitals.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 6, 2026.

stories.title: These are all the key tax changes and credits impacting you from the budget
stories.summary: Budget 2026 includes a large swath of tax changes, threshold and credit updates aimed at reducing the 'time tax' Canadians pay every year to file their returns.
stories.author: Ariel Rabinovitch
stories.content:
Budget 2026 includes a large swath of tax changes, threshold and credit updates aimed at reducing the “time tax” Canadians pay every year to file their returns at tax season by making some elements simpler.

From new receipt-free flat rate tax deductions to a tax installment threshold increase and a top-up to the Grocery and Essentials Benefit, Ottawa says these measures will “reduce the time and effort Canadians are required to spend managing their tax affairs.”

“Budget 2026 proposes practical changes to simplify deadlines, filings, and interactions with the CRA, ultimately reducing the time tax on Canadians,” the budget says.

Here’s a look at some of the key tax changes that could impact Canadians.

May 15 is now the deadline for both Canadians and self-employed workers to file their tax returns and pay all taxes owed to the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA).

By consolidating all previous tax deadlines into one, the federal government says tax filing will be simpler and afford most Canadians a few extra weeks to get their information in and taxes paid.

The previous deadline was April 30 for most Canadian filers to both submit their returns and pay the taxes owed, while self-employed individuals had until June 15. For self-employed filers, even though the deadline was later, they would still have to pay the taxes they owe to the CRA by April 30.

“The date change is expected to save the number of taxpayers potential interest and penalties from late filing,” says Rob Jeffrey, national tax policy leader and a partner with Deloitte.

“It will remain to be seen if those that file late will continue to file late with the extended deadline.”

By allowing for two more weeks to file and pay taxes, the federal government says changing the date is expected to save Canadians $230 million in interest and penalty payments over five years, starting in the upcoming tax year.

Jeffrey continued: “The other thing that I think the extra two weeks will do is that when individuals are preparing and filing their personal tax returns, they’re relying on information from a number of different sources.”

“Having an extra two weeks should allow more of those slips to automatically come through and hopefully reduce the amount of back and forth or potential disputes after the fact.”

The budget also extends the timeframe for Canadians to file a notice of objection with the CRA from 90 days to one year.

Canadians can file a notice of objection with the CRA if they disagree with how it applied tax laws, calculated income or deductions, or assessed penalties and interest.

Sometimes, Canadians would have been able to request an extension to file an objection to the CRA for up to a year, but by extending the timeframe to file an objection to a year, the budget says Canadians can remove the need to request those extensions. This, Ottawa says, not only simplifies the process for Canadian tax payers, but also for the CRA by not having to review and approve extension requests.

The budget says Canadians will have the option to claim preset tax deduction amounts for certain expenses rather than having to provide receipts and other documents to verify specific amounts.

This means Canadians won’t have to keep track of receipts throughout the year and itemize their expenses when it comes time to submit their taxes, which the budget says will reduce the burden of complying with a tax system that “can discourage Canadians from claiming the deductions and credits they are eligible for.”

Tax deductions reduce the total amount of income subject to taxes by the CRA, and Canadians still have the option to submit expenses using an itemized list and receipts if they choose.

One of those preset deductions is if someone has to relocate for a job or spends money on travelling for work. Eligible Canadians can either continue to submit individual receipts and itemize each expense to the CRA, or they can claim a flat amount of $1,000, and those in the trades can claim $1,500 through the Labour Mobility Deduction for Tradespeople.

There are also preset deductions for the Home Accessibility Tax Credit of $1,000 for qualifying renovations.

Eligible parents adopting children can also claim a flat-rate deduction of $1,200 per child.

Other preset deductions include the Medical Expense Tax Credit of $2,000 for service dog care and maintenance, and an optional flat $500 for incontinence products required for medical purposes.

Individuals with celiac disease would also be allowed to claim an optional flat $1,000 for some gluten-free food expenses.

Eligible clergy members can claim a flat deduction of $1,000 for some housing expenses as well without the need to track and document these expenses

For Canadians and businesses that pay their taxes in regular quarterly instalments to the CRA, Budget 2026 is proposing changes to take effect in 2028 that will allow for fewer payments in a year by increasing the individual payment thresholds.

This, the government says, will mean spending less time on complex paperwork, and being able to pay off taxes earlier can even give the opportunity for improved cash flow that can be invested in Canadians’ businesses and daily lives.

Ottawa says it will look to increase instalment thresholds from $3,000 to $7,500 and index them to inflation.

This means, if someone owes $12,000 a year in taxes and normally pays the CRA with quarterly instalments of $3,000 each, they could instead pay all of that owed tax in two installments instead of across four.

Self-employed business owners would be able to make a single payment of two-thirds of their net tax owing by the end of the calendar year if these proposed changes go into effect in 2028, the budget says.

Seniors would also benefit from these changes because income generated from Old Age Security, Canada Pension Plan and a Registered Retirement Income Fund are not subject to tax withholding like most employment income. Most seniors receiving this income have to withhold their own tax and pay to the CRA via instalments, which are currently under the $3,000 threshold.

By increasing the threshold to $7,500 each, more seniors could pay off their taxes in fewer or one instalments, and reduce complex paperwork.

Canadians who file their taxes with the CRA, and have incomes that qualify them for the Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit (Cgeb) will also be getting a 50 per cent top up.

Budget 2026 says the top up will be delivered to eligible Canadians by early 2027, although benefit dates have not yet been released.

The top up is equivalent to 50 per cent of the total annual benefit qualifying Canadians are entitled to receive, which is calculated based on the most recent tax year.

There are also a handful of tax measures introduced in Budget 2026 designed to empower small businesses and self-employed business owners and entrepreneurs.

This comes as many have been struggling with U.S. tariffs weighing on sales, while higher fuel costs have reduced already razor-thin profit margins.

One of the measures is the Productivity Mega Deduction, which allows businesses of all sizes to permanently deduct the full cost of eligible capital assets in the first year they are purchased rather than over the life of the asset. This can include equipment like a new coffee machine for a cafe, a fleet of vehicles for a plumbing company or new software for a tech startup.

By deducting the full cost in the first year, it sharply lowers taxable income much sooner, which can free up cash to pay workers, make repairs, or reinvest in other ways.

Budget 2026 also includes the Canada Growth Incentive, which helps Canadian business founders attract investment and grow by offering a tax exemption on up to $15 million in capital gains, which happens when someone sells an investment and makes a profit that is subject to tax.

This can also help successful entrepreneurs to keep growing their business because they can rollover the profit made from selling their previous business if they reinvest it into their next Canadian success story.

This means Canadians won’t have to keep track of receipts throughout the year and itemize their expenses when it comes time to submit their taxes, which the budget says will reduce the burden of complying with a tax system that “can discourage Canadians from claiming the deductions and credits they are eligible for.”
Tax deductions reduce the total amount of income subject to taxes by the CRA, and Canadians still have the option to submit expenses using an itemized list and receipts if they choose.

One of those preset deductions is if someone has to relocate for a job or spends money on travelling for work. Eligible Canadians can either continue to submit individual receipts and itemize each expense to the CRA, or they can claim a flat amount of $1,000, and those in the trades can claim $1,500 through the Labour Mobility Deduction for Tradespeople.
There are also preset deductions for the Home Accessibility Tax Credit of $1,000 for qualifying renovations.
Eligible parents adopting children can also claim a flat-rate deduction of $1,200 per child.
Other preset deductions include the Medical Expense Tax Credit of $2,000 for service dog care and maintenance, and an optional flat $500 for incontinence products required for medical purposes.
Individuals with celiac disease would also be allowed to claim an optional flat $1,000 for some gluten-free food expenses.
Eligible clergy members can claim a flat deduction of $1,000 for some housing expenses as well without the need to track and document these expenses

For Canadians and businesses that pay their taxes in regular quarterly instalments to the CRA, Budget 2026 is proposing changes to take effect in 2028 that will allow for fewer payments in a year by increasing the individual payment thresholds.

This, the government says, will mean spending less time on complex paperwork, and being able to pay off taxes earlier can even give the opportunity for improved cash flow that can be invested in Canadians’ businesses and daily lives.
Ottawa says it will look to increase instalment thresholds from $3,000 to $7,500 and index them to inflation.

This means, if someone owes $12,000 a year in taxes and normally pays the CRA with quarterly instalments of $3,000 each, they could instead pay all of that owed tax in two installments instead of across four.

Self-employed business owners would be able to make a single payment of two-thirds of their net tax owing by the end of the calendar year if these proposed changes go into effect in 2028, the budget says.

By increasing the threshold to $7,500 each, more seniors could pay off their taxes in fewer or one instalments, and reduce complex paperwork.

Budget 2026 says the top up will be delivered to eligible Canadians by early 2027, although benefit dates have not yet been released.
The top up is equivalent to 50 per cent of the total annual benefit qualifying Canadians are entitled to receive, which is calculated based on the most recent tax year.
There are also a handful of tax measures introduced in Budget 2026 designed to empower small businesses and self-employed business owners and entrepreneurs.
This comes as many have been struggling with U.S. tariffs weighing on sales, while higher fuel costs have reduced already razor-thin profit margins.

One of the measures is the Productivity Mega Deduction, which allows businesses of all sizes to permanently deduct the full cost of eligible capital assets in the first year they are purchased rather than over the life of the asset. This can include equipment like a new coffee machine for a cafe, a fleet of vehicles for a plumbing company or new software for a tech startup.
By deducting the full cost in the first year, it sharply lowers taxable income much sooner, which can free up cash to pay workers, make repairs, or reinvest in other ways.

Budget 2026 also includes the Canada Growth Incentive, which helps Canadian business founders attract investment and grow by offering a tax exemption on up to $15 million in capital gains, which happens when someone sells an investment and makes a profit that is subject to tax.

This can also help successful entrepreneurs to keep growing their business because they can rollover the profit made from selling their previous business if they reinvest it into their next Canadian success story.

content_blocks.text: From new receipt-free flat rate tax deductions to a tax installment threshold increase and a top-up to the Grocery and Essentials Benefit, Ottawa says these measures will “reduce the time and effort Canadians are required to spend managing their tax affairs.”
“Budget 2026 proposes practical changes to simplify deadlines, filings, and interactions with the CRA, ultimately reducing the time tax on Canadians,” the budget says.
Here’s a look at some of the key tax changes that could impact Canadians.

content_blocks.text: Tax filing deadline change
May 15 is now the deadline for both Canadians and self-employed workers to file their tax returns and pay all taxes owed to the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA).
By consolidating all previous tax deadlines into one, the federal government says tax filing will be simpler and afford most Canadians a few extra weeks to get their information in and taxes paid.

The previous deadline was April 30 for most Canadian filers to both submit their returns and pay the taxes owed, while self-employed individuals had until June 15. For self-employed filers, even though the deadline was later, they would still have to pay the taxes they owe to the CRA by April 30.
“The date change is expected to save the number of taxpayers potential interest and penalties from late filing,” says Rob Jeffrey, national tax policy leader and a partner with Deloitte.
content_blocks.html: “The date change is expected to save the number of taxpayers potential interest and penalties from late filing,” says Rob Jeffrey, national tax policy leader and a partner with Deloitte.

content_blocks.text: “It will remain to be seen if those that file late will continue to file late with the extended deadline.”

By allowing for two more weeks to file and pay taxes, the federal government says changing the date is expected to save Canadians $230 million in interest and penalty payments over five years, starting in the upcoming tax year.

Jeffrey continued: “The other thing that I think the extra two weeks will do is that when individuals are preparing and filing their personal tax returns, they’re relying on information from a number of different sources.”
“Having an extra two weeks should allow more of those slips to automatically come through and hopefully reduce the amount of back and forth or potential disputes after the fact.”

The budget also extends the timeframe for Canadians to file a notice of objection with the CRA from 90 days to one year.
Canadians can file a notice of objection with the CRA if they disagree with how it applied tax laws, calculated income or deductions, or assessed penalties and interest.

Sometimes, Canadians would have been able to request an extension to file an objection to the CRA for up to a year, but by extending the timeframe to file an objection to a year, the budget says Canadians can remove the need to request those extensions. This, Ottawa says, not only simplifies the process for Canadian tax payers, but also for the CRA by not having to review and approve extension requests.

stories.title: Police officers 'must have the public’s trust,' says Quebec security minister
stories.summary: Montreal - Quebec’s newly minted internal security minister touted the importance of public trust as he waded into a scandal that has rocked Montreal police.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
MONTREAL - Quebec’s newly minted internal security minister touted the importance of public trust as he waded into a scandal that has rocked Montreal police.

Nov. 6, 2026

Copied to clipboard

JQB[](https://www.thestar.com/news/canada/quebec/police-officers-must-have-the-public-s-trust-says-quebec-security-minister/article_8d3d5a24-b13d-5537-9b0f-a0b2942eaa38.html)

By The Canadian Press

Guy Jr. Lapointe made the comments after reporters asked him whether he trusted Montreal’s police chief, Fady Dagher.

Lapointe says the public’s trust is what matters.

The minister was in Montreal to meet with the director of the provincial police, Johanne Beausoleil.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Smart glasses are showing up in Toronto nightclubs. Not everyone’s ok with it

Dagher announced Monday that seven Montreal officers have been fired following allegations of discriminatory and racist misconduct that have dogged the service in recent months.

Civil society groups have criticized Dagher and the police force for not moving fast enough to dismantle a patrol unit in a multicultural Montreal neighbourhood after starting an internal investigation into criminal allegations last March.

Dagher held a late Friday evening news conference in mid-June to announce that he was dismantling the 16-member patrol unit in the Montréal-Nord neighbourhood of the city.

One officer at the station is also facing allegations of obstruction of justice after an incident in which evidence from a domestic violence complainant was allegedly destroyed. Other officers from a downtown Montreal station have been under investigation over misconduct allegations related to interactions with unhoused people.

Dagher has said public prosecutors are reviewing evidence to determine whether to press charges against officers on the force.

Lapointe said the allegations against Montreal police officers are extremely troubling and unacceptable.

“This is not the kind of behaviour that can be tolerated under any circumstances by police officers, who must have the public’s trust,” said Lapointe. “The premier has given me a very clear mandate: to work on the public’s sense of security.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 6, 2026.

— With files from Samira Ait Kaci Ali

The Canadian Press

stories.title: CN freight train collides with tractor trailer towing flatbed near Brighton, Ont.
stories.summary: A collision involving a CN freight train has shut down a section of road in Brighton, Ont. near the city of Quinte West.
stories.author: Rebecca Lau
stories.content:
An collision involving a CN freight train has shut down a section of road near Brighton, Ont.

OPP confirmed officers were called shortly before noon Friday to a collision near the intersection of Stoney Point Road and Lawson Settlement Road.

Quinte West Fire Chief John Whelan told Global News that a tractor trailer towing a low flatbed became stuck on the tracks as it was driving over the crossing.

According to Whelan, the driver was able to jump out of the vehicle and tried to use the emergency phone at the crossing to alert CN. However, an oncoming train came down the tracks and hit the flatbed trailer.

The fire department says the train was significantly damaged.

OPP has taken over the scene, and traffic has been shut down in the area.

There were no injuries reported.

stories.title: ‘Manifesting millions’ pays off for winners of record $90M Lotto Max jackpot
stories.summary: A group of four friends were "manifesting millions" in a group chat when they decided to buy a lottery ticket. That manifestation came to fruition when they won $90 million.
stories.author: Tavi Dhillon
stories.content:
A group of four friends from Calgary claimed the historic $90 million Lotto Max jackpot after deciding to buy the ticket in a text message group chat called “Manifesting Millions.”

Last month’s draw was the largest lottery prize awarded in Canadian history . It was won by Eidelson Elchico, Hazeline Ong, Velna Ramirez and Lovelyn Malvar.

Elchico said he found out around 3 a.m. the day after the late-October draw, when he awoke and sat up.

“(I was) planning to go downstairs to get some water,” the father of two said. “I grabbed my phone and was just scrolling down my email and I saw the winning (notification).”

He and his friends bought the ticket on Play Alberta, which notifies winners electronically.

“I actually did not count the numbers because it’s hard to count, for me, at 3 a.m. So, I thought it was only $9,000 (or) $900, but I woke up my wife and double-checked, and she told me to open the website,” Elchico said at a news conference with all four winners.

“It was true: $90 million was on hold, and we needed to call our friends. So, at 3 a.m., they didn’t wake up easily, obviously, but suddenly they started to wake up. One by one. And nobody could believe it, even me.”

The group has known each other for more than five years after meeting through their families, Malvar said.

She told reporters they decided to make the purchase at the beginning of October in a group chat called “Manifesting Millions” that was created when they heard the prize value, which was climbing after several unclaimed jackpots.

“It’s pretty overwhelming. It’s nerve-wracking. It took a week for (it) to actually sink in,” Malvar said. “You just feel shocked. It’s not something you would expect. Not in a million years.”

“When I saw the email I (was) like ‘we definitely got scammed.'”

Divided equally four ways, the $90 million will amount to $22.5 million per person.

None of the winners know how they will spend the money on themselves outside of using it to support their families. The group noted that they will donate part of their $90 million winnings to benefit the community.

Elchico said he feels a calling to use the money to do good.

“There’s a lot of people that need help. So, for me, this is the way,” he said.

All four of the winners are still working, they said, explaining that they need the distraction while the news, and sudden influx of cash, settles. Outside of their respective spouses, the group said nobody in their lives knew they are now millionaires.

They acknowledged that this fact May change after Friday’s announcement.

content_blocks.text: “(I was) planning to go downstairs to get some water,” the father of two said. “I grabbed my phone and was just scrolling down my email and I saw the winning (notification).”
He and his friends bought the ticket on Play Alberta, which notifies winners electronically.

“I actually did not count the numbers because it’s hard to count, for me, at 3 a.m. So, I thought it was only $9,000 (or) $900, but I woke up my wife and double-checked, and she told me to open the website,” Elchico said at a news conference with all four winners.

“It was true: $90 million was on hold, and we needed to call our friends. So, at 3 a.m., they didn’t wake up easily, obviously, but suddenly they started to wake up. One by one. And nobody could believe it, even me.”
The group has known each other for more than five years after meeting through their families, Malvar said.

She told reporters they decided to make the purchase at the beginning of October in a group chat called “Manifesting Millions” that was created when they heard the prize value, which was climbing after several unclaimed jackpots.
“It’s pretty overwhelming. It’s nerve-wracking. It took a week for (it) to actually sink in,” Malvar said. “You just feel shocked. It’s not something you would expect. Not in a million years.”
“When I saw the email I (was) like ‘we definitely got scammed.'”

content_blocks.text: Divided equally four ways, the $90 million will amount to $22.5 million per person.

None of the winners know how they will spend the money on themselves outside of using it to support their families. The group noted that they will donate part of their $90 million winnings to benefit the community.
Elchico said he feels a calling to use the money to do good.
“There’s a lot of people that need help. So, for me, this is the way,” he said.

All four of the winners are still working, they said, explaining that they need the distraction while the news, and sudden influx of cash, settles. Outside of their respective spouses, the group said nobody in their lives knew they are now millionaires.

stories.title: Doerkson's a fan of Carney's budget, but it might not work as a template for B.C.
stories.summary: Victoria - British Columbia's premier-designate Lorne Doerkson is a fan of this week's federal budget, but an economist says he'll have trouble emulating it.
stories.author: Wolfgang Depner The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Victoria - British Columbia premier-designate Lorne Doerkson is a fan of this week’s federal budget, but two economists caution that it May not be easily emulated provincially.

Marc Lee, senior economist with the Canadian Centre for Policy Alternatives, said the province is facing greater urgency than Liberal Prime Minister Mark Carney to deal with deficit problems.

Even though the federal and provincial deficit-to-GDP ratios are about the same, Lee said B.C. “can’t continue to run large deficits” year after year.

Lee said Ottawa has “a lot more room, the license to do things, partly because it is the federal government.”

The province has less room to reduce spending, he said, since it has primary responsibility for health, education and other social services, and residents would notice cuts.

Doerkson, whose Conservatives toppled the NDP government in the provincial election last month, praised Thursday’s federal budget as “encouraging and ambitious,” with a focus on resource industries and growth-oriented tax measures.

The premier-designate has said his government’s budget would likewise be “very committed” to growth.

Asked by reporters on Thursday whether the federal budget was an “approximation” of what his provincial budget would look like, Doerkson said the Conservatives are committed to growing B.C.‘s economy.

“We will be looking to improve our revenue from forestry, LNG and certainly we’ll be contemplating all of that going forward.”

The Conservatives have promised to cut this year’s forecasted deficit of almost $14 billion through economic growth, without new taxes.

Yet it faces certain challenges.

Jairo Yunis, policy director at the Business Council of B.C., said the Conservatives’ ability to mitigate a fiscal situation he called “dire” will be constrained by its campaign-trail commitments, last year’s public sector wage settlements, and rising debt-servicing costs, which make up the fastest-growing budget line item.

Like Lee, Yunis said the province has more “direct program spending” than Ottawa.

But the size of B.C.‘s public sector has grown by 44 per cent since 2019, compared with just three per cent for the private sector, he noted.

“So, I think there is an argument to be made about trying to have a more rigorous and more principled approach to public spending in the province.”

Yunis said Doerkson’s government must also work on regulation and permitting to stimulate economic growth and revenue.

Ottawa’s budget includes the so-called productivity mega deduction, allowing companies to immediately and fully expense eligible assets, such as machinery.

Yunis said the deduction is “arguably the most important pro-growth tax change Ottawa has made in years.”

Doerkson specifically praised the measure in his remarks on Thursday and said it would dovetail with his party’s plan to exempt some machinery, equipment and business software from the Provincial Sales Tax for three years.

“Together, they can supercharge investment in this province and create jobs right here,” he said.

Lee said the exemption would be “hugely beneficial” to the oil and gas industry, but it would push B.C. in the wrong direction when it comes to climate change.

The economist also said cuts to public services could trigger a recession, and he was not sure tax changes would create more revenue, because politicians had mostly “pushed all the buttons” around growth.

“So, I’m more skeptical about that,” he said.

Yunis was more optimistic, but acknowledged difficulties ahead for B.C.

“I don’t envy the next finance minister,” he said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 6, 2026.

Explore All News

Western University is receiving provincial funding to support 5,013 new student seats in science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) and health care, announced by the Ontario government on Nov. 6.

It comes as part of the government’s ongoing $1.7 billion investment to fund 70,000 new post-secondary seats in high-demand sectors at universities and colleges across the province.

“The recently announced funding from the Ministry of Colleges, Universities, Research Excellence and Security helps Western meet the substantial demand for our programs and ensures we can continue to prepare world-class graduates in critical fields that serve our region, the province and Canada,” said Western President Alan Shepard.

“This investment in multiple programs will expand access for students and create opportunities for more future leaders to pursue their career goals.”

With the latest investment, Western will receive funding to support an additional 5,013 seats, distributed over several years.

The 5,013 newly funded seats at Western University include:

3,515 seats for STEM programs

1,117 seats for health programs

298 seats for education programs

83 seats f or other, labour-market driven programs

Nolan Quinn, Minister of Colleges, Universities, Research Excellence and Security, visited Western and toured labs led by engineering professors Mehrdad Kermani and Mohamed Zaki in October, exploring innovative research and meeting students in the fields of advanced robotics, artificial intelligence and autonomous systems, among others.

Minister Nolan Quinn visited two engineering labs at Western University on Oct. 21. (Ayan Imtiaz Boghani/Western Engineering)

Minister Nolan Quinn met with Western University engineering students during a visit to two labs on Oct. 21. (Ayan Imtiaz Boghani/Western Engineering)

Minister Nolan Quinn met with Western Engineering professor Mohamed Zaki during a tour of his lab on Oct. 21. (Christopher Kindratsky/Western Communications)

Minister Nolan Quinn visited two engineering labs at Western University on Oct. 21. (Christopher Kindratsky/Western Communications)

[](https://news.westernu.ca/2026/11/western-receives-ontario-government-funding-5000-students/#)[](https://news.westernu.ca/2026/11/western-receives-ontario-government-funding-5000-students/#)[](https://news.westernu.ca/2026/11/western-receives-ontario-government-funding-5000-students/#)

Kermani leads the Advanced Robotics and Mechatronics L ab, developing new approaches for human-robot collaboration to perform common tasks, including those in farms, factories and hospitals. Zaki’s multidisciplinary research is focused on smart mobility and transportation through the Emergent Mobility for Resilient Communities Lab.

“Our province’s greatest strength is our highly skilled workforce – and those workers are trained at our world-class colleges and universities,” Quinn said.

“This investment is supporting the largest seat expansion in Ontario in more than a decade and will ensure more students have the opportunity to train for good-paying careers that protect and strengthen our communities, industries and province.”

Learn more about how Western is preparing future leaders and global citizens.

stories.title: Joly seeks Competition Bureau probe of Stelco as more layoffs loom
stories.summary: The federal government is asking the competition commissioner to 'thoroughly examine' if Stelco owner Cleveland-Cliffs breached the Competition Act.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
With the deadline for Cleveland-Cliffs ‘ layoffs at Stelco fast approaching, Industry Minister Melanie Joly is asking the commissioner of the Competition Bureau to investigate whether the company’s U.S.-based owner is breaking Canadian competition law.

The federal government is asking the competition commissioner to “thoroughly examine whether Cleveland-Cliffs’ conduct in the Canadian marketplace warrants enforcement action under the Competition Act,” Joly said in a statement Friday.

In her letter to the commissioner, Joly said she cited remarks by Cleveland-Cliffs CEO Lourenco Goncalves, who said he “bought Stelco because I could not afford anymore having Stelco flooding the market here in the United States to the determinant of my own company.”

Ottawa has issued several warnings to the steel company, which has already started issuing layoff notices to employees at its Hamilton, Ont., steel plant.

In a letter dated Oct. 29 obtained by Global News and addressed to Stelco’s president, Paul Simon, Joly said she expects a “concrete and credible plan for re-engagement with these workers.”

Stelco began issuing layoff notices to about 500 employees at the beginning of October following an announcement of its plans to pull back on operations at its Hamilton plant.

The company has said some of the employees laid off in Hamilton will be offered jobs at their Lake Erie facility but the union representing Stelco workers told Global News only 40 jobs have been offered to the impacted employees.

In a letter sent last month, Joly warned Stelco that if they do not reverse the layoffs within 15 days, the federal government will start legal action against the company that could ultimately lead to the parent company Cleveland-Cliffs being forced to divest of the Canadian steel firm.

Cleveland-Cliffs has maintained its position that one of the reasons for the layoffs is the 50 per cent tariff on aluminum and steel imposed by the U.S., which the company’s leadership has publicly supported.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said last month that Cleveland-Cliffs would be making a “mistake” by not respecting its obligations and commitments.

The comments came at an event in Ottawa when Carney was asked by a reporter if, given what has transpired in recent weeks, the federal government felt it was a mistake to allow Cleveland-Cliffs to acquire Stelco in 2024.

“The mistake here would be Cleveland-Cliffs not respecting the obligations, the commitments that they made in the acquisition,” Carney said in response.

–with files from Global’s Rachel Morgan and Ari Rabinovitch

stories.title: Tumbler Ridge families argue for OpenAI lawsuits to be heard in San Francisco
stories.summary: New court filing counters the company’s argument to have the U.S. cases dismissed and heard in B.C.
stories.author: David Ebner
stories.content:
Claims for damages against OpenAI and its chief executive Sam Altman in the Tumbler Ridge mass shooting lawsuits should be heard in a San Francisco court, argue lawyers for the affected families in a new legal filing.

The filing, submitted late Nov. 5 in United States District Court, is from the lead plaintiff, the husband of an educational assistant who was killed. It is among about three dozen related lawsuits from the many families affected by the killings.

Lawyers from Chicago-based Edelson PC allege that “British Columbia does not provide an adequate forum” and that “California is an appropriate forum for claims that a California company acted negligently while operating in California.”

OpenAI is headquartered in San Francisco, but the tech company argued in a submission filed on Sept. 2 that the lawsuits should be dismissed and heard in British Columbia instead because the plaintiffs live there and the B.C. government has a “uniquely strong sovereign interest in having these actions resolved at home.”

The Tumbler Ridge mass shooting happened on Feb. 10. Jesse Van Rootselaar killed her mother and half-brother before stalking through Tumbler Ridge Secondary School in the small northern B.C. town. In total, the shooter killed six children and two adults before dying by suicide.

In the lead lawsuit, from Mark Stacey, the husband of Shannda Aviugana-Durand, lawyers seek to blame OpenAI’s alleged negligence over its failure to warn Canadian police of the danger indicated in the shooter’s use of the company’s ChatGPT product.

“In the weeks that followed the attack, a sickening truth emerged: ChatGPT played a role in the mass shooting and OpenAI could have, and should have, prevented it,” the lawsuit filed on April 29 alleges, calling on the U.S. court for a jury trial. (Vancouver-based Rice Parsons Leoni & Elliott LLP is also representing affected families.)

The suit further alleges OpenAI aided and abetted a mass shooting and cites a design defect of its chatbot.

Lawyers for Mr. Stacey declined comment. OpenAI and its lawyers did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Friday.

The first big legal step in the cases is the debate before U.S. District Court Judge Jacqueline Scott Corley in San Francisco over jurisdiction.

The lawyers for the families said jurisdiction is clearly in San Francisco because the case is about “choices OpenAI made” there. Three-quarters of the company’s 2,500 workers are in California. Only 11 are in Canada.

In the latest Nov. 5 filing, some information is redacted. The filing alleges: “Jesse Van Rootselaar asked ChatGPT to [redacted]. During the ensuing exchange, Van Rootselaar admitted to [redacted] ... OpenAI did not act on this information.”

The lawyers further said “the vagaries of Canadian law” mean a case in B.C. would offer “essentially no remedy” to the parents of the dead children. They added that plaintiffs would struggle to compile evidence in a B.C. court because provincial law has no provisions to compel pretrial testimony or documents from “unwilling witnesses” outside the province.

OpenAI, in its Sept. 2 filing to dismiss the U.S. lawsuits, said a B.C. court makes sense in part because of questions about the province’s mental-health system repeatedly releasing the shooter from involuntary hospitalizations without ongoing supervision and about Canadian police permitting the shooter to retain firearms.

Outside experts and people involved in the case say key reasons to take on the company in the U.S. include OpenAI being headquartered in San Francisco and the potential for larger damages. While a survivor of the shooting, such as 13-year-old Maya Gebala , could win a large cash award in a Canadian court, pain-and-suffering damages are limited because of a long-standing Supreme Court of Canada precedent.

Lawyers need to think about a potential victory, said Marina Pavlovic, a University of Ottawa law professor who specializes in private international law.

“I could teach my entire course on this case. I talk to students about strategy. You start at the end: Where are the assets? You build a case around the assets. If these were my clients, this is what I would suggest.”

Outgoing B.C. attorney-general Niki Sharma said the provincial government filed its lawsuit on Sept. 21 in San Francisco, rather than British Columbia, to back the Tumbler Ridge families whose legal teams had already launched their cases in the United States.

“There’s a lot of value in bringing the fight to where the headquarters of the company is,” she said.

Ms. Sharma, who will soon sit as an NDP Opposition MLA after her government was defeated in last month’s provincial election, added that her goals while in government had also included “accountability and changing behaviour” in cases of public-interest litigation.

B.C. has long been a leader in Canada in corporate negligence cases, from tobacco to opioids. In the OpenAI case, Ms. Sharma said a victory in the San Francisco court could help force changes in U.S. government regulation and oversight of artificial intelligence products, alongside damages and recovered costs for families, the province and the regional school district that includes Tumbler Ridge.

The United States is widely known as a litigious country where civil cases can lead to multimillion-dollar damages, whereas Canada is not. The U.S. Constitution enshrines the right to a jury trial in such cases but jury trials in civil lawsuits have long been rare in Canada.

A demarcation of how the justice systems in the two countries settle civil cases was decided at the Supreme Court of Canada in 1978. The Andrews case maintained an opening for pecuniary damages – where an injured or harmed person can be paid for things such as the loss of future income – but strictly limited non-pecuniary damages, colloquially known as pain and suffering.

The case involved James Andrews of Edmonton, who became a quadriplegic after a traffic collision when he was 21. The Supreme Court, after conflicting rulings in the lower courts, settled on total damages before some adjustments of $817,000, of which $100,000 was for non-pecuniary pain and suffering.

Justice Brian Dickson, who later became chief justice, said the $100,000 “should be regarded as an upper limit of non-pecuniary loss in cases of this nature.” The “Andrews cap,” adjusted for inflation, is currently at about $460,000.

He warned against sizable awards for pain and suffering because there was no “objective yardstick” to measure such claims in monetary terms, and cited such awards in the U.S. that had “soared to dramatically high levels in recent years.”

stories.title: Carney says he’s yet to talk to Democrats on tariffs: ‘Short answer is no’
stories.summary: Trump will be a lame duck president as the legislative powers are overtaken by the Democrats, but he still holds executive powers which he used to impose the Section 338 tariffs.
stories.author: Rachel Morgan
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney said he has not spoken with Democrats in the U.S. about whether the party — which is set to take control of Congress in January after the midterm blue wave — could pursue legislation to get rid of tariffs on Canada.

“The short answer is no, I haven’t,” he told reporters at an unrelated news conference Friday.

“Obviously we welcome any moves to restore a free trading arrangement between Canada and the United States, which is in the interests of American families struggling with affordability, in the interest of American workers looking for good high-paying jobs and stability. And it’s fundamentally in the interests of Canadians and we will continue to work with the Americans to get a deal for Canada.”

The Section 232 and Section 338 tariffs imposed by U.S. President Donald Trump on Canada are done under executive orders, not legislation, however, meaning even with Democratic control of Congress, that power remains with Trump who has shown no inclination to remove them.

The Democrats took the House and the Senate in a sweeping win of the midterms Tuesday, reigniting questions around the U.S.-Canada trade relationship.

Since his win of the Senate seat in Michigan, senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed has not been shy to share his feelings on the trade war between Canada and the U.S., calling it “insane” in a post-win media interview.

El-Sayed is not the only newly elected Democrat who is seeking to change the American trade agenda. Representatives in Oregon, Massachusetts and Vermont have publicly spoken about wanting to see the tariffs on Canada repealed.

But these promises are just “symbolic,” Carlo Dade, the director of international policy and New North America Initiative at the University of Calgary, told Global News.

Trump will soon be considered a lame duck president as the legislative powers are overtaken by the Democrats, but he still holds executive powers.

The sweeping 50 per cent Section 338 tariffs on more than $20 billion of Canadian products were imposed via executive order, not Congress.

In April 2025, the Senate voted 51 to 48 to pass a joint resolution aimed at ending the national emergency declaration used to justify the tariffs on Canada, but ultimately that did nothing.

The Democrats have 54 seats in the U.S. Senate.

Dade said the other question is whether the newly elected Democrats would end the tariffs on Canada even if they could.

“When we think about Democrats, we’re also thinking about Democrats as we understand them. We’re thinking about Bill Clinton, thinking about Hillary Clinton, Obama,” he said.

But that might not be the type of Democrats that will soon hold some powers, he added.

Dade said there could be up to 10 Democrats who are also members of the external organization Democratic Socialists of America, which is a progressive populist group which endorses candidates running for political office who align with the group’s goals and values like seeking universal healthcare.

He said some DSA members oppose tariffs, but they remain “America first” and are likely to favour protectionist policies, as many members of the Democrats already do.

“Protect jobs, protect workers, be the working class in the U.S.,” he said.

“The shift in Democrats May be good for us in some issues, but not all.”

stories.title: DNA expert likens B.C. bear attack investigation to human crime scene
stories.summary: A forensic DNA expert says investigators assessing the scene of the fatal bear attack will likely use techniques to identify the animal similar to those used on a human crime scene.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A forensic DNA expert says investigators assessing the scene of this week’s deadly bear attack in Bella Coola, B.C., will likely use techniques to identify the culprit animal very similar to those used on a human crime scene.

Dean Hildebrand, who oversees the accredited forensic DNA lab at the British Columbia Institute of Technology, says the main difference is that animal scene investigators don’t need to worry about cross-contaminating bear samples with their own DNA.

Though he is not involved in the Bella Coola investigation, Hildebrand says they would collect samples, including saliva, blood or hair, to be tested in a forensic lab that would then compare the DNA sequence with any animals they capture.

The BC Conservation Officer Service continues its search for a bear or bears that killed a mother and daughter in Bella Coola.

School art therapist Jenny Balcarras and her adult daughter, Selah Reed, were reported missing on Sunday and their bodies were later found near a set of trails.

The service has previously said DNA from the attack would be compared to samples collected in the same area last year after a grizzly attacked a group of about 20 elementary school students and teachers, leaving an adult and three children badly injured.

In its latest post to social media on Wednesday, the service said no bears had yet been captured, but “various trapping techniques are being implemented as these efforts continue, with officers being rotated into the community.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 6, 2026.

Brieanna Charlebois, The Canadian Press
