stories.title: U.S. midterms and rate hikes leading to buyer uncertainty and the Home of the Week: Canadian real estate news for the week of Nov. 6
stories.summary: Plus, one Red Deer couple searches for the perfect home
stories.author: Jacob Dubé
stories.content:
This week: The Liberal government has released their latest budget, putting billions towards building new homes. Plus, the housing market adjusts after the Bank of Canada’s rate hike, and experts weigh in on the practicality of home-built saunas.

On Nov. 5, Prime Minister Mark Carney’s Liberal government tabled its second federal budget . Over the five-year horizon, net new spending will amount to $151.5-billion, spread across a variety of initiatives, including boosting Canada’s housing supply.

Ottawa said it would add $13-billion in new capital over ten years on a cash basis to Build Canada Homes, an agency it launched in September 2025 to accelerate home construction. That would bring its total capital to $45-billion, and the government said the new investment would set the agency “on a path” to build 200,000 new homes across Canada over the next decade.

Ottawa said it would also spend $1.5-billion over four years, starting in 2027-2028, and $387.4-million in subsequent years to ready federal land for new housing projects.

At the same time, the government said it would introduce legislation to extend a ban on foreign residential property purchases to January 1, 2029. The restrictions had been set to expire this coming January.

From business investment to increasing the debt, read the highlights from the budget .

Variable-rate mortgages were having a moment – until the Bank of Canada raised its trendsetting interest rate last week, citing concerns about high oil prices.

Canadians had been flocking to variable rates over the past few months as turmoil in the bond market pushed up fixed mortgage rates. Nearly half of consumers taking out or renewing a mortgage in 2026 signed up for a variable one, as of September, compared to less than 10 per cent who did so in 2024, according to data from National Bank of Canada.

But, as Mariya Postelnyak writes, the BoC’s rate hike had variable rates inching up a notch last week. The potential of a few more hikes in the coming months has left mortgage shoppers wondering whether a variable rate is still worth it .

The answer hinges on a number of variables, including risk tolerance, the availability of financial buffer room, and whether the borrowers are first-time homebuyers or more experienced homeowners. But experts say going variable might still turn out to be the cheaper option for many mortgage shoppers , especially for those choosing longer terms.

Derek and Jordanna Gibeault first met in 2017, but it wasn’t until 2023 that they reconnected and began dating. By May, 2023, Jordanna, a realtor, purchased a five-bedroom, three-bathroom semi-detached home in Red Deer, Alta., for $330,000.

While the home had a spacious interior, the couple thought about buying a detached home together one day, with more storage and better exterior spaces, including a bigger backyard and a larger garage. They began to consider what they could afford and what they wanted out of their new home, given a budget of around $550,000.

The couple wanted at least four bedrooms so that they could have personal office spaces, host visiting family, and convert one bedroom into a gym. A larger private backyard space was also a must-have, not only for their two large dogs – a mixed breed named Crue and a black lab named Tikka – but also for themselves.

From a home in Southeast Red Deer with a loft space above the garage, a five-bedroom bungalow with a spacious yard and a split-level home in Deer Park, find out which property the couple decided to buy .

Rates shown are the lowest available for each term/type and category (insured vs. uninsured) as of market close on Thursday, Nov. 5 .

Market watchers in many tranches of Toronto real estate are detecting a palpable fear of commitment this fall: Buyers are reluctant to submit a bid and sellers are balking at making a counter-offer.

As Carolyn Ireland writes, steady activity in the first half of October became quieter in the second half as consumers watched the lead-up to U.S. midterm elections and waited for more clarity on tariffs, interest rates and Canada’s economy.

The Bank of Canada’s rate hike has many consumers fretting about their own budgets and economists predicting a slow grind towards the end of the year in the Greater Toronto Area.

As for potential buyers, they are trying to gauge how much farther home prices have to fall and whether the potential for a lower price offsets the risk of higher rates. Realtors share how buyers and sellers might come to a deal in these times .

Studies show saunas can reduce stress, soothe sore muscles, relieve pain and improve heart health. Some research suggests they could also lower the risk of dementia. But, Matthew Hague writes, are those benefits worth the sweat and headache of a home installation?

Building a home sauna can be tricky. For starters, there are several different kinds to consider: wood burning, electric and infrared. Placement is up for debate, too. Common options include basements, backyards, bathrooms or even bedrooms.

According to Alan Jalasjaa, who hosts a sauna podcast and serves as Canada’s Sauna Ambassador, at-home saunas tend to have lower ceilings compared to commercial ones, which help keep the heat on you.

One sauna designer said the best place to install a home sauna is the backyard. Basements and ensuites can also work, but it’s vital to ensure proper insulation and drainage to avoid mould.

7 Colchester Court, Toronto – Full gallery here

Elena Stavreska was mother to a toddler, with another baby on the way, when she and her husband decided to move from their King Street West penthouse to the Edenbridge area in suburban Etobicoke – full of winding streets, expansive lots and plenty of parkland along the Humber River.

When thinking about renovations to the modern two-storey dwelling, the couple aimed to create a more calming interior and a tranquil backyard retreat.

On the main level, the foyer opens to a double-height living area with a ceiling height of 28 feet. Stairs lead to a raised dining area with temperature-controlled wine storage. The kitchen has custom cabinetry, integrated appliances, a geometric island and a breakfast bar.

Upstairs, the primary suite has floor-to-ceiling windows in the sleeping area, a bathroom with a double vanity and stand-alone tub, and a large walk-in closet. Four additional bedrooms on that floor each have ensuite bathrooms and built-in cabinets.

Outside, the couple built an in-ground pool and integrated hot tub, surrounded by 5,500 square feet of heated patios and walkways. The pool is heated year-round, in an effort to prolong the short Canadian summers.

What do you think is the asking price for the property?

You might think that a $56-million penalty would be an effective deterrent for pretty much anything, but it has done little to stop an alleged cult leader from publicly attacking three Canadians.

In August, a Honolulu jury awarded the Canadians C$56 million after finding that the self-described spiritual teacher, Liana Shanti, defamed them. The trio from Saskatchewan was not a part of the Liana Shanti community, but were targeted because they were in disputes with estranged family members who were Shanti students.

Liana Shanti believed the Canadians were behind a social media account and online posts that called her a cult leader and a fraudster. She filed a defamation suit against them. The Canadians filed a counter-suit because of her online posts that called them, among other things, “pedo supporters,” “Satanists” and child abusers.

If you have tips on this, or any other story, reach out confidentially to avery.haines@bellmedia.CA .

At a civil trial in Honolulu in August, the jury sided with the Canadians and handed out one of the largest awards in Hawaii history.

The attacks continue

Since that August verdict, Liana Shanti has continued to post online content about the three - by name - 207 times. Some of that content is similar to what was found to be defamatory by the jury.

One of the Canadians who successfully counter-sued Liana Shanti, Byron Horvath has been mentioned in 142 posts on Instagram. Many include vile accusations, which were rejected by the jury, involving abuse of his young daughter.

For example, ON Oct. 27, 2026 Shanti posted an Instagram story that said, in part, “...her dad locks her in her room and won’t let her out to pee so she has been peeing on her bedroom floor.”

At trial, one of the statements that the eight-person jury found to be untrue and defamatory included the similar phrase, “Byron Horvath…Locked her in a room for hours where she had to pee on the floor.”

On Oct. 26, 2026, she posted that Horvath “sexually and physically abused their child,” and attributed it to his ex-wife, Haley, who used to be a Liana Shanti student.

Shanti has repeatedly posted old messages from Haley to lend credence to her new online attacks.

But it’s clear that Haley is no longer a supporter of Liana Shanti or what she posts online.

In a statement to W5, Byron’s ex-wife, Haley writes, “Byron, his wife Stefanie, our daughter, our families, others and myself have walked through hell and back because of my involvement in [Shanti’s] programs.”

“[We] lovingly co-parent our daughter, who is thriving…I choose to focus on love and repairing all that was broken after my time spent in a cult.”

Haley’s statement is included, in full, at the bottom of this article.

On Oct. 7, 2026, Liana Shanti posted on Instagram about Byron’s wife, Stefanie, with the caption, “IS [sic] Stefanie covering up abuse?” She posted another version of that story the following day.

During the trial, similar statements were deemed to be untrue and defamatory including: “[e]vil dark satanic people like Byron Horvath, Stefanie Vogt, manipulate and use corrupt systems to gag and silence mothers speaking out about abuse.”

Liana Shanti has also put out a call to her followers to feed her content about Byron’s wife, Stefanie, posting, “Do you have any information regarding Stefanie Horvath?”

Shanti has made similar posts on X, formerly Twitter, naming all three Canadians repeatedly in the past few days.

Her promise to the court

All of this comes despite the fact that after the verdict, Shanti signed a declaration to the court that read, “I will not post in the future any statement about the defendants that I know to be false…”

In an email, W5 asked Shanti about the new posts and their similarity to statements found to be defamatory. She defended her actions, writing, “I have no intention of sharing anything I know to be false.” Her defence is that what she writes was told to her by other people and she believes it to be true.

She writes in one online post, “Truth is a defense to defamation. But I wasn’t alllwed [sic] to Speak on the truth I was given.”

And then Shanti turned her attention to W5, suggesting that we have been bribed. She writes, “Shortly after I finished my recent stories, a Canadian news reporter who has been obsessed with this case emailed me about my intentions… I have no doubt they are being paid by [the father of one of the defendants].”

She followed that up with a post on Wednesday of this week that says, “Imagine the fool who considers themself a ‘journalist’ and doesn’t actually seek out facts. Those with a cognition level beyond a second grader see right through it.”

W5 has repeatedly offered Liana Shanti the opportunity to sit down and tell her side of the story. We also offered to hear from her current students. She refused both requests and has now blocked W5 from her Instagram account.

Secrets are weapons

Amanda Brady, who was a Liana Shanti student for more than eight years, says that her former teacher collects and then weaponizes information that she gleans from her followers.

“Especially if it’s somebody who has knowledge of Liana’s inner workings and her life, the online attacks start,” she says in an interview from her home in Regina. “She goes after that person on her social media as an attempt to shut them up.”

Amanda says that when she was kicked out of the community, Shanti shared - and continues to share - hundreds of posts about personal and private information.

“Now you have to worry about the fear and the fallout of what’s going to happen if all of my deepest, darkest things that I’ve ever shared with my teacher who I trusted are blasted on the internet for everyone to see,” says Amanda. “Of course no one’s going to want to leave on their own accord, right?”

On Thursday, Liana Shanti wrote on Instagram, “I Will speak until ALL OF THE Evidence Proof Facts Documents Timeline are for all the world to see…I don’t give a Fuck what anyone says about me because Jesus knows me by name.”

Full statement from Haley Winter, Byron Horvath’s ex-wife:

I have not seen internet posts from Liane Wilson for over three years. Others have shared that Liane Wilson [aka Liana Shanti] has consistently continued to speak and post on the internet about myself and others involved in recent legal judgements.

I do not consent to anyone using a public platform in any way to control, slander and publicly humiliate myself, family or anyone else connected to me. I experienced first-hand the cost of trusting Liane Wilson, taking her advice and believing her to be an authority over my life.

My family is one of many targeted. Byron, his wife Stefanie, our daughter, our families, others and myself have walked through hell and back because of my involvement in her programs. I have taken accountability for my choices and the consequences of them.

We have moved on. I have rebuilt my life. Byron, his wife Stefanie and I lovingly co-parent our daughter who is thriving. I wish for anyone reading this to choose peace and love over chaos, gossip and illusion. For myself, I choose to focus on love and repairing all that was broken after my time spent in a cult.

stories.title: Budget 2026 proposes 1st deposit insurance limit increase in 2 decades
stories.summary: The Cdic limit is moving from $100,000 to $250,000 under the federal budget, an increase many have urged for years to protect consumers.
stories.author: Rachel Morgan
stories.content:
The federal government is proposing to raise the deposit insurance limit under the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation (Cdic) to $250,000, its first increase in more than 20 years.

The measure, proposed in the 2026 budget , would “modernise the deposit insurance framework,” the government said.

The Cdic limit is the amount of a consumer’s deposits that is protected in the event of a bank failure.

Since 2005, that limit has sat at $100,000.

In 2023, the Bank and Trust Companies Association wrote to former finance minister Chrystia Freeland, urging the Cdic to double its coverage to $200,000 per depositor.

Canada has the lowest level of deposit insurance among G7 countries, a letter from the group said.

About 65 per cent of deposits at Canada’s top six banks — Royal Bank of Canada, TD Bank, Bank of Montreal, Cibc, Scotiabank and National Bank of Canada — are uninsured, according to Dbrs Morningstar.

In 2025, the Department of Finance said it would conduct a review of the deposit insurance limit and that “a deterioration of the real value of available coverage due to inflation,” the limit would need to be adjusted to $150,000 to protect the “real value” of deposit protection as it was set in 2005.

At the same time, the department said a limit set at $250,000 per deposit category “would align with that of the United States and some Canadian provinces, and May provide better protection for non-retail depositors.”

As part of Budget 2026, the federal government said it proposes to legislate a periodic review of the deposit insurance framework every 10 years to ensure the Cdic “can access data to support evidence-based policy development” as well as “updating the framework so provincial trust and loan companies seeking to become a Cdic member May only do so by continuing as a federal trust and loan company.”

According to the Cdic’s 2025 annual report, it has 85 members.

As part of the proposed amendments to the Cdic, the government also plans to provide a temporary high balance for life events like selling a home and remove the deposit insurance limit for eligible deposits in registered and tax-free accounts.

With files from Reuters.

stories.title: A design-forward house in Toronto with a four-season pool
stories.summary: Couple aimed to create a more calming interior, tranquil backyard retreat in Etobicoke
stories.author: Carolyn Ireland
stories.content:
7 Colchester Court, Toronto

Asking Price: $6,745,000

Taxes: $22,482.21 (2026)

Lot Size: 54.1 by 181 feet (irregular)

Agent: Stephanie Anne Newlands, Royal LePage Real Estate Services)

Elena Stavreska was mother to a toddler, with another baby on the way, when she and her husband decided to move from their King Street West penthouse to the Edenbridge area in suburban Etobicoke.

The neighbourhood west of the core has winding streets, expansive lots and plenty of parkland along the Humber River.

The couple chose the property at 7 Colchester Court for its location on a cul-de-sac and a verdant pie-shaped lot. The original ranch-style house had been torn down and replaced with a modern two-storey dwelling a couple of years earlier.

From the time they purchased the house in early 2020, the couple saw potential for improvement, Ms. Stavreska says, but they lived in the house for two years while they thought about which elements they would change.

The aim was to create a more calming interior and a tranquil backyard retreat.

“Everything was quality, but it wasn’t necessarily our style,” Ms. Stavreska says. “The house was contemporary, but it wasn’t as design-forward.”

The newer house was built on top of the basement of the original house, Ms. Stavreska says, so the first undertaking was to excavate the lower level to create more ceiling height.

Today that level has a Scandinavian-style dry sauna, steam room, gym, home theatre, and a nanny suite with a separate entrance.

On the main level, the foyer opens to a double-height living area with a ceiling height of 28 feet. Stairs lead to a raised dining area with temperature-controlled wine storage.

The kitchen has custom cabinetry, integrated appliances, a geometric island and a breakfast bar. There’s also a separate servery and prep kitchen.

A staircase in the living area was replaced with a more open, floating design, Ms. Stavreska adds.

The work also included improving the flow between main living areas and the connection to the outdoors, Ms. Stavreska says. Today, doors in the lounging area open to a large above-ground terrace.

In total, the house has 8,125 square feet of living space.

Upstairs, the primary suite has floor-to-ceiling windows in the sleeping area, a bathroom with a double vanity and stand-alone tub, and a large walk-in closet.

Four additional bedrooms on that floor each have ensuite bathrooms and built-in cabinets.

Throughout the house, dark wood floors were changed to pale oak, baseboards and crown mouldings were stripped away, and pocket doors replaced traditional doors in some places. The sound, lighting and security systems were upgraded.

Outside, the couple undertook extensive grading and underpinning of the sloping lot in order to build an in-ground pool and integrated hot tub, surrounded by 5,500 square feet of heated patios and walkways.

A passageway inside the house leads to the year-round lounging area next to the pool. The space with a bar, bathroom, ping pong table and television has become the setting for kids’ birthday celebrations and Super Bowl parties.

The exterior has a fire pit and fire table where people gather in the evening.

“We like to spend a ton of time outside,” says Ms. Stavreska, who makes nutrition and wellness a key part of their lifestyle. “We really wanted our children to grow up seeing movement.”

The family has expanded to three kids now, and the home gym and backyard provide lots of space for lacrosse, soccer, dance and swimming.

The pool and surrounding patios are heated year-round so the family can swim outside in four seasons.

“Canadian summers are very short as we all know – we really wanted our kids to experience the outdoors as much as possible,” Ms. Stavreska says.

The couple’s eldest son is a competitive swimmer who works on his form while his coach bundles up in cold weather and walks along the perimeter, she says. A local instructor visited throughout last winter to give the couple’s youngest daughter her first swim lessons after she turned one.

Guests sometimes balk at crossing the short distance from the house to the 30-degree water, but the commute is made easier by the warmth underfoot, she says.

“It’s quite a comfortable jump.”

While some people wonder about the expense of heating an outdoor pool in the Toronto winter, Ms. Stavreska acknowledges, she adds that the pool is insulated, and the technology includes commercial-grade heating and efficient boilers.

A cover slides across when the pool is not in use.

“A lot of thought was put into the infrastructure. It’s actually quite efficiently run,” she says, adding that the driveway is also heated. “You never have to shovel snow here.”

stories.title: One-bedroom loft in Vancouver sells below what owner paid in 2018
stories.summary: Unit had been listed at a higher price, and had to be adjusted downward to get the one offer
stories.author: Kerry Gold
stories.content:
1275 Hamilton St., No. 308, Vancouver

Asking price: $749,000 (August, 2026)

Previous asking prices: $799,000 (June 1, 2026); $769,000 (June 17, 2026)

Selling price: $714,000 (September 2026)

Previous selling price: $770,000 (March, 2018)

Taxes: $2,480.10 (2026)

Monthly maintenance fee: $504.11

Days on the market: 38

Property days on the market: 121

Listing agent: Bronwyn Bertles, Engel & Volkers Vancouver

Listing agent Bronwyn Bertles says the buyer was an investor, a rarity in today’s market dominated by buyers who intend to live in the spaces they purchase. It had been listed at a higher price with another agent, and she had to adjust the price downward to get the one offer. The seller sold for $56,000 less than they paid in 2018.

“Honestly, the pricing is kind of back to what it was in 2018,” said Ms. Bertles. “We had to price it a bit more aggressively.”

The buyer got it rented out right away, she said. The transaction completed at the end of October.

This Yaletown loft has exposed timber beams and a custom glass-block feature wall around the bedroom in an otherwise open-concept space.

The building is a former warehouse converted in 2001 into 59 residential units. The building features tilt-and-turn windows, concrete construction, an electric vehicle charger, and is within walking proximity to David Lam Park, the Canada Line transit, and downtown shops.

The 717-square-foot one-bedroom suite has an industrial vibe typical of the area.

“Anecdotally, I’ve heard of so many people closing on presales, and they already are taking a $100,000 loss. There is this narrative that Vancouver real estate is a sure thing – well, it’s not,” said Ms. Bertles.

stories.title: Consulting firm Teneo hires ex-Deloitte executive to launch Canadian restructuring team
stories.summary: Phil Reynolds was hired to lead what is expected to be a 50-person unit in two years
stories.author: Andrew Willis
stories.content:
Global consulting firm Teneo added a financial advisory team to its domestic platform by hiring the former head of Deloitte’s restructuring and insolvency group.

On Friday, Teneo announced Phil Reynolds joined its office in Toronto as a senior managing director and head of what is expected to be a 50-person Canadian unit in two years.

Mr. Reynolds led Deloitte’s restructuring services in the Americas during his nine years at the firm and oversaw some of Canada’s largest and most complex creditor workouts and bankruptcies. He also worked at Alvarez & Marsal and was a partner at Kpmg.

Restructuring experts such as Mr. Reynolds are joining boutiques including Teneo in part because regulators, boards and lenders are increasingly concerned with the potential for a conflict of interest between auditors and consultants at an accounting firm when companies face financial challenges.

“I am excited to bring financial advisory expertise to Teneo’s CEO clients across all industries, in a very challenging business environment,” Mr. Reynolds said in an interview.

The decision to join Teneo was driven in part by expectations of a sharp increase in domestic restructurings, due to rising interest rates, U.S. tariffs and significant headwinds for the private credit market, Mr. Reynolds said.

Teneo is a global platform that focuses on advising chief executives. It has 60 professionals in Canada and 1,800 employees at 50 offices around the world.

In the past five years, Teneo acquired Deloitte’s entire 250-employee restructuring business in Britain, PricewaterhouseCoopers’s insolvency advisers in Australia and New Zealand, and Kmpg’s team in the Caribbean and Bermuda. In the U.S., Teneo has built a 50-person financial advisory group by hiring professionals from other firms.

Roughly a third of Teneo’s global employees are in the financial advisory business that Mr. Reynolds leads in Canada.

Teneo launched in Canada 11 years ago by hiring James Crossland, a former mining executive and president of National Public Relations.

Mr. Crossland, Teneo’s global vice-chairman, said getting the right leader for the firm’s financial advisory business has been a priority for some time because “CEOs want seasoned advice on all elements of their business, ON strategy and on finance.”

Teneo expects Mr. Reynold’s financial advisory team to be active in a number of sectors, with an initial focus on clients in banking and asset management, aviation, retail, mining and forest products.

Mr. Reynolds also has experience advising on shareholder disputes, including acting as court-appointed monitor or receiver.

“Canada is an important market for Teneo and a natural next step in the continued growth of our Financial Advisory business,” said Daniel Butters, the London-based head of the firm’s financial advisory business, in a press release. Mr. Butters is also a former Deloitte partner.

Teneo has offices in Montreal and Calgary and its adviser team includes former premiers Jean Charest and Jason Kenney, Air Canada CEO Calin Rovinescu and Desjardin Group CEO Monique Leroux.

In the U.S., Teneo has built a 50-person financial advisory group by hiring professionals from other firms.
Roughly a third of Teneo’s global employees are in the financial advisory business that Mr. Reynolds leads in Canada.
Teneo launched in Canada 11 years ago by hiring James Crossland, a former mining executive and president of National Public Relations.

Mr. Crossland, Teneo’s global vice-chairman, said getting the right leader for the firm’s financial advisory business has been a priority for some time because “CEOs want seasoned advice on all elements of their business, ON strategy and on finance.”

Teneo expects Mr. Reynold’s financial advisory team to be active in a number of sectors, with an initial focus on clients in banking and asset management, aviation, retail, mining and forest products.
Mr. Reynolds also has experience advising on shareholder disputes, including acting as court-appointed monitor or receiver.

“Canada is an important market for Teneo and a natural next step in the continued growth of our Financial Advisory business,” said Daniel Butters, the London-based head of the firm’s financial advisory business, in a press release. Mr. Butters is also a former Deloitte partner.
Teneo has offices in Montreal and Calgary and its adviser team includes former premiers Jean Charest and Jason Kenney, Air Canada CEO Calin Rovinescu and Desjardin Group CEO Monique Leroux.

stories.title: Cineplex reports $23.8M Q3 profit, record quarterly revenue
stories.summary: Toronto — Cineplex Inc. reported a third-quarter profit of $23.8 million as it saw record revenue for the period, boosted by "Spider-Man: Brand New Day" and "The Odyssey."
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Toronto — Cineplex Inc.’s new chief executive thinks the movie theatre industry has shifted from recovery mode into a period of sustainable growth.

Bill Walker pointed Friday to overall box office numbers exceeding 2019 levels and strong audience numbers at his own cinemas as proof that the industry has more than rebounded.

Movie theatres were struggling to compete with streaming, when the COVID-19 pandemic triggered temporary closures. After reopening, the industry was dealt another blow when twin Hollywood strikes reduced the number of new releases.

But these days, Walker said he feels “pretty optimistic” about the year ahead following financial results from Cineplex that included an all-time record for quarterly revenue.

Several big-name studios have committed to giving theatres exclusive screening windows for films before they head to rental or streaming platforms and there are new “Hunger Games,” “Jumanji,” “Avatar” and “Dune” movies on their way.

“In every month of 2027, there’s lots of tentpole films, as we would call them, and then there’s always the surprises, like we saw this year with ‘Backrooms’ and now, ‘You Can See Everything,'” Walker said in an interview.

“Those surprises will always show up and it’s great to see the big movies slated on the calendar that we can rely on.”

His remarks came a little over a month into his tenure as Cineplex CEO. The former Landmark Cinemas executive joined the Toronto-based chain in September, replacing longtime leader Ellis Jacob.

Walker spent the last month visiting 12 Cineplex locations and so far, said he sees “no immediate changes” to be made.

The same day Walker was given the top job, Cineplex announced plans for a review of strategic alternatives, that it said could result in a potential sale.

Walker said Friday that he was unable to provide any update on the review but reminded analysts during a conference call to discuss the company’s latest results that the point is to maximize value for shareholders.

The remarks came on the heels of Cineplex reporting a third-quarter profit of $23.8 million or 34 cents per diluted share, up from a profit of $1.2 million or two cents per diluted share a year ago.

Revenue for the quarter totalled $440.2 million, up from $348.9 million in the same quarter last year, as theatre attendance rose to 14.8 million people, up from 12.1 million.

Box office revenue per patron was $14.54 for the quarter, up from $13.23 a year ago, while concession revenue per patron amounted to $9.99, up from $9.65.

The increases were largely attributable to “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” and “The Odyssey.” The superhero flick and director Christopher Nolan’s take on the Homer epic contributed more than half of Cineplex’s total box office, Walker said.

Plenty of the ticket sales were for showings in Imax 70 mm, a premium format that is more immersive and high-resolution because it screens the movie’s full frame.

Because Walker said Cineplex has eight of the world’s 41 Imax 70 mm theatres that can project movies in the large format, it was uniquely positioned to take advantage of the film’s success.

Fans who would seldom visit the theatre were enticed to make a special trip to one of the Imax 70 mm theatres to see the movie as Nolan intended.

“They were buying tickets like it was concert tickets and we were sold out from 11 a.m. to 11 p.m.,” Walker said in an interview. “I couldn’t believe what we were experiencing.”

The movie performed so well that Walker said he will look to screen it again in Imax 70 mm next year.

After the quarter wrapped, Cineplex started showing “You Can See Everything,” Canadian director Nathan Fielder’s almost three-hour documentary on Theranos fraudster Elizabeth Holmes.

Demand for those screenings was so high, Walker said Cineplex started adding as many more showings as it could.

“There’s something magical about a sellout and being sold out sometimes drives more demand and there is a helpful cycle there overall, but once that movie went wide, we were trying to make sure we had lots of seats and screens so people can get out and see that movie,” he said.

Away from the movie theatres, Cineplex was busy at its dining and entertainment venues Rec Room, Playdium and Junxion. Some of those locations are getting expanded bowling experiences, as well axe-throwing, augmented reality and gel blaster attractions.

“There’ll be a day where axe throwing won’t be relevant, but something else will be, and so I really think about these Rec Rooms as just a platform that we’re going to continue to evolve,” Walker said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 6, 2026.

stories.title: City admits slow progress and rising costs impacting plan to stabilize Tolpuddle Housing Co-op
stories.summary: A Council-approved transition plan has experienced slower than expected progress and rising costs since the troubled Tolpuddle Housing Co-op was declared a “Project in Difficulty” more than six months ago.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
A Council-approved transition plan has experienced slower than expected progress and rising costs since the troubled Tolpuddle Housing Co-op was declared a “Project in Difficulty” more than six months ago.

The admission coming from city staff in a written statement sent to CTV News on Thursday.

Matt Feldberg, Director, Municipal Housing and Industrial Development writes that city staff have “worked with the Co-operative’s board to improve financial oversight, provide additional funding, support property management changes and address building maintenance and safety concerns. Despite these efforts costs continue to rise and progress has been slower than anticipated.”

However, Tolpuddle Co-op Board President Jo Dee Phoenix rejects Feldberg’s assertion that the city and co-op have been working together on many issues.

“One of those things is accurate, the rest of the list is not,” responds Phoenix. “They have provided some financial assistance regarding insurance payments and mortgage payments and property tax payments. They provided very limited funding for (building) deficiencies.”

“We really need some oversight from council as to what’s been happening here,” she urged.

In early March, CTV News revealed shocking conditions inside the building, including threatening graffiti, smashed drywall, damaged fire equipment, and vacant rent-geared-to-income (RGI) units destroyed by their previous tenants.

Phoenix blames the City of London’s housing waitlist for placing tenants with serious addictions and mental health conditions in a building that was never designed to provide supportive housing.

The 134 unit apartment building and townhouse complex includes 109 RGI units for low-income adults, seniors, families, and the disabled.

A tour of the building on Wednesday showcased some of the progress by the Co-op Board to restore hallways and some of the uninhabitable units, but security costs and vandalism continue to put unsustainable pressure on its finances.

Phoenix says she sent an email to every member of city council on Sept. 16 that expressed her concerns about slow progress and a deteriorating relationship between the co-op board and city staff.

“There were a couple of councillors that followed-up that they were going to look into it. A very simple one-line email. But there’s been no follow-up,” she explained. “I did receive a personal phone call from one councillor, but I’ve not received a follow-up from that phone call.”

As a result of the slow progress and rising costs, city staff have issued a request for proposals (RFP) to hire, “an independent Interim Receiver or Interim Receiver and Manager to provide temporary oversight, stabilize operations, maintain services for residents, and protect the long-term sustainability of the housing co-operative.”

It’s a decision the co-op board opposes, suggesting that council should instead look closely into their concerns.

Phoenix added, “We just had a municipal election. Every single candidate, incumbents and new candidates, had safe and affordable housing in their platform. This is where the buck stops.”

City staff will present a progress report to the Community and Protective Services (Caps) Committee on Nov. 30.

Recommendations from that committee meeting will be considered by Council on Dec. 15.

The admission coming from city staff in a written statement sent to CTV News on Thursday.

stories.title: Report alleges China linked to 18 overseas police stations in Canada
stories.summary: China has exponentially expanded its network of illegal overseas police stations, to “extend its tentacles” across a web of new community associations, according to a report by international human rights group Safeguard Defenders.
stories.author: Judy Trinh
stories.content:
Ottawa - China has exponentially expanded its network of illegal overseas police stations, to “extend its tentacles” across a web of new community associations, according to a report by international human rights group Safeguard Defenders.

In its latest report, the Spanish non-governmental organization (NGO) identifies nearly 1,250 overseas Chinese associations which they say are fronts for suspected police centres in 91 countries.

“That network is being used to watch the diaspora. To watch what they do, what they say and to essentially police them,” says Laura Harth, Safeguard Defender’s China director in an interview with CTV News.

The new figures are also a 12-fold increase from the Ngo’s findings four years earlier.

In 2022, the NGO identified 100 illegal Chinese police stations operating in more than 50 countries, including Canada.

The report, A Formula for Repression , asserts that the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) is exporting “its domestic system of surveillance and control to Chinese diaspora communities around the world.”

China has more than 60 million citizens living abroad.

Michael Kovrig, senior advisor for the International Crisis Group, says the report reveals “an early stage” of the Ccp’s efforts to expand its ability to influence the political choices of sovereign nations across the globe.

Kovrig, a former Canadian diplomat who was arbitrarily detained by China in 2018 says the “stunning” apparatus revealed by Safeguard Defenders could lead to the “slow erosion of the rights of Canadian citizens to express their own views and vote as they wish.”

The ‘magic weapon’

Safeguard Defenders says the associations are run by overseas party operatives under the direction of Beijing’s United Front Workers Department (Ufwd).

President Xi Jinping calls the Ufwd a “magic weapon” for monitoring and controlling its citizens, no matter where they live.

Safeguard was able to identify 1,247 community hubs that had acknowledged they were “liaison points” to Chinese police and prosecutor websites and in publications.

The NGO says any association connected to the Ufwd can be mobilized to participate in its mass surveillance program.

China says it has “tens of thousands” of Ufwd affiliated organizations around the world.

Instead of being chastened by the past exposure of its illegal activities, Harth, the report’s lead researcher, says China has gotten better at covering its tracks.

“They’ve learned their lesson. The public security bureaus were maybe a bit too enthusiastic. They (previously) put their own logos on walls and doors. Now post 2022, they’re more careful about (not) naming the exact associations they’re working with.”

How the network grows

A Formula for Repression , details how China’s global grid for community control works.

Researchers say that more than 10 police forces from five provinces in China are working through a vast network of Chinese Federation hubs on foreign soil.

The hubs are marketed as a place for the diaspora to connect culturally and foster business and tourism ties with various provinces and cities in China.

Safeguard Defenders lists the names of 80 regional associations linked to Chinese law enforcement. In 2022, it only found four associations that had set up police stations.

The NGO warns that the Ccp’s tentacles extend “into every part of ordinary life.”

The Canadian picture

Safeguard’s report reveals 18 alleged Chinese police monitoring stations in Canada, compared to the five that it found in 2022.

However, additional research by Jamestown, an American think tank cited in the report, uncovered 575 organizations linked to the Ufwd in Canada.

New Democratic Party MP, Jenny Kwan calls the allegations troubling.

“If true, it suggests that existing government responses have not been sufficient to deter these illegal activities,” Kwan wrote in an open letter addressed to Canada’s public safety minister.

“Canada must close the legal gaps, investigate these operations and ensure that people in our communities can speak, organize and exercise their democratic rights without coercion, intimidation or fear.”

Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree represents a riding in Scarborough, Ontario with a high population of ethnic Chinese constituents. He’s cautioning against jumping to conclusions.

“I can say that foreign interference of any sort is unacceptable. It’s something that we will not tolerate. With respect to these specific allegations – they are allegations and have not been investigated,” Anandasangaree said.

In 2023, the RCMP closed its investigation into two Chinese service centres in Montreal alleged to be police stations. No charges were laid. The organizations are now suing the federal government.

Anandasangaree says law enforcement will do their due diligence and follow up on the information in the report but says investigations must be conducted with “nuance.”

He says some of the associations are sports or book clubs, that on a day-to-day basis “just go about providing civic life to members of the Chinese diaspora.”

Will the foreign influence registry make a difference?

CTV News asked Anandasangaree if he had spoken to the Chinese embassy about registering the co-ordinators of overseas Chinese organizations as foreign agents.

Canada’s foreign-influence registry started operating in August . Under the act, failure to register foreign organizations could result in fines of $250,000 to $1 million.

Anandasangaree said the onus of education is with the individual embassies and that it’s up to Canada’s first Foreign Influence Transparency Commissioner, Anton Boegman to ensure compliance.

The minister also said he’s concerned the “unsubstantiated” numbers of reported organizations will cause difficulties for the Chinese community.

“Of course (foreign interference) is a concern. The other side is mislabelling and putting people and communities in fear unnecessarily.”

The organizations May promote recreation and culture, but Harth points out some also actively repress other communities who take part in celebrations the CPP doesn’t like, such as Tibetan or Uyghur culture.

“We can’t give legitimacy to a system that does not deserve it…We need to start sending clear signals that this kind of thing isn’t going to pass and put the United Front on notice.”

The Chinese Embassy has not responded to a request for comment from CTV News.

Fear in ethnic communities

The highest profile example of an illegal police station comes from New York City. In May 2026, Lu Jianwang, a U.S. citizen was convicted of operating a clandestine police station, to gather information on Chinese dissidents for Beijing.

In Canada, the RCMP says it has investigated five alleged Chinese police stations in Toronto, Montreal and Vancouver. However, no charges were laid.

Uyghur-Canadian Rukiye Turdush, the executive director for Center for East Turkistan National Interest, calls the massive spike in China’s overseas police stations “shocking and scary,” but not a surprise.

She has organized protests against China’s violation of human rights in Xinjiang and says she has seen firsthand how the Ufwd is suppressing dissent.

Turdush, says fellow Uyghur activists who received visas to visit relatives in China were pressured to sign documents stating support for Chinese national law.

“They come back and they’re scared…They hide and can no longer come to my organization.”

The activist is also concerned that her organization has been infiltrated by CCP operatives to launch attacks on the leadership and spy on members.

“That’s how China is dividing the community. We don’t trust each other and we don’t feel safe,” Turdush said.

Canada-China police co-operation agreement

Safeguard Defender’s new data comes 11 months after Prime Minister Mark Carney signed a new police co-operation agreement with President Xi.

In January, the two leaders committed the RCMP and China’s Ministry of Public Security (MPS) to increased co-operation in combating corruption and transnational crimes such as telecommunications fraud, cyberfraud and the trafficking of illegal synthetic drugs.

The prime minister has refused to release the text of the agreement despite calls from the Conservatives and the NDP to do so .

I’m calling on @MarkJCarney govt to stop hiding RCMP–MPS MOU signed in Beijing. Reports that RCMP needs Beijing’s “permission” to show this MOU to Canadians are a threat to our sovereignty. Our diaspora communities deserve to know how their safety and rights are being protected. pic.twitter.com/JnZAFAghEC — Jenny Kwan (@JennyKwanBC) May 12, 2026

Kovrig says Canada should not have signed the agreement because of the “political signal” it sends.

The former diplomat points out that China has a record of arbitrary detention, executions and psychological and physical torture. Kovrig himself was detained by China for more than 1,000 days.

Canada does not have an extradition treaty with China, but Kovrig says the agreement implies that the RCMP and the MPS are co-equal policing organizations that follow similar norms and behaviours.

“That’s simply not the case. The RCMP is not setting up fake police stations to influence Canadians abroad. It’s not involved in subversive activities in foreign countries. We should be calling for the agreement to be released. We need transparency and accountability.”

With files from CTV News’ Menna Elnaka

stories.title: Toronto woman’s ex-boyfriend charged with assaulting her before she was killed
stories.summary: The woman, Gregoria Alilio, died in hospital after being found with stab wounds in the area of Bathurst Street and Finch Avenue West.
stories.author: Olivia Bowden, Catherine McDonald, Noor Ra’fat
stories.content:
The ex-boyfriend of a 47-year-old woman stabbed to death on Saturday was recently charged with assaulting and threatening her, according to court documents obtained by Global News.

The woman, Gregoria Alilio, died in hospital after being found with stab wounds in the area of Bathurst Street and Finch Avenue West. Police responded around 4 p.m. Saturday and found a man alongside Alilio, also with stab wounds, who was pronounced dead at the scene.

It’s believed the man is responsible for killing Alilio, police said. While police confirmed Alilio’s identity, they would not identify the man, noting he is dead and will not face criminal charges. Multiple sources tell Global News that the deceased male is Alilio’s ex-boyfriend Reydel Del Rosario.

The court documents show that on Sept. 1, Del Rosario, 57, was charged with two counts of assault, one count of assault with a weapon, uttering threats and theft not exceeding $5,000. It indicates police were investigating the incident as intimate partner violence.

The charge details allege that Del Rosario assaulted Alilio multiple times, including with a kitchen knife. It also states that he allegedly uttered death threats towards her and stole her phone.

Bail documents obtained by Global News show Del Rosario was released on his own recognizance with a condition he not have any contact with Alilio.

The Ontario Superior Court also ordered him to not posses any kind of weapon, including knives outside of his home or workplace.

Edelyn Cabrera, Alilio’s niece, told Global News that her aunt was relied upon by family in the Philippines. “Especially her mother, she supports her mother’s medication and her daily living,” she said.

Friends of Alilio in Toronto informed the family that she had been killed. They were aware her ex-boyfriend had been charged with assaulting her, said Cabrera. “My aunt called the police after she was threatened by (him),” she said.

Alilio had been in Canada over a decade, she said. Facebook photos show she became a Canadian citizen in 2022.

paragraphs: The ex-boyfriend of a 47-year-old woman stabbed to death on Saturday was recently charged with assaulting and threatening her, according to court documents obtained by Global News.

The woman, Gregoria Alilio, died in hospital after being found with stab wounds in the area of Bathurst Street and Finch Avenue West. Police responded around 4 p.m. Saturday and found a man alongside Alilio, also with stab wounds, who was pronounced dead at the scene.

It’s believed the man is responsible for killing Alilio, police said. While police confirmed Alilio’s identity, they would not identify the man, noting he is dead and will not face criminal charges. Multiple sources tell Global News that the deceased male is Alilio’s ex-boyfriend Reydel Del Rosario.

The court documents show that on Sept. 1, Del Rosario, 57, was charged with two counts of assault, one count of assault with a weapon, uttering threats and theft not exceeding $5,000. It indicates police were investigating the incident as intimate partner violence.
The charge details allege that Del Rosario assaulted Alilio multiple times, including with a kitchen knife. It also states that he allegedly uttered death threats towards her and stole her phone.
Bail documents obtained by Global News show Del Rosario was released on his own recognizance with a condition he not have any contact with Alilio.
The Ontario Superior Court also ordered him to not posses any kind of weapon, including knives outside of his home or workplace.

Edelyn Cabrera, Alilio’s niece, told Global News that her aunt was relied upon by family in the Philippines. “Especially her mother, she supports her mother’s medication and her daily living,” she said.

Friends of Alilio in Toronto informed the family that she had been killed. They were aware her ex-boyfriend had been charged with assaulting her, said Cabrera. “My aunt called the police after she was threatened by (him),” she said.
Alilio had been in Canada over a decade, she said. Facebook photos show she became a Canadian citizen in 2022.

stories.title: Cooler temperatures, scattered showers expected Friday
stories.summary: Cooler fall conditions are expected across the region Friday, with scattered showers and temperatures holding between 7 C and 10 C, according to CTV News meteorologist Julie Atchison.
stories.author: Koylan Azofeifa Rueda
stories.content:
Cooler fall conditions are expected across the region Friday, with scattered showers and temperatures holding between 7 C and 10 C, according to CTV News meteorologist Julie Atchison.

A cold front moving across the Great Lakes is shifting winds to the northwest, bringing on-and-off showers throughout the day.

Atchison says temperatures will remain relatively steady, a significant change from the unseasonably warm weather earlier this week.

The unsettled conditions will linger into Saturday, with some lingering rainfall before skies begin to clear Sunday.

Sunday is expected to bring a mix of sun and cloud and a high of 10 C, making it the best day to get outside and tackle yardwork.

Similar conditions are expected Monday, with temperatures returning to the double digits next week. Remembrance Day is forecast to bring a mix of sun and cloud and a high of 8 C.

stories.title: Ontario’s top court won’t reduce sentence so woman convicted in bottle attack can dodge deportation
stories.summary: 'Although the immigration consequences of a sentence can be significant, as they are for the appellant, they cannot change a fit sentence into an unfit one,' the judge said
stories.author: Chris Lambie
stories.content:
Ontario’s top court has drawn the line on when the immigration consequences of a sentence veer into unfit punishment in the case of a woman who struck a stranger in the head with a tossed table and two glass bottles.

It dismissed the Mississauga, Ont., woman’s claim that the judge, who sentenced her to a year in jail for the “gratuitous” attack that left her female victim with permanent and disfiguring injuries, failed to properly consider adverse immigration consequences.

Agata Trabinska, who is not a Canadian citizen, pleaded guilty to assault causing bodily harm for the Dec. 1, 2020, attack that took place at the Mountfort Restaurant, ON Dundas Street East in Mississauga. The 43-year-old Trabinska has already served the sentence, but appealed it to fend off deportation to her native Poland, fearing she’d have to leave behind her three Canadian-born teenage sons, who are triplets.

While she was waiting to be sentenced for the assault, Trabinska pleaded guilty to possession of cocaine and methadone for the purpose of trafficking, possession of property obtained by crime, under $5,000, and possession of property obtained by crime, over $5,000, for which another judge handed her a 60-day intermittent sentence. Trabinska also appealed that sentence, which she’s already served.

“Ultimately, the appellant’s request to vary her sentences would allow the adverse immigration consequences to be the controlling factor in determining the type or length of sentence she receives,” said a recent decision from the Court of Appeal for Ontario.

“Though the appellant’s circumstances are sympathetic, the law does not permit a court to impose a sentence solely for the purpose of avoiding such consequences. Although the immigration consequences of a sentence can be significant, as they are for the appellant, they cannot change a fit sentence into an unfit one.”

The court heard that Trabinska got into a verbal altercation on the night in question with the victim’s friend at the restaurant.

“She overturned a table, which struck the victim. The appellant also threw two glass bottles, both of which struck the victim in the side of the head and caused very serious injuries,” said the Nov. 4 decision.

“The victim required 18 stitches to close a gash on her cheek and three staples to close a wound on her head.”

The sentence for the restaurant attack resulted in Trabinska — who immigrated here from Poland at the age of 20 — being declared inadmissible to Canada for “serious criminality,” said the appeal court decision.

That barred her from “appealing her inadmissibility finding to the Immigration Appeal Division, which she would have likely done on the basis of humanitarian and compassionate grounds.”

The Crown argued for a sentence in the range of 15 to 18 months for the restaurant assault, highlighting the “random, unprovoked, and violent nature of the attack, the victim’s significant injuries, and that cases involving similar assaults normally merit a custodial sentence.”

Trabinska’s lawyer recommended two years, less a day, of house arrest.

The sentencing judge “concluded that, applying the principle of restraint, a 12-month custodial sentence was appropriate and was the lowest possible sentence that would be consistent with the objectives of sentencing.”

Trabinska, who has “struggled with substance abuse since she was 16,” raised her triplets as a single parent after their father left the family shortly after she sponsored him to come to Canada, said the decision.

For the drug crimes and possession of property obtained by crime — a stolen luxury car and over $2,000 in cash — which Trabinska committed while she was on release for the assault causing bodily harm, the sentencing judge accepted the parties’ joint submission of a 60-day intermittent sentence, noting she’d already served 187 days of pre-sentence custody.

While Trabinska hasn’t been found inadmissible to Canada yet for those crimes, the appeal court pointed out she could be because the penalty exceeds six months in jail.

Permanent residents and temporary foreign workers in Canada can face deportation under the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act if they get more than six months behind bars.

Trabinska argued unsuccessfully that both her sentences are “tainted by an error in principle because they were imposed ‘without due consideration of her collateral immigration consequences.'”

According to Trabinska, “when her collateral immigration consequences are properly considered, the balance tips in favour of a conditional sentence. She argues that her forced removal from Canada will mean a return to a country where she will have no support network for her addiction and mental health issues. She also points to the collateral consequences that her deportation will have on her three teenaged sons, who will be left in Canada without their mother.”

Both sentence appeals “must fail,” said the appeal court.

It’s clear from the reasoning of the judge who sentenced her for the bottle assault that Trabinska’s “immigration status would not have resulted in a conditional sentence or a custodial sentence of less than six months,” said the appeal court.

“This was a very serious assault that had a significant physical, psychological, and financial impacts on the victim. She has suffered permanent facial scarring and nerve damage causing chronic pain. She also suffers from persistent hypervigilance, anxiety, depression, and suicidal ideation. She has suffered financially, paying for topical scar treatments and transportation for medical appointments.”

The sentencing judge concluded a conditional sentence “would be manifestly unfit,” making it clear “that the collateral consequences — including the impact of the appellant’s deportation on her sons — could not have resulted in a conditional sentence. Nor could these consequences have resulted in reducing, by half, the 12-month custodial sentence that the appellant has already served.”

The appeal court also saw no basis to reduce Trabinska’s 60-day intermittent sentence.

“Varying the sentence for the sole purpose of avoiding immigration consequences would allow collateral consequences, rather than sentence fitness, to dictate the length of the sentence on those counts,” it said.

“Such a variation would be entirely artificial and a circumvention of Parliament’s will.”

Chris Lambie is Atlantic bureau chief for National Post. He has worked for news organizations from Newfoundland to the Northwest Territories and is a three-time National Newspaper Award nominee, with a win for local reporting.

stories.title: Turning 100 in a trade war, a Quebec aluminum town makes a wish
stories.summary: Americans built Arvida, Que., into a powerhouse of industry. Now Trump’s tariffs cloud their future
stories.author: Eric Andrew-Gee, Photography by Charles-Frederick Ouellet
stories.content:
When the American tycoon Arthur Vining Davis built a company town for his aluminum plant in the Saguenay region of Quebec in 1926, he left his imprint on every part of it. Arvida would even be christened with the first syllables of his three names.

The community was a marvel from the beginning, known as “the City Built in 135 Days” after Mr. Davis’s firm, Alcoa, flung up hundreds of houses for workers almost overnight.

The speed of Arvida’s construction belied its humanity, with attractive homes in a variety of architectural styles that labourers could eventually own, large plots without fences to encourage fraternization, and winding, tree-lined streets that evoked a commuter-train suburb.

As the community celebrates its 100th anniversary, the town’s remarkably well-preserved neighbourhoods still resemble a Disneyfied vision of midcentury America deep in rural Quebec.

Its picturesque houses, guarded from changing fashions by provincial heritage laws, are often inhabited by descendants of the original workers.

It is just as Mr. Davis would have wanted it.

Only now, Arvida is shadowed by the whims of another American tycoon, this one occupying the Oval Office. The 50-per-cent tariffs imposed on Canadian aluminum by U.S. President Donald Trump are the talk of a town still dependent on the plant, now owned by the British-Australian mining giant Rio Tinto.

Mr. Trump’s stated desire to manufacture all of his country’s aluminum at home would devastate a place that was founded on American vision and capital, throwing into relief the sudden souring of Canada-U.S. relations under his administration.

Local authorities are trying to use Arvida’s centenary as a reminder of what the two countries built together, including a renewed push for recognition as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The federal government, meanwhile, is trying to further Canadianize an industry that has long been dependent on the U.S., splashing out nearly $200-million on projects in the Quebec aluminum sector last week in the name of “Canadian sovereignty.”

“In the current political context, I think it would be good for Trump to see that our aluminum saved the world,” said Marianne Salesse-Côté, director-general of the Arvida Heritage Museum, housed in a soaring Catholic church built decades ago with money deducted directly from workers’ paycheques.

Despite being nestled deep in a “North Canada steppe,” as The New York Times once remarked, Arvida owes its existence to Americans.

Mr. Davis, a pioneer in the commercial uses of aluminum who became the fifth-richest man in the U.S., conceived Arvida and hired American architects to build it.

Although Alcan was spun off as a Canadian company in 1928 amid an anti-trust investigation south of the border, and many of the worker houses were in a French-Canadian vernacular style, American executives continued to run the company and, effectively, the town.

Locals mostly accepted the bargain. Unlike in other corporate communities at the time, the housing stock was well-built and attractive, with modern amenities such as central heating. Instead of setting up a company store selling goods on credit, Alcan encouraged real banks and shops to establish themselves in town. Company-owned cinemas, skating rinks and bowling alleys provided wholesome entertainment.

In an era of dubious planned cities erected in the image of their eccentric founders, this was a success story. By the time Henry Ford’s rubber colony of Fordlandia had devolved into anarchy and been sold to the Brazilian government in the 1940s, Arvida was at its zenith.

“It was a social utopia,” said Ms. Salesse-Côté. “The dream of Arthur Vining Davis was to have his workers stay a long time.”

Alcan’s progressive paternalism had its limits. Worker safety precautions were virtually non-existent, and labour relations could be bruising. A sudden strike in 1941 made the federal government suspect enemy sabotage.

By the Second World War, Arvida was not just a company town, but a strategic cog in the war effort. It had become home to the world’s largest aluminum plant, employing 12,000 workers and cranking out 90 per cent of the aluminum used by the Commonwealth air forces. The factory was surrounded by anti-aircraft guns and protected by some 3,000 servicemen in case of Nazi attack.

“Without Arvida, we might not have had a happy ending,” said Ms. Salesse-Côté.

Arvida and its aluminum plant in 1958. Though its wartime production blitz was long over by then, the plant remained a powerhouse of the Canadian metal industry. Supplied

The company’s wartime role heralded a growing reputation as a model corporate citizen. In 1951, Alcan built a $500-million smelter in Kitimat, B.C., the country’s largest public-private partnership at the time. As chief executive in the late 1970s, Montrealer David Culver doubled down on the city as company headquarters while other firms fled a separatist government.

But for all of Arvida’s patriotic bona fides, its business model remained deeply dependent on American markets. Over the course of the 20th century, government policies began requiring the domestic transformation of certain natural resources before exportation, producing more Canadian jobs in the paper industry, for example, according to Marc-Urbain Proulx, professor of regional economics at the Université du Québec à Chicoutimi. “We never dared to do that with aluminum,” he said. “We still export raw ingots to the United States.”

The relative lack of capacity for transforming aluminum in Canada has left the domestic industry more vulnerable to U.S. tariffs. Some residents of Arvida – now part of the amalgamated city of Saguenay – feel uncomfortably exposed to Donald Trump’s hostility. “There’s a lot of anxiety,” said Ms. Salesse-Côté. “People in the community are always asking, ‘How’s Rio Tinto going? Are we going to lose jobs?’”

The answer, for now, is no. U.S. demand for Canadian aluminum is steady despite the tariffs, with Russian and Saudi sources sidelined because of global conflicts.

As for the President’s dreams of onshoring U.S. production, no one knows better than the residents of Saguenay how much electricity, capital and expertise is needed to build a smelter from scratch.

“Good luck, Trump,” said Saguenay Mayor Luc Boivin.

“Building a smelter, it takes years. The energy, they’ve given to data centres, they don’t have any more for aluminum. Right now the Americans are shooting themselves in the foot. They’re paying a tax and increasing the cost of living.”

Rio Tinto insists it’s not going anywhere. In an e-mailed statement, the company’s chief executive for aluminum and lithium, Jérôme Pécresse, pointed to its $1.5-billion investment in expanding low-carbon smelting at the Arvida complex announced in May.

“Canada is at the heart of our global aluminum strategy, and with the expertise of our teams in Quebec, we intend to keep Saguenay–Lac-Saint-Jean a global aluminum hub for the next century. We are not just celebrating 100 years of history, we are also laying the foundations for generations to come.”

In the midst of the centenary celebrations, which have included Lego recreations of the town’s famous aluminum bridge and CF-18 flyovers, the federal government has taken a renewed interest in making the country’s aluminum industry more autonomous. Industry Minister Mélanie Joly spoke just last week about reviving plans for an aluminum-rolling mill in Canada, so the country could transform its own metal into sheets on a large scale.

“We want to be able to produce our aluminum cans here at home,” she said in announcing $193-million in funding for the industry. “We want to be able to produce our aircraft and aerospace parts here at home.”

That is in line with the Carney government’s broader efforts to make the Canadian economy less dependent on the U.S. – to shift away from Canada’s long-standing role as a “basin of natural resources for the Americans,” as Mr. Proulx said.

The mayor of Saguenay is all for it. He thinks the 100th anniversary has come at a good time, deepening local pride in the middle of a trade war. Arvida may have been built by the U.S., but it is determined not to be undone by the country. “I think there’s a consciousness of the value of our industry and the need to protect it,” said Mr. Boivin.

paragraphs: When the American tycoon Arthur Vining Davis built a company town for his aluminum plant in the Saguenay region of Quebec in 1926, he left his imprint on every part of it. Arvida would even be christened with the first syllables of his three names.
The community was a marvel from the beginning, known as “the City Built in 135 Days” after Mr. Davis’s firm, Alcoa, flung up hundreds of houses for workers almost overnight.

The speed of Arvida’s construction belied its humanity, with attractive homes in a variety of architectural styles that labourers could eventually own, large plots without fences to encourage fraternization, and winding, tree-lined streets that evoked a commuter-train suburb.
As the community celebrates its 100th anniversary, the town’s remarkably well-preserved neighbourhoods still resemble a Disneyfied vision of midcentury America deep in rural Quebec.
Its picturesque houses, guarded from changing fashions by provincial heritage laws, are often inhabited by descendants of the original workers.
It is just as Mr. Davis would have wanted it.

Only now, Arvida is shadowed by the whims of another American tycoon, this one occupying the Oval Office. The 50-per-cent tariffs imposed on Canadian aluminum by U.S. President Donald Trump are the talk of a town still dependent on the plant, now owned by the British-Australian mining giant Rio Tinto.

Mr. Trump’s stated desire to manufacture all of his country’s aluminum at home would devastate a place that was founded on American vision and capital, throwing into relief the sudden souring of Canada-U.S. relations under his administration.

Local authorities are trying to use Arvida’s centenary as a reminder of what the two countries built together, including a renewed push for recognition as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The federal government, meanwhile, is trying to further Canadianize an industry that has long been dependent on the U.S., splashing out nearly $200-million on projects in the Quebec aluminum sector last week in the name of “Canadian sovereignty.”

“In the current political context, I think it would be good for Trump to see that our aluminum saved the world,” said Marianne Salesse-Côté, director-general of the Arvida Heritage Museum, housed in a soaring Catholic church built decades ago with money deducted directly from workers’ paycheques.
Despite being nestled deep in a “North Canada steppe,” as The New York Times once remarked, Arvida owes its existence to Americans.
Mr. Davis, a pioneer in the commercial uses of aluminum who became the fifth-richest man in the U.S., conceived Arvida and hired American architects to build it.

Although Alcan was spun off as a Canadian company in 1928 amid an anti-trust investigation south of the border, and many of the worker houses were in a French-Canadian vernacular style, American executives continued to run the company and, effectively, the town.

Locals mostly accepted the bargain. Unlike in other corporate communities at the time, the housing stock was well-built and attractive, with modern amenities such as central heating. Instead of setting up a company store selling goods on credit, Alcan encouraged real banks and shops to establish themselves in town. Company-owned cinemas, skating rinks and bowling alleys provided wholesome entertainment.

In an era of dubious planned cities erected in the image of their eccentric founders, this was a success story. By the time Henry Ford’s rubber colony of Fordlandia had devolved into anarchy and been sold to the Brazilian government in the 1940s, Arvida was at its zenith.
“It was a social utopia,” said Ms. Salesse-Côté. “The dream of Arthur Vining Davis was to have his workers stay a long time.”

Alcan’s progressive paternalism had its limits. Worker safety precautions were virtually non-existent, and labour relations could be bruising. A sudden strike in 1941 made the federal government suspect enemy sabotage.

By the Second World War, Arvida was not just a company town, but a strategic cog in the war effort. It had become home to the world’s largest aluminum plant, employing 12,000 workers and cranking out 90 per cent of the aluminum used by the Commonwealth air forces. The factory was surrounded by anti-aircraft guns and protected by some 3,000 servicemen in case of Nazi attack.
“Without Arvida, we might not have had a happy ending,” said Ms. Salesse-Côté.
Arvida and its aluminum plant in 1958. Though its wartime production blitz was long over by then, the plant remained a powerhouse of the Canadian metal industry. Supplied

In 1951, Alcan built a $500-million smelter in Kitimat, B.C., the country’s largest public-private partnership at the time. As chief executive in the late 1970s, Montrealer David Culver doubled down on the city as company headquarters while other firms fled a separatist government.

The relative lack of capacity for transforming aluminum in Canada has left the domestic industry more vulnerable to U.S. tariffs. stories.title: Canada expected to add jobs in October, unemployment rate to remain steady
stories.summary: Economy has faced headwinds with escalation of trade war with U.S.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Some economists are getting worried that a string of job losses in recent months is revealing cracks in the labour market.

Statistics Canada said Friday that the unemployment rate rose two tenths of a point to 6.7 per cent in October. The labour market shed 4,700 jobs last month, the agency said, and more people were also looking for work.

October’s modest decline followed a cumulative loss of 110,000 jobs across September and August. A Reuters poll of economists had expected the economy would bounce back with a gain of 13,600 jobs in October.

“For anyone hoping that October would bring a recovery in the Canadian job market after back-to-back negative surprises, today’s release is a disappointment,” said Sneha Puri, economist with jobs search site Indeed, in a media statement.

Private sector employment fell by 53,000 positions last month, marking the first decline in the segment since February. Employment in the public sector, meanwhile, was up 50,000 positions.

Statscan noted that, ON a year-over-year basis, private sector jobs are still up while the public sector is down.

Employment in the wholesale and retail trade industry has trended down over the past year and the sector led losses in October, shedding 29,000 roles. Transportation and warehousing and food and accommodation also posted losses last month, offset by some gains in construction and education.

Cibc senior economist Andrew Grantham said in an interview that he had expected more of a lift in the October labour market from one-time factors like the Alberta referendum.

While he had been anticipating the jobless rate would tick up in the fourth quarter in the face of tariff-related headwinds, Friday’s employment figures suggest there’s more underlying softness in the jobs market.

“It does look as if we’re seeing some weakness in the labour market outside of those trade-sensitive areas. So that’s a concern for us right now,” Grantham said.

That could dampen expectations for a rebound in job growth in 2027, he added.

The unemployment rate for young workers aged 15 to 24 jumped to 13.7 per cent in October, up 0.7 percentage points from September, as employment edged down and more youth looked for work.
