stories.title: Toronto and Vancouver saw first rent increase in nearly 3 years, report says
stories.summary: The average asking rent for all residential property types in Canada was $2,036 in October, a report from Rentals.CA and Urbanation showed on Thursday.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
Canada’s most expensive housing markets saw their first increase in average asking rents in nearly three years, while rents across Canada continue to fall, new report shows.

The average asking rent for all residential property types in Canada was $2,036 in October, a report from Rentals.CA and Urbanation showed on Thursday.

While this marked the 25 th consecutive month of declines, falling 3.2 per cent compared to October 2025 and 5.4 per cent compared to October 2024, the pace of the decline is slowing.

October saw the smallest annual decline in rents since February this year, the report said.

“The window for cheaper rents is closing in Toronto and Vancouver,” said Shaun Hildebrand, president of Urbanation.

Average asking rents in Canada reached a record high of $2,202 in May 2024. After hitting $2,142 in September 2024, rents have steadily declined across the country.

In Toronto and Vancouver, however, rents appeared to have hit bottom already.

“Rents in Canada’s two largest cities are starting to rise for the first time in nearly three years, driven by declining supply, a trend that will continue,” Hildebrand said.

Vancouver saw rents rise marginally (0.2 per cent) compared to October 2025, the first increase after 34 consecutive months of decline, while Toronto saw a larger increase of 1.6 per cent in average asking rent for apartments and condos, the first increase after 36 consecutive months of decline.

Rents were also up in the nation’s capital, with Ottawa seeing average rents rise 0.3 per cent in October compared to the same period in 2025.

While the window for low rents seems to be closing in the two biggest cities, renters still have an advantage in big cities like Calgary, Edmonton and major GTA markets outside of Toronto, Hildebrand said.

Among the six largest markets in Canada, Calgary posted the largest annual decline in rents (2.4 per cent).

The Greater Toronto Area saw major rent declines in Oakville (7.7 per cent), Markham (5.4 per cent), Vaughan (4.8 per cent) and Mississauga (4.3 per cent).

Condos saw the sharpest decline in rents, with rents falling to $2,048 for all condo types nationally, a drop of 5.5 per cent compared to October 2025. Two-bedroom condos saw an even sharper decline, with a 6.1 per cent drop.

Other secondary housing units, such as houses and townhomes, saw rents fall by six per cent to $2,016.

Purpose-built rents remained the most resilient of all property types, down 2.1 per cent to $2,040.

stories.title: Carney and St-Pierre Plamondon to meet during Francophonie Summit in Cambodia later this month
stories.summary: 'Both agree that an in-person meeting, as soon as possible, is preferable to a virtual meeting,' said a federal source.
stories.author: Catherine Lévesque
stories.content:
Welcome to our new, improved site!

Read a note from our editor-in-chief

'Both agree that an in-person meeting, as soon as possible, is preferable to a virtual meeting,' said a federal source.

Prime Minister Mark Carney arrives at West Block on Parliament Hill on budget day in Ottawa on Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026. (Photo BY Hyungcheol Park/Postmedia) (Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia)

November 5, 2026 at 11:47 a.m.

Ottawa — After days of discussion between their offices, Prime Minister Mark Carney and Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon have agreed to meet in-person during the Francophonie Summit taking place later this month in Phnom Penh, Cambodia.

Carney’s office had reached out to St-Pierre Plamondon’s officials on Monday, proposing two dates for a meeting in November before the summit and one right after. They said the meeting could take place in Montreal or in the Ottawa-Gatineau region.

But St-Pierre Plamondon insisted the meeting should take place in Quebec City.

He said he was respecting a provincial law — An Act to Grant Ville de Québec National Capital Status and Increase Its Autonomy and Powers — which claims that the capital of the province of Quebec is the “ideal and preferred setting for important meetings.”

But Carney’s office has claimed his packed schedule and prior international commitments wouldn’t allow him to travel to Quebec City before December.

On Wednesday, St-Pierre Plamondon said he was ready to wait until then.

“We’ll take the first date in Quebec (City),” he told reporters.

The premier also revealed there was a chance that he and Carney would have a conversation at the upcoming meeting of francophone countries taking place Nov. 15-16 which both men will be attending. He said both their teams were still “talking.”

On Thursday, their teams in Ottawa and Quebec City confirmed to National Post that Carney and St-Pierre Plamondon will be meeting at the Francophonie Summit.

“We are open to the idea of another working meeting in Quebec City at the appropriate time,” they added.

Louis Hamann, a former Quebec diplomat and former senior Liberal adviser in Ottawa, had suggested in a recent interview that maybe, if their agendas don’t align, both politicians should simply take the time to meet at the Francophonie Summit.

“That would allow Carney to avoid having to sort of bow to this Quebec City location meeting, if you will,” he said.

Jonathan Kalles, who served as Quebec adviser to former prime minister Justin Trudeau, suggested in another recent interview that “it would be weird to have to travel halfway around the world to meet each other.”

However, it wouldn’t be the first time that politicians from the same country would travel across the world to meet for the first time.

In 2012, former Quebec premier Pauline Marois met former prime minister Stephen Harper for the first time in Kinshasa, Democratic Republic of the Congo, for the Francophonie Summit. Marois said their first meeting was“very positive, very cordial.”

stories.title: Western Autonomous and Intelligent Systems Hub builds on cutting-edge research
stories.summary: will advance technologies in artificial intelligence (AI), robotics, sensing, cybersecurity.
stories.author: Jeff Renaud
stories.content:
Autonomous systems are machines that can sense their surroundings, make decisions and act with limited human intervention. They are expected to play an increasingly important role in Canada, with uses ranging from smart manufacturing and infrastructure inspection to environmental monitoring and space situational awareness.

For these systems to function, every part must work together: the sensors, software, networks and the platforms themselves. And the people developing each element must work together, too.

The new Western Autonomous and Intelligent Systems Hub brings researchers from the Faculties of Engineering and Science together to do just that, developing and testing new technologies in artificial intelligence (AI), robotics, sensing, communications and cybersecurity through shared facilities, testing environments and research platforms.

“An autonomous system is not just one piece of technology. It’s an interconnected network of technologies. The opportunity now is to connect our expertise, bring researchers together and tackle problems that require all those capabilities working at once,” said Miriam Capretz, professor of software engineering and director of the new hub. “Western has deep expertise in robotics and hardware, but what sets us apart is our strength in AI and software, the secure communications that make autonomous systems trustworthy.”

Computer science professor Zubair Fadlullah and electrical and computer engineering professor Soodeh Nikan serve as associate directors of the hub.

Unlike traditional machines such as a robot on a factory’s assembly line, programmed to repeat a specific task, autonomous systems like self-driving vehicles can perform different tasks, make decisions and adapt to changing conditions on their own. They use sensors, software and AI to understand what’s happening around them, assess their options and determine the best course of action.

Autonomous platforms, the machines that put these capabilities into action, are the visible part of the hub, but Western’s distinctive advantage lies in the intelligence layers that run across the entire system. Those are the learning algorithms, autonomy software, secure communications and trustworthy AI that autonomous systems depend on.

Western Autonomous and Intelligent Systems Hub director Miriam Capretz and associate directors Soodeh Nikan and Zubair Fadlullah in the lab with an autonomous vehicle system. (Christopher Kindratsky/Western Communications)

Researchers across Western have expertise in many of the technologies that underpin autonomous and intelligent systems, including sensor fusion, computer vision, data analytics, signal processing, aerial systems and wireless communications, including emerging 5G and 6G networks.

An autonomous platform needs to communicate with other systems and operate securely. Sensor fusion allows information from multiple sensors to be combined, helping a system build a more complete picture of its environment. Bringing together capabilities like these, along with expertise in AI, communications and cybersecurity into a functioning system requires collaboration that spans laboratories, departments and faculties.

The Western Autonomous and Intelligent Systems Hub is intended to support collaboration through shared research infrastructure and opportunities to develop and test integrated autonomous systems.

“Autonomous systems are an essential component of modern industry and society,” said Western Engineering dean Ken Coley. “I’m thrilled to say that Western has built an impressive capacity in this area over the last several years and I’m really excited to see the impact of the hub.”

An Autonomous Systems Core Facility will be part of Western’s new engineering building, currently under construction and set to open in 2027, providing a shared space for hub members to develop, test and refine new technologies. Complete with a ground floor, high-bay vehicle area and simulation lab, it will serve as a premier centre for innovation, testing and evaluation for researchers and industry partners across Ontario and Canada.

Open-source autonomous platforms – including vehicles for ground applications and drones for aerial ones – will also be developed for researchers to test new technologies. By providing shared hardware and software, the platforms will allow teams to build on existing work rather than starting from scratch with every project.

“The Faculty of Science is excited to continue collaborating with engineering researchers on this exciting hub. Our computer science faculty bring invaluable expertise on AI, network security, computing and machine learning that is essential to advancing this research. Autonomous devices are also crucial to monitoring and protecting our natural environment,” said Western Science dean Matt Davison.

In software engineering, intelligent systems are often built in layers, allowing individual components to be reused rather than rebuilt from scratch. The same principle can advance autonomous systems, where shared software for interpreting sensor data, communicating with other devices and making decisions can be adapted for different machines and tasks, including ground vehicles and aerial drones.

Capretz has designed and developed software in this way for more than 30 years. Her research, both in academic and industry settings, examines how software engineering can help different technologies work together and adapt to new applications.

For one large-scale project, she helped develop cloud-based software that uses data from building sensors to identify energy-use patterns, predict future consumption and flag potential problems. This gives building managers a clearer picture of how their facilities are performing and helps them make better decisions about energy use and maintenance.

“You don’t want to hard-code everything you create for just one particular use,” said Capretz. “If you have a common layer for sensing, communications or decision-making, you can take those pieces and use them in different applications. That makes it easier to build on what you already have rather than starting anew every time.”

This approach also makes it easier to bring new research into an existing platform, giving teams a common foundation on which to test and develop additional capabilities.

Autonomous and intelligent systems operating on land, in the air and at sea are expected to play an increasingly important role in Canada’s security and sovereignty, and in civilian applications from environmental and resource monitoring to infrastructure inspection.

Western’s existing relationship with German defence and technology company TKMS offers an example of how the university’s expertise can contribute to complex, real-world challenges. TKMS, the preferred supplier for the Canadian Patrol Submarine Project, has named Western a core academic partner in itsCanadian Defence and Dual-Use Innovation Ecosystem (CDDE), alongside the University of British Columbia and Dalhousie University, and the three universities are already at work on a TKMS-funded Arctic air-sea communications pilot.

“The TKMS project shows what’s possible when you bring the right people and technologies together to work on a problem,” said Capretz.

The partnership is exploring communications in challenging environments, where unreliable connections and harsh conditions create technical challenges. Drawing on Western’s strengths in AI, cybersecurity and communications, the project aims to develop systems that can operate within these conditions, with applications extending beyond defence.

For example, autonomous systems are increasingly being developed for infrastructure monitoring, environmental sensing, agriculture, resource management, smart manufacturing and transportation where systems must interpret complex environments and make decisions with limited human intervention.

Western’s hub gives researchers a shared environment to develop scalable, reusable technologies, while industry partners can add proprietary components for specific applications.

Western is home to a range of facilities and research platforms that support autonomous systems research, including the Wind Engineering, Energy and Environment (WindEEE) Research Institute, the Institute for Earth and Space Exploration, the Environmental Sciences Field Station, Elginfield Observatory and the Advanced Facility for Avian Research (AFAR).

The hub will make it easier for researchers from these laboratories and across different disciplines to work more closely together on complex projects. It will also give students hands-on experience with autonomous systems and the chance to collaborate across different fields of study.

“Our vision is to make it easier for researchers across Western to bring their strengths together around challenges that no single discipline can address alone,” said Florentine Strzelczyk, provost and vice-president (academic). “Through shared facilities and research platforms, we are creating the conditions for sustained collaboration across faculties and with industry partners. This hub puts that vision into practice, connecting expertise and giving students opportunities to help turn discoveries into real-world solutions.”

Learn more about how Western isturning curiosity into solutions.

“The TKMS project shows what’s possible when you bring the right people and technologies together to work on a problem,” said Capretz.

The partnership is exploring communications in challenging environments, where unreliable connections and harsh conditions create technical challenges. Drawing on Western’s strengths in AI, cybersecurity and communications, the project aims to develop systems that can operate within these conditions, with applications extending beyond defence.

For example, autonomous systems are increasingly being developed for infrastructure monitoring, environmental sensing, agriculture, resource management, smart manufacturing and transportation where systems must interpret complex environments and make decisions with limited human intervention.
Western’s hub gives researchers a shared environment to develop scalable, reusable technologies, while industry partners can add proprietary components for specific applications.
Connecting Western’s expertise

Western is home to a range of facilities and research platforms that support autonomous systems research, including the Wind Engineering, Energy and Environment (WindEEE) Research Institute, the Institute for Earth and Space Exploration, the Environmental Sciences Field Station, Elginfield Observatory and the Advanced Facility for Avian Research (AFAR).

The hub will make it easier for researchers from these laboratories and across different disciplines to work more closely together on complex projects. It will also give students hands-on experience with autonomous systems and the chance to collaborate across different fields of study.

“Our vision is to make it easier for researchers across Western to bring their strengths together around challenges that no single discipline can address alone,” said Florentine Strzelczyk, provost and vice-president (academic). “Through shared facilities and research platforms, we are creating the conditions for sustained collaboration across faculties and with industry partners. This hub puts that vision into practice, connecting expertise and giving students opportunities to help turn discoveries into real-world solutions.”

stories.title: Mexican judge arrested in Ryan Wedding case. U.S. says he took $2 million bribe to free Canadian right-hand man
stories.summary: Mexican federal judge Luis Benítez Alcántara, 49, of Mexico City, was arrested on Sunday in Colombia.
stories.author: Calvi Leon
stories.content:
A Mexican judge has been arrested on U.S. charges that he accepted a $2-million bribe to grant bail to Ryan Wedding ‘s alleged second-in-command, the U.S. Justice Department announced Thursday.

Federal judge Luis Benítez Alcántara, 49, of Mexico City, was arrested on Sunday in Colombia and charged with nine counts of being an accessory after the fact following the surprising release of Canadian Andrew Clark in early 2025.

Clark, 36, was initially arrested in Guadalajara, Jalisco, Mexico, ON Oct. 8, 2024, amid a massive crackdown on a drug-trafficking empire allegedly controlled by Wedding. The ex-Olympic snowboarder is accused of leading one of the largest cocaine pipelines into Canada, via the U.S., Mexico and Colombia, and, alongside Clark, orchestrating murders on enemies or rivals of the organization.

Benítez Alcántara was serving as the district judge in Mexico City responsible for overseeing Clark’s extradition proceedings.

Between November 2024 and February 2025, the indictment says, Clark funneled $2.75 million US through intermediaries to secure his release.

Clark was bailed in Mexico on Feb. 24, 2025 — the same day Benítez Alcántara allegedly received the $2-million bribe payment.

Canadian Andrew Clark, left, is accused of being the right-hand man to alleged drug lord Ryan Wedding, seen right after his high-profile FBI arrest.

Clark was re-arrested days later and then transferred to the U.S. alongside 28 other alleged drug traffickers in an unprecedented handover .

Mexican journalist and crime analyst Luis H. Nájera told the Star he wasn’t surprised to learn that a Mexican judge May have accepted a bribe to facilitate the release of an alleged organized crime member.

“This is, unfortunately, one of the most endemic issues the judicial system in Mexico has,” he said, noting that sometimes corrupt deals are secured via bribes, and other times through threats.

After sweeping changes to Mexico’s judicial system, which replaced appointment-based judges with ones elected by the public, Nájera worries the issue will become more frequent.

What’s unusual with the case of Benítez Alcántara, he noted, is that the judge was arrested in Colombia, not Mexico. Why exactly he was in that country, authorities have not said.

The FBI and the U.S. Attorney’s Office declined to answer questions about the arrest or whether additional charges are expected against the unknown intermediaries referenced in the indictment. The documents appear to list multiple defendants, but any information relating to their identities is redacted.

At the time of Clark’s release in Mexico, Wedding, 45, was one of the Fbi’s top 10 most wanted fugitives.

The men are accused of running a billion-dollar criminal enterprise that worked with the Sinaloa Cartel and ordered multiple murders around the globe — including the mistaken identity killings of an innocent Indian couple in Caledon, Ont., and the assassination of a federal witness who helped dismantle part of the network.

In an early 2025 news conference announcing a $10 million reward for Wedding’s capture, law enforcement officials revealed that his lieutenant, Clark, had been “somewhat inexplicably” released on bail in Mexico and that American authorities had to intervene.

“Crooked public officials, no matter where they are, who assist drug traffickers operating here at home will face justice in the United States,” U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche said in the news release.

Benítez Alcántara has served as a federal judge for six years. He was thrust into the global spotlight in 2023 following a controversial decision to acquit a man accused of using Pegasus spyware on prominent Mexican journalist Carmen Aristegui.

Aristegui was recognized for her investigations exposing government corruption and abuse of power in Mexico. In 2014, she and a team of reporters broke the so-called “Casa Blanca” scandal, exposing how the wife of then-President Enrique Peña Nieto purchased a luxury mansion from a firm that was awarded lucrative contracts with his administration.

The story, which cost Aristegui her job, triggered an intense and sustained harassment campaign against her, from break-ins at her office to personal threats and repeated attempts to hack her devices.

In his decision to acquit Juan Carlos García Rivera, Benítez Alcántara acknowledged that Aristegui’s phone was infected with the notorious spyware developed by the Israeli cyber-intelligence firm NSO Group, but said prosecutors didn’t present sufficient evidence that the accused was responsible.

If convicted of the charges announced Thursday, Benítez Alcántara faces a maximum sentence of 15 years in federal prison on each count.

After his transfer into U.S. custody, court documents suggest Clark became a co-operating witness for the FBI and RCMP, working with the lead investigators to gather enough evidence in what would become phase two of the Giant Slalom investigation. (Authorities named the probe after the snowboarding event Wedding competed in during the 2002 Olympic Games in Salt Lake City.)

Clark’s knowledge of the alleged drug operation, statements to investigators and encrypted messages seized from his phone helped prosecutors secure a second federal indictment charging Wedding and several others in connection with the Jan. 31, 2025, murder of the federal witness, Montreal-born Jonathan Acebedo Garcia, in Colombia.

After more than a year on the run, Wedding was arrested in Mexico and brought into U.S. custody in January 2026. He has pleaded not guilty to 17 federal felony counts of drug‑trafficking, running a criminal enterprise, murder and attempted murder.

In total, more than 30 people have been charged in connection with the case.

Wedding is scheduled for two trials in March and October 2027, although it’s possible the dates change due to the complexity of the case.

stories.title: Man dies after his arrest for killing Montreal woman during work video call
stories.summary: A 33-year-old man accused of fatally attacking a 45-year-old woman while she was on a Zoom call in Montreal earlier this year has died.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
A 33-year-old man accused of fatally attacking a 45-year-old Montreal woman while she was on a work video conference call has died.

Quebec’s coroner office told Global News Thursday it was notified on Nov. 2 that Youcef Moussaoui was dead. An investigation is underway to determine the cause of death.

Moussaoui was arrested last month in the Ville-Marie borough and charged with first-degree murder in the death of Leila Ben Salem , an employee of the Canada Revenue Agency.

Emergency crews were called on Sept. 22 to an apartment building on René-Lévesque Boulevard East near St-Christophe Street after receiving a request to check on a resident. When officers arrived, they found the woman unresponsive inside the apartment.

Police initially classified the death as suspicious before the case was transferred to the homicide unit. Sources later confirmed to Global News that the woman was on a work-related call when she was attacked.

Investigators remained at the scene the following day, examining the apartment building, processing the crime scene and reviewing surveillance footage as they worked to determine the circumstances surrounding the woman’s death.

Police said the killing was not related to intimate partner violence. They said evidence gathered during the investigation, including the alleged motive, will be made public during the court process.

stories.title: Police search for 3rd suspect in Mississauga arsons that sent 18 to hospital
stories.summary: The two fires happened in an apartment building in September and resulted in injuries to a police officer and a firefighter.
stories.author: Olivia Bowden
stories.content:
Peel Police said Thursday that two suspects have been arrested and a third is wanted in connection with two arsons at a Mississauga apartment building, an incident that sent 18 residents to the hospital for smoke inhalation.

The fires, which happened overnight from Sept. 20 to Sept 21, also resulted in injuries to a police officer and a firefighter . Police said the fires were deliberately set in a third-floor hallway of an apartment building in the area of Lakeshore Road West and Southdown Road.

Anyone with information on Varga’s whereabouts is asked to contact police.

stories.title: Footlab World to bring AI-powered soccer to White Oaks Mall
stories.summary: Plans to expand White Oak's Mall will 'future-proof' the iconic South London shopping destination, a spokesper...
stories.author: Ben McFadden
stories.content:
Plans to expand White Oak’s Mall will ‘future-proof’ the iconic South London shopping destination, a spokesperson said.

With Ikea recently opening in the former Hudson Bay space, the mall is now preparing for the opening of a high-tech soccer training space backed by world famous soccer player Christiano Ronaldo.

Tarik Kasem, General Manager Westdell Developments. (Benjamin McFadden/XFM News)

Portuguese-owned Footlab World is an Artificial Intelligence (AI) powered indoor soccer training facility with an indoor soccer pitch, kick practice simulators, and an equipment store. The set-up is similar to indoor golf simulators where professional players and hobbyists alike can have their kick scanned in real time.

“We believe that the traffic is going to be very intense,” said Tarik Kasem, the General Manager of Westdell Development. “There is going to be a lot of interest in checking it out and hopefully they come back for more,” said Kasem.

Other features coming to the South London location include, Swiss Chalet, Wing Stop and a Marriot hotel. Rough estimate opening date is set for spring of 2027.

This comes after Westdell Developments took over the mall and the Hudson’s Bay location closing down.

“The departure of Hudson’s Bay left a pretty wide gap in terms of our marketplace and community,” said Sarah Imrie, the marketing manager for Westdell Developments.

Sarah Imire, Marketing Manager with Westdell Development (Benjamin McFadden/XFM News)

“We are definitely filling that gap, between the 2 residential towers and Splitsville joining this project,” said Irmie.

As the mall expands so do the bus routes to the destination, with Rapid Transit bus lines preparing to setup close to the mall.

‘The south end community has always stood out and White Oaks has always been focused more on being a community hub,” said Irmie.

“White Oaks has been a part of the community for 50 years and we plan these changes will ensure we can do that for another 50 years,” said Irmie.

stories.title: Serious injuries reported after two-vehicle crash in Central Elgin
stories.summary: Around 9:30 a.m., emergency crews responded to a collision involving a pickup truck and a passenger vehicle at the intersection of Quaker Road and Elm Line.
stories.content:
A two-vehicle crash in Central Elgin sent two people to hospital and closed a section of Quaker Road on Wednesday.

Around 9:30 a.m., emergency crews responded to a collision involving a pickup truck and a passenger vehicle at the intersection of Quaker Road and Elm Line.

Police say the driver of the passenger vehicle was taken to hospital with serious injuries. A passenger in the same vehicle was also taken to hospital with minor injuries.

The driver of the pickup truck was not injured.

Quaker Road was closed in the area while emergency crews responded and investigators examined the scene.

Ontario Provincial Police continue to investigate the crash and say updates will be provided as more information becomes available.

stories.title: Board president raises concerns over delays in city’s response to troubled Tolpuddle co-op
stories.summary: The fire monitor still erroneously beeps in the lobby of the Tolpuddle Housing Co-op more than six months after London city council endorsed a plan for city staff to take a more active role in the troubled housing complex.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
The fire monitor still erroneously beeps in the lobby of the Tolpuddle Housing Co-op more than six months after London city council endorsed a plan for city staff to take a more active role in the troubled housing complex.

Board President Jo Dee Phoenix claims support promised by the municipality hasn’t materialized quickly enough to address safety concerns in the building that houses low-income Londoners, seniors, the disabled, and families.

“We reached out for help. We’re told we’re going to get the help, but the help never arrives. It’s very, very disappointing. And it is urgent [because] there are people in this community that live in fear,” Phoenix said.

On Wednesday, CTV News received no response from city officials to an inquiry about progress on their plan to address the condition, operations, and governance of the building.

Troubles exposed in March

On March 5, CTV News was granted access inside the 134-unit apartment building and townhouse complex, that includes 109 rent-geared-to-income (RGI) units, near the corner of Adelaide and King streets.

At the time, vulnerable tenants found themselves facing a sharp rise in trespassing, drug dealing, and vandalism.

Hallways and stairwells were covered in graffiti and holes had been kicked in the drywall.

Security systems to control entry into the building had been smashed, and there was a long list of fire code violations.

At the time, 15 RGI units had been so severely damaged by their previous tenants that they were uninhabitable without repairs that the co-op couldn’t afford.

Phoenix blamed city hall’s decision to place high-needs tenants with active addictions in a building that was never designed to offer adequate supports.

In April, council responded by endorsing a plan to declare Tolpuddle a “Project in Difficulty”, allowing the city to take a more active role.

Delayed request for progress report

But Phoenix suggests the promised follow-through has fallen short, “They were going to give us support. They were going to do audits. They were going to do security audits. They were going to do all kinds of things. They were going to report and appoint a mentor to the board. None of that has happened.”

On Sept. 24, Ward 4 Coun. Susan Stevenson submitted a letter to the Community and Protective Services (Caps) Committee requesting an update about:

the recommended Cpted Security Audit the appointment of a Mentor to assist the Board of Directors the release of the funding for security enhancements and maintenance previously reported to Council the appointment of an interim receiver under the Housing Services Act instead of the alternative remedies requested by the Board of Directors the status of the appeal made by the Board of Directors regarding the above appointment any third-party investigations involving the Housing Division

Instead, council referred Stevenson’s letter to the next meeting of the Caps Committee.

However, the municipal election pushed the next scheduled committee meeting to Nov. 30, and any recommendation from the committee won’t be finalized until the following council meeting on Dec. 15, the last meeting of the year.

Next steps for Tolpuddle

Phoenix says the board continues to authorize repairs that have overseen the restoration of some severely damaged parts of the building, but she claims the fire code violations have not been fully resolved.

She also credits her board for the restoration of some RGI units.

But she emphasizes the co-op does not have enough money to maintain the heightened security and repair costs.

“[City officials] have provided financial help with some big payments that we have to make for insurance and stuff like that. They have done that,” she explained. “They refuse to give us one cent for operations.”

A Request for Proposals (RFP) posted on the city’s Bids and Tenders website seeks a company to act as an Interim Receiver that will temporarily take control of many aspects of the housing co-op for the next 180 days.

The receiver would stabilize operations and governance, while developing a transition strategy for after its role concludes.

Phoenix asserted, “The housing division is trying to wipe their hands of the responsibility and hand it over to somebody else, because perhaps Tolpuddle is a little bit too advanced for them.”

A Request for Proposals (RFP) posted on the city’s Bids and Tenders website seeks a company to act as an Interim Receiver that will temporarily take control of many aspects of the housing co-op for the next 180 days.
The receiver would stabilize operations and governance, while developing a transition strategy for after its role concludes.
Phoenix asserted, “The housing division is trying to wipe their hands of the responsibility and hand it over to somebody else, because perhaps Tolpuddle is a little bit too advanced for them.”

stories.title: Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk begins 2nd spacewalk
stories.summary: Joshua Kutryk and Nasa astronaut Anil Menon stepped into the vacuum of space this morning after undergoing lengthy and detailed preparations with the help of their support team.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk is venturing outside the International Space Station for his second spacewalk in two weeks.

Kutryk and NASA astronaut Anil Menon stepped into the vacuum of space this morning after undergoing lengthy and detailed preparations with the help of their support team.

Kutryk was first to emerge, a red stripe on the legs of his space suit setting him apart from his colleague.

On Oct. 29, Kutryk became the fifth Canadian to perform the feat when he and NASA astronaut Anil Menon successfully installed seven of eight new solar arrays needed to upgrade the station’s power capacity.

The astronauts are installing the eighth and final solar array today on the starboard side of the truss, which serves as the station’s structural backbone.

The Canadian Space Agency says spacewalks are among the most difficult and dangerous tasks for astronauts but are needed to repair or install equipment or carry out manual work.

Before Kutryk, the last Canadian to perform a spacewalk was David Saint-Jacques in 2019.

Kutryk and his SpaceX Crew-13 crew members took off for the International Space Station on Oct. 1 for a mission expected to last six months.

MIDDLESEX COUNTY, ON – Middlesex County is inviting residents, builders, and members of the agricultural community to participate in a public survey to help inform the development of a new Build Ready Housing Design Program for Additional Residential Units (ARUs).

The program is supported by federal funding awarded to the Municipality of North Middlesex through the Government of Canada's Housing Accelerator Fund (HAF). The funding, confirmed by the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC), is part of a $42-million reinvestment in 32 high-performing municipalities across Canada to support continued progress in housing development.

Through a coordinated partnership with Middlesex County, the program will provide pre-approved housing designs that can be used by residents, builders, and the agricultural community, with the program being rolled out to all eight local municipalities across Middlesex County.

The public survey will help identify local preferences and design considerations to ensure the program reflects the needs of the communities it is intended to serve. Feedback received will help guide the development of a housing design catalogue featuring practical and adaptable housing options.

The public survey") will remain open until November 27, 2026.

What is an Additional Residential Unit?

An Additional Residential Unit (ARU) is a self-contained dwelling located on the same property as a principal residence. While ARUs can take many forms, including basement apartments, additions to existing homes, and garage suites, the six draft designs for Middlesex County are all detached units.

ARUs provide flexible housing options for families, seniors, caregivers, and renters while making efficient use of existing neighbourhoods and infrastructure.

What is the Build Ready Program?

The Build Ready Program aims to make it easier and more affordable for property owners to create additional housing by providing access to pre-reviewed building designs.

By selecting a design from the catalogue, homeowners can save time and costs associated with developing plans while helping to increase the supply of housing throughout Middlesex County.

Have Your Say

Residents are encouraged to review the draft designs and complete the online survey by November 27, 2026.

Survey Link: https://www.surveymonkey.com/r/8DTN9DN")

Feedback collected through the survey will help inform the final design catalogue.

stories.title: Balloon blowing kits sold by Walmart.CA recalled over chemical hazard
stories.summary: The agency said the kits, distributed by the Chinese companies Tojiyi and PawBabyBloom, were previously available on the Walmart.CA Marketplace.
stories.author: Rachel Morgan
stories.content:
Health Canada is advising the public to stop using balloon blowing kits immediately due to a chemical hazard.

The agency said the kits, distributed by the Chinese companies Tojiyi and PawBabyBloom, were previously available on the Walmart.CA Marketplace.

Balloon blowing kits containing solvents are banned in Canada under the Toys Regulations of the Canada Consumer Product Safety Act, Health Canada said.

The solvent mixture comes in a tube that is squeezed on the end of a plastic straw. Children can then blow through the straw to create a bubble.

“The safety concern is that blowing the balloons exposes a child to inhaling the vapours of any solvents present,” the Health Canada recall states. “If children blow this type of solvent containing balloon for extended periods they May experience early symptoms of central nervous system depression or dysfunction, including euphoria, hallucinations, dizziness, and difficulties with coordination of voluntary movements.”

Walmart.CA Marketplace reported that six units of the affected products were sold in Canada, according to the health agency. The products have since been removed from sale online.

Health Canada said it has contacted the foreign third-party sellers and is advising consumers to stop using the products immediately.

To date, no incidents or injuries related to these products have been reported, the agency said.

stories.title: Cadet captain unable to walk after ‘senseless attack’ during Hamilton poppy sale
stories.summary: A man who suffered life-altering injuries during an incident involving cadets selling poppies underwent same-day spinal surgery and is now in rehabilitation, his son says.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
A man who suffered life-altering injuries during an incident involving air cadets selling poppies underwent same-day spinal surgery and is now in rehabilitation, his son says.

Capt. Kenneth Kunkel cannot walk for the “foreseeable future,” according to a statement from his son, Christopher Kunkel, who said the family has been “decimated” by the “senseless attack.”

The 59-year-old was supervising the cadets outside a restaurant in Hamilton, Ont., ON Nov. 1 when two youths allegedly approached and blew an air horn directly into their ears, Hamilton police said.

Police said Kunkel followed the youths into the restaurant and confronted them. During the ensuing struggle, an adult woman intervened and allegedly assaulted him, causing him to fall, before one youth allegedly struck him several times.

Christopher said his father’s legs buckled and he lost movement during the confrontation after the woman allegedly became involved. He said Kenneth told bystanders that he needed help and could not move his legs.

“After an unforgettable Halloween evening where Captain Kenneth Kunkel walked his four grandchildren around the neighbourhood to visit friends and neighbours, we are decimated by the senseless attack that May have forever robbed four kids of their grandfather’s playful, loving tendencies,” Christopher said.

His father has been helping cadets for almost 20 years, he said, adding Kenneth was instrumental in his own journey through the cadet program and into service with the Canadian Armed Forces.

Christopher said his father’s work also influenced former cadets who later joined municipal police services, the RCMP and the military, or became more involved in their communities.

“Even as he got older, Captain Kenneth Kunkel would physically prepare for weeks in advance so he could train with cadets and be a role model as they underwent fitness evaluations as part of the cadet program,” he said.

A crowdfunding campaign has been established to help financially support Kunkel’s recovery.

A 12-year-old boy was arrested Sunday and was charged with assault level one as well as aggravated assault. A 48-year-old woman was arrested Tuesday and charged with aggravated assault.

Police did not announce charges against the second youth.

The investigation is ongoing.

Anyone with information is asked to contact police.

stories.title: Two more soldiers injured in CFB Wainwright fire out of hospital
stories.summary: The Department of National Defence also says four of the 25 soldiers who remain hospitalized have been relocated to centres in British Columbia and Ontario.
stories.author: Fakiha Baig
stories.content:
Two more soldiers injured in a deadly fire at an Alberta military base have been discharged from hospital.

The Department of National Defence also says four of the 25 soldiers who remain hospitalized have been relocated to centres in British Columbia and Ontario, so they can receive treatment closer to their families.

The update comes a little more than two weeks after a fierce wind whipped a grass fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright onto troops in a training exercise.

The Oct. 17 blaze killed four and left 39 wounded, many with serious burns.

Officials previously said 13 were in critical condition.

A total of 14 have now been released from hospital.

“Recovery will look different for each injured person and their family. Some may face a long journey ahead, but they will not face it alone,” said a news release.

“Ongoing support and services remain available to injured personnel, their families, and all CAF members as they continue to navigate the effects of this tragedy.”

Three separate investigations are looking into the fire.

stories.title: Southwestern Public Health approves move to centralized Woodstock facility by 2027
stories.summary: The health unit’s board of health has approved a move to 712 Peel St., bringing services currently spread across three Woodstock locations under one roof.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
Southwestern Public Health says it plans to consolidate its Woodstock operations into a single location by 2027.

The health unit’s board of health has approved a move to 712 Peel St., bringing services currently spread across three Woodstock locations under one roof.

Southwestern Public Health currently operates from offices at 410 Buller St. and 93 Graham St., as well as leased dental space at the Oxford County Community Health Centre.

The move is expected to take place in late summer 2027. As a tenant, the health unit said it will occupy about half of the building, while the remainder will continue to be used independently by the property owner.

The board struck a special building committee in 2023 to explore options for consolidating operations, including new construction, leased space and other development opportunities.

The committee selected the Peel Street site, citing its location, functionality and value.

“This central site offers an efficient use of existing public sector space that is currently underused,” Bernia Martin, chair of the Southwestern Public Health Board of Health, said in a statement.

“It keeps public health services local, with a more practical approach to delivering those services to our clients.”

Renovations are scheduled to begin this fall, with completion anticipated in late summer 2027.

The health unit says it will provide updates to the community as planning for the move progresses.

stories.title: 1 in 3 teens face dating violence, and doctors should be on alert: pediatric society
stories.summary: The Canadian Paediatric Society is urging doctors to talk to teen patients about healthy relationships and dating violence. In new guidance issued Thursday, the society said one-third of teens in Canada experience physical, psychological, sexual or technology-related abuse — including stalking — in relationships. Dating violence among teens is not new, but…
stories.author: Lucas Casaletto
stories.content:
The Canadian Paediatric Society is urging doctors to talk to teen patients about healthy relationships and dating violence.

In new guidance issued Thursday, the society said one-third of teens in Canada experience physical, psychological, sexual or technology-related abuse — including stalking — in relationships.

Dating violence among teens is not new, but technology like texting or social media can facilitate abusive behaviour, such as teens tracking their partners or forbidding them from communicating with friends, said Dr. Megan Harrison, chair of the society’s adolescent health committee, in an interview.

“Those types of behaviours happen to adults as well. So not just teens, but the difference is an adolescent is still, you know, forming their own identity,” she said.

“So it’s a more vulnerable time for things like that to be occurring.”

The guidance says health-care providers can normalize talking about healthy and unhealthy relationships by routinely bringing up the topic during adolescent patient visits.

“The more places where teens can feel comfortable to ask questions about relationships and to know that it’s something that they can bring up in a safe place … the better we’ll be able to prevent these unhealthy situations,” said Harrison, who is a pediatrician in the division of adolescent medicine at the Children’s Hospital of Eastern Ontario in Ottawa.

Harrison emphasized that doctors don’t need to have answers if a teen patient discloses a problematic relationship, but are providing a safe, non-judgmental space and then connecting them to other resources in the community as needed.

“You can really do a whole lot of good in actually what ends up being a really short period of time,” she said.

The guidance recommends doctors talk to teen patients alone during part of their visits and assure them that their conversation is confidential, unless the physician is immediately worried for their safety or the safety of someone else.

It also says doctors should share educational resources about healthy relationships and teen dating violence that their patient can keep or share with friends. The guidance provides an example for health-care providers on how to start that conversation.

“A lot of dating relationships are great experiences. But some patients have shared that they have experienced situations in their relationships that made them feel uncomfortable or even scared,” the sample script says.

“We now talk to all our patients about their relationships because they can impact health. We also provide education on this topic because it is likely you or someone you know could use it.”

If the teen discloses problematic behaviour in a relationship, the health-care provider should support them by thanking them for their trust and connecting them with other resources in the community that can help.

In some cases, that can include taking the first step with the patient, Harrison said.

“If the youth feels comfortable at that time, maybe I make a phone call with the youth in the office. Maybe I help them make an appointment if that’s what they’d like, or I sit there with them while they make the phone call, or we open up the web page together.”

If the patient is going to access resources later on their own, the guidance advises discussing the possibility that an abusive partner May track the teen’s online activity and asking if printed materials would be a safer option.

Some teens are at increased risk for dating violence, including those who are homeless or living in poverty, gender-diverse youth, Black and Indigenous female teens, and young people living in care systems, the guidance says.

stories.title: Merlot from the Okanagan deserves some spotlight. Here are three bottles to try
stories.summary: The underrated red wine is consistently one of the best categories from the region, say winemakers
stories.author: Christopher Waters
stories.content:
Although merlot has played an important role in the evolution of British Columbia’s wine industry, it’s less celebrated among winemakers than more expressive red varieties, such as pinot noir, cabernet franc or syrah.

In the 1990s and early 2000s, merlot gained favour among B.C. wineries because it ripens earlier than cabernet franc and cabernet sauvignon, making it a more reliable choice for the Okanagan’s relatively short growing season. Despite its role in producing some of British Columbia’s best bottles, merlot remains an underrated variety, according to Evan Saunders, winemaker at Blasted Church since 2017.

“I don’t think it gets the respect that it should,” he says. “Merlot is one of the most consistent reds that we produce in the valley.”

Saunders uses merlot to produce red blends with playful names, such as Big Bang Theory and Nectar of the Gods, as well as single variety examples. “Who doesn’t like its plummy, jammy character, with chocolate and coffee and everything else you get vintage in and vintage out,” he wonders.

Nevertheless, merlot has yet to find its place in the spotlight. Saunders wonders if it’s too successful to be taken seriously.

Before back-to-back cold events in 2022 and 2025 caused widespread crop and vine losses, it was British Columbia’s most widely planted grape, covering nearly 753 hectares, or more than 14.5 per cent of the province’s total vineyard acreage. In the aftermath, grape growers have been replanting damaged vineyards with varieties, such as pinot noir, chardonnay and gamay, which they hope will reduce the threat of frigid temperatures. (Winegrowers of British Columbia plans to release an up-to-date vine census next year that will reflect the changing face of its vineyards.)

Saunders says exploring alternative grapes helps determine what will be successful in vineyards in the Okanagan and other parts of the province. Blasted Church planted nebbiolo near the winery in 2023 and has purchased other Italian grape varieties, including refosco, teroldego, and lagrein, from a grower in the Similkameen.

Italian grapes are well-suited to the increasing temperatures experienced in the southern Okanagan, he explains. (Saunders also produces a tart and refreshing rosé from blaufränkisch, a Slovenian grape variety planted in 1996 on what is now the winery’s estate vineyard in Okanagan Falls.)

“Just because the Bordeaux varieties were planted first doesn’t mean we have to stick with them entirely,” he says. “But merlot is always going to have a place.”

Tony Holler, owner of Poplar Grove in Penticton, believes merlot is enjoying renewed interest among consumers. “Our merlot sells out before our cabernet franc,” he says.

In addition to producing a merlot under its own label, Poplar Grove uses the variety in its flagship red blend, Legacy, alongside cabernet sauvignon, petit verdot, cabernet franc and malbec. The proportions of each grape vary depending on the vintage.

Merlot is also a regular component of Poplar Grove’s annual rosé blend.

Here are three Okanagan wines that display merlot’s star power.

Blasted Church Merlot 2022 (Canada), $34

Produced with merlot grapes grown in Blasted Church’s estate vineyard on the Skaka Bench appellation, this smooth and concentrated red wine offers a charming mix of savoury, spicy and dark fruit flavours. The full-bodied style gains complexity from chocolate and tobacco notes. This has 14.9-per-cent alcohol by volume and 0.4 grams a litre residual sugar. Drink now to 2030. Available at the above price direct, blastedchurch.com , various prices in Alberta, $34 in Manitoba.

Painted Rock Merlot 2022 (Canada), $49.99

Painted Rock Merlot has consistently stood out among the labels produced by the Skinner family at its estate overlooking Skaha Lake. The 2022 vintage is the result of an exceptional growing season, which contributes to the satisfying mix of juicy berry and cherry flavours and savoury oak-derived notes. Like all of Painted Rock’s red wine portfolio, this full-bodied merlot has excellent aging potential because of its serious structure and impressive length. This has 14.6-per-cent ABV and 2.7 g/litre r.s. Drink now to 2032. Available at the above price direct, paintedrock.CA , $54.99 in British Columbia, various prices in Alberta.

Poplar Grove Merlot 2022 (Canada), $32.99

A small percentage of malbec is blended into this flavourful merlot, made from grapes grown in south-central Okanagan. The wine showcases dark fruit flavours that are enhanced by chocolate and spice notes. Its concentrated character and supple texture are balanced by a polished structure and lingering finish. Ripe and age-worthy, the winery has held back inventory to release as a 10-year-old wine to showcase its aging potential. This has 14.9-per-cent ABV and 0.39 r.s. Drink now to 2035. Available at the above price direct, poplargrove.CA , $35.99 in British Columbia, various prices in Alberta, $34.99 in Manitoba.

stories.title: Restoration plans for historic Emslie Field grandstand to be determined by 2027 budget
stories.summary: St. Thomas city council has decided it can wait a little longer after deferring restoration options to the incoming council and the 2027 budget.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
The fate of the historic grandstand at Emslie Field in St. Thomas, Ont., has been a contentious issue over the past 12 months.

St. Thomas city council has decided it can wait a little longer after deferring restoration options to the incoming council and the 2027 budget.

“The decision to defer this to the budget is good news for us,” said Derek Brooks, director of the St. Thomas Minor Baseball Association (Stmba).

Since the city closed the grandstand for safety reasons in November 2025, there have been concerns the city would tear down the structure, which was built in 1938.

Council was presented with three options:

A full rehabilitation lasting 40 to 50 years for $1,172,000.

A minimum rehabilitation for $785,950 (with $600,000 previously earmarked in the capital budget and $100,000 committed by St. Thomas Minor Baseball) lasting 15 years.

Demolition and modern replacement with bleachers for $971,000.

After a structural condition assessment was completed , city staff recommended council choose the second option . However, council was divided at the meeting.

“If we go to a full restoration of the current building for about $472,000 more, we get 45 to 50 years,” said Coun. Gary Clarke.

“I just think that with the high cost of doing a part way renewal, that 15 years from now, we’re back where we were, and it’s kind of a waste of money.”

Coun. Steve Wookey supported either of the two rehabilitation options.

“I’m okay with refurbishing it and us putting in our 600,000 and other people coming with the rest, as long as that’s revenue neutral,” said Wookey.

“I’m also okay with it being the fuller rebuild, because I talk all the time about cost-benefit analysis. If we can do something that’s going to last 50 years instead of 15 years, then we are reducing our costs later on.”

Outgoing councillor Jim Herbert was supportive of the minimum rehabilitation, while outgoing councillor Joan Rymal wondered if a new structure was a better idea.

“All I want is for it to be safe and usable,” Wookey told CTV News.

“If the baseball community wants it to be redone as opposed to something new built, I have respect for that. I’m pleased to do that as long as it’s revenue neutral for the taxpayers of the city of Saint Thomas. If we put $600,000 into it, and they want to put the other $185,000 into it, then I’m great with that and we keep something that people really want.”

With members of the Stmba in the gallery, council ultimately decided to include the options in the 2027 budget and let the incoming council decide the grandstand’s fate.

“Ultimately the restoration of the existing structure is what we wanted whether that was the first option or the second option,” said Brooks.

“We’re committed to support financially what we were willing to put forward initially, and that hasn’t changed. So, we’ll continue to work with city council and the new city council for sure when they’re sworn in.”

Brooks and many members of the community have expressed their desire to keep the historic structure, which provides shade for those attending games throughout the summer and gives a classic look to the ballpark, which opened in 1898 at Pinafore Park.

“There’s a ton of history there,” said Brooks.

“You look at Bob Emslie (former MLB pitcher and umpire) and you look at Jack Graney (former MLB pitcher and broadcaster). All of those historical baseball figures have roots here in Saint Thomas. That grandstand, with the recent dedication of the press box to Graney and obviously the name of the park after Emslie. It’s important to maintain that park as close to the way it is now for the future.”

The views of the community and the Stmba are not lost on members of city council.

“I was a history teacher for 30 years,” said Wookey outside the meeting.

“I care a lot about history, and so I’d love to see it maintained and saved as long as it makes financial sense for all the parties involved. Baseball (Stmba), as always, put their money where their mouth is and I have a great deal of respect for that. They’re doing the same thing again this time, so I’d be pleased to support them in that.”

“I’m okay with refurbishing it and us putting in our 600,000 and other people coming with the rest, as long as that’s revenue neutral,” said Wookey.

“I’m also okay with it being the fuller rebuild, because I talk all the time about cost-benefit analysis. If we can do something that’s going to last 50 years instead of 15 years, then we are reducing our costs later on.”
Outgoing councillor Jim Herbert was supportive of the minimum rehabilitation, while outgoing councillor Joan Rymal wondered if a new structure was a better idea.
“All I want is for it to be safe and usable,” Wookey told CTV News.

“If the baseball community wants it to be redone as opposed to something new built, I have respect for that. I’m pleased to do that as long as it’s revenue neutral for the taxpayers of the city of Saint Thomas. If we put $600,000 into it, and they want to put the other $185,000 into it, then I’m great with that and we keep something that people really want.”
With members of the Stmba in the gallery, council ultimately decided to include the options in the 2027 budget and let the incoming council decide the grandstand’s fate.

content_blocks.text: “Ultimately the restoration of the existing structure is what we wanted whether that was the first option or the second option,” said Brooks.

“We’re committed to support financially what we were willing to put forward initially, and that hasn’t changed. So, we’ll continue to work with city council and the new city council for sure when they’re sworn in.”

Brooks and many members of the community have expressed their desire to keep the historic structure, which provides shade for those attending games throughout the summer and gives a classic look to the ballpark, which opened in 1898 at Pinafore Park.
“There’s a ton of history there,” said Brooks.

“You look at Bob Emslie (former MLB pitcher and umpire) and you look at Jack Graney (former MLB pitcher and broadcaster). All of those historical baseball figures have roots here in Saint Thomas. That grandstand, with the recent dedication of the press box to Graney and obviously the name of the park after Emslie. It’s important to maintain that park as close to the way it is now for the future.”
The views of the community and the Stmba are not lost on members of city council.
“I was a history teacher for 30 years,” said Wookey outside the meeting.

“I care a lot about history, and so I’d love to see it maintained and saved as long as it makes financial sense for all the parties involved. Baseball (Stmba), as always, put their money where their mouth is and I have a great deal of respect for that. They’re doing the same thing again this time, so I’d be pleased to support them in that.”

stories.title: U.S. midterm results spark joy among Canadians but trust in America remains shaky
stories.summary: Many Canadians welcome the Democratic sweep of U.S. Congress, but have mixed views on whether voters’ strong rebuke of President Donald Trump’s administration will change their attitude toward America amid the ongoing trade war.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto — Many Canadians welcome the Democratic sweep of U.S. Congress, but have mixed views on whether voters’ strong rebuke of President Donald Trump’s administration will change their attitude toward America amid the ongoing trade war.

Trump’s punishing tariffs on Canadian goods, repeated musings about making Canada the 51st state and escalating tensions that include changing the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America have had a profound impact on the relationship between the two countries.

The response from Canadians has been strong, with many avoiding cross-border travel and U.S.-made products, and reconsidering the long-standing cultural and economic ties with their American neighbours.

Juli Taylor said even though she’s happy with the midterm results, she isn’t planning to visit the United States any time soon.

“I’m Canadian, we are very proud of our country and we have been picked on a lot and we are done — and we’re absolutely overjoyed with the outcome in the States,” she said in an interview in Toronto the morning after the midterms.

Taylor said she would probably consider vacationing across the border if the tariff dispute is resolved, “but it’s not my first choice, anyways.”

“We live in a beautiful country and the best country in the world, so we need to put our money back in our own economy,” she said.

Blair Coyle, who also said he stopped visiting the United States, hopes Democratic control of the House of Representatives and the Senate will help ease tensions between the two nations.

“It means that maybe I can go to the U.S. again on a vacation,” he said, adding that he instead travelled to Europe three times this year.

Uwe Richter said while he strongly favours any political change in the United States that puts a check on Trump’s power, he still plans to boycott American products “as much as it’s possible.”

“And that will not change easily,” he said, “because what Trump has done is he has damaged the situation between our two countries and the rest of the world very, very much.”

Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc said Wednesday that Ottawa’s push to diversify trade won’t change as Democrats take control of Congress, and that recent talks with Trump’s administration have been productive.

Richter said it will take a lot of work to rebuild trust and the Canada-U.S. relationship nearly two years into Trump’s second term.

“I think there would have to be quite a lot of change in the situation between our two countries before I would put any money over there, by travelling over there,” he said at a downtown Toronto park.

For some Canadians, the Republicans’ defeat in these elections doesn’t necessarily signal a change in course.

Gerry Carlin noted that Trump has stated he would use “tremendous” veto powers if his party loses in the midterms.

“I don’t trust him, first of all, and I don’t trust the policies he’s got. I don’t know that they’re going to disappear,” he said.

“I would hope that the Democrats having power in both houses now will ease those ... but we don’t know, there’s no guarantee of anything at this point,” Carlin added.

“You still got two years to go.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 5, 2026.

Sharif Hassan, The Canadian Press

stories.title: CBC to broaden personal finance programming with launch of CBC Money
stories.summary: Public broadcaster hiring 16 journalists for the unit, which will feature new and existing content dedicated to money matters
stories.author: Nicole Thompson
stories.content:
Canada’s public broadcaster is launching a slate of new personal finance programming under the umbrella CBC Money.

CBC says the content dedicated to “money matters” will launch next year, with programming “across entertainment and news” on TV, radio and online.

It will include a new video series from CBC Radio’s Cost of Living hosted by business journalist Paul Haavardsrud, offering practical tips.

CBC Money will also feature new personal finance entertainment shows.

The broadcaster says existing programming, such as Dragon’s Den , will also fall under the CBC Money umbrella.

It says it’s hiring 16 new journalists to support the initiative, including nine who will work out of a new studio in downtown Calgary.

CBC says it will also hire five new business reporters in Vancouver, Edmonton, Winnipeg and Halifax to support the programming, plus two producers in Toronto.

“With CBC Money, we will move beyond market updates and boardroom chatter, delivering essential stories of money-planning strategies and financial resilience to help Canadians make more informed decisions,” said Brodie Fenlon, editor-in-chief of CBC News, in a statement.

stories.title: A Toronto home of both function and whimsy
stories.summary: The two-storey addition engages with the older building, but nothing about it is ordinary
stories.author: Alex Bozikovic
stories.content:
The building on Jones Avenue was trying to disappear. A 1950s doctor’s office, it had been converted to apartments, carelessly clad with siding and vinyl windows. But the building found people who could see its inherent beauty, and add to it. Architect Anne-Marie Armstrong of AAmp Studio and her husband, graphic designer Todd Temporale, noticed handsome limestone window surrounds and a wall of glazed yellow brick. These things signalled a gem worth polishing.

And Ms. Armstrong revels in such a task. “There’s a belief that Toronto can feel a bit beige,” she says. “And yet there are these wonderful moments hiding in some of these buildings. Finding those excites me.”

Attentiveness to history, to detail and to the potential of an existing building: these are characteristics of any good architect, and AAmp has them in abundance. Ms. Armstrong founded the office with colleague Andrew Ashey in 2017 after meeting as architects in Los Angeles. Together, their work has emphasized hospitality projects and adaptive reuse of existing buildings, or both, as at a hotel in Georgia carved out of a mid-century bank building.

At the Jones building, the work came in two stages. A 2020 renovation reworked the building as an office and two apartments. Last year, the couple completed a 2,500-square-foot addition as a home for their family.

The two-storey addition engages with the older building, nearly – but not quite – matching its brick and adding blue glazed masonry to complement the original’s lemon yellow. But nothing about the addition is ordinary: it is an extraordinarily deft composition, the work of architects whose spatial intelligence is matched by their sensitivity. The interlocking levels and carefully orchestrated views evoke the spatial drama of Richard Neutra’s California houses. A second-floor kitchen and dining room look south across Toronto while a double-height void, framed by a wall of oak cabinetry, connects them with the bedroom above. The vertical volume is set against the horizontal sweep of the city.

The interior reflects the owners’ highly refined taste. There are Chandigarh chairs, bought second-hand, and a Carlo Scarpa table that belonged to Mr. Temporale’s father. Red marble and moss-green laminate punctuate a palette of white walls and pale wood.

But the addition is just as compelling where it intersects with the old medical building – as in the stairwell, where old pale-brown brick meets crisp new masonry and carefully crafted terrazzo. A red-painted railing provides a hit of spice.

An architect’s home is usually a manifesto, and Ms. Armstrong is explicit about her principles here. “This place is robust, it is functional, but there are these moments of whimsy that are selective. There’s a certain attitude that a building can have these moments at the scale of the person.”

Its brickwork uses stack bond, as does part of the original façade – a pattern in which the bricks are laid out in a regular grid with their long sides out – and some new windows relate to the openings below. But those alignments are selective, extending the composition of the original façade in asymmetric fashion. This is a conversation between the generations. Ms. Armstrong devoted effort even to restoring the original building: when the old yellow glazed brick couldn’t be matched in contemporary production, she convinced an Italian manufacturer, SantAnselmo, to make a small custom order.

That’s a big lift for a building with no heritage protection and no pedigree. (Its original designers are identified on the 1956 drawings as Design Incorporated, a firm that has receded into history.) But the building’s former use as a doctor’s office is well known. People have stopped to tell Mr. Temporale and Ms. Armstrong that they once came here to see Dr. Baggs and Dr. Coulter. “I really want to care for this building,” Ms. Armstrong says, “because I think the neighbourhood cares for the building too. And that means bringing new life to it.”

While architects often pay lip service to that idea, AAMp’s work builds on it. Mr. Ashey, who runs a second office for AAmp in Portland, Maine, described the studio’s design approach as open-minded. “We really consider design a democratic process,” he said. “We don’t come to the table with any preconceived ideas about how a project will evolve. The result is a product of the clients and the context where we are working – the city and the buildings.”

Not just great buildings, but ordinary ones. That specific ethos goes back to the famously jumbled streetscape of Los Angeles, where Ms. Armstrong worked for Frank Gehry and Marmol Radziner. There Mr. Ashey and Ms. Armstrong created a publication, Annotated Journal , as a way of recording aspects of the city that caught their attention: often peculiar details that might not be considered architecture at all.

Such a democratic eye is a gift in Toronto, where the buildings that define its old main streets are products of a humble industrial town. Toronto city planning has in recent years used heritage policy to lock down thousands of older buildings, good ones and bad ones alike. That censorious attitude doesn’t come with a route for the old city to change and evolve. On Jones Avenue, AAmp have defined a different attitude to the city fabric: to work with old buildings out of love and not duty, with creativity and the odd jot of colour. That is how a city can evolve and stay alive, ever changing.

stories.title: Price cut, finishing touches help find a buyer for lakefront cottage
stories.summary: Three-bedroom bungalow sells for more than $2.6-million
stories.author: Unknown
stories.content:
383 Snug Harbour Rd., Lindsay, Ont.

Asking price: $2.85-million (August, 2026)

Previous asking prices: $3.35-million (March, 2025); $3,449,000 (January, 2025); $3,449,000 (December, 2024)

Selling price: $2,625,000 (September, 2026)

Previous selling price: Not applicable

Taxes: $13,814 (2025)

Days on the market: 33

Property days on market: 332

Listing agents: Jason Challenger, John Ireland and Bryce Boyce, Affinity Group Pinnacle Realty Ltd.

This three-bedroom bungalow, newly built on a 1.04-acre lot on Sturgeon Lake northeast of Toronto, was listed around $3.4-million for about 10 months in 2025. Buyers were astonished by its custom design, but disappointed by unfinished elements, like the driveway to the attached, triple garage.

“There were only a handful of places sold over $2-million in the last two years,” said agent John Ireland. “It’s very rare for properties to go over that price point in this area.

“A lot of people in the country have gravel driveways, but if someone’s going to spend $2.5-million to $3-million, they want an asphalt driveway.”

The property, taken off the market for one year, reappeared with a new driveway and boathouse, and a reduced price tag this summer. It had visitors every week, including repeat guests who took a swim along the 32-foot shoreline before negotiating a $2,625,000 deal this fall.

“At one point, I had 22 listings, and this one had more activity than almost all of them combined,” Mr. Ireland said.

“If this house was up in Muskoka, depending on what lake it’s on and other variables, it could be worth probably double. People find value here in the Kawarthas, and you’re only an hour and a half [drive] from the city.”

This bungalow has 2,897 square feet of living space, including a kitchen, three bathrooms and a laundry room connected to well water and septic systems.

The main floor has three bedrooms and a living room with vaulted ceilings and access to a deck.

The basement has three bedrooms and a recreation area with an exit to the patio.

“It was an exceptional home,” Mr. Ireland said.

“For example, they put in under 90 tons of limestone on the exterior, and you never see that.”
