stories.title: Teacher Ruth Foster revived a B.C. creek as a salmon spawning ground
stories.summary: Half a century later, an initiative that began as a high school club has educated generations of students and nurtured countless hatchlings
stories.author: Tom Hawthorn
stories.content:
Ruth Foster’s favourite classroom had no desks, no chalkboard, no walls.

The educator gathered students along the banks of Mossom Creek, a crystalline British Columbia waterway about an hour’s drive from downtown Vancouver.

Ms. Foster, who has died at 77, was a high-school teacher who believed young people better remembered their lessons when they got their boots wet. She preferred teaching outdoors “instead of in the dry, dusty Sahara of the classroom,” she once said. You might say she excelled at streaming students.

In 1976, she and fellow biology teacher Rod MacVicar founded a salmon club with eight students at Centennial Secondary School in suburban Coquitlam, B.C.

“She wanted students to shape the place they lived in,” Mr. MacVicar said. “She wanted them to know you can think locally. You can make a difference as long as you get off your duffs and do it.”

Mossom Creek runs for about eight kilometres from a delicate web of brooks and culverts southeast of Buntzen Lake through the village of Anmore and city of Port Moody, including past an old refinery townsite known as Ioco, which took its name from the initials of the Imperial Oil Co. The creek empties into saltwater on the north side of Port Moody Arm, part of Burrard Inlet.

It was one of the few streams capable of producing salmon as the Lower Mainland became ever more urbanized. The club’s aim was to bring back a modest run of chum salmon, which had been depleted in the creek for about 15 years.

The students made an incubation box on the east side of the creek just north of Ioco Road to raise 50,000 salmon eggs. A year later, they discovered debris dumped on the banks and into the channel had destroyed the eggs and ruined their project.

The students wrote letters of protest to the environment minister and local MLAs about the dumping of debris, which was believed to have been left by contractors clearing land for an adjacent housing development.

Their protests eventually led Port Moody council to form an environmental advisory committee, believed to be one of the first of its kind in the province.

Students reintroduced an incubation box further upstream the following year. Four years later, the Vancouver Sun noted only about 20 of a batch of 19,000 chum had returned to spawn.

The creation of the province’s first student and volunteer hatchery caught the attention of the producers of the popular CBC television program The Nature of Things . David Suzuki hosted a segment on the hatchery titled, “Salmon on the Line,” in 1983.

In the fall of that year, students counted 80 returning spawners in the creek from a release of 27,000 fry four years earlier.

The slight increase in numbers also began attracting other creatures.

“Cutthroat trout eat the eggs which aren’t buried, and some of the fry,” Ms. Foster told the Vancouver Province newspaper in 1983. “Bald eagles, harbour seals and bear [populations] are all up in the area. That’s life.”

By 1991, some 700 chum returned to the stream, far more than would have made it without student assistance.

The Keta Club, which took its name from the chum’s Latin name, Oncorhynchus keta, eventually got a yellow-and-black school bus known as a Fishmobile to transport students to the site.

Every October, the students collected returning mature salmon, artificially spawned them and then mixed milt and eggs before nursing tens of thousands of fertilized eggs at the hatchery.

What began as a school club spawned an addition to the curriculum with a senior-year course called Fisheries Ecology 12.

Many of the students went on to graduate with postsecondary degrees and certificates at a time when companies, municipalities and nongovernmental organizations were looking for conservation and environmental expertise.

Government, corporate and private donations allowed for the building of a two-storey hatchery and education centre at the creek, which was administered by the Burrard Inlet Marine Enhancement Society, a nonprofit group founded by Ms. Foster, Mr. MacVicar and Centennial alumni.

The hatchery burned down in 2013. There were no injuries, though some 200,000 eggs from three species were lost. The facility was rebuilt and continues to maintain an open house on Sundays.

After retiring from teaching high school, Ms. Foster continued to mentor students at the hatchery while teaching at Simon Fraser University. She won numerous teaching and environmental awards over the years, including a prestigious Canadian Environmental Award gold medal.

Ruth Ellen Eaglesham was born in Guelph, Ont., ON Oct. 18, 1948, to the former Doris Mabel Woodfin, a nurse, and Dr. Douglas Cameron Eaglesham, a radiologist. Both parents were born in Saskatchewan. They met and married in Britain while on military service during the war.

Ms. Foster attended John F. Ross Collegiate Vocational Institute in Guelph before earning an honours degree in biology and animal sciences from what is now Western University in London, Ont. In 1975, she completed a teaching degree at the University of British Columbia in Vancouver with a major in science education and a minor in physical education.

paragraphs: Ruth Foster’s favourite classroom had no desks, no chalkboard, no walls.
The educator gathered students along the banks of Mossom Creek, a crystalline British Columbia waterway about an hour’s drive from downtown Vancouver.

Ms. Foster, who has died at 77, was a high-school teacher who believed young people better remembered their lessons when they got their boots wet. She preferred teaching outdoors “instead of in the dry, dusty Sahara of the classroom,” she once said. You might say she excelled at streaming students.
In 1976, she and fellow biology teacher Rod MacVicar founded a salmon club with eight students at Centennial Secondary School in suburban Coquitlam, B.C.
“She wanted students to shape the place they lived in,” Mr. MacVicar said. “She wanted them to know you can think locally. You can make a difference as long as you get off your duffs and do it.”

Mossom Creek runs for about eight kilometres from a delicate web of brooks and culverts southeast of Buntzen Lake through the village of Anmore and city of Port Moody, including past an old refinery townsite known as Ioco, which took its name from the initials of the Imperial Oil Co. The creek empties into saltwater on the north side of Port Moody Arm, part of Burrard Inlet.

It was one of the few streams capable of producing salmon as the Lower Mainland became ever more urbanized. The club’s aim was to bring back a modest run of chum salmon, which had been depleted in the creek for about 15 years.

The students made an incubation box on the east side of the creek just north of Ioco Road to raise 50,000 salmon eggs. A year later, they discovered debris dumped on the banks and into the channel had destroyed the eggs and ruined their project.

The students wrote letters of protest to the environment minister and local MLAs about the dumping of debris, which was believed to have been left by contractors clearing land for an adjacent housing development.
Their protests eventually led Port Moody council to form an environmental advisory committee, believed to be one of the first of its kind in the province.
Students reintroduced an incubation box further upstream the following year. Four years later, the Vancouver Sun noted only about 20 of a batch of 19,000 chum had returned to spawn.

The creation of the province’s first student and volunteer hatchery caught the attention of the producers of the popular CBC television program The Nature of Things . David Suzuki hosted a segment on the hatchery titled, “Salmon on the Line,” in 1983.
In the fall of that year, students counted 80 returning spawners in the creek from a release of 27,000 fry four years earlier.
The slight increase in numbers also began attracting other creatures.

“Cutthroat trout eat the eggs which aren’t buried, and some of the fry,” Ms. Foster told the Vancouver Province newspaper in 1983. “Bald eagles, harbour seals and bear [populations] are all up in the area. That’s life.”
By 1991, some 700 chum returned to the stream, far more than would have made it without student assistance.
The Keta Club, which took its name from the chum’s Latin name, Oncorhynchus keta, eventually got a yellow-and-black school bus known as a Fishmobile to transport students to the site.
Every October, the students collected returning mature salmon, artificially spawned them and then mixed milt and eggs before nursing tens of thousands of fertilized eggs at the hatchery.
What began as a school club spawned an addition to the curriculum with a senior-year course called Fisheries Ecology 12.

Many of the students went on to graduate with postsecondary degrees and certificates at a time when companies, municipalities and nongovernmental organizations were looking for conservation and environmental expertise.

Government, corporate and private donations allowed for the building of a two-storey hatchery and education centre at the creek, which was administered by the Burrard Inlet Marine Enhancement Society, a nonprofit group founded by Ms. Foster, Mr. MacVicar and Centennial alumni.
The hatchery burned down in 2013. There were no injuries, though some 200,000 eggs from three species were lost. The facility was rebuilt and continues to maintain an open house on Sundays.

After retiring from teaching high school, Ms. Foster continued to mentor students at the hatchery while teaching at Simon Fraser University. She won numerous teaching and environmental awards over the years, including a prestigious Canadian Environmental Award gold medal.

Ruth Ellen Eaglesham was born in Guelph, Ont., ON Oct. 18, 1948, to the former Doris Mabel Woodfin, a nurse, and Dr. Douglas Cameron Eaglesham, a radiologist. Both parents were born in Saskatchewan. They met and married in Britain while on military service during the war.

Ms. Foster attended John F. Ross Collegiate Vocational Institute in Guelph before earning an honours degree in biology and animal sciences from what is now Western University in London, Ont. In 1975, she completed a teaching degree at the University of British Columbia in Vancouver with a major in science education and a minor in physical education.

Ms. Foster, a resident of the village of Belcarra, which is part of Metro Vancouver, died at Royal Columbian Hospital in New Westminster on Sept. 28, three weeks after receiving a diagnosis of pancreatic cancer. She leaves John Foster, her husband of 55 years. She also leaves a son, Doug Foster, a daughter, Emily Foster, two grandchildren and four sisters.
Ms. Foster was in attendance for the hatchery’s 50th anniversary celebrations held just nine days before her death.

stories.title: Too broke to leave: Alberta domestic abuse victims trapped by rising cost of living
stories.summary: The Alberta Council of Women's Shelters said since 2019, the cost of housing, groceries and gas have all grown more than 30 per cent while food bank visits are up by 134 per cent.
stories.author: Karen Bartko, Kabi Moulitharan
stories.content:
The number of people seeking help from domestic violence at Alberta shelters has decreased in the past two years, but officials say that’s no reason to celebrate as a deeper dive into the data reveals many simply can’t afford to flee.

“The housing and affordability crisis is having a real impact on survivors and their ability to leave domestic violence situations,” said Cat Champagne, the executive director of the Alberta Council of Women’s Shelters (Acws).

On Wednesday, the council released its 2024-26 impact report, summarizing domestic violence trends and activities at over 50 family violence shelters across Alberta, highlighting growing pressure on survivors and the shelters that support them.

The report shows the number of people accessing shelters has declined since 2023–24.

“In so many cases, the numbers are lower because it’s just too expensive for people to leave abusive relationships,” said Miranda Pilipchuk, manager of research and evaluation at Acws and the report’s lead author.

On average, it takes a woman seven attempts to leave an abusive relationship for good and the Acws said the growing cost of starting over is making it increasingly difficult for survivors to find safety and remain safely housed.

“If you were to move into a new place, there’s a lot of costs that come along with that,” Champagne said.

“You’ve got rent, damage deposit, deposits on utilities, you’ve got to set up a whole household — whether that’s clothing, furniture, all of those things — and a lot of those times, you’re doing it for yourself and your kids.”

People in unhealthy relationships can often experience several forms of abuse or control, including financial.

“We see so many women in shelter that have never even had access to a bank account, or their accounts have been kind of frozen or kept from them, or that their abuser has used finances as a tool, you know, some type of economic abuse or financial control that they can they can manipulate with,” Champagne said.

Against that backdrop, the Acws said many survivors May choose to stay in abusive situations rather than risk homelessness and food insecurity.

Between 2025 and 2026, 82 per cent of calls requesting admission to a shelter did not result in an admission, according to The Cost of Leaving: The 2024–26 Acws Shelter Impact Report.

“That doesn’t necessarily mean that we are seeing a drop in domestic violence. It doesn’t mean that shelters have worked themselves out of a job,” Champagne said. “That’s what’s really concerning to us — where are women going and why are they not coming to shelters?”

Survivors are also staying in emergency and second-stage shelters longer, limiting the number of new people the facilities can support.

According to the report, the average length of stay in an emergency shelter has increased by roughly 50 per cent since 2019, while over the same period:

Housing costs have risen 31 per cent

Cost of food has risen by 36 per cent

Gas prices have increased by 35 per cent

Food bank visits in Alberta have increased by 134 per cent

The Acws says more than 10,000 people in Edmonton and 7,500 people in Calgary are on waitlists for affordable housing programs.

“We have a housing crisis. The housing continuum is broken,” Champagne said. “There is no safe and affordable housing for people to go to, so they’re staying in shelter longer — which of course means less people are able to access shelter.”

The report also points to an increase in the severity of violence experienced by some survivors.

Between 2024 and 2025, 72 per cent reported experiencing increasing physical violence over the previous year.

“A woman’s possibility of being killed by her intimate partner — we’re seeing those numbers higher than we’ve seen since before the pandemic,” Champagne said.

The Acws is recommending measures aimed at making it easier for survivors to establish themselves safely after leaving an abusive situation, including priority access to housing, assistance with rent and damage deposits, and faster access to financial support.

Champagne says some supports already exist, including Alberta’s Escaping Abuse Benefit, but accessing them can involve barriers for survivors. She pointed to the province’s income support system as one example.

Champagne said a shelter can work with a survivor to make a call for assistance, but if income support staff later call back and can’t reach the survivor, their file can be closed.

“The last thing any of the shelter providers around the province should have to worry about is reporting requirements, red tape issues that they’re having to go through when, at the end of the day, they just want to help pour into these survivors and ensure that they’re looked after,” Champagne said.

The council said it wants existing supports to be easier and faster for survivors to access, with fewer administrative hurdles.

Champagne noted as they struggle to serve vulnerable residents, Alberta’s shelters also have one of the highest employee turnover rates in the province.

“It’s such heavy work and with lack of resources, lack of ability to pay people properly and train them, it does impact our ability to serve survivors,” Champagne said.

The report found between 2024 and 2026, 11,332 adults and 6,277 children were admitted to Acws member shelters. During that same timeframe, Acws member shelters provided more than 35,000 referrals and 71,000 services to clients across all programs.

content_blocks.html: “You’ve got rent, damage deposit, deposits on utilities, you’ve got to set up a whole household  — whether that’s clothing, furniture, all of those things — and a lot of those times, you’re doing it for yourself and your kids.”

content_blocks.text: People in unhealthy relationships can often experience several forms of abuse or control, including financial.

“We see so many women in shelter that have never even had access to a bank account, or their accounts have been kind of frozen or kept from them, or that their abuser has used finances as a tool, you know, some type of economic abuse or financial control that they can they can manipulate with,” Champagne said.

content_blocks.alt: Click to play video: 'High cost of living impacts those fleeing domestic and family violence: report'

content_blocks.text: Against that backdrop, the Acws said many survivors May choose to stay in abusive situations rather than risk homelessness and food insecurity.
Between 2025 and 2026, 82 per cent of calls requesting admission to a shelter did not result in an admission, according to The Cost of Leaving: The 2024–26 Acws Shelter Impact Report.
content_blocks.html: Between 2025 and 2026, 82 per cent of calls requesting admission to a shelter did not result in an admission, according to The Cost of Leaving: The 2024–26 ACWS Shelter Impact Report.

content_blocks.text: “That doesn’t necessarily mean that we are seeing a drop in domestic violence. It doesn’t mean that shelters have worked themselves out of a job,” Champagne said. “That’s what’s really concerning to us — where are women going and why are they not coming to shelters?”
Survivors are also staying in emergency and second-stage shelters longer, limiting the number of new people the facilities can support.
According to the report, the average length of stay in an emergency shelter has increased by roughly 50 per cent since 2019, while over the same period:

items: Housing costs have risen 31 per cent
Cost of food has risen by 36 per cent
Gas prices have increased by 35 per cent
Food bank visits in Alberta have increased by 134 per cent

content_blocks.text: The Acws says more than 10,000 people in Edmonton and 7,500 people in Calgary are on waitlists for affordable housing programs.
content_blocks.html: The ACWS says more than 10,000 people in Edmonton and 7,500 people in Calgary are  on waitlists for affordable housing programs.

content_blocks.text: “We have a housing crisis. The housing continuum is broken,” Champagne said. “There is no safe and affordable housing for people to go to, so they’re staying in shelter longer — which of course means less people are able to access shelter.”
The report also points to an increase in the severity of violence experienced by some survivors.
Between 2024 and 2025, 72 per cent reported experiencing increasing physical violence over the previous year.
“A woman’s possibility of being killed by her intimate partner — we’re seeing those numbers higher than we’ve seen since before the pandemic,” Champagne said.

content_blocks.alt: Click to play video: '‘Unprecedented’ 45% turnover rate in Alberta domestic violence sector: ACWS'

content_blocks.text: The Acws is recommending measures aimed at making it easier for survivors to establish themselves safely after leaving an abusive situation, including priority access to housing, assistance with rent and damage deposits, and faster access to financial support.

Champagne says some supports already exist, including Alberta’s Escaping Abuse Benefit, but accessing them can involve barriers for survivors. She pointed to the province’s income support system as one example.
content_blocks.html: Champagne says some supports already exist, including Alberta’s Escaping Abuse Benefit, but accessing them can involve barriers for survivors. She pointed to the province’s income support system as one example.

content_blocks.text: Champagne said a shelter can work with a survivor to make a call for assistance, but if income support staff later call back and can’t reach the survivor, their file can be closed.

“The last thing any of the shelter providers around the province should have to worry about is reporting requirements, red tape issues that they’re having to go through when, at the end of the day, they just want to help pour into these survivors and ensure that they’re looked after,” Champagne said.
The council said it wants existing supports to be easier and faster for survivors to access, with fewer administrative hurdles.

content_blocks.alt: Click to play video: 'Alberta women’s shelters are under-resourced, leading people to be turned away: 2022 report'

content_blocks.text: Champagne noted as they struggle to serve vulnerable residents, Alberta’s shelters also have one of the highest employee turnover rates in the province.
“It’s such heavy work and with lack of resources, lack of ability to pay people properly and train them, it does impact our ability to serve survivors,” Champagne said.

The report found between 2024 and 2026, 11,332 adults and 6,277 children were admitted to Acws member shelters. During that same timeframe, Acws member shelters provided more than 35,000 referrals and 71,000 services to clients across all programs.

stories.title: Public asked to shape future of Hudson's Bay royal charter
stories.summary: The four institutions sharing Hudson’s Bay’s royal charter are launching a public consultation to help decide how access to and education around the 356-year-old document are handled in the future.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The four institutions sharing Hudson’s Bay’s royal charter are launching a public consultation to help decide how access to and education around the 356-year-old document are handled in the future.

The museums and archive that form the Hudson’s Bay Co. Royal Charter Consortium say the public consultation will be led by consulting firm First Peoples Group with support from Nanos Research and Lord Cultural Resources.

The public consultation will have several phases, beginning with a focus on Indigenous relations. It will include virtual gatherings and in-person meetings starting this month to collect feedback from Indigenous people in Winnipeg, Timmins, Ont., Yellowknife, Vancouver and Iqaluit.

The second phase will include a national survey with all Canadians invited to participate.

The feedback generated will form a framework the Archives of Manitoba, Manitoba Museum, Canadian Museum of History in Gatineau, Que., and the Royal Ontario Museum in Toronto will use to guide how they promote access and learning around the charter.

The charter issued by King Charles II in 1670 established Hudson’s Bay and gave it immense control over land, trading and Indigenous relations for decades to come.

The holding companies of the Weston family of Loblaw Cos. Ltd. fame and media baron David Thomson purchased the charter for $18 million in December, months after Hudson’s Bay filed for creditor protection in March and put its assets up for sale.

Once the purchase was complete, they donated the charter to the quartet of public institutions and asked the group to consult the public on the document’s future care, stewardship, public access and display.

The Manitoba Museum will be the first member of the consortium to display the charter in late 2027, with the Canadian Museum of History and the Royal Ontario Museum to take on hosting duties eventually.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 4, 2026.

Tara Deschamps, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Supportive housing provider Indwell wins tribunal appeal for new residence in Sarnia
stories.summary: Non-profit housing provider Indwell has won an appeal with the Ontario Land Tribunal, clearing the way for a 35 unit supportive housing building at 353 George Street in Sarnia.
stories.author: Bryan Bicknell
stories.content:
For some Lambton County residents in precarious living situations, it’s a step closer to having a place they can call home.

Non-profit housing provider Indwell has won an appeal with the Ontario Land Tribunal, clearing the way for a 35 unit supportive housing building at 353 George Street in Sarnia.

“Obviously the need is apparent to everyone that homelessness, outdoor encampments, the impacts of that on individual peoples’ lives is horrendous. And we should not be overlooking the reality that people need help,” said Graham Cubitt, the president of Flourish, the development arm of Indwell.

The land for the project was donated by Lambton County. The appeal by Indwell came after Sarnia city council backed a Committee of Adjustment decision against the proposal. An earlier plan had included 50 units of affordable housing.

“The tribunal said, ON balance, the evidence points to the application being on line with the bylaw and meeting the intent of the official plan. And so therefore it should proceed,” explained Cubitt.

The decision in Indwell’s favour, however, comes with the community still divided. Some area residents are concerned about the effect their future neighbours will have on the area.

Neighbours Kelly O’Connor Beausoleil and Chris Beausoleil explain their fears are based on the experience with an existing nearby shelter.

“We’re afraid that those few residents who are moving from the encampments and the shelters are going to pose a danger to the vulnerable people who live here,” said Chris.

“It’s saturating the neighbourhood. Like what possible logic can there be in putting one facility a block from another facility,” added Kelly.

Sarnia’s outgoing mayor, Mike Bradley, says it will be up to the new council to continue to support those in need.

“The new council and the new mayor have got to recognize that you’ve gotta stand strong and you’ve gotta stand up for those who need help and don’t have a voice. They don’t have a voice. So that’s what this project is about. We went through some very, very contentious council meetings on this. But I’m glad the majority of council supported it, and now the Land Tribunal has,” Bradley exclaimed.

Graham Cubitt says with the appeal process complete the final structural hurdle has now been cleared.

He says they expect to break ground on the project in spring of 2027.

stories.title: Quebec man pleads guilty to fatally stabbing pregnant wife dozens of times in 2024
stories.summary: Montreal - A Quebec man has pleaded guilty to second-degree murder after admitting to stabbing his pregnant wife nearly 50 times in 2024.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - A Quebec man has pleaded guilty to second-degree murder after admitting to stabbing his pregnant wife nearly 50 times in 2024.

Mustapha Khalil Mechken acknowledged in a statement of facts presented in court that he didn’t feel ready to have a child and was worried that a maternity leave would hurt the couple’s finances.

stories.title: Edmonton entrepreneur Irving Kipnes had twin passions: business and philanthropy
stories.summary: He played a major role in shaping the city, first through real estate development, and later by supporting health, education and arts institutions
stories.author: Jeremy Appel
stories.content:
The number of buildings in Edmonton named after Irving Kipnes provides a glimpse into his influence on his adopted home, as well as his range of philanthropic interests: the University of Alberta’s Dianne and Irving Kipnes Health Research Academy and Dianne and Irving Kipnes Urology Centre, the CapitalCare Kipnes Centre for Veterans, and the forthcoming Oshry-Kipnes Jewish Community Centre. There’s also the five-storey Kipnes Lantern at Ottawa’s National Arts Centre, a testament to the influence of its namesake beyond Edmonton.

But the scale of the real-estate developer and liquor magnate’s imprint on Edmonton far exceeds the several facilities bearing the Kipnes name. Over the past 65 years, Mr. Kipnes played an outsized role in physically shaping Edmonton into the sprawling metropolis of today, as the owner of Delcon Development Group, which also oversaw developments in Calgary and Scottsdale, Ariz.

“A lot of the south side of Edmonton would have been crafted in a way that Irv envisioned it, simply because he made it happen and was just determined over a longer haul,” said Craig Corbett, a business associate of Mr. Kipnes and close friend of almost 20 years. “That’s the real estate game in general, but he did it at scale.”

Mr. Kipnes’s family foundation also contributed millions of dollars to the Alberta Cancer Foundation, University Hospital Foundation, Mazankowski Alberta Heart Institute, Edmonton Symphony Orchestra, Citadel Theatre, Art Gallery of Alberta, Edmonton Opera, the Jewish Archives and Historical Society of Edmonton, and the Beth Shalom Synagogue, among other beneficiaries.

“If you just drive around Edmonton, it’s hard to drive for five minutes without seeing a building or an organization that has benefited from their time or generosity,” added Mr. Corbett, who described Mr. Kipnes as a “boss, mentor and quasi-grandfather.”

Irving Kipnes died in Edmonton on Oct. 19 of kidney failure at the age of 90. He leaves his daughters, Rozanne Kipnes and Ronee Kipnes; stepdaughter, Kendra Walker; seven grandchildren, two great-grandchildren and extended family. Mr. Kipnes was predeceased by his spouse of 36 years, Dr. Dianne Kipnes, and son, Harry Kipnes.

Throughout his life, Mr. Kipnes was hyperfocused on his twin passions: business and philanthropy. “He didn’t have any hobbies,” Ms. Walker said. “There was no sudoku. There was no music.” Dr. Kipnes, who earned her PhD in clinical psychology from Fielding University in Santa Barbara, Calif., was the “impetus for their support for the arts,” according to Mr. Corbett, who once served as board chair of Edmonton Opera. “Irv and Dianne had an awesome partnership in life, business and philanthropy.”

Mr. Kipnes’s passion for philanthropy extended to his social circle. “To be associated with him, you had to be a giver,” said lawyer and business partner David Margolus, a longtime friend. “If you were involved with him and you had a cause and he was close with you, he would want to give to that cause.”

Mr. Margolus, now 76, was a 28-year-old lawyer representing Delcon when he first met Mr. Kipnes. The two men had much in common. Both had lost their parents when they were in their early 20s and shared a strong work ethic that often resulted in late nights at the office. Mr. Margolus described himself as a “young, green lawyer” at the time, whereas Mr. Kipnes was already a well-established businessman.

Decades later, Mr. Kipnes’s extraordinary fastidiousness in reviewing legal paperwork stands out to Mr. Margolus. “He was the only client then, and the only client to this day that would read every line. He would sit across from me – he’d have his document, I’d have mine, and he’d ask me what this meant, what that meant, and what this Latin term meant,” Mr. Margolus recalled. “I learned more law from him than I did in law school.”

Mr. Kipnes was born in Calgary on Sept. 10, 1936, to Harry and Rose Kipnes, Russian-Jewish immigrants who fled antisemitism from territory located in modern-day Ukraine. In Calgary, the elder Mr. Kipnes owned a confectionery shop. Mr. Margolus said that Mr. Kipnes’s philanthropy was rooted in his Jewish upbringing, referring to the Jewish liturgical concept of tzedakah , which obliges all Jews to donate a portion of their earnings to charity .

When he was 18, Mr. Kipnes moved to Edmonton to study chemical engineering at the University of Alberta, and soon began working for Imperial Oil. In 1962, he got into the real estate development business. “He got bored being an engineer,” Mr. Corbett said. “He liked actually building things. I used to walk construction sites with him. He got a kick out of taking raw land and 10 years later, there’s 4,000 families there.”

Mr. Kipnes met social worker Dianne Walker (née McFarlane) in 1977 when he stopped in Montreal for dinner with mutual friends on the way back from a trip to Israel. At the time, Mr. Kipnes was married to his first wife, Brenda Kipnes (née Bishop), the mother of his children, and Dianne was married to her first husband, David Walker. The Walkers eventually moved to Edmonton, but their marriage ended. Dianne soon reconnected with Mr. Kipnes, who had also recently become single.

Kendra Walker was a preteen when her mother started dating Mr. Kipnes. “I loved my little life with my mom, so I was obviously not too impressed when he came on the scene,” she recalled, adding that she rejected his efforts to assume a “father figure role.”

Ms. Walker, who left to study abroad when she was 18 and now lives in Paris, came to develop a “profound respect” for her stepfather through years of visits home. “He taught me so many lessons, and I think one of them is how to love someone who you’re not obliged to love as your parent, but you love them anyway as your parent,” she said.

Irving and Dianne Kipnes got married in 1988, with the couple vowing to spend half of their time on charitable projects. Their wedding came at the tail end of a rough patch for Mr. Kipnes’s business empire. A year earlier, he was president of North West Trust, a fund he cofounded, when it was taken over by the Alberta government after losing millions of dollars due to collapsing real estate values and defaulted mortgages, with the federal government providing bailout funds to the tune of $275-million.

But after premier Ralph Klein privatized Alberta liquor sales in 1994, Mr. Kipnes sensed a chance at redemption, founding the Liquor Depot, which grew from a single store in Edmonton into a publicly traded North American behemoth, with locations from Kentucky to Alaska. “Irv could just see an opportunity and chase it,” said Mr. Corbett, who served as an executive vice-president for Liquor Depot’s parent company, Liquor Stores N.A. In 2014, when Mr. Kipnes retired from the company’s board, its chairperson was Mr. Klein’s former treasurer, Jim Dinning.

While they’re dwarfed by his charitable contributions, Mr. Kipnes also made substantial political contributions, chief among them to the former Alberta PC party, but also contributed varying sums to the UCP, Alberta NDP and Alberta Party, according to Elections Alberta financial disclosures. Mr. Margolus described his late friend’s political views as more akin to the moderate Toryism of former PC premier Peter Lougheed than the hard-right populism of Premier Danielle Smith. “Like every developer, you probably give to both parties,” Mr. Margolus surmised.

Mr. Kipnes was close friends with former Edmonton mayor and provincial health minister Stephen Mandel, who shared Mr. Kipnes’s real estate background. The pair first met playing on a team that Mr. Kipnes had sponsored in a Jewish baseball league and have been close ever since. “Irv was instrumental in me getting involved in politics and philanthropy. He’s always thought that nobody should wander through life and not give back,” Mr. Mandel said .

Mr. Kipnes supported Mr. Mandel’s mayoral aspirations, in addition to Mr. Mandel’s brief tenure as a PC MLA and leadership of the Alberta Party. “It really was not a political relationship at all. It was a friendship,” Mr. Margolus said, adding that the pair and their wives were “as close as can be.” After Mr. Mandel’s daughter Rachel died of lymphoma in 2017, the Kipneses established the Rachel Mandel Lymphoma and Blood Cancers Research Fund with a $1-million donation that was matched by the Alberta Cancer Foundation.

When he announced a $25-million donation to establish the Dianne and Irving Kipnes Health Research Institute in September 2025, Mr. Kipnes reflected on his philosophy of philanthropy.

“Giving back – whether with your time, your ideas, or your resources – is one of the most meaningful things you can do. It connects you to something larger than yourself. It ensures that the values you hold dear will carry forward, long after you’re gone,” Mr. Kipnes said. “My goal has always been simple: leave things better than I found them.”

paragraphs: The number of buildings in Edmonton named after Irving Kipnes provides a glimpse into his influence on his adopted home, as well as his range of philanthropic interests: the University of Alberta’s Dianne and Irving Kipnes Health Research Academy and Dianne and Irving Kipnes Urology Centre, the CapitalCare Kipnes Centre for Veterans, and the forthcoming Oshry-Kipnes Jewish Community Centre. There’s also the five-storey Kipnes Lantern at Ottawa’s National Arts Centre, a testament to the influence of its namesake beyond Edmonton.

But the scale of the real-estate developer and liquor magnate’s imprint on Edmonton far exceeds the several facilities bearing the Kipnes name. Over the past 65 years, Mr. Kipnes played an outsized role in physically shaping Edmonton into the sprawling metropolis of today, as the owner of Delcon Development Group, which also oversaw developments in Calgary and Scottsdale, Ariz.

“A lot of the south side of Edmonton would have been crafted in a way that Irv envisioned it, simply because he made it happen and was just determined over a longer haul,” said Craig Corbett, a business associate of Mr. Kipnes and close friend of almost 20 years. “That’s the real estate game in general, but he did it at scale.”

Mr. Kipnes’s family foundation also contributed millions of dollars to the Alberta Cancer Foundation, University Hospital Foundation, Mazankowski Alberta Heart Institute, Edmonton Symphony Orchestra, Citadel Theatre, Art Gallery of Alberta, Edmonton Opera, the Jewish Archives and Historical Society of Edmonton, and the Beth Shalom Synagogue, among other beneficiaries.

“If you just drive around Edmonton, it’s hard to drive for five minutes without seeing a building or an organization that has benefited from their time or generosity,” added Mr. Corbett, who described Mr. Kipnes as a “boss, mentor and quasi-grandfather.”

Irving Kipnes died in Edmonton on Oct. 19 of kidney failure at the age of 90. He leaves his daughters, Rozanne Kipnes and Ronee Kipnes; stepdaughter, Kendra Walker; seven grandchildren, two great-grandchildren and extended family. Mr. Kipnes was predeceased by his spouse of 36 years, Dr. Dianne Kipnes, and son, Harry Kipnes.

Throughout his life, Mr. Kipnes was hyperfocused on his twin passions: business and philanthropy. “He didn’t have any hobbies,” Ms. Walker said. “There was no sudoku. There was no music.” Dr. Kipnes, who earned her PhD in clinical psychology from Fielding University in Santa Barbara, Calif., was the “impetus for their support for the arts,” according to Mr. Corbett, who once served as board chair of Edmonton Opera. “Irv and Dianne had an awesome partnership in life, business and philanthropy.”

Mr. Kipnes’s passion for philanthropy extended to his social circle. “To be associated with him, you had to be a giver,” said lawyer and business partner David Margolus, a longtime friend. “If you were involved with him and you had a cause and he was close with you, he would want to give to that cause.”

Mr. Margolus, now 76, was a 28-year-old lawyer representing Delcon when he first met Mr. Kipnes. The two men had much in common. Both had lost their parents when they were in their early 20s and shared a strong work ethic that often resulted in late nights at the office. Mr. Margolus described himself as a “young, green lawyer” at the time, whereas Mr. Kipnes was already a well-established businessman.

Decades later, Mr. Kipnes’s extraordinary fastidiousness in reviewing legal paperwork stands out to Mr. Margolus. “He was the only client then, and the only client to this day that would read every line. He would sit across from me – he’d have his document, I’d have mine, and he’d ask me what this meant, what that meant, and what this Latin term meant,” Mr. Margolus recalled. “I learned more law from him than I did in law school.”

Mr. Kipnes was born in Calgary on Sept. 10, 1936, to Harry and Rose Kipnes, Russian-Jewish immigrants who fled antisemitism from territory located in modern-day Ukraine. In Calgary, the elder Mr. Kipnes owned a confectionery shop. Mr. Margolus said that Mr. Kipnes’s philanthropy was rooted in his Jewish upbringing, referring to the Jewish liturgical concept of tzedakah , which obliges all Jews to donate a portion of their earnings to charity .

When he was 18, Mr. Kipnes moved to Edmonton to study chemical engineering at the University of Alberta, and soon began working for Imperial Oil. In 1962, he got into the real estate development business. “He got bored being an engineer,” Mr. Corbett said. “He liked actually building things. I used to walk construction sites with him. He got a kick out of taking raw land and 10 years later, there’s 4,000 families there.”

Mr. Kipnes met social worker Dianne Walker (née McFarlane) in 1977 when he stopped in Montreal for dinner with mutual friends on the way back from a trip to Israel. At the time, Mr. Kipnes was married to his first wife, Brenda Kipnes (née Bishop), the mother of his children, and Dianne was married to her first husband, David Walker. The Walkers eventually moved to Edmonton, but their marriage ended. Dianne soon reconnected with Mr. Kipnes, who had also recently become single.

Kendra Walker was a preteen when her mother started dating Mr. Kipnes. “I loved my little life with my mom, so I was obviously not too impressed when he came on the scene,” she recalled, adding that she rejected his efforts to assume a “father figure role.”

Ms. Walker, who left to study abroad when she was 18 and now lives in Paris, came to develop a “profound respect” for her stepfather through years of visits home. “He taught me so many lessons, and I think one of them is how to love someone who you’re not obliged to love as your parent, but you love them anyway as your parent,” she said.

Irving and Dianne Kipnes got married in 1988, with the couple vowing to spend half of their time on charitable projects. Their wedding came at the tail end of a rough patch for Mr. Kipnes’s business empire. A year earlier, he was president of North West Trust, a fund he cofounded, when it was taken over by the Alberta government after losing millions of dollars due to collapsing real estate values and defaulted mortgages, with the federal government providing bailout funds to the tune of $275-million.

But after premier Ralph Klein privatized Alberta liquor sales in 1994, Mr. Kipnes sensed a chance at redemption, founding the Liquor Depot, which grew from a single store in Edmonton into a publicly traded North American behemoth, with locations from Kentucky to Alaska. “Irv could just see an opportunity and chase it,” said Mr. Corbett, who served as an executive vice-president for Liquor Depot’s parent company, Liquor Stores N.A. In 2014, when Mr. Kipnes retired from the company’s board, its chairperson was Mr. Klein’s former treasurer, Jim Dinning.

While they’re dwarfed by his charitable contributions, Mr. Kipnes also made substantial political contributions, chief among them to the former Alberta PC party, but also contributed varying sums to the UCP, Alberta NDP and Alberta Party, according to Elections Alberta financial disclosures. Mr. Margolus described his late friend’s political views as more akin to the moderate Toryism of former PC premier Peter Lougheed than the hard-right populism of Premier Danielle Smith. “Like every developer, you probably give to both parties,” Mr. Margolus surmised.

Mr. Kipnes was close friends with former Edmonton mayor and provincial health minister Stephen Mandel, who shared Mr. Kipnes’s real estate background. The pair first met playing on a team that Mr. Kipnes had sponsored in a Jewish baseball league and have been close ever since. “Irv was instrumental in me getting involved in politics and philanthropy. He’s always thought that nobody should wander through life and not give back,” Mr. Mandel said .

Mr. Kipnes supported Mr. Mandel’s mayoral aspirations, in addition to Mr. Mandel’s brief tenure as a PC MLA and leadership of the Alberta Party. “It really was not a political relationship at all. It was a friendship,” Mr. Margolus said, adding that the pair and their wives were “as close as can be.” After Mr. Mandel’s daughter Rachel died of lymphoma in 2017, the Kipneses established the Rachel Mandel Lymphoma and Blood Cancers Research Fund with a $1-million donation that was matched by the Alberta Cancer Foundation.
When he announced a $25-million donation to establish the Dianne and Irving Kipnes Health Research Institute in September 2025, Mr. Kipnes reflected on his philosophy of philanthropy.

“Giving back – whether with your time, your ideas, or your resources – is one of the most meaningful things you can do. It connects you to something larger than yourself. It ensures that the values you hold dear will carry forward, long after you’re gone,” Mr. Kipnes said. “My goal has always been simple: leave things better than I found them.”

stories.title: What can Trump do—and not do—with Congress in the hands of Democrats?
stories.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump faces an uphill battle in Washington now that the Democratic Party is projected to win control of both chambers of the U.S. Congress in the midterms.
stories.author: Ariel Rabinovitch
stories.content:
U.S. President Donald Trump will face an uphill battle in Washington with the Democratic Party set to take control of both chambers of the U.S. Congress in January after Tuesday’s midterm elections.

But experts say little of what the administration has done so far will change anytime soon because of the power Trump still holds as president, even as a lame duck.

The midterms saw a decisive defeat for the Republican Party , as voters cast their ballots following almost two years of the Trump presidency and his administration’s agenda, with the results reflecting frustration among the majority of voters.

“Those who had the courage to stand against the Trump administration’s policies were vindicated by the checks and balances of the U.S. political system that ultimately pushed American voters to issue their bold verdict on less than two years of Trump 2.0,” said Derek Holt, Scotiabank vice president and head of Capital Markets Economics, in a note to clients.

“Voters saw this period as marked by inflamed deficits, unwise trade policies, overstimulation of growth and capacity pressures that sparked affordability challenges, broken promises about ending forever wars, attacks on public institutions, a revenge agenda and overly harsh immigration policy.”

Although the midterm results send a strong message to Republicans and the Trump administration, it’s unclear if there will be any major near-term changes in Washington.

Here’s a look at how things could change now that American voters handed the Democrats more control of the U.S. government.

There are three main branches of the federal government in the United States, including Congress, which is made up of both the House of Representatives and the Senate, as well as the executive branch, with Trump at the helm.

Since Trump’s second term began in January 2025, Republicans have held the majority of both the House and the Senate, but Republicans will hand over that majority in January 2027 as dozens of new Democrats take their seats in Washington.

At the same time, Trump is set to remain as president of the United States and the executive branch of government will continue to grant him the power to change certain regulations, including tariffs. He can also veto bills Congress passes and use executive orders to authorize some actions without their approval or without needing legislation.

Having two opposing political forces in Washington means there will likely be some gridlock for the next two years, and a Democratic-controlled Congress May find other hurdles to make it harder for Trump to get his agenda over the finish line.

“It is now harder for the president of the United States to enact legislation to pursue his agenda,” says political science professor Aaron Ettinger at Carleton University.

“Now that we have a divided government, with Congress being controlled by Democrats and the White House — the executive branch — being controlled by a Republican, you have two fiercely oppositional, antagonistic parties who are probably going to be at loggerheads. So it’s going to be very difficult to pass laws.”

A Democrat-controlled House of Representatives, Senate, and their respective committees will also get significantly more power around launching investigations and issuing subpoenas, which could force Trump onto a more defensive footing and lock his focus on more domestic pressures.

The U.S. launched a trade war with countries around the world last year when Trump slapped tariffs on thousands of imports — particularly against Canada with tariffs escalating in recent months.

Since tariffs were enacted through Trump and the executive branch of government, it would be very difficult for Congress to reverse those policies.

“The power of tariffing still resides within the executive branch of the U.S. government, and certainly in Donald Trump’s presidency. He is still using a legislative foundation from Congresses yonks ago to impose the kind of tariffs that are afflicting Canadians right now,” says Ettinger.

“Canadians, unfortunately, can’t just say, ‘Team Blue won the election yesterday, everything is going to be better.’ We’re still in for a really hard ride over the next two years.”

Trump’s tariff policies have impacted both the Canadian and U.S. economies and job markets by making it more expensive to import certain goods. The impact on local communities in Maine and Michigan are just some examples where tariffs likely fuelled a blue wave in the midterms as those tariff impacts became a sticking point for voters.

Affordability for Americans was top of mind in these midterms, with tariffs, as well as the Iran war, leading to volatile price spikes for gasoline and other goods.

In the weeks ahead, Trump and the Republicans will be in the so-called “lame duck ” session, where lawmakers May try to get as much done as they can while still holding power in Congress.

At that point, the Dems control the issues and May seek greater input over matters like labour controls and the environment. A smaller deal and reversal or watering down of prior executive orders is also a possibility outside of Congress,” said Holt in a note to clients.

If either he or GOP members read the room last evening, then tariffs, assaults on key trading partners and allies and divisive trade policy were among the factors that cost them the vote.”

But experts say little of what the administration has done so far will change anytime soon because of the power Trump still holds as president, even as a lame duck.

The midterms saw a decisive defeat for the Republican Party , as voters cast their ballots following almost two years of the Trump presidency and his administration’s agenda, with the results reflecting frustration among the majority of voters.

“Those who had the courage to stand against the Trump administration’s policies were vindicated by the checks and balances of the U.S. political system that ultimately pushed American voters to issue their bold verdict on less than two years of Trump 2.0,” said Derek Holt, Scotiabank vice president and head of Capital Markets Economics, in a note to clients.

“Voters saw this period as marked by inflamed deficits, unwise trade policies, overstimulation of growth and capacity pressures that sparked affordability challenges, broken promises about ending forever wars, attacks on public institutions, a revenge agenda and overly harsh immigration policy.”
Although the midterm results send a strong message to Republicans and the Trump administration, it’s unclear if there will be any major near-term changes in Washington.
Here’s a look at how things could change now that American voters handed the Democrats more control of the U.S. government.

He can also veto bills Congress passes and use executive orders to authorize some actions without their approval or without needing legislation.

“Now that we have a divided government, with Congress being controlled by Democrats and the White House — the executive branch — being controlled by a Republican, you have two fiercely oppositional, antagonistic parties who are probably going to be at loggerheads. Since tariffs were enacted through Trump and the executive branch of government, it would be very difficult for Congress to reverse those policies.

“Canadians, unfortunately, can’t just say, ‘Team Blue won the election yesterday, everything is going to be better.’ We’re still in for a really hard ride over the next two years.”

stories.title: Hydro-Québec to sell portion of New York transmission line to Kahnawake
stories.summary: Montreal - Hydro-Québec is proposing to sell a share of a segment on a new power transmission line to New York to the Mohawk community of Kahnawake.
stories.author: Marieke Glorieux-Stryckman The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - Hydro-Québec is proposing to sell a share of a segment on a new power transmission line to New York to the Mohawk community of Kahnawake.

The First Nations community south of Montreal could become a shareholder of a 58-kilometre segment of the transmission line in Quebec under the proposed deal.

Hydro-Québec estimates this segment of the line, which is in large part underground with a smaller section underwater when it reaches the Richelieu River, cost around $800 million to build.

However, the utility said in filings to the province’s energy regulator that the asset the council of Kahnawake would invest in is worth $310 million.

The council of the First Nation plans to buy an ownership stake worth about half of this value, said Eric Doucet, a lawyer for the council.

The utility has asked the province’s energy regulator to approve a transaction that would transfer ownership of the segment to Horizon Kahnawà:ke Hydro-Québec, a new company jointly owned by Hydro-Québec and the council.

If the deal goes through, the Mohawk community would pay Hydro-Québec for the ownership stake. Hydro-Québec would then pay fees to the jointly owned company to use the transmission line, generating revenue for the community.

This is the first such partnership between Hydro-Québec and an Indigenous community, said spokesperson Lynn St-Laurent.

Keisha Goodleaf, director of revenue and business development for the Mohawk Council of Kahnawake, believes this partnership is a recognition of First Nations territory and of the need for economic reconciliation.

“There’s been some history with First Nations and Hydro-Québec — not so pretty history. I think that this is a really significant step toward bettering those partnerships and relationships with First Nations,” she said.

Goodleaf said she hopes the partnership will allow Kahnawake to build wealth for future generations and to create a model for future partnerships between Indigenous communities and Hydro-Québec.

Doucet said this project shows that Hydro-Québec understands it needs social acceptability and partnerships with Indigenous communities in future developments.

“The way of doing things of the past in terms of just kind of saying, ‘OK, we’re gonna build a dam here or we’re going to put a transmission line there’ — it doesn’t work anymore,” he said.

“It is a huge mindset shift for Hydro-Québec,” he added.

Hydro-Québec has faced legal battles over claims it destroyed First Nation and Inuit land through its hydroelectric infrastructure development.

In its 2025 Action Plan, Hydro-Quebec acknowledged the “major impact” these projects had on Indigenous communities and said it wants to create more opportunities for First Nations and Inuit to be shareholders in and profit from its projects.

“(The agreement with Kahnawake) is an example of the type of economic partnership we aim to build with First Nations and Inuit communities — sustainable partnerships in which all parties invest and benefit from the value created,” St-Laurent said.

The planned partnership allowed the Mohawk Council of Kahnawake to weigh in during the development of the project, including with environmental concerns or on Indigenous rights, said Doucet.

As part of the agreement, Hydro-Québec also donated $10 million to help build a new cultural arts centre in Kahnawake that now hosts language lessons and other events.

“That was a really great way to show that relationship building and contributing to language and culture, things that are really core community values,” said Goodleaf.

This is part of a growing number of energy partnerships with Indigenous communities including renewable energy projects, energy storage and natural gas infrastructure.

In October, TC Energy announced that five First Nations had invested in the company’s Coastal GasLink project in British Columbia. The project had previously drawn criticism, namely from the Wet’suwet’en community.

In Alberta in 2022, a group of First Nations signed a deal with the energy company Enbridge to buy shares in oil pipeline projects.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 4, 2026.

stories.title: Bedford residents raise concerns about density, traffic at waterfront project open house
stories.summary: The revitalization project includes a high-speed ferry service linking Bedford to downtown Halifax that's expected to begin in 2030.
stories.author: Rebecca Lau, Angela Capobianco
stories.content:
Concerns about density and traffic were raised during a community open house on the Mill Cove and Bedford Waterfront project, which will redevelop the area and include an electric high-speed ferry service.

Residents filled the Bedford Legion on Wednesday to share their thoughts on the early stages of the project.

Mill Cove has been designated an Urban Local Growth Center by the municipality and as a Suburban Opportunity Site by the province of Nova Scotia.

In addition to the ferry service linking Bedford to Halifax, which was announced in 2024 as part of a joint investment by all three levels of government, the revitalization will include a new public library, housing and park improvements.

“All of those combined is essentially a strong reason for us to study the area and look at a transit-oriented development or community,” said Dali Salih, a senior planner with the Planned Growth and Strategic Projects division at HRM.

“Some of the comments that I received (so far are), ‘This is exciting, build it already,’ or ‘This is exciting, but you know some improvements are required relating to whether it’s infrastructure or whether it is parkland.'”

Planners have set out key objectives, including creating pedestrian-friendly public spaces, addressing coastal hazards, enhancing the waterfront, and identifying mobility network upgrades to support the ferry.

Many attendees said they were excited about what the early stages of planning have included, but some had reservations about traffic and the proposed density of housing.

“You have to pick out the proper areas for the high density, and you still need people who want to buy single-home dwellings. So a lot of that has to be addressed,” said Kelly Bentham, president of the Fernleigh Park Homeowner Society.

Fellow resident, Jacqueline Levert, pointed out that access is a key consideration too.

“We need to make it a space where everybody has access to it. So I think those things are really important before we get into housing, but I think the ferry needs to happen quick,” she said.

Salih said she welcomes all input from residents to help build a plan the community can get behind.

“I’m hoping that they come in with all of their passion, all of their ideas, what they value, what they love about their community, so we can reflect that in our planning policies and planning recommendations,” she said.

The Mill Cove ferry is slated to transport passengers between Mill Cove and downtown Halifax using zero-emission ferries. The service is expected to reduce travel time on the Bedford Highway and help alleviate demand on existing corridors, including Hammonds Plains Road.

The federal government committed $155.7 million to the ferry project, while the province committed $65 million and the municipality was set to pitch in about $40 million.

The ferry service was initially set to begin in 2027-28 but was delayed due to land negotiations. It is now expected to begin operating in 2030.

Residents who want to submit feedback online can visit engagehalifax.CA/mill-cove.

stories.title: Alberta Premier Smith says U.S. midterm results 'vindicate' her approach to tariffs
stories.summary: Edmonton - Alberta Premier Danielle Smith says sweeping Democrat wins in the U.S. midterm elections are a vindication of her approach to the cross-border trade war.
stories.author: Jack Farrell The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Edmonton - Alberta Premier Danielle Smith says sweeping Democrat wins in the U.S. midterm elections prove her province was on the right path in the cross-border trade war.

“It is a vindication of our approach when it comes to tariffs,” Smith told the house during question period Wednesday.

“We always have objected to tariffs. We know it hurts us. It hurts the Americans.”

The Democrats on Tuesday took control of both houses of Congress and flipped long-held Republican Senate seats and state-level positions.

The results are seen as a widespread rebuke of U.S. President Donald Trump and his policies, including his treatment of trading partners like Canada.

Smith said she hopes the midterm results are an opportunity to improve the relationship between Canada and the U.S.

She pointed to her government’s efforts to build relationships across the aisle, including with Adam Schiff, a Democrat senator from California.

Smith’s government has stood apart from other provinces in the trade dispute. Alberta has for the most part resisted retaliatory tariffs or trade action while encouraging continued diplomacy.

Alberta only briefly halted sales of U.S. liquor in 2025, and Smith has steadfastly opposed the idea of leveraging oil and gas exports as an economic weapon in the fight.

But earlier Wednesday, as a result of the ongoing trade dispute, her government announced a new policy to prioritize Albertan and Canadian companies for small government contracts.

“We’re putting local businesses first, supporting Canadian suppliers and making sure more of our government spending helps create opportunities and jobs here at home,” Smith said in a news release.

The new measures apply to future contracts but existing deals are also to be reviewed when they come up for renewal.

Service Alberta Minister Dale Nally said it gives qualified local companies a better shot at bidding on about $350 million in government spending, or five per cent of procurement contracts.

He said 95 per cent of government contracts already land with Canadian companies.

“This is just a practical, common-sense way that we can help businesses that we know could be struggling or impacted because of the current tariffs,” Nally said in an interview.

Opposition NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi told reporters that the United Conservative Party government is two years too late.

“We’ve been asking for this exact thing for over two years, from the day Trump was re-elected,” Nenshi said.

“Imagine the wealth you could have created and the jobs you could have created in Alberta, if you had just done it two years ago when everyone else did.”

Nenshi said that beyond tariffs, he feels the U.S. midterm results were a sign that voters everywhere are tired of “culture war” politics — which he accused Smith of championing.

In question period, he pointed to a government bill tabled this week that would require post-secondary schools to develop neutrality policies.

“Who exactly asked the premier for this, and what difference is it going to make to a single student?” he asked.

Smith, in response, said her government was only trying to counteract NDP policies and influence. “They bring in the wokeism and the cancel culture. They create a hostile environment for free speech,” the premier said.

“We’re undoing their culture war.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 4, 2026.

— With files from Lisa Johnson

stories.title: Spy watchdog flags privacy risk from military’s online intelligence activities
stories.summary: The review agency says information publicly available online can still raise privacy concerns when it's collected and analyzed by government organizations.
stories.author: Jim Bronskill
stories.content:
A national spy watchdog report says the military’s policy on the collection of information about Canadians doesn’t sufficiently address the privacy risks posed by online searches.

The National Security and Intelligence Review Agency found the Defence Department and the Canadian Armed Forces have the legal authority to collect publicly available information from the internet for intelligence purposes, but the watchdog noted shortcomings on privacy protection and oversight.

The review agency says information publicly available online can still raise privacy concerns when it’s collected and analyzed by government organizations.

It says Canadians should be able to trust that intelligence collection has a clear, lawful purpose and that their privacy rights are respected.

The watchdog found the military does not systematically record the link between open-source collection activities on the internet and the approved operation or defence activity.

It also says policies and record-keeping do not adequately address all privacy risks or demonstrate that collection involving Canadians is necessary.

stories.title: Bombers expected to wait before naming starter
stories.summary: Head coach Mike O'Shea knows the Winnipeg Blue Bombers will be in Montreal on Saturday playing in the East Division final.
stories.author: Dan Ralph
stories.content:
Head coach Mike O’Shea knows the Winnipeg Blue Bombers will be in Montreal on Saturday playing in the East Division final.

Who will be his starting quarterback, though, is an entirely different matter.

Dru Brown orchestrated last weekend’s 25-22 East semifinal win over the Toronto Argonauts. Brown hit Nic Demski on a 23-yard TD pass with 44 seconds remaining, then found Demski for the two-point conversion.

Zach Collaros didn’t suit up due to a rib injury suffered in Winnipeg’s playoff-clinching 34-10 win over B.C. on Oct. 23. Brown replaced Collaros and went 11 of- 1 passing for 185 yards and two TDs as the Bombers outscored the Lions 24-10 in the fourth quarter.

Winnipeg didn’t confirm Brown would start the East semifinal until releasing its depth chart the day before the game. The expectation is the same will happen this week.

Winnipeg will face a rested Montreal squad that hasn’t played since a 33-16 road win over Toronto on Oct. 23. Quarterback Davis Alexander’s last start was a 44-24 win over Saskatchewan on Oct. 12, a game where he threw for 403 yards with five TDs and an interception while rushing three times for 40 yards.

Dustin Crum started both of Montreal’s final regular-season games, with Caleb Evans playing the second half of the regular-season finale in Toronto.

The win over Saskatchewan was also the last time Canadian Tyson Philpot and Tyler Snead — who finished 1-2 among CFL receivers — both started. Montreal and Winnipeg split their season series 1-1, with each winning at home.

The Alouettes were 9-0 during the regular season at Molson Stadium.

Alexander threw for 697 yards with five TDs versus Winnipeg while completing 70.4 per cent of his passes.

Philpot and Snead were both key figures versus the Bombers. Philpot registered 18 catches for 294 yards and a TD while Snead had 14 receptions for 224 yards and three touchdowns.

Alexander and Philpot are finalists for the CFL’s outstanding player award, along with Edmonton quarterback Cody Fajardo. Philpot is also up for the top Canadian honour.

Winnipeg’s Brady Oliveira rushed for 95 yards on 20 carries last week versus Toronto. The CFL rushing leader (1,493 yards, 6.3-yard average) ran for 150 yards on 25 carries (six-yard average) and a TD versus Montreal.

Ontaria Wilson was Winnipeg’s leading receiver against Montreal with 14 catches for 223 yards and three TDs. The Bombers were 5-3 versus East Division teams and 4-4 during the regular season on the road.

Pick: Montreal.

B.C. Lions versus Edmonton Elks (Saturday afternoon)

At Edmonton, the Elks are in the playoffs for the first time since 2019 and host their first post-season contest in 11 years. They split their season series with B.C. 1-1, with each team winning at home.

Edmonton was 8-1 at Commonwealth Stadium this season while B.C. was 4-5 on the road.

Nathan Rourke threw for 320 yards with a TD and two interceptions in B.C.’s 36-24 win over Edmonton on July 4. But he was injured in the Elks’ 19-17 win on July 17 as Chase Brice finished 20 of 34 passing for 226 yards with a TD and four interceptions.

Last week, Rourke had 366 passing yards and three TDs in the Lions’ 33-26 victory over the defending-champion Saskatchewan Roughriders.

Keon Hatcher Sr. registered nine receptions for 175 yards and a TD versus Edmonton, while defensive back Jackson Findlay had 13 tackles and an interception.

Edmonton’s defence should provide a stout test. The Elks led the CFL in fewest offensive points allowed (23.6 per game), offensive yards (338.6), most interceptions (27) and fumble recoveries (15) and were second against the pass (272.7 yards) and run (81.4).

stories.title: Police watchdog investigating death of armed man found in burned Fredericton home
stories.summary: The police watchdog says crisis negotiators tried to communicate with the man for a couple of hours before the home started burning.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
New Brunswick’s police oversight agency is investigating the death of an armed man inside a Fredericton home.

The Serious Incident Response Team says the man had recently barricaded himself inside the home, which caught fire.

The man’s body was later found inside the burned residence, but the agency did not say how he died.

When officers from the Fredericton Police Force were dispatched to the home on Murray Avenue on Sunday night, they learned the man had a weapon.

The police watchdog says crisis negotiators tried to communicate with the man for a couple of hours before the home started burning.

After the man’s body was found inside, the municipal police force immediately referred the case to the agency.

stories.title: Canada’s focus ‘hasn’t changed’ despite U.S. midterm blue wave, minister says
stories.summary: Canadian leaders say it would be “dangerous” to assume relations with the U.S. will change immediately following a major sweep of the House and the Senate by the Democrats Tuesday.
stories.author: Rachel Morgan
stories.content:
Canada’s focus on trade talks with the United States “hasn’t changed” following a major sweep of the House of Representatives and the Senate by the Democrats Tuesday, says Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc.

LeBlanc cautioned that the current Congress remains in place until January and Canada must continue to collaborate with the representatives who are currently in office.

“Our focus hasn’t changed. Yesterday we went to work on issues of affordability for Canadians, ON building major projects, ON strengthening the Canadian economy, ON diversifying our trade relationships,” he said. “That is actually our focus today and will be the focus tomorrow in the budget.”

LeBlanc said it would not be “constructive” to interpret what drove the results, where the war in Iran and the cost of living — which has soared due to both the conflict and the U.S. administration’s trade war on Canada and other countries — played a significant role, according to polling.

“Our job is to focus on what we can control, and that’s to work with the people that Americans have elected,” he said.

The Democrats swept both the House and the Senate Tuesday night in a blow to the Republican Party.

Some experts have said the results south of the border show how fed up Americans were with the ongoing trade war. Trade talks between Ottawa and Washington blew up in August igniting a fire that led to even broader tariffs on Canadian goods.

Canada retaliated by implementing counter-tariffs ranging from 15 to 50 per cent on approximately $27.6 billion worth of U.S. imports.

But Canada has also looked to diversify its trade portfolio, with recent trips to China and India, and signing on as an associate member with the European Union.

“I think it’s dangerous to make assumptions about what might take place before you actually have the opportunity to sit down with partners,” Minister of Justice and Attorney General Sean Fraser told reporters Wednesday.

“The strategy for Canada going forward remains the same: to defend our economic interests by diversifying trade partners, seeing if we can work through the challenges that we continue to have vis-a-vis the United States.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney said Tuesday that “more intense” trade negotiations with the U.S. had already begun following a phone call with President Trump over the weekend.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said Carney needs to take advantage of the “immense leverage” of the midterms to get a good deal with the U.S.

“The results yesterday demonstrate that Americans hate tariffs,” he said. “A tariff on Canada is a tax on Americans.”

Ontario Premier Doug Ford said that while he was elated with the midterm results , the strained relationship between the U.S. and Canada would remain.

Ford, who has been heavily critical of tariffs in the past, said he will be directing his ministers to head down to Washington to connect with senators, congresspeople and governors about their trade relationship as soon as the newly elected officials are sworn in at the end of January.

“We’re going to be down there, communicating, building those relationships,” he said. “We have to continue making sure that we move faster, quicker, immediate on everything across the board.”

Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon said his government is planning a “diplomatic offensive” to launch south of the border.

“I think we’re in a better position to possibly find a solution because Americans have spoken, the situation has changed,” he told reporters in Quebec City. “So what we’re going to do is prepare a diplomatic offensive of discussion with the Americans to see if there isn’t a solution.”

Quebec has been one of the provinces hardest hit by U.S. tariffs which target softwood lumber, aluminum and various manufactured foods.

But St-Pierre Plamondon said he doesn’t plan for Quebec to carry out direct trade notifications just yet.

“I think before positioning ourselves on that, we’ll open up the channels of discussions,” he said.

In a statement on social media, Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew said he looks forward to working together to lower costs on both sides of the border “by ending the war in Iran (gas & diesel prices) and the Trump tariffs (the price of everything else).”

He also gave a special nod to Minnesota Senator-elect Peggy Flanagan, the first Native woman elected to the Senate; Deb Haaland, who will lead New Mexico as the first Native woman to serve as a U.S. governor; and Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, who is the first Muslim elected to the Senate.

Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe said the Democrat win is an opportunity for Canada to “reset our relationship” with the U.S. and to “restore free and fair trade between our two countries.”

“I know Canada is ready to do this,” he said in a statement on social media. “Hopefully the U.S. is as well.”
