stories.title: Google AI lets Canadians buy from Lululemon, Shoppers Drug Mart without leaving app
stories.summary: Canadians using Google's artificial intelligence tools for online shopping will have an easier time checking out with some retailers.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Canadians using Google’s artificial intelligence tools for online shopping will have an easier time checking out with some retailers.

The U.S. tech giant announced a new partnership Wednesday that will allow Canadians to make purchases with select brands without leaving the Gemini app or Google’s AI search mode.

The brands included in the partnership are Lululemon Athletica Inc., Shoppers Drug Mart, La Maison Simons and some Shopify Inc. merchants.

Through the partnership, customers will be able to ask Gemini or Google’s AI search tool to find items that have specific features or are a certain style or colour.

Shoppers will then be able to buy any options Gemini and the tool present from partner retailers without exiting the app or search page.

A demo Google released of the new feature showed someone telling Gemini their face is dry, irritated and burns when most moisturizers are applied. The person requests Gemini suggest a gentle recovery balm that would heal their skin and could be purchased from a local drugstore.

Gemini surfaced a balm that could be bought directly through the app from Shoppers Drug Mart.

Retailers did not pay to access the feature and Google did not pay the merchants for their participation, Google spokesperson Wendy Manton said in an email to The Canadian Press.

Fees are also not exchanged by either side when consumers make purchases using the feature, and the program does not make items from Lululemon, Shoppers, Simons or the participating Shopify merchants more likely to be surfaced by Google, she said.

Google’s partnership comes after other tech firms like OpenAI and Meta have introduced features to make checking out through their AI platforms more seamless.

Last year, Shopify announced it would start helping its merchants make hundreds of millions of their products be instantly discoverable through ChatGPT.

The Ottawa-based e-commerce software provider also began integrating Shop Pay — its checkout technology — into AI tools including Muse, Claude Duet, Grok Bot and Instinct.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 4, 2026.

Companies in this story: (TSX:L, TSX: Shop)

stories.title: Tariff relief for Canada not guaranteed after Democrats sweep U.S. midterm elections
stories.summary: Bangor — Political watchers in Atlantic Canada say the Democrats' sweeping midterm election victory in the United States likely won't provide immediate relief from tariffs.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Bangor — The premiers of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick say they’re hopeful the Democrats’ sweeping midterm election victory in the United States will improve the country’s relationship with Canada.

Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston told reporters Wednesday that Prime Minister Mark Carney is representing Canada well and he’s putting his faith in Ottawa to improve relations.

“The American people spoke pretty loudly, I would say, and pretty clearly, and I’m hopeful that’s a message that obviously (President Donald Trump) and his team receive as well on the expectations of the people,” Houston told reporters following a groundbreaking ceremony for U.S. e-commerce giant Amazon in Dartmouth, N.S., ON Wednesday.

“And I believe that a part of that is a better relationship with Canada, their neighbours, their friends. We have long-standing relationships and we just need to get those to a better place.”

Meanwhile, New Brunswick Premier Susan Holt said Wednesday morning that her Liberal government is “looking forward to building relationships” with newly elected U.S. officials.

Holt, in a brief statement to The Canadian Press, said she expects “their leadership will result in improved trade conditions for (New Brunswick) entrepreneurs and workers.”

Trump told Fox News on Tuesday that “a great deal” with Canada was imminent. For his part, Prime Minister Mark Carney said the two sides have “made progress” after the U.S. backed down on some of its demands.

Political watchers in Atlantic Canada say midterm results likely won’t provide immediate relief from tariffs.

The trade war with Canada became a ballot-box issue in several races in states along the border and Democrat victories there are seen as a rebuke to the Republican president’s policies.

In Maine, Democrat Troy Jackson unseated long-standing incumbent Republican senator Susan Collins. Both say the U.S.-Canada trade war has hit their state’s economy hard and that tariffs should be removed.

Some Jackson voters said tariffs on Canada played a role in their decision, accusing Collins of not doing enough to curtail Trump.

But Donald Wright, a political science professor at the University of New Brunswick in Fredericton, said Trump still has the executive powers he used to enact the tariffs and he isn’t likely to back off because of election results.

Instead, he said the president could take the result as an excuse to punish Maine by ramping up the levies on Canadian goods.

Last month, in the lead-up to Tuesday’s midterms, Trump exempted some Canadian forestry products and agricultural equipment from his 50-per-cent levies in an attempt to help Collins.

“A vindictive president might want to hurt Maine … he could re-implement some of the tariffs that he lifted,” Wright said in an interview.

Scott Matthews, head of the political science department at Memorial University in Newfoundland and Labrador, said Canada May have lost an advocate in Collins.

Without Collins, the Republicans lose one of their moderate voices in Washington, Matthews said by phone.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 4, 2026.

stories.title: AFN chief says no one besides Carney, Kinew talked about abolishing Indian Act
stories.summary: Talk of reforming or abolishing the Indian Act comes as Mark Carney works to speed up development of major projects alongside the provinces and Indigenous Peoples.
stories.author: Alessia Passafiume
stories.content:
The national chief of the Assembly of First Nations says the only leaders to discuss abolishing the Indian Act during a landmark meeting last week were Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew and Prime Minister Mark Carney.

Carney said after the meeting that the idea was raised by chiefs in the room.

Kinew, who is Anishinaabe, called for the act to be abolished during the historic gathering of federal, provincial and First Nations leaders in Ottawa.

The Indian Act, which dates from 1876, gives Ottawa sweeping powers over First Nations communities and people, including the authority to decide who qualifies for status and what reserves can and can’t do.

Both Kinew and Carney said the idea to change or abolish the Indian Act was raised and supported by some chiefs in the room. AFN National Chief Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak said on Tuesday that’s not true.

Woodhouse Nepinak said the chiefs were focused more on the major projects legislation they say threatens their rights, and those conversations “went to the wayside” when Kinew and Carney made their remarks.

The prime minister said after the meeting he was “very open to” the idea but later said the Indian Act could be reformed rather than abolished.

“Not everybody, but other participants raised the desirability. So it’s already starting from the right place in that it’s not the federal government deciding something should be done. It’s responding to a request,” Carney said at the time.

In an emailed statement issued Friday, a spokesperson for Indigenous Services Minister Mandy Gull-Masty’s office said Kinew was not the only one to raise the possibility of reforming or removing the Indian Act at the meeting.

“As the meeting was held behind closed doors, it would be inappropriate to provide more specificity on the details of the conversation,” Livi McElrea said.

While First Nations chiefs generally agree the law is outdated and restrictive, there is little consensus on whether it should be repealed and what might take its place.

First Nations leaders broadly support changing the rules on how the Indian Act determines who qualifies for status. The federal government has not committed to changing those rules.

Previous prime ministers have tried and failed to reform or eliminate the Indian Act. In 1969, years before he became prime minister, Jean Chrétien introduced what was known as the “White Paper” when he was minister of Indian Affairs in the government of Pierre Trudeau.

The document called for the abolition of the Indian Act, an end to Indian status, the absorption of First Nations people as ordinary Canadian citizens, the termination of treaties and the privatization of reserve lands.

The proposal received widespread pushback from First Nations leaders led in part by Harold Cardinal and the Indian Association of Alberta. They called Chrétien’s plan assimilationist and warned it would lead to the erasure of their cultures.

In the emailed statement from Gull-Masty’s office, McElrea said Carney has acknowledged the Indian Act is racist and it’s necessary to have a broader conversation with First Nations about its future.

There are policies in place if a First Nation decides to opt out of the Indian Act and move toward self-government.

Gull-Masty’s community, the Cree First Nation of Waswanipi, is one of those self-governing communities under the 1975 James Bay and Northern Quebec Agreement — the first modern land claim in Canada and one in which Chrétien played a leading role.

Talk of reforming or abolishing the Indian Act comes as Carney works to speed up development of major projects alongside the provinces and Indigenous Peoples.

His government’s Building Canada Act initially gave Ottawa the power to sidestep the Indian Act. That provision was removed in response to calls from the Conservatives and the Bloc Québécois.

stories.title: Amend firearms regulations to allow security guards protecting synagogues to be armed, urges Jewish advocacy group
stories.summary: The need for armed deterrence was evident on Sept. 20, when armed police officers protected a Belleville Jewish congregation from an armed attacker, says Tafsik
stories.author: Stewart Lewis
stories.content:
A Toronto-based Jewish advocacy organization is urging immediate action to amend federal firearms regulations.

Tafsik wants licensed, trained security guards to be able to carry firearms while protecting places of worship and private faith-based schools.

“We are asking Ottawa for one targeted change to an existing regulation, so that licensed, trained and vetted security guards can protect people at prayer and children in private faith-based schools, under the same strict rules that already apply to armoured-car guards,” says Sofia Marquez, head of Tafsik’s operations.

Tafsik put this proposal forward at an emergency security meeting that it organized for Toronto’s Jewish community on Sept. 30, 10 days after a gunman opened fire outside a Belleville, Ont., synagogue on Yom Kippur.

“Canada’s own intelligence agencies have warned that an attack on our community is a realistic possibility, yet the only armed protection a congregation can lawfully hire today is a paid-duty police officer, at about $125 an hour,” says Marquez, adding that “most synagogues, churches, mosques and temples cannot afford that week after week.”

Tafsik is lobbying federal members of parliament and senators, Marquez says. It already received support at the provincial level during the emergency security meeting, she adds. Community members, Jewish organizations, community security providers, Toronto police and government, including Ontario’s Solicitor General, Michael Kerzner and Toronto City Councillor James Pasternak, were present.

“We are now beginning meetings with federal ministers in Ottawa, MPs and senators,” Marquez says.

Legal “authorizations to carry” set out in federal Firearms Act regulations allow private security guards to carry firearms when transporting cash and commercial valuables. However, notes Merquez, the regs deny that same protection for “people at prayer and children in religious schools.”

Tafsik is calling on the Minister of Public Safety to introduce a regulatory amendment to change this.

The advocacy organization’s push comes amid intelligence warnings and increasing numbers of hate-motivated incidents across the country.

Federal assessments from the Integrated Terrorism Assessment Centre and Csis have repeatedly warned that the Jewish community faces acute threats , particularly from lone actors targeting vulnerable community sites.

Police-reported hate crimes against Jewish Canadians accounted for 71% of all religion-motivated hate crimes in 2025 despite representing only 1% of the population.

The urgency for armed deterrence was evident on Sept. 20, 2026, when an armed attacker opened fire outside the Sons of Jacob synagogue in Belleville during Yom Kippur services. “A mass casualty event was averted because armed police officers were protecting the site,” says Merquez.

However, she notes, at present, the only avenue for having armed deterrence at a religious institution or private faith-based school is hiring off-duty, paid police officers.

She says that the published York Regional Police rate for a constable is $89.06 an hour, plus a 24 per cent administration fee and 13 per cent HST. So, about $125 an hour, before a $39 hourly vehicle charge, with a four-hour minimum. For one post covering eight hours a day, that’s about $1,000 a day, or $365,000 a year.

Tafsik estimates it would cost about $30 an hour, based on current rates, to pay for licensed security guards. That is about $240 a day, or $87,600 a year, roughly a quarter of the paid off-duty police officer cost.

“For the vast majority of congregations, the present expense is impossible to sustain,” says Marquez. While federal grant programs such as the Canada Community Security Program provides limited, short-term funding for high-risk periods (capped at 90 days), it explicitly excludes recurring weekly services.

Tasfik is advocating for quick adoption of legislative reform. It suggests that proposed amendments would involve strict safeguards akin to those governing armed guards governing movement of cash and valuables. That includes stringent qualifications, authorizations restricted to active duty on the premises of the designated place of worship or private faith-based school, integration with police and firearms officers, and a prohibition against armed volunteers.

Stewart Lewis is a writer and editor with National Post. A journalist and lawyer, he has worked in newspapers, radio and TV, and served a legal stint with Global Affairs Canada at the United Nations in New York City.

“We are now beginning meetings with federal ministers in Ottawa, MPs and senators,” Marquez says.

Legal “authorizations to carry” set out in federal Firearms Act regulations allow private security guards to carry firearms when transporting cash and commercial valuables. However, notes Merquez, the regs deny that same protection for “people at prayer and children in religious schools.”
Tafsik is calling on the Minister of Public Safety to introduce a regulatory amendment to change this.
The advocacy organization’s push comes amid intelligence warnings and increasing numbers of hate-motivated incidents across the country.

Federal assessments from the Integrated Terrorism Assessment Centre and Csis have repeatedly warned that the Jewish community faces acute threats , particularly from lone actors targeting vulnerable community sites.
Police-reported hate crimes against Jewish Canadians accounted for 71% of all religion-motivated hate crimes in 2025 despite representing only 1% of the population.

The urgency for armed deterrence was evident on Sept. 20, 2026, when an armed attacker opened fire outside the Sons of Jacob synagogue in Belleville during Yom Kippur services. “A mass casualty event was averted because armed police officers were protecting the site,” says Merquez.
However, she notes, at present, the only avenue for having armed deterrence at a religious institution or private faith-based school is hiring off-duty, paid police officers.

She says that the published York Regional Police rate for a constable is $89.06 an hour, plus a 24 per cent administration fee and 13 per cent HST. So, about $125 an hour, before a $39 hourly vehicle charge, with a four-hour minimum. For one post covering eight hours a day, that’s about $1,000 a day, or $365,000 a year.

Tafsik estimates it would cost about $30 an hour, based on current rates, to pay for licensed security guards. That is about $240 a day, or $87,600 a year, roughly a quarter of the paid off-duty police officer cost.

“For the vast majority of congregations, the present expense is impossible to sustain,” says Marquez. While federal grant programs such as the Canada Community Security Program provides limited, short-term funding for high-risk periods (capped at 90 days), it explicitly excludes recurring weekly services.

Tasfik is advocating for quick adoption of legislative reform. It suggests that proposed amendments would involve strict safeguards akin to those governing armed guards governing movement of cash and valuables. That includes stringent qualifications, authorizations restricted to active duty on the premises of the designated place of worship or private faith-based school, integration with police and firearms officers, and a prohibition against armed volunteers.

stories.title: Green Line LRT extension study proposed, north Calgary councillors seek bus service improvements
stories.summary: A city committee endorsed exploring curbside bus lanes along Centre Street in north Calgary to improve rapid bus-service in lieu of a future Green Line LRT extension.
stories.author: Adam MacVicar
stories.content:
As construction work dots the future route for the first phase of the Green Line LRT project in southeast Calgary, project officials hope to secure more funding to study extending the line further north and south.

In an update to the city’s executive committee Tuesday, city administration noted it would be requesting an additional $16.6 million in the upcoming four-year budget cycle to advance planning and design on future extensions to the project.

Roughly $4.1 million would be dedicated to study a southeast extension of the future line from the Shepard to Seton areas, while the bulk of the funding, $12.4 million, is proposed to examine extending the line further north from Eau Claire to 160 Avenue N.

Project officials said the difference in funding is due to a broader scope of work required for the northern leg, which is expected to take two years.

“In the north there was a functional plan done up to 16 Avenue in 2021 but no further work has been done on that,” Green Line director Wendy Tynan told reporters. “There’s much more work to progress: utilities, land, understanding technical considerations.”

Tynan estimated the study on the southeast extension would take one year to complete.

According to city administration, the studies will help improve project readiness for both extensions by updating technical information and assumptions as well as strengthening further cost certainty.

High-level estimates currently peg the cost for the south extension at $3 billion from Shepard to Seton and $4 billion to build the Green Line from Eau Claire to 40 Avenue N, according to city administration.

Calgary Mayor Jeromy Farkas said having those figures will help the city advocate for funding from both the provincial and federal governments; conversations he said he hopes to start having within the course of the next year.

“This is absolutely essential, not just for moving Calgarians, but also for the long-term financial viability of the Green Line,” Farkas said. “We need more riders on the system so it can be safe and so we can achieve some of the cost recovery requirements.”

Construction on the Green Line is currently underway from Shepard in the city’s northeast to 10 Avenue in the Beltline at a cost of $6.2 billion. The line is expected to be operational by 2031.

Funding for the studies will be decided by city council during budget deliberations later this month.

However, two city councillors representing Calgary’s northern communities aren’t convinced the Green Line will cross the Bow River anytime soon, and instead are seeking improved rapid-bus service in the area.

“I can’t wait 20 years for the potential of a Green Line to reach Ward 3,” said Coun. Andrew Yule, who represents that area. “What we need now is service because we’ve been put off and put off with these (bus-rapid transit) upgrades.”

In a separate report to committee Tuesday, city administration said fully building out the MAX Green BRT line along Centre Street from downtown to Keystone Hills would cost at least $511 million.

City administration said that would cover dedicated curbside bus lanes along the length of Centre Street and would come with the shortest delivery timeline.

More expensive options that would mean a smoother transition from a bus to the LRT up Centre Street in the future have already been explored, Yule argued, with little progress to date.

Some upgrades have already been completed along the MAX Green BRT with heated bus shelters and roadway improvements after it was converted into a rapid-bus route in 2025.

City councillors in the area argued for increased capacity for transit users in the area as the route is one of the busiest in the city with roughly 30,000 daily riders.

“We need to be able to make these improvements to be able to get dedicated lanes where they’re appropriate, signalized intersections in order to be able to speed up the bus, in order to be able to add more buses to Centre Street,” Ward 4 Coun. DJ Kelly said.

Yule’s motion to explore the $511 million option was endorsed by committee Tuesday, but still requires a final decision by city council.

If city council approves exploring the idea, administration would study the impacts and report back by mid-2027.

“My focus is service and it’s not about wasting years and years on studies,” Yule told reporters. “It’s about getting service to Calgarians that desperately need it.”

stories.title: Second night for community questions on Nova Scotia’s first proposed AI data centre
stories.summary: Cape Bretoners with questions about Nova Scotia's first planned artificial intelligence data centre have a second chance to speak up.
stories.author: Lyndsay Armstrong
stories.content:
By Lyndsay Armstrong The Canadian Press

Posted November 4, 2026 9:30 am

Cape Bretoners with questions about Nova Scotia’s first planned artificial intelligence data centre have a second chance to speak up.

The second of two information sessions by EverWind Fuels is set for this evening in southern Cape Breton, in the rural town of Lower River Inhabitants, N.S.

2:27 Legal expert weighs in on calls for regulations surrounding data centre development

Tuesday’s information session in D’Escousse, N.S., ran late as more than 200 people filled a community hall to hear from company officials.

Speakers asked about safeguards and environmental protections for the $10-billion, 18,600-square-metre AI data centre in Point Tupper, N.S., that’s set to come online by the end of 2027.

An information session on a planned AI data centre in Cape Breton ran late as residents lined up to ask what safeguards and environmental protections would be in place and to voice concern about the American AI giant that would lease the centre. (Nov. 4, 2026)

American tech company Anthropic has signed a 20-year lease for the centre that would draw 95 megawatts of electricity during its first phase, before a 325-megawatt expansion in 2028.

Everwind officials said residents had valid concerns, ranging from environmental protections to jobs, and there would be more consultations to come.

stories.title: Ex-RBC employee found guilty after viewing PM’s data, opening fraudulent accounts
stories.summary: Ibrahim El-Hakim was recruited by someone he believed ‘to be associated with organized crime,’ court document says
stories.author: Jim Bronskill
stories.content:
A former Royal Bank of Canada employee has been found guilty of three criminal charges after opening fraudulent accounts and viewing the personal banking information of Prime Minister Mark Carney.

Ibrahim El-Hakim, who worked at a downtown Ottawa bank branch, was recruited by someone he believed “to be associated with organized crime,” says an agreed statement of facts in the case filed in an Ontario court.

The RCMP began an investigation last year following a complaint from RBC.

The agreed statement says El-Hakim opened at least 43 fraudulent accounts at the bank between November 2023 and June 2025.

In late June 2025, El-Hakim admitted his involvement in the fraud to an RBC corporate security official, saying he was recruited on Telegram, a social media messaging app, by a person using the alias AI World, the statement says.

“Mr. El-Hakim stated that he participated in the scheme because he was experiencing financial difficulties,” it adds.

Court documents show El-Hakim pleaded guilty in August to fraud over $5,000, unauthorized use of a computer and identity theft.

El-Hakim did not turn up for a sentencing hearing late last month.

His lawyer at the time told Ontario Court Justice Norm Boxall that El-Hakim was no longer in Ottawa.

The court has set a new date for sentencing later this month.

The agreed statement of facts says El-Hakim described how he created bank profiles and opened credit products after receiving requests from AI World via Telegram.

AI World would send instructions and personal identifying information, including name, date of birth, social insurance number, driver’s licence information, passport data and customer profile information. It would request that a credit card be linked to a particular account.

El-Hakim would also send identity information back to AI World, including online banking passwords.

El-Hakim received at least $5,000 in compensation – $500 for each account issued in the form of an e-transfer deposited into one of his accounts at other banks, the statement says.

It adds that, shortly after interviewing El-Hakim, RBC became aware he had used his work computer and software to conduct unauthorized queries on customer profiles.

On June 17, 2025, El-Hakim accessed the customer banking profiles of Carney, Justin Trudeau and another individual, the statement says. The Trudeau account he accessed “was determined not to belong to the former prime minister,” the statement adds.

While accessing these profiles, El-Hakim was observed consulting a smart watch, the statement says. On the surveillance video, he was seen at one point taking a cellphone out of his pocket, using it and alternating his gaze between the phone and the computer screen of his bank workstation.

“Mr. El-Hakim committed these offences despite having received training in ethics, privacy, security and fraud prevention as part of his employment at RBC,” the statement says.

“He used customer information provided by third parties, opened fraudulent accounts, attempted to obtain credit products, accessed customer information without authorization, verified and transmitted identifying information, and received compensation for his participation.”

RBC has had to pay $14,634 for 27 clients to receive a two-year credit monitoring service as a result of their identity being stolen, the statement says.

RCMP Cpl. Erique Gasse said in September 2025 the investigation did not lead Mounties to believe there was any threat to Carney’s safety or to national security.

Since the investigation involved the prime minister, it was assigned to the RCMP’s Integrated National Security Enforcement Team in Montreal, where the report was made.

stories.title: Midterm blue wave sweep comes amid tariff backlash in Maine, Michigan
stories.summary: The world woke up on Wednesday morning to control of the U.S. Congress shifting to Democrats in a clear rejection of President Donald Trump's turbulent second term.
stories.author: Kelly Geraldine Malone
stories.content:
The world woke up on Wednesday morning to control of the U.S. Congress shifting to Democrats in a clear rejection of President Donald Trump’s turbulent second term.

In a clear rebuke of the second Trump administration, Democrats flipped long held Republican Senate seats in Texas, Maine and South Carolina. A blue wave also washed over House seats and down-ballot votes in an unprecedented Democratic tsunami set to send shock waves through the Republican party.

Polling showed that Americans were frustrated with the president and his policies. Trump’s approval was plummeting due to rising gas and diesel prices, high inflation and the unpopular war with Iran.

Many Americans have shown anger regarding Trump’s policies, which have driven up costs at gas stations and grocery stores.

The trade war with Canada became a ballot box issue in close contests in Maine and Michigan.

Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed — a constant target of Trump and the Republicans — beat out GOP candidate Mike Rogers while Democrat Troy Jackson ended the nearly 30-year run of Republican Susan Collins in Maine.

Trump’s attacks on Canada were so unpopular in Michigan that it forced Rogers to distance himself from Trump over the duties. El-Sayed has long called the trade war nonsensical.

Republicans and Democrats casting votes in Michigan on Tuesday said they wanted to see the trade war end. Mark Pospisil, 43, said it’s not good for Canada or the United States to have trade tensions.

“We should be friendly with our neighbours,” Pospisil said after voting for Republicans in White Lake, Mich.

The Michigan race was contentious and achieved national attention from Trump and Republicans, who made derogatory comments about El-Sayed linked to his religion and heritage.

In a speech after his win was announced, El-Sayed called out Trump and members of his administration for repeatedly mispronouncing his name.

“So after JD (Vance) swears me in in January, you can just go on and call me senator,” El-Sayed said to applause.

In Maine, the president had tried to give Collins a boost in the tough contest by making changes to 50 per cent tariffs on a range of Canadian goods to offer a reprieve to industries hit hard in Maine. The move was not enough to stop the blue wave from sweeping the state in response to high energy prices and a plummet in Canadian tourism.

Voters in some of the most Republican-safe areas showed their frustration with the president and the GOP. In Texas, James Talarico broke a decades-long Democrat losing streak by trouncing Trump-aligned Ken Paxton.

stories.title: Man seriously injured in Hamilton assault involving cadets selling poppies
stories.summary: A 59-year-old man suffered life-altering injuries after intervening in an incident involving air cadets selling poppies over the weekend, Hamilton police say.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
A 59-year-old man suffered life-altering injuries after intervening in an incident involving air cadets selling poppies over the weekend, Hamilton police say.

The man was supervising the cadets outside a restaurant at 1223 Barton St. E. Sunday afternoon when two youths allegedly approached and blew an air horn directly into their ears, police said in a news release.

He then followed the youths into the restaurant to confront them.

“A struggle ensued and an adult female who was not initially involved in the altercation jumped in to assist the youths,” police said.

Police allege the woman assaulted the man, who fell to the ground. One of the youths then hit the victim several times before leaving the restaurant. The woman also left the scene before police arrived.

“Upon arrival, officers located the adult male victim inside the restaurant suffering from serious injuries. Hamilton Paramedic Services attended and transported the victim to a local hospital for treatment. His injuries are considered life-altering,” police said.

“A short time later, officers located the two youths at a nearby retail store after receiving reports of a new, unrelated disturbance.”

A 12-year-old boy was arrested and charged with assault level one as well as aggravated assault. A 48-year-old woman was arrested Tuesday and charged with aggravated assault.

The investigation is ongoing.

Anyone with information is asked to contact police.

stories.title: Stock markets rally in early trading after U.S. midterm election
stories.summary: Stock markets rallied in both Canada and the U.S. early Wednesday after the U.S. midterm election yielded Democratic majorities in both houses of Congress.
stories.author: Elaine Lai And David Mchugh
stories.content:
Stock markets in both Canada and the U.S. rallied early Wednesday as Wall Street tries to sort the winners from the losers following stunning losses for U.S. President Donald Trump’s party in the midterm elections.

First Solar soared, while companies controlled by Trump ally Elon Musk fell. The parent company of Trump’s social media company plunged.

The S&P 500 jumped 1.1 per cent in early trading Wednesday and was potentially on track for its best day in six weeks. The Dow Jones Industrial Average soared 983 points, and the Nasdaq composite rose 1.7 per cent. Treasury yields fell in the bond market.

On Bay Street, the TSX surged at the open of trade, gaining more than 500 points, or about 1.4 per cent as of 9:35 a.m. Eastern time. The Canadian dollar’s U.S. exchange rate also rose about a quarter of a cent to 71.66 cents.

Investors parsed the potential impact on artificial intelligence, the defence and wind energy sectors, as well as Big Oil.

The results usher in a new era of congressional resistance to the agenda aggressively pursued by Trump. One overarching theme was that divided government might not be such a bad thing.

Markets generally prefer that control of Washington be split between Republicans and Democrats. That is seen as offering less risk of sweeping policy changes that could upend the economy.

“The magnitude of the gains for the Democrats in the midterms does not change too much for the near-term policy outlook, given the party still lacks a filibuster-proof majority in the Senate and President Trump has veto power to block legislation,” Stephen Brown of Capital Economics said in an analysis.

Get expert insights, Q&A on markets, housing, inflation, and personal finance information delivered to you every Saturday.

Some Asian markets briefly retreated amid concerns that the Democrats might slow the buildout of AI because of safety concerns and local resistance to data centres. Investors have questioned whether a major run-up in stock prices for artificial intelligence companies signals a bubble in the sector.

3:36 2026 U.S. midterm elections: Democrats ride ‘blue wave’ as early results show bad night for GOP

Defence stocks were largely in retreat on the possibility that the war in Iran will be dialed back.

Much remains impossible to predict, since Trump retains executive authority over key areas such as defence, foreign policy and in some instances trade.

A downbeat forecast could be that “Trump is not now a lame duck, but an angry duck” who might restart tensions over tariffs and Nato allies’ levels of military spending, said Carsten Brzeski, global chief of macro at ING Bank.

1:25 Trump strikes Iran hours before polls open in U.S. midterm elections

An optimistic view, Brzeski said, is that Trump becomes “a tame duck … that he will slow down any disruptive efforts and that he will put more focus on trying to win the Nobel Peace Prize by ending the two big wars without big disruption, and on trade, nothing happens but a few words.”

In Asia, Japan’s Nikkei 225 dipped 1.4 per cent to 62,188.63 while Taiwan’s Taiex lost 0.8 per cent. South Korea’s Kospi index rose 0.6 per cent to 5,683.80, as memory chipmaker SK Hynix edged 0.1 per cent lower, while Samsung Electronics slid 0.7 per cent. Japanese memory chipmaker Kioxia Holdings tumbled 5.4 per cent.

In early European trading, the CAC 40 in Paris rose 1.6 per cent to 8,148.42. Britain’s Ftse 100 was up 1.25 per cent to 10,770.95, and Germany’s DAX climbed 1.5 per cent to 26,249.34.

The price of Brent crude, the international standard, fell 1.2 per cent to US$102.35 per barrel, while U.S. benchmark crude oil gave up 0.8 per cent to $95.31 per barrel.

The U.S. dollar fell to 158.30 Japanese yen from 158.69 yen. The euro rose to $1.1255 from $1.1194.

stories.title: Canadian Tire putting $200 million into opening, revamping Mark’s stores
stories.summary: Toronto — Canadian Tire Corp. Ltd. is hoping to "reinvent" Mark's by pouring $200 million into opening and refreshing more of the apparel retailer's stores.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Toronto — Canadian Tire Corp. Ltd. is hoping to “reinvent” Mark’s by pouring $200 million into opening and refreshing more of the apparel retailer’s stores.

The cash infusion announced Wednesday will both expand Mark’s overall footprint and help revamp stores. By the end of 2028, the goal is for at least 40 of its expected 387 Mark’s locations to be new or converted to an updated model the company has been experimenting with since 2023.

That new format uses bigger spaces — roughly 25,000 square feet — to give stores a brighter, more airy and welcoming feel. The locations also tend to offer more expansive women’s and children’s sections as well as brand-specific shops nestled within broader Mark’s stores.

The model has been adopted by 21 stores in Alberta, British Columbia, Manitoba, Ontario and Quebec so far.

Mark’s president PJ Czank sees it as an opportunity for the nearly 50-year-old company to “change how customers see us.”

While trades workers have been accustomed to visiting the retailer since 1977 for apparel, the acquisition of Mark’s by Canadian Tire in the early aughts sparked an expanded modus operandi for the company. Under Canadian Tire, Mark’s was shaped into a destination for casual wear.

The forthcoming transformation of some stores and launch of others is meant to build on that journey by luring in customers who haven’t realized the brand is more than a place to get work boots or jeans.

“We’d like to be more inspiring and more relevant, particularly for women who don’t traditionally shop us, but also younger customers,” Czank explained.

“We’re appealing to more new Canadians and we really want to change people’s minds and say to customers who haven’t considered us, this is the time to consider us.”

Stores already using the new format have seen improved customer acquisition metrics, including among women and younger shoppers.

Both are valuable demographics to capture because some research suggests women tend to make most household purchasing decisions and young people often formulate lifelong opinions and affinities for brands in their early years.

Canadian Tire decided to launch the new format at Mark’s in 2023, when it was looking at its real estate portfolio.

“What we realized is that our biggest stores are actually the most productive,” Czank said.

It snatched up five former Bed Bath & Beyond locations to test the concept and has been building on that momentum ever since.

Its biggest store using the concept yet recently opened in Thunder Bay, Ont. It spans 36,000 gross square feet and includes shop-in-shop spaces for Columbia, Silver Jeans, Carhartt, Timberland and Levi’s.

While Czank initially fretted that bigger stores would hinder the number of sales Mark’s scored per square foot, they actually drove double-digit increases and triggered promising results from less tangible metrics like how people feel about shopping there.

“Some of these metrics I actually had to go ask the team to go back and double check them because they were so good,” he said.

The model doesn’t fit every market though. Czank concedes it’s not really suitable for downtown Toronto or Vancouver, where space is at a premium, but it works well in metropolitan and suburban regions.

Even stores that aren’t converted to the new format are benefiting, he said, because the company applies learnings and hit features from the refreshed locations to its other sites.

“There’s plenty of opportunity, I think, for us to continue to grow with this,” Czank said. “This concept is a scratching of the surface.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 4, 2026.

Companies in this story: (TSX:CTC.A)

Tara Deschamps, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Researchers call for ban on popular kitchen countertops over silicosis fears
stories.summary: Study found significant rates of death and serious illness among workers fabricating or installing engineered stone or quartz surfaces
stories.author: Shane Dingman
stories.content:
Canadian researchers are calling for a ban on engineered stone or quartz surfaces after publishing a study that found significant rates of death and serious illness among workers fabricating or installing the glossy countertop product.

The study Silicosis Among Engineered Stone Workers in Ontario reviewed the cases of 20 workers over a 10-year period and found three early deaths (the median age was 43 among the deceased, compared to 52 for the whole group), six lung transplant referrals, and in 35 per cent of cases, workers left with chronic hypoxia, or an inability for their bodies to get enough oxygen on their own.

The study, by Dr. Susan Tarlo and researchers at the University of Toronto/University Health Network, underlined that, because there’s been no industry-wide surveillance studies of workers exposed to dust from quartz countertops, “the true burden of engineered stone–associated silicosis in Canada remains uncertain.”

Engineered stone was invented in the 1960s but began to rapidly gain market share among home-builders and renovators over the past two decades in Europe, Asia and North America. Market research from The Freedonia Group has reported that demand for the glossy countertops and hard surfaces made by manufacturers such as Caesarstone May be worth as much as $1-billion in Canada, and account for close to 50 per cent of countertop installations nationwide.

Researchers aren’t clear on the size of the exposed work force, though simple Google searches showed 200 installers in the Toronto area, suggesting potentially hundreds or thousands of exposed workers nationwide.

“There’s a ton of workers who don’t realize how hazardous it is,” said Victoria Arrandale, a researcher with University of Toronto’s Dalla Lana School of Public Health, who said the disease has been showing up in engineered stone worker populations in Europe, Australia and California as the product has expanded to new markets. “It’s a new exposure scenario, it’s not a new hazard. We know it’s problematic.”

Silicosis is a lung disease caused when the tiny flecks of silica are inhaled along with rock dust, which can damage the air sacs in lungs (alveoli) and can cause inflammation or scar tissue around the airways. In the study, 70 per cent of the men had silicosis, but in 30 per cent the nodules of scar tissue formed large lumps called progressive massive fibrosis that impede breathing.

“Silicosis is a very old disease and originally it was mostly in miners,” said Dr. Tarlo, a respirologist and clinician investigator at UHN, who authored the study along with Dr. Abeer Abdelsayad and Dr. Ambrose Lau.

Dr. Tarlo noted a key difference in these new cases was the quartz material being worked with is typically composed of 90 per cent silica, whereas, in the past, miners dealt with rock dust that carried just 5 to 20 per cent silica.

While silica is a known carcinogen, the amount of the material present in engineered stone means that a better way to think of the risk of illness associated with it May be to compare how Canada cracked down on asbestos. “We no longer use asbestos for new projects because it carries too great a risk,” Dr. Tarlo said.

In the last decade, as medical research in other countries has found high levels of the disease among quartz countertop workers, some jurisdictions – such as Australia and California – have moved to restrict or even outright ban the substance.

The Ontario government has issued alerts on the dangers of the material in 2020 and 2023 and provided $1-million in funding for educational tools for safer practices such as wet-cutting (instead of dry cutting that produces more dust) and rolled out a voluntary occupational exposure registry for workers.

However, Dr. Tarlo notes that in the past governments did more to gain insight into the scope of the silica exposure and give workers early diagnoses before the disease progressed. “In Ontario, there was a surveillance program with breathing tests and chest X-rays: every year that the Ministry of Labor used to run and the miners would be screened with these tests,” she said, adding that surveillance is still less effective than prohibition.

Courts May also put pressure on engineered stone companies, with several successful lawsuits in recent years out of California. On Oct. 28, a court awarded $67-million in damages to Dennys Rene Rivas Williams, an engineered stone fabricator who was diagnosed with silicosis at 35 and had a double-lung transplant at 37.

The legal challenges are serious enough that one of the largest manufacturers of engineered stone, publicly traded Caesarstone Ltd., noted the litigation risk in its 2025 annual report.

“We are unable to obtain insurance coverage for future claims relating to silicosis,” Caesarstone warned investors. “As of Dec. 31, 2025, we were subject to lawsuits with respect to 618 injured persons globally, of which 40 were in Israel, 151 in Australia and 427 in the United States.”

stories.title: Home buyers and home sellers ride a wave of uncertainty in the GTA
stories.summary: Market watchers are detecting a palpable fear of commitment this fall
stories.author: Carolyn Ireland
stories.content:
Market watchers in many tranches of Toronto real estate are detecting a palpable fear of commitment this fall: Buyers are reluctant to submit a bid and sellers are balking at making a counter-offer.

Cheri Dorsey McCann, broker with McCann Realty Group, estimates that negotiations end with a deal about 80 per cent of the time – but that outcome can only occur when the two sides engage.

“You really have to know how to get people to put things on paper,” she said.

Steady activity in the first half of October became quieter in the second half, Ms. McCann said, as consumers watched the lead-up to U.S. midterm elections and waited for more clarity on tariffs, interest rates and Canada’s economy.

In another twist to an unpredictable fall housing market, the Bank of Canada raised its key interest rate to 2.5 per cent from 2.25 per cent at the end of October.

The central bank’s first move since October of last year has many consumers fretting about their own budgets and economists predicting a slow grind towards the end of the year in the Greater Toronto Area.

For buyers trying to navigate the market, the move raises the prospect of more rate hikes in the coming months as central bank Governor Tiff Macklem keeps a concerned eye on the rate of inflation.

Benjamin Reitzes, macro strategist at Bank of Montreal, notes that policy-makers indicated they have heightened concerns around inflation but easing worries about economic growth.

While the Bank of Canada statement suggested a possible need to increase the policy rate further, Mr. Reitzes notes the pace of hikes is extremely uncertain and will be driven by incoming data.

As for potential buyers, they are trying to gauge how much farther home prices have to fall and whether the potential for a lower price offsets the risk of higher rates.

Ms. McCann said buyers’ agents will sometimes call to discuss the amount a client is willing to pay for one of her listings in order to get a sense of the seller’s resolve. Ms. McCann urges those agents to formalize their verbal offers.

“It’s not an offer if you don’t put it on paper,” she said. “I always work with all the offers – even if they’re ridiculously low – and 80 per cent of them get done.”

In Ms. McCann’s opinion, the biggest mistake sellers and their agents can make is to reject a bid without making a counter-offer – no matter how far the divide.

Ms. McCann points to the recent example of a house with an asking price around $2.8-million.

She submitted an offer on behalf of her buyer, but the seller refused to sign back, and the deal died.

“It would have sold that night,” she said. “It’s still sitting on the market six weeks later.”

Ms. McCann said she directs her own sellers to make a counter-offer. Whether they accept the final price is their decision.

“You have nothing to lose by signing it back,” she advises, even if nothing comes of the negotiation. “At least you know what that buyer was willing to pay.”

Ms. McCann said some homeowners with equity in their existing property are taking advantage of the drop from peak prices to move up.

She recently gathered listings for a meeting with a client with a budget between $3-million and $4-million; the assembled properties had price reductions ranging from $300,000 and up.

First-time buyers are also active, she said, because prices have decreased to the level where some who were priced out in the past can now afford to buy.

Victor Tran, mortgage and real estate expert with Rates.CA. observed that some buyers are now picking up the pace of their search before a preapproval for financing expires.

Some buyers feel an increased sense of urgency because the central bank’s first hike since the summer of 2023 May be the first in a series, Mr. Tran pointed out.

Higher rates May also affect a buyer’s ability to pass the Canadian mortgage stress test, Mr. Tran said.

Borrowers are required to show they can handle mortgage payments at 5.25 per cent – or the contract rate plus 2 per cent – whichever is higher.

For house hunters who haven’t yet nailed down a purchase price with a signed deal, Mr. Tran runs through the numbers to show them the outcome if rates soar beyond the stress test level.

“It’s very important to use assumptions as worst-case scenarios,” he said.

The mortgage broker has been spending time crunching numbers for buyers and helping them to determine the impact of rising rates. In some cases, first-time buyers will save or scramble to come up with a larger down payment, he said, while others will reduce the amount they spend on a house or condo.

“Interest rates are certainly creeping up very fast,” Mr. Tran said. “It’s just important to get ahead of it by revising the budget.”

Many buyers with tight budgets are willing to go with variable-rate mortgages because lenders are offering rates just below 4 per cent compared with rates just below 5 per cent for mortgages with rates locked in for three- or five-year terms.

That nearly 1 per cent spread sometimes allows buyers to qualify for a loan and pass the stress test more easily than if they paid the higher freight on a fixed-rate mortgage, Mr. Tran said.

Buyers understand their monthly payments May tick up with each Bank of Canada hike but, for some, going variable means they can get into the market sooner.

“Some homeowners are willing to take that risk to go for variable for immediate savings – and ride the wave, basically,” Mr. Tran said. “Many people are desperate.”

stories.title: Arriving at next station: A comfy home
stories.summary: Former train station was converted into a property on a sizable piece of land in Mono, Ont.
stories.author: Dave LeBlanc
stories.content:
A close friend of mine, no longer with us, worked for much of his life at CN Rail. Through him, I learned of train aficionados (he had a different word for aficionado) in the 1990s. As a conductor, he’d see them on bridges, notepads in hand, writing down the reporting marks and numbers found on freight cars, recording lengths, or snapping photographs. Sometimes, if the train was stopped, they’d ask him questions, and he’d indulge them as best he could, but, to him, it was just a job, so they’d often know more than he did.

In talking with Mike Lander about his house in Mono Township, Ont. – the former 1914 Shelburne train station that was moved to its present location in the early 1970s – I can tell he’s in my friend’s camp. After poking about for an hour and admiring all of the building’s original features, he pulled out his phone and called up a document sent to him by a train aficionado.

“Here’s a drawing of the bench,” he said. “The different sizes and the different types.” The bench in question is the weathered, silvery, slatted curved bench parked on Mr. Lander’s deck; according to these shop drawings, it’s original to the station, and one of a few configurations Canadian-Pacific would install.

To wit, Mr. Lander swiped to an old black-and-white photograph of a station: “He said this one is close, this one is a No. 11.” The building Mr. Lander lives in, he was told, is a “Type 19.”

Or something like that.

So, with the old Shelburne station now up for sale, the question is: will the next owner be the kind of person who knows (and cherishes) every little detail, or just someone who wants a unique vacation or retirement property on a nice piece of land that’s not too far from the big city?

“You don’t have to deal with the 400 [highway], and lakes, over the years, have just gotten more noisy and busy,” says listing agent David Visentin, who also co-hosts the long-running Hgtv program Love It or List It . “You can come up here, and for the same price … you’re getting privacy and quiet, and there’s tons of water: there’re ponds that you don’t even see.”

And while there is no pond on the four hectares that come with the old train station, there are so many trees it takes a few seconds to spot the building after turning into the driveway from Blind Line. But, once those red-shingles and that hip roof held aloft by prominent corbels comes into view, that pang of romance, travel and nostalgia quickly follows.

It’s the same once inside: the eye immediately falls upon the massive, dark oak ticket booth with amber glass, semi-opaque window-inserts because it’s so romantic, not because it divides the space into two large ‘rooms’ – dining and living – and houses the kitchen. Upon closer inspection, the public, corridor-facing side of the booth still sports the worn counter where passengers would rest their forearms as they’d open their purses and wallets, and, inside, the cashier’s drawer remains. Facing the window is an original, built in desk with filing cabinet, likely for employees to watch for (and make records of) incoming and outgoing trains. Decorating the security cage that rises from the booth up to the high, lath-and-plaster, coved ceiling are railroad tools collected by the building’s former owners (Mr. Lander is third owner).

And speaking of owners, while in the heated-floor kitchen, Mr. Lander produces a photo-album filled with old, square Polaroids. These photographs, gifted to him with his purchase in 2012, document the 1970 closure and transport of the station to its present location, which necessitated removing the roof. It’s an album he says he’ll give to new owners as well.

Still in the same configuration are the station’s two washrooms. The men’s washroom is now the full bathroom, complete with claw-foot tub, while the women’s has been converted to a powder room/laundry room; interestingly, the women’s is where the original fuse panel was located: “If they put it in the men’s, kids would’ve screwed with it,” Mr. Landers says with a laugh. “Young boys would get in there and get clever.”

The living area benefits from an enormous grouping of large windows, all original and double-hung (with storms as well). While there is grandeur and formality to the room, one can also sense the new openness of the Edwardian era, which embraced light and airiness more than the Victorians before them.

And while the four bedrooms are small and suffer from fairly low ceilings (a portion of the building was divided into two storeys by lowering the floor slightly), there is a high-and-dry basement that could be converted into bedrooms for tall teenagers; better yet, there are a few outbuildings on the property that would make excellent youth habitats.

After inspecting the original, broken-down ‘station’ wagon outside, Mr. Visentin and I walk one of the property’s two kilometres of trails, perfect “for cross-country skiing or for ATVs, whatever,” he says. Pointing at a stand of trees, he continues: “You’ve got hardwood but you’ve also got the evergreens, which is great for the winter, because the winds get kind of howl-y out here … and you’re close to everything: Shelburne, Orangeville, you’ve got Hockley Valley [and] access to Toronto pretty quickly.”

Quickly by automobile, of course; despite thinking I can hear a faint steam-whistle in the distance, I know the trains don’t run in these parts any more.

For more information, visit this website .

stories.title: Maple Leaf Foods’ profit falls in third quarter as sales edge higher
stories.summary: Company now expects full-year adjusted earnings to come in at lower end of forecast
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Maple Leaf Foods Inc. MFI-T , which spun off its pork business as Canada Packers Inc. Cpkr-T last year, reported a third-quarter profit from continuing operations of $22.3-million as its sales edged higher compared with a year ago.

The poultry and prepared foods company says its profit amounted to 18 cents per share for the quarter ended Sept. 30.

The result compared with a profit of $23.3-million or 19 cents per share in the same quarter last year.

On an adjusted basis, Maple Leaf says it earned 36 cents per share in its latest quarter up from an adjusted profit of 21 cents per share a year ago.

Sales for the quarter totalled $1.03-billion, up from $1.01-billion in the third quarter of 2025.

Maple Leaf says poultry sales increased by 4.3 per cent, while prepared food sales rose by 1.3 per cent.

The company is now expecting its full-year adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization to be at the lower end of the projected $520-million to $540-million range, CEO Curtis Frank said in a statement on Wednesday.

“We entered 2026 expecting a relatively stable external environment. That has not been the case,” he said.

“Renewed inflation in food production worldwide has raised costs and pressured consumers, particularly in the second half.”

RBC analyst Irene Nattel wrote in a report that she is encouraged the company will remain within the guidance range for 2026.

While some, she noted, are likely going to be disappointed with the tightened guidance, “we remind investors of our forever caveat on (Maple Leaf): the road from here to there inevitably is bumpy.”

stories.title: CTV News in Latvia: Near Russia’s border, Canadian soldiers face both ‘insults’ and ‘open arms’ from locals
stories.summary: For nearly a decade, Canadian troops have led Nato’s multinational mission in Latvia. However, this week marked a significant shift: the alliance’s entire brigade – 2,000 of whom are Canadian – has been deployed close to the borders of Russia and Belarus.
stories.author: Adrian Ghobrial
stories.content:
Daugavpils, Latvia -- Canadian soldiers in eastern Latvia, just 50 kilometres from the Russian border are training to get comfortable in the chaos.

Inside the charred remains of a Soviet-era school, a battle battalion made up of more than a dozen Canadians is conducting a close-quarter battle (CQB) training exercise, in lockstep with a group of Italian soldiers. Two countries, both part of the same Nato brigade.

As the sound of gunfire echoes along the abandoned school’s concrete walls, the multinational battalions sweep through multiple floors, securing the building in a simulated combat scenario.

“An actual clearing like this (of a building) would include a lot of casualties and medevacs. It’s one of the most dangerous things we can conduct on any given day during an actual combat mission,” said a master corporal who spoke to CTV News during the training operation.

While embedded with Nato soldiers, CTV National News was asked to withhold the names of infantry members to protect their identities.

The master corporal helping command the CQB exercise said training days like this in a highly charged environment are invaluable.

“If this (close quarter battle) was to happen in a real war scenario, we have to be ready because what we will be doing is so dangerous,” he said.

For nearly a decade, Canadian troops have led Nato’s multinational mission in Latvia. However, this week marked a significant shift: the alliance’s entire brigade – 2,000 of whom are Canadian – has been deployed close to the borders of Russia and Belarus.

This marks the first time the entire brigade has mobilized to Latvia’s eastern border, arriving at a time of heightened tensions in eastern Europe.

Latvia along with Estonia to the north and Lithuania to the south, makes up Nato’s eastern flank.

CTV News is embedded with Nato troops near the city of Daugavpils, which is 30 km from the border of Belarus and 50 km from the Russian border.

Nearly 50 per cent of Daugavpils’ population is ethnic Russian, creating a complex region with differing political views.

The city’s mayor, who was unavailable to speak to CTV News has been painted as pro-Russian by some Eastern European media. Multiple reports allege he refused to fly the Ukrainian flag at city hall following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

A Canadian Armed Forces lieutenant who spoke to CTV News said he and some of the other Nato soldiers operating in Daugavpils have experienced friction from area residents.

“Some people are more receptive than others to our presence here,” the lieutenant said. “Some have shouted insults at us but others have welcomed us with open arms.”

While working to connect with the community, the lieutenant, whose name CTV News has been asked not to publish, has been tracking drone activity and potential incursions near Nato training areas in eastern Latvia.

At times they’re civilian drones, other times they could be military drones,” he said. “Sometimes the drones are flying overhead taking pictures, (of us) as they go low and then go high as well.”

It is an operational reality in this region, Latvia is now home to the largest number of Canadian Armed Forces members abroad.

On this day, the Canadian-led Nato brigade is projecting a show of force, hoping to deter any looming threat to the east.

stories.title: ‘They’re not going to be the same’: Top burn surgeon on the painful road ahead for Wainwright victims
stories.summary: Two Ontario soldiers severely burned in the fire on the Alberta military base are now under the care of the country's largest burn centre
stories.author: Sharon Kirkey
stories.content:
Soon after operating on one member of the Armed Forces and before he was due to operate on a second, Dr. Alan Rogers described how the lives of his patients, both “young, healthy guys” severely burned in the deadly fire at CFB Wainwright, have been forever altered.

“For me, it’s devastating to see young boys getting injured like this, honestly,” said Rogers, a plastic and reconstructive surgeon at the Ross Tilley Burn Centre at Toronto’s Sunnybrook Health Sciences Centre, the country’s largest burn unit.

“On the other hand, I appreciate that I have some of the skills and knowledge, and I’m part of an excellent team, and we can help these guys.

“But what we can do doesn’t bring back how they looked before, how they functioned before.

unfortunately,” he said.

“We’ll do our very best.”

The two men were transferred by air ambulance Friday to Sunnybrook from a specialized Edmonton burn unit. “We’ve essentially repatriated our own patients,” Rogers said of the two service members who are from Ontario.

He could not divulge personal details because of patient confidentiality. He didn’t want to get into specifics, for fear of crossing a boundary.

“But I can say that they both have very extensive burns.”

A third service member from Ontario was discharged from hospital and is being followed as an outpatient at Sunnybrook.

All three were among those injured when a grass fire broke out during training exercises at CFB Wainwright in Alberta on the afternoon of Oct. 17. According to military officials, the fire ignited in the area where soldiers were using live munitions and spread rapidly because of high winds. The inferno claimed the lives of four soldiers and left 39 others injured, 19 critically.

As of last Wednesday, 27 remained in hospital, 13 in critical condition.

Ten specialized burn nurses and a burn surgeon from the Sunnybrook burn centre arrived in Alberta days after the fire.

“I think this has been one of the most traumatic experiences for them,” Rogers said of his colleagues, some of whom are close friends

“Many of them have been doing burn nursing for 30 years or more. Some of our most experienced nurses. For them to say that this is one of the most traumatic experiences that they’ve observed says a lot.”

The burn injuries in otherwise fit and healthy young people are extensive. That’s traumatic enough on an individual level, but the sheer scale of the tragedy makes it even more devastating, Rogers said.

A major burn goes beyond the skin; it affects the whole person, he said. “Fluid requirements are higher, nutritional requirements are higher” and people are at dramatically heightened risk for infection because they’ve lost the barrier to the environment, their skin.

People can get pneumonia, urinary infections, or bloodstream infections. “And of course most of the bacteria come from the wounds, because the wounds are not yet closed; they’re open.”

The advantage of young people is that they tend to heal well. “Assuming we do all the right things, they should heal,” Rogers said.

But with severe burns, the greatest surgical challenge is that there often isn’t enough unburned skin left to use for traditional skin grafts.

With deep, extensive burns, skin is no longer viable, Rogers said. It undergoes cell death, or necrosis. The dead tissue needs to be removed and replaced with the person’s own healthy skin, because the skin is the body’s primary protection against infection.

Burned skin is often temporarily replaced with cadaver skin, “and then we change it for their own (skin) by way of skin graft surgery,” said Rogers, who is also an associate professor of plastic, reconstructive and aesthetic surgery at the University of Toronto.

With conventional skin grafting, thin layers of skin are taken from unburned areas and moved to burned ones. But sometimes there isn’t enough skin to go around, and unburned skin needs to be reused more than once, which means waiting for the donor site to heal before moving to the next section.

Donor skin can be expanded and stretched to cover larger areas. More revolutionary treatments might also be used on the soldiers, including a product developed by Laval University researchers that involves using a skin substitute grown from the patient’s own cells.

Later, people need reconstruction, scar treatment, rehabilitation, and help returning to family life and jobs, Rogers said.

But the psychological toll begins with what happened at the time of the burn, he said. People can experience a form of post-traumatic stress, re-living the fire in recurring nightmares. Some might experience feelings of guilt for those who didn’t survive. Some witnessed people dying.

Some of the patients will be disabled. Some will be completely dependent on their families. Some will never go back to work. It has a massive socioeconomic and psychological effect

At the hospital, care involves balancing the patient’s level of awareness.

“We can’t keep them completely sedated the entire time. That has ill effects too,” Rogers said.

But being awake not only means having to deal with the physical pain of dressing changes; being awake also means having to confront the harsh realities of their injuries.

“These are young patients, many of whom have been disfigured by the burn injury,” Rogers said.

“They’re never going to look the same. However good the surgery we do, their skin is not going to be normal. They’re going to have a number of contractures. They’re going to have some disability. Range of motion is going to be affected. Strength is going to be affected,” Rogers said.

“Some of them will lose fingers. Some will have amputations. Each and every part of that is traumatic.”

While the psychological burden is tied to the physical injuries, “it can be so much greater, and so much more enduring, well after all the wounds have healed.”

Families can feel relatively powerless at first, Rogers said.

Many of the injured have young families — partners, wives, young children. “Many are in their mid-20s,” Rogers said.

“The impact is enormous.”

The goal while in hospital is “to do as good as a job as we can (so that) they survive. They survive with reasonably well-healed wounds, and they rehabilitate as best they can,” he said.

Some who survive severe burns ultimately become supporters to others experiencing similar trauma, “because they have that to offer, and it’s very rewarding for them,” Rogers said.

“Some really struggle.”

The Wainwright tragedy is especially heartbreaking “because it sounds as if there were circumstances that were preventable,” Rogers said.

Military police are investigating, and a separate independent board of inquiry will be conducted, officials have said.

Sharon Kirkey is a national reporter with National Post focusing on health and science stories. She is also a three-time National Newspaper Awards nominee, with a win for beat reporting.

stories.title: Canadians can’t keep up with their debt: Benchmark Canada
stories.summary: One insolvency firm says its clients carried average unsecured debts of more than $67,000 last year, up 37 per cent over three years
stories.author: David George-Cosh, Special to National Post
stories.content:
Countries don’t typically get report cards, but there are hard facts that can be collated, assessed and compared. Enter Benchmark Canada , a new project from the Macdonald-Laurier Institute that brings together more than 40 different metrics that measure this nation’s performance. This fall, the National Post is examining many of those findings.

Canadians are falling further behind on car loans, credit cards and personal loans, with arrears in all three categories hitting their highest levels in the decade-long period tracked by Benchmark Canada.

Canada’s debt strain is greatest in instalment loans, which include unsecured personal loans and point-of-sale financing. The share of those loans that are at least 90 days overdue reached 2.95 per cent, more than triple the 0.95 per cent recorded in late 2015, the Macdonald-Laurier Institute project showed.

Meanwhile, auto-loan arrears stood at 0.87 per cent, up from a pandemic low of 0.39 per cent in 2021. Credit-card arrears reached 0.80 per cent, nearly double from their 2021 low of 0.44 per cent.

Doug Hoyes, co-founder of insolvency firm Hoyes, Michalos & Associates Inc., said borrowers often tap a line of credit to make up for lost income. When that runs out, they turn to credit cards, then higher-cost instalment loans and payday lenders.

“You cannot keep layering borrowing on top of borrowing,” he said.

Hoyes said many of his clients use those loans to cover bills after exhausting cheaper sources of credit, hoping their income will recover before the payments become unmanageable.

His firm’s clients carried average unsecured debts of more than $67,000 last year, up 11 per cent from a year earlier and 37 per cent over three years, and owed money to an average of 10 creditors.

Matt Fabian, TransUnion Canada’s senior director of financial services research and consulting, said that while Canadians are having trouble paying back their loans, they’re still relatively managing their debtload. Payment deferrals, government support and reduced spending during the pandemic helped pushed overall arrears to unusually low levels from the recession of 2008-2009 before bouncing higher in the past year, he noted.

“For some products, in some segments, it’s higher than it was pre-COVID. For some, it’s just returning,” he said.

Your governments are to blame for high gas prices: Benchmark Canada

Canadians quickly falling behind on their mortgages: Benchmark Canada

Instalment loans performed worse partly because of the type of borrower who takes them out, Fabian said. Borrowers seeking debt-consolidation loans likely already have financial problems, while alternative lenders serve higher-risk customers who May not qualify for traditional bank loans.

Those borrowers pay higher interest rates and have less room to absorb increases in living costs or a loss of income. Fabian described subprime consumers as “constantly living in their own personal recession.”

TransUnion’s latest quarterly credit report found average non-mortgage debt in Canada reached $28,118 per customer in the second quarter, up 7.6 per cent from a year earlier. Total consumer debt, including mortgages, hit a whopping $2.64 trillion.

The TransUnion data showed the share of borrowers who were at least 30 days overdue on their payments fell to 4.27 per cent from 4.34 per cent a year earlier. But the share of those at least 90 days overdue rose to 1.81 per cent from 1.77 per cent. Benchmark Canada’s figures, drawn from Bank of Canada calculations using TransUnion data, measure the share of loans at least 90 days overdue.

The share of debt balances falling into arrears is also rising faster than the share of income coming into one’s accounts, Fabian said. That suggests borrowers with larger debts are having more difficulty keeping up their payments, and face increased pressure with higher minimum payments, he said.

A C.D. Howe Institute report published this month found that national debt figures are masking growing strain among younger and lower-income Canadians.

The share of household disposable income used to pay debt fell to 14.5 per cent in the second quarter, from a 2023 peak of 15.2 per cent, the C.D. Howe analysis found. But younger Canadians carry unsecured debts without the cushion of home equity older Canadians can enjoy thanks to Canada’s frothy real estate market.

More borrowers are also seeking formal debt relief. Consumer debt proposals accounted for nearly 80 per cent of insolvency filings in the second quarter, up from about 60 per cent before the pandemic, TransUnion reported. Banks often have established programs to help restructure payments and have an incentive to preserve relationships with customers who hold chequing and savings accounts with them, Fabian said.

Saul Schwartz, professor at the School of Public Policy and Administration at Carleton University, cautioned against reading the rise in consumer proposals as a sign of worsening borrower behaviour. Instead, Canada’s banking system is inducing more borrowers to pay more of what they owe, he said.

Proposals can help borrowers protect assets and spread payments over time, but most pay more than they would in bankruptcy, Schwartz said. Governments can help, he noted. “Establishing publicly funded debt advice services, either nationally, provincially or even municipally, would be a big step forward.”

He also pointed to the Breathing Space program in England and Wales (Scotland runs its own separate debt program), which freezes most interest and charges on qualifying debts for up to 60 days while borrowers seek advice on how to make their repayments.

Hoyes said he expects rising arrears to lead to more insolvencies as borrowers exhaust their remaining credit.

“Nobody files bankruptcy at the first missed payment,” he said. “They file when they’ve run out of ways to keep going.”

The need for armed deterrence was evident on Sept. 20, when armed police officers protected a Belleville Jewish congregation from an armed attacker, says Tafsik

Two Ontario soldiers severely burned in the fire on the Alberta military base are now under the care of the country's largest burn centre
